The JMGO N3 Ultimate pumps stunning color and brightness through very flexible optics, making it a killer projector when ideal theater conditions aren’t possible. It also works great for gaming, but it lacks some of the finesse of rivals such as the Valerion VisionMaster Max or Xgimi Titan Noir

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Price: $2999 Resolution: 4K Lumens: 5800 ISO Audio: 2x12.5W Light: RGB Laser Projection: 0.47" DLP Screen size: 40-300 inches HDR: HDR10, HLG, Dolby Vision Refresh Rate: 60Hz/240Hz Ports: 2x HDMI 2.1 (1x eARC), 1x USB-A Smart TV Software: Google TV Size: 12.14 x 9.05 x 10.79 inches Weight: 15.32 lbs Lifespan: n/a

The JMGO N3 Ultimate continues the brand's efforts to make better and better projectors within the constraints of an almost unchanging form factor. In fact, it’s hard to tell this new one apart from its predecessors. That almost makes it more impressive that JMGO has packed in so many upgrades. This model has motors in its gimbal stand for remote adjustment, extensive optical zoom and lens shift, and enough laser to simply blast out light while also enjoying VRR support.

All that packed into a $2,999 package is something of a steal. It may be more than the Xgimi Horizon 20 Pro, but JMGO drowns that thing in brightness and tops it in contrast, too. Among the best projectors we’ve tested, the N3 Ultimate has rivals in the Xgimi Titan Noir line and Valerion VisionMaster Max, which offer superb black levels, but when ambient lighting can’t be eliminated, the JMGO N3 Ultimate will be hard to beat.

The JMGO N3 Ultimate launched in mid-2026, and it landed with a $2,999 price tag. For a projector with its capabilities, that’s an exceedingly reasonable price.

JMGO is no stranger to significant discounts either. During my testing, I’ve seen the JMGO N3 Ultimate on sale for as much as $600 off. JMGO also offered a lot of bundle deals if you need a tall stand, 3D glasses, or a projection screen to go with the projector.

JMGO hasn’t been one for shaking up its designs. Looking at the JMGO N3 Ultimate, it’d be easy to mistake it for even the JMGO N1 Ultra. It still has the signature gimbal stand with a power button on the base and a two-tone chassis with two different shell sections, and JMGO still can’t get the seam between those to line up cleanly at the top.

This generation, the gimbal stand is considerably advanced. It has motorized control built into both its rotational and vertical axes, letting you shift its orientation remotely. One lingering downside to this design is that the base of the stand has no levelling feet. So you might be able to square the projection away easily enough, but it may appear rotated slightly if you set the N3 Ultimate on an un-level surface. In one case, this left me to stuff a wedge of paper underneath one side.

You can, of course, use digital correction to sort out rotation issues, but that’d be a shame to do since the JMGO N3 Ultimate has excellent hardware for optical adjustment this generation. The N3 Ultimate has zoom to let it go from a 0.88:1 throw ratio to as far as 1.7:1. That gives it a much wider range than the Xgimi Horizon 20 Pro, though not quite as much as the Hisense XR10. JGMO tops this off with considerable horizontal (53% in either direction) and vertical lens shift (130% in either direction).

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

This range of zoom and lens shift is awesome for flexibility in setting up the projector. You basically can pick where you want to project to, and if you set the N3 Ultimate anywhere close to a decent spot (heck, even pretty off-center spots will do), you can use the zoom and lens shift to get a perfectly squared image without any digital adjustments that would crop away some of that 4K picture. Well, at least you can get it almost perfect if you don’t need to level the projector.

The JMGO N3 Ultimate shifts its ports away from the rear of the main projector housing to instead fit at the back of the base. JMGO is still stingy with its connections, though. The N3 Ultimate only gets two HDMI 2.1 ports (one with eARC) and a USB port.

The rear of the main projector housing is now solely dedicated to cooling. The sides of the projector can pull in fresh air while the rear pumps it all out. It does a good job, too. N3 Ultimate makes a lot of light in a fairly small chassis and manages to do so without the fans getting noticeably loud even when you sit at just arm’s length from the projector.

As with prior models, the JMGO N3 Ultimate comes with a foam carrying case that can hold the projector, power supply, and remote. It’s a convenient way to gather and protect everything when you’re moving the projector from place to place, but I wouldn’t count on it to handle much abuse or even rough handling, as the plastic clips that keep it closed are fairly flimsy.

The JMGO N3 Ultimate looks great, but its staggering brightness levels and slightly elevated black floor make it a better match for brighter viewing environments. Since its black levels don’t bottom out very low, you’ll pretty much always see some of the light it’s casting in a very dark room, and that can be distracting. Competing projectors like the Xgimi Titan Noir and Valerion VisionMaster Max do a much better job clamping those black levels down for dark room viewing.

It’s far less distracting if you’re viewing bright content, as your eyes will adjust to the brightness and turn the dark areas perceptually black. When you have a little light on in your viewing space, the black floor becomes less of an issue and the extreme brightness of the JMGO N3 Ultimate becomes a key advantage. This thing is incredibly bright. Most content can still look great even with some ambient light. Bright enough content can stand up even to overhead lighting in a well-lit room (just avoid sunlight).

With the RGB lasers offering extreme gamut coverage, bright and colorful content like “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” is simply stunning. Princess Rosalina’s fight near the start is a splendid showcase of the color and explosive lighting with her magic effects dazzling the screen.

In some picture modes, the JMGO N3 Ultimate uses a dynamic black level, dimming down for dark scenes and ramping up for brighter scenes. It’s not fast enough, though. When video jumps between bright and dark shots, it’s possible to see the projector shifting its illuminance. In the opening to “Blade Runner 2049,” the camera jumps from bright outdoor shots to dark interiors; the projector quickly tries to dim itself for those dark interior shots but lags behind the cuts. It’s a little jarring, but gradual shifts are not as distracting.

Like most of its competition, the JMGO N3 Ultimate uses extensive motion smoothing by default. This works out well enough for panning shots, but it introduces heavy artifacting in most other motion and becomes a serious distraction. Motion looks better with this MEMC setting turned off, though some panning shots will stutter. I’ve found the Low setting looked decent without too much artifacting. JMGO doesn’t include a dedicated 24p/Film mode, unfortunately.

Like other DLP projectors, the JMGO N3 Ultimate displays colors in sequence, and this can create some visible artifacts that look like a rainbow to the eyes. Some projectors have gotten pretty good at diminishing this effect. The JMGO N3 Ultimate’s DLP rainbow effect isn’t horrendous, but I find it noticeable from time to time, especially on subtitles or large white areas of the projection.

The brightness and vivid color of the JMGO N3 Ultimate is plain to see, but objective measurements confirmed its quality. I used a Spyder X2 Ultra colorimeter and 1.1-gain matte white projection screen for color testing and a lux meter for brightness and contrast testing, and the JMGO N3 Ultimate delivers.

With a full white screen and an ANSI lumen measurement pattern, I saw the JMGO N3 Ultimate hit 5,215 lumens. That may be a bit shy of its rated brightness, but it was with a picture profile that didn’t introduce horribly skewed color or extra fan noise. Displaying an evenly black and white checkerboard pattern, the projector offered 93.9:1 contrast ratio at full brightness and a better 115:1 ratio at its minimum brightness, which is on the high end of what I’ve seen from projectors.

For a more extreme case, I measure the brightness of white boxes in the corners against the black level at the center of the projection. This produced a solid 480:1 contrast ratio. To assess the ideal contrast possible in a highly light-controlled room, I use the same test pattern to measure the white levels, then I block most of the projection with black velvet, only letting the center of the projection shine through a hole in the fabric. I then measure the black point of the projected light coming through the hole. In this setup, the JMGO N3 Ultimate hit a respectable 2,270:1 contrast ratio.

Using the colorimeter and projection screen, I measured the JMGO N3 Ultimate’s color at 99.8% coverage of the sRGB color space, 94% of DCI-P3, and 92% of BT.2020. This is a great result, especially when considering there’s less precision in measuring the color gamut of reflected light as opposed to the direct light coming from a monitor or TV.

The speakers on the JMGO N3 Ultimate are nothing to get excited about. While they might deliver stereo sound, you’re only likely to get a real sense of that separation if you’re sitting directly in front or behind the projector.

The speakers are fine for small room listening, and they’ll do in a pinch if you’re in a slightly larger room and everyone is quiet. If you want explosive, powerful home theater sound, the JMGO N3 Ultimate won’t cut it. There’s a little punch to the bass, but not deep thunder.

Given this, you’ll likely be forced to use one of the two HDMI ports for eARC as it’s the only quality audio output. There’s no optical audio or even a 3.5mm jack, so your options are limited for connecting to one of the best soundbars. You can send audio over Bluetooth, but that’ll come with its own drawbacks.

The JMGO N3 Ultimate is very well cut out for gaming. With its optical adjustments, you can be sure you’re getting a crisp image that lets you see the little details you might need. If you’ve ever strained your eyes trying to figure out what you’re looking at in a game because the visuals were too dark, this is where the high brightness level helps.

By default, the projector has some noticeable latency. I measured 126ms between a 120Hz OLED and the projector running at its default settings. Turning on Game Mode cut that down nicely to 51ms.

That was comfortable for 4K/60Hz gaming, but the JMGO N3 Ultimate can still go further. It can drop down to 1080p and ramp up to 240Hz with VRR support, at which point I measured no latency at all behind the OLED display. A photo taken of both displays with a 1/1000-second shutter speed captured both displaying the exact same count on a millisecond counter.

To minimize lag, you won’t be able to use keystone or digital image adaptations, but even keeping these enabled saw just 50ms of latency. At this level, I was still comfortably able to keep up with the frantic pacing of combat in Hades 2 and successfully make my way through the first phase of the fight with Chronos.

Without the High Refresh Rate and VRR settings enabled, you’ll get crisper visuals, but you won’t get a 240Hz refresh rate and risk screen tearing. Latency still feels reduced by sending the projector 240 frames per second, but it skips many of them without that former setting.

You get standard Google TV with the JMGO N3 Ultimate. This gives you access to a massive assortment of streaming services and other apps. The JMGO N3 Ultimate can be a little slow to navigate after it boots up, but once it’s been running for a minute, it tends to feel quite responsive.

JMGO isn’t doing much special on top of Google TV. It has its own Projector settings menu where all of the important controls for focus, keystone, zoom and the like are conveniently gathered. Smartly, it’s the first option in the full settings menu, since it’s hard to do much else if the projection is askew or out of focus. Tucked in here are a few of the projectors' niftier features, including a wall color adaptation that calibrates the projection to compensate for non-white walls. I ran it against a piece of pink insulation, and it noticeably reduced the pink material’s effect on the white areas of the projection.

There’s also a tool for spatial memory, which lets you save projection settings for different setups/spaces and then quickly re-apply them. When shifting the projector back and forth between my office and living room, this was a handy way to quickly dial it back to ideal settings. That said, manual adjustments to the gimbal can confuse it, and it won’t correct the direction it’s facing if you set it down wrong, which all takes some of the smarts out of that feature.

The remote that comes with the JMGO N3 Ultimate is compact and simple, perhaps too much so. You get your standard circular navigation ring, and underneath that is the home, back, and voice assistant buttons that you’ll find with any Google TV device. Tucked into the middle of those is a pill-shaped volume control that’s easy enough to feel out in the dark, though you won’t have to since all of those controls (except the navigation ring) have backlighting.

Beyond those controls, you get a power button in the top left corner and a shortcut to “Free TV” in that top right corner that launches Google TV Freeplay. Lower down, you get shortcuts to Prime Video, Netflix, and YouTube. A fourth custom shortcut button lets you set a custom app or Google Home device to access with it. A few extra shortcut buttons would have been nice. Plenty of other projector remotes have additional control shortcuts, like to picture and sound modes, and many further differentiates between full settings and a more focused menu. The lack here makes diving into specific settings a bit more tedious. The lack of a mute button is also annoying.

The JMGO N3 Ultimate has one special button tied to its unique gimbal stand. Holding this button activates the motorized gimbal and a gyroscope in the remote, and then moving the remote will correspondingly move the projector. It’s a neat trick useful for quick adjustments, though ultimately isn’t precise enough to avoid needing further fine-tuned adjustments.

The JGMO N3 Ultimate is a stunner. From the jump, it offers flexible optics that ensure you can get a near-perfect projection even if you plunk it down almost randomly. Its RGB laser light source pumps out stunningly bright visuals that can simply drip in color, and its contrast is strong.

The JGMO N3 Ultimate commands a high price, but not an unreasonable one (especially with frequent discounts) considering the prices of the massive TVs it would replace. With its portability, it’s also much easier to bring for a movie night in the yard or at a friend's place than a competing TV. You’re also going to want to bring along an extra speaker if you want the audio to match the quality of the video.

If you’re outfitting a pitch black home theater, I’d look to the Valerion VisionMaster Max or Xgimi Titan Noir instead, which offer much better black floors. In any other conditions, the N3 Ultimate can look exceptional, especially if you’re trying to combat a bit of ambient light.

#50. Khosla Ventures doubles down on Even Healthcare to challenge India’s hospital economics

Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

Even Healthcare has raised $50 million in a funding round led by Khosla Ventures, as the Indian startup seeks to change how hospitals in the world’s most populous country make money and how doctors are rewarded.

The all-equity Series B round also saw participation from Alpha Wave and valued it at $300 million, triple its valuation 18 months ago, according to Even. The latest funding brings Even’s total capital raised to more than $120 million.

Hospitals in India typically earn more when patients undergo additional tests, procedures, or longer stays, even when they may not need them. Even wants to change that by focusing on patient care rather than pushing unnecessary treatments that drive up medical bills.

That approach has continued to appeal to Khosla Ventures, which has invested in Even since its seed round in 2021. The Silicon Valley venture firm is doubling down as Even moves to build and operate hospitals of its own, giving it greater control over patient care and costs.

Vinod Khosla, founder of Khosla Ventures, said Even’s approach goes beyond fixing individual parts of a fragmented healthcare system by bringing financing, technology, and care delivery together. The goal, he said in a prepared statement, is to reward better health outcomes rather than greater use of healthcare services.

“The clinical and economic results so far give us conviction that this can become an important new model for healthcare in India and beyond,” Khosla said.

Initially, Even relied on partner hospitals to treat its members, but Mayank Banerjee, who founded the startup in 2021 with Matilde Giglio and Alessandro Ialongo, said in an interview that the startup began questioning that model after finding that patients had undergone tests or been recommended surgeries it considered unnecessary.

“We think patients are getting not only a bad experience, but insurers are getting a bad economic deal. And as a result, we decided to fix it by building our own hospitals,” Banerjee told TechCrunch.

Even has since opened two hospitals in Bengaluru, both of which reached operational profitability, excluding depreciation, within a year of opening, Banerjee stated. The startup plans to open five more hospitals in the southern Indian city over the next six months, funded by its latest round.

Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even leases hospital buildings on 20-year agreements and spends on fitting them out and buying medical equipment.

Unlike hospitals where doctors may have financial incentives to recommend more procedures, Even pays its doctors fixed salaries — not tying their compensation to the number of tests or surgeries they perform, though Banerjee said doctors can earn bonuses based on patient-reported clinical outcomes.

The same principle extends to hospital management, whose compensation is not linked to the number of procedures performed, Banerjee told TechCrunch. Managers, he said, receive salaries and company-wide incentives, while marketing teams focus on bringing in patients instead of the revenue those patients generate. Moreover, every employee, including doctors and other hospital staff, receives equity in Even. The idea is to give employees a stake in the startup’s long-term performance, not to reward them for generating more medical bills.

Most of Even’s revenue comes from patients paying for treatment, Banerjee said. The startup also generates revenue through its relationships with insurers. It is also working with insurer partners on a model that could compensate it for hospitalizations it helps prevent, not simply for providing more treatment.

Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even tracks how patients recover after treatment using established medical scoring systems. In the case of knee replacements, for instance, it uses the Oxford Knee Score to measure pain and mobility. The startup publishes results on its website, alongside figures from other healthcare systems for comparison.

Even says its hospitals have an unplanned readmission rate of less than 1%, compared with an industry benchmark of 8% to 15%. Furthermore, it claims patients spend 40% less time in the hospital and that its approach has saved insurers more than ₹500 million (about $5.27 million).

Jai Sajnani, a partner at Khosla Ventures, told TechCrunch that the early performance of Even’s hospitals was a key reason the firm led the round. “We look forward to helping the Even team put quality care within reach of every family in Bengaluru and across India,” he said.

Even is still losing money, though. The startup posted a net loss of ₹902 million (about $9.50 million) in fiscal 2025, nearly 25% more than the previous year, on revenue of ₹272 million (about $2.86 million), regulatory filings show.

In August, Even also laid off about 350 employees, according to Indian startup news website Entrackr. Banerjee acknowledged the restructuring and called it a difficult decision. He said the affected employees received severance, extended health insurance, and accelerated equity vesting.

Even currently employs about 650 people, including around 300 doctors full-time. The startup has about 250,000 members and has recorded more than 750,000 patient interactions since its launch in 2021, including consultations, diagnostic tests, and surgeries, Banerjee said.

Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even could turn profitable within months if it stopped spending on expansion, but the startup is choosing to grow instead. He declined to say when the startup expects to become profitable.

“Right now, we’re investing in growth and serving more patients,” Banerjee said.

Elon Musk says he plans to give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in the US starting next year. With around 72 million children in the US as of July 2025, Musk would be giving away about $10.5 billion worth of shares, according to a report from CNBC.

Musk, who runs SpaceX and Tesla, writes on X that this giveaway “will be the first of many.” It comes just months after SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell announced that she’d be giving shares of her SpaceX stock to 2 million Trump Accounts, the tax-advantaged investment accounts given to American children. Dell’s founder similarly poured $6.25 billion into Trump Accounts, while Micron also announced a $250 million investment.

Along with giving away SpaceX shares, Musk has made large contributions to Republican midterm election efforts. Musk donated $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund PAC in September, making up more than “half of the super PAC’s total receipts in the third quarter of this year,” according to CBS News. He also dumped $76 million into the Super PAC he founded in 2024, America PAC.

#52. The Story of Billy Evans and ‘Theranos 2.0’

Warning: Light movie spoilers below. Read at your own risk.

Even before becoming the stars of Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s much-buzzed-about new documentary, Elizabeth Holmes and Billy Evans were a special kind of couple. Holmes “may have ultimately failed to change the world in the way she set out,” Evans wrote in a letter at the time of Holmes’ sentencing in 2022, “but she has undeniably changed mine.” The Theranos founder, in the hardest years of her life, taught her husband “a patience” that he “would have previously dismissed as unnecessary and soft.”

She brought out his inner light, another sentencing letter from a friend of the couple reports: When they returned from a “monthslong camping trip,” Evans “displayed a new level of compassion in his demeanor, a strong sense of intention with his actions, and a heightened desire to listen to and look at others with purpose.” Whatever others might think, Evans was saying, Holmes wasn’t the only one of the pair that had been given a second chance. And they might get a second second chance with Haemanthus, a company that Evans is keen to reassure social media followers is absolutely—most definitely— “not Theranos 2.0.” A person familiar with the business told The Wall Street Journal that Holmes is not involved.

🔗 The New Fan’s Guide to the Unreal World of Nathan Fielder

🔗 How Elizabeth Holmes Tricked WIRED—and Everyone Else

🔗 From the Archive: This Woman Invented a Way to Run 30 Lab Tests on Only One Drop of Blood

But viewers of You Can See Everything will watch Evans agreeing to the characterization that he and Holmes are making Theranos 2.0. They discuss the trajectory to make a working prototype of something on camera; they talk about collaborating on product ideas from prison. “To meet her, to spend time with her, that was the intention of the film,” the Austin, Texas-based Evans told David Friedberg, a cohost of the podcast All-In. “I haven’t seen it yet. I might think this is the dumbest thing that I have done.”

So who is Evans? And what is he building?

Long before fathering two children—son William and daughter Invicta—with Holmes, Evans grew up in San Diego in one of the city’s more prominent families, heir to midcentury pioneers in the Southern California tourism industry. His grandparents, William and Anne Evans were “two young hoteliers [who] saw the future,” according to the family’s company website, and opened up what would become a popular resort hotel on a mudflat in Mission Bay in 1953. They added a second nearby, and today own a third in La Jolla. This brought generational wealth. The business passed in part to Billy’s father, also named William.

Billy went to the Francis Parker School, one of the most prestigious private schools in the city. “The Evans family is very well respected in San Diego,” said a contemporary of Evans’ who worked for the family as a teenager, but Billy “always a source of drama, would try to fight to start fights.” He had “affluenza” and was “just your classic spoiled rich kid” in a way that was not true of all his relatives. The inner light would come around later. (Evans did not want to be interviewed for the story and did not answer specific questions.)

After graduating from MIT with a bachelor of science in economics, Evans reportedly tried to launch a startup offering medical concierge services. This failed. He then took jobs in a handful of tech companies, including LinkedIn and Luminar Technologies, a self-driving car company. In 2017, at a “Fleet Week charity event” in the Bay Area, the then 25-year-old met Holmes and was “captivated,” he later wrote the judge at her sentencing, “by her childish wonder and authenticity.”

There was some reporting in the early years that the Evans family was not entirely enthused by this courtship, but doubts seemed to have dissipated by the time of the Holmes trial. Billy’s father, William Evans, showed up to the courtroom incognito, under the alias “Hanson,” identifying himself as a kind of mechanic. (He owns an enormous classic car collection.) To journalists, he defended Holmes’ honor. In court, he turned heads by unwrapping a “large Rice Krispies Treat” whose crinkling foil drowned out the judge on the first day of jury selection, NPR reported.

While in the film Evans and Holmes are both shown on fundraising calls, her name doesn’t appear in any of the incorporation documents of Haemanthus, the company Evans founded in 2022. There is little publicly available information on the company; to date, it has released no products and barely has a LinkedIn page, let alone a website. Yet its name can’t help but conjure up Theranos, and, indeed, its stated goal is to bring blood, urine, and saliva testing to American homes in the form of a countertop-size machine, which was more or less the goal of Theranos.

But the technology of Haemanthus seems to be a bit different than that of Theranos. Where the earlier company’s machine hoped to perfect the “miniaturization” of existing diagnostic techniques such that they could fit in a box on a counter, using a very small blood sample, Haemanthus’ machine uses “light.” To employ a cooler word, it uses lasers. The company’s Raman Spectroscopy System, a patent for which was granted January 21, 2025, suggests a machine capable of firing high-power light sources into biological samples and reading the resulting information accurately.

Raman Spectroscopy is a real and promising diagnostic tool and the subject of research since its discovery by, among others, C. V. Raman in 1928. Shine a light source at a material and perhaps one in 1 million photons will shift in frequency in relation to the molecular vibrations of the material it bounced off of. That shift can be measured and analyzed, and a century of work has gone into making this process a little easier and a little more useful, carried out today by specialists at research universities and hospitals.

It may someday be even more useful. WIRED contacted Eric Potma, a professor of chemistry at UC Irvine, to shed some light on the technology. “Given that I act as one of their consultants, I am not sure if it is appropriate for me to delve much further into this,” he wrote back. “All I can say is that from an engineering perspective, they have some interesting ideas that are worth exploring.”

“It is not a technology concept pulled out of thin air, as people may be inclined to think based on the fact that the company is run by Elizabeth's husband (and thus an automatic repeat of the Theranos story),” he continued over email. “My own assessment is that Haemanthus is not Theranos. The engineers at Haemanthus are legit, and they are really trying to push the Raman detection technology into interesting directions.”

The challenges of putting this highly sensitive and difficult diagnostic technique into home appliances able to assess human health markers with a level of accuracy in seconds that will pass regulatory scrutiny—as promised in the company’s promotional materials—are great, though. Last year, The New York Times said that the company had garnered a $3.5 million investment from “friends and family.” It now reports as much as $20 million in funding.

Press accounts of the company’s marketing materials seem to promise investors that the company faces “no regulatory oversight,” in part because the machine would only be developed to test veterinary diseases at first. The New York Times, though, confirmed with the USDA that the agency had regulatory oversight over “vet diagnostics.”

Evans told the Times, which had other questions, that the company was “in stealth” and would remain so: “They aren’t going to find anything associated with the name Haemanthus.” There are a few things out there, among them the patent, but stealth mode continues. The addresses that turn up are mostly connected to private homes in one of Austin’s more desirable neighborhoods, near Barton Springs. Contacted by phone, a few folks who seem likely to be employees of the company declined to talk or even confirm or deny their role.

The desire for “stealth,” though, is a little discordant with the desire to participate in a yearslong documentary project with a graduate of one of Canada’s top business schools. Perhaps it will help raise money: Once the laser system is perfected, the company hopes, according to materials reviewed by the Times, to put the whole thing in a stamp-size wearable device, a research process it told investors will take “three years and $70 million.” Holmes will be reportedly moving from prison to a halfway house next summer. The world may yet be changed.

#59. No agenda, no rush, no leaving San Francisco: Benchmark’s partners on investing in a frenzied market

Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

The players sometimes change. I sat down with four of Benchmark’s partners three years ago, and three of those individuals are no longer with the firm. The capital commitments have changed, too. This summer, Benchmark announced $2 billion across two funds, marking only the second time in its 31-year history that it has veered from raising a far smaller vehicle.

But at this week’s TechCrunch Disrupt, the venture firm’s five partners convincingly portrayed a close-knit team that’s not about to put the pedal to the metal, even as many of their rivals do exactly that. The world may be speeding up, but they’re investing at the pace Benchmark always has: just two or three new bets per year per partner. The world is drowning in information, yet their Monday partner meetings still have no agenda. And while economic indicators point to trouble ahead, they don’t seem too bothered, seeing many of the warning signs as products of X-fueled hysteria.

Here’s what Benchmark’s full partnership — gathered publicly for the first time on our stage — had to say at the show. Some of the comments below have been edited for length and clarity; you can watch the full interview at the end of the article.

Benchmark has evolved in some ways, including a bigger core fund and a new growth fund. How do you think about adapting without losing what makes you Benchmark?

Peter Fenton: The craft that hasn’t changed is the core fund: working closely with founders at the beginning. It’s usually a 10-to-15-year commitment, [working] shoulder to shoulder, and that doesn’t scale. There’s also been inflation. We held the core fund at $500 million for 20 years, and it has just inflated to be consistent with the existing economy, which we hadn’t done and that was probably a tactical error on our part.

[As for the growth fund] it’s an expansion of our mandate. In some ways, we get permission from the ecosystem to do more than just the core early-stage business. [Not having this previously] was a fork in our eye. A number of opportunities that came to Benchmark would have returned somewhere between 10 and 1,000x to Benchmark, and we were constricted by our early-stage focus.

Are you thinking to make a handful of bets with that $1.25 billion growth fund?

Fenton: We all have different answers, which is the beauty of a partnership. I’d love for us to have, as that great J.P. Morgan paper puts it, the agony and ecstasy of a concentrated portfolio. If the fund is successful, one or two investments will generate 90% of the returns. So I think it’s four to six, maybe seven to eight.

Ev, you joined Benchmark late last year. You’ve worked at Founders Fund, Bond, and Kleiner Perkins. How does Benchmark differ?

Ev Randall: Every firm is ultimately a collection of the people within the firm and how they work together. Some are very hierarchical, with a 50- or 60-person investment team and investment processes that are federated into product groups. And then you have small partnerships. Very early in my career, I was drawn to small partnerships because they allow a higher level of throughput and fidelity in your conversations, where you don’t feel like you’re making decisions through some Byzantine corporate structure. You’re going out on the field together, like a sports team.

And then the other piece is: You have to find your people, You have to find people who you not only like but admire. With Benchmark, with the current crop of GPs, it was obvious that everyone liked each other and got along, but it went deeper than that. It’s a group that admires each other and learns from each other. That mix of attributes is very rare, and when I saw it, I immediately wanted to join, and I think Jack felt the same way also as a newcomer.

Jack, you joined in February, but it was just a year ago that you raised a second, $275 million fund for your own firm in what you told the Wall Street Journal took one week. You also have a hugely popular podcast. Why join Benchmark?

Jack Altman: It’s funny. I did the podcast with these guys at the start of this year, and during that podcast, obviously we talked about the commitment to being a small fund, but more than that, what I heard was that they want to be the first people who founders call, they want to be concentrated, and they just care. So much in this industry gets tied up in money and status, and what I felt from the Benchmark team then, and ten times more as I’ve gotten to know them so well, is it’s a group that really cares about founders and helping companies. And I did enjoy being an individual investor. . .but in a market this crazy, I don’t know how I’d feel, figuring it out on my own. Having a group of people who are so smart and focused and driven to learn it with and from has been awesome.

I’m told you meet on Mondays with no agenda.

Chethan Puttagunta: Jack tried to make an agenda. [Laughs.]

Altman: I’ve got an agenda for next Monday.

Eric Vishria: It’s weirdly arbitrary, honestly. It’s an ongoing conversation. In a time of rapid change, you’re trying to figure out what’s becoming possible that wasn’t possible six months ago, and who’s bending light. We talk about what companies we’re meeting, what piqued our interest and why, what we’re seeing in board meetings. You can try to systematize it, but one of the beauties of five people is you don’t have to. It’s a decades-long conversation that only works if you’re small and actually enjoy spending time together. After this session, we’re having dinner with one of the very few entrepreneurs who has built a multi-hundred-billion-dollar company, someone we’re not invested in, just to stretch our thinking.

Puttagunta: Part of not having an agenda is you need space to be reactive. If a founder needs help landing an executive or a strategic partnership, the five of us can be at their disposal.

You’re an equal partnership. Can one person put the kibosh on a deal?

Puttagunta: Nobody knows. We don’t have rules around it.

Altman: I actually don’t know. I was waiting to see what someone else [said].

Altman: Because the firm is structured around a low volume of deals, you don’t actually want to have all of this rigor. If we invested in 100 or 200 companies a year, you’d want a CRM and a formal voting process. Because it’s so rare, the lack of structure is a huge asset.

Fenton: One of the differentiating aspects of our brand is we’re not so cocksure to come in and say ‘winner’ or ‘loser.’ It’s not Shark Tank. We sort of feel awe, for lack of a better term, at all the possibilities . . . The occasional case where someone comes in who’s polarizing — the entrepreneurs feel that. If someone in the room doesn’t like you, we’re not a great partner.

Companies are growing faster than ever. I’d think it’s easier to feel you’re missing out on opportunities if you don’t invest with greater frequency. Have you picked up the pace?

Puttagunta: I think the pace is consistent. I think part of the reality of venture capital in our business is that we are not going to be part of every successful company, and that’s okay. There are companies that we identify, we find that the entrepreneur has some great strength, and we want to amplify that strength. And it’s our job to find a way to work with that person. It kind of doesn’t matter how much capital they want to raise, or what structure, or where they are. You just have to work through all that stuff.

One thing that founders are interested in as a trend is VCs backing competing companies. Has that VC-founder pact changed because companies are growing so quickly and expanding into one another’s territory?

Vishria: One of the things we have an ethos around is, we are making a commitment to an entrepreneur, and through that commitment, we’re saying we’re going to work with you in this thing, and whatever that thing is, and we are working closely enough where it matters, and it should matter to them, and as it matters to us. The harsh reality of this world is every company is evolving very quickly, and so you do have companies that will naturally evolve from one thing to another, or pivot or change, and you are going to get conflicts. That’s just the reality of the of the kind of current dynamic. . .

Of course, we’re maintaining confidentiality and doing those things and fortunate to not end up in in that type of insane direct conflict [as happened recently with rival companies Factory and Cognition]. . . that commitment of exclusivity in that area is really important. But things are evolving. There’s no doubt about that.

Puttagunta: And I think people are ultra ambitious in this AI era. As the cost of coding new products effectively goes to zero, founders see a surface area and they want to attack the surface area, and so I think it’s probably going to happen more, where you start to run into each other. But there’s a way to be there’s a way to maintain that relationship and be respectful.

Jack, have you made an investment for Benchmark yet, and if so, did you feel a lot of pressure with that first deal?

Altman: I have, a few, and some are recent, so not all are disclosed. My background was software, but since joining, I’ve done chips, robotics and infra. Someone asked me when I joined, ‘How was the onboarding?’ And I was like, ‘It was perfect. There was no onboarding.’ Either Chethan or Eric told me early on, ‘Hey, you’re going to feel tight on your first one. Don’t. You’re going to make many investments while you’re here. This whole game includes crazy power laws. The odds of it being your first are low.’ . . . I trusted they understood what my shape was as a person, as an investor, and I was going to just try to stay as consistent to that as I could.

It really is a group dynamic on a lot of these. The investments I’ve made, I don’t think we would have won them if I didn’t have my partners. I don’t know that I would have been able to know how to get to a yes without them.

Eric, the AI chip company Cerebras was an unusual bet for Benchmark at the time it was made. What persuaded you to move forward with it?

Vishria: We invested in the spring of 2016, in the first round. We hadn’t made a hardware investment in 10 years. The founders seemed good, they had a very simple thesis, and I didn’t understand most of the rest. On the Sunday night before they came back to pitch the partnership, Peter told me it went against everything he’d learned in venture. Then, after the Monday pitch, he had flipped. A big part of it is understanding each other’s instincts. That began a journey of lots of ups and downs and many potential deaths of the company along the way, and it’s far from over. The romanticism of falling in love with a founder and an idea is why we do this.

Fenton: Andrew and his co-founders are heretics. What they were saying was unorthodox, and you see it today, with people dumping on the stock because it’s polarizing. That’s exactly where we have to be as investors. If it’s consensus, why is there a startup?

On that point, Cerebras priced at $185 when it went public earlier this year, jumped to $350, and is back near $185. Why?

Vishria: About six weeks before the IPO, I showed the company stock chart after stock chart: CoreWeave, Datadog, DoorDash, Amazon. Peak to trough, it’s insane how many of them move 500% in a year, up and down. So who knows? You control what you can control, and you update the public markets every 12 weeks. Being a public company takes a stomach of titanium, and the employees have to understand that.

Your former colleague, Bill Gurley, has long argued that the traditional IPO process is broken, that that IPO ‘pop’ benefits bankers and their clients — not the company. He’s a proponent of direct listings. Does anyone here agree with that thinking?

Vishria: I think maybe of this group, I’m the only one who’s worked on a direct listing. It can for sure make sense. I think the reality is for this crop of AI companies, it’s going to be unlikely because they need capital, and they need a lot of capital. At the end of the day, IPOs raise money. Cerebras raised $6 billion. That matters, so I think it’s probably unlikely for this crop just because most of them need capital.

Could a severe correction be coming? A lot of AI companies have exhausted their free cash flow. It’s very expensive for companies to borrow. We also just saw the first AI bankruptcy with Character AI.

Randall: Macro is always a fool’s errand to predict with precision. What has changed most since I started investing is the information environment. Character.AI was the leftover corpse of a company whose founder and team were acqui-hired into Google a year and a half ago, and it was already sold for $2.3 billion; its Chapter 11 being read as an AI chill effect shows that the info environment for public equities in tech has been drawn so much into this, like, hyperactive X echo chamber.

If you look at the market today and you see where CoreWeave and Nebius and all these things are trading, those numbers are are due to the ARR figures of two private companies that will probably be public in the next 12 months . . .There’s so much capex and there’s so much investment that runs through the estimated and projected health of OpenAI and Anthropic.

Our companies see so much demand that they can’t get enough compute to serve customers who are willing to pay them at good gross margins. There’s nothing inherently unhealthy about the AI ecosystem. What’s unhealthy is the volatility from data points that are often untrue or exaggerated for clicks. I do think OpenAI and Anthropic going public would be healthy, so the market stops swinging 5% to 10% every time an anonymous account updates an estimate.

Those two companies have also really pulled the center of gravity back to San Francisco. Do you have to be in San Francisco to be a founder now? Are you interested in companies outside of California?

Altman: I don’t know that you have to be here as a founder, but I think it is right now by far the easiest place to get talent, capital, and customers. Probably everyone [on the team] works with companies that are not in San Francisco, but we’re also here in San Francisco every day, so I wouldn’t say you have to, but I’d say: strong bias for our particular setup.

Fenton: Historically, 90%-plus percent of the capital returns have come from companies founded here. There are beautiful stories outside that dense probability distribution — Shopify is a great example, Ramp — but the ecosystem effect that occurs when you have a successful company and that leads to a background of great executives [and] ambitious people, the bar of success gets raised. I don’t think it has systemically happened anywhere quite like here.

Randall: I’m trying to think of a non-SF based company that I’ve met with in the last 18 months that wasn’t actively saying that they were spending time in San Francisco. They’ve either opening an office in San Francisco, they’re spending half of their time in San Francisco, or they’re planning to move out to San Francisco. Iron sharpens iron. If you want to be around peers who are going to make you the best version of yourself, and it’s hard to think of a city that does that better than San Francisco in the current era that we’re in now with AI here.

If you’re on the hunt for lightweight wireless headphones but wearing earbuds or clip-ons never feels comfortable or secure, a relatively obscure Japanese headphone maker could have the solution. Final’s new Porta headphones feature an on-ear design supported by a headband but with a structure made from a single piece of wire so they weigh just 40 grams. For comparison, Marshall’s recently-launched Milton A.N.C. are also designed to be smaller on-ear headphones but weigh 200 grams.

The Final Porta are available for preorder now through the company’s online store for 12,800 yen (around $80) with black or orange ear pads and shipping expected to start on October 23rd. The company also has an Amazon shop for US-based customers, but the Porta aren’t listed there yet.

Sporting a design that looks loosely inspired by the lightweight headphones Sony bundled with its Walkmans decades ago, the Porta’s functionality is unsurprisingly basic. A 57mAh battery charges over USB-C and provides up to eight hours of use while the Porta are wirelessly paired to a device using Bluetooth 5.4 and streaming audio over the SBC and AAC codecs. There’s no active noise cancelation which is not uncommon for on-ear headphones that don’t create a full seal, but with an IPX4 rating you should be able to use the Porta in the rain or while working up a sweat without worrying about them getting damaged by the moisture.

#61. How Elizabeth Holmes Tricked WIRED—and Everyone Else

Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder of the fraud-ridden blood-test company Theranos, made her national press debut in The Wall Street Journal in 2013. The article—“A Drop of Blood, an Instant Diagnosis”—wasn’t a science story, or even a business story. It ran in the Opinion section, by a writer on the Journal’s editorial board named Joseph Rago, winner of a Pulitzer Prize for critiques of the Affordable Care Act.

He wrote that he was impressed by the prospect of individuals having more direct control of their health care; no less an eminence than former secretary of state George Shultz, a Theranos board member, had told Rago that Holmes was the next Steve Jobs or Bill Gates.

By 2014, Holmes was the youngest woman billionaire ever, and the mid-2010s were electric with tech-industry success stories—the iPhone, Tesla, Airbnb, Twitter. I was an editor at WIRED back then, and Theranos-as-presented felt very WIRED. It looked like evidence that a Silicon Valley approach to innovation would work in every industry, including medicine. And at the magazine that first published the idea of the “quantified self,” Theranos’ pitch validated the notion that individuals could take charge of their own health with innovative tech and access to data.

🔗 The New Fan’s Guide to the Unreal World of Nathan Fielder

🔗 The Story of Billy Evans and ‘Theranos 2.0’

🔗 From the Archive: This Woman Invented a Way to Run 30 Lab Tests on Only One Drop of Blood

One of my colleagues, an editor named Caitlin Roper, saw a story in Theranos and in Holmes, but no one was sure what shape it should take. The executive editor suggested Roper just go talk to Holmes and see what was what. The result was an influential long-form Q&A headlined “One Drop, Infinite Data: How Elizabeth Holmes Built a Better Blood Test.” Because print magazines move with the agility and speed of a post-Panamax cargo ship, the story didn’t run until the March 2014 issue.

Over the next few months, other publications followed. Fortune put Holmes on the cover. The New Yorker did a profile. In October 2015, Inc. put her on the cover, calling her “the next Steve Jobs”—and a couple of weeks later, The Wall Street Journal did another article on Theranos, by the reporter John Carreyrou. The headline was deceptively humble: “Theranos Has Struggled with Blood Tests.”

The speedy and accurate blood tests were fake, the innovative tech didn’t exist, and Walgreens, a major partner, terminated its deal with Theranos. It was a grift. A new documentary film, out this week, follows Holmes in the weeks leading up to her incarceration.

Get a bunch of old WIRED editors together these days and it doesn’t take more than one drink before we start asking each other whether we enabled the worst parts of the tech world’s rise to power. Sometimes it seems like every antichrist-lecturing, panopticon-building, machine-god-bothering weirdo with $100 billion and a government contract made his debut in our pages. So, with Theranos and Holmes back in the news, the current administration at WIRED wondered what we were thinking back then.

It was a long time ago. I called Caitlin.

As always, we were looking for good stories. “I was interested in this female founder, but also the idea that her actual goal was disruption of health care, that there could be more transparency and reduced costs,” says Roper, who today is executive producer for scripted film and TV at The New York Times. “I was going through some medical stuff at the time and having constant blood tests, and I was curious about what this could do.”

Roper got a go-ahead to report and write something, execution to be determined. In the house jargon: Green light, format TK. She and I talked it through separately. “The conversation I remember with you, which I thought of many years later, was looking at the board of directors, her board, which was just completely batshit. It had military figures and government officials, and just seemed very odd,” Roper says. “You said there was something weird about that. It raised your suspicious hackles.”

It did—a few of us thought we saw hints of red flags. The company hadn’t published any peer-reviewed data. Colleagues had heard unconfirmable rumors of shenanigans inside the company. But that didn’t mean it wasn’t a story. We’d just have to figure out how to handle all that. WIRED had been, in years past, overly credulous, especially of scientific claims. But primarily WIRED covered innovation and stuff that sounded futuristic. This felt like it qualified.

“I remember that with dramatic irony, looking back,” Roper says.

Holmes agreed to an interview, and Roper went down to the Valley, to Theranos’ offices. She was only the second reporter to be there, and she got the performance that Holmes would become famous for. “There’s a lot of weird things about her. She was speaking in this strange, low voice. She was wearing a Steve Jobs outfit—black turtleneck,” Roper says. “She seemed like she was very precisely trying to project something.” (That first WSJ story ran with an illustrated caricature; WIRED shot a photo, professionally styled, of Holmes in her signature look.)

They spent an hour talking. Roper got her blood drawn, a tiny pinprick from the tip of her finger. “I said, ‘I’d love to see the box, can I follow my blood sample?’” Roper says. “They said, absolutely not.” Company reps implied it was a health-and-safety issue.

Instead, Holmes took Roper to the Palo Alto Walgreens, one of the few where Theranos had actually set up shop. “That part seemed like a snow job,” Roper says. “It was clear even from my own basic research that it hadn’t rolled out.” The booth at Walgreens was not in service. Holmes told her the company was going to open Walgreens labs across the Southwest.

Roper’s blood results came back. “The panel they took was similar to a panel I’d just had. I looked at them, and they matched,” Roper says. That seemed roughly confirmatory, at the time. It’s impossible to know now how it pulled that off, but later it turned out Theranos maintained a fully kitted-out lab in its Palo Alto offices, in addition to the lab for the company’s supposed new tech.

Interview done, Roper drove back up to San Francisco, to WIRED. “It didn’t feel like there was a feature to do,” she says. The Walgreens stuff wasn’t happening yet; it was too hard to report out how the technology worked. What was hard, in retrospect, was validation. Roper and the bosses weren’t sure that investment money from bold-faced names made up for an absence of hard scientific evidence.

So Roper wrote it up as an interview—a Q&A. “It seemed more like an interesting founder story,” she says. Roper asked every hard question, and got answers. They just turned out to be lies. But Roper acknowledges some cracks in the story’s origin. “If she had not been a woman, I would have been less motivated. That was part of what compelled me,” she says. “I felt sympathetic to the idea of her outfit and her weirdness, because I related to the idea that she was passing in some way in that environment, needing to assert herself.”

It’s tempting to see in that a DEI-run-amok story. It isn’t. All of us at WIRED were trying to wrestle with sexism in the world we covered, and at our magazine. Holmes’ board was all non–Silicon Valley types—was that because venture investors and scientists had identified her as a bad risk, or was it because Silicon Valley venture capitalists don’t support women founders?

Just a month after Roper’s Q&A ran, a team of researchers at the Harvard Business School and MIT Sloan School published a paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences showing that investors were far more likely to fund the same pitch if it came from a man than if it came from a woman—and that conventionally attractive men did even better. Today, roughly 75 percent of venture investors are men, and the proportions were worse a decade ago. There’s even research showing that male venture investors are more likely to promote women to partner if the men have daughters. Roper and WIRED were trying to fight that tide and ran aground on a grifter instead.

“Partially, yes, it’s a woman founder, and that’s a nice change of pace. It would’ve been nice if you guys could have beaten John Carreyrou and figured it out,” says Dave Karpf, an associate professor at George Washington University who has read every issue of WIRED and uses them to teach a class about Silicon Valley’s visions of the future. “But it wasn’t a new, untested claim. It was an active fraud.”

It’s fair to imagine a timeline where WIRED dug in deeper and was more critical, or at least didn’t further drive the hype cycle. “That story and the way we photographed her was absolutely fuel to lauding her and drawing attention,” Roper says. “I do feel partially responsible for that.”

We probably were, but I’m not sure WIRED’s Q&A was any more or less credulous than stories other magazines did. I know I sound defensive here, but even WIRED’s rigorous fact-check process wasn’t designed to unmask fraud. We all got got; it’s easy to see red flags when they’re in the rearview mirror. Was it weird to believe a 19-year-old college dropout had noticed something about pathology and microfluidics no one else had? Sure, but as Karpf points out, the system valorizes those kinds of iconoclasts. Steve Jobs was a dropout, man!

“If she had done all the graduate work, she wouldn’t have been nearly as fundable. They would just find someone else to tell them the stories they want to fund,” Karpf says. “It’s the people promoting it who, I think, have a bunch of answering to do.”

In 2019, as Sam Altman was leaving his role leading the tech incubator Y Combinator to become CEO of OpenAI, he wrote a blog post extolling the virtue in founders with “too much self belief … almost to the point of delusion.” Venture investors will tell you they invest in people as much as ideas, and the ideas are sometimes early-days, or half-baked. The system encourages exaggeration—right up to the line of deception. It can favor charismatic hucksters. If Theranos’ technology didn’t quite work yet, well, that’s a core tenet of Silicon Valley: Fake it till you make it.

And for a long time, WIRED helped. The magazine touted big ideas, and sometimes those ideas turned out to be dumb. Sometimes we were too early; sometimes we were wrong. Pitch meetings for stories big and small were a bit of a Thunderdome, actually. Eventually we developed some heuristics to encode skepticism in the process. For architecture stories, renders weren’t enough—ground had to have been broken. Physical objects had to exist in physical space; reporters had to be able to visit a thing. A flying car had to, you know, fly. In stories about new drugs or medical devices, the gating rule became “phase 3 trials or get the fuck out.”

Today, every responsible tech journalist has had to don new kinds of armor to prepare for the future that WIRED helped create. It’s possible to marvel at robot cars navigating cities as if driven by ghosts—while acknowledging the ways they sometimes fail, are often remote-piloted by humans, and pose new questions about regulating Big Tech. It’s possible to be awed by generative artificial intelligence’s capabilities while also interrogating the motives and practices of the companies that build it. And, yes, the personal politics of tech trillionaires matter when they’re donating more than a quarter of a billion dollars to support one political party over another. All of that was probably WIRED’s responsibility back then; it’s everyone’s responsibility now.

The tech business hates all that, reasonably. Not rarely, some longtime Silicon Valley dude will learn I spent most of my career at WIRED and say something like, “What happened to that place? I miss the old, optimistic WIRED.”

But you know, in the same issue of the magazine that carried the Holmes Q&A, another of our colleagues, Bill Wasik, wrote an opinion piece touted on the cover as “Silicon Valley’s Douchebag Problem.” Wasik, today the science editor at The New York Times, wrote then that dead-eyed misbehavior in pursuit of profit would kill tech’s magical status. Peter Thiel–derived ideas about secession and business models that relied on surveillance capitalism risked a backlash that would burn it all down, Wasik warned. The Valley and its toys, he wrote, would end up “a punch line—a hallucination of a future that no one believes in anymore.”

Science and tech journalism have to be about more than investors and returns. The future is too important; the stakes are too high. Case in point: As part of Joseph Rago’s reporting on Elizabeth Holmes and Theranos, he got his finger pricked. Rago’s blood test results were back “by the time I walked out the door,” he wrote. “(Phew: all clear.)” Four years later, Rago, 34, died alone in his New York apartment.

The city medical examiner said the cause of his death was sarcoidosis, a rare (and rarely fatal), hard-to-diagnose inflammatory disorder. Doctors usually figure it out by excluding other possibilities. Rago didn’t even know he had the disease. But among its signs are elevated levels of vitamin D and angiotensin-converting enzyme. Maybe an honest blood test would have spotted it.

#69. Anthropic says it’s committing 5% of its shares to a ‘public benefit fund’

Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

Anthropic announced on Sunday that it’s creating a “public benefit fund” that will give the company “increased flexibility and scale” to support projects for societal good.

Anthropic said that it will commit 5% of its shares to the fund — structured as a wholly owned entity within the company — with the option to contribute an additional 2% for every 50% increase in Anthropic’s value. And it offered some broad-strokes ideas for how this money might actually be used, such as “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.”

There’s also the impact that AI might have on the job market, which Anthropic has already committed $200 million to study. But, the company said, “given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.”

Anthropic’s announcement comes as the AI industry faces increasingly negative public sentiment, which CEO Dario Amodei has described as “fundamentally a crisis of trust.”

If you’re wondering who will actually decide which public benefits are worth funding, Anthropic said it will share more information about structure and governance in the coming months.

#70. A hacker broke into John Deere and SharkNinja with an army of AI agents

A hacker broke into more than 100 websites using an army of AI agents that mostly operated on their own, according to findings from the AI security firm Norforge. Though Norforge doesn’t name the targets, Reuters reports that the victims included companies like John Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins.

Concerns over AI-powered cybersecurity breaches have grown as the technology grows more advanced, with hackers using the tools to carry out large-scale attacks. At the same time, rogue AI agents are carrying out attacks of their own after escaping from testing environments.

Researchers at Norforge uncovered the attacks through exposed work on Cairn, an open-source AI platform that describes itself as a “general-purpose problem-solving engine.” With Cairn, users set a start and end point for the AI agents, which document their progress as they move forward with the task. However, as noted by Norforge, hackers can also use the tool to orchestrate cyberattacks using AI agents.

The hacker who broke into more than 100 sites was the “most active” among the exposed Cairn instances discovered by Norforge, waging attacks on companies based in the US, Canada, Australia, and Japan, as reported by Reuters. This attacker laid out “preferred intrusion tactics” using fewer than 100 Chinese characters, with successful breaches taking about 23 hours, according to Reuters. Overall, Nordforge found more than 20 exposed Cairn instances that are “likely malicious.”

In a statement to Reuters, a John Deere spokesperson said there is “no indication that ​sensitive information was accessed” as a result of the attack, while Cummins said it’s “investigating the report of a potential cyber-attack on a website operated by one of our third-party vendors.”

Meanwhile, SharkNinja says the breach impacted a standalone site with product support information, and that it has contained the threat. John Deere, Cumms, and SharkNinja didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

Nordforge says it’s working to get the malicious Cairn instances taken down. Cairn’s creator, who goes by @le1xia0, said earlier this month that the platform “was never a ‘hacking tool,’” adding that “misuse is a human decision, not a feature of the engine.”

#71. 15 Best White Elephant Gifts, Plus a Prank Box to Put Them In (2026)

You Can’t Escape the white elephant parties. My friend who hosts an annual white elephant debated sending out an invite before October even began, and my mother’s ornament-themed white elephant has split into two parties this year. On top of all your regular Christmas and holiday shopping, trying to pick a gift that won’t embarrass you at multiple gift exchanges feels like mental torture.

That’s because white elephant parties in particular present a unique challenge: Can you find a cool or funny white elephant gift within a set budget that a group of people—who are potentially strangers—will battle each other to take home? None of us wants to be the person who brought the gift nobody wanted. Some folks bring joke gifts, some bring booze to be safe, and some gifts will feel like garbage to you but gems to others. Some of my favorite white elephant gifts include a coffee-pot-shaped mug, a fun Lego set, and sushi-shaped magnets. Here’s every white elephant gift I recommend bringing, ranging from quirky to cool to actually useful.

Looking for more gift ideas? Don’t miss our other awesome gift guides as the holiday season ramps up.

Updated October 2026: I’ve added Verloop Mosaic Slide Slippers, Final E500 wired headphones, Jenny Lemons hair accessories, and Cync Dynamic Effects Smart Light Bulbs to this guide.

Maybe you’re headed to your book club white elephant, or maybe you’ve talked everyone into getting an e-reader this year. Maybe that’s just me, though. Either way, if you know there are people with e-readers coming to your gift exchange, a cool new case makes for an easy win. PopSockets has an entire Kindle case line that has a lot of really cool and gift-worthy designs. This dragon sterling case is one of my favorites. The black opaque base allows Kindle colors to show through, or it can dress up the plain black Kindle models. It also has a built-in MagSafe ring so the winner can attach their favorite PopSocket Grip to it for easier reading—or you can include one for them. This one’s my personal favorite. PopSockets only has models for the 12th and 11th generations of the Kindle, so don't get these if you're shopping the new 13th generation models that were just announced earlier this month.

If your group is more of a Kobo club, I also really love Kobo's SleepCover cases ($40) that can prop the e-reader up thanks to the foldable portion of the cover. You might want to include a gift receipt so they can exchange it if you get the wrong size—Kobo has SleepCovers for both Libra and Clara models, but PopSockets’ cases only fit the Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft.

In this economy, no one wants junk from the white elephant exchange, especially if your buy-in is around $50. If you're looking for something your gift receiver could use every day that also has a little style to it, try these knit slippers from Verloop. The Mosaic Slide Slippers have interlocking stripes for a fresh look while still being a cozy, comfy house slipper.

There are other designs you can explore, but my husband's eyes lit up at this design, so it's a fun option if you're struggling what to bring a group of men. The only gamble is sizing, but these slippers only come in two sizes anyway, so I'd get the L/XL so that it fits most attendees. I wear a size 8 in women's, which Verloop says is the S/M, but the larger size isn't so large that I can't wear these around the house on a chilly fall morning.

Wired earbuds are back, baby. A lot of the latest models will cost you a pretty penny (or rather, several $20 bills that would push it out of the white elephant gift budget), but WIRED reviewer Harry Rabinowitz says these earbuds from Final are surprisingly good for the $20 price point. They even come with five pairs of silicone and foam ear tips, so whoever wins it can find their perfect fit.

Everyone hydrates, so a drinking vessel is a safe gift all around. And most people drink some kind of caffeinated drink, whether it’s coffee or tea or perhaps an energy drink. This fun mug looks like a miniature coffee pot and can handle hot drinks. It even comes with a plastic lid so you can take it on the go. I like how comfortable the handle is to hold, and it’s just so funny to look at while still doing a great job holding my morning tea. The lid is pretty flimsy, so I usually just drink out of the glass top instead, but I still like that there is an included lid rather than none at all.

Jazz up someone’s fridge with adorable sushi magnets. They almost look a little too real—the salmon nigiri looks ready to eat—but are still fun to look at on a fridge. Every single visitor I have comments on how cute these magnets are. After two years of rocking these on my fridge, they’re all holding up strong.

While the magnets on the plastic rolls are small, they’re still plenty strong enough to hold up papers and children’s artwork on someone’s fridge without slipping or falling. I'd only put two corners of paper underneath one of these max since they’re not massively strong, and I usually put two magnets for each piece of art. I’m craving ikura just looking at them, and the foodies at your white elephant can battle it out for who gets to take these home and deal with the same cravings.

Jenny Lemons (Micro Fish Hair Claw Clip Set)

Jenny Lemons (Large Hot Sauce Hair Claw Clip)

I've seen some failed attempts at whimsy at a white elephant party. The worst I've seen recently was a confetti-filled rolling pin that got zero steal bids and broke as soon as the party ended.

But I like the concept of something fun to look at that doubles as being useful. These hair clips from Jenny Lemons check that box in a much more fun way, and are something I could see any of my girlfriends being excited to open. (My long-haired husband would even be amused to open the larger hot sauce clip if his hair weren't so thick that we have to buy special hair ties for it.) I love that the set of six micro fish clips comes with a container to look like it's a set of tinned fish. Jenny Lemons has a ton of other designs too, both for the larger clips and sets of six, so you can pick the set that works best for your crew of friends or family.

I’ll tell you right now: The Big Enter Supersized Key enter key is a little too much fun to have on my desk, and a great thing to bring for a white elephant with your coworkers, fellow work-from-home folks, or friends who are allowed to really decorate their cubicle. The punchable enter key’s function is simple: You punch it to hit enter. It connects to a computer via a USB cord, and is nice and responsive so you don’t have to punch it super hard. It’s a fun addition to lively Slack chats, or a secret way to be passive-aggressive without anyone knowing. Unless the winner of this supersized key has a cubicle partner. But that’s their problem—if they can manage to win in the first place during the game.

Being a nerd isn’t as lame as it used to be, nor does it seem so weird to play Dungeons & Dragons like it used to, either. If you’ve got a few dungeon divers in your white elephant group (or maybe it’s a white elephant with your D&D party!), as I do, these Lego sets are a hit. My husband was the lucky last grabber for a white elephant gift that included three of these. They’re mystery bags, making it a fun discovery for the winner, and with 12 different designs you should be safe to buy a couple without doubling up on the model type. But even if you do, that’s something for the gift winner to discover and laugh about.

I have a lot of tea lovers in my various circle of friends, so this delicious cozy beverage set would be safe to bring to a myriad of white elephant parties. I have Diaspora Spice Co’s collaboration set with East Fork that includes the Masala Chai and Madhur Jaggery to sweeten it, and it’s one of the best cozy chais I’ve ever been able to make at home. Starbucks’ watery chai really won’t hit after a cup of this.

While I haven’t tried the Golden Milk yet, this set feels like something really delicious anyone could enjoy for the chilly months to come after the holidays. It’s a good price point for those $40 limits, too.

I love these smart light bulbs, and they pack more smarts than you'd express to wow your party crowd. Not only to Cync's Dynamic Effects A19 Smart Light Bulbs pair with your Wi-Fi without needing a hub, have tons of options for routines and light shows and a full range of color options, are compatible with Amazon and Google's smart home ecosystems, but these light bulbs actually have a built-in speaker to hear music and fluctuate the lights to match the mood. Let your gift receiver know they'll need to specifically turn on a Music Shows setting in the app to have their bulbs react to music.

I’m over gifting puzzles, and instead I’m gifting stylish paint-by-number kits this year. I’ve started on this pretty one from Galison—I’m two hours in and have likely two more hours to go, which surprised me. It comes with 12 paint colors and three brushes, and while I’d maybe include a few more brushes or some other painting accessory if the spending threshold is above $30, it makes for a great gift for your hobby-loving friend group.

I’ve never been a big fan of drink cozies. They’re useful, of course, and I like packing them for a camping trip, but they’re usually a little ugly to look at. Enter: Puffin Drinkwear, which makes drink cozies that recommend our favorite outerwear layers. It’s like playing Barbie with your drinks—if Barbie were really outdoorsy. You might’ve seen these in Netflix’s Will & Harper, and I encourage you to give your drinks their own fancy names to match these sweet fancy jackets. My husband keeps stealing the Alpine puffy style for his daily energy drink, but he has yet to name it; instead he’s giggling about how fun it is to give his Red Bull a little hood to wear.

Grab a couple that best embody your friend group, whether they love their hoodies or their leather jackets, or even a spa robe that can wrap around a bottle of wine. The spa robe is my favorite, and that with a nice bottle of wine might become my new go-to white elephant for a group I don’t know well (or that I know loves wine!).

Finding a good group game is hard, especially one that can accommodate both small and large groups. The best one I’ve tried is Listography, which is designed for three to six players, but I’ve seen it successfully accommodate up to 10 people (but you’ll need to bring your own extra pieces for the board!). To play, one person will pull a card with a prompt—things like “states that border Canada”—and everyone needs to make a list of answers. How many things you write down and how obscure you want to get varies, since there are three different card styles and requirements for that round. There’s a board your group can move around, but my group of friends loves to use it without the board and instead just keep score for each person.

One of the white elephant gifts I fought for last holiday season was this set of iridescent glasses. It’s a pretty little set with a vintage vibe to it that works great for cocktails or even just a fun little glass of water. I was also excited that it came with a bottle of lychee vodka, and I’d definitely recommend including a bottle of something fun that makes for a fight-worthy set (and to help you hit the price minimum, if it’s higher than $25).

Nowadays Cannabis Infused Beverage, Starting at $36: Bringing a bottle of booze is a white elephant classic; my husband’s work team almost exclusively exchanges bottles of liquor as a safe bet for enthusiasm. I think you can do better, though, and bring a THC spirit instead. This spirit is light and a little fruity, sitting somewhere in between the flavor profile of a floral gin and a sweet sake. My friends and I tried it mixed into a pomegranate cocktail instead of tequila, which was fantastic, and we also loved it with seltzer as a THC twist on a gin and tonic. It’s delicious alone, too. I’d skip this for a work party or any group that might not be green-friendly, though.

Booze in general: This is always a safe pick! You could also bring a bottle of nonalcoholic wine if you wanted an option that everyone can have.

Here’s what was the least fought over at the white elephant parties I attended last year, or the most inappropriate ideas our team has heard of:

If you’re headed to your first white elephant gift exchange, here’s a quick explainer on what’s about to happen.

Everyone will bring a wrapped gift (often under a certain price, like $25) and place it into a pile or central spot. Then, each person will draw a number that indicates their place in the gift-choosing order. When your number is called, you can either choose and unwrap a gift from the pile or steal one that has already been unwrapped by someone. Most exchanges will have a limit on how often a gift can be stolen—usually around three times—so if you have the best gift in your hands when it’s time for someone else to choose, there’s no guarantee you’ll get to keep it. If your gift is stolen, you can either unwrap a new one or steal someone else’s gift (no take-backs, sorry).

These rules can vary based on the host and their house rules, so make sure to ask what the rules are at the start of the game. Happy exchanging!
