#110. CERN and Mistral join forces to accelerate AI for science

CERN and Mistral sign a statement of intent to advance AI for science and strengthen Europeâs scientific and technological capabilities

CERN, the European Laboratory for Particle Physics, and Mistral, a European developer of large-scale AI models, have signed a statement of intent to establish a long-term strategic partnership focused on developing foundation models for scientific discovery.

The partnership brings together CERNâs expertise in fundamental physics, scientific data and large-scale computing with Mistralâs leadership in large-scale model training, leveraging these combined capabilities and resources to advance AI for science on an exceptional scale. While the initial focus is on high-energy physics, the partnership has the potential to contribute to the development of AI approaches that can serve the broader scientific community.

At the heart of this work is the ambition to develop a single pretrained Large Physics Model â the first foundation model for collider physics. It will be trained on billions of simulated proton-proton collisions at CERNâs Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the worldâs largest and most powerful particle accelerator, and designed to support multiple tasks, from reconstructing particle collisions and identifying particles to flagging unexpected signals and evaluating future detector designs.

The model is intended to address a fundamental challenge in analysing LHC collisions. Today, reconstruction relies on a chain of specialised algorithms that progressively transform detector signals into the particles and other objects used for physics analysis. Machine learning has long played an important role in this process, improving performance across a range of specialised tasks. Foundation models offer the potential to build on these advances, learning across the whole reconstruction chain and supporting multiple tasks within a single model.

âHigh-energy physics provides a unique environment in which artificial intelligence can be developed and tested with exceptional rigour. We are partnering with Mistral, a leading European AI company, to advance AI capabilities that can serve the whole physics community and be shared,â said Enrica Porcari, CERN’s Chief Information Officer.

CERN is home to one of the worldâs largest volumes of scientific data, with around one exabyte â one million terabytes â of experimental data from the LHC stored to date. The number of collisions is set to increase tenfold with the HL-LHC, which is expected to begin operation around 2030. This combination of scale and scientific precision provides exceptional conditions for developing and testing AI.

âWe are proud to work with CERN to explore what large-scale AI models can bring to the growing complexity of particle physics. Together, we have the opportunity to push the frontiers of high-energy physics, developing AI capabilities that have the potential to lead to new scientific discoveries,â said Johannes Brandstetter, Vice-President of AI for Engineering at Mistral.

By bringing together European excellence in AI and fundamental science, this partnership marks a step towards a new generation of AI tools capable of addressing the scale, precision and complexity of modern science in Europe and beyond.

Mistral is a global AI lab building state-of-the-art open-weight models, products and infrastructure that enable enterprises, public institutions and advanced industries to own, customise and control their AI. Headquartered in France, Mistral has a strong international presence across Europe, North America and Asia.

For more information, visit www.mistral.ai.

#112. I Test Home Security Tech. Here Are 4 Devices I Rely on to Guard My Porch

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Porch security is the best, easiest safety project for anyone new to smart homes.

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Your front door is your first line of defense against, well, anything you don’t want in your home. It’s also one of the first places burglars check when they’re looking for an easy break-in, and the spot porch pirates watch if they think lucrative packages are going to show up. That means your door is also the best place to start improving home security, especially as the holidays ramp up and you get more visitors and deliveries.

Here’s the technology I use to protect my front door and porch, in four easy steps anyone can start with. You don’t need to install a full security system or pay a high monthly subscription for home monitoring with these devices, either. Setup is totally DIY and takes very little time, too. See which you should start with.

Old deadbolts do well, but any entryway can get a powerful upgrade by adding digital features via a smart lock. Smart locks allow you to control your front door lock from anywhere using your phone, as well as creating temporary passes for guests. They can support digital wallet keys for touchless unlocking, and many have keypads or fingerprint readers. Plus, you can enable settings like auto-locking, so you never have to worry about forgetting to lock the door.

Smart locks come in two flavors: retrofits that leave your deadbolt largely intact and only replace your indoor thumb turn, and full deadbolt replacements that give you new locking power, inside and out. Don’t worry about installation: If you’ve never installed a deadbolt before, the process is generally easy and doesn’t take much time. I have a full guide where you can find more details.

Say goodbye to dusty doorbells of the past. Today’s high-tech doorbells do far more than chime: Video doorbells keep an eye on your front porch, while also giving you a two-way audio intercom right on your phone to hold a conversation — or even let an LLM do the talking for you.

Video doorbells also have particularly useful object recognition features, sometimes even for free. That includes recognizing packages and alerting you whenever one shows up at your door, or when one suddenly vanishes. Video storage options can save recordings of key events, so you can check who came to the door if you need to.

These advanced doorbells come in both wired and wireless versions. I’m a fan of the battery-powered, wireless models, which you can set and angle to get just the right look at your porch, doormat and other key places. Many can also work with your current door chime, although you probably don’t need it anymore with phone-based chimes.

Yale’s delivery boxes are larger, so you need room for them in the right spots.

Package theft concerns have reignited a centuries-old tradition of protecting mail. Today’s modern delivery boxes are specifically designed to allow delivery people to put packages inside, but make it difficult or impossible for thieves to take packages out, through clever lock models, auto-locking, smart controls and other various tricks.

I’ve been using a delivery box myself for a couple of years and find it very handy, as long as you have the space by your door. Some versions even come weighted or screwed down if you’re worried about a porch pirate absconding with the entire box. It’s a good idea to put notes in your deliveries to use the box, since despite signs not all delivery people will notice it’s there.

As a final plus, these boxes also keep your packages protected from the elements, which is nice when you live in an area that gets frequent winter snowstorms, as I do.

Smart bulbs are cheap, support multiple voice assistants and have lots of fun tricks.

Where front doors exist, there’s usually a light nearby, like an overhead porch light or a wall-mounted lamp, to illuminate the entryway and surrounding area. These lights can also get a major makeover if you switch to an LED smart bulb, which are available as both BR30 floodlights and standard A19 home bulbs.

These lights also give you phone app controls, which is more important than it might seem. With my apps, I can control brightness, set schedules for bulbs to turn on or off, and even adjust the color to whatever I want, say for a holiday event. All it takes is screwing in the bulb and connecting it to Wi-Fi, so you can be done in seconds.

If you feel like experimenting, you can usually link smart bulbs to other devices, too. For example, you could set the light to turn on automatically when a smart lock is unlocked, or when a security system is disarmed.

Now that your front porch is up to date, take a look at the latest home AI tricks I’ve found are actually worth using and how to get them.

Just looking at the specs, there doesn’t appear to be many fundamental differences between them, with the exception that the Edge is Google’s first repairable Fitbit, and it’s $20 more.

Also: The 5 most popular Garmin watches of 2026: What readers are buying most, and last chance Prime Day prices

Like the Fitbit Air and Charge, the Edge also includes a week-long battery life, with one big caveat. You’ll get seven days of battery life with always-on display disabled. With always-on enabled, the battery drops down to two days.

Unlike the Charge, Google adds a side button — similar to Apple’s Action Button — for activating workouts and selecting information. Under the hood, sleep tracking improves in the Edge by 15%.

Like the Pixel Watch 5, wearers will be able to see their workout details, health metrics, and other messages on the Fitbit Edge. This visual guidance is displayed on a vibrant hybrid OLED screen built with Corning Gorilla Glass 3. It also syncs to your phone for incoming texts, Google Maps directions, and other notifications.

When it comes to the price, I was expecting something similarly priced to the Fitbit Charge, and am wondering whether the small upgrades available on the Edge justify a $20 price increase. If the two most substantial upgrades are sleep tracking accuracy (which is software driven) and repairability, what part of this device is $20 more expensive to build?

Also: Google’s Fitbit Air is a $99 screenless wearable that I can actually take seriously

The Fitbit Air was perfectly priced at $100, and, though I haven’t tested the Edge yet, I’m skeptical the added screen will justify the $80 price difference between the Air and the Edge — especially when the Air lasts seven days, while the Edge with always-on enabled only lasts two.

The Fitbit Edge is available to pre-order now, and it’s available everywhere on Oct. 27.

#116. Tips for building an AI-powered PC

AI is here to stay, it seems, and a lot of people have leaned into the change rather than resisting it. Many people engage with AI over their web browser since major AI services are available there, thereby bypassing the need to have a strong PC that’s optimized to run AI. However, other folks want to run AI directly on their PCs. That is a different category entirely.

To run AI, you need a pretty strong computer. You can probably run something simple like Nvidia’s ChatRTX without a ton of resources, but if you’re generating images, video, or doing development work, you probably want more than just the bare minimum. So, if you’re getting ready to build an AI, here are some tips on how to do it.

An AI-powered PC needs to run an operating system that can actually use AI. All three major computer operating systems can do this, including Windows, MacOS, and Linux. Generally speaking, Ubuntu and Windows are the two most popular operating systems for running AI, and they should be at the top of your list if you’re building an AI-powered PC.

Windows is a little better for basic stuff because Copilot is built in. Copilot is in several of Microsoft's apps and in the OS itself, plus you can download the native Copilot app from the Microsoft Store. Ubuntu is superior if you want to build an AI PC from scratch, as all the tools work there and you have the freedom to set things up the way you want. However, Ubuntu is harder to learn if you’ve never used it before.

An AI-powered PC requires some hefty specs if you want your AI to run well. That includes a large amount of RAM and storage. The more you have of both, the better your AI will run. If you’re wondering why these two things are so expensive right now, this is why. AI data centers are eating up all the RAM and storage so each company’s AI runs better.

The baseline you want to shoot for is about 32GB of RAM and around 1TB of storage, although the more you have, the better things will be. If you skimp here, you won’t have enough space to download AI models or enough RAM to run them.

I am a fan of AMD GPUs myself, but if you want a PC to run AI, then Nvidia is the way to go. Many of the biggest tools have direct compatibility with Nvidia, and run better when compared to similar AMD GPUs. You want the highest-end card you can afford with the most possible VRAM. Most guides have a floor at 8GB of VRAM, but there are AI models that can easily make use of the 32GB of VRAM in the exceedingly expensive RTX 5090, so there’s no ceiling here.

A good start is the Nvidia RTX 5070, which comes with 12GB of VRAM, but if you can swing for the stronger RTX 5080 or RTX 5090, you’ll be much better off.

The CPU is still important, just not quite as much as the GPU, RAM, and VRAM. Modern CPUs have what is called an NPU, which stands for neural processing unit. These are used specifically for AI tasks, and having a PC with one sets you up for success. All of the major chipmakers have this, including the Intel Core Ultra series, the AMD Ryzen AI series, and even the Snapdragon X series, although you won’t be making a PC with that last one. Pick whichever one you like most.

All of the above advice applies to people who are building a PC, but they also apply to people shopping for laptops. Look for ones with a high-end Nvidia GPU with plenty of VRAM and a CPU that includes an NPU. Most laptops that fulfill these qualifications are user-upgradeable, so you can always add more RAM and storage later, although if you can find one with 32GB of RAM and at least 1TB of storage, you’ll be pretty well set for a while.

#118. Data Centers Have a New PR Plan: Your Kid’s Field Trip

Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. They’re out this week, so Caroline Haskins is reporting for duty. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Caroline an email at [email protected] or reach her securely on Signal at carolinehaskins.61.

The nonprofit 7x24 Exchange International wants to promote data centers, which they believe are "mission critical” infrastructure. As part of this work, the group recommends a children’s story, “What is a Data Center?,” which follows a honey badger named Honey who gets a guided tour of a data center from a worker named Oliver. Oliver explains that the job of data center employees is to make sure that the “functions supported by the data center” are available to anybody, “no matter what time it is.”

"Like when my mom shops online late at night because my dad is sleeping and won't know about it?" Honey asks.

The story is part of a broader pattern across the data center industry. In addition to lobbying, job creation programs, tax breaks, companies and interest groups are trying something a bit more creative: winning over the youth. As pushback to massive data center build-outs and energy-guzzling campuses intensifies, the industry is apparently taking a softer approach to community building using a tactic other industries with a public relations problem have tried.

Alex Molnar, a research professor at the University of Colorado Boulder and the director of the National Education Policy Center, tells WIRED that, for over a century, industries with an image problem—fast food, tobacco, oil and gas—have brought their messaging to schools.

“A very, very big reason why corporations get involved in the schools is, quite simply, corporate propaganda—for the purpose not necessarily of selling a product, but of telling their ‘story,’” Molnar says.

In May, the Potomac chapter of the Association for Computer Operations Management (AFCOM), a trade group for the data center industry, sponsored Memorial Day-themed flag-making kits to be distributed to 3,100 first graders across 37 schools in Loudoun County, Virginia, also known as Data Center Alley. In addition to the flag kits, kids received an informational card with statistics about “the positive impact” that the data center industry has on the local economy.

Besides promoting heartwarming tales about how women can shop, 7x24 Exchange is also the brains behind a holiday it calls “International Data Center Day,” which is “designed to create awareness of the data center industry and inspire the next generation of talent.”

The nonprofit encourages people to pitch the holiday to school administrators. For participating high schools, it offers a celebratory crossword puzzle and information about data center training programs. For elementary schools, it offers data center-themed coloring pages, instructions for an evaporation-themed science project, and print-out activities like “Draw a picture of the cloud" and “Draw a data superhero.” It also promotes several data center-themed books for young readers, including one in which two sisters visit a data center and meet a robot named JB and another that features two brothers who visit a "vibrant digital world" and save the internet. Then there’s “Polly Packet's Precious Payload,” which follows a mother who teaches her daughter about data centers.

7x24 Exchange has also visited or organized at least a half-dozen K-12 events at schools across the country this year. In Minnesota, it brought Fridley High School students on a field trip to a local Cummins diesel power generation facility in order to learn about the “generators that power data centers worldwide.” (7x24 Exchange, Cummins, and Fridley High School did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)

The nonprofit is far from the only organization sponsoring school activities that are friendly to data centers. WIRED’s tally of public blogs and social media posts found that, since 2025, at least eleven companies and industry groups have hosted student field trips to local data centers.

Sabey, a company that runs seven US data centers, has hosted a number of field trips for Washington-based high schoolers, including one in May for Eastmont High School students, one in January for Manson School District students, and another last October for Quincy High School students.

Manson School District publicized the trip in a blog post showing what appears to be adults and students in a conference room. The image labeled us “AI-generated content,” though, and several people in the photo have missing limbs. The blog says that students learned about “the role data centers play in storing, processing, and protecting information” and “the wide range of careers” in the data center industry.

Quincy School District communications coordinator Jessica Blancas tells WIRED that the district “has organized data center visits for many years” at the facilities of companies like Microsoft, Vantage, Yahoo, and Sabey. She described the latter company as a “long-standing” district partner, citing its consistent work offering “guest speakers,” “mock interviews,” and “internship opportunities.”

Blancas adds that the district has organized “all-girls visits to Sabey,” as well as tours for students who intend to go into specific fields like construction or engineering. (Manson School District and Sabey did not respond for comment.)

Amazon, meanwhile, hosted a field trip last February at its Arlington, Virginia, “Skills Center,” a free community space for anyone “curious about cloud computing and future job possibilities.” It was open to any high school in the DC metro area, though Jackson-Reed High School was the only one to attend.

Molnar says he doesn’t get what’s in it for kids. “Why would a third grader be interested in a data center?” he says.

“You're going to see miles after miles of the most boring things imaginable,” he adds. “Lines after lines of these servers generating enormous volumes of heat. You're also going to hear some fair amount of noise. And you're not going to see many people because not many people work there when they're built.”

It’s common for companies to sow goodwill through public outreach, and as tech companies have reckoned with the backlash to data centers, these field trips are taking place in an increasingly fraught environment.

A Pew Research poll conducted over the summer found that about half of the 10,000 Americans surveyed see data centers as “mostly bad” for the environment and quality of life, and across the country, an ideologically diverse cohort has started rallying against them. In some places, the negative sentiment toward local data centers has been amplified by their proximity to local schools.

Providing educational materials and offering field trips are ways that industries can maintain their social license to operate in a community. The data center sector is, in many ways, following the playbook other industries have to sow goodwill with children as well as their parents. The oil and gas industry has sponsored university research projects and STEM programs in K-12 schools. The tech world has similarly funded STEM programs, as well as advocated for in-school coding programs while lobbying to make computer science count as a science credit.

Fossil fuel companies have also spent millions of dollars developing K-12 lessons with pro-industry talking points, particularly in states like Oklahoma and Texas.

Molnar believes this kind of corporate influence shouldn’t be allowed because kids are “in an absolutely powerless position.” Kids “need to be protected” by their school districts and communities, he says.

“As an adult, I have access to alternative information—I have a critical ability to assess what I'm hearing, and to render some kind of judgments,” Molnar says. “None of that is true of children.”

Data centers may be for kids, but some of the products that rely on their server racks sure aren’t. When Meta launched Muse, it looked like a cute little AI agent for the masses. But my colleague Reece Rogers recently discovered that Muse has a naughty side. When Reece asked Muse if it was able to sext, it told him to “shoot your shot.” Reece did, and Muse was receptive. Enthusiastic, even! We published the chat logs—well, the PG-13 ones since WIRED is a family site, after all—and Reece spoke to consumer advocates who were alarmed at Muse’s sexy demeanor.

Meta, for its part, says this is all part of the plan. “Muse is an app for people 18 and over that allows them to engage in adult conversations, if they choose, using a private and secure VM only accessible to them,” company spokesperson Daniel Roberts told Reece. So if that’s your thing, have at it!

#119. Timestral: Mistral release time-series foundation models

Timestral, Mistral’s first family of time-series foundation models, delivers state-of-the-art probabilistic, multivariate forecasts with just 209M parameters, outperforming larger models on key benchmarks while supporting past and future covariates. Available in four sizes (5M to 209M parameters), it balances accuracy and efficiency, running efficiently on CPUs and excelling in zero-shot forecasting for diverse domains. The model combines synthetic pre-training, covariate-aware attention, and long-context learning, with fine-tuning options for domain adaptation via Mistral Forge.

Today, we’re releasing Timestral, our first family of time-series foundation models. Our largest model, at just 209M parameters, ranks first on all three of the field's main public benchmarks, GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, outperforming the previous state of the art with only two-thirds of the model parameters.

Timestral delivers probabilistic, multivariate forecasts and supports past-only and known-future covariates. Our family of models sits on the Pareto front of forecasting accuracy versus model size, delivering leading performance at each size. Results have been submitted to the GIFT-Eval and TIME leaderboards.

Time series is one of the most common data types in enterprise, from sensor telemetry to observability metrics. Forecasts built on it drive decisions in capacity planning, energy, supply chains, risk and maintenance.

Industrial plants forecast process sensors against the production schedule, catch equipment drift before it fails, and plan capacity and spare parts across thousands of assets. Finance teams forecast flows, volumes, and volatility to inform positions, hedging, and treasury across thousands of accounts.

Classical models such as ARIMA and linear regression remain well-established tools for forecasting time series. These models are usually fitted to a single series and learn only from that series' history.

Deep learning models such as PatchTST add the capacity to learn nonlinear patterns across many related series, but they are still typically trained from scratch on each dataset, so what they learn doesn't carry over to new domains.

Time series foundation models bring the pre-training approach to time series. Trained on a large and diverse corpus, our model learns patterns that transfer across series, forecasting zero-shot on data it has never seen, even in domains where data is scarce.

We evaluated Timestral on the three main public forecasting benchmarks: GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench. Among pre-trained, zero-shot models, it ranks first across all five metrics. These results come from a single checkpoint, without ensembling.

GIFT-Eval, top ten of 83 comparable pretrained and zero-shot entries. Lower is better.

TIME, top ten of the 35 leaderboard entries. Lower is better on both metrics.

fev-bench, top ten of the 37 leaderboard entries, by SQL skill score. Higher is better.

Timestral has been optimised as a family of four models: 5M, 28M, 123M and 209M parameters. The larger models improve forecast performance, while the smaller ones are faster and cheaper. All four share the same architecture and training recipe. Every size sits on the Pareto front of accuracy versus model size: for each model size, no public model forecasts better.

Score vs model size on GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench (shown as 1 − skill score). Lower is better. Our 28M model beats Chronos-2, about four times larger, on GIFT-Eval and TIME. Our 209M model beats TimesFM-3 and Falcon-2.0 with fewer parameters.

Timestral does not need a GPU at inference. On a standard server CPU with 8 threads, forecasting one day ahead from three weeks of 15-minute history takes 10 ms with the 5M model and 140 ms with the 209M model. Smaller models trade some accuracy for speed: the 28M model is five times faster than the 209M model, and the 123M model comes within 0.2% of the 209M score at three quarters of its latency.

Consider an industrial plant with thousands of sensors across its equipment. Timestral can improve the forecasts on that data in several ways.

Multivariate forecasting. A pump's vibration, temperature and pressure don't move independently. A rise in one often explains or causes a change in another. Timestral models related series jointly, so it can use those dependencies instead of forecasting each sensor in isolation.

Probabilistic forecasting. A single predicted value may not show the full picture. Timestral predicts a full set of quantiles, so teams can see how wide the uncertainty is, set alert thresholds that reflect it, and plan maintenance around risk rather than a single number.

Categorical covariates. Some covariates take values from a set of categories rather than continuous numbers, such as the day of the week, or a machine's state (running, idle, under maintenance). Encoding these as numbers would impose an order or scale they don't have. Timestral takes them as categorical inputs directly to improve forecasts.

Known-future covariates. Some drivers of sensor behaviour are known in advance, such as production schedules, planned shutdowns, weather forecasts. Timestral can condition on them to improve forecast quality, so a scheduled load increase is expected rather than flagged as a surprise.

Timestral is a numerical model that can run inside existing monitoring pipelines, or be paired with our language models in multi-modal agentic workflows.

Timestral running continuously on the plant's sensor streams, detecting anomalies as they occur.

When it flags an anomaly on a pump, an agent embeds the signals and compares against embeddings of past sensor data to find similar historical failures.

The agent then starts sub-agents to run a root cause analysis, drawing on context from that plant, such as maintenance records, shift logs and operator notes, equipment manuals, past work orders, and readings from related equipment.

The agent drafts a suggested diagnosis based on the findings, with supporting evidence and possible next steps.

The plant manager gets a diagnosis and a plan backed by the sensor data, rather than just an alert.

Several ideas have been combined to produce these results. Each will be described in detail in the technical report.

Decoupled Horizon Forecasting. Causal decoders trained with contiguous patch masking, as in Toto 2.0 and TimesFM-3, mask out the values to be forecast, so they look like missing values and are also lost as context for later forecasts. Our approach, DHF, separates the two: the full history stays in the sequence, and learned forecast tokens read the history before them. Every observed value thus serves as both target and context, true gaps stay flagged as missing, and training horizon lengths and missing-data augmentation can be tuned independently of each other.

Covariate-aware attention. Each input series is assigned a role: target variate, past-only covariate or known-future covariate. Known-future covariates are visible across the whole window while targets stay causal, and information flows only from covariates to targets. Timestral can therefore use a holiday calendar or a weather forecast without leaking a target's own future into its forecast.

Synthetic-first data. The majority of the training data was synthetic. We first generated univariate processes with coherent temporal dynamics, including trends, seasonality and diverse noise patterns. We then used a multivariate synthesizer to construct multivariate series by introducing nonlinear dependencies between these processes.

Two-stage training. Timestral is first pre-trained at scale on purely synthetic data with context size 8192, then post-trained on a mix of real and synthetic data with a 4x longer context. The objective is a pinball loss over 21 quantiles, a discrete approximation of CRPS.

Public benchmarks measure general performance, but production data can be significantly different in behavior and structure. It may also shift over time as markets change regime, equipment degrades and demand patterns move. The lasting value lies in being able to adapt a model to in-domain data and keep retraining it as the distribution moves.

For organisations that want to go further, Timestral is available through Mistral Forge, the same training pipeline we use for our language models. It supports:

Architectural extensions, such as domain-specific covariates.

Fine-tuning on proprietary data, specialising to a domain while preserving general performance.

Control over the training data, including adjusting the training mix, replaying pre-training data, and generating synthetic data samples to reflect the target domain. Full control over the data ensures that nothing we backtest was seen during pre-training.

The full pipeline can be deployed on our clients’ hardware, including air-gapped environments.

We have published a GitHub repository so you can run Timestral on your own data. A technical report with the full results will follow. For more specialised forecasting problems, or to collaborate on research, please reach out to us.

Multivariate targets, past-only and known-future covariates

Mistral's time-series foundation models. State-of-the-art probabilistic forecasts, 5M–209M params, runs on CPU.

#125. Windows update patches a whopping 1,400 security bugs –  including 2 zero days

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

This month’s update also marks the first official one for Windows 11 26H2 and the end of support for Windows 11 24H2 Home and Pro.

Microsoft continues to break bug-squashing records, with October’s Windows update patching more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities. As usual, the actual number of bug fixes varies based on which ones are counted, but hovers around 1,410.

Also: How to upgrade your ‘incompatible’ Windows 10 PC to Windows 11 – for free

Released Tuesday, the latest update is also the first official one for Windows 11 26H2 and the last one for Windows 11 24H2 Home and Pro editions. Plus, it resolves specific issues with built-in features like File Explorer and Bluetooth, and even lets you remap the Copilot keyboard key to trigger a different action.

As usual, the updates are aimed at all supported versions of Windows 11. These include all editions of Windows 11 26H2, 26H1, 25H2, and 24H2, as well as 23H2 Enterprise and Education. Windows 10 PCs enrolled in Microsoft’s Extended Security Updates (ESU) program also receive the latest security patches.

With such a large collection of bug fixes, you’ll want to install this one. In Windows 11, head to Settings and select Windows Update. You may find the update already installed and just waiting for a reboot. If not, click the button to check for updates to download and install it. In Windows 10, go to Settings, select Windows Update, and install the latest one.

Each new annual version of Windows, such as 24H2 or 23H2, loses support after 24 months, which means no more security updates or bug fixes. With Windows 11 24H2 hitting this milestone, you’ll need to jump to the latest version to keep your PC updated. For that, head to Windows Update and check for updates. You should see a notice telling you that Windows 11, version 26H2 is available. Click the link to download and install it.

Also: My favorite Windows app makes moving to a new PC so easy

The same deadline looms for Windows 11 23H2 Enterprise and Education editions, which reach end of support next month on November 10. Here, you or your organization will also need to update Windows to the latest version to stay protected.

Surpassing the almost 1,000 security flaws patched in September, the October update marks yet another record. For that, the company can thank AI. Microsoft uses its own internal “multi-model agentic scanning harness,” codenamed MDASH. This AI-powered tool identifies real Windows vulnerabilities, reduces false positives, and sends the results to engineers more quickly.

Specifically, the October update fixes 80 critical vulnerabilities and two zero-days, according to patch management provider Action1 in a new advisory.

One of the zero-days has already been exploited in the wild. Designated as CVE-2026-96951, this one could allow a remote attacker to bypass security protection by exploiting a flaw in Windows Shell.

Also: I tried the free Microsoft Word clone on Linux

“This vulnerability presents a serious security threat because it allows attackers to bypass an important Windows security defense designed to protect users from potentially dangerous files,” Action1 said in its advisory. “Attackers can exploit this weakness remotely by convincing users to open specially crafted files or interact with malicious content. Successful exploitation could weaken Windows security protections and increase the risk of malicious content reaching users without the expected security warnings.”

Labeled CVE-2026-108398, the other zero-day was publicly disclosed before the fix was rolled out and could let an attacker skirt past security measures by exploiting a flaw in Microsoft’s .net Framework.

Aside from the security patches, the October update fixes some glitches in File Explorer. You can now more easily preview downloaded files using the Preview pane. File Explorer also now retains the state of sections (expanded or collapsed), so you can more quickly pick up where you left off. Plus, thumbnail previews for cloud-based files in the Details pane will render more reliably.

Also: Microsoft’s new Nvidia PCs are cool for extreme power users

For those of you who grapple with Bluetooth issues, the update also improves the accuracy and stability of connected Bluetooth devices and accessories.

And last but not least, the update adds a new setting in Windows 11 that lets you remap the Copilot key. Instead of triggering Microsoft’s AI, the key can function as the right Ctrl key or the right-click context menu on the desktop and in File Explorer.

#126. Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings

Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year, according to a report that the AI company published on Friday.

Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at how the company currently operates.

Notably, Anthropic is making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior-level employees in technical departments falling from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the proportion of junior technical hires falling even more sharply, from 27% to 9%.

Anthropic also says that technical teams now represent a smaller share of the overall workforce, falling from 61% to 56% — a trend that it attributes to  “natural expansion of business functions as the company scales,” as well as “coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves.”

One employee reportedly described an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.” In an April 2026 survey, 27% of employees said they had become more productive because of Claude  and 20% said their job had shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes”; apparently one engineer compared this to babysitting: “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.”

In fact, the report suggests “human attention and judgement” are becoming a “bottleneck” for productivity, as Claude produces a “deluge” of text that needs to be read and organized.

Unsurprisingly, the report argues that AI adoption has made the company more productive, as indicated by “more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts.” The company acknowledges that “more code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact,” but it also hasn’t found any indications that code quality is declining.

The report says that based on calendar data, meeting time per employee is up 20% compared to a year ago, and it’s up 16% for technical contributors. The company attributes this to the importance of “human trust and accountability,” with employees repeatedly describing “face-to-face coordination as indispensable.”

#127. 5 Windows settings most people dont know about

Windows is a massive operating system and you can go years or even decades without interacting with most of the features. There are over 100 native system-wide hotkeys in Windows 11 and it’s a pretty safe bet that most people don’t know much beyond Select All, Copy, and Paste.

It would take a year to list everything, so instead we’re going to focus on Windows settings that you may not know about. These settings can increase functionality, add some nifty options, or just make your life easier. Every feature below is available on Windows 11 Home and Pro, and they should also be available on Windows 10 in case you’re one of the many people who held out after official support ended last year.

People copy and paste stuff all the time, and sometimes, they have to go back and find something they’d copied before. Windows has a built-in feature to handle that. To use it, simply hit Windows Key + V together. This opens up the Clipboard History box. The feature is off by default, so you have to turn it on, but after that, it’ll store up to 25 of the most recent things you copied, provided they are HTML (links), text, or images up to 4MB.

You can also pin items to keep them in the clipboard history forever. The rest are deleted when you shut down or reboot your PC. You can also access Windows’ native emoji selector from this Window, which works in any app where you can enter text.

It’s pretty common knowledge that closing an app from the Windows Taskbar doesn’t necessarily fully close it down. Sometimes it sits in the System Tray and has to be closed again there, or a process continues to run unseen in the background until you go into the Task Manager to turn it off manually. You don’t have to do it this way.

Go to Settings > System > Advanced to find a setting called End task. Click this option on. Now when you right-click an app in the Taskbar, you have the option to end the task directly, shutting down the app and all of its background tasks from there without taking a second trip to the Task Manager or the System Tray.

Prior versions of Windows tucked the Start menu in the lower left corner and then moved it to the center in modern versions of Windows. You can actually move it back over if you want to. Right click a blank spot on your Taskbar and select Taskbar Settings. Find the Taskbar icon alignment option. You keep everything in the center or move it to the left.

There are some really interesting settings in here, like hiding the Taskbar on your extra monitors, turning Widgets off, putting your Taskbar on a different edge of your screen, and more. It’s worth rooting around in there to customize your Taskbar experience further.

Windows has themes, not unlike Google Chrome or Mozilla Firefox. Go into Settings > Personalization > Themes to locate their settings. You have three main options. You can download a theme from the Microsoft Store, edit an existing theme on your machine, or create a custom theme. Each theme saves your background, including a slideshow if you want one, the accent color scheme, your mouse appearance, and sounds.

The Settings menu is pretty big, but there’s a whole other settings menu you can unlock with one simple install of Microsoft PowerToys. This powerful software adds several other features that you can tick on and off, along with many other things that you can adjust. For example, you can use the Keyboard Manager to create new hotkeys and then bind them to your keyboard.

This sounds more like a feature than a settings option, but it’s actually both. PowerToys plugs into Windows in a way the stock Settings menu doesn’t and there are plenty of previously inaccessible settings options there. Root around and have fun, there’s a lot of extra stuff to check out.

#128. Valerion VisionMaster Max 4K Projector Review: Looks Great, Sounds OK

Valerion’s VisionMaster Kickstarter campaign raised more than $8 million in 2024, making it the most-funded campaign on the platform that year. After spending the past few weeks with the flagship VisionMaster Max, I’m confident there are plenty of satisfied backers.

At $3,999, it costs far more than excellent point-and-play rivals, such as the Nebula X1 (9/10 WIRED Recommends), but considerably less than native 4K home-theater projectors from brands like Sony and JVC. That leaves the Max straddling two very different camps.

Its compact design, built-in Google TV, and automated setup suggest the classification of a premium lifestyle projector, while optical zoom, vertical lens shift, a mechanical iris, and sophisticated black-level processing point toward something far more capable. It’s easy to use and almost too pretty to ceiling-mount, but arguably too sophisticated to spend its life propped up on a side table. So the question remains: Who is the VisionMaster Max actually for?

The 16.5-pound VisionMaster Max is simple to get up and running. Google TV grants instant access to many streaming services, while auto-keystone and autofocus make positioning a frictionless process. (However, because keystone correction digitally reshapes the image, when used heavily, it can reduce resolution—but that’s true for all devices with the feature.) Optical zoom, with a 0.9 to 1.5:1 throw ratio, lets you resize the picture without moving the projector. There’s also vertical lens shift, which moves the image up or down without needing to resort to digital correction. All of this means that if you’ve got a blank wall and five minutes, you can stream Emily in Paris on a 90-inch screen in no time.

It’s clever tech, though not fully unique, with the XGIMI Horizon range and Nebula X1 offering similar optical-image manipulation. Even so, the VisionMaster Max offers considerably more control than most point-and-play designs. Praise is also due for the remote, which looks and feels great. Many brands scrimp on details like accessories, but Valerion maintains its premium feel throughout.

The VisionMaster Max produces a seriously bright image. Its 3,500 ISO lumen RGB triple-laser light source easily projected a 75-inch picture I could happily watch during the day in a bright room. Valerion says it’s good for images between 40 and 300 inches. I maxed out at 130 inches but was impressed by how even the detail remained right to the edges at that size.

While I watched during the day, the colors appeared a bit washed out in this environment, but much less so than I expected. Once I watched in the dark, however, I enjoyed punchy high-dynamic-range (HDR) highlights, excellent detail, and smooth motion.

In terms of color, the Max has 110 percent Rec.2020 coverage, meaning the lasers can reproduce an exceptionally wide range of colors, far exceeding the needs for ultra-high-definition (UHD) and HDR video. In my living room, colors looked rich without becoming cartoonish, while the combination of brightness, detail, and contrast gave movies cinematic quality.

Black levels with most home projectors are good, but not brilliant. Here, however, the proprietary six-stage iris self-adjusts the aperture from scene to scene, closing for darker images to deepen blacks, and opening up when a scene calls for more brightness. Enhanced Black Level (EBL) works alongside the iris, electronically reducing laser output in darker scenes, adjusting the image curve to maintain details. Together, these features dramatically reduce the charcoal-gray blacks common with this type of projector. I was astonished by the depth and shadow detail it produced without losing brighter details. Even the film The Dark Knight, with its muted color grading, looked good.

Though I didn’t put the VisionMaster Max through its paces for video-game testing (I’m not much of a gamer, unless you count Mario Kart battles on the Nintendo Switch), the projector’s specifications are nonetheless impressive. It supports refresh rates up to 240 Hz at 1080p, with claimed input lag as low as 4 milliseconds (ms); for 4K, 60-Hz gaming, that input lag is rated at 15 ms. Two HDMI 2.1 inputs and auto low-latency mode further strengthen its gaming credentials, although it lacks a variable refresh rate (VRR) to dynamically smooth out delays.

Less impressive than its picture is its sound: The VisionMaster Max has two 12-watt speakers, and audio is clean, detailed, with effects neatly separated from dialog. But it still suffers from its box form factor. To be fair, with the exception of Anker’s removable satellite speaker designs like the Nebula X1, audio fails to keep up with image quality in many lifestyle projectors. I’d contend that at this price, an all-in-one projector should provide audio that matches the pixel-perfect picture. The Max’s speakers are fine, but push it beyond level 25 of 100, and it just sounds loud.

Thankfully, since the projector supports both DTS and Dolby Atmos, you can connect it to a decent 5.1/7.1 home theater audio system. You can also wirelessly link to a Bluetooth speaker, which makes for a clean living-room setup, although latency can be an issue. For reliable synchronization and true surround sound, HDMI eARC remains the better audio option.

Valerion is not without stiff competition, and that includes against itself. The Nebula X1 offers a similarly simple Google TV setup and 3,500-lumen brightness, with optional wireless surround sound making it better suited to casual living-room or outdoor use. The Leica Cine Play 1 (9/10, WIRED Recommends) combines superb optics with a more lifestyle-friendly design. Valerion’s cheaper VisionMaster Pro 2 ($2,999) retains key features, including Google TV, RGB triple-laser projection, optical zoom, and EBL, but it loses the Max’s iris and vertical lens shift. For casual movie nights, I’d be happy with this compromise that keeps extra money in my pocket.

While not necessarily casual, the Max is great and likely best suited for the viewer who wants to enjoy its capabilities. Its weight, extensive picture controls, and exceptional brightness encourage a proper screen, external sound, and careful setup, where its superb black levels and cinematic image can be fully exploited.

The brand seems to agree, as it’s strongly encouraging customers to go all-in with its baffling array of deals. At the time of publication, you can opt to bundle the $3,999 Max with a choice of screens and four stands—including a tripod and ceiling mount—without paying any additional fee.

It may be overkill for occasional big-screen streaming, but as a compact projector at the heart of a home theater, I highly recommend it.

#135. Replit makes OpenAI its default over Anthropic, CEO says

Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic.

“I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.”

It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser.

After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default. This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves.

Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s.

“Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.”

Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.

There is evidence on the company’s website, blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities.

Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue.

“We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.”

Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027.

Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures.

“In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.”

This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT. It has been updated to include more context around Replit’s partnerships with Anthropic and OpenAI. Its title has been updated, as well.

#136. 5 tips to customize your smartphone like a cyberdeck

Cyberdecks are interesting pieces of tech. They are, essentially, sci-fi inspired portable computers that people build that can kind of bridge the gap between smartphones and laptops. You’ve probably seen them all over the sci-fi genre, including games like Cyberpunk 2077 and movies like Ghost in the Shell or Hackers. You may be interested in building your own. It turns out, you can do that.

Alternatively, you can take an existing piece of tech and turn it into a cyberdeck. A smartphone is a great candidate for this because it’s already a portable computer attached to a screen, giving you the ability to add a few more touches to turn it into a cyberdeck. It may not be as cool-looking as a Raspberry Pi board built into a custom enclosure, but it’s a quick way to get into it with tech you already have.

This is the hardest part of this whole process. A lot of people use something like a small tacklebox, dremel it out so that the phone fits, and buy a small keyboard like the K808 Mini Bluetooth Keyboard to complete the effect with minimal effort and resources. Your enclosure and keyboard will depend on the size of your phone, but hopefully this gives you a good place to start.

There are also custom 3D printing services that will make you something on request. Prices vary wildly here, but the first and most important step is getting your enclosure and keyboard set up since cyberdecks are supposed to be used out and about.

The enclosure is arguably the hardest and also most important part, but preparing your software to work with everything is also necessary. One app that works well for this is Rotation Lock. This app locks your display in a specific orientation, bypassing your phone’s auto-rotate function and letting you use your phone in whatever orientation you set it to. The app doesn’t work with every phone, though, so make sure to check that yours is compatible.

Next up is adding some software chops to your smartphone-turned-cyberdeck. Termux is a good app to do this. It is an Android terminal emulator and Linux environment app that lets you run commands. The real win here is that it lets you set up and run a Linux environment, which grants you access to all sorts of other cool things.

There are limitations to this technology, and you’ll want to look for Linux apps compiled specifically for Termux, but there’s a lot of additional functionality you can add to your cyberdeck with it.

Some Android phones have a desktop mode that is perfect for cyberdeck use. The most well-known and obvious one is Samsung DeX, which turns your smartphone into a native desktop environment, making it friendlier for keyboard and mouse activities. This is doable in the settings menu of Samsung phones, so you don’t need an external display to use it. Google added a desktop mode to Android in 2026 but you need a Pixel device to use it for now. Either of these solutions will work just fine.

Most of the stuff above gets you most of the way there, but recommending anything further really depends on what you want to do with it. You can download a custom launcher to give it a more cyberdeck vibe, like this retro launcher on Google Play. Another option is Tasker to set up automations, like turning on all the cyberdeck stuff once it’s plugged into a certain device. You can even use a remote desktop app to connect to your PC at home. There are apps for cybersecurity and productivity, or you can turn your phone into a video game emulator box with all the various emulators. The sky is really the limit here, so let your imagination run wild.

We’re getting ever closer to Halloween, and there’s plenty of scares to be had in Prime Video’s top 10 movie chart this week. I’ve combed through the platform’s weekly hits to find the films worthy of your precious streaming time.

Prime Video’s top 10 usually isn’t stuffed full of bona fide classics, and this week is no different. Still, I think you’ll enjoy the trio of picks I’ve gone with, which include an emotional new drama starring Margaret Qualley, the latest entry in an iconic horror series and a light-hearted criminal caper led by Stanley Tucci.

The movies below are taken from Prime Video’s top 10 as of Monday, October 19, 2026. So break out the teeth-rotting treats and prepare to laugh, cry and gasp at my pick of flicks that are actually worth streaming.

Get your hankies ready for a new weepy. Following nurse Maya (Margaret Qualley), a pandemic-related tragedy sees the Boston healer up sticks to Europe, where she becomes a reclusive digital nomad. Unlike the rest of us who spent our time rewatching old episodes of "DuckTales" during lockdown, Maya ends up flitting through unfulfilling casual relationships, which only worsens her grief.

Qualley once again impresses in a leading role, even if the material is a little sappy. Still, the supporting cast, including Patrick Schwarzenegger, Aaron Pierre and Gabriel Basso, is reasonably strong and the globe-hopping plot, which takes in Lisbon, Luxembourg and Tokyo, is handsomely shot. Perhaps the most surprising thing about “Love of Your Life”? It’s produced by Ryan Gosling. Sadly for fans of “Drive,” there’s a distinct lack of action in this sincere, well-meaning drama.

Watch "Love of Your Life" on Prime Video now

Sidney Prescott returns to the iconic horror franchise after star Neve Campbell sat “Scream 6” out due to a pay dispute. One of the OG Final Girls, it’s great to see the series’ main star back and dueling yet another version of Ghostface. Considering we’re now seven slashers in, it’s impressive that “Scream 7” still has the appetite for the kill.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

This time out we’re treated to a very different version of Sidney. Now happily married and a protective mom to Tatam (Isabel May), our hero’s suburban life is turned upside down when a new Ghostface turns up to slice and dice. Or should that be an old Ghostface? The movie has some fun playing around with the notion of AI deepfakes, resulting in a few surprising cameos. The opening scene set in the original film’s infamous house and one kill that feels like it’s been lifted from “Final Destination” are particular highlights.

You’ve got to admire Stanley Tucci. Not only does he seem to spend most of his existence travelling while making fettuccine so delicious you want to dive into your TV, he seemingly has a “movie must be set in Italy” clause in any new project. In fairness, only part of “Masterplan” is set in the land of pasta (an early heist in Lake Como), with the main action taking Tucci’s talented thief to Paris.

Why is this pilfering scoundrel in the City of Love with a couple of up-and-coming heists artists? To steal the Mona Lisa from the Louvre. Obviously. #138. Climate Change Has It In for the World’s Best Surfing

This story originally appeared on The Guardian and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

The climate crisis is coming for some of the world’s greatest surf breaks, submerging some as sea level rises and wiping out others as classic breaks get crushed against coastal developments.

Analysis of dozens of famous waves in World Surfing Reserves (WSR) found that more than three-quarters were at high risk because of changing tide levels, hardened shorelines, and shifting sands.

The impacts matter not only to the surfers catching the waves but also to the communities that depend on the multibillion-dollar surf economy, often located in places with little else.

The waves rated at most risk in the study include the “bombing barrels” of Croyde Beach in North Devon, UK; the point breaks at Noosa in Australia and Oriente Salvaje, El Salvador; and Santa Cruz reefs of California such as Sewer Peak and Wind and Sea.

The best surfing waves are created by intricate combinations of seafloor shape, swell direction, and tide. “Surf breaks are incredibly unique oceanographic phenomena—a confluence of all these factors that fit together just right to make the wave happen—and so those processes are really sensitive,” said Dan Reineman, an associate professor at California State University Channel Islands and a coauthor of the study.

Global heating is pushing up sea level and changing rainfall patterns that affect sediment movement, which can upset the delicate balance and destroy the wave. However, the researchers said the expert local knowledge of surfers could be tapped to help protect the waves.

Trent Hodges, a coauthor of the study and a senior programs manager at Save the Waves Coalition, which launched the WSR program in 2009, said: “Climate change will impact surf breaks all over the world in different ways, depending on their unique geographies. We learned directly from the local surfers how they are seeing their waves change. It’s a canary in the coal mine too—when a wave changes, that often means the beach is changing, and everybody enjoys the beach.”

The study, published in the journal Climatic Change, concludes: “Climate change and coastal management both have significant negative implications for the future viability of multiple surf breaks of global significance and, therefore, the myriad distinct local communities, cultures and economies they support.”

Almost 200 local experts analyzed 57 surf breaks in all but two of the 13 WSRs, spread across eight countries. The researchers said thousands of other surf waves around the world faced similar peril.

A key finding was that where coastlines were more natural, they could adapt better to the changes brought by the climate crisis, by shifting inland and relocating sediments. Development such as sea walls, jetties, and groynes made the beaches and waves less resilient, Reineman said.

Adam Hall, a cofounder of the North Devon WSR, was one of the local surfers who contributed to the study. He said: “North Devon is so special. We have Saunton Sands, a world-renowned longboarding wave with really long, mellow rides, and the UK’s best beach break at Croyde. We’ve got left- and right-hand point breaks and a sheltered spot for when it gets too windy and too big. Whatever you want to do, we’ve got it.”

He said surfing was very important for the local economy, and not just in summer. “Surfers will come throughout the year. They fill up the pubs, restaurants, and car parks when the swells are good in January, February, and March, where if you go to any other tourist destination that doesn’t have surf, they’re dead on their knees.”

#144. Linus Torvalds is using AI to develop Linux kernel code now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The move is a turning point in the developer's relationship with AI and Linux.

It had to happen. Linus Torvalds announced to the world that he used AI to write code for the Linux kernel. Who’d thought it? Well, me for one. Over the last few years, I’ve seen Torvalds’ attitude change from skeptical to seeing AI as a useful tool for programmers and maintainers.

Also: Nvidia’s new Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is another step forward for US open-weight AI

In his Git submission, he wrote, “The code, the test programs, the review behind the list above and the first draft of this text were done with an LLM coding assistant (Claude Code) under my direction.”

His new code consists of an eight-patch series. It’s published on the branch noref-filemap-read-with-llm in Torvalds’s repository. These patches aim to remove a bottleneck that arises when multiple threads make small reads from the same file.

Specifically, the fix addresses contention in Linux’s page cache, which holds file data in memory. When several threads repeatedly read small amounts of data from the same cached file, they take and release references to the folio backing that data. Those reference-count updates require atomic writes to a shared cache line. This in turn forces processor cores to compete over it.

Doesn’t sound like that big a problem, does it? Wrong. In some workloads, it can really slow things down. Torvalds found that when eight threads issued 16-byte pread() calls against the same page on a four-core, eight-thread Intel Core i7-8565U laptop, the shared cache line accounted for 99.92% of the measured cross-core load, according to Hit in Modified cache line (HITMs). That slows work down considerably.

This isn’t just Linus scratching a personal itch. It’s been a known issue since 2024. Earlier attempts to fix it, though, have come to naught.

Torvalds and Claude Code’s proposed patches change when the kernel can reuse memory removed from the page cache. Rather than returning that memory to the allocator immediately, the patches defer reuse until a read-copy-update (RCU) grace period has elapsed. That lets a reader protected by an RCU read-side section copy data directly into a user buffer without taking a folio reference.

Also: Someone made a free Photoshop clone – so I had to try it on Linux

This approach trades immediate memory reclamation for a read path that avoids repeatedly updating a shared reference counter. The reported performance gains are substantial within that specific test. Eight-thread throughput rose from approximately 9.9–10.4 million reads per second to 30–33 million, while kernel cycles per read fell from roughly 2,950 to 725. Single-thread reads improved more modestly, from about 452–454 cycles to 408–409 cycles per read. Torvalds added in his pull request (PR) that “A machine with more CPUs, or more than one socket, should gain more; nothing bigger has been measured.”

This doesn’t mean Linux as a whole runs three times faster. Hardly! Instead, this describes experimental results from a particular small-read workload on Torvald’s personal laptop, which he had with him in Prague at Linux Plumbers.

That’s not to say Torvalds and Claude Code have fixed this issue. We’re far from being able to say that. The performance gains come with engineering trade-offs. Delaying memory reuse means pages can remain unavailable while the kernel waits for an RCU grace period. In his Git submission, Torvalds described that reclamation issue as “the part of this series that is least solved.”

Also: I’ve used Ubuntu for 22 years – and 26.10 might be its best release yet

There is also a regression when a read targets a user page that is not yet mapped. The new path incurs an additional failed exception before falling back to the existing implementation. As of Oct. 13th, the branch remained outside the mainline Linux 7.3-rc6. Whether it will ever be merged, and on what timetable, remains up in the air.

Torvalds’s decision to use Claude Code reflects a long-term evolution in his attitude toward AI. This hasn’t been a simple reversal from opposition to support.

In December 2023, he described AI as a potential aid to developers, saying, “I see AI as a tool that can help us be better at what we do.” At the time, his interest in AI was around how it could help identify bugs, rather than writing code. No one was giving serious thought to using AI to write serious programs (hard to believe now).

By late 2025, Torvalds was calling himself “a huge believer in AI as a tool, and saying he was more interested not just in finding bugs, but in maintaining code and reviewing patches. Generating new, serious code for Linux was still largely off the table. Still, in January 2026, he began toying with AI-assisted coding for a Python audio visualizer in a hobby project.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code – here’s why they choose it over Codex

His latest remarks, reported Oct. 9 following a conversation with Dirk Hohndel at Open Source Summit Europe in Prague, were more enthusiastic.

“I used to think it was just not very good — but now I’m at the point where I actually really like using AI,” Torvalds said. “I think AI is a wonderful tool if you use it correctly and treat it as a tool, and I find it makes programming much more enjoyable.”

Even so, he cautioned, “I think that you need to be very careful using AI when you’re doing something real and important.” It doesn’t get much less real and important than Linux.

The page-cache experiment puts both sides of his position on display. Claude Code helped produce kernel code, tests, and review materials. The resulting branch shows promising benchmark gains, but also the unresolved memory-reclamation questions and performance regression that must be addressed before the experiment can become production kernel code.

Still, we’ve reached a turning point. Torvalds, arguably the world’s foremost developer and maintainer, is now using AI to develop new Linux kernel code. This would have been unthinkable even a year ago, and even now some people still struggle to imagine AI adding new code to Linux or any other important program.

#145. Ember’s new temperature-controlled mug makes my nightly tea ritual even better

Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

With the nights getting chillier, I’ve been reaching for a cup of tea more often. And if there’s one thing that can make a cozy fall night even better, it’s a warm drink that actually stays warm. Enter Ember’s new Mug 3, the latest version of the company’s temperature-controlled smart mug, which is designed to keep your drink at just the right temperature for as long as you sip.

Ember first introduced its smart mug in 2016 to solve a problem most coffee and tea drinkers know all too well: getting distracted for a few minutes, only to return to a lukewarm drink. Now, the company is back with its third-generation mug, which brings a handful of practical upgrades.

The biggest change is that you no longer have to open the app to adjust your drink’s temperature. Instead, you can use the button on the bottom of the mug to cycle through five preset temperatures, starting at 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Each press raises the temperature by five degrees, up to a maximum of 145 degrees, so you can easily make your drink a little hotter with each click.

Honestly, this is the feature I ended up using the most during my time testing out the mug. At night, when I’m curled up in bed with a book and a cup of tea, my phone is usually somewhere across the room. Being able to adjust my drink without getting up to find it is a small convenience, but one I genuinely appreciate.

It’s also a welcome change for users who have reported running into connectivity or pairing issues with the Ember app.

That said, I do have one complaint: the button is located on the bottom of the mug. It’s a peculiar design choice when you’re dealing with a cup full of hot liquid, and it isn’t particularly easy to press, either. I often found myself tilting the mug and pressing down firmly to get it to respond. So, while I appreciate the addition of on-mug controls, I wish Ember had made the button easier to reach.

If you prefer using your phone, the Ember app still offers plenty of customization. After pairing the mug with your phone over Bluetooth, you can choose presets based on what you’re drinking. Ember recommends 136 degrees Fahrenheit for black coffee, 132 degrees for green tea, and 142 degrees for lemon water. You can also create your own temperature presets, which is handy if you like your drinks a little hotter or cooler than the recommended settings.

The Mug 3 also comes with a few other upgrades, including a sliding lid designed to help prevent spills. The mug can also keep your drink at its desired temperature for up to three hours on a single charge. And it’s the first mug in Ember’s lineup to be top-rack dishwasher-safe, making cleanup easier. (Just keep in mind that it isn’t microwave-safe.)

The Ember Mug 3 comes in two sizes: a 10-ounce model for $129 and a 14-ounce version for $149.

The smaller mug is available in black, white, and stainless steel, while the larger size comes in eight colors, including sage green, lavender, powder blue, salt blue, sandstone, white, black, and matcha green.

Alongside the new mug, Ember also introduced the Tumbler 2, which replaces both the Travel Mug 2 and the original Tumbler in its lineup. The 16-ounce tumbler features a slimmer, taller design intended to fit standard car cup holders. It’s available in black for $179, while the Travel Mug 2 will remain available until supplies run out.

The products are available to purchase on Ember’s website, Target, and Amazon.

#147. Magnesium May Not Reach Your Brain, Despite Supplement Label Promises

Most of us probably don’t think about how much magnesium we’re consuming, but our bodies couldn’t function without it. We each typically contain about 25 grams of magnesium, more than half of which is stockpiled in bones. The rest is distributed in cells throughout the body, taking part in hundreds of essential chemical reactions, including building DNA and proteins and sending signals within our nervous systems and between our brains and the rest of our bodies.

But just because our cells—and especially our neurons—need magnesium doesn't mean that extra magnesium will make them function any better. Not only that, but ingesting more of the element doesn’t mean it’s reaching your brain or really any specific part of your body.

In supplement pills, magnesium isn’t just on its own but part of a compound usually called a “magnesium salt.” This must dissolve to release Mg²⁺, the ionic version that our bodies use. How much of this actually gets into your system—versus gets excreted—depends on a variety of factors including the dose, your stomach contents, and how much magnesium is already in your body. In other words, the higher the dose, the less magnesium gets absorbed.

That’s all if the supplement dissolves in the first place. Magnesium oxide, which is usually the basis of the cheapest pills offered, doesn’t break down all that easily. In reality, magnesium oxide supplements mostly act as laxatives, drawing water into the intestines to flush out the excess salt.

This is where the marketing comes in. There are other types of magnesium compounds that do dissolve better. Magnesium citrate, for example, has been shown to have the highest bioavailability in laboratory tests. Despite the fact that all these salts still break down in the intestine, some supplement labels also claim that their specific chemical blend targets the magnesium directly to certain parts of your body, like your muscles or your brain.

These claims are often based on experiments using rodents, and the animals are typically supplied with magnesium long-term at higher doses than found in a pill. One study in rats found that a salt called magnesium L-threonate increased the amount of magnesium in the brain and improved some manifestations of learning and memory. This is the basis of some of the more overzealous marketing in the supplement world, which proclaims that this special salt will take the magnesium right to your brain.

There are some human studies, but that’s not really what they say. A few small randomized trials reporting improvements in some cognitive tests or sleep have been conducted—but there are several important caveats. Some studies tested a mixture of substances, lasted for only a few weeks, or analyzed a very limited number of outcomes. Many of these studies can also not be considered independent, because they were funded by supplement manufacturers or led by their staff.

Moreover, the studies—for extremely understandable reasons—didn't measure magnesium content in the brain. So maybe a little more sneaks into your gray matter, but based on the scientific understanding of how these salts are processed, in all likelihood, a brain-focused magnesium supplement is still just an expensive laxative.
