If your cleaning cupboard is bulging at the seams, you’re likely juggling a different bottle for every mess — from grease on clothing and makeup-stained carpets to those frustrating white deodorant marks on black shirts.

But without realizing it, you probably already have a cleaning solution at home, and instead of taking up space in your cupboard, it could be hiding in your bathroom cabinet, ready and waiting to be used.

Plus, using stain-removing products you already have at home lets you declutter your cleaning cupboard and save dollars on unnecessary purchases.

Cleaning expert Lynsey Crombie, at Lynsey Queen of Clean, shares in an Instagram post how the household products you already have can work just as well. In the post, she says, “Some of the best stain-fighters could already be hiding in your cupboards… and a few might really surprise you!”

A post shared by Lynsey Queen Of Clean (@lynsey_queenofclean)

At Tom’s Guide, we already cover how to shift stains with items you already have in your pantry, such as how to remove sweat stains from clothing with baking soda and how to deep-clean the grimiest part of your toilet with vinegar.

However, you might already own a few other powerful stain removers you haven’t considered. Beyond baking soda, white vinegar and dish soap, Crombie recommends plenty of other products to lift stains.

Micellar waterOne of the toughest stains to remove from carpet and clothing is makeup. Dense pigments, stubborn waxes and oils all resist water, making them hard to shift. So instead of resorting to off-the-shelf products, Crombie recommends using micellar cleansing water, which I already use as my regular makeup cleanser.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Aside from cleansing your skin, it can remove greasy marks around your home, since it’s designed to lift dirt and oil. Struggling to clear those sticky fingerprints off chrome surfaces? Add some micellar water to a microfiber cloth and wipe the smudges away.

ToothpasteAnother staple in your bathroom cabinet is toothpaste. It contains baking soda, a mild abrasive that breaks down oils but is gentle enough not to scratch. It can be used to clean tarnished silverware (but avoid using a gel or whitening toothpaste) and to remove mineral deposits on an iron’s soleplate. Plus, rubbing a small amount of toothpaste onto your faucets with a cloth can bring back their shine.

Shaving foamWhile you’re reaching for your toothpaste, pull out your shaving foam. The grooming essential is the perfect product to stop your mirrors from misting. Wiping over your mirror with shaving foam leaves behind a thin layer of surfactant that causes condensation to spread out evenly into a flat transparent sheet, rather than forming individual droplets. What’s more, shaving foam can also lift stains from carpet. Apply the foam to the flooring, let it sit for 3-5 minutes, then blot with a damp cloth.

Cut the cost of cleaningBy thinking outside the box, you can remove stains already in your cupboards, without spending out on targeted stain removers.

These 12 x 12 inch microfiber cleaning cloths leave a streak-free and lint-free clean. They are versatile, absorbent cloths that can be used throughout your home.

#155. 5 tips to maximize your tech’s performance amid the RAM crisis

If you haven’t looked at the cost of RAM recently, then don’t. They haven’t changed in any positive way since the RAMpocalypse began, and if anything, it’s going to get a lot worse before it gets any better. That makes almost any upgrade untenable, whether it’s buying a new laptop or upgrading your existing desktop PC.

There is another way, and that’s the wonderful world of software optimization. A few tweaks here and there can add a little extra performance to your tech, preserve it for a little longer, and hopefully last you long enough to get to the other end of the RAMpocalypse when prices finally drop. It’s not quite as potent as doubling your RAM or buying an extra storage drive, but they can definitely make a difference.

The best part is that these tweaks are free, so it won’t cost you anything to use them, and depending on your setup, you might be looking at some decent performance gains.

This first tweak is pretty common practice and that’s disabling startup apps that you don’t need. It helps performance in two notable ways. First, it makes your boot times faster since the PC is starting fewer apps right when it turns on. The other way is by helping performance while you use the PC, since fewer apps are running in the background, freeing up system resources. This is free, quick, and reversible in case something goes wrong.

Windows users can learn how to do it here, while Mac users can also do this with this method.

Brand new SSDs are right up there with RAM in terms of price, and so a nearly full SSD can be quite a problem. Instead of buying more hardware, take some time to clean out the old junk to see if you can get some of your storage back for free.

There are many methods to do this, including built-in Disk Cleanup tools on Windows and Mac. Uninstalling apps on a smartphone to free up space is also pretty easy. Specialized apps like WinDirStat can also help you find and remove large files, freeing up more space, and if you have external storage, you can offload files there to save even more.

Uninstalling stuff has a dual benefit. Apps and especially modern games take up tons of space, and removing apps and games you don’t play can help free up valuable storage. Additionally, many old apps still run in the background, so uninstalling them claws back some system resources as well. The effectiveness of this one depends entirely on how much junk you have on your computer.

This works for Windows, Mac, smartphones, and tablets, since apps are ubiquitous. The only thing to note is that Windows has two methods to uninstall apps, including the Apps section of the Settings menu and the Control Panel. You’ll want to check both places since they don’t house the same list of apps on your computer.

Your power settings can have a pretty decent impact on performance. Most computers — at least laptops — are defaulted to a setting that balances power consumption and battery life. This means most PC laptops and MacBooks are running at a decent clip, but they can do better. This minor adjustment is pretty easy to do, but be forewarned that a higher performance setting will reduce battery life.

Windows users can edit their Power Options to change this, and on Macs, it’s called Power Modes. Some smartphones and tablets also have options like a gaming mode that helps goose performance, but you’ll have to check for your specific smartphone.

When any piece of tech gets hot, it lowers performance because the CPU or GPU throttles itself to stay within reasonable temperatures. Thus, if you keep your computer or phone cooler, it can run harder for longer. This is tougher to do with smartphones, but for PCs and laptops, it mostly involves making sure your computer is clean and gets enough air.

Some canned air can work wonders here, as dust buildup can impede fan operation and make your computer hotter. Laptop coolers and even reapplying your thermal paste can help lower PC temps, which can have a remarkable impact on your performance.

#156. Mark Wahlberg wants to take on the longevity-startup crowd with an affordable gym concept

Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

Mark Wahlberg has started companies of his own and backed plenty of others. But he says the gym he’s opening in December has him more excited than anything he’s done in his entire career. It also goes after a corner of the market where venture money keeps flowing: pricey, diagnostics-heavy wellness.

Speaking with us at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, the actor said the first Municipal Gym opens in December. It’s a 32,000-square-foot club outside Las Vegas with blood work, epigenetic testing, recovery gear, compression therapy, cold plunges, and a café that serves up protein muffins, among other things. He’s pitching it as the affordable alternative to the longevity clubs that charge tens of thousands of dollars a year for much the same thing.

It’s the second part of a scheme that was, in some ways, first hatched seven years ago with a casual sportswear line.

The clothing brand Municipal launched during COVID, which Wahlberg freely volunteered “was not a good idea,” given that clothing was a lousy business to enter in 2020, with retailers from J.Crew to Brooks Brothers going bankrupt.

It grew out of what he’d been seeing as a celebrity fitness spokesperson. He’d done collabs with various brands, and other companies kept approaching him to be their brand ambassador, but they all seemed to want the same thing, he said. “Everybody just kind of wanted to sell T-shirts and sneakers. And I was like, well, I want to kind of have a bigger impact on people’s lives as a whole.”

By that, he meant what people eat, what supplements they take, how they train, and how they recover. “We figured, okay, we’ll start in the apparel space, and then we’ll build from there.” He says he only takes swings at “things that I’m very passionate about and things that are a direct extension of who I am.”

Even without a pandemic, clothing is a brutal business, as we pointed out, citing Lululemon’s repeated quality-control challenges. But Wahlberg didn’t seem fazed, talking instead about why the gym fits his vision. He thought it “always could be great for the brand” in part because it gives people a place to “actually feel and touch the clothes” before they buy. Besides, he continued, how people exercise is “another big part of people’s lives.”

Most in the space have been laser-focused on the high end. Fountain Life, the longevity company co-founded by Tony Robbins, raised $18 million last year to expand its centers for wealthy clients, and a full subscription runs $21,500 a year, according to reports. The Estate, a company co-founded by Robbins and hospitality executive Sam Nazarian, is still mapping out plans to charge $35,000 memberships to its wellness centers. Equinox is similarly building a waitlist for a $36,000 longevity add-on that it plans to launch atop a traditional gym membership.

Wahlberg says Municipal aims for that same luxury tier but for a lot less. “We have a better price point than our competitors, and we’re going to get far more results,” he said. For $99, he said as an example, members will receive three rounds of blood work and an hour with a doctor to flag what they’re predisposed to. Supplements and hormone therapy are also “right there.”

When we asked whether the gyms will double as storefronts for his other products (he owns a supplements brand, for example), he said “kind of.” What he’s really building, he said, is a “health and wellness ecosystem” with “everything there, soup to nuts.”

He didn’t put a number on how many gyms he wants, but he called the growth strategy “aggressive,” telling us that “landlords and developers who toured the Las Vegas site have offered “AAA locations at very favorable terms, with great TI” (tenant-improvement allowances that help pay for the build-out).

Wahlberg’s last big bet on a gym chain might have scared off someone else. We told him we’d recently watched “Wahl Street,” his reality show, in which an early episode shows him getting deeply involved with the fitness chain F45 in 2019, and that we wanted to warn him about what was coming. “How did you know about the pandemic?” he joked, to laughs from the crowd. He bought into the company, known for its 45-minute classes, at a $450 million valuation. It went public in 2021, then was delisted from the NYSE in 2023 after its stock collapsed. Wahlberg said he learned a lot from the experience.

“I think the biggest takeaway was just making sure that I’m involved with people that share the same approach that I do.” He also said he always thought big box was the better model. F45’s classes suit people who are short on time, but he wants members to hang around Municipal for hours. Plenty of gyms run on a “join up but don’t show up” model, he said, adding, “I can’t understand that philosophy.”

The name Municipal is very intentional and clearly means a lot to Wahlberg, who grew up poor in Boston, one of nine kids, playing on public basketball courts and golf courses. “You learn a lot on the blacktop,” he said. “You learn to win, to lose, to compete, and hopefully to get back up and do it again.”

He has never hidden his rough youth. (He was sentenced to two years for assaults as a teenager and served 45 days.)

In fact, earlier in the afternoon on Thursday, surrounded by friends and business associates in a seating area backstage at Disrupt — this is the man who inspired the show “Entourage,” after all — he said he was turned around by two people, including Father Jim Flavin, a Boston-area parish priest who has been in Wahlberg’s life since he was 13.

He wants the gyms to carry that same spirit. “It’s a place to work, but have fun and support each other and create community and really challenge people to be better versions of themselves,” he said. “I’ve come from next to nothing to being in an amazing position,” Wahlberg continued. “I try to constantly remind myself that I can inspire other people growing up in similar situations, especially inner-city kids and at-risk youth, that there is a way to overcome your circumstances if you’re willing to go out there and do the work.”

At 55, his goals have changed, naturally. While he was once focused on looking good, “I just want to feel good when I wake up in the morning,” he said. “I want to be able to conquer all the things that I have planned for the day.”

He also said his plate is exceedingly full right now, between the gym, a film role as Pete Rose, and his daughter’s equestrian career. He’s so eager for the gym to open, he said, that visiting the construction site feels like “literally watching paint dry.” Indeed, asked if he was open to taking on new ventures, he shrugged. “I’m not out there hunting, looking for the next thing for sure.” But he wouldn’t rule it out, he added quickly. “If something amazing were to come along, obviously I wouldn’t turn it down.”

Pictured above with Walhberg, friend and business partner Bruce K. Lee.

#157. The Best AirPods Cases We’ve Used In Our Day-to-Day Lives (2026)

The best AirPods cases are subjective, but luckily, you have thousands of options to match your style and mood. You can find a ton of novelty cases online, most of which are just fine. For this guide, we focused on cases with a WIRED angle. Rather than another case that looks like food or a licensed character, the recommendations below add some functionality or protection beyond the basics.

For more recommendations, check out our guides to the Best AirPods, Best Wireless Headphones, and Best iPad Accessories.

Compatible with AirPods Pro (1st, 2nd, and 3rd generation) and AirPods (3rd and 4th generation).

The Dbrand Grip Case looks fantastic, and it doesn't add an irksome amount of bulk or weight to my headphones. The case is made of black rubber and can then be personalized with your choice of skins, plus an optional lanyard. There are more than 40 options, and you can swap them out whenever, though the sticker-like skins aren't reusable. Dbrand provides installation instructions, but I winged it and found it easy to get everything lined up. The skin options are slick, too. I'm partial to the UV-reactive Holo White, but there are some with an x-ray or pixelated aesthetic, circuit patterns, plain colors, and more. This case offers solid protection while still being eye-catching, which is why it's my favorite.

Compatible with AirPods Pro (3rd generation) and AirPods (4th generation).

UAG is in the business of making tough accessories, and this sturdy option adds a thick layer of rubber around the original AirPods case to protect it from drops. It has a nice grippy texture and snug fit, with squared edges that help me get a better grip when walking around. It also comes with a sweet-looking carabiner that is optional but I quite liked. The action is smooth, and it's not too big. Every feature works as intended, and there are 10 different color options to choose from.

Compatible with AirPods Pro (3rd generation) and AirPods (4th generation)

Most cases in this guide have support for wireless charging, but if you're all in on MagSafe accessories, you'll love ESR’s Orbit case. It comes with magnets that attach securely to a MagSafe charger. The top and bottom pieces also snap shut with magnets, which helps keep the lid from accidentally sliding off (a common issue I've experienced with other AirPods cases). It's protective, with a shock-absorbing hard shell that helps protect against drops. This also means it's bulkier than other cases I've tested, but that's not a deal-breaker for me. As someone who constantly drops her AirPods case, I'll take all the extra protection I can get. —Brenda Stolyar

Compatible with AirPods Pro (1st, 2nd, and 3rd generation) and AirPods (3rd and 4th generation)

This leather case is made from Horween leather, which is minimally treated and develops a rich patina over time. It feels slippery, which I didn't love, but it's still protective without adding meaningful bulk to your headphones. It fits snugly and has cutouts for the light and speaker holes. There's a lanyard attachment point, but no lanyard is included. I haven't tried a better leather case.

Compatible with AirPods Pro (1st, 2nd, and 3rd generation) and AirPods (4th generation)

This case actually improved my AirPods experience. Sliding the front switch pops the lid up, so I can easily place my headphones in with one hand. The colors also come in coordinating schemes with the iPhone 17 lineup. The case stays on when I accidentally drop it, and it has a spot for a wrist lanyard, too. I also like that I can still see the charging light through the case, and the bright colors help me spot my AirPods from a distance.

Compatible with AirPods Pro (1st, 2nd, and 3rd generation) and AirPods (3rd and 4th generation).

Most AirPods cases come with a clip you can attach to your bag or keys, but this case from Bandolier elevates the look. I keep it clipped to the outside of my tote bag, but you can attach it to the inside if there's a pocket.

Since it's a pouch, it doesn't attach to the top and bottom of the AirPods case like the other cases in this guide. But it's still protective, covering the entire case (except the charging port). It's made of genuine pebbled leather, giving it a bumpy texture that adds a nice high-end touch. It's also available in several colors, including black, pink, lavender, metallic blue, and more. —Brenda Stolyar

Soft-touch silicone cases are great because they're usually thin, lightweight, and come in tons of colors. But they're also dust magnets. Casetify's Ripple Case is dust-proof thanks to an antistatic coating. This is important considering the AirPods Max don't have a dust-resistance rating. That way, you can worry a little less about dust seeping in.

The Ripple case includes cutouts for the buttons, making them super easy to access. They also fit perfectly over the earcups. And, as the name suggests, they feature a ripple pattern that adds definition to the earcups. I like the color options, though I wish Casetify's logo wasn't stamped smack dab in the middle. —Brenda Stolyar

Burga AirPods Max Case ($25): This snap-on case for AirPods Max keeps your ports accessible and is pretty easy to snap on and remove. It's available in dozens of prints, and you can coordinate it with various iPhone accessories like cases and ring holders, too.

Alpaka x Twelve South Micro Tote ($30): What is it about cute tiny tote bags that drives people cuckoo bananas? Because I really want this limited-edition collaboration between two makers of high-quality accessories, Alpaka and Twelve South. Originally intended for Twelve South's PowerClip portable battery, it's also the perfect size for an AirPods case. Made from Alpaka's durable X-Pac material, it includes a D-ring to hook onto the outside of your bag, belt loop, or keychain. You can also use it for coins and other small items. Although I haven't tested this long enough for a full recommendation, I have had positive experiences using Alpaka and Twelve South products long-term. —Les Shu

Compatible with AirPods Pro (1st, 2nd, and 3rd generation).

Bellroy Pod Jacket ($39): Sadly, it's time to replace my trusty Incase Woolenex AirPods Case because it's reached the end of its useful life; I am upgrading to the AirPods Pro 3; and Incase no longer makes this product. Bellroy has stepped in to become my accessories maker of choice, and I love the luxe leather feel of the Pod Jacket, and it's a great alternative to our leather pick above. It includes a corded lanyard, which I don't use since I prefer to keep it in my pocket, and the lanyard just gets in the way. I like that I can still charge it wirelessly. If leather is not your thing, the Pod Jacket is available in other materials. —Les Shu

Compatible with AirPods Pro (2nd and 3rd generation).

Spigen Classic LS Case: This case makes your AirPods Pro look like the classic Macintosh mouse, but the aesthetics don't outweigh its mediocre functionality. The lid constantly pops off, and while I appreciate that Spigen includes extra adhesive, I don't want to have to deal with it. It was also annoying to open and too bulky to fit conveniently in my purse or pocket.

How do you know which case to buy? Apple has several generations of its AirPods, whether you have the standard AirPods or the AirPods Pro, so be sure the case you select works with your model. (Some cases are interchangeable, particularly the first- and second-generation AirPods and the first- and second-generation AirPods Pro.) To find what you have, go to Settings > Bluetooth on the Apple device you paired them with. Tap the “i” icon next to your AirPods' name to see the model number. If your AirPods aren't connected to an Apple device, you can find the model number on the device itself. It's on the underside of each earbud—you may need to use your smartphone's zoom feature to read it.

Once you have the model number, you can cross-reference it with this tool to identify the generation. You can also just check the receipt in your order history if you purchased them online.

You probably know if you bought a different case for your AirPods, but it's worth checking the case's model number, too, as Apple has released stand-alone models with wireless charging and MagSafe support. You can find those details here.

I make sure these cases provide adequate protection in day-to-day life. I keep my AirPods in most of the time and always tote them around, so these cases get a lot of field testing. I also make sure they allow the full use of AirPods' features, like hearing the Find My tone or allowing wireless charging. I tested most of these cases with my AirPods Pro 3, but am hoping to check out more options for the AirPods 4 and the AirPods Max soon.

#158. It's still OK to enjoy programming

Reading Hacker News makes me feel like I need to write this: it's still OK to enjoy programming.

Yes, at work, where you are paid to produce value for a business, the economics of purely hand-written code have changed. But that's work. Work is not life. The loudest voices on the internet are the saddest and most infectious.

To throw a tiny counter example in the sea of despair: I still program on the weekends because it is fun. I'm currently learning game programming! My current level of sophistication is a buggy Breakout clone with terrible collision detection. I write it by hand because I enjoy it. I struggle with problems because solving them makes me happy. It doesn't bother me that Claude could one-shot it, because that's not the point.

I also get side-tracked from working on this "game" to study random programming topics. Last weekend was exploring how far I could push type safety in Java using ideas from dependently typed languages like Agda. There is no point to this. It gets tucked away under "interesting ways of thinking about a particular problem." Maybe it will come up in work life. Maybe not. I did it because exploring is was fun[0].

A few weekends ago: recursion schemes. Technically, this was not fun. I spent hours of banging my head against a wall. In the end, I still don't even know what's valuable about the ideas[1]. But I do know that many of the most beautiful ideas in programming only become clear to me after years of baking in my mind. It's why entire papers get written about Monoids. Maybe one day I'll find a problem that this applies to. Maybe not. I did it because understanding hard things is rewarding.

I write this because I increasingly feel a strange social pressure. It's like I'm not "supposed" to enjoy this any more. As though there's no point or joy to be had in continuing to grow as a human. The more of this doom stream you consume, the more it starts to infect you. Maybe "there is no point," you find yourself thinking. But this disappears as soon as you disconnect.

It's OK to enjoy things[2]. Doing so requires no economic justification.

Footnotes: [0] Take the time to understand Fin one day. It is beautiful. [1] I'm not there yet, but the goal of studying this is to give myself another tool for reasoning about program correctness algebraically (a topic I cover in my book!) [2] I also have a blast vibe-coding. I've got a suite of apps for which I've never looked at a line of code. I suspect doing so would horrify me. "Programming" this way is also fun. Often extremely so. But in its own unique way.

This homemade weed killer is in your kitchen

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If there is one gardening chore that always feels like a losing battle, it’s dealing with those unruly weeds. Be it taking over my lawn and front yard or surfacing between my patio pavers, they seem to be everywhere.

While larger, visible weeds with clear taproots are easy enough to pull out, weeds stuck deep in narrow cracks and crevices are a whole different challenge.

But before you splurge on commercial weed killers or expensive tools, a surprising pantry staple can do just the trick — and it’s not white vinegar. In fact, this chemical-free, natural hack will not only make light work of your everyday weeding chores, but can banish pests too. Win-win!

It seems like baking soda can do so much more than enhance tasty bakes and cakes. Known for its miraculous cleaning powers in the home and odor-neutralizing abilities, baking soda can also tackle young weeds — making it a cost-effective weed killer.

Essentially, baking soda acts as a contact herbicide. Although it burns and destroys the specific green foliage and tissues it comes into contact with, it doesn't penetrate deep taproots. Which is why this method is more effective for dealing with shallow roots only.

Simply sprinkle baking soda directly from the box over the weeds and grass growing in between the crevices. If you’re dealing with scattered weeds or blades of grass shooting up, experts recommend sprinkling about one teaspoon of baking soda directly onto the foliage and stems of each plant.

And if you’re tackling larger weed patches, scatter about 1 cup (225 grams) of baking soda per 100 square feet of paving.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Afterwards, take a bristle broom or brush to sweep the baking soda into the cracks to stop new weeds from settling into the soil.

If, like me, you’re worried about the unsightly mess of baking soda all over your patio, you can make an easy homemade spray. Simply dilute about 10 tablespoons of baking soda into a gallon of water in a bottle before spraying directly over the weeds and along the pavers.

Just be sure to steer clear of any nearby flowers, vegetables, or delicate plants to prevent accidental harm. The idea is to just focus on where the weeds are coming through, without affecting the rest of your yard.

What’s more, now is the right time to tackle weeds in your pavers. This is mainly because current fall mild temperatures and moisture create prime conditions for young weeds. Which means you’ll need to act fast before those deep taproots take hold.

So the next time you’re out of your usual weed killer (or even white vinegar), you might want to check out your pantry essentials for a fuss-free solution this season.

#165. Porsche’s electric Macan Turbo is an automotive existential crisis

Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

Maybe it was the grey color, the slightly bulbous roofline, or the vaguely SUV-like proportions of the electric Porsche Macan, but as I shuttled kids and groceries around city and suburban streets, I never once noticed a longing stare from other drivers. Unlike with other cars I’ve tested, no enthusiasts stopped to ask me questions.

The 2026 Porsche Macan Turbo simply blended in, leaving in its wake a raft of existential questions. What is a sports car, anyway? Does it need to be overwhelmingly extroverted? Should it match the leaner, lighter look of its gas-powered sibling?

Drive one and the questions cease. Maybe that’s because the acceleration makes it hard to breathe? Or maybe it’s because, by the numbers, the Macan is a sports car at heart despite its rather humdrum crossover body style.

My passengers would agree. The kids I drove to soccer practice, both my own and others, gave the punchy acceleration high marks. The G-forces it reports on the head-up display ($2,660) can easily mimic the pull of gravity. Stab the accelerator at 70 mph and it lurches as though it were standing still. (Don’t worry, fellow parents. I did not try that with children on board.)

On winding roads, the car comes alive, thanks in part to the four-wheel steering ($2,150). Drop it into Sport Plus mode, and the car literally drops on its air suspension. Are we sure this is another anonymous crossover? Maybe anonymity is a useful trait in a car this responsive and powerful.

Unlike most two-row crossovers, you get the feeling of sitting in the Macan, not on it. The wheel extends far enough to make a sporty driving position possible, and the classic Porsche chronometer ($1,040) perched atop the dash ticks off the seconds it takes to get the kid to soccer practice.

The 2026 Porsche Macan Turbo EV is a two-row crossover with 630 horsepower and a 100-kilowatt-hour battery. The EV, which the automaker provided to me for a week, starts at $112,700. However, the one I drove rang up at $149,610, including destination fees. Yes, the options alone could buy a nicely equipped Chevy Bolt. With Porsche and options, if you have to ask…well, it’s better not to.

The Porsche Macan Turbo EV I drove came in Slate Grey Neo (a $2,620 upgrade), which was really well executed and among the best greys I’ve seen. If you crave luxurious anonymity, then this grey is your color.

There were a slew of other options, and in my view, not all of them are worth it. I’d skip the passenger display ($1,710); my kids liked that it could play YouTube videos, but they can’t ride up front, and my wife was underwhelmed. “Our washing machine can play YouTube videos,” she said.

I’d also forgo the illuminated Porsche wordmark on the front seatbacks ($690), puddle lamps that shine “PORSCHE” onto the pavement ($420), Porsche crests on the headrests ($640), and an illuminated Turbo badge on the door sills ($1,230).

That Turbo badge became a point of contention for some of my friends, who were quick to point out that EVs technically can’t have turbos. That is true, though automotive names have long been divorced from reality. Almost every Porsche these days has a turbo, even those not labeled as such.

It’s not just Porsche: BMW’s model numbers, for example, stopped reflecting engine displacement decades ago, and the Ford Galaxie never traveled between star systems using its hyperdrive. Sorry, friends, I’m not taking the bait.

At least the Macan Turbo’s EV qualities don’t raise too many questions. It charges fast — exactly 20 minutes from 19% to 80% on a 350-kilowatt charger — and gets about 285 miles of highway range. Those big wheels ($4,110) and sticky tires ($660) sapped some range, but it was still more than enough to get from New York to Boston with charge to spare.

The advanced driver assistance system ($1,140) works well enough, even if it hunts a bit in the lane. The AI-powered voice assistant did a solid job of interpreting my queries and commands. For a while, I thought it was the only way to turn on the heated steering wheel ($720), which was actually fine because it worked so well. (Surprise! There’s a small button hidden on the inner rim of the steering wheel between two spokes. IYKYK, I guess.)

When it’s time to leave the Macan, you can just open the door and walk away. The Burmester sound system ($4,960) will keep bumpin’ until you lock the door, which is a helpful reminder. If you’re a Porsche traditionalist, you can also hit the vestigial power button to the left of the driver’s display. Good to have choices, I guess? At least Porsche doesn’t charge you for that.

The navigation system, and specifically how it integrates with the EV, was underwhelming.

When the car was at a 22% state of charge, I asked it to find the nearest fast charger. It directed me to two. Not two different options, but two chargers that I was supposed to use sequentially. The first was a 50-kilowatt charger in a mall parking lot 10 minutes away. There, I was supposed to add a few percentage points before unplugging and driving across the street to another mall’s parking lot, where I would finish at a 350-kilowatt charger.

Wait, what? I ignored the machine and drove straight to the 350-kilowatt charger, arriving at 19%. As I backed into the stall, the car was still commanding me to drive to the slower charger. I guess it didn’t want the battery to dip below 20%? Too late. There’s probably a setting to change that somewhere, but it wasn’t obvious. At least the charge rate peaked at 245 kilowatts, close to the 270-kilowatt maximum.

The electric Macan is like the answer to an esoteric Jeopardy! question: What does an identity crisis look like in the automotive industry? I’ll take a Porsche Macan Turbo for $150,000, Alex.

For anyone with deep enough pockets, EVs have blurred the line between sports cars and everything else. True gear heads will have another car to race, but if you want to spend a few hours carving corners, the Macan will do just fine. As a bonus, you can also use it in real life and won’t pay through the nose to keep it filled up.

Actually, that raises another question, this one for my editor: Can I get a fatter paycheck?

#166. Everything AI allows you to do in Windows 11 that saves you time

AI is becoming a major part of our digital lives, and Microsoft has adopted the new tech with open arms. So much so that Microsoft now offers a huge range of AI tools straight from Windows 11, led by Microsoft’s new digital assistant, Copilot.

The real advantage of AI is that it can help you do your work faster. AI tools, at least right now, are excellent at helping users save time, so they can spend that time on other tasks. And, many more AI tools that can help you save time are on the way – so expect to be able to save more and more time over the next few months and years.

Curious about how you can save time in Windows 11 using AI? Here are the best features right now.

The first thing that AI tools became reasonably good at is search. To be clear, AI tools do hallucinate information – which is to say that when it comes to search, they sometimes confidently get things wrong. That means that you should double-check important information, especially if the information is highly consequential.

That said, Copilot is still pretty good at search, and it provides sources for its information too – so you can click on the sources and double-check that the information is accurate as needed. Plus, Copilot allows you to ask follow-up questions, which is a whole lot quicker than having to search multiple topics on the web.

With AI in Windows 11, you don’t necessarily need to read full, long documents. Instead, you can ask Copilot to summarize documents for you, and this can be done in a few different apps and services. For example, you can ask Copilot to summarize articles in Microsoft Edge, or ask it to summarize documents in Word.

There are some handy image creation AI tools in Windows too – and more tools are coming. For now, you can use Microsoft Designer to create images for you. Simply input a text prompt, and Designer will create an image. From there, you can edit the image, and refine it – both using AI tools, and using manual graphic design tools.

As you might expect, Copilot can generate text of its own too, which can be helpful in a variety of settings. For example, from the Pages app, you can enable Copilot and ask it to generate text by describing the kind of text that you want the assistant to create. From there, you can have Copilot change the tone of the text, or ask it to rewrite the text based on additional prompts. Then, simply hit the “Add to page” button and your new text will show up in your document.

One of the most powerful upcoming AI tools for Windows 11 will first show up in Microsoft’s new generation of computers, called Microsoft Copilot+ PCs. These computers feature powerful new AI processors that can handle local AI features, like Recall.

Recall essentially keeps an eye on the things you do on your computer, and allows you to easily find documents, websites, images, and more, by asking Copilot about them. Remember when you found a recipe you wanted to cook a few weeks ago, but now you can’t find the web page again? That’s the kind of thing that Recall will be able to help with. Using the tool, you should be able to simply ask Copilot to help you find it, and it’ll look through the log of what you’ve done on your computer.

You’ll be able to turn this feature off if you wish, and set which apps and websites it works with, or doesn’t work with. And, Microsoft is quick to point out that these snapshots are stored locally, and not uploaded to the cloud.

Cocreate takes image creation tools to the next level. Using Cocreate on Copilot+ PCs, you’ll be able to sketch designs in paint, and couple that information with text prompts to have Cocreate create a new image for you. The feature will also be available in Microsoft Photos, and could be perfect for those who simply need graphics for a document, for example.

#167. Encryption Is Getting Squeezed From All Sides

Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

Oh, Canada. The Great White North is the latest country to contemplate legislation that could essentially mandate backdoors and increase data retention in encrypted services. The proposed changes have prompted the Canadian anti-censorship company Psiphon VPN—which keeps millions of Iranians online during repressive internet shutdowns—to say it will leave the country if the bill passes. And Psiphon is not the only one.

Encrypted messaging app Signal has said it would exit the Canadian market because the legislation would require unacceptable changes to its open source projects. Apple and Meta have criticized the bill, and DuckDuckGo and NordVPN say they would consider pulling their services, too. But as countries around the world contemplate similar legislation, even larger questions begin to emerge about which states or regions could differentiate themselves as being safe havens for privacy services if global hostility to encryption continues to rise.

It’s been maddening and disturbing to see more and more democratic countries around the world propose changes to their surveillance and data collection laws, with the aim of giving cops and intelligence agencies greater powers to access people’s information. Governments already have broad digital surveillance powers and investigative tactics to solve crimes that involve encrypted data, but legislative proposals almost inevitably include provisions to expand this access even more—mandating additional logging and what amounts to backdoors or intentional flaws in encrypted products, which cryptographers and security engineers have consistently said cannot be built safely. Truly everyone who understands the issue has said it as much for decades. Yet policymakers return again and again to the idea, somehow expecting a different conclusion or a new breakthrough that will make it all possible.

“There have always been some officials within certain agencies that tend to view technology as a crime scene in and of itself, and it becomes a myopic point of fixation where access is desired,” says Kate Robertson, a senior research associate at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab. “But that type of siloed thinking forgets that technology needs to be the secure operating platform for hospitals, for banks, for national security agencies, for police services themselves to protect victims who report private information to them.”

In recent years, the UK and Australia have introduced sweeping surveillance reforms that can compel companies to break their encryption. Other encryption-threatening proposals have also emerged in the EU, France, India, Ireland, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, and others. While not all measures have passed into law or been enacted, the hostility is clear.

First proposed in 2025, and partially revised due to blistering criticism from tech companies and civil society, Canada’s C-22 bill can broadly place requirements on tech companies, including those outside of Canada, to introduce “technical capabilities” that allow data to be accessed for law enforcement purposes. Like many such bills, C-22 says that companies will not have to introduce a “systemic vulnerability” into their systems. But opponents have pointed out that any capability to access end-to-end encrypted data amounts to a backdoor that could be discovered and abused by anyone. And this risk is only heightened even more by the ease with which anyone can now use AI tools for reverse engineering and system mapping.

“Companies could be asked to introduce vulnerabilities, build backdoors, bypass, weaken or otherwise defeat encryption,” members of the US House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committee said in a May letter to Canadian officials.

In addition to potential impacts on encryption, C-22 also includes provisions that could require companies to retain metadata about user activity, something that many privacy focused services (including VPN services from Psiphon and DuckDuckGo) intentionally avoid. As a result, these companies say, they would be forced to change their business models to collect data they do not need or want to collect about their users. And researchers say that such product changes would diminish user trust while increasing the potential for widespread surveillance.

“If you are asking and requiring for this infrastructural change—that they retain metadata by default—it is creating a surveillance capability within a tool that didn’t have it,” says Afsaneh Rigot, the founder of the De|Center, a research organization that aims to reduce the risk of technological harms. “There are contexts like Iran and other contexts globally, who all of this has a trickle effect on. It's not going to stay in Canada because these types of laws always get copy pasted around the world.”

As more countries contemplate such laws, developers focused on privacy and anti-censorship tools are increasingly casting around for safe jurisdictions to operate in. But this still doesn’t solve the problem of reaching users in all countries around the world and for now, there are no sure bets.

“Changing your headquarters isn’t much of a plan B when the law follows your users, as C-22 would,” says Joseph Lorenzo-Hall, security portfolio lead at the Internet Society. “The strongest protection is holding as little user data as possible, but ‘we don’t have it’ is no defense if governments can force you to start collecting it. A safe haven needs more than favorable winds in strong encryption. It needs laws that let companies keep their privacy promises and defend them against foreign threats to confidentiality and integrity.”

Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.

#170. Alternatives to Animal Testing Are Finally Taking Off

Changing habits may be the hardest engineering challenge of all

Lab rats have long been a mainstay of biomedical research and drug development. Now, technologies such as Emulate’s Lung-on-a-Chip aim to model human biology without relying on animals.

Seventeen years ago, cell biologist Donald Ingber and his colleagues at Harvard University’s Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering submitted a paper to the journal Science describing their model human lung. It was smaller than a USB stick and made of a clear polymer slab containing narrow channels, which were lined with the type of cells that line a lung’s air sacs and blood vessels. When air was pumped through hollow chambers beside the channels, the device rhythmically expanded and contracted—it “breathed.”

This lifelike movement was a dramatic change from previous generations of lung models, which typically used static cultures of lung tissue that were unable to simulate the movements essential to lung function. When exposed to inflammatory proteins and bacteria, Ingber’s artificial lung reacted much as living lungs would. And exposure to silica nanoparticles used to model the effects of ultrafine particulates revealed that movement affected how tissues absorbed them.

Donald Ingber led the team that developed the first human lung-on-a-chip at Harvard University’s Wyss Institute. Sam Ogden

It was a powerful proof-of-principle demonstration of a system that could be used to test drugs and other chemicals, providing a complement and even an alternative to testing in tissue cultures or in animals. Even so, the editors at Science were hesitant. They rejected the paper and suggested that Ingber’s team also run the tests in mice.

It wasn’t an unreasonable request: Harvard’s lung system was new and comparing the results it generated to results from mice would help validate it. Ingber’s team ran the suggested experiments and resubmitted their study a year later, in 2010, at which point it was published. (It has since been cited by nearly 5,400 other papers.) Still, the incident spoke to how animal models have been the default of modern biomedical research.

An early lung-on-a-chip developed at Harvard’s Wyss Institute used microfluidic channels lined with human cells to reproduce key features of lung function. Wyss Institute at Harvard University

A recent story told by Ilka Maschmeyer, a translational toxicology researcher and executive at the German biotech company TissUse, shows how much things have changed. TissUse specializes in building organ-on-a-chip systems—the conversational name for systems like Ingber’s lung—that are used by pharmaceutical companies for research. A few months ago, says Maschmeyer, a pharmaceutical company approached TissUse after being denied permission by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to run a clinical trial of a new drug. The problem: It had presented animal data, but the FDA wanted data from organs-on-a-chip or some comparable alternative. The standards had come full circle.

A Breathing Lung-on-a-Chip The lung chip re-creates the interface between an air sac and a blood vessel, with human lung and endothelial cells growing on opposite sides of a porous membrane. Vacuum channels rhythmically stretch and relax the tissue to mimic breathing, reproducing mechanical forces that can affect how lung cells respond to substances they encounter. In one experiment, researchers added bacteria to the air channel and white blood cells to the blood channel; the immune cells crossed the membrane and engulfed the bacteria, reproducing an inflammatory response. GyGinfographics.com

The lung chip re-creates the interface between an air sac and a blood vessel, with human lung and endothelial cells growing on opposite sides of a porous membrane. Vacuum channels rhythmically stretch and relax the tissue to mimic breathing, reproducing mechanical forces that can affect how lung cells respond to substances they encounter. In one experiment, researchers added bacteria to the air channel and white blood cells to the blood channel; the immune cells crossed the membrane and engulfed the bacteria, reproducing an inflammatory response.

The moment spoke to a trend, perhaps even the early days of a fundamental shift, away from the use of animals in toxicology and drug development. “It’s rare still,” says Maschmeyer, “but I think it’s going to be more and more frequent.”

A host of these kinds of alternatives to experiments on animals have been developed over the years. Collectively they’re known as NAMs, an acronym that stands, depending on whom you’re talking to, for new approach methodologies, novel alternative methods, or nonanimal methods. Most NAMs have yet to be rigorously tested, but early studies suggest their potential.

As NAMs have become more sophisticated, the question of how they will be implemented has become less about their technical qualities and more about the practical next steps needed to realize their potential. Validating NAMs—standardizing the systems, conducting head-to-head comparisons with animal experiments—is an enormous challenge. Moreover, simply outperforming animal models is necessary but not sufficient. The adoption of NAMs will require changes in policy, training, and culture.

“This transition process is much more complicated than you would think,” says Thomas Hartung, a toxicologist and director of the Center for Alternatives to Animal Testing at Johns Hopkins University. “It is more about change management than it is about the technology.”

For decades, animal advocates and many scientists have criticized both the morality and usefulness of experimenting on animals. An estimated 92 percent of all drugs that enter U.S. clinical trials fail to reach the market, sometimes for business reasons but often because the drugs prove ineffective or unsafe in ways that were not predicted by animal experiments. Failure rates are even higher in drugs for heart disease, cancer, and diseases of the brain.

These statistics don’t automatically mean that a reliance on animals is to blame. Flawed study designs are a problem too, and also the sheer confounding complexity of disease. But there’s little question that animals have made poor surrogates for many conditions. And just as animal experiments may mistakenly suggest efficacy or fail to predict harm in humans, they might also erroneously suggest that drugs are ineffective or harmful when they could actually work in humans. Some researchers argue that if aspirin or acetaminophen had been discovered after the advent of modern testing requirements, they might have been abandoned.

TissUse’s Humimic systems use microfluidic chips to culture human tissues and model interactions between organs. A researcher images tissues in a chip during an experiment [top], Humimic chips sit in a temperature-controlled unit [center], and a researcher prepares chips for use [bottom].TissUse (3)

Researchers developing NAMs have pushed these systems far beyond old-fashioned tissue cultures. The new technologies include organoids that more closely mimic the structure, composition, and function of human organs. More humanlike still are organ-on-a-chip systems; alongside Ingber’s lung-on-a-chip are brains, hearts, kidneys, and even placentas on a chip. As many as 10 such organs have been linked together, yielding multi-organ systems that promise to recapitulate many aspects of human physiology—not perfectly, but better than a mouse or a monkey would. Supporting these systems are computational simulations of organs and organisms, and also artificial intelligence tools that analyze data generated by other systems and inform future experiments in a high-powered iterative loop.

Yet even as studies piled up and some pharmaceutical companies started using NAMs in-house, the U.S. regulatory system governing drug developing and testing remained an obstacle to their wider use. NAM proponents were overjoyed, then, when in late 2022 the FDA Modernization Act 2.0 passed into law. It explicitly authorized the use of NAMs in the preclinical studies required of new drugs before they could enter human trials. Previous regulations had mandated animal testing; now the door was open to alternatives. It was a landmark moment. “That was something I didn’t expect to see in my life,” says Maschmeyer.

Although immediate in-the-lab impact was limited, the FDA’s decision was a harbinger of things to come. In 2025, the FDA pledged “to make animal studies the exception rather than the norm” for drug safety testing. Then, in September 2026, the agency followed up by issuing a rule that, if it takes effect, will replace references to “animal tests” in its drug-development regulations with the broader term “nonclinical tests.” The change makes explicit that validated alternatives such as human-cell systems, organs-on-chips, and computer models can be used when appropriate.

Also in 2025, the U.S. National Institutes of Health, the world’s largest public biomedical research funder, announced that researchers applying for grants to study animal models would also need to incorporate nonanimal research, such as real-world data or studies of NAMs. Meanwhile, the European Commission and United Kingdom have announced their own plans to phase out animal testing, and the intergovernmental Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development updated its influential guidelines to allow for expanded use of NAMs.

NAM proponents say these shifts were essential: If regulators won’t accept NAM results, there’s less incentive to adopt them, especially for researchers already working with animals. Maschmeyer says TissUse’s clients increasingly include scientists whose research has been focused on animals. “I see, within the last year, a change,” says Maschmeyer. “It’s more people who are working with animal models who now have to also add in vitro models.” She traces it mainly to the regulatory shift—a trend Ingber calls “game-changing.”

It’s not enough for regulators to say that NAMs can or should be used, though. Even more important is the regulatory apparatus dedicated to assessing how they should be used. This begins with their validation: the process by which experimental methodologies and devices are determined to be reliable and trustworthy. A prototype brain-on-a-chip designed to model a rare neurological disease might work fine in the lab that developed it—but to be validated, the system needs to work in the real world.

“You read about all the organ chips that come out of academic labs, which is great—but that’s not going to change their uptake by the FDA, because you have to get the same results anywhere in the world. It has to be a commercial product. It has to be mass-produced and meet very fine performance criteria,” says Ingber. For example, even minute variations in the hydrogels used as tissue scaffolds in organ chips can produce very different growth patterns.

Emulate’s Organ-Chips are connected to the company’s automated culture system, which supplies the chips with nutrients and controls the flow of fluid through them. Emulate

Workflows and procedures need to be uniform, too. One obstacle to wider use of vascularized tumor-on-a-chip platforms in developing cancer therapies, for example, is the different metrics used by different research groups to characterize blood-vessel function and geometry. Experimental guidelines, workflows, checkpoints, metrics, reporting criteria: All need to be standardized in order for researchers to compare their work and collaborate across platforms. Members of Ingber’s lab coach industry researchers on how to use chips developed by Emulate, a company founded by Ingber. But even with instructions, they still need help with the finer points of tending to stem-cell cultures.

When a NAM is ready for commercial use and researchers know how to use it, the most important test—whether it provides clinical benefit—still remains. A rare-disease organ chip might be reliable, but are the biomarkers it measures actually relevant? If so, are the algorithms that extrapolate chip results to the drug’s in-body effects truly predictive?

Microscopic images reveal the human tissues grown inside Emulate’s Organ-Chips. Bacteria, shown in magenta, interact with mucus and airway cells in a LungChip [top]; an IntestineChip develops structures resembling those that absorb nutrients in the small intestine [center]; and tiny hairlike cilia grow on cells in another LungChip, where they help move mucus and trapped particles out of the airway [bottom].Emulate (3)

Such questions have been answered for some NAMs. For example, a liver-on-a-chip system from Emulate correctly flagged about seven out of every eight drugs that had safely passed animal trials but proved toxic to human livers. A similar study was conducted by researchers from Oxford University and Janssen Pharmaceutica (later renamed Johnson & Johnson Innovative Medicine). That team showed that their computational simulations of human heart cells flagged compounds that caused a type of dangerous heart arrhythmia with 89 percent accuracy, compared to animal studies that were 75 percent accurate.

Such studies, however, are complicated and costly. Emulate’s study required 870 chips and the labor equivalent of 16 full-time employees working for 16 weeks—efforts far beyond the reach of the average lab. If the researchers wanted regulatory approval to use their chip to predict large-molecule drugs rather than the small-molecule drugs they tested, they would have needed to run another such study for that particular use. And comparable studies ostensibly need to be conducted for every commercially available NAM and every context in which they would be used—a vast undertaking. “That’s a challenge,” says Kathy Archibald, founder of Safer Medicines Trust, a United Kingdom–based group that considers animals to be poor models of human biology. “It takes too long and costs too much, and small companies can’t afford to do it.”

Ingber thinks that academic scientists need to collaborate more with industry researchers on NAMs, and that governments should fund those projects. He and other NAM proponents also stress the importance of having access to the necessary data: Without information from preclinical animal studies and human clinical trials, comparisons are difficult, but much of that data is now proprietary. Pharmaceutical companies and regulators need to share it, they say, and the FDA has called for an open-access repository of drug toxicity data. Hartung of Johns Hopkins also suggests that new animal experiments be run in parallel with NAMs, producing side-by-side comparisons.

To Christian Maass, a computational biologist at the German biotechnology company ESQlabs, NAMS are overdue for a showdown with animal models. His company makes “digital twin” systems in which data from organ chip systems inform whole-human simulations of drug outcomes and disease progression. “I love what we are doing,” says Maass, speaking not only of his company but of the whole field. But he adds that researchers have not yet provided “the evidence and the proof that we are doing better or as good as the animal models.”

Maass thinks that head-to-head comparisons are essential to good science. After all, if a NAM doesn’t outperform an animal model, or works best as a complement rather than a replacement, that needs to be known. He also believes such studies could convince skeptics. Maass mentions the debut of the iPhone, when people saw for the first time how well a phone could work without buttons. “That was an ‘aha!’ moment,” he says. But for NAMs, “that moment is still lacking.”

Even when those head-to-head comparisons are made, though, and regulations are appropriately changed, adoption can be slow. In the mid-1990s, researchers developed and validated the monocyte activation test—an assay that uses human blood cells to predict immune response—to replace the rabbit pyrogen test, which involves injecting a compound into a rabbit’s ear and monitoring the animal’s rectal temperature. But it wasn’t until 2010 that the European Pharmacopeia—the official Europe-wide standards for such testing—accepted the monocyte activation test as a replacement. And rabbits are still widely used for this test worldwide.

Why the slow pace of change? In part because updates to guidance documents referring to animal tests lagged behind, but also because of inertia within the culture and institutions of science. “The formal requirement may disappear, but the informal expectation persists,” says Kathrin Herrmann, a veterinary scientist and colleague of Hartung’s at the Center for Alternatives to Animal Testing. Regulators, grant reviewers, peer reviewers, journal editors—the human infrastructure of science—often still expect to see animal data and are unfamiliar with NAMs.

Herrmann is now overseeing a survey of early-career researchers working with, or trying to make the switch to, NAMs. “We consistently hear concerns that NAM-only proposals are perceived as risky by funders, that there is pressure to ‘add an animal experiment’ for credibility, that access to NAM infrastructure is limited, and that career trajectories become uncertain when departing from established animal models,” says Herrmann.

The vast majority of drugs entering clinical trials in the United States fail to reach FDA approval, with particularly high failure rates in some therapeutic areas.

Animal models are embedded in databases, training programs, and the very culture of research. Scientists who use animals may be reluctant to change; their identities as researchers are tied to animals and, more practically, they’ve spent their careers learning the techniques. A toxicologist who has used rats for decades might understandably look askance when asked to take a chance on unfamiliar chunks of polymer and stem cells—especially when human well-being, or millions of dollars, may ride on the choice. Likewise, an academic scientist whose career was built on animal models may not welcome NAMs; a switch may represent the loss of jobs for lab members whose expertise is no longer relevant. “I could see why it’s a hard thing for people to take it up,” says Ingber.

Education and training is vital, say NAM proponents. The NIH and FDA now offer resources for researchers interested in NAMs, as do their counterparts in other countries embracing the technologies. Herrmann helps run webinars where researchers and regulators learn to use and evaluate NAMs; Hartung’s modules on Coursera, the online learning platform, have been taken by about 12,000 students so far. “These trainees will set up their own labs. They will go to industry. They will replace the old guard,” says Joseph Wu, director of Stanford University’s Cardiovascular Institute.

Wu is also a cofounder of Greenstone Biosciences, a company that uses stem-cell-derived human tissues and AI to model disease and predict drug responses. He’s used that position to introduce researchers to NAMs, helping convince the company’s directors to freely share Greenstone’s large library of stem-cell lines with any academic researchers who want to use them. “I really believe that people should understand how this platform works,” says Wu. “At the end of the day, we’re just trying to advance science.”

With enough time—and funding, incentives, training, education, collaboration, and generational turnover—the research culture of drug development and safety testing may shift. Whether NAMs will be used in other areas of science, though, is an open question. Early-stage drug development and regulatory testing account for roughly 30 percent of animals used in experiments; the rest are used in basic biological research. Replacing those animals is less straightforward, but it may be possible: Ingber describes organ-on-a-chip-based insights into inflammatory bowel disease, preterm birth, and treating viral infections that couldn’t have been made in animals. Hartung calls the adoption of NAMs in toxicology a “lighthouse function,” helping guide the way for other types of research.

“Suddenly, all the dams have opened,” he says.

What a silly article. It wonders why people aren't training to use a product that, by the article's detailed admission, isn't fit-for-purpose yet and only focusses on individual organs when it does. There is, in fact, training in place for generic skills like nurturing cell cultures and it's good that governments have firmly indicated support for NAMs but they're a way off replacing animals yet. The article also consults with numerous activists which is why it's inaccurate - its own reference for drug attrition rates doesn't even contain any mention of animals!

It's always interesting to identify the barriers to adoption of a promising technology. I like how this story describes how scientists live and work in cultures and asks what it will take to update their cultural biases toward working with animals. There's also the question of how to compare studies that are often proprietary. Makes me wonder how we strike the balance between trade secrets and healthy openness.

#173. India becomes the latest country to report rogue AI agent activity

Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday.

The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.”

The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.”

This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal.

At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers. CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around.

Still, the Indian cases appear to be worse in one respect, which is what the agents saw: In Australia, OpenAI said it found no evidence its agents touched individuals’ medical or criminal records, even after they wrote files inside a Medicare statistics system, while in India, agents read personal data and confidential business records. And unlike earlier incidents, each disclosed by a single lab, India’s case involved agents from multiple providers.

CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations, or say whether the agents altered any systems. TechCrunch has reached out to CERT-In for more information.

For now, the closest parallel seems to be Anthropic’s July disclosure of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords.

In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own. The disclosures have left governments relying on AI companies causing these breaches to voluntarily disclose rogue AI agent activity.

#174. Moon phase today: What the Moon will look like on October 19, 2026

The Moon is getting closer to full, with most of its surface now lit up as it moves through the Waxing Gibbous phase. There's a lot more to see tonight than a week ago, so be sure to look up tonight.

As of Monday, Oct. 19, NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waxing Gibbous phase, with 56% of its surface visible.

Tonight, you should be able to spot the Mare Crisium and Mare Fecunditatis without any visual aids. If you have binoculars you'll also see the Endymion Crater, the Alphonsus Crater, and the Appenine Mountains. Plus, if you have a telescope, you'll also see the Apollo 15 and 16 landing spots, plus the Rima Hyginus.

The next Full Moon will take place on October 25 or 26, depending on your timezone.

The Moon takes around 29.5 days to travel around Earth, and its appearance changes throughout the month. As it moves around our planet, we see different amounts of its sunlit side, from a slim crescent to the quarter phases and eventually a Full Moon. It then begins the cycle again. As NASA explains, these phases are caused by the Moon's changing position relative to Earth and the Sun.

New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere)

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

#177. The Best LED Grow Lights for Houseplants This Winter (2026)

Summer is officially over, along with its allotment of free sunlight. You might be sad about this, but your indoor plants might be even sadder. A good LED grow light can replicate sunlight with full-spectrum light and day/night cycles, keeping plants lush and thriving even in a dark, windowless corner or basement.

I have no fewer than 40 houseplants in my home at any given time, as well as a fair number of grow lights, and what I've found to be important for a general consumer (i.e., someone not doing that kind of indoor grow) isn't necessarily certain colored light wavelengths but whether a grow light is easy to live with in your house.

Many grow lights are more or less going to serve the same purpose, so what you really need to know is this: Is the light so bright that it's disruptive? Does it require complicated installation? Is it easy for kids or pets to knock over? The grow lights recommended below are ones that WIRED staffers have lived with for months, if not years, and have found them both effective and easy to integrate into our lives.

Also be sure to check out our guides to the Best Indoor Gardening Systems, Best Gifts for Plant Lovers, and Best Kitchen Composters.

Photosynthetic photon flux Ddensity, or PPFD, expressed in micromoles per square meter per second (μmol/m²/s), is a measurement of how much light reaches your plant that's usable for photosynthesis. In general, the higher the plant's energy needs, such as producing a flower or a fruit, the higher the PPFD number you want. Though different lights have different height requirements given the plants they're made for, for standardization purposes, I measured the PPFD of each grow light at 18 inches with the Photone app and a light diffuser. Keep in mind these measurements are general and approximate.

Some of these grow lights I bought myself, with my own money, before I even began working at WIRED. Others were owned by staffers and recommended to me. I also have press samples from other guides I worked on, which I liked so much I ended up keeping around.

For the traditional grow lights, I tested them at home under normal-life conditions. I put them where they'd fit, tested their timers, and noted whether or not they were dimmable. I also measured each light's PPFD (see above) and noted whether certain lights could be daisy-chained for more extensive coverage.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

There are a lot of options out there for starting seeds and helping houseplants along in the winter, and many of them are bulky, fussy, or require elaborate hanging setups. This simple, 15-inch-long light from Vego sticks to its 3M adhesive mount with a magnet, so it's easy to take on and off and use with existing racks or, as I do, under a kitchen cabinet. Up to four Vego lights can be daisy-chained together, and the five preprogrammed modes (Seeds, Leafy, Fruits, Herbs, Microgreens) have varying intensities and automatic built-in off periods to simulate nighttime. I have not found this light especially disruptive, especially since it's easy to turn on and off with the button on the back.

WIRED commerce SEO director Stewart Savin used these lights to start her garden earlier this year and had 138 successful germinations across 144 seedling cells. ("The vast majority of those plants went on to have long lives in my garden after I hardened them off," she says.) Note that because this light can only go beneath a rack, shelf, or cabinet, it’s not inherently adjustable, and therefore is best for small plants (like seedlings) that aren’t going to grow especially tall.

This do-anything light, with a broad 2 x 3-foot head, can hang from the ceiling or swivel on its included stand where you need it. (Up to 20 of these lights can be daisy-chained.) Note that while the stand is useful, the 1-inch-diameter pole and offset base aren't the sturdiest, and it's easy to knock over, so I'd recommend hanging it if you have pets and small kids. I learned this the hard way while trying to revive a corn plant in a dark corner at the top of my stairs.

While this light is quite bright and potentially disruptive, it's easily dimmable via the remote, which hangs on a cord. At first I thought this was weird, but I found it extremely useful when the light was behind plants or in another hard-to-reach spot.

Also worth noting: While the stand height is supposed to be adjustable up to 72 inches, mine only goes up to about 64 inches, so it may not be the best option for extremely tall plants.

Vivosun is a long-respected brand among indoor growers, and its LumaLight panels are sturdy and all business. In fact, you'll be hard-pressed to find a higher-quality grow light for the price. This is not necessarily a light for casual houseplant parents—the 100-watt, 12 x 12-inch model weighs 4.4 pounds and needs to be attached to the ceiling or inside one of Vivosun's grow tents using the included adjustable ropes and carabiners.

If you're growing fruiting or flowering plants, though, this is the grow light you want—none of the other lights I tested even came close to its level of brightness. That said, you probably won't want it in a main living area, though it is dimmable via a dial on top. The LumaLight is IP65-rated for water resistance, and up to seven units can be daisy-chained if you need.

Former WIRED commerce director Martin Cizmar loved and recommended this grow light for his houseplants, which features three bendable heads on a clip you can attach to a table or shelf. It has a timer for three, nine, or twelve hours, plus a 10-foot cord if you need to place it away from an outlet. It also has warm and cool lighting options in addition to full spectrum, if you want to use it for ambiance (despite it looking, in my opinion, sort of like a creepy Freddy Krueger glove), plus 10 dimming modes. Right now, the base price on Amazon is for a two-pack.

If you don’t have the space or desire for a classic grow light, I’ve used all three options below for at least a year, and all resulted in happy plants.

This stylish structure is designed to fit Ferry-Morse seedling trays, but it could be limiting in many households given the square footage it requires (18 x 22 inches). I have, however, been using it for years to revive smaller houseplants and start seedlings for my indoor gardens.

This grow light is more decorative than anything—in fact, it makes a great wow-factor gift—and is a bit limited by its size and the height of the bottom panel (anything too small and you won't see it). However, I have one in my living room for cuttings and succulents, and anything I've put in it has thrived.

This full-spectrum light bulb can go in any compatible fixture, whether that’s a floor lamp or a table lamp. I even put it inside one of my overhead can lights to see if I could grow a tall corn plant in a no-light corner, and it worked.

Sansi Pot Clip-On Plant Lights for $30: These Sansi grow lights came in handy when I was living in a dark basement with minimal light for plants and hardly any space to store them. They clip directly onto the pot, so you don't need a dedicated stand or extra space, and they run on a three-, six-, or twelve-hour timer. The long cord (just over 6 feet) also helps in awkward or tight spaces. These lights helped my Monstera stay alive over winter with almost no natural light. Just be aware that the clips work best on thin pots, though you can also stick them on a chopstick or stake if needed, thanks to the adjustable gooseneck, depending on how tall your plant is. —Louryn Strampe

Ferry-Morse Indoor Grow Light Fixture for $40: This T5 fluorescent bulb is meant to sit in a fixture on little metal pole legs over a 10 x 20-inch seedling tray, but it seemed a bit rickety when I assembled it and set it up, and the light bulb wouldn’t turn on for me despite extensive troubleshooting.
