#179. Tesla Roadster Fires Up SpaceX Tech for ‘Flying Car’ Demo

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

I'm no rocket scientist, but I'm not sure the vehicle on display was a fully functional car that a human can drive.

On Thursday night in Texas, Tesla unveiled the long-awaited, production-intent second-generation of its Roadster electric sports car, showcasing a wild array of unbelievable party tricks, including driving upside down, performing aerial barrel rolls and hopping over other cars with the aid of SpaceX thruster and suction technology.

Surprisingly, the angular coupe that rolled onto the stage looked almost nothing like the curvaceous concept car that the automaker revealed almost nine years ago. Back in 2017, Tesla’s would-be halo car targeted a 1.9-second 0-60 time, 620 miles of range and production in 2020. That deadline came and went, and the Roadster was delayed multiple times as Tesla CEO Elon Musk shifted his focus from robotics to robotaxis to politics. The new-look Roadster seems to be built as a showcase of the combined might of the cross-owned, Musk-helmed tech giants: Tesla, xAI and SpaceX.

The demonstration opened with the new Roadster showcasing its angular Cybertruck-inspired design from an unconventional angle: by driving up a massive ramp and onto a wall where it was held vertically by suction fans. Tesla Vice President of Engineering Lars Moravy, on stage at the event, later said the underbody system can generate up to 2Gs of suction, allowing the EV to stick to the road — and apparently walls as well.

“I mean, this car really sucks,” Musk added. “This car could suck the chrome off a trailer hitch. It could suck a tennis ball through a hose pipe.”

Next, the Roadster backed up, stopped and accelerated toward the C-shaped ramp again, driving upside down momentarily before launching into the air, performing a barrel roll with the aid of 10 SpaceX cold gas thrusters located under and around the vehicle’s body — the same tech used to adjust the position and attitude of satellites and craft in zero-g space. As the night continued, the Roadster was shown hopping over a lineup of Tesla vehicles while performing another barrel roll, its thrusters causing the EV to pivot in midair and cushion its landing.

I’m no rocket scientist, but I’m not sure the vehicle on display was a fully functional car that a human can drive. The windows appeared completely opaque, hinting at no cockpit, and the aerobatics seemed implausible for a long-range EV, often laden with hundreds of pounds of battery. More likely, this was a stripped-down, remote-controlled mule with just enough battery onboard to complete the demo, and it’s highly unlikely that we’ll see a true production flying car equipped with this tech.

Aside from the promise of pirouetting over traffic, the Tesla Roadster’s on-road performance is said to be impressive.

In addition to the promised ability to corner at more than 2 g of lateral acceleration, the company says the electric sports car will complete a 0-60 mph sprint in 1 second, or 0.81 second with the aid of the SpaceX thrusters. The automaker says the top “Rocket” spec will be a limited-edition, “invite-only” model not available to the public. (I’d wager these “flying cars” wouldn’t exactly be street-legal and would be limited to closed-course shenanigans.) All of these figures are Tesla’s own and have yet to be independently confirmed.

Musk said the car would be offered in three trim levels, including the Rocket Roadster, and that Tesla is aiming for a production target sometime in 2028. Tesla did not reveal final prices, updated range estimates or any other relevant details, but reservations have opened at a hefty $50,000 apiece on the Roadster reservation page.

#181. Apple’s $299 HomeView smart hub is here: 8 highlights, including the wall model

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

As an Apple Home user, here’s what stands out about Apple's new smart home hub - and what I want to test firsthand.

Apple just announced it’s releasing the HomeView for purchase on Nov. 13, with preorders beginning today, Oct. 13. The new device acts as a smart home hub, complete with a touchscreen, smart speaker, Siri AI, and a security camera dashboard.

Also: How Apple’s video doorbell privacy compares to Ring, Wyze, and Blink

The HomeView is designed to work with Siri AI as the brain of your Apple smart home. As a central smart home hub, the HomeView competes directly with the Amazon Echo Show and Google Nest Hub.

The Apple HomeView is available for preorder at $299 on Oct. 13, with general availability on Nov. 13.

With Siri AI, the Apple smart home is finally getting the generative AI upgrade we’ve wanted for the past couple of years. As a loyal Apple Home user and smart home devices reviewer, I’ve had to watch Siri fall behind Alexa+ and Gemini for Home in my house.

In a world where generative and agentic AI is king, Siri has become obsolete.

Also: Forget Wi-Fi: Apple is betting on Bluetooth with its new home devices

With HomeView, Siri AI will be capable of holding natural conversations, handling multiple commands at once, maintaining context across personal devices, and answering general questions unrelated to your smart home.

The Apple HomeView can recognize up to six people and automatically switch to their personalized home screens when one approaches the device.

“It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home,” Greg Joswiak, Apple’s SVP of worldwide marketing, said in a press release.

Apple claims that the HomeView keeps everyone’s information private and secure. The device uses the built-in camera and presence sensors to detect when someone is approaching it and allows each user to customize their home screen apps and widgets.

Users can also set up shared photo albums and music for others to enjoy in the home.

Apple said the HomeView works with Apple Home accessories and supports Matter, but it’s unclear whether it’ll act as a Thread border router. It’s also unclear whether the new HomePod mini supports Thread, as its predecessor does.

Also: Google Home Speaker vs. Amazon Echo Dot Max

You can use the Apple HomeView as a Matter and a HomeKit hub in your home. This means that you can connect any Matter-certified smart home devices and any others that feature the “Works with Apple Home” label.

Aside from serving as your smart home hub, the HomeView also provides extra peace of mind for your safety and security. Like the HomePod, this device can detect the sound of smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and subsequently send notifications to the user’s iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch.

Acting as a smart home dashboard, the Apple HomeView can display up to 9 camera feeds at once, giving you a complete look at what is happening throughout your home on a single screen. You can easily view your HKSV (HomeKit Secure Video) feeds on HomeView, provided you have an iCloud+ subscription and compatible cameras.

Like the Amazon Echo devices, HomeView makes it easier than before to stay in touch with your family at home and everywhere else. It can handle FaceTime calls, check locations with Find My, and send Intercom messages to other Apple devices.

Apple’s Intercom feature has been notoriously unreliable in my experience, so I resort to Amazon Alexa’s announcement features to share quick notes with my family. Unfortunately, Intercom messages can take minutes to arrive from one device to another in my home, so we’ve given up on it entirely.

#182. Let's Encrypt is adding two additional remote perspectives for domain validation

Let's Encrypt is adding two new remote perspectives for domain validation. This change is motivated by the fact that increased perspectives provide more domain validation security and is required by the Baseline Requirements which is quoted below. Increasing the number and coverage of our domain validation perspectives improves visibility and protection against BGP attacks.

BR 3.2.2.9 Multi Perspective Issuance Corroboration Effective 2026-12-15, the CA MUST implement Multi-Perspective Issuance Corroboration using at least five (5) remote Network Perspectives. The CA MUST ensure that the requirements defined in Quorum Requirements Table are satisfied, and the remote Network Perspectives that corroborate the Primary Network Perspective fall within the service regions of at least two (2) distinct Regional Internet Registries. If the requirements are not satisfied, then the CA MUST NOT proceed with issuance of the Certificate.

During domain validation, this means that we will make seven total validation requests, one from the primary datacenter and six from remote perspectives (previously four). For validation to succeed, the primary server and a quorum of remote perspectives must receive the correct challenge response. This makes it more difficult for attackers to hijack validation requests. To learn more about multi-perspective domain validation, please see our earlier blog post when Let's Encrypt first added new perspectives.

We expect little to no impact to users. Let's Encrypt will begin performing domain validation with the new regions in staging on Tuesday, October 27th, 2026. Assuming all goes well, we will do the production rollout on Tuesday, November 10th, 2026. Updates will be posted in this thread.

According to my Apple Watch, I'm sleeping deeper, staying asleep longer, and waking up refreshed. A sleep doctor explains why this simple habit works so well

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Deep sleep (also known as slow-wave or N3 sleep) is one of four sleep stages we cycle through every night. It's where your body carries out repair work and produces high levels of growth hormone. Essentially, it's where a lot of 'the magic happens'. For most healthy adults, deep sleep should make up 10-20% of their overall nightly sleep.

According to my Apple Watch 12, deep sleep makes up around 23% of my nightly sleep on average, which is already in the upper tier. However, I'm still dealing with stress-fuelled 3 a.m. wake-ups, and because deep sleep is associated with a higher tolerance to stress, I've been wondering if more deep sleep is the answer to helping me sleep through the night.

To test this, I've adopted a new, simple 10-minute daily habit that science says can help you get more deep sleep. After just 6 days this habit has helped me go from 23% to 28% deep sleep (roughly an extra 38 minutes) a night.

The habit? Daily exercise. In fact, a study by the University of Texas indicates that getting as little as 10 minutes of moderate to vigorous exercise per day could help you get more deep sleep.

Here Dr. Jeffrey Durmer, a neuroscientist, neurologist, and sleep medicine physician explains how it works and why you should try it if you keep waking up through the night.

At first, I started a daily exercise regime by accident. Walking my son to school four times a week is a 30 minute leisurely round trip through a beautiful wooded valley, or a 15 minute white-knuckle cycle ride that leaves me gasping for air on the uphill leg. Guess which one he prefers.

People who don’t usually exercise may see an especially strong effect, because even a short and intense workout raises their adenosine levels beyond what they normally experience

Once he went back to school in September, our twice-daily cycle ride commenced. And, in a way, I was happy to get the workout. I know I should make time for exercise, but I rarely do — so this felt like a routine I could stick to. Not that I had much of a choice. However, I soon noticed that these short bursts of exercise were having a positive impact on my sleep. Falling and staying asleep is something that I can struggle with, but I found myself feeling ready for sleep come bedtime and, occasionally, waking up feeling more refreshed than usual.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

When I read the study this week that linked a minimum of 10 minutes of daily exercise to longer time spent in deeper sleep, I wanted to compare that to my own experience.

I track my sleep with an Apple Watch, so I was able to see that, compared to a sedentary period in August before starting my daily exercise regime, my time spent in deep sleep had increased by 5% on average. That sounds like a paltry amount, but for me 5% equates to an extra 38 minutes of deep sleep per night. According to Dr. Durmer, there's a good reason why I — someone who previously rarely exercised — had such a significant uptick in time spent in deep sleep. "This study shows that even a small amount of exercise can increase deep non-REM sleep, the stage that drives much of the brain and body’s restoration," explains Dr. Durmer, Chief Medical Officer of Happy Health."People who don’t usually exercise may see an especially strong effect, because even a short and intense workout raises their adenosine levels beyond what they normally experience."

"Exercise and sleep have a two-way, virtuous relationship: better sleep improves performance, and regular exercise improves sleep," explains Dr. Durmer, who works with elite athletes to help them sleep better in order to unlock better physical performance.Here, we take a closer look at how regular exercise can help increase the time spent in deep sleep.

From the moment we wake up, our sleep pressure begins to build, enabling us to fall asleep at the right time.

Also referred to as our homeostatic sleep dive or sleep hunger, sleep pressure is largely dictated by a neurotransmitter called adenosine.

"When we exercise, our bodies burn ATP, our main energy source, and that releases adenosine," says Dr. Durmer.

"Adenosine naturally builds up over the day, and as it accumulates in the brain, it activates receptors that make us sleepy. Exercise speeds up that build-up, which helps us fall asleep."As exercise becomes a habit, it strengthens both the daily adenosine cycle and the regularity of sleep and wake times, reinforcing the virtuous cycle between the two."

For me, stress is a big disrupter of my sleep, making it harder to both fall and stay asleep. However, as Dr. Durmer explains, exercise can help reduce stress for better sleep. In turn, we sleep better and we're better equipped to deal with stress, which perpetuates the positive relationship between sleep and exercise.

"Exercise also shifts the body toward parasympathetic, or 'rest and digest,' dominance afterward, so the early stages of sleep tend to be deeper and less disrupted," says Dr. Durmer."That deep non-REM sleep is when the body does much of its repair work: releasing growth hormone, calming inflammation, supporting immune function, and improving insulin sensitivity.

"Keeping a regular sleep-wake schedule adds to these benefits by supporting energy storage in the muscles, cardiovascular health, and nervous system balance."

I cycle my son to school in the morning, come rain or shine. In addition to the exercise, part of the benefit of this on my sleep is the sunlight exposure. This helps cement my circadian rhythm, which is my body's internal clock. Dr. Durmer explains that the harder you work, the better the sleep benefit. But if you can only do one thing, spending time in natural light in the morning is the most important, as this helps regulate key sleep hormones."Any exercise is better than none for improving sleep and keeping a regular sleep-wake cycle," he explains. "On days you can’t work out, get outside in the sunlight, especially in the morning, and take a short walk to keep your body moving."

#187. Apple keeps making the Phone app better; here’s how

9to5Mac is brought to you by Tello Mobile. Switching to Tello Mobile can bring the cost of your plan down to as little as $5 a month, or an unlimited plan for just $25 a month, all on America’s largest 5G network. See all of the available plans at tello.com.

You might not think about it often, but the Phone app on your iPhone keeps getting more powerful. Here are two features you can use today, plus one coming next month in iOS 27.

With iOS 26 last year, Apple added a new feature called Hold Assist to the Phone app. When you’re on a call, the feature can detect when you’ve been placed on hold. Then you’ll see a pop-up you can tap to enable Hold Assist.

When the person on the other end of the call returns, your iPhone will notify you.

Here’s how Apple describes Hold Assist: “Automatically detect when you are placed on hold, so you can step away. iPhone will then notify you when it’s time to pick up.”

You can enable Hold Assist by going to the Settings app, scrolling down to Apps, then choosing Phone. In this menu, you’ll see a toggle: “Hold Assist Detection” that you can turn on.

Call Screening is another new feature in the Phone app, introduced as part of iOS 26 last year. Here’s how Apple describes it: “Calls from unsaved numbers will be asked for more information before iPhone rings.”

When someone from an unsaved number calls you, Call Screening kicks in and asks who they are and why they are calling. You can then view their explanation right on your iPhone’s Lock Screen and choose to answer or send them to voicemail.

In an age of ever-increasing spam calls, Call Screening is a must-enable feature. You can find it in Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Phone.

Finally, Call Context is a new feature coming to the Phone app with iOS 27. It’s an Apple Intelligence feature that proactively surfaces relevant information when you call a business.

For example, if you call an airline to change your flight, Call Context will automatically find your confirmation code in Mail and show it on the screen while you’re on the call. If you call a company about a recent order you placed, it will proactively surface the order number and other relevant details.

Call Context is a well-done feature that uses AI to proactively help you during what is often a frustrating process. It also does so with privacy in mind, and only looks at who you’re calling, not what you’re saying, to show the necessary information.

Call Context is available on iPhone 15 Pro and later.

I try to avoid using the Phone app at all costs, but unfortunately it’s a necessary evil. These new Phone app features at least make the experience more enjoyable. In particular, I’m a huge fan of Call Screening. I get an absurd number of spam calls every day, and Call Screening really helps me preserve my sanity.

What are your favorite Phone app features? Do you use any of the new options? Let us know down in the comments.

#188. Surprise! Meta and Apple Worked Together on a New Open-Source AI Model

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Think of Muse Spark Open as the result of Meta and Apple's enemies-to-lovers arc.

It’s the enemies-to-lovers trope, tech edition. Two tech titans have teamed up to create a new open-weights AI model. Meta is the owner of the new AI model, called Muse Spark Open, and it worked with Apple’s hardware team to ensure the AI model can run efficiently on the M5 Mac Studio Ultra.

Muse Spark Open is an open-weights AI model, which means developers can understand how it works and customize it to their needs. It has a robust 42 billion active parameters and a context window of a million tokens, with multimodal capabilities that Meta says are good at agentic and coding tasks. Translation: It’s a big model that can handle different kinds of tasks, including powering AI agents, aimed at engineers and developers. The model’s weights are publicly available now on Hugging Face under Meta’s Muse Model license.

Note that if you want to run the model on Apple computers, it requires two Mac Studios with M5 Ultra chips. Right now, the base price for a device with the M5 Ultra chip (with 96GB of memory and 1TB of storage) starts at $5,499 each. If you want the device to have the full 512GB of RAM — which isn’t even on sale yet — it’s going to be far more expensive. Safe to say, as 256GB of RAM adds $4,000 to the price, that it would be a pricey investment.

Meta and Apple could not have taken more divergent paths in the AI race, or even in the pre-AI era. Apple has been hesitant to throw itself into AI development, whereas Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg couldn’t push his company fast enough, burning through billions of dollars to do so. Apple’s decades-long focus on privacy, while not perfect, is existentially at odds with Meta’s entire targeted advertising business model reliant on collecting as much information on its users as possible. Remember when Apple offered iPhone owners the ability to opt out of app tracking and cost Meta $10 billion in 2022?

But this new collaboration is a clear sign that both companies are determined to travel down their set paths in the AI race: Meta, to build open-weights AI models, and Apple, to build the hardware needed to run AI. Or as Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, told Axios, “We’re excited for mommy and daddy to be playing nice again.” In X posts, Zuckerberg put it a bit more diplomatically; new Apple CEO John Ternus focused on the reason for the team-up, namely on-device AI.

On-device AI is a way to run AI models and tools without relying on a cloud service. It requires a little more setup than simply opening up your ChatGPT app, but developers and businesses can configure the AI system to keep their data more secure. Depending on the scale of the operation and hardware used, it can also be a cheaper, long-term option than continually paying a monthly subscription.

It’s not totally surprising to see Apple taking part in AI development, despite its own meager AI tools. The Californian company has carved out a place in the AI race through its hardware. At the beginning of 2026, when tech circles were excitedly using the OpenClaw agent, Apple’s Mac Minis were the computer of choice for many AI fans. During Apple’s hardware launches, including the M5 MacBook Air in March, Apple boasted that its chip tech could power impressive performance, and CNET’s testing mostly verifies those promises. The Mac Studio, released in August, is the latest example of Apple focusing on hardware capable of running compute-intensive AI tasks.

#189. These 12 Automatic Cat Feeders Were the Best We Tested in 2026

An automatic cat feeder may just change your life. No more begging at 4 am. Plus, it can give you peace of mind while you're away from your fur baby. As seen with the rise of automatic litter boxes and pet tracking, technology has made it so we can closely monitor our pets without doing a lot of the manual labor normally involved.

Gravity-fed automatic dry-food dispensers were invented nearly a century ago, but today most automatic cat feeders use Wi-Fi and connect to a phone app that lets you set a schedule or feed on demand from afar, all while monitoring your pet’s eating habits. Newer models have taken this tech further, like the Petkit YumShare Dual-Hopper 2 Automatic Feeder With Camera ($170), which has a built-in, AI-enabled camera that analyzes the remaining food in the bowl and stops dispensing to prevent overfeeding. Automatic wet-food dispensers—our top pick in this category is the Petlibro Polar Smart Wet Feeder ($170)—are relatively new, often using ice packs or mini-refrigeration cooling systems to keep the food as fresh as possible.

Automatic feeders are also helpful for pet parents who want to monitor their pets’ health, maintain specialized schedules, or foster healthier eating habits. (A customizable automatic cat feeder can help with the endless gorging-vomiting cycle many cats struggle with.) Nearly all of the automatic cat feeders on this list are marketed toward cats, but some can be used with smaller dogs, and I’ve noted these below.

Check out our related guides, like the Best Automatic Litter Boxes, Best Cat Water Fountains, Best Smart Cat Collars, and Best Pet Cameras.

Updated October 2026: I've added the Neakasa Riko Automatic Cat Feeder and Petlibro Granary 2 Vision and removed the out-of-stock Cheerble Match G1. I've also updated prices and links throughout.

This model is an upgrade of one of my favorite models below, the Petkit YumShare Dual-Hopper Automatic Feeder With Camera, with added AI features. It offers a crystal-clear video feed, night vision, customizable meal calls, and a dual-hopper for two types of food. Through the connected app, you can set feeding schedules or feed on demand from both tanks, use two-way audio, and monitor the feeder from your phone. Unlike most other brands, the AI-enabled camera doesn't require a subscription and can identify up to 20 pets and log when each has eaten. The camera also uses AI to analyze the remaining food in the bowl and will stop dispensing to prevent overfeeding.

This feeder performed very well throughout testing, and I appreciate that you don't need to opt into the subscription plan for AI to recognize different pets. However, I still think the connected Petkit app isn't as reliable or as easy to use as Petlibro's app.

This updated Petlibro Polar Wet Food Feeder solves nearly every gripe I had with other automatic feeders for storing wet food—it’s essentially a mini-fridge that keeps food fresh, and it’s connected to an app where you can schedule and customize feedings and keep a feeding log. Food is dispensed into three wide, shallow stainless-steel bowls, which means less chance of whisker fatigue with wide bowls or feline acne from bacteria-harboring plastic. When it’s time to feed, the cover slides back from the hole, revealing the food beneath.

The refrigerator uses thermoelectric cooling and stays at 50 degrees Fahrenheit or below. Cooling is paused 30 minutes before scheduled feeding time to ensure it’s at the ideal temperature. The bowls are now numbered, so you can easily match feedings to specific bowls in the app. Through the app, you can adjust schedules, manually feed on demand, and control how long it's open—there's even a sensor to make sure it doesn’t close while your kitty is feeding. This is the best automatic wet feeder on the market, in my opinion—I even bought a second one for my other cat.

Note: For certain Amazon locations, this feeder is marked as a “Frequently Returned Item.” I haven't experienced any issues with reliability or performance, and it's worked well for the past six-plus months of testing.

This model is the new-and-improved version of one of my long-standing favorite models below, the Petlibro Granary Smart Camera Feeder. As before, it still has an excellent connected app for scheduling and monitoring feedings, two-way audio, and a 1080p camera with night vision. But this new version also has a built-in bowl scale to track levels and prevent overfeeding, an AI-powered camera that differentiates pets and tracks eating habits, and “smart refill mode” that keeps the bowl filled automatically.

These improvements make this feeder one of the best on the market. I love that it now has a built-in scale (that measures food within one gram) to prevent overfeeding, which is especially helpful when you're out of town and may not be monitoring your pets' eating habits as closely. The multi-pet recognition is also helpful because, through the app, you can look back at the log and see exactly who is eating and how much they are eating. However, some of the cooler features, like AI camera multi-pet recognition logged by each pet and enhanced eating insights, are only available with the paid subscription service ($96 to $160/year). During testing, the only issues I ran into were that the live camera footage was slow to load and sometimes gave me a “timed out” error message, a bright light automatically turned on when the cat approached at night, and there is no window to visually see how much kibble is left in the tank.

I've never tested an automatic feeder like this. If you've read my cat water fountains guide, you know how crucial it is to keep your cat hydrated to avoid potentially lethal UTIs and blockages (especially in males, like my cat Basil). The Riko has a brand-new design that turns freeze-dried food into wet, soup-like meals at feeding time. Through the connected app, Riko uses the information you provide about your cat(s) to personalize a feeding plan of up to 20 meals a day, with portions ranging from 0.04 to 0.7 ounces—this is also ideal, since experts generally agree that cats prefer smaller, frequent meals. You can also customize the water-to-food ratio, adjustable from 1:1 to 5:1, with a traditional “mix” that grinds freeze-dried and adds water; water-only mode; and food-only mode, which just grinds the freeze-dried pieces. The Riko is only compatible with freeze-dried food and treats measuring less than 0.6 x 1 inch in length/width (more info can be found in the product specifications section). I used Smalls freeze-dried food ($24) during testing.

During testing, I primarily followed Riko's suggestions for how often and how much to feed, which ended up being about once an hour. I liked that if you didn't want to plan it yourself, you could put it on autopilot like this, and that there are also options for whether you want it to be a wet mix or not. It's a great concept in theory, and fresh, hydrating meals are preferable to kibble. However, my cats didn't like the rehydrated food and refused to eat it, so I'd make sure your cats like this style before buying. (My cats had eaten the Smalls brand in its freeze-dried form previously and liked it.)The whole grinding and rehydrating process takes about five minutes and produces a noticeable grinding noise. Then, a little jingle, and the bowl automatically pops out with the chunky soup. I love this fully automated system and appreciate that Riko is attempting to address cats' dehydration problems. It's just a bummer my (very spoiled) cats didn't take to it.

Designed especially for cats, but small dogs could use.

Although this isn’t the most expensive automatic feeder on this list, it’s reliable, tech-savvy, and highly customizable. It's controlled via an app and dispenses food from its 5-liter capacity based on the feeding schedule you create. It has a 1080p HD camera with night vision so you can watch and hear your pet eat even when far away, and you can communicate with them via the speaker. Through the Petlibro app (for Android and iOS), you set up a feeding schedule (up to six meals a day) or feed snacks in your desired amount, from one-twelfth of a cup to four cups. The app is easy to use, with extremely customizable feeding plans and meals you can label individually. Our runner-up pick below, the Petkit YumShare Dual-Hopper Automatic Feeder with Camera, is similar in many ways, but the app is a little more intuitive, reliable, and user-friendly on this one (plus we love the built-in camera to spy while afar).

This model is being phased out in favor of the newer Petkit model above, but you can still find it on third-party sites, and it's still one of my favorite models I've ever tested.

This automatic feeder is essentially the same model as above, but it doesn't include an AI-enabled camera. It does have an HD camera with a 140-degree viewing angle, infrared night vision, two-way audio with customizable meal calls, and a dual hopper that lets you store and dispense two different types of food. Through the connected app, you can customize and set feeding schedules for the two separate tanks, give snacks, and monitor the feeder from your phone. Plus, the camera will analyze the remaining food in the bowl and stop dispensing (to prevent overfeeding).

I love that the dual hopper can store different types of dry kibble and freeze-dried food and dispense them separately. I recommend saving your moolah and just going with this model—unless you need AI to identify your cats, you can spot the difference between cats through the camera yourself for $70-ish less.

This is a sleek, more pared-down pet feeder from Petlibro. Although it has a simpler design and smaller capacity (2 liters) than others tested, this auto feeder features a hygienic stainless-steel bowl, a rotor design, a tight seal, and a button that opens the top to keep kibble fresh (and is kitty-tamper-proof). It connects to Petlibro's easy-to-use app, where you can schedule up to 10 meals a day in one to 16 portions, or feed on demand. Plus, unlike the other Petlibro feeders I've tested, this goes down to a super small 1/24-cup dispense amount, which makes it easy if you just want to dispense a small snack.

It also has a rechargeable battery that lasts for up to 30 days, so you have freedom in movement or placement. Unlike many others on the list, it doesn't offer two-way audio or monitoring of when each pet is fed, and it only works on 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi. But if you're looking for a cheaper, more basic auto-feeder (and don't need a camera or audio), I'd recommend this model.

It can be used with cats or very small dogs.

This automatic feeder doesn't have all the bells and whistles, but it's a solid, inexpensive dual feeder. There’s an app where you can customize feeding plans for up to six meals a day, each meal being 1/12 of a cup. It also has a front knob to plan meals if you don't want to use the app. (I found the app could be very buggy, and I often relied on manually programming.) You can also record a 10-second meal message to play before mealtimes. It can be plugged in or run on four AA batteries in case of a power outage, for extra peace of mind. I love that the bowls are almost a foot apart to give more space for my greedy cats, and the hygienic stainless-steel inserts can be removed for easier cleaning. The app is very bare-bones and could use work, but this dual feeder worked reliably, and I consider it a great deal at this price point.

This automatic feeder features dual storage, a built-in camera, two-way audio, and a connected app for scheduling and on-demand feeding. It’s AI-enabled to differentiate between pets and identify their behavior. Setup is super easy and takes only a few minutes; then you’ll need to upload pictures of your cats for their profiles and set up customized feeding plans for up to three pets, in increments of ⅛ of a cup. In theory, you can create customizable feeding plans for each pet, but there’s no way to ensure each cat gets their own portions and doesn’t steal the others'. Plus, you can’t just set up a general daily plan; you have to set a schedule for each individual pet.

The AI didn’t distinguish or label my cats in the video feed, which I found odd, but it did identify and log behaviors it recorded, such as feeding, napping, and walking. Through the app, you can watch highlights and activity logs, communicate via the speaker, and feed on demand. It was cool to watch past video feeds and see the labels the AI creates based on observed behaviors, but the promised custom, individualized feeding plans underdeliver.

I was pleasantly surprised by this relatively affordable automatic feeder. It has a scale at the bottom of the stainless-steel bowl, which ensures your pet gets the exact right amount of food. It'll even adjust how much it dispenses based on how much is left in the bowl, helping prevent overeating. The feeder includes anti-jam technology, low-food-detection sensors, and a backup battery in case of a power failure.

From the app, you can schedule and adjust feedings with an optional meal call recording, and it logs when and how much your pet has eaten. This is super helpful for tracking and understanding your cats' eating habits. But because I have two cats, the tracking feature isn't as reliable, as the feeder doesn't know which cat was eating when it logs. For that reason, some of the cooler aspects of monitoring feedings with this feeder work best for single-pet homes.

For this feeder, the pet wears a collar with a tag that allows the feeder’s lid to open only when that tag is present. When the sensor in the pad in front is activated, the stainless-steel food bowl (which is removable for washing and dishwasher-safe) is uncovered, and the cover retracts over the kibble when the cat leaves, ensuring that only the chosen pet with the collar can access the food. Through the app, you can create up to 10 feeding schedules, and the amounts can be modified anytime, including on-demand feeding. The automatic lid is customizable too. In the app, you can leave the lid in “open mode” or adjust how long it stays open after your pet walks away from it.

Overall, I think this is a nearly perfect device for a particular kind of pet owner. It works best for a cat in a dog home where the owner doesn’t want the dog getting into the cat’s food; if each pet in the home has an RFID feeder; if one particular cat has special dietary needs; or if you have a multi-cat home with an aggressive eater. In these cases, I truly think this product would be a life-changer. (If you get a One RFID for each pet, it’s recommended that you space them at least 10 inches apart to avoid any interference.)

It can be used with cats or very small dogs.

This expensive, techy automatic feeder has buttons and an app that let you control feeding schedules and portion sizes, including monitoring levels to make sure there is enough (when the food level is low, it alerts you via the app and via a light on top of the feeder). I love how customizable meals are: You can set multiple schedules for different days of the week, and it dispenses anywhere from one-eighth of a cup to half a cup of food. It also has gravity mode, where the feeder checks levels every six hours and dispenses food automatically if the bowl is empty.

The app is intuitive and easy to use, with customizable settings, and it tracks every time a cat is fed. Although the plastic food bowl is food-safe and BPA-free, plastic is still prone to harboring bacteria, and I’d prefer stainless steel. (Whisker has a stainless-steel insert for $20 or a glass bowl insert for $30.) I can’t really find any other faults in this feeder—it has worked perfectly and just feels sleek and elevated.

Oneisall 2-in-1 Automatic Cat Feeder and Water Dispenser for $60: Generally, I'm a fan of all the Oneisall pet products I've tested. While they aren't the most technologically advanced, they are always reliable and affordable. This model is relatively simple. To set up, you'll need to attach the bowl supports and dishwasher-safe stainless-steel bowls, fill the water and kibble compartments, and plug in. This model runs on corded power but also has an optional 4 AA batteries in case of a power outage. There is no connected app. You'll just set the clock and adjust meal settings, and you can schedule one to six meals per day with adjustable portions, from one to 10 portion sizes. I don't love having food and water so close, since cats prefer them separate to prevent cross-contamination in the wild. I always recommend automatic pet fountains instead for a fresh source of water, but if you don't have a lot of space, are on a budget, and need a temporary solution for getting fresh water to your kitty while you're out of town, the gravity-fed water system helps keep water relatively fresh (plus, the translucent tank makes it easier to check water levels). I'd recommend this basic option if you're on a budget and need a temporary solution for when you're out of the house (and don't mind not having a connected app).

Closer Pets C200 2-Meal Automatic Pet Feeder for $50: This automatic feeder is super simple, which is both its weakness and its strength. It’s essentially two shallow plastic containers with stainless-steel inserts (both dishwasher-safe) and tamper-resistant lids that lock and automatically open using an old-school egg-style timer that runs on an AA battery rather than electricity. Although the container has an ice pack to keep the wet food cool, after one night it lost virtually all of its coolness. There’s a lid-link clip attachment, a small piece of plastic that links the lids to ensure they open at the same time, which is super helpful for owners of two cats like me. I wish the timer were electric so I could program it to the exact time I want it to open, rather than guesstimating the timing on the little marks. However, this is a simple solution to help make sure both my cats are given wet food without me having to wake up at the crack of dawn.

Oneisall Cordless WiFi Automatic Cat Feeder for $53: I had high hopes for this cordless feeder, which boasts a rechargeable battery with a 100-day life and an integrated app, but it's just too unreliable. Through the app, you can program up to 10 daily meals (in 1-12 portions each), monitor pets' eating habits, and customize meal calls. Unlike other apps, you can't choose portion size; instead, you have to multiply the number of servings. The app gave me constant problems and would often disconnect from the feeder and be unable to reconnect to WiFi. Luckily, I was able to program meals via the screen and buttons, but it would've been much nicer if the app had worked reliably.

Catit Pixi Smart 6-Meal Feeder for $86: Like others on this list, the Catit Pixi wet and dry feeder uses ice packs to keep wet food fresh and rotates meals among six compartments on a set schedule. The schedule can be programmed via the app or adjusted on the feeder itself. At this price point, the app shouldn’t be this limited and glitchy. The schedule is available in military time only, and the app is extremely limited—you can only set the meal schedule for the same day. When I wanted to do only two to three meals a day spread over two days, I had to reschedule the meals for every new day. The feeder didn't keep it cold enough to spread the meals out, and the wet food was not at a safe eating temperature. At this price point, just get the Petlibro Polar wet feeder.

Catit Pixi Smart Cat Feeder for $112: Kibble is stored in the feeder’s body, but it lacks a window to visually check food levels. The meal-planning calendar shows only a week at a time, and although it should repeat daily based on the schedule, I found that some days had no schedule despite setting one up. The Pixi also doesn’t tell you how much food was dispensed; it just refers to it as a “portion”—I manually measured and found the portion was less than a tablespoon of kibble. After using it continuously for more than a month, I found it was extremely glitchy and almost never reliably stuck to the programmed schedule, sometimes skipping meals altogether. This feeder is potentially dangerous, and I'd caution pet parents against relying on it.

Closer Pets C500 for $77: This automatic wet and dry feeder can schedule up to four pre-portioned meals (and one meal given manually) and opens them on a timer using three AA batteries (sold separately). The user sets the four times they want the bowls, which have ice packs underneath, to rotate. The bowls are quite deep and narrow, and they aren’t super easy for cats to reach, which could cause whisker fatigue. Although there are two relatively large ice packs, when I checked on the feeder after a night’s sleep, the packs weren’t very cold. This may be OK for kibble, but wet food was kept at unsafe temperatures, and my cats couldn't reach all of the food.

Automatic feeders are great for pet owners who want to help manage their pets’ weight and monitor eating patterns. Plus, they allow for a lot more control and precision, so owners can learn exactly how much their cat is eating and when. Because cats are naturally more nocturnal, many have the annoying habit of waking you up in the early hours, demanding food. These feeders allow you to set up a schedule that fits their schedule better without inconveniencing yours.

Of course, it’s never recommended to leave pets alone for long periods, but these automatic feeders give more peace of mind and are much healthier for your pet than leaving a huge amount of food out for free-feeding while you're away for the night. Simply put, it’s an easier way to feed and monitor your cat’s health with less work for you, the human.

I have two rescue cats, ages 4 and 5, and they eat two wet-food meals a day, along with small amounts of dry kibble throughout the day. Vets (and TikTokkers) have successfully persuaded me to move toward a primarily wet-food diet, which has a higher water content. This provides more moisture in their diet, which helps with potentially life-threatening problems like UTIs, which are especially prevalent in male cats. I still like to give smaller dry-food meals throughout the day to satisfy their need for crunch.

For dry food, I use Hill’s Science Diet, and for wet food, I use Friskies Shreds. (Yes, only Shreds. Fellow cat owners will understand.)

I set up the feeders, noting ease of setup, potential problems, and app navigation. I also tested various schedules and manual feedings in the app, documenting any issues. I used each feeder for at least a week, if not longer.

Although cats are generally considered less high-maintenance than dogs, it’s still not advisable to leave your cat alone for extended periods. In dire circumstances, you can leave a cat alone for 24 to 48 hours with scheduled feedings and a clean water source, but it’s not ideal—especially for cats with health issues, kittens younger than a year, or very elderly cats. Although these feeders are automatic and meals can be scheduled in advance for multiple days, our pets still need their human pals around for enrichment, care, and, well, love.

#190. Dutch tax authorities cancel Microsoft 365 cloud rollout – and turn toward open source

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Another European move toward digital sovereignty has curtailed adopting the US workplace suite.

The Netherlands’ Tax and Customs Administration has abandoned its planned Microsoft 365 public-cloud rollout.

Why? The reasons were clear at the Open Source Summit Europe conference, where the Linux Foundation (LF) released the 2026 State of Open Source in Europe. In it, the nonprofit, pro-open-source organization revealed that 94% of European Union (EU) organizations say digital sovereignty is important, with 61% considering it very important. As Thierry Carrez, the Linux Foundation Europe GM, said in his keynote, “Europe has clearly heard the message on digital sovereignty.”

In an interview onstage at the summit, Nithya Ruff, chair of the LF board, added that it’s not just Europe: “Digital sovereignty is a need that the entire world feels, whether it’s Sierra Leone or the US or China.”

It’s not just the Dutch tax collectors, though. The Netherlands is also exploring switching from Windows and proprietary software to Linux and open-source programs across the board. That follows the Swiss military and other agencies announcing they were moving to Linux and openDesk, a German open-source office suite. Before that, European governments shifting to Linux included Austria, France, Germany, and Ireland.

Also: Windows October update patches a whopping 1,400 security bugs –  including 2 zero days

Indeed, according to the LF Europe report, 94% of organizations care about AI as much as they do about digital sovereignty. We all know how businesses are moving to AI as fast as they can. Outside the States, the move to digital sovereignty is garnering just as much support.

The Netherlands had planned to switch to Microsoft 365 in 2025. The idea then was to complete the rollout by the end of 2026. About 5,000 employees had already migrated when the Dutch Advisory Council on ICT Assessment recommended reversing the public-cloud rollout in June. The government paused the plan in July; the latest announcement replaces that rollout with an on-premises/open-source approach.

The Tax and Customs Administration isn’t replacing all of Microsoft Office with a single open-source suite, at least not yet. Instead, the government will keep the existing Microsoft software for now.

Looking ahead, State Secretary for Finance Eelco Eerenberg set out the replacement timetable in a letter to Parliament: “In 2027, the provision for mail and calendar will be realized on-premises. Later in 2027 and 2028, European open-source solutions for personal storage and collaboration will follow. This allows us to work toward a sustainable and more autonomous solution for these functionalities.”

The ICT assessment found that the chosen Microsoft 365 public-cloud design fell short on “information security, information processing and future-proofing.” Another key concern was preserving data confidentiality and control. In particular, the ICT assessment raised concerns about sending confidential documents through American servers rather than the government networks previously used.

The Dutch government is also concerned about 365’s encryption. The proposed 365 setup relied on standard Microsoft encryption rather than Double Key Encryption. The latter would have given the administration greater control.

Another worry was that end-to-end encryption wouldn’t have been enabled by default for one-to-one Teams calls. This has long concerned the Netherlands government. On top of that, it would have been unavailable for group calls under the selected configuration. These were criticisms of the deployment design, not claims that every Microsoft 365 configuration has identical disadvantages.

Also: Got a Microsoft 365 subscription? Your storage is about to shrink

Finally, the assessment identified vendor lock-in, reduced flexibility, concerns about digital sovereignty, and the absence of an adequate exit strategy as showstopping issues. In my view, based on my coverage of the European Union’s push for digital sovereignty, they don’t trust American companies under the current US government.

For now, the on-premises email/calendar environment will still use Microsoft software, including Outlook. The open-source portion concerns personal storage and collaboration, not a wholesale replacement of Word, Excel, PowerPoint, or the entire desktop environment.

What exactly will this look like? We don’t know yet. No particular open-source programs or software stacks have been chosen yet. What we do know, though, is that other Dutch government agencies have started developing Digitaal Autonome Werkomgeving Overheid (DAWO), which translates to “Digital Autonomous Work Environment for Government.” DAWO starts by replacing the Windows desktop with the Dutch Linux distribution NixOS.

Also: I tried the free Microsoft Word clone on Linux – and it’s my new default (on Mac too)

On top of NixOS, France’s La Suite and Germany’s openDesk are being considered for the desktop suite. Another possibility is that the Netherlands will move to a homebrew of MijnBureau. This self-hosted suite combines open-source projects, including Nextcloud for storage and collaboration, Collabora for office documents, Element for messaging, and OpenProject for work management. This is a more ready-to-run office suite than what I’d call a Netherlands agency’s built-from-scratch “Dutch Office” suite.

Still, while the replacement details remain foggy, Dutch tax authorities have canceled the Microsoft 365 cloud rollout in favor of an on-premises email/groupware suite, followed by a full-fledged open-source office suite.

#191. The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build

Agility Robotics’ first practical robotic worker is nothing like I dreamed

Author and Agility Robotics co-founder Jonathan Hurst next to his new Digit 5 humanoid robot worker.

Agility Robotics, the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5. It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do.

Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined.

My dream has always been to build robots that combine locomotion and manipulation to move through the world and interact with it as people do. I seek a mastery of motion, achieved through devices designed to navigate the constraints of physics with elegance. When I started the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory at Oregon State in 2008, we began with a theory derived from decades of work in biomechanics: that a simple “spring-mass” model (a body supported by legs that act like springs) should be able to reproduce every known walking and running gait found in animals.

We put theory into practice by building the bipedal robot ATRIAS—short for “Assume The Robot Is A Sphere,” a joke among physicists about reducing a complex system to its simplest possible form. ATRIAS looked like a large microwave on stilts because it was only intended to demonstrate the physics of human walking and running. This was the first glimmer of achieving my dream; even though ATRIAS wasn’t designed to look like us, it still seemed natural, and even somehow alive, when it settled into a walking gait.

With the success of ATRIAS, the barriers to progress shifted from scientific to engineering and organizational, and a startup company seemed like the way to bridge the gap from a one-off research concept to an actual robotic product. I felt confident of two things: that I would be able to build robots that could go where people go, and that this capability would be incredibly useful. This combination of ambition and naivete is necessary for anyone to found a new company—how hard could it be?

Good advice for starting a company is to understand a customer problem, and then find a way to solve it using your unique capabilities. My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones, and I did not do this. We relied on our belief that this technology would enable new possibilities and trusted ourselves to figure out the business as we went. So we simply focused on building our first product: the bipedal robot Cassie.

Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot that researchers could buy, able to maintain its balance through active, fluid motion rather than careful, rigid steps. It had ostrichlike legs, not because we were imitating ground-running birds, but as a result of engineering strictly for performance. It was not intended to be commercially useful, and had no torso, arms, or head. We sold Cassie robots to Harvard, Caltech, the University of Michigan, the University of California, Berkeley, and a handful of other research institutions, ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them.

ATRIAS, Cassie, and Digit 4 EVT [left to right] are on display at Agility Robotics’ RoboFab in Salem, Ore. The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year.Agility Robotics

Because Cassie’s hardware enabled research into the physics of walking and running, the legged-robot research frontier shifted to control software. Traditionally, engineers controlled legged robots with detailed mathematical models that determined how the machines should move. With Cassie, researchers pioneered the new approach of reinforcement learning for bipedal legged locomotion: A simulated robot learns through trial and error, and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine. This approach is what enables virtually all of the dynamic behaviors that you see on legged robots today, and Cassie looked alive as it recovered from stumbles while climbing stairs, ran 5 kilometers across the Oregon State campus, and broke the robot world record for a 100-meter dash.

Cassie got us closer to being able to move through the world with confidence and grace, but to make it useful, we needed manipulation. After exhaustively exploring different configurations, we found that an upright torso helped the robot balance, while two arms mounted near the top of the torso allowed it to pick up large objects and to catch itself when it fell. Digit 1, which added a torso and arms to the Cassie legs, was our first mobile manipulation robot, and another step on the path toward a product that could do useful work for commercial customers.

As we explored the first applications for Digit, potential customers kept asking us: Why legs? And why a humanoid? These were tough questions for me to answer, because they exposed a core business reality: It didn’t matter to Agility Robotics if we solved a cool science problem in a beautiful way. What mattered to the business was solving real problems for customers.

After years of engagement with industry partners, we found one answer in warehouses and manufacturing facilities: moving bins. Bin handling is a clearly defined task where two arms are needed to lift large bins up high and legs are the best way to balance and move in narrow spaces. Because the task can vary widely from one deployment to another, it hasn’t been broadly addressed by single-purpose automation. Yet it was constrained enough to give Digit an economically viable first job while it developed a broader set of skills.

In 2019, Digit began demonstrating its capabilities to do real work. With Ford Motor Company, we showed how Digit 1 could carry packages from an autonomous vehicle to a front porch. We developed Digit 2 and 3 while working with a certain global package delivery company on moving and sorting cardboard boxes. Amazon tested Digit 4 on moving and stacking bins, and it became the world’s first commercially deployed humanoid at the logistics provider GXO. In 2024, Digit appeared on the cover of Time magazine.

Despite Digit’s apparent success, we began to run into conflicts between my dream and the needs of actual customers. We were no longer working with relatively patient university research labs. Agility has to sell robots to survive, and customers will only purchase robots that provide value. If bins weren’t moving, our customers were losing money. We spent a huge amount of time and effort keeping our first deployments operational, which arguably eliminated any profit we made. Yet this also kept our company learning and alive the way no lab demo ever could.

I had no idea how hard it would be, or that running a company would involve so many things that have nothing to do with solving technical problems: deployments across the country; shipping, service, and customer support; fundraising and investor relations; more fundraising; human resources and IT; developing fleet-management software; managing a supply chain; and even more fundraising. I had no experience with any of these things. My career had focused on solving the technical challenges of robots interacting with the world, and it turned out that was only a tiny piece of building a successful robotics company. But Agility was the only path I saw to continuing the technical work and having an impact.

I knew that Agility needed to focus more on robots as a product, but I didn’t know how to make that happen. Hiring the people we needed to run the company meant giving up an immense amount of control, but we had no other choice. We recruited a new executive team with the experience required to commercialize this new technology, and they quickly made changes that were both painful and necessary.

Digit versions 1, 2, and 3 [left to right] show the evolution of the robot from a dynamic walking platform into a useful mobile manipulator. Agility

We had intended the next revision of Digit, Digit 4 EVT (Engineering Validation and Test), to be a relatively minor upgrade. But Agility’s new leadership insisted that the robot was missing key features that were essential if Digit was going to become a real product. So Digit 4 EVT instead incorporated a series of major changes in a highly compressed timeline, such as larger batteries and system-wide upgrades for safety and regulatory compliance, which added enough mass to dramatically alter the robot’s appearance and capabilities.

While early Digits were headless, Agility Robotics was able to justify a head for Digit 4 to optimize antenna and camera placement, and it turned out to be surprisingly useful for human-robot interaction.Christie Hemm Klok

I could only watch as others brought their own talents to bear to make Digit into a successful product, in gut-wrenching ways that didn’t always align with my vision. There were some especially difficult times when I felt like there were compromises made that didn’t seem necessary, but making those decisions was no longer my sole responsibility. I had to accept that Digit had grown far beyond me, and look for ways of influencing decisions rather than directing them. In the moment, it was incredibly frustrating, as Digit 4 EVT took a few steps backward from my vision of how humanoids should look and move.

Agility is in our name because agility is core to the future of the company. I want Digit to be lithe and graceful. When people see Digit, I want them to like the robot, to understand what it can do at a glance, and to feel that it’s there to help. But with Digit 4 EVT, all of that was sacrificed to functionality, because of course it had to be—the customer just needs the robot to do the work. The design process became a ruthless triage, with aesthetics and elegance of movement being delayed over and over again in favor of brutal functionality. For an engineer whose mind lives more in the future than in the present, it has been hard for me to accept this trajectory. And yet, through Digit 4 EVT’s commercial deployments, we began to really understand specific applications and what they required. We mapped the first 10 use cases Digit would perform, and then began designing Digit 5 from scratch based on everything we had learned.

Digit 5 will be Agility’s first real step toward a general-purpose robot. It marks our transition from imagining what a future humanoid robot should be to designing a product around the realities of customer deployments. These realities include things like European CE regulatory compliance, North American UL electrical-safety certifications, and Federal Communications Commission limits for electromagnetic radiation—all of which felt tangential to my dream for Digit, but were absolute requirements.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers while working 20 hours a day and lifting more than a human can.Christie Hemm Klok

Customer requirements helped us realize that safety in particular was one of the most critical barriers to scaling. In Digit 4’s commercial deployments, the robots had to work behind physical barriers, separated from humans at all times, to meet insurance and regulatory demands. This seemed silly to me, because I’ve never felt that our robots were dangerous, but we have to prove that they’re safe. And since keeping the robots in safety cages severely limited their usefulness, enabling Digit 5 to operate safely around people became a primary design goal. We spent two years on this challenge.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers. It will rely on an array of sensors to locate nearby people in a manner that’s certifiably safe, and then take actions based on that information. As a person approaches, Digit 5 is programmed to stop what it’s doing, set down its payload, sit on the floor, and cut power to its motors before the person gets close enough to touch the robot. This conservative approach reduces the risk to nearby people in a verifiable way, and we believe it’s the only approach that makes sense as a first step toward working alongside humans.

Yet this strategy also feels like a massive slowdown on the path toward robots becoming part of everyday life. Enabling coexistence with humans has influenced almost every aspect of Digit 5’s design: the shape of the legs and the body, the safety-rated sensors within protective housings, the isolated computers dedicated to safety, and more. All of these features increase the robot’s complexity, power consumption, mass, and physical size.

Digit 5 is Agility’s largest, heaviest, strongest, and most capable humanoid robot worker.

The robot’s design was driven by safety, with integrated protection for the robot and for the humans it will work around.Agility Robotics

Weighing over 120 kg, Digit 5 is a huge robot. It needed to achieve the lifting limits recommended under the U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health guidelines for human workers, which include repeatedly lifting 23-kg bins and reaching shelves 1.75 meters high. Digit is designed to perform tasks like these for 20 hours a day—something no human can do. This requires motors with enough power and torque to lift the load, but also enough precision to delicately control the force Digit applies when it makes contact with the world. To power those motors, we needed a large battery and a dock for rapid autonomous charging. The dock will deliver 240 amperes at 48 volts, which is enough current to make its thick charging cables visibly wiggle under the induced magnetic forces, while powerful fans blow air through cooling channels in the robot’s torso to keep the battery from overheating. The battery and cooling system takes up about 75 percent of Digit’s torso, but it will allow the robot to operate for 90 minutes and fully recharge during a 9-minute break, enabling near-continuous work.

All of this extra bulk means that Digit 5 can no longer run or jump the way previous generations could, and the svelte form I imagined has become physically impossible. In some ways, Digit 5 feels more like a forklift than the graceful humanoid I set out to build. But looking at the situation rationally, I believe this trade-off is necessary for any company that claims its humanoid can do this kind of work today: If you see a robot that looks like a human working in a factory or warehouse, it either can’t lift the required weight or can’t make it through the whole shift. And if it’s not covered with sensors, it’s likely not safe to stand next to.

The most visible change with Digit 5 is that humanlike legs replace the ostrichlike legs of our earlier versions. While the “backward” leg configuration was optimized for walking and running, we discovered that it created problems with squatting because the ankle will strike the ground. Digit 5 will spend a lot of time lifting heavy objects from near the floor, so we used a humanoid leg configuration with knee and hip motors that both contribute torque to help the robot stand up again.

When Digit detects an approaching human, the robot will lower itself to the floor and cut power to its motors. Agility believes this is the only near-term approach to verifiably reduce risk when the robot is working near people.Agility Robotics

Other companies building humanoid robots have copied the human form without ever understanding its purpose. It’s very frustrating that, to an outside observer, it now looks like we discarded Agility’s distinctive leg design and simply did what everyone else was doing. Yet I know that we arrived at this shape based purely on functional engineering choices. Making a robot look like a human is the easy part—without the function to match, and the understanding of the physics underlying that function, the whole point of the human form may be lost.

With the power, battery life, and safety features that we are designing into Digit 5, we will have a truly useful robot. But it also compromises on some things that are core to my vision and mission. I understand why we made the choices we did and can justify them all, but together they leave me unsatisfied. It’s the curse of the engineer.

I believe Digit 5 will be the scaling moment for Agility Robotics, the inflection point where we can begin deploying robots in large numbers. While the robot will continue carrying bins, our road map includes many more tasks, from picking individual items and tending machines, to preparing parts for assembly and shipping, and eventually doing assembly work itself. Its interchangeable tool interfaces and modular design will enable us to gradually upgrade its subsystems. It will be a platform for improvement, a source of data for future behavior training, and a viable product all at the same time.

Hurst stands between the previous version of Digit, Digit 4 EVT [left], and Digit 5.Christie Hemm Klok

But I cannot love Digit 5. It’s the largest, heaviest, most expensive robot Agility will ever build, full of design compromises that enable it to be exactly the robot it needs to be right now rather than the robot I dreamed of. In the beginning, I envisioned steady progress on agility and dexterity, with each version becoming more dynamically capable. Instead, developing Digit 5 has required large detours to incorporate requirements that seemed unrelated to my original vision. However, I now recognize that tackling these challenges was always necessary. Customers and product requirements didn’t ruin my vision; they revealed what my vision was missing. This is how robots will achieve commercial success and make a real-world impact, which will bring me closer to my scientific dream as well.

We won’t have a humanoid that matches the capabilities of humans until it achieves that mastery of motion that inspired me to found Agility over a decade ago. I saw glimmers of it with the spring-mass locomotion of ATRIAS, and more glimmers with Cassie’s running gait.

I know that such mastery is physically possible with the tools and hardware that we have right now, and despite all of its compromises, Digit 5 will give us a practical foundation for pursuing that dream. I want every future version of Digit to be lighter and more graceful, to interact more naturally with humans, and to be better at manipulating objects and moving through the world, enabling robots to enter aspects of our lives that they haven’t been able to help with before. By the time I’m old enough to need assistance at home, I expect Digit will be up to the task.

With Digit 5, Agility has built a robot that will be useful in our world. Now I’m getting back to work to make it beautiful, too.

Jonathan W. Hurst is the co-founder and chief robot officer of Agility Robotics and a robotics professor at Oregon State University.

#194. Monday.com launches Harmony, a voice AI platform for sales calls

The platform runs on voice tech from OneAI, which Monday.com bought for $14.1M in cash in May.

Monday.com has launched Harmony, a voice AI platform that calls, qualifies and follows up on sales leads, then hands them to human reps. It uses small, task-specific AI models and claims replies in about 200 milliseconds. It is available in the US, UK, Australia and Singapore.

Monday.com has launched Harmony, a voice AI platform that phones sales leads, qualifies them and passes the best ones to human reps, the company said on Monday. It is aimed at mid-market and large companies in the US, UK, Australia and Singapore.

Harmony runs on voice technology from OneAI, which Monday.com bought in May for $14.1M in cash, according to a company filing. The deal was meant to speed up the launch of voice AI tools, the filing said.

Instead of one large AI model, Harmony uses a set of small models trained on real customer calls. Each handles one job, such as qualifying a lead or dealing with an objection. Because they run largely on Harmony’s own servers, the company says its agents reply in about 200 milliseconds.

“Unlike generic solutions that rely on third-party LLMs, our specialized models and structured logic translate into conversations that sound human and a response time that feels human,” said Vitali Margolin, who leads Harmony.

The platform also dials numbers, routes incoming calls and records consent, using telephony from Twilio. It writes call notes back to CRM systems such as Salesforce and HubSpot. By default, its agents tell callers they are AI, according to Harmony’s website.

Monday.com said Harmony reaches up to 70% of the people it calls, but did not share how it measured this. It did not publish prices.

One early user, UK car finance broker Bright Car Finance, said Harmony helped it close 9% more deals in less than a year. Before, it turned only about 5% of approved applications into finance agreements, because leads went cold.

The launch comes as Monday.com tries to reinvent itself around AI. In July, it said it would cut about 620 jobs, a fifth of its staff, and in June it set up a $200M fund for workplace AI startups.

Harmony enters a busy market. Voice AI startups such as Bland and Vapi have each raised $50M this year.

#198. HTC Made Smart Glasses That Are Way More Private

You can’t really talk about smart glasses without bringing up Meta. HTC, the company behind 2010-era virtual reality headsets and a failed smartphone business, seems quite eager to tackle that comparison directly.

In September, HTC started selling its $499 Vive Eagle smart glasses in the US. The Eagles have lots of the same features as other glasses on the market—cameras for capturing photos and video, speakers in the frames for music playback and calls, an embedded AI agent you can ask questions of and even get recipes from by taking pictures of stuff in your fridge.

But HTC also wants to steer clear of the ongoing debate about privacy in camera-equipped smart glasses. Meta has been dogged by controversy for its smart glasses, with people worried about the company’s interest in enabling face-recognition features, and calling the people who wear them creepy. HTC is aware of that discourse and thinks it is completely possible to make smart glasses that aren’t a privacy nightmare.

“It's not just about protecting the consumer, but it's also about protecting people around the consumer,” Dan McDowell, HTC Vive’s head of enterprise sales, tells WIRED. “People can usher in, I think, what are really tremendous experiences with a new layer of confidence and protection.”

I’ve been wandering around with the glasses for a couple of weeks, and so far they meet my expectations for what smart glasses have become. They protect my eyes from the sun. They snap good photos and videos. You can record and transcribe voice notes. The music playback has decent sound quality. (I’ll always prefer a solid pair of headphones if I’m actually trying to listen to music, but the speakers work just fine.) They come in two styles—one with square Wayfarer-esque lenses and the other more rounded.

The Vive Eagle glasses can get 4.5 hours of battery life on continuous music playback. They can last 36 hours on standby. HTC also sells a companion clip-on battery pack called Power Boost that costs $49. It clips right onto the frame and is noticeable but not as obnoxious as you might think.

Don’t forget the AI assistant, Vive AI, which can utilize OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Google’s Gemini. It doesn’t require a login, so users are “de-identified” in a way that keeps the services from retaining personal information. (That also means, by default, you won’t be able to enjoy many of the personalization features these chatbots offer by gleaning information from your emails and messages.) The glasses come with Vive’s AI Plus, free for the first two years. After that, users must pay a monthly $2.50 subscription fee.

Right by the cameras is a bright indicator light. If you cover the light, it won’t record. If someone around you says stop recording, that will stop the recording. Video footage you capture is encrypted and stored on the glasses—it’s not automatically sent to the phone or cloud. If you want to import photos or videos, you have to do it manually in the app.

Meta has faced scrutiny over the indicator light before, as some users have blocked the LED with stickers or broken into the hardware to turn it off. Meta has responded with software updates that disable the camera if someone tampers with the indicator light, along with other privacy-focused measures.

I ask McDowell how HTC, and really any smart glasses maker, can get past the “trust me, bro”–style privacy promises companies tend to make.

“We're not a social media company,” McDowell says. “There's no benefit to me to have any of your info. We don't train our AI model or any third-party AI models with any of the information that is used on the glasses.”

The real problem may be that with cameras on the frames, smart glasses are hard to distinguish between brands. The Vive Eagles look a lot like Meta glasses, and people worried about those privacy issues may not know that the Eagles are different and not tied to Mark Zuckerberg’s company. I’ve had friends see me wearing them and ask if they’re smart glasses. Yeah, I replied, but not the ones they’re thinking of. That didn’t seem to dispel any of their suspicions.

The hope, at least how HTC frames it, is that more players with better privacy practices will help shift cultural disdain for smart glasses. A bunch of other companies are going cameraless, like Even Realities, Viture, and Halliday. Others are building theirs with privacy shields or focusing on virtual displays instead of capturing the world around you. That said, no one has captured the market quite like Meta.

“We'd like to make sure that our technology adapts to society's expectations, not the other way around,” McDowell says. “I hope that everybody that's making products like these takes steps in the right direction.”

Smart city deployments have historically relied on cameras, sensors, and dashboards that capture data without delivering timely insight. Edge AI changes this by letting inference happen close to where data is generated. This supports faster decisions, stronger data sovereignty, and lower operating costs than cloud-only designs. This guide traces the progression from automation and perception to prediction, agentic coordination, and physical AI, where urban systems continuously perceive conditions, reason about them, and act within a tiered edge architecture spanning far-edge sensors, regional infrastructure, and the cloud.
