#204. Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook could debut on November 6: Here’s what to expect

After over a decade of not adopting touch displays on its Mac notebook lineup, Apple will finally be releasing its first touchscreen MacBook as early as November 6th, after announcing it as early as October 27th.

Of course, rumors are rumors – though essentially every reputable source has aligned on the idea of the MacBook Pro gaining support for touch very shortly. Apple even left a few hints in macOS 27: Touch Support in Sidecar, pull to refresh support, and slightly bigger menu bar items.

One could call all of this a mere coincidence, but it’s probably exactly what it looks like. Regardless, here’s what the first touchscreen MacBook will have to offer.

On the display panel side of things, the redesigned MacBook Pro will come with a Tandem OLED display. This will be similar to the iPad Pro, which is often touted as one of the best mobile displays on the market. Tandem OLED comprises of stacked OLED panels, which allows for incredible colors, strong contrast, and increased brightness.

Reports also suggest it’ll come with a Dynamic Island, and it’ll be a bit smaller than the one on the iPhone. It won’t, however, come with support for Face ID.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple will have some special optimizations for the first touchscreen MacBook Pro, beyond what’s already visible in the betas of macOS 27:

“For instance, if users touch a button or control, the interface will bring up a new type of menu surrounding their finger that provides more relevant options for touch commands.

The software will also display the most appropriate set of controls based on users’ prior interaction. And if a person taps an item in the menu bar at the top of the screen, the set of controls will enlarge to be more easily selectable with a finger.”

Despite initial reporting suggesting that we’ll be seeing the debut of the M6 Pro and Max in the redesigned MacBook Pro, Apple is now skipping the release of those chips to accelerate the M7. This means that the first iteration of 2nm chips won’t be making their way to the redesigned MacBook Pros, and they’ll instead offer the existing M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

There won’t be a base model version of this computer quite yet, though rumors suggest that Apple will be launching a base version of the redesigned MacBook Pro with an M7 chip as early as next spring.

One design rumor for the new MacBook Pro is the fact that it’ll be slightly slimmer and lighter – though it’s unclear how meaningful this will be. The last MacBook Pro iteration made the computers look and feel quite chunky, so a bit of progress here would likely be welcome – so long as it doesn’t come at the compromise of thermals.

Bloomberg has also reported that these computers will be ‘significantly lighter,’ thanks to re-engineering of internal components.

Seems odd that they’d release this m5 in October, then March-May release the M7 version. Certainly would make me not want to buy it.

According to the Power On newsletter, Apple will potentially release these new MacBook Pro models on November 6th, making a straight four weeks of new Apple launches with iPhone Duo, HomePod mini 2, the new MacBook Pro, and HomeView + Apple TV 4K.

As of now, there’s no Apple release scheduled for November 6th, so it would make sense to be the new MacBook Pro:

Now, I have a little more to share: Apple is planning to hold a “reset” at its retail stores on the evening of Thursday, Nov. 5, into Friday, Nov. 6, that implies new signage and products will be placed on store tables. Given that this Friday is a week after the Mac announcements (when Apple would typically release products), it would make sense that this is the date when at least some of the new items become available to customers.

#205. Four European carriers to explore a joint bid for satellite spectrum

They would build the ground network in Europe, while a satellite partner still to be chosen supplies the constellation. Every mobile operator would get access.

Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica and Vodafone have signed a letter of intent to explore a joint bid for satellite spectrum in Europe. The four companies announced it on Monday in a joint release.

The spectrum is for mobile satellite services (MSS), the radio frequencies that link satellites with mobile devices. The bid would be for its future allocation in Europe. The letter commits the four only to explore a bid, and they gave no timetable.

They said the plan supports the European Commission’s aim of strengthening Europe’s sovereignty, security and resilience in critical connectivity. The four would give every mobile operator open, non-discriminatory access to offer direct-to-device (D2D) services to its customers. The model is meant to foster competition and expand consumer choice, they said.

The four plan to set up the key ground network in Europe, along with critical coordination and monitoring functions. They will not invest directly in a satellite constellation. The constellation would come from a satellite partner they have yet to select.

They said they aim to bring coverage to underserved areas, make public networks more resilient and protect critical communications. They also want to support the development of a European constellation.

The letter does not replace existing satellite partnerships, the four said. AST SpaceMobile, which counts all four as partners, also announced the letter on Monday. It said it supplies ground stations in Europe through its joint venture, Satellite Connect Europe.

TNW reported in September, citing Bloomberg, that the four carriers were in early talks about a joint satellite venture.

In May, the European Union said it was considering a plan to reserve part of the 2 GHz band for European companies. They would use it to offer satellite services. SpaceX criticised the idea, saying it would worsen service in Ukraine, The Verge reported, citing the Financial Times.

In the US, AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon announced their own collaboration earlier this year. It would combine their spectrum in rural areas and dead zones.

Luke Kehoe, lead industry analyst at Ookla, called it a commercial concern, in comments carried by Advanced Television.

“Europe’s operators want to avoid becoming effectively MVNOs for satellite coverage, selling somebody else’s service on somebody else’s terms. Securing MSS spectrum would give them a stronger hand in negotiations.” Luke Kehoe, lead industry analyst, Ookla

Amazon just upped its game with new Android tablets for entertainment and work.

Amazon just announced three new Alexa Tablets, a trio of AI-powered Android tablets for work and entertainment with a more “Pro” build. The new tablets are an unexpected upgrade for Amazon, and an indication that the company is moving away from budget-focused tablets to more premium devices.

Also: 6 ways to make Android look and work more like iOS

The lineup starts at $230 and includes the Amazon Alexa Tablet 8, the Amazon Alexa Tablet 11 at $330, and the Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, which starts at $500. All three tablets are currently available for pre-order, and will start shipping on October 14.

Compared to the older Fire Tablets, the new Alexa Tablets have been completely reimagined, which means they include features that had never been available on a Fire Tablet before.

Aside from being designed to work with Alexa+, the biggest change with these tablets is that they’re the first of the newer Amazon tablets to support access to Google Play, not just Amazon’s walled app store.

Amazon also announced a set of new Kids’ Tablets in bright colors and ready-to-go bundles with access to Google Play, though parents will still be able to control which apps their kids can access and download.

As the name indicates, the Alexa Tablets feature the Alexa+ virtual assistant integrated throughout. Instead of just having Alexa+ as a voice assistant, the new tablets feature the AI assistant woven into the interface, similar to how Gemini is for typical Android tablets.

Also: I recommend this Android tablet over flagship models, especially at this price

The new Alexa Tablets can have Alexa interpret what is on your screen and answer questions about it. You can also have live, ongoing conversations without repeating the wake word before each one.

On the hardware side, the Alexa Tablets also feature a major upgrade. The Tablet 8 features 4GB of RAM and 64GB of storage for everyday use. The Tablet 11 has 8GB of RAM and 64GB of storage for extra entertainment and light work.

The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, however, has a 4nm 8-core processor, 8GB or 16GB of RAM, and 128GB of storage. It also features a 12-inch display with a 120Hz refresh rate and comes with the option of a Nanomatte anti-glare display tablet for $50 more, starting at $550. Also: This rugged Android tablet goes everywhere I’m uneasy taking my iPad Pro – and it’s only $340

Amazon also sells a Pro Keyboard for this flagship tablet, which is magnetic, features a trackpad, and requires no Bluetooth pairing. Instead of a simple iterative update, the new Alexa Tablets are an entirely redesigned lineup that could reposition Amazon tablets as full-fledged Android tablets.

Amazon also launched two new, upgraded Kids Tablets: the Amazon Kids Tablet 8, starting at $230, and the Amazon Kids Tablet 11, starting at $330. The Kids’ tablets come in an 8.7-inch and 11-inch form factor, the latter of which has a 2.5K display and 8GB of RAM.

The Kids Tablets also feature Android instead of FireOS, improved hardware and screen resolution, AI-powered storytelling, and more convenient parental controls. Unfortunately, the Kids Tablets feature a one-year limited warranty, which is a considerable reduction from the previous tablets’ two-year, worry-free guarantee.

#207. Everything You Should Know About Mail Categories on Your iPhone

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems

These categories can be nice, but you can turn them off if you don't like them.

Finding a particular message can be difficult if you get a lot of emails. If you want to check on the status of a package, scrolling through newsletters and random ads can be irksome. Luckily, Apple introduced Categories for the mail app when the tech company released iOS 18.2 in 2025.

“The Mail app automatically sorts your email messages into categories to help you find and manage messages more quickly,” Apple wrote online.

Categories are on by default, but if you don’t like how it works in Mail, no worries. Apple gives you a few options to either ignore Categories or revert your app to look like it did before the iOS 18.2 update.

Here’s what you need to know about Mail Categories and how to turn the feature off so your app looks like it did before the update.

Mail Categories are similar to categories you would find in other email services, like Gmail. The app filters your emails into one of four categories: Primary, Transactions, Updates and Promotions.

Emails with receipts, as well as order and delivery information, fill the Transactions category, and news, social and other subscription emails go to Updates. Emails with special offers and deals go to Promotions, as you might imagine.

The Primary category is more difficult to pin down. Apple says in the app that Primary is for “Messages that matter most.” I’ve used the redesigned app since it launched in beta, and during that time my Primary category was filled with emails from my wife, customer service and even refund information. It’s a little bit of a catch-all category.

Categories aren’t perfect so sometimes an email lands where it probably shouldn’t, like an ad in the Transactions category instead of the Promotions. There is a way to change an email’s category for any future messages you might receive from that sender. Here’s how.

1. Tap Mail.2. Tap the Transactions, Updates or Promotions tab then tap a message.3. Tap the three dots (…) in the top right corner.4. Tap Categorize Sender.

Then you can manually categorize messages from a given sender to another category. You can also recategorize an email from Promotions to Deals and then back to Promotions. The only emails that can’t be recategorized are those in Primary — which can be annoying.

Once, I ordered tickets for a show at a local theater, and the email was filtered to Promotions. I moved the email with those tickets to Primary, but now all emails from that theater — including deals and sales — go to my Primary category. Not being able to change that categorization back is annoying.

If you don’t like Mail Categories, you have a few options to see all your mail at once. The easiest way is to swipe the categories bar near the top of Mail to the left to reveal the option All Mail. Swiping left to view this option automatically selects All Mail. Now all your mail will be displayed from top to bottom as each message comes in, but you will still see the Categories tabs across the top of the app.

You can also remove Categories altogether so the app looks like it did before the update. Here’s how.

1. Tap Mail.2. Tap the three dots (…) in the top right corner of the app.3. Tap Show Categories.

Now your emails will populate in Mail from top to bottom as they arrive in your inbox.

#208. Don’t Let a Crypto Inheritance Get Stuck on the Blockchain

If someone you know has cryptocurrency that you might inherit, let me just say ahoy matey! I hope your pirate spirit is alive and your treasure-hunting skills sharp, because that's what it might take to get those assets. And if you're the one holding crypto, know that if you do nothing, it's very possible those funds will die with you.

In the US, cryptocurrency is considered a digital asset rather than money in terms of probate and estate law. With money and physical assets, you can sign a beneficiary form and create an estate plan or write a last will and testament naming who should get what when you die. With digital assets, however, the law says we should not assume that a deceased person wanted their private materials—everything from emails to photos—given to another person unless they explicitly said so. This puts cryptocurrency, as a digital asset, in an awkward position.

The options for arranging a transfer of cryptocurrency upon one's death or incapacitation breaks down by one big division: whether the crypto is held by a custodian or in a noncustodial crypto wallet.

A custodian or custodial wallet means a third party, such as a bank or a cryptocurrency marketplace, holds and manages the assets for you. Typically, transferring assets after death is much easier with a custodian, especially if it's a bank.

Noncustodial wallets eliminate the middleman and let a person hold their assets directly. For crypto enthusiasts whose interest in digital currency is driven by a distaste for the traditional banking system, then using a noncustodial wallet is kind of the whole point.

Noncustodial wallets can be software or hardware-based. It can even be a piece of paper with the instructions and passwords for accessing the cryptocurrency on it. (I use "password" here and throughout to refer to any string of letters, numbers, and characters needed to gain access to someone’s cryptocurrency.) Whatever kind of noncustodial wallet you choose, passing on your assets will require a DIY solution.

When you use a third-party custodian to hold your cryptocurrency, you can choose one that has a beneficiary process in place.

Charles Schwab and Chase are just two examples of large, well-known financial institutions that offer crypto services and have experience transferring assets after death. Schwab, for example, houses its cryptocurrency services within brokerage accounts. Signing a beneficiary form for a brokerage account applies to the crypto account as well. One and done.

Another benefit of using a bank is that at least three entities know you have an account: the bank, the government, and the credit reporting bureaus. Avenues exist for finding the banked money of deceased people. With a noncustodial wallet, this is not at all the case.

Similarly, if you get locked out of your online bank account, you can go to a bank branch with ID (I've had to do it) and get back in. More important to your heirs, it doesn't matter if you were locked out of the online portal when you died—that has no bearing on the account or a beneficiary's ability to receive the funds. This is not the case with noncustodial wallets.

Note that cryptocurrency accounts, even when held through a bank, are not FDIC-insured.

Other custodians include crypto marketplaces, such as Coinbase, and peer-to-peer payment services, like PayPal. Neither Coinbase nor PayPal have beneficiary forms as of this writing, though they do have a clear process for proving a person is entitled to a decedent's account. In both cases, you must have legal documents saying you are the executor of the estate (for PayPal) or are entitled to inherit the account (Coinbase), as well as a death certificate and other documentation. So the process is clunky and takes some advance planning, but it's still straightforward.

How many disadvantages there are to using a custodian depends on your outlook. As mentioned, crypto enthusiasts who eschew traditional banking may not see any value in using a custodian. Banks require ID, so you cannot hold the crypto anonymously. Banks and many other custodians report your transactions to the federal government, holding you accountable to an honest tax filing. Custodial wallets also cost money. They typically charge transaction fees, usually a small percentage of each trade.

The primary benefit of a noncustodial wallet is that everything is in your control. You hold the assets directly. You're responsible for knowing and keeping safe the information you need to access your assets. You also have to come up with a plan for informing your beneficiaries that a crypto account exists and making sure they can access it.

The first and biggest problem is that if you get locked out while you're alive, it's game over. "If you lose your cryptographic key, there's no company that you can appeal to," says Benjamin Orzeske, chief counsel for Uniform Law Commission and a staff attorney for the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act, the law that guides how digital inheritance is handled in most states.

In the case of a hardware key, a corrupted device or one lost to fire or theft may also cut off a person and their heirs from their crypto, permanently and irreversibly.

The other major hurdle is that your fiduciary needs to know the crypto exists. No government or credit reporting bureau has a record of you holding the account. The only people who know are the ones you tell.

Now let's get procedural. Because of how the blockchain works, you must figure out a secure way to give your heirs instructions for obtaining the assets. Your system has to be safe. It doesn't come with any backups or failsafes unless you create them. And whether you can test your system to make sure it works before you die will require a huge amount of trust.

Ideas from Reddit users for how to build a system for passing on cryptocurrency include email dead-man switches, printed instructions given to a trusted person, and splitting instructions across two people who will need to come together to obtain access. All these solutions could work but have obvious flaws: the failure of an email system, a trusted person dying alongside you, someone forgetting you gave them instructions, and so forth.

The best option may be to put the bulk of the instructions into your estate plan, including your named fiduciary, but crucially omitting any passwords. As Catherine Hodder, a senior attorney editor at FindLaw, explained to me, “The will is a public document,” and you should never put any usernames or passwords in your will.

An excellent place to put your password is inside a safe-deposit box at a bank. The existence of the deposit box should also be listed in your will. Some crypto owners have suggested stamping the password into a metal plate, which I suppose is a fine idea if you don't trust ink and paper to last longer than you.

One potential flaw is still that you can't do a dry run to make sure your system works unless you trust your fiduciary completely. Something as simple as needing your fingerprint to unlock a device could spell the end of your plan.

An objection that some staunchly anti-capitalistic investors may have is that by including your cryptocurrency in your estate plan, you've returned it to the realm of traditional law and governance.

#209. A death, a plagiarism scandal and a quest for revenge: the tale of Otto Z

After his mother died, Otto became convinced he’d been wronged by the forensic investigators – and that one of them was a fraud. The truth was even stranger

On a balmy, quiet evening in June 2020, Otto’s elderly mother, Doria, was fading in her Munich apartment. As she lay with her eyes closed, her pale face, framed by her white hair, was calm.

Otto, masked, gloved and draped in a sterile apron, dozed in a chair beside her. Otto, who sometimes goes by the name Rainer, and whose last name is only known as “Z” because of Germany’s strict privacy laws, was a doctor who had cared for his mother for years, ever since she had suffered a stroke and moved in with him. He described the course of that night to me. He woke to the sound of her short breath and tried to sit her upright. Her eyes were shut, and her lips pursed. She stopped breathing. Otto reached for his phone to call for help, but then Doria opened her eyes and stared into his. She smiled, drew one last deep breath, shut her eyes again, and lay still.

Otto sank into his chair. As a doctor, he had seen death many times, but his own mother’s passing sent him into shock. He felt frozen, watching the windows glisten in the fading light. He was 66, and his brother and father had died years before. He had no friends. He had given all of his time, energy and attention to his mother’s care, and now that his task was suddenly over, he had no one to turn to. He mourned in solitude, with an impromptu ritual. He lit candles and set metal plates at the four corners of her bed. He sat beside her and thought about her soul.

Once the rite was complete, Otto picked up the phone and called a funeral home. He knew the procedure: as a doctor, he could issue his own mother’s death certificate. After he hung up, Otto waited. It was the last calm moment he would experience for many months.

After he called the funeral home, Otto told me, he waited beside his mother all night and into the next afternoon before he heard a knock at the door. He was surprised to see that, rather than doctors, the two men in the hallway were police officers. They wore bulletproof vests and carried guns. He invited them inside, where they scanned the rooms. He directed them to his mother’s bedroom and followed close behind, but the officers stopped him and asked him to take a seat.

While the officers inspected his mother’s body, Otto sat in his office. Forty-five minutes passed, and then he heard someone else enter the flat without knocking. A tall, stylish woman approached and introduced herself as a coroner from the Munich Institute of Forensic Medicine, before walking off to the bedroom.

Otto knew that a coroner – as opposed to a doctor or nurse – is only sent to the scenes of suspicious deaths. He followed her to the bedroom, where she had begun inspecting his mother’s body. Otto wasn’t easily rattled, but he told me that the way the coroner handled Doria threw him off. He found her elegant attire unprofessional, given the circumstances, and her bedside manner lacking. He said that he tried, however, to remain polite and helpful. As she went about her work, he offered his recollections from his mother’s final hours and an account of her long illness, which he had documented minutely over the years. Otto informed the coroner that he was a doctor, but it seemed to him that she was uninterested. She turned to the police officers and, without explanation, told them that this was a matter for law enforcement, before leaving the flat. Otto told me he wondered why nobody was listening to him, the grieving son, the doctor?

More armed police officers arrived and searched the rooms. A commissioner approached Otto and told him to gather his things, as they needed to conduct their work uninterrupted. Sleep-deprived and grief-stricken, Otto was ushered on to the street and ordered not to return. He drifted along Munich’s wide, lamplit streets. As darkness fell upon the city, Otto told me he felt that he “didn’t understand the world any more”.

He checked into a hotel, but found it intolerable to sit in his room. Later that night he wandered back to his flat and found the door sealed with police tape. He was desperate to check in on his mother and thought she might still be inside. He broke the police seal and entered the dark rooms, which were a chaotic mess, as if burglars had turned it over before fleeing the scene. He entered the bedroom. His mother was gone.

Otto went back to his hotel but still found it impossible to sleep. He returned to his flat a second time at about 2am, and this time he found several police officers stationed there. They spotted him and put him in the back of a police car. He was taken to the Institute of Forensic Medicine, where doctors extracted samples from him: hair, urine and blood. When they had finished, Otto was taken back to the police station and found himself alone in what he described as a tiny, windowless cell with only a mattress, a stainless steel toilet and bars on the door.

The next morning, two officers questioned him. How did he care for Doria? Why did he document her condition so precisely? Had he given his mother a concentrated saline injection? Only then did Otto understand: the police believed he had murdered his mother.

After two nights in jail, or possibly three (his memory of this time is confused), Otto was released and allowed to return to his flat. While it was a relief to be home, he told me he still didn’t understand why he was under suspicion. He had not yet been formally charged with any crime. Otto wrote to the head of the Institute of Forensic Medicine, Prof Matthias Graw, to ask if his team had discovered anything suspicious while inspecting Doria’s body. Eager to prove his innocence, Otto offered to send Graw all of his day-to-day notes on Doria’s health. He suggested, boldly, that they co-author a paper about the cause of her death.

Graw never answered Otto’s emails, and Otto fell into a depression. He told me he began blaming himself for his mother’s death. Had he made a mistake? Overlooked some critical detail? Was there some way he could have saved her? Over the years, he said, he had taken her to see 19 different specialists to ensure that she received the best care. He made sure she exercised and spent time each day in the fresh air. He had tried his best, hadn’t he?

Doria was his whole world. Before the pandemic he used to take her into the city centre each night, where she was a favourite among the buskers for her generous tips. In her younger years, Doria had been an avid traveller, and Otto had taken her, in a wheelchair, on one last holiday to Italy. Now she was gone. Otto’s despair grew until he was unable to eat or sleep.

In January 2021, the authorities dropped their investigation into his mother’s death, and Otto was cleared of any wrongdoing. But he still couldn’t get over her death. He checked himself into a psychiatric treatment centre, hoping to quiet his mind.

Through therapy and exercise, Otto slowly regained his strength. Meanwhile, he had received a copy of the results of his mother’s toxicological report, signed by Graw and two of his institute’s specialists, but he was too disoriented to examine them carefully. Months passed. It was mid-summer, after Otto had moved back into his apartment, when he finally sat down with Doria’s medical files and the report.

With two PhDs and decades of experience in medicine and chemistry, Otto knew how to interpret lab reports. He told me that something seemed off. Data seemed to him to have been highlighted selectively. Other details seemed to him to have been glossed over. In the toxicological report, he said he spotted a chemical compound – commonly associated with exposure to cold – in her bloodstream. In his telling, an impossible, unspeakable idea crept into his mind: could his mother have somehow still been alive when she was taken away and stowed in the mortuary’s freezer? Could she have actually died at the Institute of Forensic Medicine, under the coroner’s care? And if so, how? The report also mentioned unusual traces of a substance contained in the autumn crocus flower, a poison called colchicine.

Otto began researching the Institute of Forensic Medicine. He started with its director, Prof Matthias Graw, and discovered that decades earlier, when Graw was a doctoral student at the University of Hamburg, he had written his dissertation on a certain naturally occurring poison found in the autumn crocus flower, called colchicine – the same poison found in Doria’s blood. Otto told me that a dark theory took shape in his mind: what if the institute had tried to frame him, to cover up the fact that they had actually killed his mother?

He did not go to the police – who, he reasoned, must work closely with the head of the institute of legal medicine. He would take the matter into his own hands. Hoping to perform his own examinations, Otto again wrote to the institute and requested access to his mother’s remains. Once more, his letter received no reply. In his apartment, hunched over his computer, Otto dug deeper into Graw, looking for evidence of negligence or criminality in the records of the man who oversaw his mother’s autopsy. He scoured scientific literature to research colchicine, the poison in which Graw was an expert.

By mid-February 2022, Otto had on his desk a book, dated 1982. Its title was Colchicine – 100 Years of Research. One of the chapters – its experiments, findings, tables and conclusion – was nearly identical to Graw’s dissertation, published five years later. Otto was convinced that he had in his hands the evidence he needed to bring Graw down.

At the end February 2022, a man named Stefan Weber was sitting in his office on the outskirts of Salzburg when an intriguing email landed in his inbox. The message claimed that Graw, the head of the Institute of Forensic Medicine at the University of Munich and one of the most respected forensic scientists in Germany, had plagiarised his doctoral thesis.

This was the kind of message Weber lived for. Fifty-six years old, baby-faced, broad, energetic and unrelentingly serious, Weber is the German-speaking world’s most-feared plagiarism hunter. His investigations have previously targeted Austria’s former labour and family minister Christine Aschbacher, who stepped down after Weber claimed her master’s thesis showed “never-before-seen depths of gobbledegook, nonsense and plagiarism”, and the German politician Annalena Baerbock, whose once-promising bid for the chancellorship was torpedoed when he investigated her book. The New York Times has called Weber the “undisputed terror of academics, politicians, [and] celebrities”.

Weber does not go out of his way to be liked. A former communications professor, he failed on eight occasions at eight universities to attain tenure. His colleagues in academia often found him brusque and inflexible. He told me he was hated because of his insistence on high standards.

Weber dresses in black and conducts his affairs with extreme scrupulousness. Fearing diabetes, he fasts for long periods. He spends his days in almost complete solitude, moving between his office, the library and the copy shop. He receives numerous requests for investigations each month, mostly from law firms and private individuals who want him to look into an applicant, competitor or colleague. Weber told me he charges up to €350 an hour for his work. He frequently pillories both public figures and obscure academics on his blog, where he also rails against “the Wokistan ideology” and has written: “Rightwing extremist must be understood as a title of honour!” In his spare time, he writes lofty books of philosophy and theory, with titles such as Language, Humanity, Universe.

The email, sent by one Otto Z, claimed that Graw’s entire career was “built on deception”. From Otto’s description, the colchicine book would have been an easy source to pilfer. It had been published in East Germany at the height of the cold war, which meant that it most likely wasn’t known to western academics when Graw published his dissertation. It was also, in plagiarism-hunter parlance, “grey literature”: informal material that isn’t peer-reviewed and therefore lies outside the reach of digital research platforms. Without Otto’s tip-off, it would have been impossible for Weber to discover the book’s existence.

Weber accepted the case and, with the help of an assistant, got to work researching the book. The archive of the East German publisher had been lost after reunification, and the book had never been cited by another source. Weber went searching for a physical copy. At the library, the elderly archivist told him they didn’t carry it. After consulting her databases, she informed him that no other library in the world did, either. But she found a single copy on eBay, for $220, and soon Weber held the book in his hands: a bright red hardcover. When Weber sat down to read it, he discovered that the red book told an incredible story nearly lost to history.

It was a record of an academic symposium held in 1981 at a hospital in the small Romanian city of Târgu Neamţ. Present were eminent experts on colchicine – biologists, pharmacists, zoologists – who gathered to present their work. Their lectures and conversations were assembled into chapters that chronicled the history of their niche field of research. Since at least the first century, the autumn crocus has been known to be toxic. Since the sixth century, the toxin responsible, colchicine, has been used to treat gout. Throughout the 20th century, new uses for colchicine were discovered: its ability to disrupt microtubules, for example, helps scientists study cell division, disease mechanisms and drug toxicity.

More surprising than any discovery presented at the symposium, however, was the guest list. Experts came from both sides of the iron curtain. At least two Americans were present: zoologist John Julius Biesele and obesity researcher Jules Hirsch. Had these westerners risked their reputations, careers and possibly their freedom to take part?

Perhaps the explanation had something to do with the symposium’s host, Elena Ceaușescu, the eccentric and ruthless wife of Nicolae Ceaușescu, then-dictator of Romania. Adding a bizarre twist to Weber’s investigation, Mrs Ceaușescu was, herself, an infamous academic cheat. Despite only completing elementary school, she believed that she was “born a great chemist”, and coerced the Polytechnic Institute in Bucharest into awarding her a PhD in chemistry. Throughout her husband’s reign, she forced Romanian chemists to produce work under her name. Had she somehow blackmailed western scientists into attending her conference? Or could they have been spies sent by the CIA to gather intelligence?

When Romania’s Soviet-backed regime collapsed in 1989, Elena Ceaușescu, along with her husband, was executed by firing squad. Weber’s research turned up no other references to her groundbreaking conference. By 2022, most of its attendants had also passed away. The conference seemed destined to remain a footnote in the history of science. But poring over the pages of Colchicine, Weber was soon convinced that one man had not overlooked the book: Matthias Graw.

After cross-referencing the red book and Graw’s dissertation, Weber and his assistant concluded that nearly 80% of Graw’s work was not original. Two of his thesis’s central chapters and many whole sections were word-for-word copies, with images and tables reproduced wholesale.

On 6 June 2022, Weber finally filed his report. In the 70-page document, which he sent to several media outlets, he claimed that Graw had plagiarised deliberately and with intent to deceive. “The case smells of severe scientific misconduct,” he declared in his blog. “The head of a forensic medicine institute … obviously has a corpse in the basement himself.”

Graw was on holiday in northern Norway when word reached him. On 20 June 2022, a reporter from the investigative magazine Der Spiegel contacted the University of Munich’s Institute of Forensic Medicine, asking if Graw would like to comment on allegations that he had plagiarised his thesis. Graw, a stern man of 66, told me through his lawyer that he remembered being baffled by the call. He explained that he had gone on holiday and left his laptop behind in Munich, about 1,500 miles away. Without it, he couldn’t possibly respond to each of the many accusations, which were anyway baseless. Soon after, the legal department of Graw’s employer, the University of Munich, called Graw to say that they could not support or represent him, as they had to maintain impartiality until the end of the investigation.

Der Spiegel broke the story on 1 July 2022 with an article headlined: “Serious plagiarism allegations against Munich forensic pathologist”. The Munich-based Süddeutsche Zeitung quoted Weber saying that Graw should be suspended while the allegations were investigated. Then came the tabloid Bild, which reported that several lawyers were calling for all the institute’s reports published under Graw’s directorship – thousands – to be reviewed, and the cases re-examined, potentially causing an “earthquake in the Munich judiciary”.

There were calls for Graw to resign. His underlings at the institute began speculating about his successor. The German government asked him to step down from his position as vice-president of the Society for Forensic Medicine. Finally, Graw’s alma mater, the University of Hamburg, opened an inquiry. If its investigation corroborated Weber’s report, Graw’s doctorate would be rescinded. He would lose his office, tenure and pension.

While Weber waited for the results of the Hamburg inquest, in late August he was surprised to read a follow-up story in Bild. Without alerting Weber, Otto had granted the paper an interview in which he claimed that Graw had stolen a gold tooth from his mother during the autopsy. In the article, Otto also claimed that his mother, Doria, was a Jewish Holocaust survivor – which immediately evoked a parallel between the gold tooth theft and the Nazi concentration camps. It was Weber’s policy never to investigate his clients’ motives. He was only interested in the truth, not in hearsay or petty grievances. But reading the article, he began to wonder whether Otto’s interest in Graw might go beyond academic integrity.

Three months after opening their investigation, the University of Hamburg’s panel of ombudsmen finished their internal inquiry. Graw’s detractors expected his disgrace to be complete. But the story was to take a new, unexpected twist.

The university team did not agree with the conclusions of Weber’s report accusing Graw of plagiarism. In fact, they pointed the finger in an entirely new direction. In the university’s view, it wasn’t Graw’s dissertation that was fraudulent. The panel had examined the red book on colchicine, which Graw had supposedly plagiarised for his thesis. And in their expert opinion, it was the red book that was fake.

Weber was stunned. He began looking into the university inquiry’s claims. First, it stated that the publisher’s address listed on the copyright page didn’t correspond to any real location in the former German Democratic Republic. Second, a certain technical term was translated awkwardly into English. And third, the text cited a 1983 source, which was impossible for a book printed in 1982 and based on a 1981 conference.

This evidence struck Weber as weak. It could all be the result of sloppy socialist-era publishing, rather than proof of a forgery. And why would anyone go to such lengths to destroy Graw’s reputation as to create an entirely fake book with such an elaborate backstory?

Still, Weber felt his abilities as an investigator had been called into question, and he set out to crush the accusations. He began by contacting Otto, who had first sent him a pdf scan of the red book, before Weber’s librarian found a print copy on sale on eBay. He asked where exactly he had first found the red book. Previously, Otto had explained that he had seen it cited in a patent, then happened upon the volume he had in his possession at a Serbian flea market. Weber asked, which flea market? And could he provide the patent where it was cited?

Otto, who had previously been helpful in all of his interactions with Weber, became evasive, then angry. Without answering Weber’s questions, he insisted that the University of Hamburg had performed a sham investigation designed to clear Graw’s name. Then, turning conspiratorial, he flooded Weber’s inbox with hundreds of pages of documents chronicling his mother’s death and his reasons for believing that Graw had mishandled her remains.

Weber tried to make sense of Otto’s behaviour by working through the twists in the story on his blog. “If [this is a] forgery, then all this is as unlikely as researchers finding out tomorrow that the Earth is flat,” he wrote on 6 October 2022. Weber saw only two options: either the academic elite had conspired to protect Graw by conducting a shoddy investigation, or Otto had forged the book with the intention of using Weber as a pawn in a shockingly elaborate scheme to sabotage Graw. He announced that if the latter was true, he would renounce plagiarism hunting for ever.

Weber cleared his schedule and turned his attention to the red book. He looked through old GDR phone books for the name of the translator – but no person under that name seemed to live in East Berlin at the time. Weber brought the book to an antiquarian, who claimed that the volume’s cloth bookmark was unusual for that era of East German publishing. A graphic designer informed him that the book’s primary font, Scotch Modern, was only released in 2008. Finally, Weber tracked down the photographer responsible for a key photo of the autumn crocus, who told him that he had uploaded the picture to Wikimedia Commons in 2005.

Weber realised he had been duped. On 13 October, he publicly apologised and revoked his accusations against Graw in a blog post that called the affair “a disaster for plagiarism research”. Then, in a new blog post titled Chronology of a Failed Character Assassination, he set out to document how the book had been produced.

Graw was perfectly sure he had not copied his PhD dissertation, but in a recent phone call, he told me how unsettling the accusations had been: “One thing was clear: the plagiarism hunters had been commissioned by someone, but the question was who, and why?” He spent months trying to calm people in his circles, convincing them he’d done nothing wrong. When he received a pdf of the red book he was supposed to have plagiarised, he was struck by how many glaring errors it contained – and how many people had overlooked them.

During this time, Otto had initiated a series of civil proceedings against Graw, accusing him of copyright infringement. In August 2022, Graw read the interview with Otto in Bild, in which Otto further accused him of stealing a gold tooth from his dead mother. It was then he realised that Otto, the bereaved son, was behind the plot to destroy his career. In October, Graw filed a criminal complaint against Otto, asking for a police investigation of the whole affair.

On 8 November 2022, police burst into Otto’s apartment. Officers found extensive literature on colchicine and several of Graw’s scientific papers. They seized correspondence and data-storage devices containing sprawling documents in which the name “Graw” appeared more than 28,000 times. Otto’s laptop contained folders named Graw and Dissertation, and images of the autumn crocus flower. Investigators also found correspondence with a Pakistani ghostwriter and a contract with a Serbian printer. Out of these disparate ingredients, it seemed, Otto had carefully assembled the red book.

As investigators pored over Otto’s records, a picture emerged of his past, his mother’s final days and his strange, obsessive quest for revenge. Though he had lied about practically everything else, Otto was, in fact, a doctor – albeit one with a chequered clinical history. After practising in the US, Switzerland and Germany, he settled in the UK, but concerns raised by a pharmacist about “bizarre” prescriptions he’d written had prompted a review by Lambeth primary care trust and an investigation by the General Medical Council. In 2010, he had been barred from practising medicine in the UK, but by then, he had returned to Munich to focus on just one patient: his mother.

Otto believed that movement was key to improving Doria’s health. He insisted that Doria walk every day, even when she was so exhausted she could barely get out of bed. He brought her down into the streets and observed as she hobbled along the pavement. He told me that he would leave marks on the buildings to track her progress, and took her to her favourite park bench. “Come on, Ma!” he remembered saying to cheer her on. “Just another three metres!”

For years, he monitored her day and night, noting signs of progress or deterioration. Every day, he inspected her urine and weighed her faeces to make sure she was getting enough nutrition.

After Doria died, Otto called the funeral home, asking for her to be picked up as late as legally possible, 36 hours after her death. When the company asked for a death certificate, Otto issued one himself, noting “rigor mortis” as a sign of death. It was then that the funeral company got suspicious and alerted the police, who sent a patrol unit and a coroner.

When the coroner arrived, Otto’s erratic behaviour and desire to share his copious records of his mother’s health made her suspicious, too. “Extremely odd behaviour of the son; questionable medical treatment; extremely poor condition of care,” she noted in her report. Noting “indications of an unnatural death”, she ordered an autopsy. The examiners’ prevailing theory was that Otto had accidentally killed his mother with an overdose of insulin, then covered up his mistake by administering a glucose injection to stabilise her vitals.

In the weeks after the coroner issued her report, Otto launched legal action against her, including for invoicing irregularities, but his suit was dismissed. Police opened a manslaughter investigation against Otto for the death of his mother, but dropped the case after the autopsy. Graw told me he didn’t perform the autopsy himself. His name was on the report merely as the institute’s director. The report found no conclusive evidence that Doria’s death was unnatural.

During those long, uncertain months, Otto became tormented by trying to recover his mother’s corpse and discovering the exact cause of death – wondering whether it was due to a mistake he had made. He wrote to Matthias Graw to suggest they co-author a paper on the conditions that led to Doria’s passing, and recommended they perform a histological examination of the brain, which he later described in court as entailing “a circular cut with a butcher’s knife, then pulling the skin off and going at it with a saw”.

Graw said he never received the letter, but if he had, he wouldn’t have responded to Otto for the same reason that Otto was kept in the dark about the examinations of his mother’s body – the ongoing criminal investigation forbade any contact with a suspect. Otto seems to have become obsessed with Graw, the keeper of his mother’s remains, and his fixation gradually twisted into a conviction that he was hiding something sinister.

Barred access to Graw, Otto sought to learn everything he could about the man and find a fatal flaw. He fixated on Graw’s dissertation on the poison colchicine, hoping to undermine the foundation of the doctor’s entire career. He launched a flurry of bizarre proceedings against him, claiming that the doctor had failed to recognise inconsistencies in the colchicine levels in his mother’s blood, and accusing him of using the “flesh of the Jewish woman Mrs Z” for experiments.

On 1 March 2024, the Munich public prosecutor concluded its investigation and charged Otto with document forgery, copyright infringement and multiple counts of defamation and fraud. The case came to trial in early 2025. The prosecution argued that Otto had attempted to “completely obliterate the livelihood” of Graw by commissioning the creation of the red book, inventing the 1981 conference on which it was based, and listing the book on eBay in order to fool Stefan Weber into carrying out his plan. Carbon dating corroborated these claims – the paper on which the book was printed was produced no earlier than 2015. When the furore failed to cost Graw his job, the prosecution claimed, Otto had fed the press the gold tooth accusation.

During the trial, Otto repeatedly claimed that his mother was a Holocaust survivor. Reporters for Die Zeit, the weekly magazine that published an extensive article on the case, contacted the main organisations that document survivors, and concluded that her name does not appear in the records.

On 6 March 2025, Otto was sentenced to two and a half years in prison. The court cited his “almost unprecedented criminal energy”. Otto appealed against the court’s decision. When convicted, he was offered a suspended sentence if he confessed, but he maintained his innocence, claiming he and his mother were the victims of a string of bureaucratic errors, then a conspiracy to cover them up. Finally, in July 2026, he confessed to commissioning the red book and agreed to pay €210,000 in damages to Graw. He received a two-year suspended sentence.

When I spoke to Graw recently, he told me he was satisfied with the outcome and hoped for peace and quiet now. But he was still coming to terms with the case, which had consumed the past few years of his life. He remained baffled by Otto’s motive in targeting him – he hadn’t performed the autopsy or started the investigation, and his institute’s report was the reason why Otto had been exonerated. He lamented that Otto had never explained, or apologised.

He complained that “some of the media had no interest in investigating the allegations and carried stories before giving me a chance to respond”. And while, as a scientist, he was bound to test hypotheses before publishing them, “plagiarism hunters didn’t even check whether the source was genuine at all”. (Despite his vow, Stefan Weber has not retired from plagiarism hunting, but he has sworn to never again work with “grey literature”.)

At trial, questions were raised about Otto’s mental health, but he refused to submit to psychiatric evaluation. According to experts called by the court, the assiduous attention to detail with which he carried out his forgery seems to rule out a full psychotic breakdown or a schizophrenic episode, but he may have experienced temporary delusions brought on by grief.

Otto dismisses mental illness allegations as attempts to discredit him. He told me he has bought a house in Serbia to transform it into a memorial dedicated to his mother. With the slow, reverent precision with which he does everything, he has been attempting to retrace the steps of Doria’s entire life. In this memorial exhibition, he said, he will show she was a Holocaust survivor, and detail the true sequence of events that led to her death.

#212. This Hidden Device Could Free Up Gigawatts of Grid Power

Variable frequency drives can slash motors’ power use

Zurich-based ABB is one of several manufacturers of variable frequency drives (VFDs), such as this ACH580. VFDs could help make the millions of electric motors running in industrial facilities more energy efficient.

This article was originally published by Canary Media.

America’s energy supply crunch is driving a surge of federal and private investment in new electricity generation — from polluting gas turbines to cleaner developments like solar farms and geothermal plants. But gigawatts of power are already available for the taking across the U.S. economy in the form of wasted energy from an unexpected source: motors.

Some 50 million electric motors drive the fans, pumps, and compressors found in virtually every factory and building. Together, they gobble enough electricity to equal nearly a third of total U.S. power demand. Often, the motors use far more energy than they actually need to keep America’s machines humming.

Companies can install devices known as variable frequency drives, or VFDs, to make motors run super efficiently. Yet adoption remains relatively low, in part because of the perceived hassle of retrofitting equipment and because they’re typically not required. On average, only 16 percent of motor systems at industrial facilities and 4 percent of commercial-sector motors use VFDs, according to a 2021 market report by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

However, there are now more reasons than ever to equip the nation’s motors with power-saving devices, energy experts and device manufacturers say. They’re urging federal agencies, utilities, and deep-pocked tech giants to spur a wider rollout of VFDs through financial incentives and efficiency standards.

For one, slashing motors’ power use would free up grid capacity for large electricity users like data centers and electric vehicles, they argue. It would help curb costs for factories that are switching from fossil-fueled heating systems to electrified, motor-based solutions like heat pumps — all at a time when industrial power prices are climbing fast. Plus, VFD technology has become far more sophisticated and less expensive to install than earlier iterations.

“This is low-hanging fruit that gives a lot [of energy] back and is reasonably simple,” Nik Sawe, a senior policy analyst at the nonpartisan think tank Energy Innovation, says of the technology.

Energy-wise, the main problem with electric motors is that they’re always running at full capacity. Consider an office building, which empties out in the evening. The heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning system can wind down in those hours, with dampers and valves restricting the flow of cold or hot air. But the motors and fans that drive the whole setup are still working in the background, wasting energy.

VFD technology, such as the Danfoss iC7 series has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings trying to combat rising electricity costs. Danfoss Drives

VFDs are electronic controllers with temperature sensors that continually adjust the speed of motors, automatically ramping up or down to match demand. The technology, which is also called adjustable speed drives, has the potential to curb a motor’s energy use by around 40 to 60 percent, says Neal Elliott, director emeritus of the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy.

All those energy reductions add up. Toyota, for example, installed VFDs on over 200 motors inside the HVAC system at its auto manufacturing plant in Georgetown, Kentucky, as part of a US $1.25 million pilot project in 2015. The automaker saved more than $700,000 in annual electricity costs thanks to the VFDs, and it continues to use the technology at other manufacturing facilities across the U.S., the company said by email.

“We’ve known for many, many years that there’s a huge opportunity for energy savings by varying the speed of the motor,” says Elliott, who noted that he literally wrote the book on energy-efficient motor systems in 2002.

Certain aspects of the technology have historically held the drives back since they debuted in the late 1960s. Measuring the flow of water, air, refrigerant — whatever is moving through the system that the motors are driving — was for decades an expensive engineering process. Accurately controlling motors to deliver the right amount of juice, at just the right time, faced similar issues.

But recent advances in sensors and machine-learning algorithms have significantly slashed the cost and complexity of using drives, Elliott says. Modern VFDs have also benefited from the increased production of advanced power chips that are used in high-voltage applications such as electric vehicles and solar power inverters.

Another long-standing challenge has been that commercial and industrial building developers often prioritize reducing up-front costs over netting long-term energy savings, and so don’t always build to the highest efficiency levels, says Zack Valdez, senior director of regulatory and industry affairs at the National Electrical Manufacturers Association, whose members include drive and motor makers.

“If the facility that you’re putting it into doesn’t require it, then oftentimes people will overlook [VFDs], because they’re just trying to build to a minimum set of energy requirements,” he says. And if companies don’t install drives from the start, they’re likely less inclined to take time to retrofit an operating system.

The trade association recently launched a pilot program with manufacturers, utilities, and energy-efficiency groups to collect real-world data about how VFDs reduce motors’ electricity use and lower utility bills. The goal is to demonstrate how the technology can benefit not only individual facilities but also the wider grid — giving utilities a concrete reason to provide rebates for industrial customers.

Proponents say they hope the results will help the U.S. Department of Energy shape future efficiency measures and incentives that encourage adoption of the drives, including in federally owned buildings. Despite the Trump administration’s open hostility toward home appliance and equipment mandates, agency staff have apparently been receptive to discussing solutions that could meet the soaring power needs of data centers.

“If you added a drive to all the motors that are out there, you could provide [power for] up to five years of data center growth without having to build any new generation,” says Kirk Anderson, director of government relations and public affairs for ABB. The global manufacturing giant makes VFDs domestically near Milwaukee.

Anderson floated the idea of having tech companies help pay for factory owners to install VFDs to free up room on the grid. After all, hyperscalers are already spending many billions of dollars to revive shuttered nuclear plants, support next-generation geothermal projects, deploy fleets of grid-scale batteries, and supercharge the buildout of gas turbines and power plants.

“Instead of ‘bring your own power,’ it should be ‘offset your own power,’” he says, referring to a growing effort by states to get data centers to secure their own power resources and prevent rising costs for regular customers.

Michael Reckamp, the director of enterprise strategy for Danfoss Drives, North America, another VFD manufacturer, said that despite the traditionally low adoption rates, the technology has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings as rising electricity costs and other grid-wide challenges make it harder to justify wasting energy.

Still, “it hasn’t permeated enough to get everyone utilizing it,” he says. “In the current situation, where we’re having so many issues with grids, brownouts, and now data centers wanting to take the load, I think there should be a renewed focus on putting drives out there to really reduce the stress on the grid and improve energy savings.”

Maria Gallucci is a clean-energy reporter with Canary Media.

Apple is reportedly developing a premium HomeView built around a motorized arm that spins 360 degrees and turns the display toward whoever's speaking, per Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. A larger 9-inch screen, a 2027-2028 target, and an identity crisis about whether it's a "Max," an "Ultra," or something with its own name.

We’ve only just got the first HomeView, but the Cupertino crew is thinking about the long-game here, and it expands into a companion era I’m not sure we’re ready for — with a fascinating backstory.

Per Gurman, the arm-equipped device pairs the motorized base with a bigger 9-inch display — up from the 7-inch panel on the standard HomeView just announced. But what’s key to note is that this is not HomeView 2.

It’s a more premium experience, and a companion that is actually able to rotate on its base and look at you as you walk around a room. Less of a passive device on your kitchen countertop and one that can actively engage with you — with a rumored $1,000 price tag penciled in for a 2027 launch.

In February 2025, Apple Machine Learning Research published a video of a robot lamp research demo — a little articulated Pixar-looking lamp that watched a person move around a room, and responded with something uncomfortably close to personality. Head tilts. Leaning in. The unmistakable energy of Pixar’s mascot coming to life with a machine learning degree.

Nobody treated it as a serious thing at the time. But here we are in October 2026, watching how things can come full circle. The more I watch it, the more I realize this wasn’t just a lamp demo. It was Apple workshopping the idea of making your furniture behave like it notices you.

And soon, we may see what that looks like in a real product. But that’s not the only place where Apple may have already been unintentionally working on the HomeView Max.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Here’s the story underneath the story: the $10 billion electric car is the most expensive graveyard in Apple history. When it was gutted, we all thought that everything was scattered into the wind.

Gurman’s reporting suggests something more deliberate — the robotics lived on, moving the arm from the driveway to the living room. And all that gesture recognition, smooth motion and spatial awareness of that car arm is reportedly being repackaged as this screen that turns its head when you walk in mid-Siri.

As a tech nerd, this is an absurdly cool use of some serious engineering.

So, it’s time to put the tin hat on, together.

First, the swivel is the whole thing — and the entire privacy conversation. Apple’s pitch has always been privacy-centered, and for good reason when you see what other companies are doing.

And while that may well be the case with this arm version of HomeView, I think there’s a creep factor to a screen following you around the room that will cause some spirited discussions around the Thanksgiving table.

Second, that rumored price is going to turn some heads. Compared to other smart home hubs, the current HomeView is already pretty pricey and kind of limited in functionality. Now we have a premium robot sibling option set for launch next year? That’s a big test of household budgets.

Third, Siri has to be good. A robot arm that turns toward you only matters if there’s something worth saying to it once it’s looking. The HomeView ad does show how it can fit into a chaotic family household, but if my iPhone’s Siri response time is anything to go by, those pauses between people asking questions and getting answers would actually leave some awkward silences.

When it’s just a screen on your countertop, that can be forgiven. But when you make it a companion, it has to be near-instantaneous. The arm, ironically, is probably the least important component of this device when it comes to actually using it.

Gurman’s report uses the word “companion,” and I couldn’t agree more. For the past decade, smart home devices have been appliances — helpful, static and furniture-adjacent.

This robot arm is the moment the real hub is elevated above being just a screen with a speaker, but a feeling that something in your house knows you walked in.

Are people going to be comfortable with this? That’s something we’ll find out. Apple’s $299 HomeView is a slightly high, but rational price for a smart display, and it’ll get the software updates the robot needs anyway.

This rumored arm version is for a different person entirely: the smart-home early adopter with a spouse who’s stopped asking where the money went, and the Apple watcher reading the tea leaves.

So to figure this out, I turn to you, dear reader!

#214. Apple sets 28 October event, expected to bring its first touchscreen Mac

The Los Angeles "Pro and tell" launch is also tipped to bring an M6 iMac and an OLED iPad mini.

Apple has confirmed a “Pro and tell” event in Los Angeles on 28 October. Bloomberg reports it will show its first touchscreen MacBook Pro with an OLED screen, an entry-level M6 MacBook Pro, a new iMac and an OLED iPad mini. Apple has not confirmed any products.

Apple will hold a launch event in Los Angeles on 28 October under the tagline “Pro and tell,” the company confirmed on Monday. Press releases are expected at 10am Pacific Time, followed by hands-on sessions for media.

Apple has not said what it will show. But the event is expected to bring its first touchscreen MacBook, Bloomberg reported. Mark Gurman had earlier said the launch was planned for 27 October.

According to Bloomberg, the new 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models will have OLED touchscreens and a Dynamic Island, the cut-out at the top of the iPhone screen. They are also said to be much lighter than current models.

Apple is also expected to add a cheaper 14-inch MacBook Pro with its M6 chip, and a refreshed iMac. Both are set to keep their current designs, Bloomberg said. Apple launched the M6, its first 2nm chip, in the Mac mini in August.

The fourth product is likely an iPad mini with an OLED screen, better speakers and a moved front camera, 9to5Mac reported, citing Gurman. Bloomberg first reported the OLED iPad mini in July, with an October launch target.

The touchscreen Mac is part of a wider plan to overhaul every Mac over the next year. Apple has long rejected touchscreens on laptops, saying macOS is designed for a mouse and trackpad.

“Pro and tell” will be Apple’s third launch this autumn and the second under chief executive John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook on 1 September. It follows the HomeView smart home display, a second HomePod mini and a new Apple TV, Bloomberg said.

Ternus’s first event in September brought the foldable iPhone Duo, which goes on sale this Friday.

#216. ‘I use AI to do the things that I’m bad at’: Linus Torvalds on why it works for him

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Linux

The Linux creator calls vibe coding 'a wonderful way to find joy in programming,' but not for running Linux development. (Finding bugs is OK.)

PRAGUE – Many open-source developers still dislike AI. The latest example is System76 banning AI-generated content from its COSMIC desktop. At Open Source Summit Europe, Linux creator Linus Torvalds offered a different take: “I actually really like using AI,” Torvald told Dirk Hohndel, his good friend and head of Ericsson Software Technology, in their latest discussion.

Also: Linus Torvalds is using AI to develop Linux kernel code now

But that enthusiasm comes with a distinction worth keeping in mind. Using AI to make a hobby project more enjoyable is one thing. Using it responsibly in the Linux kernel, where generated patches and bug reports can overwhelm maintainers, is another.

Torvalds said, “I think that you need to be very careful using AI when you’re doing something real and important.”

Torvalds explained he hadn’t always felt that way about AI programming. “I used to think it was just not very good — but now I’m at  the point where I actually really like using AI.”

“To be fair,” he continued, “I don’t do a lot of kernel programming. I’m a maintainer. The Linux kernel is a project where other people do the real work, and I act as the collection point. But I still enjoy programming immensely. I think AI is a wonderful tool if you use it correctly and treat it as a tool, and I find it makes programming much more enjoyable.”

Torvalds recalled, “I started programming in 1981 or so, and back then computers were much simpler, and you could understand what they were doing, and also the programs you compared your own programs to were much simpler.”

Also: Someone made a free Photoshop clone – so I had to try it on Linux

“It’s a different story today,” Torvalds said. “The bar in software engineering has grown so high that it’s hard to see your own small efforts as worth anything, because you’re used to all these polished, professional programs. “

“A lot of people make fun of vibe coding, but I think it’s a wonderful way to find joy in programming. It makes you feel like you’re doing something relevant. It allows you, as a new programmer, to do things that you would otherwise have a really hard time with.”

He continued: “I love the concept of AI as a gateway drug because I was working on my own toy project, the guitar pedal, and I knew what I was doing. I had a user interface that I had written myself in C that was running on a microcontroller that was running on this small screen, and I was like, “This is just stupid. It looks like something from the ’80s; I wanted it to look like something from this century. But I don’t do Java. I do kernels.”

Also: My 5 favorite Linux distros for security

“So, I use AI to do the things that I’m bad at,” Torvalds went on, “I’d seen all the same YouTube videos you have. Give AI a prompt, and it will do it. So I gave it a prompt, and it did it, and it was horrendous. Then I said, ‘Hey, look! I already did this in C. I did it the right way. It’s just ugly.”

That’s not to say AI isn’t useful for finding and fixing mistakes in the Linux kernel. Hohndel asked about Sashiko, an agentic Linux kernel code review system. Torvalds said its public reviews now appear on the Linux Kernel Mailing List (LKML). Indeed, some subsystem maintainers now expect patches to have received such a review before accepting them.

That doesn’t mean all pull requests have to go through an AI review. Some maintainers do require it, though, and it seems likely that all will eventually require it.

Also: Why the future of Linux is rolling – thanks to AI

AI tools can identify genuine security problems. They can also surface issues in old, no-longer-used drivers that have gone unnoticed for years. Torvalds sees value in the resulting fixes, while acknowledging their cost. “It is, I think, improving our code base… Although it is also stressing maintainers out to the point that it’s a problem.”

As Torvalds said in Mumbai earlier this year. convincing but fabricated bug reports can require substantial human effort to disprove, while narrowly targeted patches may fix one symptom without addressing the underlying problem. Torvalds called some submissions “mindless band-aid kind of patches.”

That said, AI code checking is here, and it’s here to stay. For example, Torvalds said, “three-quarters of the preceding day’s Linux Kernel Maintainer Summit discussion concerned making AI generation and review less stressful and more useful. The bottleneck isn’t getting patches. It’s getting useful work through review without exhausting the people responsible for it.

Because it was Linux’s 35th anniversary, Torvalds also talked about how the process of making Linux has changed over the years. In the beginning, Linux had no development infrastructure at all to speak of. Instead, Torvalds tracked changes through tarball patches and regularly distributed updated source code.

“I made patches every single day internally, and I released them at least weekly,” he recalled. “And it actually worked surprisingly well for a small project.”

Also: ‘I’m not a programmer’ anymore: Linus Torvalds on the only two tools he uses now

Hohndel noted that the distribution of new tarballs and their accompanying changes continued until 2002, when Linux had become a much larger undertaking. Back in those days, Torvalds said, “It was really just me, myself, and my computer.”

His reluctance to adopt existing source-control tools was not simply stubbornness. He wanted developers to work independently, with their own local environments. “I really felt very strongly that everybody should have their own local setup,” he said.

As I explained in my 2025 account of Linux’s growth, drawing on Jonathan Corbet’s history of the project, Linux’s openness attracted an expanding development community. But relying on Torvalds to apply incoming patches manually became a bottleneck. Accepting contributions by hand was no longer enough; the project needed a better way to integrate them.

The BitKeeper version control system provided that improvement, although its proprietary licensing divided the kernel community. Some developers refused to use it. Torvalds, however, found that distributed source control made it substantially easier to merge work from subsystems such as networking and ARM. Torvalds said, “BitKeeper, as far as I’m concerned, was a huge success.”

He didn’t consider it flawless. Rather, it showed him what source control could do and helped him identify what he actually wanted. Nor did its adoption require every maintainer to use the same tool.

Also: Linux after Linus? The kernel community’s plan for replacing Torvalds

Then the 2005 BitKeeper licensing dispute took away the tool he had come to depend on.  After experiencing distributed source control, returning to the old approach was no longer appealing. Git was Torvalds’ answer.

Hohndel recalled that Torvalds took 11 days to produce the first working version: a new object model, code, and a functioning tool in under two weeks. The early Git was not universally popular. Developers accustomed to CVS found it unfamiliar, and its first versions had rough edges.

Its eventual success still surprises Torvalds. Today, according to a 2022 Stack Overflow Developer survey, Git has become the de facto standard for version control: Nearly 94% of respondents, and almost 97% of professional developers, use Git. All Torvalds wanted was a tool for Linux, not to remake software development everywhere. As he put it,  “I sometimes get way too much credit for Git.”

After roughly six months, he handed over its maintenance. His point was that the subsequent decades of development belonged to other people, not that the initial work was unimportant. “It’s worth noting that Git today is a lot better than Git in 2005.”

Linux’s release process underwent another major change, moving away from long-lived, separate stable and development trees toward frequent releases, a merge window, and release candidates.

Under the older model, work accumulated in the development tree while distributions backported desired changes into stable kernels. Releases intended to happen annually could stretch into years, making planning difficult. Torvalds proposed a dramatically shorter cycle. The reaction was not enthusiastic. “People looked at me like I had grown a third head.”

Also: Even Linus Torvalds is vibe coding now

His initial five-week target was intentionally aggressive. The process ultimately settled into the familiar nine-to-ten-week rhythm. The result is a development model Torvalds still finds remarkably effective. “We now, for the last 20 years, have a really stable, working model.”

He also rejected the idea that Linux should organize itself around dramatic feature launches. “I’m a big believer in the whole incremental small changes that, over time, turn into big features.” As he had said this summer in Mumbai, Linux’s development goal remains “incremental improvement and steady progress all the time.”

So, while AI is changing Linux’s problem-finding and fixing mechanisms, the name of the game for Linux remains rapid, small improvements to an essential, stable operating system.
