#217. The Unusual Item I Use to Degrease a Pan Before Washing It

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Keep oil out of the kitchen sink with this nifty trick.

My mother kept a large jar under the sink to store rendered fat or used oil from bacon, burgers, fried chicken and the like; its distinct layers represented the geologic eras of family dinners from previous months. Once full, we would presumably discard it in the trash.

This was before we recycled everything, and before we knew food waste was one of the largest contributors to greenhouse gas emissions. Surely large jars of cooking grease set out on the curb with other refuse isn’t exactly a winning move on either the recycling or food-waste front.

While we have vastly improved how we dispose of many things, excess cooking grease still presents a regular quandary. It’s not exactly cooperative to slither inside biodegradable food-waste bags, if you’re fortunate enough to live somewhere that collects food waste. You also can’t toss it into your countertop composter without disrupting its yuck-free operation.

So, is it ever OK to pour excess grease or used cooking oil down the sink? Even if you run the hot water tap at the same time? Short answer: no. Long answer? Here’s an expert for the “no.” “When grease cools, it solidifies, coating the interior of the pipe,” says Jacylyn Basilone, chief operating officer of Brooks Plumbing. Even if you’re running hot water, the grease will eventually cool further down the line and cause future problems. “Over time, the solidified grease in the pipes can catch debris, thus making a partial clog grow larger and larger,” she says, reducing the pipe’s circumference little by little if you do this repeatedly.

Unlike a clogged shower drain, which you can usually clear easily, “a normal sewer machine or ‘snake’ can’t alleviate this type of stoppage,” says Basilone. “While grease solidifies, it can’t be captured by the claw head. Grease removal is best remediated with a hydrojetter, which tends to be more expensive than the traditional drain-cleaning services.”

Bread is the real answer, and I can’t believe I haven’t been doing this all along. (*Hangs head in shame as someone fully guilty of relying on the obviously very sketchy hot water method.*)

Bread has always been a superb grease-mopping tool; we usually think of it in a culinary context rather than for waste removal. Just as you’d drag a crusty baguette or hunk of ciabatta across the drippings on your plate, bread is an excellent sponge for all manner of oil, whether or not it is appealing to consume. Using bread to soak up excess oil essentially turns liquid food waste into a solid, making disposal much easier.

If it’s not obvious, this is also an excellent way to use bread that might otherwise go to waste: the ends of the loaf you can’t bring yourself to eat, or bread that’s gone stale or starting to show the first mold spores. If you’re going to discard the bread anyway, at least put it to good use.

The bread trick comes in handy in almost endless ways. If there’s a pool of oil, it’s the mop for the job. I initially tried it after cooking bacon. A single, small slice of bread was enough to absorb what was easily four to six ounces of liquid grease left in the pan. I dragged the slice around the pan like a mop, but even after letting it sit a few extra moments, it kept working and eventually soaked up all the liquid grease. (If you’re feeling indulgent and used a fresh bread slice for this purpose, the temptation to make pretty epic croutons here is quite strong — another upside.)

If your air fryer has space between the drawer and the basket, you can place the bread there to soak up grease while cooking. Even for oily, slow-cooked proteins like pork shoulder, you can press the bread onto the meat to soak up grease before serving.

Once the bread has absorbed the oil and needs discarding, responsible food-waste methods are much easier to manage. Depending on how much oil the bread has absorbed, you can safely put the soaked bread in the compost bin or countertop composter without risking a major oil spill and a mess to clean up later. Oil can slow decomposition, so composting large amounts isn’t recommended. Small amounts, such as a few tablespoons at a time, are safe.

Even if you have no other option but to throw it away — and if that is the case, please consider getting a small composting appliance — at the very least, you’re not involving an easily recyclable glass container.

For more home tips, learn this neat trick for reusing frying oil and learn the 10 worst things to pour down your drain.

#218. Microplastics React With Water, a New Study Says. That’s a Problem for Biology

One of the reasons plastic has become so ubiquitous is that, generally, it’s very chemically stable, meaning it does not readily react with the substances around it. That’s why this material is so often used for food packaging and water bottles.

The same was thought to be true of microplastics—those tiny pieces of debris that break off from larger plastic objects and which, according to numerous studies, have spread to virtually every ecosystem on the planet. But scientists at Columbia University and UC Berkeley have just discovered that water can make the surfaces of microplastics chemically active and turn them into a potential hazard.

According to the findings of the article published in Nature, this activity can trigger the spontaneous formation of chemicals capable of altering other molecules, like those that are essential for living organisms. The phenomenon, the authors note, occurs even under normal environmental conditions, without the need for sunlight or other agents that cause plastic degradation.

So how can microplastics be so reactive when bigger plastics generally aren’t? The scientists suggest this has to do with the greater available surface area for these reactions to occur.

“As plastic fragments into smaller and smaller particles, its surface area increases enormously,” Wei Min, a professor of chemistry and biomedical engineering at Columbia University, said in a press release. “Then microplastics change the water that surrounds them, generating high-energy, reactive radicals that very likely contribute to biological damage that we see in animals and potentially in humans as a result of microplastic exposure.”

Among these potentially dangerous chemical products—called reactive oxygen species—a variety known as hydroxyl radicals stands out. They are particularly dangerous because they can snatch electrons from the proteins and fats that make up cell membranes, disrupting their structure and function. These “are textbook examples of the kinds of molecules that can damage animal and human tissue,” added Naixin Qian, a postdoctoral researcher in Min’s lab who helped lead the research.

Our body has some defenses against this kind of damage. This is the biological function of the buzzy molecules known as antioxidants. These neutralize the reactive chemicals, but if the reactive compounds greatly outnumber antioxidants, this line of defense can be overwhelmed.

This can develop into a scenario called oxidative stress, leading to the damage of cells. Previous research had already identified oxidative stress among the cellular responses associated with exposure to microplastics, although the mechanisms responsible for this damage are not yet fully understood.

The extent to which microplastics have pervaded our bodies remains an open debate, with some of the more sensational findings having been called into question. But if even a small amount of microplastics are present in our tissues, they could be reacting with the water in our bodies.

The researchers were particularly concerned with the potential effects on blood, which is largely composed of water. If contact with this fluid can chemically activate the surfaces of microplastics, their presence inside the body could pose an additional danger beyond that of the pollutants they carry or release.

When the researchers exposed red blood cells extracted from mice to different types of microplastics, the cells became deformed and ruptured—a phenomenon known as hemolysis. The effects were greater with plastics that were more reactive with water, indicating that this activity was the cause of cellular damage.

Research into the effects of microplastics has long focused on other chemicals leaching from the particles or on their physical effects, often considering the plastic itself chemically inert. The larger pieces generally are, but these findings challenge the assumption that what is true of plastic on a grand scale is also true of the microscopic pieces it breaks down into.

#219. Show HN: KiviDB, a faster Redis-compatible memory database and vector cache

A fast, multi-threaded Redis® and Valkey alternative written in Rust: drop-in compatible, with full-text and vector search built in

KiviDB is a fast, multi-threaded alternative to Redis® and Valkey, written in Rust. It speaks the Redis protocol (RESP2 and RESP3), so existing Redis clients, redis-cli and libraries work unchanged, and it has full-text and vector search built in. It runs every core on a sharded in-memory key-value design, and persists to snapshots and an optional append-only file.

On the same 32 cores, KiviDB serves 21 million pipelined GETs per second: about 9× Redis 8 and 2.3× Dragonfly, with under half Dragonfly's p99 latency (benchmarks).

KiviDB listens on 6380, not Redis's 6379, so the two can run side by side; point your client at that port, or pass --port 6379.

Repository: github.com/kividbio/kividb · Website: kividb.io

As of October 2026. Something out of date or wrong? Please open an issue.

Throughput, latency, vector search and vector ingest. Click for the full-resolution video.

All figures below are from one session in October 2026 on AWS Graviton3 bare metal: the server on a c7gn.metal (64 vCPU), confined to 32 cores, and the load generator on a second c7gn.metal in the same placement group. Each engine ran alone on the server, one after another.

memtier_benchmark through kivi-benchmark's run-matrix.sh: 10 million keys, 100-byte values, 30 s a scenario, mean of two rounds; 300 connections pipelined, 1,200 without pipelining.

redis/vector-db-benchmark on glove-25-angular (1.18M vectors, 25 dimensions): HNSW with M=16 and EF_CONSTRUCTION=256, 100 clients uploading in batches of 64, then queries at ef 64, 128, 256 and 512.

Results depend on the environment. Treat published figures as one controlled capture, not a guarantee, and measure on your own hardware and workload.

KiviDB implements Redis Stack–compatible search and vector commands, so existing clients and tutorials largely work unchanged. Use them for full-text (BM25), tags / numerics, and vector ANN (FLAT or HNSW) on hash fields.

Store vectors as raw FLOAT32 little-endian bytes in a hash field (DIM × 4 bytes), the same convention as Redis Stack and redis-py / numpy blobs. Use your client's binary-safe HSET (the integration tests under tests/e2e/ have examples).

Query with KNN (Dialect 2), passing the query vector as a named binary parameter:

The full command surface, filters, hybrid search and edge cases are in COMMANDS.md (search for FT.CREATE, FT.SEARCH, FT.HYBRID, and so on).

KiviDB comes in four variants, chosen by Cargo features at build time:

In a build without Lua, the scripting commands return an error. A build without TLS refuses to start if --tls-port is given, rather than serving plaintext.

Requires a stable Rust toolchain (rust-toolchain.toml selects stable with rustfmt and clippy). The crate uses the 2024 edition; the oldest toolchain it is checked against is Rust 1.89, the version the Dockerfile builds with.

On Linux the server uses io_uring when the kernel allows it and falls back to Tokio otherwise (--io-model auto, the default).

To build the Docker image yourself, docker build -t kividb . builds the default variant; docker build --build-arg KIVIDB_FEATURES=lua,tls -t kividb:full . builds another one.

Any Redis client works; point it at port 6380.

Protected mode is on by default, as in Redis. While it is on, no bind address has been set (--bind or bind in the config file) and the default user has no password, only clients on the same machine (loopback) may connect. Any other client receives a -DENIED error that explains the options, and is disconnected.

To accept clients from other machines, do one of these:

If you turn it off or bind to a public address, make sure the server cannot be reached from the internet without a password.

Images are published to Docker Hub and the GitHub Container Registry, with the same tags in both:

latest and version tags such as v1.1.0 are the default variant; v1.1.0-lua, v1.1.0-tls and v1.1.0-full are the others. Images are built for amd64 and arm64.

A container is reached through its network, never from loopback, so the image's default command is --protected-mode no. Arguments you pass replace that default, which turns protected mode back on. When you pass your own flags, set a password (recommended) or add --protected-mode no yourself:

With AOF persistence (mount a volume so data survives restarts; the server runs as user kividb in /home/kividb):

With --aof, every write is appended to appendonly.aof and the file is replayed on startup, so a crash loses at most about the last second of writes (the fsync interval) rather than everything since the last snapshot. When an AOF is present it is the source of truth and the snapshot is not loaded; see docs/PERSISTENCE.md for why.

io_uring in containers: Docker's default seccomp profile blocks io_uring on recent versions, and KiviDB then falls back to Tokio. To allow it on a Linux host, run with --security-opt seccomp=unconfined (understand what that permits before using it in production).

Release binaries for Linux (x86_64, aarch64) and macOS (Apple silicon, Intel) are published on GitHub Releases. The latest/download links below always resolve to the newest release; replace latest/download with download/v1.1.0 to pin a version.

Each variant other than the default has its name in the file: kividb-lua-linux-x86_64.tar.gz, kividb-tls-…, kividb-full-…. The default variant is also packaged for Linux as kividb_amd64.deb / kividb_arm64.deb and kividb.x86_64.rpm / kividb.aarch64.rpm, built with nfpm from packaging/nfpm.yaml. A SHA256SUMS.txt file lists the checksum of every file in a release.

KiviDB is configured with command-line flags, or with a Redis-style configuration file (one directive per line, such as port 6380 or appendonly yes). The file is read from /etc/kividb/kividb.conf if it exists; --configfile names another one. A flag given on the command line wins over the same setting in the file. Run kividb --help for the full list.

TLS clients connect on a separate port, --tls-port; plain traffic stays on --port.

Client certificates (mutual TLS). With --tls-ca-cert-file ca.pem, clients must present a certificate signed by that CA; others are refused during the handshake. --tls-auth-clients optional accepts clients without a certificate but still refuses an invalid one, and --tls-auth-clients no does not ask for one. With redis-cli: redis-cli --tls -p 6381 --cacert ca.pem --cert client.pem --key client.key.

Clients must use TLS on the TLS port. A plain connection to it (for example redis-cli -p 6381 without --tls) fails the handshake, and the server logs [TLS] handshake failed. For memtier_benchmark, add --tls (and --tls-skip-verify for a self-signed certificate).

The log goes to standard error, or to --logfile. docs/LOGGING.md describes the log; docs/ERRORS.md explains the warnings, errors and error replies, and what to do about each.

When it starts, a release build of KiviDB makes one HTTPS request to https://github.com/kividbio/kividb/releases/latest, the same page you would open to find the newest release. GitHub answers with a redirect to that release's tag; if it is newer than the running build, KiviDB prints a short notice with the link before the startup banner. Nothing is sent but the request itself, with a User-Agent of kividb/: no host name, configuration, keys, data or identifier. GitHub sees the request's source IP address, as any web server would.

Startup waits at most 1.5 seconds for the reply; a failure is logged at debug level only and never affects clients. Only a version-shaped tag is accepted from the reply, and nothing else from it is printed.

It is also never made by a debug build or when the CI environment variable is set. --update-check-url points it at another https:// address, such as a mirror inside a closed network. docs/UPDATE_CHECK.md has the details.

Contributions are welcome. See CONTRIBUTING.md for how to build, test and submit changes. Contributions are accepted under the Contributor License Agreement, which you sign on your first pull request.

Please follow the Code of Conduct. The Changelog lists what changed in each release.

Please do not report security vulnerabilities in public issues. See SECURITY.md for how to report one privately.

Using KiviDB does not put your application under the AGPL. The big question when buying trading cards on Amazon is whether or not you're actually getting value for money. Amazon is a reliable pick for finding readily available stock, but you often pay above market price.

#221. IEEE Offers More Services to Cities That Want to Be Smarter

They include webinars, educational resources, and conferences

Georges Zissis is an IEEE Fellow and chair of the IEEE Smart Cities Technical Community.

Satish Sani is an IEEE senior member and chair of the IEEE Smart Grid Technical Track.

More and more city governments are using advanced technologies to improve livability for their residents. Municipalities use data from smartphones and sensors for traffic enforcement, traffic control, and waste management. They also have implemented artificial intelligence and deep learning programs.

Dubai, Paris, and Coral Gables, Fla., are among the cities that have invested heavily in programs to become smarter.

But along with the conveniences that come with a smart city transition, there have been challenges including safety and privacy issues and eroding relationships between residents and city officials.

Although many initiatives have delivered real innovations, not all have been successful. Inefficient global coordination has hindered projects with unclear standards, socioeconomic differences, and a lack of worldwide governance, leading to a disconnect between the technologies and the ability to adapt to them.

Citizens’ trust in the technologies suffers because of privacy breaches, personal data leaks, and other issues.

Smart city projects are complex and expensive endeavors that involve politicians, citizens, technocrats, and engineers. Successful projects require citizens to be fully engaged and to have strong collaborations with the participants, especially engineers, as engineering is the cornerstone.

Collaboration with universities, research institutions, and technology experts can bridge knowledge gaps on the behavior of complex socio-technical systems. What’s missing, though, is a global platform where those involved can discuss their experiences.

To help solve those and other challenges, the IEEE Smart Cities Technical Community (formerly the IEEE Smart Cities Initiative) was launched in 2013 by IEEE Future Directions, which incubates emerging technologies and new applications of current ones. The technical community provides city leaders and others with credible, unbiased information and educational content developed by IEEE experts.

Since then, IEEE Smart Cities has launched services including its flagship International Smart Cities Conference, a media center with educational and technical resources, and a contest to recognize the best smart project completed by city officials. The platforms bring together practicing engineers, academic researchers, policymakers, and city leaders to collaborate and exchange ideas and experiences about moving toward a smart-city model.

In 2021 the IEEE Power & Energy Society began managing the Smart Cities program, which is supported by the IEEE Communications, Industry Applications, and Intelligent Transportation Systems societies and other IEEE entities.

Thanks to volunteers’ dedication and determination, IEEE Smart Cities launched several services. But the initiative’s structure limited the development of long-term projects and the creation of new activities.

To address the situation, the IEEE Technical Activities Board (TAB) created the second-generation technical community ad hoc committee, also in 2021. It was a pilot program whereby IEEE Smart Cities formed a board of governors to oversee the community’s operations and leadership, and created a policies and procedures manual.

In November 2025 IEEE Smart Cities became a TAB technical community.

Today more than 7,000 volunteers collaborate on various aspects of the community within at least one of the following technical tracks:

New webinar series, workshops, conferences, educational resources, and other offerings are being created.

Two events were launched recently: the IEEE European Technology and Engineering Management Summit, held in May 2025 in Belgium, with the next one planned for 2027; and the IEEE Sustainable Smart Lighting World Conference, scheduled for 2 to 6 December in Athens.

The Smart Cities Ambassadors program aims to raise the technical community’s visibility outside IEEE by holding roundtables and other events at non-IEEE functions.

IEEE Smart Cities volunteers are working on launching journals. In addition, standards are being developed in collaboration with the IEEE Standards Association, societies, and councils.

The program is collaborating with the Open and Agile Smart Cities and Communities network, the Instituto de Competitividad e Innovación para el Desarrollo y Transferencia de Tecnología, and the International Project Management Association.

All of those actions have the ultimate objective of boosting IEEE Smart Cities’ growth and sustainability, as well as strengthening the leadership and educational offerings to technical community volunteers.

If you would like to volunteer, visit the Smart Cities website.

Georges Zissis is an IEEE Fellow and chair of the IEEE Smart Cities Technical Community.

Satish Sani is an IEEE senior member and chair of the IEEE Smart Grid Technical Track.

It's official, Apple's foldable has a 4,883 mAh battery

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first iPhone Duos will be landing in users' hands by the end of this week, and it means we finally get a chance to find out all the things we still don't know about the phone. One thing we can cross off the list is the phone's total battery capacity, thanks to the newly published EU energy label.

According to EU law, all phones that go on sale in the region also need a publicly accessible Energy Label, which offers key details about the device in question. Alongside information like IP rating, drop test performance and repairability, the labels also lists the phone's energy performance and battery specs. In the case of the iPhone Duo, it confirms the long-standing rumor that the phone packs in a 4,883 mAh battery pack.

For reference the eSIM-only variants of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max both have respective 4,288 mAh and 5,567 mAh batteries. Which means the iPhone Duo falls somewhere in the middle of the two.

However, considering this is a dual screen phone, one of which is almost 8-inches in size, it's not entirely clear whether the actual battery life will do the same. We'll have to wait and see how the Duo fairs in our own battery life testing.

As you can see, the iPhone Duo's battery life isn't dissimilar to that of other foldables out there. It's slightly below the Z Fold 8 Ultra, and slightly higher than the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, though both of them are full size book-shaped foldables with a little more space for larger batteries. As is the Motorola Razr Fold, which has a hefty 6,000 mAh battery hiding inside.

The closest we have to Apple's passport-shaped design is the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, which has a slightly smaller 4,800 mAh battery.

This phone lasted just shy of 13 hours during testing, which may give us a benchmark of what to expect from the Duo. Not only is Apple's battery store an extra 83 mAh of power, it also features the same energy-saving features as the 18 Pro series — including the A20 Pro chipset and C2 modem.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

I'd expect the iPhone Duo to last a little longer than the Z Fold 8 based on those two factors, but we can't know for sure until we actually get it into the Tom's Guide lab.

The EU Energy Label also confirmed some other details. One of which is that the Duo's battery is rated for 1,000 full recharge cycles (zero to 100% and back), which means it should keep at least 80% of its total capacity for that duration.

The Duo also lasted 140 free falls without causing problems, though this number dropped to 35 when it was dropped with the screen fully open.

So as durable as it may be, the iPhone Duo is still a lot more fragile if you leave the inner screen open and exposed. For comparison the Z Fold 8 and Z Fold 8 Ultra both lasted 210 drops, which dropped to 45 when opened, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max lasted 180.

As for water, the phone is IP68 rated (as expected) and is capable of being immersed in up to six meters of water. The screen is also listed as scratch-resistant up to 5 Mohs on the hardness scale, compared to just one on the Z Fold 8 series. Since this is the same as the iPhone 18 Pro Max, which has a Ceramic Shield 2 display, my guess is that only the Duo's outer display was tested.

The Duo's repairability index score of 2.65 is also lower than that of the other three phones. The 18 Pro Max hit 3.14, while the Z Fold 8 and 8 Ultra score 2.79 and 2.78, respectively.

#227. Amazon’s TorchNeuron lets PyTorch code run on AWS Trainium chips

The open-source tool enters public beta on 20 October, and Amazon says it needs no code rewrite.

Amazon has launched TorchNeuron, an open-source backend that lets PyTorch code run on its Trainium AI chips with a one-line change. It goes into public beta on 20 October under the Apache 2.0 licence and supports Trainium2 and Trainium3. Some PyTorch features are not yet supported.

Amazon has launched TorchNeuron, a tool that lets developers run their existing PyTorch code on its Trainium AI chips without rewriting it, the company said on Monday. PyTorch is the most widely used software framework for building AI models.

TorchNeuron will go into public beta on 20 October at the PyTorch Conference in San Jose, according to a PyTorch blog post by Amazon engineers. It will be open source under the Apache 2.0 licence and supports Trainium2 and Trainium3.

Until now, moving AI code to a new chip often meant months of rewriting and testing. With TorchNeuron, developers point their code at Trainium by changing a single device setting, Amazon said.

In a demo, Amazon ran the same training script on a standard chip and on Trainium, and said the model learned at the same rate on both. The tool plugs into PyTorch’s built-in system for adding new hardware, so standard testing and scaling tools still work.

However, the first release has gaps. It does not yet support some PyTorch features, such as dynamic input shapes, and about 22,000 PyTorch tests are skipped, according to the PyTorch blog post.

Early users include voice AI startups Cartesia and Deepgram, as well as the Lieber Institute for Brain Development, which uses it in drug research. Hugging Face has also added Trainium support to its AI tools. Uber recently signed up to use the chips in an AWS expansion deal.

The launch is part of Amazon’s push to compete with Nvidia, whose chips and CUDA software dominate AI computing. In April, chief executive Andy Jassy said Amazon’s custom chip business could be worth $50B, and Amazon now says it has passed a $25B annual revenue run rate.

One of TorchNeuron’s launch partners is Decart, an AI chip software startup that Amazon was reported to be in talks to buy.

#228. Why AI Isn’t Ready to Tackle Our Convoluted Genomes

The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.

Since its molecular structure was deduced in the 1950s, DNA has been hailed by many biologists as the secret of life. They’ve read and studied the information stored in the DNA found in the cells of living organisms, known as their genomes, and claimed that this genetic database must be some kind of blueprint, code script, or computer. But if DNA really does harbor some greater secret about how life works, biologists have yet to find it.

In fact, the human genome is less a script than a puzzle that gets harder the closer they look. Knowing the entire sequence—the order of all 3 billion or so of our DNA’s chemical building blocks, nearly fully deduced by the international Human Genome Project between 1990 and 2003—hasn’t helped much. That investigation showed that barely 2 percent of the human genome consists of actual genes, the information-coding sequences of DNA.

It’s now clear that understanding the human genome is no longer a matter of figuring out what each gene does. The deeper and much harder question is how those genes are used, or regulated, a question that seems to involve some and perhaps much of the rest of the genome. By switching suites of genes on and off, the many different cell types in our bodies can all be created from the same material. Cells also regulate their genes from moment to moment in response to a constant inflow of signals from their neighbors and surroundings. But the processes that govern gene regulation are proving so complex that some biologists wonder whether a full understanding of it—of how the genome really works—will ever be within the grasp of our puny minds.

Some are counting on outsourcing the analysis to artificial intelligence. Genomic “foundation models” such as Evo 2, Genos, and Google DeepMind’s AlphaGenome are trained on vast quantities of genomic data, which biologists use to make predictions about how differences in DNA sequence affect biological processes and ultimately the traits (including disease risk) of a whole organism. These algorithms don’t worry about the complicated regulatory stuff going on. All of that is supposedly subsumed by the algorithm’s “training,” through which it deduces correlations from cases we already know about.

This approach is likely to be useful, but for those who crave real understanding of how the genome, and ultimately life itself, works, a computational black box will never suffice. And perhaps more to the point, the genome might not submit to the kind of straightforward input-output approach that such AI models ultimately assume.

That’s because the genome is no blueprint or algorithm. It’s something else.

Given that it’s the product of around 4 billion years of evolution, perhaps it’s not surprising that our genome is complicated. The surprise has been what those complications are. “Our genome is not what we might make it if we sat down at the drawing board,” said the biologist Karen Adelman, who studies gene regulation at Harvard Medical School.

The traditional view posits that a small proportion of our DNA holds the code for making the protein molecules that orchestrate our cells’ chemistry. Each instruction for a protein is held in a corresponding gene—we have around 20,000 of these—and gene sequences can range in length from a couple of dozen to almost 3 million DNA “letters” (representing molecules called nucleotides).

Making a protein from its gene is a two-stage affair. First the DNA is read, letter by letter, by an enzyme called a polymerase, which creates a copy of that code in a related molecule called messenger RNA (mRNA). This is called transcription. The mRNA is then read by a piece of molecular machinery called the ribosome, which constructs the protein—a process called translation. The proteins made by the ribosome then go off to do their jobs in making and sustaining the organism.

This picture is still more or less correct. But it turns out that “the genes are probably not the most interesting part of the genome,” Adelman said.

What matters more is how our genes, many of which we share with simpler organisms, are regulated—turned on and off. Which proteins a cell needs changes over time and according to cell type: muscle, brain, skin, and so on. How the genes that encode those proteins are regulated depends on some of the genome that doesn’t code for proteins.

Biologists have known about gene regulation, and the involvement of “noncoding” DNA, since the 1960s. But for many years, most of what they understood about this came from studies of simple organisms like bacteria, where the principles are generally straightforward. It has gradually become clear, though, that in complex eukaryotic organisms like us, gene regulation is far more complicated, involving overlapping systems of oversight and control, each with its own intricacies.

Transcription gets started by proteins called transcription factors, which are like the operations managers of gene regulation. These proteins stick to sections of DNA (typically close to the target gene) and recruit the polymerase enzyme to make an mRNA copy. In bacteria, transcription factors are rather like keys that fit the locks of unique binding sites on DNA. But that’s not how they work in complex organisms. In us, the logic of transcription factors is more difficult to parse.

For one thing, our transcription factors don’t show strong preferences for particular DNA binding sites. What’s more, they tend to work in pairs or groups. And a given transcription factor might have different effects in different contexts, such as activating gene transcription in one cell type but suppressing it in another, depending on which other transcription factors are around.

In bacteria, regulation tends to have an “OR” logic, Adelman said, whereby a particular signal turns a gene on or off: It’s either this or that. But in the human genome the logic is more like what computer scientists designate “AND.” Many signals are integrated to reach a regulatory decision: This and that and also that other thing. In this case, regulation can be more responsive to nuances of context, and the regulatory knobs are tunable rather than being just on or off. “This is part of the beauty” of our regulatory complexity, Adelman said.

When they interact with the genome, transcription factors bind to pieces of DNA called enhancers—which present a puzzle of their own.

Enhancers are gathering points for transcription factors, and they are thought to be the decisive influence on transcription: They deliver the “go” signal for a waiting polymerase to make an mRNA version of the DNA sequence. Seems simple enough, but mapping enhancers to their respective genes is far from straightforward. Our genome has hundreds of thousands, perhaps millions, of enhancers. That means we have many more of them than we have genes. Each gene might be influenced by many enhancers, and each enhancer might influence multiple genes.

“It’s embarrassing that 25 years after the Human Genome Project, we don’t know where all the enhancers are in the genome, let alone what they do when they act and which genes they control,” said Wendy Bickmore, a genome biologist at the University of Edinburgh.

Biologists do know that most enhancers won’t respond to a single transcription factor. Their activation “requires a cocktail,” Bickmore said. “That’s what gives [an enhancer] that exquisite specificity—because it’s only in a particular cell at a particular time that you have the right combination of factors to bind and activate that enhancer.”

Some enhancers are, as you’d expect, close to the genes they regulate, or even sit on DNA inside a gene. But others sit far away from the gene—perhaps millions of nucleotides away, with more genes in between.

The existence of such so-called “distal” enhancers “seems bonkers,” Bickmore said. “How do you get that information from over there to over here, to the gene that needs to be activated? That’s a largely unanswered question.”

One of the answers comes in the form of a loop.

Distal enhancers are brought to the gene they regulate on great loops of DNA or, more strictly, of chromatin, the combination of DNA and its packaging proteins that are unraveled as if from a ball of wool. The loops are created by a protein motor called cohesin, which runs up and down the DNA strand and extrudes it as needed.

Once cohesin has formed a loop to bring elements together, what then? It was once thought that they then stick together or assemble into a molecular machine, but they don’t. Rather, the components appear to form a loose but dense blob in which they interact rather weakly, fleetingly, and indiscriminately—a sort of committee, sometimes called a condensate.

These transcription hubs are extremely fluid and differ from one cell to another. “There’ll be a bit of loop extrusion going on over here, in the next cell it might be over here, and the whole thing is turning over incredibly fast,” Bickmore said. Even if the cells are notionally identical—both skin cells, say—exactly what the gene-regulatory machinery is up to at any moment is never quite the same in any two of them.

Chromatin loops are just one reason why a gene’s transcription depends on the shape and structure of the chromatin around it.

The textbook image of a chromosome—one of the 46 units into which our genomes are divided—is of a compact, X-shaped cluster of chromatin. But any time a cell is not actively dividing, its chromatin is unwound into what looks like a tangled mess. There is order to the chaos, however. Some parts of chromatin are densely packed into a form called heterochromatin. The compacted DNA there is relatively inaccessible to transcription factors; the genes it contains are typically silenced. Meanwhile, other parts are relatively loose, open, and accessible: This is called euchromatin.

There are special enzymes involved in packaging and repackaging chromatin, thereby controlling transcription. In other words, what matters is not just the encoded information in the DNA but also how it exists physically and dynamically in space. “We’ve stopped thinking about the genome as a linear piece of DNA code,” Bickmore said. “Thinking about this incredibly dynamic three-dimensional folding as absolutely inherent to regulation is a very exciting change.”

One aspect of this 3D organization is the clustering of segments of chromatin into compartments called topologically associating domains (TADs). Within a TAD, the genes seem to be coregulated: switched on or off in groups. Such groups keep suites of genes active or silent together to form and provide function in different cell types. Cohesin is also involved in the shuffling of chromatin to construct TADs—a dynamic process in which the chromatin is constantly rearranged in our cells.

Chromatin shape can also be influenced by chemical modifications called epigenetic marks: small molecules attached to DNA packaging proteins called histones or stuck directly to DNA. Some of these epigenetic modifications can alter the electrical charges on histones, which changes how the proteins attract or repel one another and so rejigs the chromatin packing. Epigenetic modifications to chromatin are like annotations of the DNA script that change its meaning in a given context. When cells divide, the epigenetic annotations are copied, too.

How and when the marks get added and changed, and what each type of mark means for gene activity, are complex questions with no simple answers. Some researchers talk of an “epigenetic code” governing this aspect of gene regulation, but it’s far from clear if anything so systematic really exists.

All of these processes and others can determine whether a gene gets transcribed into mRNA. But there are further layers of regulation that determine whether the mRNA is then translated into a corresponding protein—and which protein arises.

This post-transcriptional regulation is often controlled by RNA molecules that are said to be noncoding. These short-lived molecules aren’t templates for proteins, as mRNA is, but have other jobs of their own. While mRNA is produced from the protein-coding areas of DNA (so-called “coding genes”), noncoding RNAs are transcribed from other DNA regions now generally described as noncoding genes. These noncoding RNAs are versatile, taking on varied roles in a cell. Researchers are learning more about what they can do every day, and many if not most of them seem to be involved in gene regulation.

Small noncoding RNAs called microRNAs, for example, can silence mRNAs before they can be translated into proteins. They do this by guiding special enzymes to a particular mRNA to degrade or chemically modify it. The microRNAs don’t do this job alone but, not unlike transcription factors, act combinatorially, in groups, and in a rather promiscuous manner: A given microRNA might regulate many mRNAs, and a given mRNA might be regulated by many microRNAs.

Why make an mRNA only to stop it getting translated in a protein? This sort of post-transcriptional regulation is like having another checkpoint: Does the cell really need this protein? MicroRNAs can be mobilized to allow cells to adjust gene expression depending on the immediate context. In this way, the workings of the genome are less like a program’s inevitable progression and more like an adaptive and responsive process.

Another post-transcriptional complication is that mRNAs get translated to protein only after they have been reorganized. Fresh from transcription, an mRNA contains sequences that encode bits of protein, called exons, as well as sequences that shouldn’t be translated and need to be snipped out, called introns. (Strictly speaking, this pre-edited RNA is called pre-mRNA.) The job of editing introns out and splicing exons together is done by a molecular assembly called the spliceosome, which is made from several proteins together with various noncoding RNAs.

The spliceosome too can be sensitive to context, so that it might splice the pre-mRNA to encode one protein in one cell type and a slightly different protein in another. Sometimes these different protein “isoforms” can have very different roles. Transcription factors, for example, are often alternatively spliced in this way, and their isoforms can take on different regulatory tasks—some might activate gene expression, for instance, while others repress it.

All told, these and other regulatory mechanisms show that the genome is far from some automated program running in the background to build us and keep us alive. Our cells are, in effect, making complex decisions about how to use their genes—both the information they contain and the structure they assume.

Thus, cells need to assemble a rather loose and fuzzy committee of components, such as transcription factors and enhancers, to get transcription underway, which also depends on how the chromatin strand is shaped and molded at that moment. Then there are further layers of decisionmaking and action-taking in between mRNA and the final, functional protein.

Remember, too, that all the players—from transcription factors to noncoding RNAs—are themselves produced from the genome in the same kind of context-dependent process. That makes the genome rather like a recursive, self-referential system that the computer scientist Douglas Hofstadter dubbed “a strange loop.” It acts on itself, mindful of its own history—which determines chromatin conformation and epigenetic markings, say—and heedful of messages from inside and outside the cell. Not, then, a blueprint.

And for that reason, not at all easy to understand. “I wouldn’t have designed it this way if I was God,” Bickmore said. “But here we are!”

Why is gene regulation in animals like us so darned complicated? One potential answer is that evolution doesn’t have the foresight to design with efficiency and transparent logic, but merely tinkers with what it has already available. Maybe so—but eukaryotic gene regulation isn’t just a messy version of what happens in bacteria. It has different principles, and there’s surely a reason for them.

Bickmore suspects that the complexity of regulation and of genome organization might have been the only means of generating complexity in the organism. For example, organisms with many tissue types and varied lifestyles required more control over which genes were on or off in a given cell. One thing this demanded was more and more noncoding regulatory sequences in DNA. But then they couldn’t all fit close to the gene itself.

“As you get more complexity, you need to add more and more enhancers,” Bickmore said. “But where are you going to put them? You start to put them farther and farther away. Once they are [far enough], you start to need TADs and three-dimensional [chromatin] folding to allow those things to work.”

We also need regulatory complexity because, over evolutionary time, the human genome has accumulated DNA from parasitic viruses in the form of jumping genetic material called transposable elements. These sequences have inserted themselves all over our chromosomes and are good at replicating themselves. To sift the good DNA from the bad, we needed additional layers of regulation to ensure that cells weren’t translating RNAs they don’t really need or that could be actively harmful.

With so many context-dependent checks and balances in the workings of our genome, it is evidently not a program or algorithm that predictably generates the same outcome in every situation. It’s an open informational system that responds to external inputs and the genome’s dynamic internal conditions. This poses a challenge if AI relies solely on the genetic sequences within genomes to predict what genomes will do.

Researchers Developing AI-based genomic foundation models, such as AlphaGenome, hope that all these layers of regulation—transcription factors, splicing, epigenetic marks, loops, chromatin packing, and so on—will be implicitly included in the correlations that the algorithms learn between genetic sequence and organismal traits. They’re content for the complexity described above to be in a black box, so long as the model generates accurate predictions. But will that work?

“I’m sure [AlphaGenome] is going to be useful, but with limitations,” Bickmore said. “To me the big gap is in the complexity of the human body—in all the cell types and how they change over time in development. And all that data is missing.”

Fundamentally, the challenge is that the genome is not a set of static, linear instructions. It is highly dynamic, and it uses its information contextually, with combinatorial and promiscuous logic. “Whether we’ll ever be able to capture that aspect” in algorithms like AlphaGenome, “I don’t know,” she said.

Yet the problem goes even deeper because the functioning of specific organisms, including each of us, doesn’t just depend on genomes. Other factors, such as diet, environment, microbiome, and, for us at least, culture, can matter hugely, too—not just in terms of how we act and how healthy we are but also in the state of our genome itself. The biologist Adrian Woolfson, cofounder of California-based biotech company Genyro, which aims to use AI systems for so-called “generative biology,” calls this information cloud the “informiome.”

“While the human genome forms the foundation of the human informiome, other layers of extra-genetic information are equally important,” Woolfson wrote in his book On the Future of Species, published in April 2026. Genomic foundation models won’t even be able to predict all the consequences of genetic mutations, he argued, because the relevant information is not in the genome sequence in the first place.

So how should we think about the genome? Maybe the only metaphors that can capture the way the genome really works must come from biology itself. In 2020, the biological historian Evelyn Fox compared the genome to “an exquisitely sensitive reactive system.” Rather than a sequence of genes leading to the formation of traits, she said, it’s more of “a device for regulating the production of specific proteins in response to constantly changing signals it receives from its environment.”

That sounds close to the picture painted by the geneticist Barbara McClintock in the address she delivered upon being awarded the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for her discovery of transposons. The genome, she declared, is “a highly sensitive organ of the cell, monitoring genomic activities and correcting common errors, sensing the unusual and unexpected events and responding to them, often by restructuring the genome.”

Research since that time has fleshed out this image, revealing how the shape of chromatin can matter as much as the information its DNA sequences encode and how an army of molecules collaborates to reorganize it and make collective decisions about how to use its genetic information in context-dependent ways. There is no human technology that works this way, so metaphors such as blueprints, programs, or computers will always fall short.

Bickmore is optimistic that the workings of the genome are understandable, despite its complexity. “We’ve got a handle on it now,” she said. “We might not know the details, but I think the whole field is coalescing now into a framework where we’re thinking along similar lines.” AI can surely help with this sense-making, but in the end, human reasoning will be needed to discern the fundamental principles.

“McClintock was far more on point than people realized at the time,” Adelman said. “What she said was that the genome isn’t static—it’s living.”

#229. ESA's Hera Will View Asteroid Scars from DART's Strike

The ESA spacecraft will capture results of a planetary defense test

David Dickinson is a freelance science writer and long-time sky watcher.

A rendering of Hera shows the spacecraft approaching the Dimorphos asteroid, with a portion of the larger Didymos asteroid on the left. In November and December, Hera will acquire baseline measurements of the asteroids from 25 to 30 kilometers away.

In one month, the European Space Agency’s Hera mission will make history. Moving at 12 kilometers per second relative to Earth, the mission is about to rendezvous with the binary Dimorphos-Didymos asteroid pair. NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission slammed into Dimorphos in 2022, and now Hera will provide a follow-up view of the mission’s resulting handiwork. The European Space Agency (ESA) recently released a thought-provoking look at the perspectives of Hera and what an astronaut might see from the surface of the asteroids as the mission speeds by.

But what would it be like to hitch a ride aboard Hera? Launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral, Fla., on 7 October 2024, Hera is ESA’s first Space Safety Programme-class mission. The spacecraft took just over two years to reach its destination. Even now, the pair of asteroids is little more than a few pixels across in Hera’s view. The mission imaged Didymos in July 2026.

Discovered by the Kitt Peak Spacewatch survey on 11 April 1996, 65803 Didymos is 780 meters in diameter, and it orbits the Sun once every 2.1 years. In 2003, the asteroid was discovered to have a small moonlet, a 151-meter rock named Dimorphos. Scientists are finding that more and more asteroids are in fact binary pairs in their own right.

Like our Moon, the pair are dark and silicon-rich. The meetup with Hera also occurs 1.5 astronomical units from the Sun. This makes for a dimmer view, though it still provides enough juice for Hera’s two 5-meter long solar panels.

Didymos is a fast rotator, spinning once every 2.2 hours. DART saw Dimorphos as a ‘rubble pile asteroid’ shortly before impact, similar to 101955 Bennu or 162173 Ryugu, visited by NASA’s Osiris-Rex and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s Hayabusa2 missions respectively. These rock piles are thought to be at their limits in terms of holding together versus flying apart. DART’s 6.6 km/s impact did shorten the original 11 hour, 55 minute orbit by about 32 minutes, and a debris stream was seen from the binary pair in the weeks after impact.

An arrival preview should provide the first close-up views of Dimorphos post-impact. This sort of study could prove handy, if we ever need to move an Earthbound asteroid out of harm’s way.

Certainly, standing on the boulder strewn surface of either asteroid would provide an alien vista of a spinning sky dominated by the other nearby asteroid companion. The feeble gravitational pull of either asteroid would allow a would-be astronaut to fall to the surface of either at a days-long leisurely rate.

Hera’s pair of CubeSats will put that to the test. Juventas and Milani—built by GomSpace in Luxembourg and Tyvak International in Turin, Italy, respectively—will leave Hera shortly after rendezvous next month. Milani will analyze the dust field around both asteroids and study the spectral composition of the pair, while Juventas will make comparisons of the internal structure of the asteroids and may even approach and come to rest on Dimorphos.

After Hera is done with its nominal mission in 2027, controllers may opt to extend its life as a technology demonstrator, testing autonomous spacecraft control techniques.

It’s going to be exciting to get a look at the Didymos-Dimorphos system again. And although we can’t be there in person, we can still get a close look at these alien worlds through Hera’s eyes.

#231. Simulation App Speeds Up Electric Truck Battery Design

Using a laser-welding simulation app, Volvo Trucks has accelerated the design of long-lasting, high-performance batteries

A consortium including Volvo Trucks used COMSOL-based multiscale simulation and a custom app to optimize laser-welded battery pack design and manufacturing, improving the robustness and lifetime of batteries for electric trucks to enable longer-range, more reliable heavy-duty electric fleets.

This article is brought to you by COMSOL.

These days, no one blinks an eye at two-day, one-day, and even same-day package deliveries. Despite the plethora of localized fulfillment and distribution centers that have cropped up to meet the demand, delivery trucks still need to make considerably long drives, often over highways. To reduce fuel and maintenance costs as well as carbon emissions, companies are investing in electric trucks for their delivery fleets. While turning to electric trucks is a promising solution, the battery packs incorporated into these automotive designs often fall short in the lifetime needed to make long-distance highway travel feasible.

To help overcome the issue of battery lifetime, a consortium of universities and industry partners incorporated multiscale simulation and a custom simulation app into the battery manufacturing process. The organizations involved in this project were Aurobay, Resolvent, the European Commission, the Technical University of Denmark (DTU), Vinnova (the Swedish Agency for Innovation Systems), Innovation Fund Denmark, and Volvo Group Trucks Operations.

The simulation app, built by Resolvent, a Denmark-based engineering consultancy that specializes in green energy, enables the R&D department at Volvo to easily test battery lifetime performance.

The Multiscale Simulation of Laser Welding for Optimal Battery Pack Manufacturing project — referred to as “LaserBATMAN” — was initiated in May 2022 and wrapped up in May 2025 (Ref. 1). Although BATMAN here refers to battery manufacturing and not the famous masked superhero, the goals for the project also strove for greatness.

The LaserBATMAN project aimed to optimize two key performance metrics for battery packs: robustness and lifetime (Ref. 1). One element of the battery manufacturing process that affects both of these metrics is the laser welding used in component joining processes (for example, to connect battery cells in a pack via a busbar). If done correctly, laser welding can positively impact battery life, but if done incorrectly, laser welding can increase the risk of battery degradation. Computational modeling can be used to analyze and predict the effects of welding and joining processes at different stages of the manufacturing process.

Martin Refslund Nielsen, former chief commercial officer and partner at Resolvent, explained that for this type of multiphysics and multiscale problem, “COMSOL Multiphysics is just the right tool.”

The Resolvent team used the COMSOL Multiphysics software to study how laser welding affects the electrochemistry and degradation of battery cells. At least, that’s how the project started.

“Ambitions grew,” Nielsen said, explaining that the team ended up modeling the performance of the entire battery, from cell to pack level, and even “turned [the model] into a design tool in the end”, in reference to the app.

After training the deep neural network of the battery model, the team built a custom simulation app to efficiently optimize busbar tabs in the configuration of a battery pack.

First, the team built an electrochemical model of a battery cell by inputting the formulas for the relevant chemical reaction kinetics (Figure 2). The resulting cell-layer model was then fed input data, and the output data was used to train a deep neural network (DNN). With this reduced-order model, the team was able to quickly gain insight into cell behavior.

After training the DNN of the battery model, the team built a custom simulation app to efficiently optimize busbar tabs in the configuration of a battery pack.

Figure 2: The Resolvent battery model.COMSOL

The different features of the simulation app, as described by Nielsen, include its options to input dimensions for the pack geometry (Figure 3), the number of cells, and operating conditions such as ambient temperature and charge–discharge current profiles. The app also makes it possible to apply a simple charging current and load customized cycles. Users are then able to see how the battery performs with each set of specific inputs.

Figure 3. The battery pack model developed by Resolvent.COMSOL

Another important aspect of Resolvent’s app is the Busbar Weld Design Tool button, which Nielsen described as “a tool within a tool.” This button can be used to efficiently calculate busbar weld performance after a number of cycles. After clicking the button, a window opens with options for setting different parameters, including the shape of the weld, busbar thickness, and penetration depth of the laser (Figure 4).

“[This button] is interesting from a robust design perspective,” said Nielsen. Users can apply a variant to the input parameters to see what happens in production if the weld does not reach far enough into the busbar.

Figure 4. Resolvent’s simulation app, showing how certain parameters can be customized. The model shows how the busbar weld is affected by a cooling airflow.COMSOL

“We certainly get deep technical insight here, and we can dimension the design in the sweet spot. Deep technical insight is also key to optimizing product performance,” Nielsen said. For example, if the results suggest better cooling, the team could potentially reduce the design by two battery cells and retain the same performance, easily quantifying the tradeoff between cooling and setup.

The app’s user interface also includes a Compute Battery button, which can be used to see the temperature of the weld in a given state, the state of charge, and the solid–electrolyte interface (SEI) layer thickness (Figure 5). The results can help the engineering team further determine if there is room for optimization in the design. For instance, a user can apply a cooling flow in the app and see if turbulence or standing air occurs.

As explained by Nielsen, simulation apps offer more consistent analysis and reporting, and the intuitiveness of custom apps makes it easier to share knowledge. “We are in a much better place to optimize performance and increase robustness,” said Nielsen.

Figure 5. Temperature in the given state (left), state of charge (middle), and SEI layer thickness (right) in the battery pack.COMSOL

The custom simulation app developed by the LaserBATMAN consortium can be used to help produce more robust battery designs with ranges that can support highway travel over longer distances with fewer failures — all while promoting the use of green energy. A heroic project indeed.

#234. I no longer care to work on any Ruby gems so I've archived all my repositories

I’ve decided to archive the source code of my Ruby gems to make it clear that I’m no longer working on them; I’ve written this post to link from them in order to explain why.

In an article published in 2000, Yukihiro Matsumoto (a.k.a. “Matz”), designer of Ruby, wrote,

For me, the purpose of life is, at least partly, to have joy. Programmers often feel joy when they can concentrate on the creative side of programming, so Ruby is designed to make programmers happy.

And as recently as a 2019 interview, he said,

I designed Ruby for humans, not for machines.

It was during that era, when Ruby was ostensibly for joy, for creativity, for humans, that I developed this code. But that age, of doing things for humans, has passed, and with it my enthusiasm for working on Ruby gems. I won’t say it was always great, but at least we were working with and for people.

The pre-eminent application of Ruby has been making web applications using Rails. Rails is open source software but it’s owned and controlled by a man whose views I find abhorrent, although there is an ongoing effort to fork it. To judge by his keynote at Rails World this year – the conference that he himself set up in pique after he wasn’t invited to RailsConf a couple of years ago – he is no longer particularly interested in Ruby, Rails, or even programming itself. (He’s now using LLM agents to churn out apps in Rust, a language which he compares to “pouring acid into [his] eyes”, but that’s apparently fine because he doesn’t even look at what they generate.)

But even beyond Rails, the Ruby language itself is now substantially developed using LLM agents. Matz is giving talks repositioning Ruby as a “Programming Language for AI age”, to be emitted by LLM agents, and stating that to be able to do that LLMs need to consume more good human-written Ruby code. You might already have seen the problem here.

In that context, I no longer feel inspired to contribute to a commons that’s being strip-mined by massive corporations to feed the very machines whose unthinking output pollutes it. When people claim that it’s no longer sustainable to write code by hand, they’re not entirely wrong, but only in the same way that it’s no longer sustainable to sleep in a bed once someone has taken a shit in it.

You want changes? Go ask your agent or something. I’m told that’s what you’re supposed to do now. I’m out.

My name is Paul Battley. I live in Rotherhithe in London and I work with software and the internet for a living.

po-ru.com is my personal website, in which I write about my interests: languages, music, programming, food, politics, and anything else. Read more about me.

#235. Regulators are trying to protect you from being fired by AI – here’s how

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Regulating AI at work is happening slowly, but it's still stuck at the state level.

AI use at work is up, touching everything from everyday tasks to hiring and performance reviews. An April survey conducted by MyPerfectResume found that of 1,000 HR professionals, 73% said they use AI to make hiring decisions and 52% said they use AI to inform “restructuring and role planning.”

Hiring managers are also turning to AI for deeper behavioral insights when screening candidates: Over half of respondents (51%) use it to “flag ‘risky’ candidates.” Only 26% of respondents said they don’t use AI to make decisions about layoffs.

Also: How to beat the AI algorithm and get the job of your dreams

California Governor Gavin Newsom recently signed new legislation protecting workers from certain AI-powered decision-makers in the workplace. The bill covers these issues from a few angles — here’s what the regulation is trying to address, and how it could set the tone for future state or federal legislation.

SB 947, somewhat cheekily called the “No Robo Bosses Act,” prohibits employers from outsourcing disciplinary and termination decisions entirely to AI, referred to in the bill as automated decision systems (ADS). The bill requires employers to check any AI decisions on employee discipline or termination, as well as provide the employee with a description of the reasons for the decision. That includes any data used to make the decision, including personnel files, evaluations, work product, peer reviews, and “witness interviews.”

“If an employer cannot corroborate the ADS output or the human reviewer has concluded that the ADS output is inaccurate, incomplete, or misleading, the employer shall not use the ADS output to make a disciplinary or termination decision,” the bill states.

Also: AI just broke your career ladder – here are 6 new ways to the top

The law, which goes into effect on July 1, 2027, lets affected employees file complaints with the California Labor Commissioner if they believe this process was not followed correctly in a firing decision. It does not fully prohibit the use of automated systems for these determinations. It also requires employers to clarify whether “a mass layoff, relocation, or termination is caused by an AI system,” according to a brief on the governor’s website.

While AI regulation at the federal level remains less specific, mired in voluntary agreements with labs, and arguably focused on distractions, states have risen to the challenge of creating initial protections for workers. Still, when it comes to AI in hiring and other workplace processes, some states like Colorado and Connecticut have opted for mandating disclosure of AI use rather than actual intervention.

California and New York have tended to lead the charge on stricter laws, though Illinois passed a landmark bill this summer, becoming the first state to require third-party audits of frontier labs.

Also: 73% of tech job listings require AI skills now: How to show off yours

Lily Li, a lawyer specializing in AI and founder of Metaverse Law, told ZDNET she sees California’s latest law setting the precedent for other states. But she also anticipates companies finding loopholes in the law’s required human review process.

“We could see employers engaging in check-the-box reviews rather than meaningful human review, to avoid the operational costs of an additional layer of review,” she said. “The ability for an employee to request an explanation is a helpful check against this, however.”With that concern, it’s possible the onus of tackling unvetted AI-driven firings will fall on complainants contesting their own firings in court. Still, protections like these will remain patchwork across the country until some version of them is adopted at the federal level.

#236. A successful AI pilot doesn’t mean your AI strategy is working

Zacharie Lahmi, founder of Ellis Partners, says companies should cost each AI use case and agree on success criteria before a pilot starts.

Zacharie Lahmi, founder of Ellis Partners.

Launching an AI pilot is relatively straightforward. But integrating it reliably and at scale into business operations is a far greater challenge. McKinsey’s global 2026 survey found that only 37% of respondents said AI had improved their company’s earnings, unchanged from the previous year. Yet eight in ten said AI had helped them become more productive at work.

An AI tool may work well during a small test, when the task is simple and the data is clean. But using it across a company brings new challenges. It must integrate with existing software, comply with data access and security requirements, and have a clear process for handling failures. Someone must also take responsibility for its performance. Meeting these requirements means coordinating across IT, operations, finance, and risk teams.

Costs create another challenge. Companies are used to setting budgets for software projects and estimating staff time. AI costs can be harder to predict. They depend on how much information the system processes, which model it uses, and how often people use it. Without a clear estimate, finance teams may struggle to judge whether a project is worth the investment.

Zacharie Lahmi, founder of Ellis Partners, recommends that companies assess AI opportunities one business process at a time. He has ten years of experience in technology, including work helping launch monday.com in France. His approach focuses on estimating the cost and resources required for each use case before testing it.

“Companies need to understand the cost of a use case and the resources it will require. The return-on-investment discussion should happen before the pilot, not after.” Zacharie Lahmi, founder of Ellis Partners

Every AI test needs clear goals and a plan for when things go wrong. Lahmi recommends setting measurable targets for usage, maintenance costs, and errors.

“Useful pilots are the ones we really want to see in production. We should agree on success criteria beforehand, so there is no debate after the pilot about whether it worked.” Zacharie Lahmi

Lahmi also urges companies to look beyond sales and marketing when choosing AI projects. While these functions offer benefits that may be easier to link to revenue, he believes everyday operational processes can offer greater opportunities.

“The most boring operational tasks, the core processes of your industry, are the ones you should be thinking about with AI. Ask yourself how you can fundamentally change the way your industry operates, rather than simply maximizing short-term gains.” Zacharie Lahmi

Some enterprise AI projects remain in testing for several months, according to Lahmi. Often, nobody has defined what the project must achieve to justify wider use. He recommends assessing each AI project based on the business problem it would solve.

“Companies should then weigh the expected benefits against the effort required to implement it and the time it would take to see results. A smaller project that delivers results quickly may be a better starting point than a larger one.” Zacharie Lahmi

He suggests examining everyday business operations, too. Improving a process can change how a company works, rather than simply helping employees complete tasks faster.

Company size also affects how easily AI projects can be introduced and adjusted. Lahmi notes that smaller businesses often have fewer layers of approval, allowing them to make decisions and change direction more quickly. Large enterprises may face more hurdles because changes can affect multiple teams and existing systems.

Regardless of company size, businesses might need to assess whether an AI system delivers the results they expected. They can track how much time it saves, whether it reduces mistakes, and what it costs to maintain. These measures can help leaders decide whether to continue with a project, make changes, or stop it altogether. A successful demonstration alone might not be enough to justify wider adoption.

For stakeholders, the final litmus test for enterprise AI is not just doing the same thing faster, but fundamentally changing how value is created. Launching more pilot projects does not necessarily mean a company is making progress. Each project needs a clear goal and a realistic budget, along with limits on the risks the business is willing to accept.

Companies can review performance after launch and ensure someone has the authority to pause and audit a system if problems arise. These steps can help turn AI experiments into tools that businesses can depend on.

#239. Chasing China’s Monazite Monopoly

Billions are driving a race against Beijing’s decades-long lead

Glenn Zorpette is editorial director for content development at IEEE Spectrum.

The Baogang Tailings Dam, near the industrial city of Baotou, in Inner Mongolia, is one of the most polluted bodies of water in the world. The 11-square-kilometer artificial lake holds the effluent from decades of rare-earth and other industrial-processing operations.

One of the singular features of Baotou, an industrial city of 2 million people in Inner Mongolia, is a 10-square-kilometer (4-square-mile) lake that is among the most polluted in the world. The artificial lake, referred to by the name of the dam associated with it, Weikuang Dam (or Baogang Tailings Dam), has for decades collected the effluent from minerals processing for China’s globally dominant iron, steel, and rare-earths industries.

Built in the late 1950s, the lake contains a highly toxic stew of industrial chemicals with substantial amounts of radioactive thorium, the latter resulting primarily from the processing of monazite ores for rare-earths. China has since greatly tightened its environmental regulations and restrictions on mining and minerals processing. For example, largely because of the environmental disaster that is Weikuang Dam, the country doesn’t permit the development or operation of stand-alone monazite mines—that is, mines where nothing is mined except monazite ore.

Now, with industrialized nations in North America, Asia, and Europe spending billions to shore up their rare-earths supply chains, and counting on monazite to help them do it, China’s history and experiences with monazite offer important lessons.

This article is a collaboration between Foreign Policy, the global magazine of politics and ideas, and IEEE Spectrum, the flagship magazine of the IEEE.

Monazite ore is a pillar of China’s rare-earths industry because it is a prime source of some less common but extremely important rare-earth elements, notably dysprosium, terbium, yttrium, and erbium. The country mines and processes vast quantities of monazite ore; it also imports huge amounts of monazite ore for processing.

Most of the domestically mined monazite ore comes from a single mine: the mammoth Bayan Obo complex, 150 kilometers north of Baotou, in Inner Mongolia. Bayan Obo, which is primarily an iron-ore mine, also happens to contain the largest known rare-earth deposit in the world. It’s the source of nearly half of all the rare-earth ore mined on the planet in a typical year. Most of the rare-earth ore mined at Bayan Obo is a type called bastnaesite; it’s the mining of that bastnaesite that makes it legal to mine monazite ore at Bayan Obo as well.

Related: Can a Radioactive Ore Break China’s Grip on Rare Earths?

All told, ore from Bayan Obo was used to produce 170,000 tonnes of rare-earth metal last year, according to David Merriman, research director at the minerals intelligence firm Project Blue. Roughly 30 percent to 40 percent of the rare-earth ore mined at Bayan Obo is monazite. That amount alone would be enough to make China the world’s largest processor of monazite for rare-earths.

But a more detailed picture of China’s interest in monazite emerges when you consider the country’s imports of the ore. Last year, they amounted to more than 70,000 tonnes, says Thomas Kruemmer, a Singapore-based consultant on minerals and metals. That figure becomes more impressive when you consider the unique challenges of shipping monazite by sea. Because of its radioactivity, concentrated monazite ore is classified as Class 7 dangerous cargo under the International Maritime Dangerous Goods Code. That means, Kruemmer notes, that the ore can be imported through only four ports in China.

In addition, importation of some kinds of monazite into China is supposed to go through a joint venture consisting of the China National Nuclear Corp. and Shenghe Resources, which are at least partly state-owned. But lots of imported monazite doesn’t go through those organizations, notes Merriman. That’s because heavy mineral sands, which may contain roughly 2 percent or 3 percent monazite by weight, are not subject to the same import controls as concentrated monazite ore. So companies import the heavy mineral sands; separate out various profitable concentrates, including the monazite mineral concentrate; and then process the monazite concentrate to recover the rare-earths.

China has lately stepped up its efforts to secure rare-earth ore around the world. One reason, says Kruemmer, is simply to make up for recently lost supplies. In 2025, the U.S. government invested US $400 million in MP Materials, which operates the Mountain Pass mine and processing facility in California. The deal put an end to long-standing contracts under which MP Materials had been selling tens of thousands of tonnes of rare-earth concentrate annually to a trading affiliate of Shenghe Resources.

But other Westerners speculate that China has strategic reasons for stepping up its efforts to acquire heavy mineral sands or other rare-earth assets abroad. By locking down rights to deposits or projects abroad, Chinese organizations are making them unavailable to non-Chinese developers, according to this reasoning.

Merriman points out that your view of these activities largely depends on where you sit. The U.S. government recently made a conditional loan commitment of up to $725 million to U.S. monazite processor Energy Fuels, which has been aggressively securing substantial monazite supplies in Australia, Brazil, and Madagascar. To a Chinese observer, those moves probably look rather strategic.

China, meanwhile, is doing what it has been doing for decades. “China’s playing its game,” says Merriman.

Glenn Zorpette is editorial director for content development at IEEE Spectrum. A Fellow of the IEEE, he holds a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from Brown University.
