#258. I Tried the 'Normatec Go' Compression Boots, and My Calves Have Never Felt Better

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

If you've ever been on your feet all day and your calves felt like two sandbags, you know how tough it can be to find relief. I'm a marathon runner, so I know it well. Training blocks mean high mileage, and calves take a beating on every mile. I've tried foam rollers, massage guns, stretching, and my favorite maneuver: lying with my legs up against the wall.

This week's upgrade is the first recovery tool that seems to do all the work for me, and hey—after a long run, I'm not complaining. It's my first foray into compression boots: the Hyperice Normatec Go.

The Normatec Go is a pair of wearable compression sleeves that wrap around your calves and give you a dynamic air compression massage. Hyperice describes it as a fully portable version of its Normatec line, which pro athletes and recovery rooms have used for years.

The sleeves inflate and deflate in a pulsing pattern (as opposed to just squeezing constantly). Hyperice calls this compression "gapless": There are three overlapping zones of 360-degree compression working through the calf. In theory, the wave of pressure helps push fluid and blood through your lower legs, which is why Hyperice says the massage increases circulation and reduces tension and swelling.

Hyperice also points out that the calf is often called the body's "second heart" because it helps push blood back up from your lower legs. That matches my experience: After a long run, calves are where the heaviness and tightness show up first.

The biggest upgrade over traditional compression boots is that you don't need to set up a whole system. You strap on the sleeves, open the app, pick an intensity, and relax. I've worn them at my desk, on the couch, and while answering emails after a long run. I show up to my next run feeling fresher, and for a marathon runner, that's the whole point of recovery.

A few features make the experience better:

Seven compression levels (40 to 200 mmHg), so you can go gentle after an easy run or firm after a long one

The two sleeves always stay in sync for a symmetrical massage

Bluetooth control through the Hyperice app, so you adjust everything from your phone

1.2 pounds total, and TSA friendly, so they can travel with you

Hyperice recommends sessions of about 20 to 30 minutes. You can go up to 60 after a tough workout, or use a shorter 15- to 20-minute session at medium intensity before a run to warm up your legs.

The Normatec Go costs $379. Full-size compression boots that cover your whole leg usually run well over $1,000, so that's a big difference. These only cover the calves, but if calves are where you need relief, you don't have to pay for coverage you won't use. They're also FSA/HSA eligible.

At the same time, the obvious limitation is that these are for calves only. I suppose it's a testament to the product that I've never been more tempted to spring for full-size boots, so that my quads and hamstrings can experience the same treatment.

The battery life also leaves something to be desired. Hyperice claims they last three hours per charge, but in my experience, you're better off charging between every hour or so of use.

If you're training for a race, spending long days on your feet, or just tired of tight, heavy calves, the Normatec Go is the upgrade I'd recommend. I can't imagine my recovery routine without it now.

When installing macOS 27 (Golden Gate), Rosetta is automatically removed. If you manage a fleet with any legacy Intel-only software still in use, you need a plan in place before your users start experiencing issues. Here is what I’m doing, and I have some thoughts on vendors who are waiting until the last minute to deploy Apple Silicon-native tools.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

One thing I need to clarify is that macOS 27 removes it, but macOS 28 will no longer support it. For traditional apps, macOS 27 will prompt the user to reinstall it with an easy-to-follow GUI prompt. That’s actually the workable scenario, because at least the user knows something is wrong, and macOS reinstalls it. The tools I’m worried about are the ones that won’t do that. I have a handful of menu bar utilities from vendors who haven’t shipped a native Apple Silicon build yet, and in my testing this summer, they are just silently failing. There’s no error prompt. It just fails to work. That makes auditing your fleet before macOS 27 rolls out more important than it might seem at first glance.

My short-term fix is to automatically push a Rosetta reinstallation script to every Mac that joins my macOS 27 Dynamic Device Group. In Mosyle, the setup is really straightforward. You create a new script profile, name it something obvious like “Rosetta Install macOS 27,” and enter the following command in the script tab:

Under Execution Settings, pick your preferred trigger, then assign the profile to your macOS 27 Dynamic Device Group and save. When a device appears in that group, Mosyle automatically pushes the script, and Rosetta (hopefully) gets installed before the user ever runs into a problem. It’s not a permanent fix, but it buys time while I work on the real solution: getting vendors to ship native builds.

I want to be direct about this. Apple Silicon shipped in late 2020. We are now in late 2026. Any vendor still telling customers that a native Apple Silicon build is “on the roadmap” before Rosetta stops working in macOS 28 has had five-plus years to solve this problem and has chosen not to. That is not a resource issue or a technical challenge at this point. It is a prioritization choice, and one that falls squarely on the IT teams managing their software. Even if these vendors ship Apple Silicon-native versions before macOS 28, the shipping delay makes me question their commitment to macOS.

If you haven’t audited your fleet for Rosetta-dependent software yet, do it now while there’s still time to either push a script workaround or have the harder vendor conversations before users start running into problems. Most enterprise fleets are likely doing a 90 day block on Golden Gate for final testing/QA, so now is the time to work on your final plan. The script fix in Mosyle takes about five minutes to set up. Vendor conversations will take longer, and migrating to new solutions will take a bit longer.

#260. Here’s Exactly How Tesla Made Its New 230-Mph Car ‘Fly’

Last night, with considerable showmanship, Tesla CEO Elon Musk proudly unveiled the Roadster 2 just nine years after first announcing the car, and made it “fly.” While undeniably impressive, you could also describe the spectacle as Tesla making its long-delayed luxury car “do a big hop” and then, as Buzz Lightyear would say, “fall with style.”

During the reveal in McGregor, Texas, at SpaceX’s rocket development and testing facility, the two-seater Roadster 2 launched itself over the automaker’s entire lineup, shot from 0 to 60 mph in less than a second, and then drove upside down off a high ramp to then flip over midair and land back down on the ground, cushioning its rapid descent using onboard thrusters.

All this was pure gold for social clips (though at the time of publication, Tesla’s stock price was down after the event), but how did Tesla make its new EV prototype perform these tricks? Tesla vehicle engineering head Lars Moravy went into detail with auto lifestyle and insurance brand Hagerty before yesterday’s event, explaining how the Roadster 2 works.

The Roadster 2's gravity-defying demonstration in Texas used a combination of suction and rocket thrust.

Franz von Holzhausen, Tesla’s chief designer since 2008, designed the angular exterior. He also helmed the aesthetic of the Cybertruck, Models S, X, 3, and Y, as well as the Semi. Blacked-out windows obscured any view inside the EV, which carried no human driver anyway because, as Musk said, Tesla wanted “to make sure we don’t kill anyone” during the gravity-defying demonstration.

The Roadster 2 will be rear-wheel-drive only, a departure from Tesla’s track record of all-wheel-drive EVs. Two motors will deliver over a megawatt of power (1,341 horsepower) and over 1,400 newton-meters (Nm) of torque, meaning this car will have more torque and power than a three-motor Plaid. But all of that power goes through just the rear wheels.

The car will be light, at “just under 1,700 kilos” (under 2 tons), according to Moravy, not significantly heavier than the original 1,300-kg (1.4-ton) Roadster, despite a larger size.

Tesla claims a range of over 300 miles for the Roadster and hopes to mitigate this distinctly average range by also giving the EV the fastest-charging battery the automaker has ever produced, supposedly capable of zipping from 15 to 80 percent in 10 minutes.

At a 2013 auction, Elon Musk bought the iconic "Wet Nellie" Lotus Esprit S1 submarine car from the 1977 James Bond film The Spy Who Loved Me for just shy of $1 million. Musk is so taken with his Bond memorabilia that it apparently inspired one of the Roadster 2's key abilities.

That submarine Bond car has four propellers at its rear, so Tesla decided to ape this with four 20-kilowatt fans on the Roadster 2. Moravy says these fans break the laws of tire physics and dramatically increase the EV's traction by becoming what Tesla calls the car’s “sucker system.” Four independent replaceable skirts drop down on the sides of the car, allowing the Roadster 2 to stick (or suck) to the road at lower speeds where its aerodynamic wings aren't yet contributing to downforce. Moravy claims the system can produce over 2 g's in a corner when accelerating, even below 50 mph.

This type of aerodynamic manipulation also appears on the McMurtry Spéirling Pure, which uses two high-speed electric fans spinning at up to 23,000 revolutions per minute to actively suck air from underneath the chassis, generating up to 2,000 kg (around 4,400 pounds) of downforce.

This extreme suction lets the Roadster 2 drive up the vertical ramp at the Texas demonstration and hold onto the surface even when upside down.

So how does the Roadster 2 hover, correct itself, and dampen its fall? That's thanks to what Tesla calls the car’s “SpaceX system,” referring to Musk’s aerospace company, which helped with this part of the car’s development.

Originally, the Roadster was meant to have a 2+2 cabin. Now it’s a two-seater because behind the seats sits a 200-liter carbon-overwrapped pressure vessel (COPV) that holds up to 10,000 PSI to supply the car’s cold gas thrusters, which use expansion of pressurized nitrogen gas to generate thrust, a tech predominantly used for spacecraft stabilization. Cold gas thrusters are the simplest manifestation of a rocket engine.

This combination of suction system and thrusters helps the car hit 0 to 60 mph in supposedly under a second. In this launch mode, Moravy says the rear thrusters produce more than 80 kilonewtons of thrust, which, staggeringly, matches the Dassault Falcon 10X jet. Tesla has seemingly cracked the sub-second race, while the aforementioned McMurtry Spéirling Pure can only manage this feat in a bowel-clenching 1.3 seconds. During this astonishing acceleration, the driver will endure up to 5 g's.

The Roadster 2's Performance model will feature the sucker system and no thrusters, so 0 to 60 will take a touch longer at 1.6 seconds and a top speed of 210 mph. The Thrust model gets the whole package and a top speed of 230 mph.

Moravy says the “flight system,” as he calls it in Hagerty’s walk-through, requires yet another 400-liter cold gas COPV, occupying the space where the passenger seat is, making the car a single-seater and bringing total thrust fuel up to 600 liters. This “flight system” also requires six extra thrusters: one in each corner, plus two at the front to yaw.

Unlike in space, where cold gas thrusters provide consistent levels of thrust until the last drop of fuel is used, on Earth the “flight system” will lose thrust as the compressed gas depletes. Moravy likens it to blowing up a balloon then letting the air out: “When I open the end of a balloon, all the gas comes out, and at a certain point, it starts tapering off. That same thing will happen here.”

The Roadster 2 requires six additional thrusters around the car to operate its “flight system.”

Apparently, refilling the 600-liter nitrogen tanks takes Tesla six to seven hours, but the company is supposedly working on a system to dramatically reduce this to 30 minutes.

The current Roadster 2 prototypes are being used for further development, and production won’t begin until 2028—but remember that Musk previously said Roadster deliveries would begin in 2020, so take this with a very large pinch of salt. That's without talking about how the Federal Aviation Administration will react to this "flying" car.

Still, for the Tesla faithful, a reservation page is already live where a $5,000 reservation fee secures the Performance variant, with an additional $45,000 due within 10 days. The Thrust is available for an initial $5,000 fee, with a whopping $245,000 due within 10 days.

If you thought Pokémon TCG collectors were already losing their minds over 30th Celebration Booster Bundles and Elite Trainer Boxes, Amazon just opened preorders for the crown jewel of the anniversary expansion: the 30th Celebration Ultra-Premium Collections.

Both high-end boxes are currently available for preorder at Amazon for under $700 ahead of their official Nov. 6 release date.

Pokémon TCG 30th Celebration Ultra-Premium Collection Night (Umbreon): Includes the exclusive Umbreon ex promo card with a Futuristic-rarity Pikachu ex promo card and an Umbreon playmat.

The big question when buying trading cards on Amazon is whether or not you're actually getting value for money. Amazon is a reliable pick for finding readily available stock, but you often pay above market price.

I’ve always struggled with sleep. I’ve never been able to nap as most people can, and once my head hits the pillow, I’m usually wide awake—not the best sleep routine. And trust me, I’ve tried it all. From lavender pillow sprays to hot showers before crawling under the sheets, nothing seems to make me sleepy.

The only time I ever fall asleep is when I’m in a moving vehicle. This tells me two things: 1. That I’m probably the worst person to have in the passenger seat on a road trip, and 2. A combination of white noise from the road, vibrations, and motion knocks me completely out.

To dive deeper into how I can improve my sleep quality, I started using an Oura Ring, and this shows me how my daily activities and even what time I eat can influence the number of Zs I’m getting each night. I also recently added the Hatch Sleep Clock to my nighttime routine, and now I’m getting eight hours of sleep almost every night. So what is this super pairing actually doing? Let’s find out.

The Hatch Sleep Clock brings sleep-tracking technology to your nightstand with motion sensors that can detect what stage of sleep you're in. The app logs all this information, and you can set alarms and wind-down routines for when you get into bed.

I upgraded from my Hatch Restore 3 to the Hatch Sleep Clock because it can track habits, and I wanted to know if there was something else I should be doing during my wind-down routine to fall asleep. Admittedly, there’s not much difference between the software for the Sleep Clock and the Restore 3, but the Sleep Clock tracks your sleep, and it held the key to my sleepless nights.

The Hatch Sleep Clock uses motion sensors to understand your movements at night and denote your sleep stages into core, REM, and deep. I have to say, at first I thought it wouldn't be accurate, but the data I get back is almost identical to my Oura Ring, even though it doesn’t track any physical metrics like heart rate or breathing regularity.

Because the clock could track my sleep, it recommended wind-down routines that would benefit my sleep patterns. It’s a very intuitive device without being too intrusive. As soon as I started seeing my sleep scores climb higher and higher in my Oura app. Oura can show me what affects my sleep during the day, but the relaxation comes from the Hatch.

I never take my Oura Ring off. This tiny device has taught me so much about my body that I appreciate everything it tells me and take it on board as if it’s gospel. But the catch is that it can only tell me what’s going on and what’s wrong, not why. That’s why the ring needs the Hatch as a partner in crime.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

According to the CDC, 14.5% of adults in the U.S. have trouble falling asleep, and women are more likely than men to have trouble falling asleep. But once they’ve fallen asleep, 17.8% of adults have trouble staying asleep. Advice from Harvard Medical School says good sleep hygiene can help you fall asleep and improve sleep quality. Sleep hygiene includes practices like structuring a bedtime routine and creating a comfortable sleeping environment.

The Hatch Sleep Clock has helped me create that environment, and now I look forward to getting into bed every night to wind down with calm, red-toned lighting, white noise, and my book. Maintaining this structure, as recommended by the Hatch, has meant my body and mind now understand the routine. My heart rate lowers and my thoughts clear.

When I plugged in the Hatch Sleep Tracker, I really didn’t have high hopes. Why? Well, I honestly didn’t understand how a motion sensor could detect my REM and deep sleep. Surely it needs some biometrics to get the full picture. Oh, how wrong I was.

When I checked the app in the morning, it mapped my whole night’s sleep, and it matched my Oura Ring's sleep analysis almost perfectly.

There are only a couple of minutes between the time spent asleep on both devices, but wake-ups and deep sleep are logged accurately, as you can see.

Using both the Oura Ring and the Hatch Sleep Clock has helped me build a routine and use advice from both apps to figure out what works best for relaxing. My sleep has improved so much in the last few months, and I owe it all to this duo.

#263. Nvidia reportedly wants all its HBM suppliers to use TSMC’s 3nm process

Nvidia wants Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron on one process for its custom NVHBM chips. Samsung agreed after an internal review, dropping its all-in-house approach for Nvidia.

Samsung Electronics will make a core part of Nvidia’s custom memory chips on TSMC’s 3-nanometre process. The Seoul Economic Daily reported the move on Sunday, citing industry sources. It would be the first time the two have worked together on making high-bandwidth memory (HBM).

The part is the base die, the logic layer at the bottom of an HBM stack. Until now, Samsung has made both the base die and the memory dies above it for all of its HBM. That is called a turnkey approach. It has decided to change that for Nvidia, according to the report.

NVHBM is Nvidia’s custom HBM, unveiled in August. Nvidia has asked all three of its NVHBM suppliers to make the base die on TSMC’s 3nm process. Those suppliers are Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron. Nvidia also wants the memory dies standardised on 1c, the sixth generation of DRAM technology. NVHBM uses the design of HBM4E, the seventh generation of HBM.

The reason is consistency, the newspaper said. When suppliers use different methods, one design is hard to make perform the same way across all of them. A common process also means Nvidia does not have to validate each supplier’s chips separately. Samsung’s Device Solutions division agreed after an internal review.

The two companies worked together four years ago, when Samsung made sure its HBM fitted TSMC’s packaging process.

NVHBM moves the memory controller off the GPU and onto the base die. That is according to a second Seoul Economic Daily report. That frees space on the GPU for more computing circuits. To make room, the physical layer that talks to other chips is 60% smaller than in standard HBM. The result is up to 30% more bandwidth and 15% less power than standard HBM4E, the report said.

The industry puts TSMC’s 3nm yield at more than 90%. That compares with about 60% for Samsung Foundry’s comparable 2nm process, SF2.

UBS expects HBM demand of about 61.5 billion gigabits next year, up 91%. It expects new shipments from memory makers of only 54.6 billion gigabits. That leaves a shortfall of about 10%, the newspaper said.

TSMC is adding two 3nm lines at Fab 18 in Tainan. Mass production is due to start in the first half of 2027 and of 2028. It also plans 3nm lines at its second plants in Arizona and in Kumamoto, Japan.

Samsung will keep the turnkey approach for its standard HBM4 and HBM4E, which use its own 4nm base dies. It will also keep it for custom HBM for other customers, including AMD. It is also testing whether its own foundry could make the NVHBM base die on its 2nm process. That is a hedge in case demand outgrows TSMC’s capacity, an industry official said.

Progress continues in restructuring IEEE’s geographic regions, as outlined in The Institute’s February 2023 article “IEEE Is Realigning Its Geographic Regions.”

The restructuring is defined in the image of the redrawn map in this article.

Although the new regional alignment will not officially take place until 1 January 2028, several activities have begun within IEEE Member and Geographic Activities (MGA) and across other IEEE organizational units. Within MGA, volunteers and staff have been actively addressing system enhancements, director/director-elect elections, governance updates, communications, and regional finances and offerings.

Work will continue from now until the effective date of realignment in 2028. The change will not affect your IEEE membership, nor will it change either your local IEEE section or chapter.

If you have any questions regarding the realignment, contact Reg-Realignment@ieee.org.

IEEE Member and Geographic Activities oversees IEEE membership and the activities of its geographic units worldwide.

#265. Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Is 'Loser Core'?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's Out of Touch Guide delves into the musical genre/sub-culture of "Loser Core," a pointed response to overly polished music and Instagram-polished fashion. We also define some slang, so if a young person says you have EBK or nods and says "GiGis" to you, you'll know whether you're being insulted or complimented. And then there's Biddy Blas, Star Wars fandom's newest Glub Shitto.

Loser Core is a growing subculture and musical style among young people. The music is influenced by indie, alternative, and lo-fi, with lyrics that tend toward depressing. They're usually about alienation, teen angst, and how hard it is to talk girls. Loser Core is like emo, but more homemade and more hopeless, or like grunge with less anger. Prominent Loser Core artists include Memo Boy and Wifiskeleton. Notable influences include Radiohead and Weezer.

The Loser Core look is anti-fashion: over-size, slouchy hoodies, anime T-shirts, digital watches, and beat-up sneakers. The personality type is alienated nerd with niche hobbies and few friends. So basically, depressed young people who gravitate to depressing music and a slobby look. No matter your age, I'm sure you knew (or were) this type of person when you were 17.

Here's a video that explains it a bit more:

So that's Loser Core, the genre and lifestyle. Explaining the prominence of the Loser Core Playlist is a little more complicated. Created on Spotify by depay178, LOSERCORE is a playlist of 155 songs in the Loser Core genre. Back in June, a TikTok user called @user406398991 started posted AI-generated cartoons to promote the LOSERCORE playlist. The videos feature a recurring cast of characters, are usually about music, and end with a recommendation to visit the LOSERCORE playlist. Here's an example:

The videos started appearing on a lot of people's feeds in October, raising the profile the musical genre and generating reenactment videos like this:

...as well as videos from artists who are confused at their own inclusion on the list, people selling rip-off merch, and people gate-keeping what Loser Core is and questioning the inclusion of some songs on what is becoming the canonical list. Also: a ton of videos asking, "why does this keep showing up on my feed?"

Online chatter about the playlist revolves around the perceived lack of quality of the videos, and why, exactly, someone would spend so much time promoting a playlist on Spotify when you can't monetize the followers it gets.

It's a good question. There are indirect ways this list could be making someone money—maybe there's a connection between the promotion and the bands on the list who get paid per stream—but I like to think it's just kids who identify with these artists and want other kids to hear what they're into, like people did with zines in the old days. We don't have to monetize everything, right?

EBK stands for "Extreme Baller Knowledge." It goes beyond the sports reference to apply to to anyone who has deep knowledge of a subject. It's usually used ironically.

Pronounced like the name Gigi, "GiGis" comes from sports by way of gamer culture. The post game pleasantry "good game" has been a staple in sports since forever. Gamers adopted it and shortened it to "GG" in text. So GiGis is a way of saying "good game."

This week's viral video comes by way of a video game cut-scene. Star Wars: Galactic Racer was released on Oct. 6, and its breakout star has emerged: Biddy Blas. You won't find him in any of the Star Wars movies or TV shows. Biddy is only in this one game, and basically only exists as an opponent to be beaten in a race. But Biddy is too great to go out in obscurity. Just check him out:

Soon after the release of the game, fans dubbed Biddy the "best Glup Shitto (Star Wars background character with a silly name)" and started making memes to celebrate him, like these:

Biddy Blas' popularity is the result of voice actor Richard Summers-Calvert's spirited performance, particularly his reading of Biddy's catchphrase, "scrib doon," (i.e.: "Write that down."). The phrase gets caught in your brain:

and there are so many occasions when "scrib doon" is the perfect thing to say:

#267. Gdynia and the Dream of a Maritime Poland

A century ago, a Baltic fishing village began its transformation into a bustling port. Gdynia embodied interwar Poland’s modernising ambitions, but it could not guarantee the country’s security.

The penultimate point in Woodrow Wilson’s Fourteen Points for peace negotiations to end the First World War was the most idealised of its goals. It called for an independent Polish state to be created, and not, as the eminent Polish-American historian Piotr Wandycz notes, resurrected – and certainly not ‘based on historical principles’, mapped on to the old Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth that had been erased from the European map in 1795. This would be a new Poland. Wilson called for it to include ‘territories inhabited by indisputably Polish populations’ (this would become difficult to ascertain and haunt the future of the region); and the document called for ‘political and economic independence and territorial integrity […] guaranteed by international covenant’ (plans, again, which were difficult to put into practice). It was a puzzle.

There was another clause in the mix, too: that Poland ‘should be assured a free and secure access to the sea’.

Poles, who had pushed for this, saw the nautical sphere as a necessity for the country. As the historian Marta Grzechnik argues, Poles also wanted to shed the country’s image as a fragile land-locked nation. It was also essential if Poland was to become a modern nation – ‘far-sighted’, as Grzechnik puts it – and a global nation, even an imperial one.

The problem was that access to the sea in the interwar period had a German-shaped obstacle, or, rather, two of them. Poland had been awarded a small strip of land in the north to provide maritime links, but it was pincered between Germany proper and East Prussia, with no sizeable ports in sight; nor could it rely on the Free City of Danzig for any maritime ambitions, because although Poland had the right to use the port, Danzig was predominantly German in population, and hence tensions were frequent. In 1920, Poland decided it would have to build its own port in the region. In the end, experts selected a fishing and holiday village, Gdynia, as the best spot to put the plan into action due to hydrographic conditions and rail connections – and it was promptly overhauled as a modern port, fit for a modern nation.

Gdynia, more than any other city, might be seen then as a sort of microcosm for interwar Poland itself – it was an alternative Polish capital. Yes, Warsaw, the real capital, was the glorified location of the Miracle on the Vistula: the decisive triumph of Polish forces against the westward march of the Soviets in 1920, which pushed back the spread of communism into Europe. Warsaw was glitzy and glamorous, a true urban marvel, featuring revolving dance floors, Art Deco skyscrapers, prosperity, but also mounting tensions and poverty. Yes, Vilnius (then Wilno) was also a bulwark of patriotism, although to the chagrin of the newly independent Lithuania, which had broken ties with Poland because of Poland’s seizure of the city. Lviv (then Lwów), too, had a claim to be the nation’s capital of culture.

Yet Gdynia was a new city, symbolising the modernisation of the country, and its high hopes in the interwar period. Work on the port began in 1921; by 1926, 100 years ago this year, the once sleepy fishing village had been granted city rights and, by the end of the 1930s, it was a bustling maritime metropolis. Its construction into the jewel of modern Poland was matched by suitable architecture: functionalist buildings, sparkling in whitewash, with curves and perpendicular lines, and sweeping, grinning windows on every façade, wide to the hopeful Baltic Sea beyond. It was a Bauhaus fever dream.

Poets, writers and filmmakers celebrated Gdynia, too, in modernist art. Grzechnik notes that poets wrote of the city’s machinery and its modernist architecture, while the 1935 melodrama film Rapsodia Bałtyku (Rhapsody of the Baltic), about two navy officers, celebrated Gdynia for its military prowess as well as its maritime prosperity. By the 1930s, Gdynia was the hub of the Polish navy, and served commercial and passenger traffic.

It was also a place that illustrated the darker side of Poland’s burgeoning modernity. Tens of thousands used the new port as a point of departure for a new life across the Atlantic, from a modernist three-storey passenger hall, constructed at the port in 1933 for this very purpose. While the construction of Gdynia was testament to utopian ideas of a modern Poland, many did not see their future in the country, where modernity was still uneven and poverty rife. The building they departed from now houses the Emigration Museum, witness to centuries of Polish émigré history. Moreover, Gdynia was a stronghold of the Maritime and Colonial League – a mass Polish social organisation promoting the creation of colonies for Poland. The city’s construction was a political statement that spoke to a new Polish prosperity and self-confidence, but it could not escape the shadow of conflict with Germany, and the difficulties of creating a new Polish future alongside neighbours with expansionist designs.

Gdynia was the fulfilment of Wilson’s promise in part, but not in whole – it was a gateway to the Baltic, and a symbol of Poland’s freedom. It was also a place where, however much Poles tried, they were not able to guarantee the one element of the sea-life they thought indispensable for the future: security.

#269. Razer Barracuda V2 Pro Review: A Gaming Headset for the Office

I transition between different pieces of audio equipment on any given day. I listen to music with my earbuds, but they always fall out when I talk, so for meetings I tend to go without. If I’m in a loud setting and need to speak in a virtual meeting, I reach for my old, reliable headset for its higher-quality mic, but I often sacrifice call quality in non-gaming environments. And when I’m gaming, I love my light-up kitty-ear headset, but I don’t necessarily want to wear that at a coffee shop or in a professional setting. Which is why the new Razer Barracuda V2 Pro is made for people like me. It’s an elegant, multipurpose headset that does the job, no matter what the job is.

The Barracuda V2 Pro feels more like a good pair of over-ear headphones than a traditional gaming headset. During my testing period, I regularly listened to music with it. It sounds clear and balanced—there’s a bit of quality loss in the lows and highs, but it’s still perfectly acceptable, and the hybrid active noise canceling (ANC) is fantastic. Press the Multifunction button to cycle between ambient, ANC-on, and ANC-off modes. Hold it to activate your voice assistant or customize it in the Razer Synapse Windows/Mac software or Razer Audio smartphone app. (Customizations include cycling ANC modes, adjusting volume via Bluetooth, or using your voice assistant, so you can choose what each button press does.) You can tweak the EQ in Razer Audio and cycle between presets—Movie, Music, Game, and Default—with the press of a button. Press the same button twice to cycle between connectivity modes, including Bluetooth, HyperSpeed Wireless, and Simultaneous Listening. You can also go wired with the included cable.

I love that the HyperSpeed wireless dongle is cleverly stored behind a magnetic panel in the left earcup. The wide range of connectivity options means this headset is compatible with PC, Mac, PlayStation, Steam Deck, and mobile devices. You can also use it with your Xbox in Bluetooth mode. Simultaneous audio lets you answer a phone call while still in the game, or play a video in the background while you’re in a matchmaking queue. THX Spatial Audio makes gaming on my PC feel even more immersive.

Onboard controls include two buttons for volume adjustment. I wish this was a wheel, but that boils down to personal preference. There’s also a dedicated mute toggle, and you can tap the power button to pause, double-tap to skip the next song, or triple-tap to go back; you can also use this button to accept or reject incoming calls.

The Barracuda V2 Pro features internal beamforming mics and an optional, detachable external boom microphone (HyperClear Full Band Mic). Both offer clear, concise sound, according to the colleagues and gamers who helped me assess them. The leatherette-covered memory foam earcups are soft, squishy, and comfortable, though the base felt a little tight on my jaw and earlobes after hours of use. I have a smaller-than-average head and can imagine this would be more of a nuisance for people with impressive noggin circumferences. The headset is lightweight, coming in at 285 grams.

I have yet to deplete the impressive 70-hour battery (50 with ANC on), even while listening to music and playing games every day. A fifteen-minute USB-C charge gets you about six hours of battery life.

There are a couple of quirks. I wish it folded down more compactly, and I need to find a carrying case that has space for the external microphone when it isn’t attached. This headset also lacks Razer’s well-known RGB lights, which may be a draw for users taking it to the office or on the train. But if you see the brand name and expect a Chroma-compatible confection, this isn’t the right set for you. Ultimately, though, it’s very well-rounded and versatile, and it’s an easy recommendation for anyone seeking a headset that can work during the day and into the night.

#270. Meet the Anthropic Engineer Keeping Its AI Agent Trustworthy

His data systems make sure Claude’s answers are accurate

IEEE Senior Member Gurmeet Saran is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind Claude’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs.

If you’ve ever wondered how Claude and similar AI agents can answer complex questions in seconds and where they get the information, you’re not alone.

Gurmeet Saran works to find that answer every day as an engineer at Anthropic in San Francisco, the AI research company behind Claude. The IEEE senior member is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind the chatbot’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs.

Gurmeet Saran Employer Anthropic in San FranciscoTitle Member of technical staffMember grade IEEE senior memberAlma maters University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India

University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India

“My job is to make sure the data is accurate, structured, and trustworthy, and that private data stays private,” he says. “As I learned earlier in my career, privacy can’t be a layer you bolt on—it has to be part of the architecture from the start.” If you can’t trust the logic, he adds, you can’t make reliable claims about the behavior, and that has real safety implications.

Safety is a priority for Anthropic, he says. According to Claude’s mission statement, the company wants the AI agent to be “genuinely helpful to the people it works with or on behalf of, as well as to society, while avoiding actions that are unsafe, unethical, or deceptive.” Crucial to the mission is ensuring that researchers can observe and understand how AI models behave, a challenge that is especially acute for large language models, Saran says.

“We have decent tools to monitor databases and web services,” he says, “but for LLMs, we’re still figuring it out.”

Saran’s interest in computing systems dates back to his childhood in Kolkata, where he logged as much time as he could in the school computer lab.

“I remember the first time I used one of the computers,” he says. “What struck me was that you could write instructions, and the machine would follow them exactly. No ambiguity.

After graduating from high school in 1999, he stayed in India to pursue advanced degrees. He earned a bachelor’s degree in electronics and telecommunication engineering in 2004 at the University of Kalyani. In 2010, he earned a master’s degree in software engineering from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science in Pilani.

While a graduate student, he began his career in 2007 at Yahoo as a technical lead of the data team in Bengaluru, India. While there, he encountered the project that shaped his career trajectory: working on web analytics and business intelligence reporting solutions.

“We kept running into a frustrating problem,” he recalls. “Different teams would calculate the same website metric—something like daily active site users—using slightly different logic, and end up with conflicting answers. It sounds like a small issue, but when leadership is making decisions about resource allocation and product development using that data, not knowing which number is correct becomes a problem.”

The team built a central data repository with defined metrics, essentially serving as a single source of truth. Saran created a model that defined what “daily active site users” means, breaking down which events counted, how to handle edge cases (or when standard code fails), and more.

With the new model, data teams across the company could rely on a standard method to determine the number of daily active users for the projects and sites they were responsible for and obtain comparable results using the same logic.

From there, Saran and his team built Yahoo! Digits, an internal web analytics tool used for all the company’s products.

Saran left Yahoo in 2010 to join Intuit as a staff engineer in Mountain View, Calif. He helped build the analytics infrastructure that unified data across the company’s products, including TurboTax and QuickBooks accounting software. During his tenure, Intuit developed a feature that detected fraudulent tax filings in real time. It required Saran and other engineers to build a system to protect taxpayer data while adhering to strict U.S. Internal Revenue Service policies.

“IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations.”

“This taught me that privacy and governance can’t be layers you bolt onto software after the fact,” he says. “They have to be part of the architecture from the start.”

Saran joined Meta (known as Facebook at the time) in 2016 as a lead software engineer in Menlo Park, Calif. The company was facing controversy over its video metrics: Meta publicly acknowledged an error that caused it to overstate the number of views for posted videos.

“This wasn’t a coding bug; it was an architectural problem,” Saran says. He built a system that worked similarly to what he had developed at Intuit, whereby one single truth was defined to govern all video view metrics across the site.

That system, Metric360, eventually became part of the site’s architecture. By the time he left Meta in 2021, he says, Metric360 was being used across the company to calculate video metrics.

He left the company to become a principal software engineer at Wealthfront, a financial services company in Palo Alto, Calif. He helped build the company’s data infrastructure.

Saran joined Anthropic in 2025 as a member of the technical staff.

To describe the implications of his work, he uses a medical analogy: “Imagine a doctor is monitoring a patient’s vital signs and making treatment decisions based on those numbers. What if one or a few of the medical devices used were slightly miscalibrated? Even if most readings are fine, it’s a serious problem because the difficult decisions happen in the margins.

“It’s the same with AI systems. My job is essentially to make sure the instruments are giving accurate readings—that the data means what it says it means.”

His job comes with high stakes and complex problems to solve.

“AI agents are especially tricky to observe,” he says. “When a system is taking sequences of actions [generating conversational responses with different users], you need a way to capture what it did, what information it was working from, and whether outcomes matched what the end user expected. And you have to do all of that without exposing anyone’s private information—the systems are designed to recognize sensitive data and keep it protected as it flows through. It’s a much more demanding observability problem than anything I’ve worked on before.”

Solving for system reliability while AI is still in its early days of adoption is both Saran’s passion and the problem that keeps him up at night, he says.

“I think making AI systems genuinely auditable and transparent is one of the more important engineering problems of the next decade,” he says, “and it doesn’t get talked about as much as model capabilities do.”

“After more than 20 years of building data infrastructure across organizations like Yahoo, Intuit, Meta, and Wealthfront,” he says, “I wanted to contribute back to the technical community through peer review, publishing, and engaging with the broader engineering research ecosystem.”

He says he believes IEEE can play an essential role in shaping the future of AI through its standards work.

“We have standards for everything, from building codes to software testing,” he says. “AI infrastructure needs something similar, and IEEE has the credibility and the reach to do that.”

Another problem that IEEE can solve for, he says, is access: “IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters, especially as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations in a few cities.”

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

#271. US orders civilian federal agencies to remove DeepSeek from their systems

A Homeland Security order also bars agencies from buying DeepSeek products or tools built on its models.

The Department of Homeland Security has ordered US civilian federal agencies to remove DeepSeek products from their IT systems and stop buying them, under a 2018 supply chain security law. The order covers third-party tools built on DeepSeek’s models, and cites the risk that sensitive data could be shared with the Chinese government.

US government agencies must take DeepSeek off their computers and stop buying its tools, under a new Homeland Security order. The department posted a notice of the order on the Federal Register website on Monday.

The ban applies to civilian agencies. It also covers tools from other firms that are built on DeepSeek’s AI models. It was issued under a 2018 law that lets the government cut risky suppliers out of its buying.

The order is dated 24 July and was signed by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Bloomberg reported. It also bars DeepSeek from taking part in federal contracts.

In the order, the government said DeepSeek collects a lot of user data that could be passed to Beijing under Chinese security laws, according to Bloomberg. The department also said the models pose “multiple threat vectors” and may hide malware or security flaws, Reuters reported.

The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to Bloomberg’s request for comment. DeepSeek did not comment in either report.

Some parts of the government had already limited the Chinese startup’s tools. A Pentagon IT agency blocked its chatbot in January 2025, and the Commerce Department and the Navy have banned it on work devices. New York, Tennessee, and Virginia have taken similar steps.

The move follows months of pressure on Chinese AI firms in Washington. In June, the White House held off on blacklisting DeepSeek and more than 100 other Chinese firms, even after a panel of officials cleared them for a US trade blacklist.

US officials have also accused Chinese AI labs of copying US models through a technique called distillation. In February, OpenAI told US lawmakers that DeepSeek had used the method to build its R1 chatbot, Bloomberg reported.

#272. Verizon confirms $10 monthly fee for new iPhone Handoff feature

Following T-Mobile and Deutsche Telekom, Verizon has now confirmed how much it will charge customers to use Apple’s new iPhone Handoff feature. Here are the details.

During Apple’s “Surprise and Shine” event last month, the company shared more details about iPhone Handoff, a new iOS 27 feature first previewed at WWDC that lets users share a single phone number across two iPhones.

Apple announced that the feature would initially be supported by T-Mobile and Deutsche Telekom, with Verizon and EE expected to follow before the end of the year.

Shortly after the event, T-Mobile confirmed a $5 monthly fee for iPhone Handoff, while Deutsche Telekom made the feature available through its existing MultiSIM service, which costs €6.95 per month unless already included in the customer’s plan.

eSIM promised us easier handling of SIM cards but instead it just lets carriers exploit us in new ways.

Today, as spotted by MacRumors, Verizon also confirmed its pricing for iPhone Handoff, announcing that it will charge $10 per month, twice as much as T-Mobile.

Verizon will support iPhone Handoff, giving customers the flexibility to use a single Verizon phone number seamlessly across two compatible iPhone models. Whether using the pocketable iPhone Duo on the go or iPhone 18 Pro for work, customers can switch active status between devices at any time while keeping full access to Verizon’s 5G network. iPhone Handoff will be available from Verizon for $10/month on compatible iPhones models running iOS 27.

AT&T, meanwhile, seemingly has no plans to support Apple’s new iPhone Handoff feature. When CNET asked about it last month, the carrier acknowledged its potential benefits but said it was focused on its existing eSIM activation and transfer options instead.

This 2026 model combines a soundbar and wireless subwoofer in a 5.1.2-channel setup, with dedicated channels for dialogue, surround sound, and overhead effects, plus a separate subwoofer to handle the bass. That layout makes it a sensible upgrade for anyone who keeps turning up the TV volume to catch a conversation—only to turn it down again when the action gets loud—since most built-in TV speakers lack a dedicated center channel to separate voices from the rest of the soundtrack.

Samsung builds on that center channel with two dialogue enhancement modes and a new feature called Sound Elevation, which attempts to raise the apparent height of voices so dialogue seems to come from the actors on screen and not from beneath the TV. That could be particularly useful if your soundbar sits on a low entertainment unit. And if you already have a compatible Samsung TV, Q-Symphony lets its speakers work alongside the soundbar, potentially creating a broader soundstage without buying any extra hardware.

The HW-Q800H also supports Dolby Atmos, adding a greater sense of height and space to compatible movies and shows, though the lack of DTS support is worth considering if you regularly watch Blu-rays with DTS soundtracks. Also, since there are no separate rear speakers included, surround effects won't feel quite as immersive as they would with a full home theater setup. Samsung does include automatic room correction, though, which adjusts the sound to suit your space without requiring much manual tweaking.

#275. Thank Gen Z for the ‘Girls’ Revival

It’s official: Lena Dunham’s millennial magnum opus Girls is coming back, and it’s in large part thanks to Gen Z giving the show its long overdue redemption arc.

Using their native tongue: the internet, Gen Z proselytized the show through memes, clips, and podcasts, and now, as if by collective manifestation, it’s being rebooted for five episodes, which HBO announced Wednesday.

When Girls first aired in 2012, it was cataclysmic. Rave reviews were usurped by the relentless onslaught of sexism and misogyny, which commented on Dunham’s body, the kind of sex depicted onscreen, and the nepo baby allegations against the show’s stars—as well as the series’ lack of diversity. There was endless backlash and backlash to the backlash; it became everyone’s favorite show to both fairly criticize and willfully misunderstand, and creator Dunham was the one stuck grasping onto the lightning rod of so much ire, as she began to stand for everything wrong with millennial white women.

But then something happened. A decade after it aired, everyone started rewatching Girls. It’s not just that people were talking about it online; the series’ viewership doubled between November 2022 and January 2023, compared with the previous three months, The New York Times reported. On Tiktok and Instagram, memes and supercuts started unfurling: Marnie poised with a microphone in the infamous teal dress; Hannah snapping “I am busy, trying to become who I am,” or Shoshanna saying, “Obvi we’re the ladies!” It finally clicked for viewers, spawning a cultural and critical resurgence. While the reviews aged like milk, the show had aged like wine.

It was a phenomenon largely fueled by Gen Z viewers who had missed the show the first time around. (As well as prominent millennial Girls “truthers” like Hunter Harris, Peyton Dix, and Evan Ross Katz.) Among these Gen Z viewers were Amelia Ritthaler and Evan Lazarus, Brooklyn comedians who launched the Girls Rewatch podcast in 2023.

“I think the rest of society caught up to (Dunham),” says Ritthaler, 28. “Everybody was kind of under the impression that they weren’t allowed to be publicly saying that they loved the show and thought it was great. But me and Evan were like, this show is amazing. Why is everybody mad at her?”

Gen Z especially was able to identify with a style that so many millennials had failed to grasp. “So much of what we were raised on was this post-ironic, emotionally removed, ‘world is burning, but let’s dance through it’ kind of social media,’” she says. “I feel like when it was coming out, millennials were just kind of in their earnest era. The millennial optimism of it all. I feel like Gen Z never got that, so we were always watching it from this satirical lens that Lena wrote it in.”

Ritthaler and Lazarus posted Girls memes on TikTok and Instagram, amassing a following that allowed them to have guests like Dunham, as well as cast members Allison Williams (Marnie), Andrew Rannells (Elijah), and Zosia Mamet (Shoshanna) on the show. “I think this was like 70% cuz of you guys,” Jemima Kirke (Jessa) commented on the podcast’s Instagram account the day the revival was announced. “I feel like I loved my favorite show back to my life,” Lazarus said in a teary-eyed video.

The show’s redemption arc coincided with Dunham’s memoir Famesick, published in April, further fueling the Girls nostalgia. “I feel like reading Famesick felt like getting a director’s cut of girls,” says Dix, who hosts the podcast Lemme Say This with Hunter Harris.

The book was an instant New York Times bestseller with a buzzy tour. More importantly, there was a public reckoning around the way culture mistreated Dunham. It felt like a bow tied neatly around the physical and mental toll making Girls. She had moved to London, gotten sober, written extensively about chronic illness, worked on shows like Industry and Too Much. Last month, she announced she’d welcomed a baby via surrogacy.

There were never explicit fan calls for a reboot, particularly after the universally-panned Sex and the City reboot And Just Like That… But the swell in the show’s popularity undoubtedly caught the attention of HBO execs, thanks to the tenacious Gen Zers who spread the good word online. In a Substack post published Wednesday, Dunham credited the fans for helping her be ready to return to the series. “Maybe there was once a part of me that wanted to outrun Hannah and her ladies,” she writes. “Seeing the love you’ve so generously shared for it helped to turn me around.”

“The fans are just tender queers and sensitive girls who journal and heart their eyes,” says Dix. “The people she’s reaching and nurturing aren’t critics anymore, it feels like, or people who want to make weird comments about her body. It’s just young people, she wants to help inform or entertain.”

Part of the reason for the revival is, of course, that everything has come back: Gossip Girl, Pretty Little Liars, iCarly, and countless others have also seen reboots and sequels in recent years. “It’s nostalgia-core for sure,” Ritthaler says. “But it sucks that we don't have any new IP that has topped it. I walk around Brooklyn every day, thinking ‘how did we make Girls in 2012 and then everything went back to being worse?’”

But Gen Z is also ripe for a millennial optimism they never got to experience. Nostalgia for the mid-2010s has been cropping up online, with people posting photos of themselves in 2016, longing for fixed gear bikes, sepia toned photos, and stomp-clap music.

“I think there’s an energy, particularly in New York right now, that really embodies millennial optimism, and I think that Girls is absolutely a part of that cultural conversation,” says Dix. “It falls neatly into this new world we’re building that is kind of based on ‘Obama first-term joy.’ It’s nice to feel joy again when it’s really difficult to find it.”

#276. Starbucks is launching an incredibly cute Winnie the Pooh collection — how to buy

Starbucks is teaming up with Disney for a 20-piece Starbucks x Winnie the Pooh collection celebrating 100 years of the Hundred Acre Wood. The limited-edition lineup drops on Oct. 20, delivering honey-drip cold cups, ceramic beehive mugs, and plush Bearista keychains.

It's an incredibly cute collection that is bound to cause a stir, but there's a catch. We hate to break it to you like this, but the collection is exclusive to the Asia-Pacific region.

The 20-piece range mixes aesthetic drinkware with lifestyle accessories:

Hunny Pot Tumblers and Cold Cups: Cold cups with honey-drip lids, golden-yellow straw toppers, and Pooh illustrations.

Ceramic Beehive Mug: A textured, beehive-shaped ceramic mug featuring Pooh stuck in a honey pot entry.

Bearista Costume Keychains and Phone Straps: Collectible Starbucks Bearistas dressed in plush costumes of Pooh, Piglet, Eeyore, and Tigger.

Packable Tote Bag: A reusable Hundred Acre Wood tote that folds into its own matching pouch.

We want everything, but here's where it gets complicated.

If you live in North America or Europe, you won't find these on local Starbucks shelves.

On launch day (Oct. 20), the collection will be available at participating Starbucks coffeehouses in Australia, Indonesia, Malaysia, New Zealand, the Philippines, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand, and Vietnam. Unfortunately for collectors elsewhere, the secondary market is going to be your best bet.

Exporters will begin listing inventory from Oct. 20, but you should expect a significant markup over retail prices on high-demand pieces like the ceramic beehive mug and plush Bearista straps. Head over to eBay and good luck.

If you desperately want official Disney x Starbucks drinkware without paying reseller markups, the Disney Store regularly stocks collaboration tumblers that ship directly to U.S. and UK addresses. In fact, we've spotted a cute Winnie the Pooh tumbler going for $27.99.

The Bearaby SoftForm is one of the coolest, comfiest pillows I've tested. It has a bit of bounce, a touch of sink, and a soft finish that gently cradles your ear and jaw to relieve pressure. It's also highly breathable, maintaining a cool feel even on hot nights. However, with just one loft—its height and thickness—available, its appeal is inherently limited. Some will find it too short, others too tall, but if you're lucky enough to find it 'just right,' it's a fantastic choice for cooler, pressure-relieving sleep.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

When I think of Bearaby, I think of snug sleep comforts, like stress-busting weighted blankets and knot pillows. So I was eager to get my hands on the Bearaby SoftForm pillow, to see if it can deliver the same signature coziness and land a place in our guide to the best pillows for every sleep style.

Type: LatexBest for: Side sleepers, hot sleepersSizes: 28" x 16"Trial: 30 nightsWarranty: 1-yearPrice: $149 at Bearaby

The SoftForm pillow is made from Melofoam, a latex foam developed by Bearaby. Latex foam is known for its spring, a natural bounce back that means the pillow won't go flat when you change position. And the SoftForm pillow has some of that, with materials that return to shape as soon as you move.

But it's a softer version of a latex pillow. You don't properly sink into it (you'll need memory foam for that) but it does gently contour to the ear and jaw to relieve pressure build-up. And there's one feature of latex that the SoftForm pillow has in spades: temperature regulation. It's incredibly breathable, staying a neutral feel even on hot nights.

The 6" loft should keep most side sleepers happy and the softer feel can accommodate back sleepers as well. But the single loft with no adjustability feels like a missed opportunity.

It's too high for me as a stomach sleeper, and I suspect side sleepers with wide shoulders will find it too shallow. For me, and considering the Bearaby SoftForm Pillow costs $149, this is a key drawback in the pillow's design.

The Bearaby SoftFormPillow is a luxury buy, with an MSRP of $149 for the standard size. While Bearaby sales do happen occasionally, they're rare and they don't always cover every product. In other words, while you might be lucky and stumble on a sale, I wouldn't count on it.

While $149 is a premium pillow, it's not an unusual price for a latex design. The Saatva Latex pillow, for example, is $165, while the Birch Organic pillow typically sells for $159 and the Coop Adjustable Latex pillow is $149.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

You can pick up a latex pillow for less but it's rare to find a pillow made from this natural material at a low cost. The Helix Talalay Latex pillow is an affordable choice, but you can still expect to pay around $89.

Bearaby offers a 30-night trial and a 1-year warranty with the SoftForm pillow. These extras are okay but we might expect better at this price. Coop gives a 100-night trial and 5-year warranty with its latex pillow (although this is unusually generous.)

Bearaby's SoftForm Pillow is a latex pillow with a cotton cover and a breathable build. At $149 it's a premium design and Bearaby sales are rare, but keep an eye out for discounts over the major holidays. A 30-night trial and 1-year warranty are included.

The Bearaby SoftForm pillow is made from a simple design; a single, seamless slab of foam wrapped in a natural cotton cover. There are no adjustable layers or removable fill to contend with, and no plumping or fluffing required (something I'll get into later).

But this is no ordinary foam, this is Melofoam, Bearaby's own design. Made from the sap of hevea trees in Sri Lanka, it's gentle steamed until a bouncy latex foam is formed. Air channels are then cut into the foam, to increase breathability.

The pillow is 6" tall and measures 28" x 16". The air channels give the pillow a softer feel at the center and a touch more firmness at the sides, to support different sleeping positions.

I slept on the Bearaby SoftForm Pillow for three weeks. Here's everything you need to know about the comfort and performance.

There isn't really a set up process for the Bearaby SoftForm pillow. It comes in a large zippered bag and is delivered flat. Once the pillow is out of the bag, it's ready to sleep on straight away.

While latex foams can have a strong smell (the Helix Latex Pillow had a distinct scent), I didn't notice any noticeable off-gassing from the SoftForm pillow. So even sensitive noses should be comfortable using this design.

The hardest part of set-up was putting the pillow in its case. The measurements aren't standard, which meant I had a slight overhang.

The previous latex pillow I slept on was a bit of a trampoline — any movement was accompanied by some boing. I was expecting the same from the SoftForm pillow, seeing as it's also an all-latex build.

However, this is a latex pillow with a difference. It feels halfway between latex and memory foam: there's not quite a bounce, not quite a slow-moving sink.

So what does that actually mean to sleep on? When you first lie on the SoftForm pillow it feels soft beneath the head, gently conforming around the ear and jaw. But you soon meet the support core, which holds up the neck to keep your head at the correct angle. You sink slightly and then you stop and when you move the surface eases quickly back to form.

I used a 10lb weight to get a clear idea of what's happening. My kettlebell (roughly equal to the weight of a human head) did sink significantly into the pillow; that's the softness at play. But as soon as the weight was lifted, the materials jumped back. That's the latex bounce.

At 6" tall it has a high pillow loft, which should best suit side sleepers. With the tall design and lack of sink, my head felt well supported when lying on my side. It neatly filled the gap between my neck and the bed. However, some side sleepers with broader shoulders will need a taller loft and there's no way to adjust the feel.

I also found it largely comfortable for back sleeping, although it would take a minute to get my head in the right position on the soft foam at the center of the pillow. Stomach sleeping, however, is uncomfortable. The pillow pushed my head upwards, resulting in neck ache.

With just the one loft, no adjustability and no stacking, it's a bit of a Goldilocks pillow. You might find it just right, but for many it's going to be too tall or too short.

Latex is one of the most breathable pillow fills, as the natural material allows for plenty of airflow. Add on the air channels cut into the Bearaby SoftForm foams, and I was expecting the pillow to stay cool overnight.

During testing, the Bearaby pillow has lived up to my cooling expectations. The temperature regulation is excellent, as heat quickly escapes to ensure no warm spots pool beneath my head.

I've been dressing my pillows in Bearaby's Second Skin sheets, which add to the cooling feel (these have a silky finish and are chill to the touch.) However, I've also been wearing an eye mask and various sleep headbands, both of which can increase heat build-up. Despite that, I've stayed cool.

Pillows typically need to be replaced every two years, although some pillows will lose their loft muh quicker than that.

To check if your pillow needs replacing, we recommend a 30-second test: fold your pillow in half and see how long it takes to bounce back. If your pillow is hard to fold or bounces back insantly, it's in good shape. If it folds slowly and stays folded, the fill is probably worn out.

I've been sleeping on the Bearaby SoftForm pillow for over a month and so far it's showing no signs of sagging. But that's the bare minimum, particularly for a pillow in this price bracket.

Overall, however, the pillow has a sturdy, durable design. The foams and fabrics seem high quality which should contribute to a longer lifespan. And while the most recent reviews for the SoftForm pillow are all within the past few months, the Bearaby Cuddler, which is made from the same Melofoam, has reviews dating back years and no mention of excessive wear or tear.

While a one-year warranty is on the short side for a premium pillow, it's still within the industry average. All factors considered, I think you should get at least two years use from the Bearaby SoftForm pillow.

Whether its yellow sweat stains following a warm night or unwelcome marks from your favorite retinol night cream, all pillows need a clean from time to time. Maintenance helps extend the lifespan of your pillow by keeping the materials fresh.

The SoftForm core is spot clean only and Bearaby recommends allowing the pillow to dry completely before using it again. The cover can be machine washed in cold water with a mild detergent.

While it's not unusual for a latex pillow to require this level of care, it's still a slightly laborious process. Especially considering some pillow types can be machine washed. However, you don't need to plump it back into shape, as it returns to form naturally — that's a few seconds saved every morning.

The Bearaby SoftForm Pillow is supportive and springy but with a soft hug that relieves pressure at the shoulder and jaw. When you lie on it the materials gently ease around your head to hold you in a cradle and when you move they subtly respond to ensure you never miss out on comfort.

Made from natural latex and cotton, this eco-pillow is also highly breathable. Even on hot nights sleeping laden in eye masks and headphone bands, I haven't felt my head overheat. It's a good pick if you often wake up feeling sweaty.

However, it does have some flaws, the most prominent being the build. It should be high enough for most side sleepers and soft enough for many back sleeper but this is a $149 pillow — another loft option wouldn't go amiss. If a 6" loft sounds right for you, then this is an excellent design with plenty to celebrate. If not, then expect a sore neck in the morning.

✅ You're a hot sleeper: The latex foams and built-in air channels allow for heat to escape, so you can stay a neutral temperature during the night.

✅ You're a combination sleeper: Easy to move around on and with a loft that suits most sleep styles, the Bearaby SoftForm pillow is supportive on those restless nights.

✅ You want an eco-friendly design: Bearaby's Melofoam and natural cotton cover are better for the environment than petroleum-based foams and textiles.

❌ You sleep on your stomach: The 6" loft is too tall for most pillow sleepers — try the Helix Latex Pillow in a low loft for a similar design without the neck strain.

❌ You have wide shoulders: Most side sleepers should be supported by the SoftForm but with just one loft, it's too short for those who prefer to stack their pillows.

❌ You like a traditional feel: With its soft-yet-responsive design and single slab build, this pillow feels nothing like a classic down or down alternative design. The Birch Pillow, which uses wool and shredded latex, is a better option for a traditional feel.

Like the Bearaby SoftForm, the Helix Talalay Latex pillow is made from a single piece of foam with holes to increase air flow. It has a bouncier feel than the Bearaby, with a quick response rather than a gentle sink. Available in two lofts (low and high), it has an MSRP of $111 for a standard size but the Helix mattress sales run year-round, so expect to pay around $89.

Like the Bearaby SoftForm, the Birch Organic Pillow is made from latex foams. Only here you'll find a core of shredded latex, wrapped in a layer of wool padding. The result is a cool feeling design that can be easily adjusted to suit your needs, although the medium-loft won't suit stomach sleepers or side sleepers with wide shoulders. It's $159 in the Birch sale (was $198).

If the SoftForm pillow delivers subtle softness, the Tempur-Pedic Tempur-Cloud pillow takes it to the max. This sink-in pillow is like a luxurious marshmallow with a low loft for back and stomach sleepers. But watch out for heat retention, as it can sleep hot. A queen is $84 at full price but stay alert for Tempur-Pedic mattress sales, as you can often find a bundle deal.

#279. Power To The Players Act would make the games you buy yours to own

The bill would also require an offline mode before a game’s servers go dark. NBA 2K25 loses its online servers on 31 December.

Ritchie Torres, US representative for New York’s 15th district, speaking in Washington, DC, in 2024.

Ritchie Torres, a Democratic congressman from New York, plans to bring a video game ownership bill to Congress. He announced the Power To The Players Act on 15 October.

The bill would direct the Federal Trade Commission to write new rules. They would protect players’ ability to own and play the games they buy. Buying a game would give you ownership of it, not a licence to play it, Torres’s office said. Games with online features would also have to offer an offline mode before their servers shut down.

“A game that can be taken away the moment a company pulls the plug is not a purchase. It is a rental disguised as a sale.” Ritchie Torres, US representative for New York’s 15th district

Torres said consumers must have the right to own, play and transfer the games they buy.

His office pointed to NBA 2K25. The game sold for $69.99, or $99.99 for the All-Star Edition. 2K Games will pull it from digital storefronts on 30 October. Its online servers will shut down on 31 December, two years after its release.

“I think there should be a simple rule: if you pay for it, you own it.” Ritchie Torres, to Kotaku

In a phone interview with Kotaku, Torres said the bill would restore how people bought and played games in the 1980s, 1990s and 2000s. He also called it an affordability issue.

The bill covers games only, not films or music. Torres said he hoped it would set a precedent for the rest of the digital economy. He did not confirm whether the bill will have cosponsors or Republican support, Kotaku reported. Torres still has to formally introduce it in Congress.

In Pennsylvania, state senator John Kane has introduced the Protect Our Games Act, The Verge reported. When a company retires a game, it would have to offer one of three things. These are an offline mode, an online mode that runs without its servers, or a refund of at least 25%.

Game ownership has drawn more attention since Sony said it plans to phase out physical game discs in 2028, according to The Verge. The Stop Killing Games campaign has called on companies to stop selling games that become unplayable when online support ends.

#280. Apple poaches longtime Meta executive to lead global litigation

Bloomberg reports that Apple has hired Scott Tucker, who spent nearly six years as Meta’s vice president and deputy general counsel for global litigation. Here are the details.

Earlier this year, Meta’s former chief legal officer Jennifer Newstead joined Apple as its new general counsel, replacing longtime executive Kate Adams.

Newstead’s responsibilities eventually expanded to include government affairs following the retirement of Lisa Jackson, who had previously overseen the division.

The changes brought Apple’s legal and government affairs teams under a single executive, with former CEO Tim Cook, now Apple’s executive chairman, also remaining directly involved in managing the company’s government relations.

As part of the reorganization, Apple also hired former American Airlines executive Nate Gatten as its new vice president of government affairs.

Now, Bloomberg reports that Newstead is bringing in a former colleague from Meta, Scott Tucker, who joined Mark Zuckerberg’s company in 2021 and previously held a senior legal position at Morgan Stanley.

The company has hired Scott Tucker, a longtime deputy general counsel and litigation chief at Meta, according to people with knowledge of the matter.

Tucker is becoming Apple’s vice president of global litigation and financial services, a newly created position overseeing commercial and patent litigation worldwide, said the people, who asked not to be named because the move isn’t public. He’ll also manage legal matters involving the company’s financial offerings.

The report adds that as a result of Tucker joining the company, Heather Grenier, Apple’s vice president of commercial and competition litigation, will now report to him rather than directly to Newstead. Bloomberg notes, however, that Grenier will retain her position on Newstead’s legal leadership team.

Finally, Bloomberg says Apple is also expanding the responsibilities of longtime legal executive Kyle Andeer, who will now oversee matters involving “international legal matters and functions involving online child safety, cybersecurity and law enforcement.”

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. The CRKD Nitro Deck (in the Renegade Raider Fortnite Edition) is down to $34.99 on Woot, a noticeable drop from its usual $79.99 and lower than its current price on Amazon. Price trackers also suggest this is the lowest it has gone so far. Shipping is free for Prime members and costs $6 for everyone else, with the deal expected to last about a week unless it sells out earlier. Keep in mind that Woot doesn't ship to Alaska, Hawaii, or P.O. Box addresses.

At its core, the Nitro Deck is trying to solve one of the Nintendo Switch’s most persistent problems: Joy-Con stick drift. But it isn't a traditional controller—it's a full shell that your Nintendo Switch slides into and locks in with a simple latch system that feels secure without being annoying to use. Once it's in place, it feels more like holding a proper controller with a screen attached—the grips are thicker and shaped more like what you would find on a standard console controller, so your hands have something to rest on instead of flattening out against the Joy-Cons. The sticks are full-sized, the triggers have more travel, and there are four back buttons you can map if you like customizing controls.

You still get motion controls and rumble, and there is also a USB-C passthrough for charging or video output. The right stick sits a bit too far out, so using it for camera control or aiming can feel cramped and slightly awkward. It is manageable for short bursts, but it can get uncomfortable over time. The kickstand is also limited—it works, but you don't get much flexibility in how you prop the system up. And because everything is built into one shell, you lose the option to detach the controllers entirely, which is part of what makes the Switch unique in the first place. And while the added bulk improves grip, it makes the system less portable. Still, if you mostly play in handheld mode and want something sturdier with drift-resistant sticks, the Nitro Deck feels great, especially at this discounted price.
