#282. First Utility-Scale Enhanced Geothermal Plant Goes Live

Fervo Energy begins selling electricity in Utah

Fervo Energy has turned on a 33-megawatt unit of its geothermal power plant in Utah. It synchronized to the grid on 24 September and began commercial operation six days later.

This article was originally published by Canary Media.

The geothermal startup Fervo Energy is now selling power to the grid from its Cape Station project in Utah—marking the first time a utility-scale, next-generation geothermal facility has achieved such a feat worldwide.

The Houston-based firm turned on an initial 33-megawatt unit late last week and has been testing and ramping up output since. On Thursday, Fervo will officially begin commercial operations, supplying carbon-free electricity to Shell Energy, a retail power provider in California.

Cape Station, a $2 billion project that will eventually be 500 MW, is unique among the world’s commercial geothermal plants. While other facilities draw on naturally occurring hot water and steam, Fervo has engineered its own geothermal resource deep underground. The startup uses drilling techniques from the oil and gas industry to create reservoirs in hot, dry rocks that generate steam to produce electricity.

“Traditional geothermal would have never been done in southern Utah,” says Dawn Owens, Fervo’s senior vice president and head of development and commercial markets.

With the first unit online, Fervo says it is working to commission two more 33-MW power blocks by 1 January, 2027. The project’s remaining 400 MW—which is supported by a new agreement with Google—is under construction and slated to come online in 2028.

Fervo already operates a 3.5-MW commercial pilot plant in Nevada, which went online in late 2023. Owens says the pilot, called Project Red, was important for demonstrating the technology itself. But firing up Cape Station proves that Fervo’s approach can achieve utility scale and export power to wider markets.

“This is massive for both Fervo and the geothermal industry at large,” she says.

Fervo, which went public in May, is leading the fast-growing movement to develop clean, always-on geothermal power to meet soaring demand from data centers and balance growing supplies of intermittent solar and wind energy. Next-generation geothermal firms have raised billions of dollars in private capital in recent years to develop and deploy technologies that can harness energy in harsh, deep environments.

Drilling continues at Fervo Energy’s Cape Station geothermal plant in Beaver County, Utah, where the company plans to ramp up production to 500 MW. Fervo Energy

Today, geothermal represents just 0.4 percent of total U.S. electricity generation every year. Expanding geothermal’s share of the mix will require not just building more projects like Cape Station but also tackling high upfront drilling costs and other economic and regulatory barriers—all while working to limit potential impacts on communities and the environment, experts say.

“Fervo’s first power achievement shows investors the size and scale of the opportunity to fuel many more such milestones across developers and sites in the future,” says Mitchell Smith, who serves as grid lead for the Mountain West Geothermal Consortium. The bipartisan initiative is calling for increased public and private financing “to help bring more projects online responsibly and at the speed of demand,” he added.

Fervo has declined to disclose the terms of its power purchase agreements for in-progress and future development, which together represent about 1,000 MW, or enough to power roughly 1 million U.S. homes every year. Phase 1 of Cape Station is set to deliver power at $7,000 per kilowatt, while Phase 2 should come at $5,500 per kilowatt, the company previously told Canary Media. (By comparison, the average cost to build a natural gas–fired power plant was $2,157 per kilowatt in 2025.)

Along with slashing drilling costs, enhanced geothermal projects could improve their economics by delivering power when it’s most valuable to utilities, according to researchers. While geothermal plants traditionally provide around-the-clock, baseload power, next-generation facilities might operate flexibly during certain periods—like in the evening, when solar output declines—to reduce overall grid costs. Geothermal plants could also operate “behind the meter” to directly power data centers so that the costs of adding new electricity capacity aren’t passed on to utility customers, Owens says.

“We’ve been saying all along that our technology makes geothermal more scalable and affordable in more places,” she says. On Cape Station’s powering-up, she adds, “That’s just something no next-generation geothermal company has ever been able to do before.”

Maria Gallucci is a clean-energy reporter with Canary Media.

#283. Elon Musk Is Almost Single-Handedly Funding the Republican Midterms Push

Elon Musk has quietly financed a major canvassing operation to help Republican candidates in the midterm elections that rivals his effort in the 2024 presidential election, according to federal filings posted Thursday night. To monitor the trillionaire’s overall influence on November’s elections, WIRED created a live-updating tracker that pulls federal filings daily.

The Musk-aligned America PAC has spent $76.7 million in the third quarter of 2026, $35.8 million of which has been spent on a field operation to drive turnout among President Donald Trump's core base across all seven Senate battleground states and a number of House races, the filings show.

That compares with the roughly $45 million America PAC had spent on putting together a field operation at the same point in the 2024 cycle, when the super PAC effectively ran the vast majority of canvassing for Trump's presidential campaign.

In short, Musk has assembled a presidential-level field operation this midterm cycle, underscoring the extent to which he has taken over the get-out-the-vote effort for the party and created something of a shadow Republican National Committee. With three weeks until Election Day, the total contributions are only set to rise even higher.

Canvassing has been America PAC’s largest expense, ahead of the $23.7 million it spent on a combination of digital ads mostly attacking Democrats, campaign literature, and phone bank efforts.

But in an effort to save Republicans' Senate majority, Musk also gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC supporting the GOP's candidates in that chamber. The same amount appears to have been funneled into Texas PAC, which was registered with the FEC in August 2026 and is backing embattled Republican candidate and Texas attorney general Ken Paxton.

Musk has been particularly focused on the Senate race in Texas this midterm cycle, where he has extensive personal and business interests. Musk lives near Austin and his businesses SpaceX and Tesla are based in the state. Musk accounted for nearly 60 percent of the $273 million that the Senate Leadership Fund raised for Texas PAC.

The stunning war chest that Musk has unleashed into all seven battleground Senate races and, to a lesser degree, a number of competitive House races, makes him the largest known donor in the midterms among both Republicans and Democrats.

Since its inception, America PAC has relied primarily on outside firms to conduct paid canvassing, in which people are hired to knock on the doors of likely Trump or Republican voters to remind them to register to vote and vote early.

The super PAC has used mostly the same contractors as in the 2024 cycle, the filings show. The biggest canvassing contract went to Blitz Canvassing, a subsidiary of the political affairs firm GP3 Partners, which helped stand up America PAC.

The other vendors listed in America PAC’s filings were the firms Patriot Grassroots LLC, The Synapse Group, In Field Strategies, Echo Canyon Group, Threshold Strategies, and GEG Strategies LLC. All but the last two also worked for America PAC in 2024.

Going into the final stretch of campaigning, America PAC has more than $12 million remaining, though Musk, the richest man in the world, may contribute more to his PAC as required.

America PAC has spent in 40 races in 17 states since July. The Texas Senate race drew the largest share, in which Musk’s team has spent $15.3 million attacking Democrat James Talarico and $3.5 million supporting Paxton.

The super PAC has also spent about $5.3 million attacking Democrat Sherrod Brown in Ohio’s Senate race against Republican Jon Husted and $3.5 million attacking Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who is running against Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan, according to the WIRED tracker.

#286. Apple’s new App Store rules crack down on AI nudification and ‘bait-and-switch’ apps

Apple updated its App Review Guidelines today with a series of changes meant to strengthen protections against harmful content and deceptive app review practices. Here are the details.

Over the past year alone, there has been no shortage of reports and controversies involving apps that skirt Apple’s App Review Guidelines and expose users, including minors, to harmful or inappropriate content.

In January, the Tech Transparency Project (TTP) identified dozens of AI-powered “nudify” apps on the App Store.

The group published a follow-up investigation in April, revealing that Apple’s App Store search suggestions and advertisements were also directing users to such apps. In July, San Francisco officials ordered Apple to remove eight apps capable of generating nonconsensual intimate imagery.

Also in July, a 9to5Mac investigation uncovered dozens of apps disguising gambling platforms as simple games and utilities to evade App Store review, many of which were available to children.

These apps behaved as advertised when accessed from outside Brazil, but revealed hidden betting platforms when opened from Brazilian IP addresses.

And then there was the Grok controversy, which saw Elon Musk’s AI chatbot used to generate nonconsensual sexualized images of women and minors, prompting lawmakers and advocacy groups to call on Apple to remove X and Grok from the App Store. Apple later confirmed that it had privately warned xAI that Grok could be removed unless the company addressed the issue.

Today, Apple updated its App Review Guidelines in an attempt to address problems such as these.

Under Section 1.2, which covers user-generated content, the guidelines now read (changes in bold):

Apps that enable users to create, generate, upload, share, or otherwise contribute content present particular challenges, including intellectual property infringement, nonconsensual intimate imagery, and anonymous bullying.

Apple’s new terms add that “Developers who fail to implement appropriate safeguards or fail to remediate identified violations after notice may be considered in violation of the Developer Code of Conduct.”

In another particularly important change, Apple strengthened its rules against so-called ‘bait-and-switch’ apps, which “misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as “nudification” — after approval,” as the company puts it.

Don’t include any hidden, dormant, or undocumented features in your app; your app’s functionality should be clear to end users and App Review. Attempting to hide undocumented features in your app binary, such as through code obfuscation or other methods, is grounds for removal of your app from the App Store and termination of your developer account.

While the prohibition on hidden functionality was already present in Section 2.3.1, Apple has now made the rule more explicit, specifically calling out code obfuscation and emphasizing that violations can lead to an app’s removal and the termination of the developer’s account.

Finally, under Section 5 (Legal), Apple also strengthened its language around apps that facilitate human trafficking or the exploitation of children, explicitly stating that they “will be removed from the App Store and blocked from alternative distribution.”

#288. Maybe Chatbots Shouldn’t Get to Say ‘I’ or ‘Me’

During four decades of studying the effects of interaction with computers, Sherry Turkle has developed a reputation as a careful if critical social scientist who approaches her work with academic rigor and distance.

Her new book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines, breaks this mold. It is a polemic warning that we have reached a state of emergency where our humanity is at risk from overreliance on soulless machines who pose as our tutors, mentors, friends, colleagues, and lovers. Turkle is aiming for the high bar of books —Silent Spring, The Jungle, Unsafe at Any Speed—that awaken the public to impending crises.

Essentially, this diminutive MIT professor is taking on a multitrillion-dollar industry backed by a government eager to accelerate AI into every corner of our personal and professional lives.

STEVEN LEVY: Your previous books reported results of your research as a social scientist, often leading to troubling conclusions about how people, especially children, interact with computers. But this book reads like you’re breaking the glass and pulling the fire alarm. Why the shift?

SHERRY TURKLE: Like I do with all my books, I went in curious. But after 10 or so interviews, conducted during the pandemic, neutral-curious was no longer my state of mind. This was terrible! Here are these people during the pandemic, their families are suffering, reaching out to them, and they're talking to me about how they really want to just hang with their chatbot. When I was able to interview people face to face, I was not happy. People don't want to do anything in politics because they just want to live in chatbot-land. So the arc of the book ended up as—reality needs you. It couldn't be a worse time to give up on reality.

You write that social media set us up for this.

Social media softened us up by getting us used to the idea that if you're feeling sad or blue, open up your computer. Then it made you mad and kept you with your own kind. But now we have this new technology that has no reason to be first-person.

Do you think that we should ban chatbots from using the first person?

Yes! After a career of having credibility as not being Luddite-crazy, I'm not in the mood to give all that away and say all chatbots are toxic all the time. But this is very dangerous, a slippery slope. This is being used to basically say we don't need to pay for psychotherapy, we can use chatbots. In every serious interview I do, people invoke this myth about practice—that you use chatbots to practice for talking to your boss, your lover, your teacher. But when you’re bathing in the warm soup of total acceptance [from LLMs], talking to chatbots becomes the endgame.

You also have a problem with reliance on chatbots in the workplace, and a particular loathing for the term “human in the loop.”

When they use that term, it means the human has been taken out of the productive process and is there to do some sort of cleanup work, to catch the hallucinations or things the AI doesn’t see. That doesn't work, because employers only have a couple of humans in the loop. Those people basically can't change anything. They are there partly to make it sound good when they're litigated, and partly to give people a false sense that the process hasn't been delegated to an AI. But it has been delegated to an AI.

Maybe powerful chatbots are a new form of interaction that isn’t necessarily worse than human conversation, but different, as people report feeling encouraged and empowered by the positive feedback they provide.

An AI won't ever replace human conversation. It’s really not afraid of death, it’s not afraid of illness, it's not afraid of pain, it doesn't love its children, and it doesn't care if you kill yourself or make dinner. So if we raise our kids with it, or have our most intimate conversations with it, we're going to lose contact.

Still, a lot of people have nobody to talk to. They feel that talking to chatbots helps them.

If there's a crisis of loneliness, it's because we're abandoning each other. Give me one data center, and I will turn it into resources for the elderly.

Studies show that most people are skeptical about AI, and there has been considerable pushback. Yet hundreds of millions of people use them. Even people who push back against data centers are using chatbots.

The goal of this book is to expand the terms of the pushback to include this more intimate connection.

Do you really feel that our growing intimacy with AI can be stopped?

I have more hope now than I did six months ago, because of all of this talk about extinction events and Hugging Face and getting into the Australian civil service by mistake. I feel that people will be willing to look at the intimate as well as the non-intimate costs.

Humanoid robots have begun to show real capability in ball sports, but preserving a professional athlete’s motion style while maintaining reliable task performance is still an unresolved problem. This guide examines an adaptive motion planning and tracking framework that learns tennis serving and rally styles directly from broadcast video and motion-capture data. A hierarchical design separates a planner, which generates stylistic kinematic motion, from a tracker, which executes that motion with minimal interference. Because tracking performance inevitably degrades when a policy trained in simulation moves to physical hardware, the framework trains its tracker on randomized execution speeds and conditions its planner on a learned motion-speed representation, reducing the compounding errors introduced by autoregressive planning and noisy perception. The paper documents real-world validation on a research humanoid platform and transfer to a full-size humanoid robot, including serving in an uncontrolled environment without motion capture, and closes with practical, transferable lessons for engineers building future humanoid ball-sports systems.

#292. The Adventure-Ready Samsung Galaxy Watch Is Over $175 Off Right Now

Samsung announced the Galaxy Watch Ultra in the summer of 2024, and then refreshed it in August of 2025 with double the storage and new color options. The Galaxy Watch Ultra emphasizes outdoor and exercise features, putting it in competition with the Apple Watch Ultra as a premium fitness watch at a premium price. Ever since the Galaxy Watch Ultra2 came out this year, the 2025 Galaxy Watch Ultra has been dropping in price, currently reaching a new low price of $471.78 according to price-checking tools, over $175 off the original $649.99 price tag. And if the extra storage isn't a big deal to you, you can get the 2024 version for $399.99 (originally $649.99).

The Galaxy Watch Ultra excels over other watches in one key aspect: its outdoorsy features. If you're an avid hiker or an athlete who spends long hours outdoors, this is a worthwhile choice. Like any good rugged watch, this one is tough, made out of Grade 4 titanium, and has an IP68 water- and dust-resistant rating. You can also take it up high altitudes (up to 9,000 meters) and it can withstand up to 10ATM of pressure (about 330 feet underwater). You also get a built-in siren in case of emergencies. The screen is a 1.47-inch Super AMOLED display, brighter than previous Samsung AMOLED smartwatches. The only downside is that it comes in just one size—47mm.

The watch runs WearOS from Samsung and comes with 2GB of RAM and 64GB of storage. The 590mAh battery is one of the best for its price point, making it perfect for prolonged outdoor use. If you don't use any power-saving modes, it'll last 60 hours, but it can go up to 100 hours if you're conservative.

One of the new features this watch brings is AI-based health metrics and advanced sleep tracking, which you can read more about in PCMag's "excellent" review. If you're looking for a more budget-friendly (and smaller) option for more general use, the Samsung Galaxy Watch 7 at $220 (originally $329.99) is a great option.

#293. Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra Review: The First Real AI PC

A new fleet of Windows laptops has arrived, and the Surface Laptop Ultra is its flagship vessel. Ever since it was announced, it's been one of my anticipated laptops of the year. It not only promises to be a beefed-up evolution of the Surface Laptop (a laptop I already really liked), but also debuts a brand-new piece of silicon: the Nvidia RTX Spark N1X "superchip."

The goal is a single laptop that can handle on-device AI, gaming, content creation, and nearly anything else you might throw at it. If that sounds a bit like a MacBook Pro, you're on the right track. But unlike previous attempts to dethrone Apple, the Surface Laptop Ultra is trading blows with the very best. I just wish it had the battery life to truly keep up with the MacBook Pro.

This isn't Microsoft's first foray into a more powerful laptop. The company first tried that in 2021 with the Surface Laptop Studio. At the time, it was the company's answer to the MacBook Pro: a laptop-tablet hybrid oriented toward the growing class of content creators and media professionals. It even came with a discrete graphics card (though not a particularly good one).

The Surface Laptop Ultra rejects the Studio's form-factor experimentation and opts for a more straightforward but polished approach. It's a powerful clamshell laptop that's designed for people who need the extra performance—whether for gaming, content creation, or on-device AI workflows. The ideal demographic, I suppose, is someone who does some of all of that.

At 4.4 pounds, the Surface Laptop Ultra is lighter than the 16-inch MacBook Pro but slightly thicker. It's actually the thickest of all the new N1X laptops, with HP's OmniBook Ultra being the thinnest. The Surface Laptop Ultra appears thinner than it actually is, though, thanks to the inventive way it hides its side vents—so discreet that it's hard to photograph them. The design has just enough small touches like that to make it stand out. There's also a soft dip into the keyboard well, with a unique look that matches the curved lip of the underside vents. I appreciate the modern vibe of the rounded screen corners, though some apps don't account for them well and nearly cut off elements of the Title Bar. One other minor annoyance is that there's no lip for your finger when the device is closed. You can slide your fingernail in between, but in most cases, you'll need two hands to open it.

But once opened, the Surface Laptop Ultra gets mostly compliments from me. The keyboard is fantastic, as is the extra-large touchpad with haptic feedback. I still dislike the power button placement (why not put it in the top right like every other laptop, as an obvious button, instead of between keys?), and the keycaps could be a bit larger. But overall, I was very happy and comfortable typing and swiping on the laptop.

I was also very pleased with the audio. The aforementioned underside vents also hide the four speakers, which sound fabulous. I was really impressed by how loud, rich, and full these sound, perhaps only second to the 16-inch MacBook Pro (and 15-inch MacBook Air). There's even a hint of bass!

Next to those speakers are lots of useful ports. You have the usual for a laptop of this type, including HDMI, USB-A, a headphone jack, an SD card slot, and three USB4 Type-C ports. The system can support up to three 4K external monitors or a single 5K display. Regardless of the resolution, you're maxed out at a 120 Hz refresh rate. This is slightly behind the latest MacBook Pro, which can support two 5K displays at a 120 Hz refresh rate. But overall, I'm really happy with this mix of connectivity—in fact, it just might be the most well-rounded offering I can imagine.

The Surface Laptop Ultra has a trick up its sleeve involving magnets. The Surface Laptop has long used the Surface Connect, a proprietary magnetic power port that can also plug into Microsoft's Surface Dock. The Surface Laptop Ultra now uses USB-C, and how Microsoft engineered it to make it magnetic is impressive. Disappointingly, only the USB-C port on the right side has this magnetic feature, but all USB-C ports deliver power. You've always been able to buy third-party add-ons that do something similar, but it's a really neat bit of innovation.

What I appreciate most about all the Surface Laptop designs is the 3:2 aspect ratio display. I often find that more vertical space comes in handy, especially if you frequently work with documents, spreadsheets, and websites. Combined with the smaller 15-inch touchscreen (compared to the typical 16-incher), this makes for a more compact laptop to carry. At a full inch narrower than the 16-inch MacBook Pro, it fits in a laptop bag a bit more easily.

The screen is extremely sharp, with a pixel density of 257 pixels per inch, just barely exceeding the 16-inch MacBook Pro. Like the MacBook Pro, the Surface Laptop Ultra's display uses Mini-LED backlighting. OLED is far more commonly used in Windows laptops, though, which make up for their lack of brightness with extreme contrast and stronger color performance. But here, the Surface Laptop Ultra clearly has its targets on the MacBook Pro. That may change soon with the rumored launch of the OLED MacBook Pro.

With 1,344 dimming zones, it's the brightest laptop screen ever made. Using my colorimeter, I measured 987 nits of brightness in SDR and 1,945 nits in HDR in a 9 percent window. The result is pretty stunning HDR performance. Games and movies look spectacular on this screen, even without the perfect black levels OLED would provide. Add in the 120-Hz refresh rate, and you have a beautiful display for gaming—especially in more visually immersive, single-player games.

But the screen is highly reflective. This was also true of the standard Surface Laptop, but it's noticeably more reflective than a MacBook. Even with the brightness fully maxed, I still found myself staring at my reflection when viewing websites with dark backgrounds—and that's despite this being unquestionably the brightest screen ever put in a laptop. The reflections are really my only complaint. Otherwise, it's one of my favorite displays I've tested.

The 1080p webcam isn't particularly impressive. It struggles in low light, and the image is pretty noisy. The MacBook Pro webcam has better image processing, brightening faces without overexposing.

The Nvidia N1X is a first-of-its-kind chip in Windows laptops. Qualcomm broke open the floodgates in 2024 with its Snapdragon X chips, of which the Surface Laptop was an early adopter. These were primarily an answer to the MacBook Air, and later to what would become the MacBook Neo. But Qualcomm's chips never scaled up to the performance needed to match something like the M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro. That's where the Nvidia N1X steps in.

Both the Snapdragon X and N1X use a System on a Chip (SoC) design, which packages the CPU, GPU, and memory together. It's the same design Apple Silicon chips use, and—importantly—it lets both the CPU and GPU access local memory. This is crucial for enabling the much faster local AI processing, which needs to feed that GPU as much memory as possible. The N1X comes in two configurations: an 18-core system (5,120 GPU cores) and a 20-core system (6,144 GPU cores). Think of these like Apple's M5 Pro and M5 Max, with the main differences being GPU performance and configuration options. For example, if you want 128 GB of memory to hammer home that AI performance, you have to go with the 20-core N1X. In fact, the 18-core model is limited to just 24 GB or 32 GB of RAM (and from what I've seen so far, the Surface Laptop Ultra is the only N1X laptop to be sold with only 24 GB of memory).

I tested the 32 GB model, paired with the higher-end 20-core CPU. In terms of core count, the graphics card in this configuration of the N1X sits right in between the mobile RTX 5070 Ti and RTX 5080. That sounds promising on a laptop this thin, but the core count alone doesn't mean you should expect it to perform at the same level in games. The N1X is capped at 80 watts, which puts a serious limit on in-game frame rates. Gaming as a whole, however, is also handicapped by the nature of this being an Arm-based system. In nearly every game you play, the Surface Laptop Ultra will need to rely on app emulation, which does reduce performance. As Nvidia points out, though, emulation has its biggest impact on the CPU. So, even if applications like games aren't optimized for Arm, they should still run OK. That's exactly what I experienced with the handful of games I tried. You'll need to play most games at medium settings or lower to get decent frame rates, and usually you'll want to play at 1920 x 1200 resolution.

Despite scoring lower than the M5 Max MacBook Pro in 3DMark tests, the Surface Laptop Ultra delivers up to 20 percent faster frame rates in games like Cyberpunk 2077. That's one of the few titles where I could directly compare the two systems. I also tested games like 007: First Light, Marvel Rivals, and Black Myth: Wukong. Seeing so many popular titles run on an Arm system is exciting, and Nvidia is clearly investing heavily in the future of gaming on Arm. However, a list of fairly high-profile multiplayer games aren't compatible yet due to anti-cheat systems, including PUBG, Valorant, and League of Legends. Those are some heavy hitters to be missing at launch, but Nvidia says support is coming. I did run into some glitches, though, such as in 007: First Light, where I couldn't adjust the display resolution in the options menu. That's frustrating as the game otherwise plays well on the system.

Regardless, these are the most powerful integrated graphics we've seen in a Windows laptop, leaving Intel's Panther Lake X9 in the dust. But if you want the best bang-for-your-buck gaming performance, you're much better off buying a dedicated gaming laptop. The RTX 5060 in a Lenovo LOQ 15, for example, can draw up to 115 watts and deliver up to 22 percent better performance in games like Cyberpunk 2077 and Marvel Rivals. It's also around a thousand dollars cheaper. If gaming were the main point of the Surface Laptop Ultra, that would feel like a disappointment.

But AI performance is the real reason this laptop (and the N1X as a whole) exists, and that's where it shines most. I ran it through Procyon's latest AI benchmarks, which include text generation, image generation, and computer vision. The Surface Laptop Ultra is around 25 percent faster than the Dell XPS 14 at generating text in these lighter models, which only range from 3.5-billion parameters up to 12-billion. Nice to see, but not exactly a dramatic leap ahead. Meanwhile, the Razer Blade 16 with an RTX 5090 (and 32 GB of RAM) posts nearly twice the scores in these tests. That's a more expensive laptop, of course, but it also doesn't go around claiming to be designed for AI.

Clearly, these entry-level configurations of the Surface Laptop Ultra are more for AI dabblers than true enthusiasts. Adding more memory doesn't necessarily solve that problem. I'm also testing a 128-GB version of the HP OmniBook Ultra right now (with the same N1X chip), and I was hoping to see it run some larger models. And while you can certainly load up a 70-billion parameter model in LM Studio, performance on it is very slow. Without more raw GPU compute on hand to speed things up, these more impactful models feel too slow to use daily work. They can, however, still be used in situations that require more complex reasoning, such as for coding, when it's worth waiting for the actual correct answer.

Running local AI models as a computing task that lots of people will want to do is still a question mark for me. As long as free cloud-based models are faster and more useful, I have a hard time seeing people spend extra cash on a computer just to run a model locally. This will undoubtedly change as models improve, but right now, it'll have a limited appeal in that regard. The real benefit might be in agentic AI that gives you access to your local files on your computer and lets you do things that aren't possible in a basic ChatGPT session. I ran a very basic test in LM Studio Bionic, asking it to analyze a folder of local text files and generate a comprehensive summary using Gemma 4 E4B, a 4.5-billion-parameter model. It took 8 minutes to process the request and another 2 minutes to deliver the 853-word response. There's enough performance here to explore and experiment with on-device AI—but the speed may get frustrating. I say all that less to criticize the Surface Laptop Ultra and more just to set expectations on what laptops can do right now.

If the N1X has one serious weakness, it's the CPU. The N1X is 20 to 24 percent slower in CPU benchmarks, in both single-core and multi-core performance tests. Switching from Balanced to Performance Mode in the Windows Settings, however, makes a big difference. It's a 20 percent increase in single-core performance when enabled, a bigger delta than on other laptops. It's fast enough not to be a major bottleneck, but I'd expect to see improvement in future generations of the N1X chip.

The Surface Laptop Ultra is not the only RTX Spark laptop launching today. Many of them major Windows laptop manufacturers has one, and they all lean into high-end hardware, including nearly every premium feature possible. I'm still testing some of these models, including the closest competitor, the Lenovo Pro 9n. It has a 15-inch screen, the same N1X chip, and 32 GB of RAM. From what I can tell so far, these laptops perform fairly similarly, within a few percentage points.

But against something like the Razer Blade 16, the Surface Laptop Ultra faces a closer rival. You can buy the RTX 5070 model of the Blade 16 with 32 GB of RAM and a terabyte of storage for $2,999—a similar configuration and price to the Surface Laptop Ultra. They are a similar size and are both well-built. The Surface Laptop Ultra has a sharper and brighter screen, but the Blade 16 has a faster refresh rate. Higher-end configurations of the Razer Blade 16 with the Intel Core Ultra 9 386H even match the Surface Laptop Ultra's battery life, which lasted only 12 hours in a local video playback test. Both devices are what I'd call “do-it-all” laptops. I think the Surface Laptop Ultra is the better overall laptop, largely because of its better keyboard and touchpad. It also has the option to configure it with up to 128 GB of memory, whereas the Blade 16 maxes out at 64 GB. But if you'll spend more time gaming than running local models, the Surface Laptop Ultra (and any of the N1X devices) is the wrong choice.

The Surface Laptop Ultra is also priced nearly the same as the 16-inch MacBook Pro. For $2,999, you get 24 GB of RAM and a terabyte of storage. Both offer a lower-tier performance option, either the M5 Pro or the 18-core N1X. The Surface Laptop Ultra lets you configure the system with 128 GB of memory with only a terabyte of storage, whereas the MacBook Pro forces you into 2 TB. The MacBook Pro still has the edge in polish, whether that's better speakers and a webcam, a less reflective screen, or more comprehensive app support. The major disadvantage, however, is battery life. The MacBook Pro offers a full nine or ten more hours of battery life than the Surface Laptop Ultra. No getting around that. The MacBook Pro also tends to stay a bit quieter. That's part of the magic sauce of what makes the MacBook Pro feel special. The problem has never been that we don't have powerful-enough laptops. The difficulty is in not having to make compromises to achieve that performance, and battery life has always been the most challenging to overcome. Unfortunately, the Surface Laptop Ultra (and the other N1X laptops for that matter) still don't quite make the cut.

And yet, I'm drawn to the brighter screen and taller aspect ratio of the Surface Laptop Ultra, as well as its 15-inch size. I've always found the 16-inch MacBook Pro to be a bit unwieldy. We may be just weeks away from seeing what Apple has in store for a lighter MacBook Pro with a touchscreen. But for now, if you want to dabble in gaming, content creation, and AI workflows, it's probably the best laptop you can buy that isn't a MacBook Pro. And even more importantly, I foresee it starting a new era in Windows laptops that will grown into something truly special in the not-so-distant future.

#296. Master AI Chip Principles With New IEEE Design Program

The AI processor architecture courses use an avatar learning method

Angelo Athens is an instructional design manager for IEEE Educational Activities.

Today’s engineers face an unprecedented acceleration in AI hardware complexity, as explained in the recent research article “Revisiting Edge AI: Opportunities and Challenges.” The article examines the rapid growth of edge AI and the challenges it creates, including resource constraints, model architecture limitations, and network demands across edge-AI deployments.

The acceleration is driven by a fundamental shift in how modern AI models are built and scaled. As the models have become much larger and more complex, they are computationally more demanding because they contain more parameters and require more calculations.

To meet the demands of scaling deep neural networks, the industry is increasingly developing AI chips that are designed for specific tasks.

One major reason is that moving data between memory and the processor has become a major limitation on AI performance.

The movement to confront the hardware bottleneck—the AI memory wall—has altered the trajectory of semiconductor innovation, shifting architectural priorities toward domain-specific accelerator platforms.

No longer can engineers evaluate systems statically; they must master joint hardware design and network-algorithm co-optimization to navigate the critical trade‑offs between throughput, latency, and operational efficiency.

The challenges are addressed in the new AI Processor Architecture, Design Principles, and Performance program, developed by IEEE Educational Activities with support from the IEEE Computer Society.

The five-course program provides a structured exploration of AI processor technologies, from fundamental design principles to advanced architectures and real-world deployment.

The program addresses the needs of professionals across the AI hardware ecosystem, including hardware architects, chip designers, embedded systems developers, data‑center hardware engineers, and innovators exploring next‑generation processor ecosystems.

It is also valuable for those transitioning into AI chip design or seeking to understand the architectural forces shaping modern machine learning acceleration. For many, it provides the bridge between theoretical knowledge and the collaborative, cross‑disciplinary reasoning required in engineering environments.

The program is designed to explore how modern AI processors are conceived, structured, and optimized. The architectural layers that define contemporary AI hardware will be covered, including compute units, memory hierarchies, dataflows, and the performance characteristics that emerge from design decisions. The curriculum bridges theory and application, enabling participants to interpret architectural foundations, analyze trade‑offs, and understand how hardware structures shape computational efficiency across diverse environments.

By the end of the courses, learners will be able to evaluate processor behavior with the analytical precision expected of professionals working at the frontier of AI hardware design.

The program also uses a dialogue‑driven learning approach. Learners view conversations between AI-generated avatars that engage in scenario‑based dialogues. The avatars represent engineers tackling the same problems from various perspectives based on their different roles. The simulated storytelling and dialogues make advanced engineering concepts approachable without sacrificing depth or interactivity, because the user is occasionally challenged to decide the correct answer that leads to the best course of action.

A hardware engineer might push back against a systems engineer’s demands, for example, revealing the friction between physical constraints and algorithmic ambition. A computational validation specialist might interrogate a chip performance engineer’s optimism, exposing the gap between theoretical throughput and real‑world behavior. A heterogeneous systems architect could debate a multiprocessor coordination specialist about synchronization overheads, while a standards development engineer discusses regulatory implications with a technology strategy and compliance architect.

In the final course, an IoT systems architect and an embedded AI optimization engineer dissect the realities of deploying AI in constrained environments.

By the end of the course, learners will be able to evaluate processor behavior with the analytical precision expected of professionals working at the frontier of AI hardware design.

The avatar-driven learning environment creates a psychologically safer environment for learners, who might feel intimidated by traditional expert‑led videos. Research published in 2024 in IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies showed that avatar‑based instruction can increase a learner’s confidence by up to 25 percent and improve retention of complex technical material.

Each course concludes with a module in which the two experts from different disciplines debate, question, and challenge each other’s assumptions.

The cross‑disciplinary conversations can do more than explain concepts; they can model how experts think. They can reveal the negotiations behind architectural choices, the competing priorities that shape system design, and the analytical rigor required to balance performance, efficiency, scalability, and compliance.

Learners observe engineering discourse, gaining insight into the reasoning patterns that drive innovation in AI processor development.

The program goes further by interrupting the dialogue at key moments and inviting the learner to step in. Instead of passively absorbing information, the learner decides how to resolve a trade‑off, predict the outcome of a design choice, or select the most defensible engineering path. The experience can feel less like a course and more like an apprenticeship inside an engineering team.

By merging rigorous technical content with an innovative, dialogue‑driven delivery model, the program sets a standard for teaching advanced engineering. It captures the complexity of real‑world problem‑solving, humanizes the learning experience, and challenges participants to think like the engineers who are defining the future of AI hardware. It is not simply a new course; it is a new way of learning.

For individual access, visit the IEEE Learning Network.

For customized organizational options, contact a content specialist to discuss volume pricing.

Angelo Athens is an instructional design manager for IEEE Educational Activities.

#297. Apple calls iPhone Duo pre-order demand ‘extraordinary’ as shipping dates slip

Apple has issued a short statement following strong initial demand for the iPhone Duo, with shipping estimates already slipping into next year. Here’s what the company said.

As soon as iPhone Duo pre-orders opened today, shipping estimates began slipping from late October into November, then December, and eventually January. In some countries, including Brazil, estimated deliveries have already been pushed into early February.

While there had been reports warning that initial iPhone Duo supplies could be limited, the speed and extent of the shipping delays still caught many by surprise.

1) Apple almost always under promises on shipping and over delivers.

2) Apple makes regular shipments to Apple Stores and carriers so check local stores.

Note: Apple prioritizes AppleStores and doesn't normally have wait lists but carriers do, so get on a waiting list and check back with that Apple Stores. You can always order online, because Apple doesn't charge cards till the order is process.

Apple, meanwhile, is putting a positive spin on the strong initial response. In a statement shared with CNBC, the company described pre-order demand as “nothing short of extraordinary”, and added:

“We are working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers’ hands as quickly as possible, and we will continue accepting orders online.”

With shipping dates slipping well into next year, scalpers on eBay and X are already looking to cash in, with asking prices reaching as high as $10,000.

This has led to criticism of Apple’s handling of pre-orders, with some calling on the company to identify and cancel orders placed by scalpers.

What’s your take on how Apple has handled the iPhone Duo pre-orders so far? Let us know in the comments.

If your phone is showing these signs, don't ignore them

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Whether you missclicked or downloaded the wrong file, malware can infect your Android device or iPhone and you might not have even noticed. There are some signs that are completely obvious, but others are a little more discreet and take some snooping around to suss out.

Here are some warning signs that you might have an unwanted guest on your smartphone.

Advertisements spamming your phone, especially outside of an app, is a dead giveaway. Don’t ignore the problem, even if you’re a fan of Neon Genesis Evangelion who really appreciates seeing “CONGRATULATIONS” spread across their screen.

If your phone is packing a ridiculous number of applications like mine, then you might not notice when a new app creeps into your system. For both the sake of spotting malware and cleaning up your library of unused apps, it's worth taking the time to audit your current apps.

Malware does a lot in the background to wreak havoc on your device, and that takes power. So one of the telltale signs of malware infecting your device is if you experience shorter battery life. Battery life can vary, especially as a phone ages, so I recommend looking up the average battery life for your device to see if there's an obvious discrepancy.

Got a brand new phone and all of a sudden everything slows down to a crawl? Are apps randomly crashing on you? This is another sign that malware may have crept onto your device. This may be more difficult to spot on phones already experiencing slower performance, so keep an eye out for other signs if that’s the case.

Unless you still have a Samsung Galaxy Note 7 hanging around, which you shouldn't, your device should not be scorching your hand. If your smartphone is spamming you with overheating warnings or is straight up crashing, especially in temperate environments, there might be a virus giving your phone a fever (my dad joke for the day).

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Unless you have a limited data plan and are remaining vigilant about your usage, it’s unlikely you’ll notice malware taking up all your data. Unlimited data users who have never checked their data metrics need to be more alert. It doesn’t hurt to check your data usage every once in a while, if not to see what apps you’re maybe spending a little too much time on.

The most embarrassing and frustrating sign of malware is all your friends and family getting hit with spam messages that can potentially affect their devices. You’ll likely hear about this sooner than later, but as someone who doesn’t actually use SMS to contact people, it doesn’t hurt to check your default messaging app. Hopefully your contacts know what you sound like versus a spam bot imitating you, but the sooner you alert people the better.

If you’re still not 100% certain whether or not your device is carrying around malware, there’s a few things you can do.

For iPhone users, navigate to Settings > General > VPN & Device Management to check if any unknown profiles are installed. If you don’t find anything here, go to Settings > Privacy & Security and check on your app permissions. This might be a bit tedious, but you should do a step by step inventory of app permissions and revoke access to apps that you aren't using, and delete ones that you don’t recognize.

For Android users, go to Google Play > tap your profile picture > Play Protect. This will scan your device for any harmful apps. It typically runs automatically, but it doesn’t hurt to do a manual check.

If you don’t find anything going down these routes, Android users can download one of the best Android antivirus software solutions, which can not only help locate malware but also delete it. Unfortunately, iPhone users don’t have access to traditional antivirus software because of how Apple sandboxes each app, but you can download security apps that can detect data breaches.

If you can’t manage to track down the issue, then resetting your device to factory settings may be the next step. In this case, you should set up your smartphone as a new device, as any backups can bring with it the malware that infected the system to begin with. Then reintroduce apps and services one by one to see if the issue continues, and if it happens again, you’ll know where the call inside the house is coming from and you can get rid of it — it could be something as simple as a browser extension.

I highly recommend changing passwords on critical services, like banking apps, using a different device. Monitor your smartphone for a while to see if the issue has been addressed before relogging into any sensitive apps.

#299. Whatever Happened to Daylight Saving Time Going Away?

It will soon be time, once again, for our clocks to “fall back.” Nov. 1 is the date most places in the U.S. quit daylight saving time for 2026 and go back to standard time. We're still on this clock-changing treadmill, despite legislation that was supposed to eliminate it a few years ago, and despite medical professionals warning that these clock changes are bad for our health.

For example, a study out of the Stanford School of Medicine found that switching the time back and forth every year probably contributes to increased rates of stroke and obesity. Permanent daylight saving time would be an improvement on that, and permanent standard time would be even better, health-wise. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine published a position paper a few years ago stating that scientific evidence supports the idea "that the United States should eliminate seasonal time changes in favor of permanent standard time, which aligns best with human circadian biology."

But despite all this, we’ll still have to turn the clocks ahead again in spring. So whatever happened to those bills in Congress aiming to abolish the time changes?

The Sunshine Protection Act was a federal bill that would have made Daylight Saving Time permanent. If enacted, it would have taken effect on Nov. 5, 2023, the date that we would otherwise have changed the clocks. The result would be that our winter mornings would stay dark an hour longer than they currently do, but we’d get an hour more of daylight in the winter evenings.

The bill passed the Senate in March of 2022, but it wasn't taken up by the House of Representatives. In July of 2026, a similar law passed the House of Representatives, and President Trump wrote on Truth Social this month that "Republicans in the Senate have to get moving on what I call the 'No More Changing of Clocks Act.'" The Senate Majority Leader said it doesn't have the support to pass, since it would mean dark mornings for commuters and for children waiting for morning buses.

We operate on two different times throughout the year: "standard time" and "daylight saving time." These even get their own time zones! For example, if a time is marked as "EST," that means eastern standard time, which is different from eastern daylight time.

Standard time is the one we use in winter, and daylight saving time is the one we use in summer. The bill mentioned above would have done away with standard time and kept us on daylight saving time year-round. Meanwhile, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine has taken the position that we should stay on standard time (that is, winter time) year-round, since screwing with our circadian rhythms twice a year has detrimental effects on our health and safety. If they got their way, we would fall back some year and then never spring forward again.

States have their own ideas about what time it should be. Currently, states are not allowed to switch to permanent daylight saving time, but they are allowed to stay on standard time year-round if they prefer. Two states do so: Hawaii and Arizona (minus the parts of Arizona in the Navajo nation).

Nineteen states have passed laws or resolutions that would allow them to switch to permanent daylight saving time if the federal government ever allows them to do so. Those states, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures, are Alabama, Colorado, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Louisiana, Maine, Minnesota, Mississippi, Montana, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming. Three other states have made attempts to join the list: Similar bills made it partway through the Kentucky and Ohio legislatures but were not signed into law. California voters have authorized a law that isn’t yet officially on the books.

Until a federal law passes, those states are stuck with their current time zones. Current federal law, as passed in 1966, allows states to opt out of daylight saving time (as Hawaii and Arizona have) but does not offer a way for states to make daylight saving time permanent or to choose their own dates for changing the clocks. If you’re sick of time changes, you can always move to one of the territories that don’t observe daylight saving, which include the U.S. Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico.

#300. AWOL Vision Aetherion Max RGB Laser UST Projector Review: A Top Buy

It takes a special home theater projector to get me to stick through a movie like Supergirl. Critics panned it for dark themes, and its visually dark tones make it literally tough to see. But when I used the AWOL Vision Aetherion Max to project it onto a 120-inch screen with Dolby Atmos sound blasting from every corner of my basement, the film looked stunning.

The Aetherion Max, with its precise picture-quality settings and sharp 4K clarity, provides an experience rivaling that of a movie theater. Supergirl might suffer from bad CGI and even worse dialog, but the projector's features, like Dark Detail and Enhanced Black Level, brought the film to life, making reds and blues pop with amazing vividness.

Priced at $4,499, this ultrashort throw model sits right next to the wall or projector screen. In some ways, it reminds me of the LG Micro RGB Evo television with highly adjustable picture-quality settings. Ultimately, though, I'm a fan of the Aetherion Max because it projects a breathtakingly colorful image.

Before taking stock of its powerhouse specs, I noticed the Aetherion Max's design. Shaped a bit like a Tesla Cybertruck, the silver projector has sharp edges that lend a modern look. The front of the machine (the side that faces you) has no buttons except a single white line that animates when you power it on—a detail I found to be distracting and then powered off. The other side (which faces the screen) is where you'll find three HDMI 2.1 ports (including one for eARC passthrough audio), a USB-A port for a local storage device, optical and 3.5mm audio-out ports, and a 1 GBps Ethernet port for wired streaming.

AWOL Vision Aetherion Max RGB Laser UST Projector

This model runs on Google TV, and that’s a relief because it meant setup only took a few minutes. Auto-keystoning with manual screen-size options worked just fine. There’s also a QR code you can use to automate keystone correction from your phone, but my room was too dark, and it didn't work for me. (AWOL Vision reps told me it should have worked fine even in a dark room like mine.)

The portable projector weighs 19.3 pounds—notably less than its 23-pound competitor Hisense XR10 Smart Projector (8/10, WIRED Recommends)—and I found it both easy to grip and move around between rooms. For wireless streaming, the Aetherion Max supports Wi-Fi 7, offering nice compatibility and speed. It also runs quite fast thanks to 8 GB of internal RAM and offers 128 GB of internal storage for storing content, though I relied mostly on streaming.

Unlike the highly rated Xgimi Titan Noir Max, the Aetherion Max's iris does not adjust dynamically as you watch content. But similar to the Hisense XR10, you can adjust picture-quality settings to match the room. For example, Dolby Vision Bright works best in a bright room, allowing the iris to let in more light.

For color accuracy, the projector hits 110 percent of the Rec. 2020 spec. That means if you watch a movie that meets that color spec, like Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 or Inside Out, you will see the entire color palette. AWOL Vision also lists the contrast ratio as 6,000:1 and lumens at 3,300 ISO, but—as I've learned from personal experience—those specs are not the final arbiter of picture quality. Many other factors come into play, including the darkness level of a room.

AWOL Vision Aetherion Max RGB Laser UST Projector

The weak spot here is the remote, which is functional if not impressive. I like its large Home button that’s centered and easy to find in the dark without looking. There’s also a button for Google Gemini and convenient shortcuts for apps like Netflix. My main issue is with the volume buttons, placed just above the shortcuts, but small and hard to find. Only the upper half of the remote is backlit, which uselessly doesn't extend to all of the buttons, including volume.

The Aetherion Max's ability to work in a brightly lit room blew me away throughout testing. I watched the movie Mayday on Apple TV+ from start to finish in broad daylight, projecting the image on a wall that measures nearly 16 feet diagonally. I didn't notice any contrast problems and could see nighttime scenes just fine. The slight warping on my wall distorted the image a bit, but that's to be expected of ultrashort throw models.

In my windowless testing room, with a full surround-sound system that even includes height channel speakers in the ceiling, the Aetherion Max performed even better. To test a projector's contrast ratio and brightness, I typically play dark scenes in the movies Awake and The Creator, and I've never seen the scenes look as great as they did when rendered by the Aetherion Max. I didn’t even have to tweak the picture-quality settings (and generally when I test these specs, such is not the case).

Dark scenes in House of the Dragon, which I streamed using the HBO Max app, did require some user intervention, though. A beach scene in the moonlight involving a mysterious dragon would be hard to render even on high-end home cinema projectors, but once I enabled Dark Detail and Enhanced Black Level, I could suddenly see everything clearly, just as the TV show creators intended.

AWOL Vision Aetherion Max RGB Laser UST Projector

Indeed, every time I ran into a slight issue with picture quality, I found a matching setting that solved the problem. In a dark hallway scene during the movie The Batman, gun flashes looked bright red and clear, but some amber tones on Batman looked a shade too dark. Once I switched to Dolby Vision Bright, I could easily make out the grimaces and muscle flexes. Some projectors look a bit out of focus on the edges, but that's not true with the Aetherion Max; in Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu on Disney+, a snowy scene showcased the extreme pixel clarity all the way to the ends of the screen.

AWOL Vision Aetherion Max RGB Laser UST Projector

For games, I tested NBA 2K27 with the new Nvidia GeForce driver on an Alienware Aurora gaming laptop. The jaw-dropping graphics, which use realistic lighting and details, made a convincing case for Anthony Edwards of the Minnesota Timberwolves being in my testing room. When I tried Onimusha: Way of the Sword on PC, I was equally blown away by the crisp graphics. At this larger size, with ultra-clear pixel depth across the entire screen, every samurai slash seemed more realistic. Great for gaming, the projector uses extremely low latency—just 1 millisecond—for no lag, graphical stuttering, or delays, allowing for quick controller responses.

Sound is strong on the projector itself. When I watched the movies Civil War and Unbroken via an Onkyo TX-RZ50 AV receiver, I felt I was in a movie theater. A slight glitch was that the audio cut out when I used height channel speakers for 7.1.2 sound (AWOL Vision is investigating why).

The Aetherion Max also passed demo-reel benchmarks with flying colors—for the most part. While scenes with flowers, white mist over a snowy mountain, water in the deep blue ocean, and two horses in a field looked mesmerizing and realistic, it was tough to make out dark trees on a dark background. The skin-tone test also yielded unimpressive results. I’m not sure why, but two faces looked way too similar in a group shot, and a few other tests showed a lack of tonal variety. Adjusting settings didn’t help. However, this detail didn’t heavily factor into my overall takeaway of the projector, since it's a subtle color benchmark.

The AWOL Vision Aetherion Max is ultimately an amazing projector: a rock star of color accuracy, with crisp pixel clarity across the entire image and superior contrast. While the price is in line with other high-end models, this is one seriously capable home cinema model.

#302. William Gibson and the trademarking of cyberspace

From the first days of the web, people have repeated the story that Autodesk trademarked "cyberspace" and Gibson retaliated by trademarking "Eric Gullichsen".

In 1989, I was working at the Autodesk Research Lab on early virtual reality, a project started after we visited Scott Fisher at NASA Ames. Our nascent system was a 386 with a pair of Matrox graphics cards on the ISA bus, a VPL EyePhone, a Polhemus tracker, and a data glove. It ran at six to ten frames per second on models with a few hundred polygons. Sluggish, but marginally enough to get us Through the Looking Glass.

Our motto was “Reality Isn’t Enough Any More”.

I was also spending a lot of time hanging out with Timothy Leary, whose suggestion was responsible for my quitting my job at MCC and moving to California. I’d met him at the Hackers 2.0 conference in 1986 and gave him a ride to the San Jose airport. We became fast friends, and I did quite a lot of writing with him, most of which remains unpublished. But that’s a story for later. Timothy, who appears in a samizdat Autodesk virtual reality video, nicknamed our VR lab “Cyberia”.

Timothy was a tremendous fan of Gibson, and considered his seminal 1984 novel Neuromancer extremely prescient about the impending digital revolution.

As our VR developments crept slowly towards becoming a product, we at Autodesk applied to register a trademark “cyberspace”. Timothy informed me Gibson was plenty miffed about this, so I wrote him what I felt was a conciliatory letter,1 though ending snarkily by quoting his own words, “The street finds its own use for things.”

In reply, Gibson had his lawyers send Autodesk a letter2. Which I recall we ignored.

Timothy - ever the incorrigible prankster - circulated the rumor that Gibson was attempting to trademark “Eric Gullichsen” in retaliation. Then Barlow, for reasons of his own, embellished that rumor. Later amplified by Rudy Rucker.

About a year later - after I'd already left Autodesk for my VR startup, Sense8 Corporation - we were invited to the inaugural Art Futura 1990 in Barcelona. And there, in the lobby of some swank hotel, I met Gibson. He opined in a laconic drawl that although the street finds its own use for things “Autodesk is not the street”.

There was plenty of cava consumed in the small hours before the time Barcelonans sit down to eat endless rounds of tapas. As I recall, after all the many Art Futura parties we'd put the matter behind us, or close enough.

And there was a memorable visit to Gaudi’s Park Güell, whose giant lizard of crazy-quilt ceramic appears in Count Zero.

So: Autodesk did apply to register Cyberspace, and Gibson really did object. But Gibson trying to trademark Eric Gullichsen was Timothy Leary's prank, propagated until it became accepted history.

#303. Report: Apple gains ground on rivals, but iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo face challenges

In a new investor note sent out this week, GF Securities’ Jeff Pu and Henry Huang project that Apple will be the only major smartphone manufacturer to grow shipments in 2026, even as the global market is expected to shrink by more than 14%. Here are the details.

For the past few weeks, several reports from IDC and Counterpoint Research have been mapping out the impact of rising memory costs on smartphone sales.

And while the numbers may vary slightly, it is increasingly clear that Apple has been able to weather the downturn better than its competitors.

This week, Pu and Huang released a new investor note reinforcing that trend, projecting that Apple will gain significant market share in 2026 as most of its major competitors see shipments decline.

According to the report, Apple is on track to close out 2026 as the only major smartphone manufacturer to increase shipments, with a projected 4% year-over-year gain to 257 million units.

That would keep Apple ahead of Samsung, which is expected to ship 241 million smartphones, essentially unchanged from 2025. Apple also topped the rankings in 2024 and 2025.

Apple’s share of global smartphone shipments is also projected to climb to 24% in 2026, compared to 20% in 2025 and 19% in 2024.

Market-wide, the report projects a 14.2% drop in total shipments to 1.08 billion shipped smartphones for 2026, and further pegs 2026-2027 as “one of the most challenging periods for the industry, driven primarily by sharply higher memory prices, which have already pushed OEMs to reduce shipments and raise device prices.”

Back to Apple, the report reiterates that the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max have received a relatively lukewarm reception, which the analysts partly attribute to competition from the iPhone Duo and criticism of their weight. The analysts also cite production constraints affecting both the iPhone Duo and the iPhone 18 Pro lineup:

Due to hinge constraints, we are reducing the iPhone Duo EMS build plan from 7m to 6m units in 2026. We also lower the iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max build plan to 72m units given the constraints associated with the adjustable‑aperture camera.

The iPhone Duo went up for pre-order earlier today and is already showing delivery estimates stretching into late January in the US and even further in other countries.

With all of that in mind, the report maintained its “Hold” rating on Apple stock, with a price target of $369. Apple shares closed at $343.46, up 0.43% on the day, making it the only major tech stock to finish in the green amid the ongoing sector-wide sell-off.
