#304. We Need to Embed Ethics Into Our Engineering Courses

Adding social responsibility to technical training prepares students to protect the public good

Cynthia J. Finelli is a professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and Education at the University of Michigan.

Susan M. Lord is a professor and Founding Chair of Integrated Engineering at the University of San Diego.

Erin A. Cech is an associate professor of Sociology and Mechanical Engineering at the University of Michigan.

In mid-September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei joined a growing group of researchers calling for the AI industry to slow down. While some have questioned these researchers’ motivation for voicing concerns about the rapid pace of development, the plea highlighted a key tension between safety and speed. The underlying problem is not simply a technical error, but a sociotechnical failure: Pressure to move quickly has made it hard for engineers to fully assess and manage new risks of increasingly powerful AI systems. It is a clear warning that responsible engineering requires more than technical expertise; engineers must also understand workplace pressures, moral and ethical rules, and the social consequences rooted in the systems they create.

Cases like this, alongside invasive surveillance technologies and biased AI tools, have exposed serious shortcomings in how engineers recognize and address the ethical and social implications of their work. While the need to educate graduates in ethics and social responsibility is widely recognized, a persistent gap remains—these topics are too often treated as afterthoughts, disconnected from the technical content of engineering coursework. This siloed approach leaves graduates ill-equipped to address real-world challenges; indeed, only about a third of engineering professionals in the United States report having received training on their public welfare responsibilities during their formal engineering education.

We are working to bridge this gap by designing two complementary instructional approaches, one that integrates social issues directly into foundation technical coursework and a second that prepares students to act as “public welfare watchdogs” through a standalone engineering course. By embedding ethics and social responsibility training directly into the core of undergraduate engineering coursework, we equip future professionals with the agency they will need to protect the public good.

Across the engineering profession, there is a persistent belief that technical skill-building is central to engineering, while ethical, social, and public welfare concerns are peripheral or distracting. This technical/social dualism is evident even in the evaluation of scholarly research. For instance, we recently submitted an academic position paper discussing this ethics education gap to a leading peer-reviewed engineering journal. It was dismissed by reviewers along the very same dualism it described.

One reviewer warned that it would be “highly irresponsible” to challenge technical skill-building as “the foundation of any kind of engineering” by adding ethics and social responsibility training into engineering classrooms. Another reviewer objected that integrating these considerations into foundational courses risks “distracting the students from fully absorbing the technology.” These comments miss the core argument of our work: that ethics and social responsibility are integral to responsible technical practice.

Today, accreditation agencies like ABET (formerly known as the Accreditation Board for Engineering and Technology) and professional licensing bodies like the National Society of Professional Engineers mandate student outcomes related to social and public welfare consequences. But these curriculum requirements tend to be unhelpfully generic and minimally enforced. As a result, engineering students often receive ethics instruction through introductory or non-engineering coursework, where the focus is on codes of conduct and academic integrity, rather than deeper topics of social responsibility. This instruction is almost always disconnected from the complex real-world dilemmas engineers face.

Indeed, we find that only ethics instruction in actual engineering courses (not in other parts of the curriculum) can effectively instill ethical awareness as professionals. Concerningly, only about 4 in 10 engineers in the United States recall receiving this kind of training, and 3 in 10 report never receiving training on their public welfare responsibilities at any point in their careers. This leaves most of the profession underprepared to handle the complex challenges of engineering practice.

To advance a new paradigm—one that embeds ethics and social responsibility issues within the undergraduate engineering curriculum—we’ve designed two innovative course-based approaches: a library of one-hour sociotechnical modules for foundational circuits courses (described here and here) and a new engineering course dedicated to public welfare responsibilities.

The first approach integrates discussions about relevant social issues directly into foundational engineering courses, where students begin to form their identities as engineers. “Introduction to Circuits” is typically the first course in the electrical engineering major and is a requirement for many other engineering disciplines, making it a powerful site for introducing social content and ethical reasoning. We designed several one-hour modules for this course, where social issues provide context for a technical topic, offering a manageable entry point for faculty who may feel ill-prepared to teach about ethics and social responsibility.

While many engineering faculty recognize the importance of teaching students about these topics, they struggle to integrate them into their courses amid heavy teaching and research demands. To overcome these challenges, each module provides ready-to-use materials, including lecture slides with scripts and homework and exam problems. Integrating these modules directly into the course signals to students that sociotechnical awareness is not an “add-on,” but a required professional competency.

Our module on hospital power prioritization, for instance, connects the technical topics of power and equivalent circuits to the ethical challenges of healthcare infrastructure. Students learn about the reality of “red outlets” in medical settings, debating the power needs of specific wards (e.g., the intensive care unit, operating rooms, and physiotherapy rooms) to decide which branches should receive emergency power during a hypothetical outage.

Our conflict minerals module connects the technical topic of capacitors to the global tantalum supply chain. Students calculate the amount of tantalum used in cell phones and identify mining locations in regions like the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where revenue often fuels armed conflict and human rights abuses. Students research the conflict-mineral policies of major companies such as Apple and Samsung and reflect on their future roles as ethical designers and consumers.

Student responses to these modules have been overwhelmingly positive. In interviews, students told us that the content helped them get away from the “stigma that engineers only worry about math” and made the work more meaningful. We plan to share the modules widely to help circuits instructors across the globe bridge the technical-social divide.

Beyond these integrated modules, our second approach is a standalone engineering course—Public Welfare Responsibilities in Engineering (PWRE)—that helps round out students’ sociotechnical education by preparing them to fulfill their professional obligations as engineers. While most dedicated ethics courses end by introducing engineers’ abstract responsibilities, PWRE helps students recognize specific public welfare concerns, enhances their motivation to act when they encounter them, and teaches concrete, practical intervention strategies.

In addition to teaching students about professional codes, such as the IEEE Code of Ethics, PWRE engages students in discussion of where these formal definitions may fall short, and how structural barriers such as workplace culture can hinder engineers from fulfilling these responsibilities. Then, the course equips students with intervention strategies. Students learn about their rights and responsibilities as whistleblowers, review tactics for seeking advice from professional societies, and practice writing op-eds to raise the alarm about ethical issues to the broader public. Our research shows that the course produces notable shifts in students’ ethical agency, strengthening their ability to serve as “public welfare watchdogs” in the modern workplace.

Today’s engineering graduates face complex sociotechnical challenges beyond AI expansion, including climate change and global supply chains; they need tools to navigate ambiguity and act ethically in uncertain contexts. To meet these evolving demands, engineering education must move beyond outdated modes of instruction that focus only on building technical skills—some of which may soon be outsourced to AI. We must fundamentally reimagine the role of ethics and social responsibility, embedding them across the engineering curriculum and throughout the professional formation of engineers.

All engineers learn to solve problems, but ethical engineers can also discern which problems are worth solving and anticipate the consequences of innovation for society. By centering ethics and social responsibility as core priorities of the profession, we can prepare engineers to be stewards of technology and trusted voices in public discourse.

As one student reflected after participating in our modules, “We are a part of the issue if we don’t decide to fix it.”

Cynthia J. Finelli is an Arthur F. Thurnau Professor, the David C. Munson, Jr. Professor of Engineering, and a professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and Education (by courtesy) at the University of Michigan. Her research focuses on advancing evidence-based teaching, fostering social responsibility through engineering coursework, and supporting the success of a diverse student body. She is a Fellow of IEEE and the American Society for Engineering Education (ASEE) and has held leadership and editorial roles throughout the IEEE engineering education community.

Susan M. Lord is Professor and Founding Chair of Integrated Engineering at the University of San Diego. Her research focuses on the study and promotion of equity in engineering including student pathways and inclusive teaching. She is a Fellow of the IEEE and the ASEE and is active in the engineering education community including serving as General Co-Chair of the Frontiers in Education Conference, President of the IEEE Education Society, and Associate Editor of the IEEE Transactions on Education.

Erin A. Cech is an associate professor of Sociology and Mechanical Engineering (by courtesy) at the University of Michigan. She holds a Ph.D. in Sociology from UC San Diego and an undergraduate degree in Electrical Engineering from Montana State. Cech's research examines cultural mechanisms of inequality reproduction. Her work has appeared in PNAS and Science Advances and has been covered by The New York Times, NPR, CNN, and the news sections of Science and Nature.

Nothing new here. Some 45 years ago I attended the graduation ceremony of the College of Engineering at the University of Maryland. In his address to the graduates the dean stressed the importance of questioning and understanding the why of proposed developments before diving into the how. The example he gave was pumping blood over long distances, which can obviously be used for good or nefarious purposes.

I teach a course that incorporates ethics into engineering design and entrepreneurship. I often recall a senior colleague's words when he handed me the course upon his retirement. He observed that students largely acquire their ethical value systems at home and through their early schooling. By the time they reach university, much of that foundation is already established. Perhaps our role is not so much to create an ethics system as to help students understand how to apply ethical principles in engineering practice. Was my colleague being pessimistic, or simply realistic?

I like the optimism here about young engineers' ability to grapple with the social implications of their technical work. It makes me think there's going to be a challenge for educators and licensing boards to agree on how to make this kind of ethics module fit their goals, of course. Different institutions might differ on ethics priorities! But asking engineers to think outside the circuit board and instead to think like empowered citizens is a great start.

It recharges to 100% in under an hour (or three hours via solar) and is expandable up to 4kWh. It supports up to 800W solar input (panels sold separately) for off-grid charging and includes five AC outlets, as well as a car outlet, RV connection, and high-output USB-C ports.

Compared to its predecessor, it’s quieter and more compact in both weight and footprint, and the added perk of app connectivity makes it easy to monitor and control. If you want reliable, high-capacity portable power, the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 is a great emergency essential, though if you want something with true grab-and-go appeal, you may want to opt for the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, which weighs about 40% less but has half the battery capacity—and also happens to be 46% off right now.

#306. AI-Generated Hot Girls Are Ripping Off Comedians to Boost Their Horny Content

Last week, the stand-up comedian Julia Jasunas was on Instagram when she got a DM from a fellow comic. Did she know, her friend wrote, that a random Instagram influencer had ripped off a joke from her stand-up act?

Initially, Jasunas was mad but not overly shocked. Plagiarism is not uncommon in the stand-up comedy world, and comics are “really sensitive about it, because there's not a ton of protection against it,” she tells WIRED. “So we all look out for each other.” Then she clicked on the link.

The video was of a purported stand-up comic named Aylen Skye, a buxom blond with leonine cheekbones and 250,000 Instagram followers. In the clip, Skye, wearing a crop top and Daisy Dukes, tells a joke about renting out a room in her two-bedroom apartment to a cute guy. To Jasunas’ shock, it was, verbatim, her joke, down to the “ums” and “ahs.”

Whoever Skye was, she didn’t appear to be a comic; the website she advertised in her video, AylenTV.com, redirected to NSFW content on Fanvue, a subscription-based OnlyFans competitor that markets itself as the “No1 AI monetisation platform for creators.” And not only did she appear to not be a comic, she also didn’t seem to be real. After looking at Skye’s comments section, Jasunas was fairly convinced she was AI.

“You look at any female comic’s comments section and you’ll see all these men berating her, objectifying her body, saying she’s not funny or the joke is bad,” she says. But with Skye, all of the comments were positive. “That’s how I knew she was fake,” she deadpans.

For Jasunas, being ripped off by a sexy AI-generated comedian was “violating on so many different levels.” “It’s one thing to have your jokes stolen,” she says. “It’s another to funnel your work into something so sexualized, for someone else’s profit.” She immediately reported the video to Meta for impersonation, but says Meta told her it did not violate community guidelines because Skye wasn’t pretending to be Jasunas; it was just passing off her joke as its own. “They just didn’t seem to care,” Jasunas says. (The majority of Skye’s posts are now flagged as AI content, though the account itself is not.)

Jasunas is far from the only stand-up comic to have been targeted by Skye. Nor does Skye appear to be the only AI-generated hot girl account targeting comics. WIRED has identified eight comics whose videos have been replicated by scantily clad, AI-generated women, many of whom follow each other on social media. All of the videos are copies of already-successful viral stand-up clips, except the AI-generated counterparts are playing to bigger audiences, with better lighting, better sound, and more skintight outfits—essentially, all the elements required to ensure virality. The accounts also post flirty, clearly AI-generated late-night TV show interviews with hosts like Conan O’Brien and Jimmy Kimmel, as well as the occasional “edgy” racist or transphobic joke catering to the MAGA crowd.

Though Instagram’s community guidelines prohibit impersonation, such policies don’t extend to copying someone else’s content, particularly if that content isn’t copyrighted. The platform also does not have any prohibitions against AI content, so long as it is appropriately labeled as such. Some of the accounts are labeled as AI-generated—but others are not, or their videos are inconsistently labeled. (Skye did not respond to a request for comment, though it has commented on many stand-up comics’ videos calling it out: “if you focused on putting out content instead of making whinny [sic] posts like this, you’d be as successful as me,” it wrote on one comic’s Instagram post.)

Particularly grating to the comics being ripped off is that some of the AI-generated videos perform better than the originals, spawning calls for increased protections for original content on Instagram. “AI is evolving very fast, and we need rules to protect creators before this becomes a bigger issue,” says Mandy Martino, who also had one of her jokes lifted by Skye. “It’s not just about a joke being stolen—it’s about this being a change that we need to get ahead of. And Instagram saying this isn’t a problem is the scariest part.”

Comics have been complaining about AI accounts stealing their content since June, with the stand-up Steph Clark regularly documenting such “weird pick-me AI slop” on her Instagram. In one early video, the AI stand-up in question is a leggy redhead sitting on a stool, awkwardly delivering a nonsensical punch line comparing faking orgasms to being a bad cook, a vacant expression on its face.

In the following months, however, the technology for such clone videos has improved exponentially, to the degree that it’s difficult to tell whether or not the women in the videos are actually real people. One such example is Tiffany Sloane, which identifies itself as an actress in its bio on Instagram, where it has more than 375,000 followers. A pear-shaped 19-year-old bombshell with a septum piercing and a BBL, Sloane does crowd work and jokes about quarter-zips and Jimmy Buffett songs on its Instagram page—which, similar to Skye, also includes a Highlights link to its OnlyFans profile.

Since starting the Instagram account in August, Sloane amassed a robust following and is also on TikTok and Facebook, where it has built out a “super horny AI-generated short-form video content farm,” as the writer Ryan Broderick puts it. On October 3, the comedian George Brett Olson posted a viral video captioned “AI stole my joke!!!” showing a side-by-side comparison of his stand-up bit—a joke about how Republicans ignore the risks of AI in favor of manufacturing panic over illegal immigration—next to Sloane’s near-identical one. In both clips, the comics are standing in front of identical backdrops and wearing similar salmon shirts and khaki shorts. Only the punch line, which features an expletive in Olson’s version, is different.

“I was kind of in shock,” Olson tells WIRED of seeing Sloane’s video for the first time. “I just thought it was so weird to see people openly stealing in real time.” He says his followers told him they reported it to Meta, and according to them, Meta responded by saying Sloane’s video did not violate any community guidelines. “I couldn’t believe it,” he says. “This is my intellectual property. I created it. And not only did this person or whatever steal it, they stole my likeness too.”

After Olson made his video calling out Sloane, he was flooded with comments from fellow stand-ups and fans supporting him and vowing to report Sloane’s account to Instagram. Even Sloane weighed in, leaving a comment on Olson’s page saying, “sorry, won’t happen again” before deleting its video, as well as many other Reels on its page. (Sloane didn’t immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)

Ultimately, however, Olson was dispirited by the inaction on Meta’s end. After tagging Instagram head Adam Mosseri, Mosseri responded by saying that while he did not think it was “practical for us to try and ban AI content” from Meta, the platform was “very invested in trying to drive more traffic to original content creators, and if an AI creator is ripping off content wholesale, it would be good for us to work out what we can do about that.”

Responding to WIRED, Francis Brennan, a spokesperson for Meta, declined to comment further, saying, “Our policies are pretty clear around this stuff, and Adam’s comment speaks for itself.” All of the AI-generated accounts flagged by WIRED are still on the platform.

As of now, there’s very little that comedians can do about AI creators “ripping off content wholesale.” Legally, jokes have historically enjoyed very little copyright protection, in part due to the ephemeral nature of stand-up and the fact that many setups and punch lines have been used in the industry, with slightly different variations, for years. There’s also the matter of the financial stakes being relatively low, according to Aaron Perzanowski, now a law professor at the University of Michigan, who told NPR in 2017, “when you're talking about accusations of infringement dealing with fairly low-dollar-value creative work, we don't see a lot of litigation." (Olson says this sentiment was echoed by an intellectual property lawyer he consulted with, who he claims told him that unless Sloane was making millions of dollars on OnlyFans, threatening a lawsuit was probably more trouble than it was worth.)

The negative sentiment against these AI-generated creators does not appear to be shared by some in the tech industry, such as Andreessen Horowitz partner Justine Moore, who publicly praised Sloane in an X post, referring to her online presence as “a genius marketing hack.”

Olson is not overly optimistic that AI evangelists will rush to the defense of the creatives whose labor is being exploited. Nor, for that matter, does he believe that the “lizard-brained” commenters rushing to post horny comments on Sloane’s and Skye’s pages particularly care whether they’re real, or who actually crafted the jokes they’re telling in their viral clips.

“To me, we're asking the essential question, does the artist matter?” he says. “And to those 350,000 people that follow Tiffany Sloane, the answer is clearly no. And that’s really demoralizing.”

#307. Cadence launched a magnetic travel pump that took 1,023 tries to get right — where to buy

TL;DR: Cadence launched The Pump ($30), a magnetic travel attachment for its refillable Capsules. Six years in the making, it features a flexible tube that fits Medium and Large sizes, an angled nozzle, and a lock-tight cap that prevents spills in your bag.

Refilling travel bottles with your favorite skincare or haircare products usually ends one of two ways: either you are stuck digging thick lotion out of a jar with your fingers, or a cheap squeeze bottle bursts inside your luggage. Design brand Cadence is smoothing out that middle ground with its newest release: The Pump.

Designed to attach directly to Cadence’s signature refillable Capsules, the $30 accessory gives you a mess-free way to dispense liquids like sunscreen, lotions, shampoos, and body oils while on the go. Instead of sticking a basic off-the-shelf plastic straw onto a jar, Cadence spent six years testing 1,023 different iterations to get the mechanics right.

The main innovation is a flexible, coiled dip tube. The tube stretches and compresses automatically inside the container, so a single pump head works seamlessly whether you screw it onto a Medium Capsule or a Large Capsule.

Operating it is simple: pull off the magnetic cap, give the fluted collar a quick half-turn to raise the pump head, and press. When you are done, twist the collar back down and drop the cap back on.

Seven heavy-duty neodymium magnets lock the cap in place, physically blocking the pump head from rising while packed away. That means no accidental squirts ruining the inside of your bag during transit. Cadence also angled the dispensing nozzle upward, directing product outward so liquids do not collect around the collar and make a mess.

Made from the same durable polypropylene as the original Capsules, The Pump comes in a sand colorway and works with Cadence’s interchangeable, magnetic Label Tiles so you always know what is inside.

You can also pair it with Cadence's Parcel organizers, which now feature customizable straps with embroidered icons for a completely personalized setup.

Your carry-on will thank you. Grab The Pump from Cadence for $30.

#309. IEEE Report Predicts Tech That Will Transform Lives

It details how AI, energy, and medicine will change by 2030

Liz Wegerer is a freelance writer based in Seattle.

By 2028, genetic engineering and gene therapy will be used frequently to treat a variety of diseases, thanks to advances in artificial intelligence, according to the recently released 2030 Technology Megatrends Report from IEEE.

“We are seeing a fundamental shift in how technology evolves,” says IEEE Fellow Dejan Milojicic, chair of the IEEE Future Directions Committee’s Industry Advisory Board, the group responsible for the report. “Artificial intelligence is no longer operating in a vacuum; it is now deeply connected to our energy, infrastructure, and physical systems.” Milojicic, a Hewlett Packard Enterprise Fellow, is a vice president at HPE Labs in Milpitas, Calif.

AI underpins many of the report’s 30 technologies and five “megatrends,” which are technology shifts with the potential to reshape industries and everyday life for decades. A megatrend isn’t a single breakthrough but a collection of related technologies.

For the 2030 report, 166 experts—from 38 countries across six continents—drawn from industry, academia, and government identified 30 breakthrough technologies across the five megatrends: AI, energy, health, space, and physical AI. The experts graded the trends against five criteria: likelihood of success, impact to humanity, maturity, market adoption, and horizon to adoption.

Interconnected systems drive the megatrends, and the connection among them is AI.

The report notes that AI technology is advancing faster than any previous revolution, including industrial, electrical, and digital. The pace has turned the technology into general-purpose infrastructure, Milojicic says.

That evolution carries risks, though, the experts say. The report cites the lack of computing infrastructure and energy sources as constraints on the ability to scale up AI, and it says the technology’s growth will require reshaping the workforce.

Workers have always needed to adapt to stay competitive, Milojicic says, adding that AI adoption isn’t an all-or-nothing approach. Businesses should decide when and how to apply it, he says.

The experts say long-term success will require both technical capabilities and attention to the human-AI relationship. Conditions including trust, security, explainability, and policymaking will determine which AI-supported technologies are most likely to scale, they say.

“This report shifts the conversation to something far more important: how these advances will intersect with one another to shape human lives,” Mary Ellen Randall, 2026 IEEE president and CEO, said in a news release about the report. “The data makes clear that trust, safety, and human connection must guide every major breakthrough in the decade ahead.”

The experts scored personalized medicine as the study’s highest-impact technology, at 4.93 out of 5, for its potential to improve human life.

The report credits AI-driven breakthroughs in personalized diagnostics and therapeutic treatments, driven by innovative biotech startups. Within two years, the experts predict, genetic engineering and gene therapy will be used in therapeutic areas.

Within five years, earlier disease diagnoses will move out of the lab and into day-to-day medical practice, the report predicts. Meanwhile, it says, researchers likely will be able to manufacture simple synthetic proteins—molecules engineered from scratch, rather than found in nature—to perform a specific job in the body, such as targeting a tumor or supplying a missing enzyme.

Increased power demand by AI is outpacing the energy sector’s ability to keep up. Tech infrastructure—data centers, networks, and computing hardware—already uses an estimated 10 percent of electricity globally, according to the news release.

The experts predict that within two to three years, energy storage will double in developed countries.

The energy industry has been relatively dormant for years, Milojicic says, with little breakthrough innovation since the times of Thomas Edison and Nikola Tesla.

“Data centers can ramp up within milliseconds, yet it takes months for the power and energy sector to ramp up,” he says. “The governments of various countries will have to rethink their approach to power generation to stay ahead of demand.”

The experts cite the Jevons paradox—the idea that efficiency gains tend to increase overall consumption. As AI chip efficiency improves, organizations will run more hardware to build ever-larger frontier models—those advanced AI systems currently in development—the experts say. Data centers will draw as much power as grids can supply, leaving no surplus, the experts predict.

Physical AI refers to systems embedded within machines that sense and act in the world, including robots and autonomous vehicles. In the report, the category originally was called “hyper-automation and robotics,” a broad, software-driven process automation paired with physical machines. The Industry Advisory Board later folded it into the single physical AI megatrend.

The experts found that human-AI interaction has the shortest adoption horizon of any of the 30 scored technologies, at two to three years. They also say physical AI has the biggest chance of technical advancement of any megatrend during the next four years.

“The data makes clear that trust, safety, and human connection must guide every major breakthrough in the decade ahead.” —Mary Ellen Randall, 2026 IEEE president and CEO

Smarter, more efficient robots will substantially cut energy consumption in the next two years, the experts say.

Communications between humans and AI—whether in an android or another device—will shift from text-based commands to predominantly audio and video instructions within two to three years, the experts predict.

Androids used in factories will use tactile and haptic feedback within two to five years, letting them sense what they’re touching and adjust their grip or force in response, the experts say. Bio-inspired skin, tissues, and sensors will advance in the same timeframe, the experts predict, giving robots perception that better mirrors human touch.

Space technology, as the report defines it, covers more than exploration. It spans satellite communications, in-space manufacturing, launch technology, and other infrastructure. It is one of the lower-profile megatrends in the report, not for lack of promise but because of where the sector presently sits.

“It’s not lagging,” Milojicic says. “It’s the current state of maturity. People are talking about satellite communication right now because it’s very cool and practical. But it’s a small segment compared to the attention AI gets.”

He says he believes the space sector will be more prominent in the coming years: “This is an area of technology that will become increasingly important, especially as terrestrial communication and transportation push the boundaries for space as well.”

The report highlights two technologies on the near horizon: semiconductor manufacturing that uses parts built in space and more affordable reusable rockets. It also sees clean energy generation in space and the commercialization of orbital garbage collection as potential technologies to watch for in the next decade.

The report recommends that academia, industry, governments, and professional associations work together.

To build a well-trained workforce, the report says, industry should partner with professional organizations on training programs and revive apprenticeships in chemistry, physics, and other physical sciences. It also calls on businesses to treat AI infrastructure—computing, data, and energy—as a long-term strategic asset.

Other recommendations include expanding access to affordable, quality education in STEM coursework and AI competence.

Governments should lead on policy and implement reintegration programs for workers displaced by AI, the report says.

The experts say professional organizations including IEEE should develop new products and services using AI, strengthen safety and data governance standards, and serve as a collaboration platform for industry, academia, and policymakers.

The report also offers recommendations for end users, content creators, investors, and company leadership on strategies for succeeding in an AI-focused future.

The same thread runs through all the report’s recommendations: Don’t lose sight of the human-AI relationship.

“As a public charity dedicated to advancing technology for the benefit of humanity, IEEE believes progress must be measured by more than technology development and implementation speed,” Sophia A. Muirhead, IEEE executive director and chief operating officer, said in the news release. “Whether retraining the global workforce or integrating AI responsibly into daily life, the success of these megatrends depends on ensuring innovation strengthens human well-being and public trust.”

Liz Wegerer is a freelance writer based in Seattle.

#311. The Difference Between Suunto's Race, Run, and Vertical Series Smartwatches

This week, Suunto launched its newest addition to its Race line of performance watches, the Race 3S. At $599, it’s lightweight with a premium feel, and to me, its most interesting upgrade is the new silicon-carbon battery, which Suunto says offers up to 38 hours of dual-band GPS, up to 45 hours in Endurance mode, 10 days of training use, and up to 12 days in daily mode. While I usually stick to my Garmin Forerunners, I’ve been personally testing the Suunto 3S and loving it on first impression.

Suunto may be one of the lesser-known fitness watch brands, but its offerings, aimed at hikers and outdoorsy people, have long been well regarded. The company sorts its sports watches into families: Run, Race, and Vertical. Three families of watches, all with several generations of models and a lot of overlapping specs, are enough to leave you staring at a product page, wracked with decision fatigue. This week’s launch of the Suunto Race 3S, the newest member of the Race family, is a good enough reason for me to help you sort it out.

Best for: Road runners, 5K-to-marathon trainers, and anyone who wants a watch they forget they're wearing, including overnight. It's also a good first step into Suunto's ecosystem.

In her review of the Suunto Run my colleague Beth Skwarecki calls this watch on of her favorite running watches, pointing to features that not only rival, but maybe even outshine Garmin and Coros watches at a similar price point. Both watches in the Run series, the Run and the Run 2, are known for being easy to wear and simple to use, but still with all the core features of a reliable running watch.

Best for: Trail runners, triathletes, and runners who want serious training tools and navigation.

The Race S is the compact option, while the Race 2 has since replaced the original Race and has a bigger screen and larger case. It might best suit people with bigger wrists who want a big display and don't mind the weight.

As of today, the Race 3S is the lightweight premium pick. It combines the Race S's compact size with a titanium and sapphire build, a bigger battery, a brighter screen, and double the storage. Suunto says its battery capacity is 46 percent larger than the Race S's, and its display is 233 percent brighter.

When in doubt, the Race series is the middle of the lineup, and it's a natural sweet spot to land on. If you can't decide between the Run and Race options, Beth's got you covered with an in-depth comparison.

Best for: Ultrarunners, mountaineers, backpackers, and anyone doing multi-day trips where charging isn't an option. It's also a good fit if you want a watch that holds up to rough use.

The Vertical 2 is marketed as an expedition-grade watch. It weighs about 87 grams and measures 49 mm, and it's available in stainless steel or titanium. It's water-resistant to 100 meters. It has a built-in LED flashlight that the lighter Race and Run watches lack, a redesigned heart rate sensor, and more storage and processing power than the original. Its main selling point is battery life—allegedly up to 65 hours of GPS in Performance mode and up to 250 hours in Tour mode.

The original Vertical is the older model, with a solar-assisted MIP display. It's still sold and often discounted, but the Vertical 2's AMOLED screen is a major step up in clarity.

The Suunto Run series is for runners who want a light, simple watch. The Race series is for performance athletes who want a premium build and strong all-around training and navigation tools. The Vertical series is for people who go far from civilization and want the longest battery life and the toughest build.

The Suunto lineup also includes Core outdoor watches and dive computers like the Ocean, but those are a different conversation. For runners and trail athletes, the choice comes down to Run, Race, or Vertical, and which of them fits how far, how long, and how rough you like to get:

If you mostly run on roads and want a lightweight entry-point watch, look at the Run.

If you race, train across several sports, or run trails and want a premium build, look at the Race 3S, or the Race if you're sticking to a smaller budget. Or you can choose the Race 2 if you prefer a bigger case and screen.

If your adventures last days rather than hours, choose the Vertical 2.

#312. The Best Digital Wall Calendar (2026): Skylight, Everblog, Greenlight

I won’t lie to you: I hated the first digital wall calendar I tried.

I tested it last year and was left unimpressed. It was bulky and expensive, and my calendar details were slow to appear (if they appeared at all). The device felt more like clutter than a useful addition to my home. So, I wrote off the idea of using one at all, but to my surprise, digital wall calendars have only picked up in popularity and options since then. After trying a few new models myself this year, I can now see why.

These gadgets work by taking your online calendar—whether your Google Calendar, the calendar app on your iPhone, or your corporate Microsoft calendar account—and putting it on a digital screen that you can mount on the wall or prop up on a countertop or table. They’re often more than just calendars, also functioning as chore charts, meal planners, and sometimes even digital photo frames. I usually have smart displays all over my home, especially in my kitchen and living area, but for the past two weeks, I’ve replaced them all with digital wall calendars. And you know what? I don't miss talking to those annoying AI-powered assistants.

Instead, as someone who already lives and breathes by her Google Calendar, I love being able to see it on a large display in the middle of the kitchen, without needing my phone—especially when it’s on a digital wall device that immediately reflects my most up-to-date calendar. My husband and I have also been using the extra features more often, particularly to guide my 4-year-old through his evening bedtime routine with the help of his own companion device. Here’s everything you need to know about the best digital wall calendars and whether they’re right for you.

Updated October 2026: I’ve added the Greenlight Family Hub as a new pick for families with teens and notes on the Skylight Buddy’s calendar feature. I’ve also ensured up-to-date links and prices.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

You might have heard these gadgets called by various names. Maybe “digital wall calendar” or “smart calendar device.” Maybe you’ve just heard the name Skylight Calendar, which is a notably popular model right now. No matter what you call them, these devices all do the same thing: replace a paper calendar with a digitized one that connects to the calendar tools you’re already using, like Google Calendar or Apple Calendar. The devices let you see your entire family’s schedule in one view, with the ability to update or add to it without needing a phone or a separate account. It also erases issues like unreadable handwriting and forgetting to write down an event you’ve already scheduled digitally, and its color-coding system makes it easy to see who’s on the hook for which activities.

While these are often called wall calendars, you can usually choose to place them on a tabletop. I preferred the models that included a tabletop stand, but I was still able to prop up the ones that only came with wall-mounting hardware during my testing.

I didn’t expect to feel this way, but having a physical version of my hyper-detailed Google Calendar in the center of my home has been a delight. My husband and I both check our calendar at a glance while we’re chatting in the kitchen, and at the start of the week, we’ll camp out in front of it for a few minutes to plan the week’s dinners and grocery needs. My top pick, Skylight Calendar 2, actually prompts us to add items to our grocery list based on what meals we picked (if it’s a stored recipe, that is).

My husband and I have found it so useful in part because we’re both good about adding events to our individual calendars, so now this device can reflect that work. It lets us skip pulling out our phones when discussing plans for the next day or the upcoming weekend.

Skylight’s calendar is the most popular for a reason. The brand is known for its digital photo frames, and now you can use the same Skylight app to operate any of its three digital calendars: The older 10-inch Calendar ($150), the newer Calendar 2 ($340), and the Calendar Max ($630). The main difference between these is size, but Calendar 2 is the newest model, with improved performance and interchangeable Snap Frames ($30 to $50) that you can purchase to change the device’s look (you can also buy these for the Calendar Max, but not the older 10-inch Calendar).

What makes Skylight great is its software. It’s easy to use, and it quickly imported my Google Calendar and the wide variety of calendars shared to it, so I could immediately add all of my family’s schedules to the device. The left-side menu bar shows all the pages you can toggle between. Calendar, Lists, Tasks, Rewards, Meals, and Recipes are the main areas you’ll use; you can also access the Photos, Sleep, and Settings pages from the same menu.

The app and device interface are clean and intuitive compared with other models, many of which feel like Android tablets with a fancy calendar mode added. I was able to easily assign calendars I created on the device to family members. For example, I assigned my husband’s calendar to him without needing him to log in or import it, and I could have assigned any calendar I created to my son as well. I also liked that shared events only appear once on the Skylight, but with both of our designated colors added to show the event in question applied to both of us.

Lists and Tasks sound similar, but Tasks are meant to function as a chore chart, connecting back to the Rewards page to build habits and earn the reward you set after hitting a certain goal. The main audience for this is children who are old enough to check the calendar. Lists are for things like your groceries. If you add recipes to the Recipe tab and then add those to your meal plan for that week, Skylight will offer to put the corresponding ingredients on your shopping list.

The Everblog HomeCal has an operating system that feels pleasantly similar to the Skylight. It has a bit of an Android undertone to it, but it doesn’t feel like a giant tablet as much as the Apolosign or Cozyla calendars (both below). Setup was pretty seamless, but there was a delay for the device to update with my calendar invites. It would also take a while for the Everblog to reflect changes I made to my Google Calendar on another device. While it worked well for the most part during testing, I occasionally noticed events missing from my Everblog. It also turned each calendar email account I connected to the device into a separate profile, which was annoying. I could toggle off the extra emails when I was on pages outside of the calendar, though, so I didn’t have three profiles for myself on my Chores page, for example.

The menu on the left-hand side is very similar to Skylight’s, with options like Calendar, Chores, and Meal Plan. There isn’t a recipe section, which I miss, but there is a Fridge section, which lets you track the groceries you already have. Part of why this exists is because Everblog also has a smaller, battery-powered version of this calendar that’s designed to attach to your fridge, aptly named the FridgeCal ($249). Still, I prefer the Recipe tab on the Skylight. The Everblog also has a Chores tab, but no additional tab for tracking regular chores or other to-dos separately.

There’s a free photo option, but the uploader tool in the app only lets you add one photo at a time. Painful, but I’m sure many would feel it’s worth the free price tag. To use the feature, you’ll need to go into the settings on the physical device to turn on photo slideshow as your screensaver. The Everblog defaults to pinging loudly at the start of any calendar event, which you can only change on the device, not in the app.

There’s a button on the bottom right-hand corner of the screen that will take you to a homepage with an overview of the calendar and chores, and access to other applications like Spotify and Netflix, if you set up your accounts on this device for streaming content. It comes enabled for wall mounting, but you can purchase the Calendar Stand ($39) if you want to situate it on a tabletop, and there’s a wooden frame ($99) you can buy to snap on to give it a nicer look.

The Greenlight Family Hub has a sleek, stylish interface that isn’t just made for family calendars and chores. It brings together various parts of the popular family finance app with the help of a calendar as a touchpoint, so it has a different feel than your typical digital wall calendar.

Greenlight started out as a tool to give your kids a debit card that you can easily track spending, and the company added chore tracking so parents could reward chores financially without needing to crack out their Venmo or have cash handy. Greenlight says parents then mentioned how they used the spending notifications to keep an eye on where their kids were, so the company added family location tracking through its apps, and launched a GPS tracker for smaller children who wouldn’t have a phone that could be tracked.

Now, Greenlight has launched the Family Hub to bring those features into a single device, plus a calendar. It’s made both for the family overall and for smaller children who don’t have a phone, so they can still use it to track their chores. The calendar aspect also works well and updates quickly to reflect changes I make on other devices, which I like.

It sounds a little Big Brother-y with all that tracking involved, but I understand the appeal as a parent who wants to be involved and keep an eye on things without expecting constant text updates. But I can feel the limitations sometimes with Greenlight’s approach to helping parents manage their kids, versus the entire family. Chores, for example, are only for children, and you can’t set up this hub without creating a child account with it. So if you’re just a married couple or household of roommates, you’ll be annoyed to list yourself as a child to use the chore tool.

But my favorite features aren’t what Greenlight is known for, at least not originally. This hub not only has free, unlimited storage for its photo screensaver, but also has the option to get voice support. That voice support is behind a paywall, requiring either $10 a month or $100 for the year, but it’s a feature I’ve long thought these devices need. It won’t connect to your smart-home devices, but will answer questions about the weather or your calendar and let you set timers, and it will prompt family members to add the parent PIN if they try to command any serious changes to the calendars or chore lists. Greenlight’s voice assistant worked well to understand my questions, but it was easy to trigger without actually saying the wake words “Hey Greenlight.”

You’ll need to make sure to follow the setup steps carefully if you don’t want to set up a financial account for your child. When I first signed up with the Greenlight app, I hit the button to create an account instead of choosing “Set up a Family Hub,” which got me stuck on the financial path. Greenlight’s support had to go in and reset my account for me, and it was spooky how fast the app pulled my legal name and information from just my phone number. Greenlight says it’s fixing this in its app so that it’s easier for people to back out and switch to hub setup only, but it’s something to look out for.

If you want a digital calendar made just for kids, Skylight has something along those lines called the Skylight Buddy. Originally it was just a chore and routine gadget, reflecting only his assigned tasks and habits from the Skylight app, but Skylight added a calendar feature so my son can now see the events tagged onto his personal calendar.

Even without the calendar feature, my 4-year-old loves his 7-inch Buddy, and it really does help get him to brush his teeth and put on his PJs in a timely (well, more timely) fashion now that it’s in his room. It also has a night-light and sound machine, but the sounds are limited, and the night-light is pretty dim. So for those capabilities, I’m sticking to the Hatch Baby my son is used to and loves.

Ultimately, this is most useful if you already have and use a Skylight Calendar, but now that it acts as a calendar itself, it can definitely be a stand-alone gadget. It highlights the routines front and center, but also makes it easy to see what events are coming up that day. My son’s schedule isn’t very busy at his age, nor can he even read his calendar invites at this point, but it’s a great add-on to an already useful device.

There are subscription options to get more features—Buddy Plus is $39 a year, and Skylight Plus is $79 a year. Skylight Plus is what you should get if you have the larger Calendar, as it unlocks paywalled features for the Buddy and Calendar devices. But I haven’t needed any subscription-only capabilities to keep my son excited about and engaged in his bedtime routine.

Apolosign’s digital calendar has three sizes: 15.7, 21.5, and 27 inches. It runs Google’s Android OS, so it operates very similarly to an Android tablet and to Google’s Pixel Tablet, if you’ve used either as a smart display, as I have. The Apolosign has two modes: Calendar and Android. Calendar mode worked similarly to Skylight. I seamlessly connected it to my Google Calendar, imported over most of my various shared calendars, and color-coded them.

The Calendar mode has a left-side menu bar (you’ll have to tap to make it appear), with sections for Home, Calendar, Routines, To-Dos, Rewards, and Meals. The Home page has a two-column design, showing you the calendar on one side and your Routines and To-Dos on the other. You can then tap into any of these sections or check off items directly from the Home page. Apolosign also has baked-in notifications that chime to remind you about calendar events and to-dos, plus phone notifications to let you know how many items are on your calendar that day.

WIRED Reviewer Kat Merck also tested Apolosign, but preferred Android mode to Calendar mode. Android mode allows you to customize widgets and layout, which was the only way she could see the monthly view she was used to from having a paper calendar. Android mode also lets you use photos from Google Photos as a background and screensaver. She says it’s nice to be able to customize the layout in this mode, but found that Android mode often struggles to sync with other programs, including Apolosign’s own app.

I don’t like the Apolosign experience quite as much as the Skylight or Everblog, and Kat agreed that this device is not very intuitive and takes a lot of patience to set up. But having no paywall is a huge plus, and many people will feel it’s worth getting used to the more Android-style experience to not pay a monthly or yearly fee. But since it’s essentially a large Android tablet, iPhone users have flagged on Reddit that they can’t two-way sync between it and their iPhone devices. The Apolosign is often on sale for the same price, if not cheaper, than the Skylight.

Cozyla Calendar Plus 2 (15.6 Inches) for $350: This calendar is similar to Apolosign with an Android-based operating system, but it didn’t import my shared calendars, meaning it took more work to set up. It was overall frustrating to navigate and didn’t guide me through its tools as effectively as Skylight or Apolosign. While Cozyla doesn’t have any subscription fees, its 15.6-inch size is more expensive than both Skylight’s and Apolosign’s.

Hearth Display for $629: This is another digital calendar and family tool that has a paywall with an affordable Family Membership ($6 a month) but a much higher initial price point. It’s only available in a large, 27-inch size, and I found it was slow to load my calendar and also bulky compared to more affordable options.

Digital wall calendars sync with your existing digital calendar app of choice, like Google Calendar, and display it on the physical screen. There are usually additional tools for recipes, to-do lists, and chores, but each digital wall calendar varies in how you import the information. You may have to manually import it or type the details into the device, but once you get used to the process, the function can be helpful for the whole family.

Will Changes to My Calendar Appear Instantly?

Changes you make on your native calendar app, like Google Calendar and Apple’s Calendar, should reflect quickly on the digital wall calendar device. But changes you make on the device aren’t always backward compatible with the native calendar. It depends on the calendar’s settings and how the information was shared; I can edit my primary personal calendar on the Skylight Calendar 2, for example, but I can’t edit my work calendar that I shared to the Skylight through my personal. There are also some syncing issues you may run into with the Apolosign, which doesn’t two-way sync with an iPhone since the digital calendar runs on an Android operating system.

How Is a Digital Calendar Different From a Smart Display?

Many smart displays look similar to these devices but have an entirely different operating system. Sure, the Google Pixel Tablet has some overlap with the Apolosign and Cozyla, since they all run an Android operating system. But unlike smart displays, digital calendar devices are designed with specific tools to run your family and none of the clutter. You’ll lose out on smart-home support, though Apolosign claims you can use Google Assistant on it (that hasn’t worked for me so far). On most devices, you’ll also compromise on extras like video streaming (you can, however, stream on Everblog). But as someone who uses a smart display regularly, I really didn’t miss it once I switched over to the digital calendar device. I do wish there were a weather-report page, as most digital wall calendars just show the current weather.

No—in fact, most of these devices come with a table-stand option. I only tested in table-stand mode since I had multiple of these devices in my house at one time, but the wall-mounting option is nice, allowing you to keep your tabletops clear. The 15-inch models are great for tabletops, and you may want to consider larger sizes for the wall-mounting route.

#314. Report: Apple’s antitrust negotiations with the DOJ spark concerns of a weak settlement

The Information reports that PayPal and Epic Games are among the developers concerned that a potential antitrust settlement between Apple and the DOJ might not go far enough in addressing the company’s allegedly anticompetitive practices. Here are the details.

A few months ago, Bloomberg reported that Apple and the DOJ were in talks to settle a 2024 antitrust lawsuit alleging that the company illegally monopolized the US smartphone market at the expense of consumers, developers, and competitors.

When the DOJ first filed the lawsuit, Apple pledged to “vigorously” defend itself and has continued to push back against the government’s allegations ever since.

Despite Bloomberg’s report about settlement talks, the case has continued to move forward, with Apple and the DOJ recently clashing over access to internal documents from federal agencies during discovery.

However, as The Information reported today, settlement talks have also continued behind the scenes, with the Justice Department apparently prioritizing iPhone interoperability.

According to the report, the “department appears to be focusing on a deal addressing interoperability issues developers face with the iPhone,” although developers are concerned that any resulting settlement might impose only limited restrictions on Apple’s practices.

As part of its talks with developers, the Justice Department has asked them for a list of ways to improve the iPhone’s ability to operate with other devices, the people said.Many developers and antitrust lawyers are concerned that the Justice Department will oﬀer Apple a settlement that imposes relatively light requirements on how its devices interact with other companies’ devices.”

According to The Information, PayPal and Epic Games are among the developers that have directly raised concerns about a potential settlement with DOJ officials.

Meanwhile, some people involved in the settlement negotiations reportedly expected a resolution much sooner, although the pending Senate confirmation of Adam Candeub, Trump’s nominee to lead the DOJ’s antitrust division, could be contributing to the delay.

The report adds that Apple has changed some of its products and policies since the DOJ brought the lawsuit in 2024, including improving messaging interoperability with Android devices, but is likely to resist more substantial changes to its ecosystem, potentially complicating efforts to reach a settlement.

Asked about the discussions, a DOJ spokesperson declined to comment on the specifics, saying only that the department would “continue to prioritize affordability for all Americans across our economy.” Other companies mentioned in the report, including PayPal and Epic Games, declined to comment, while Apple didn’t respond.

#315. Changing Your Career Isn’t Easy

But finding examples for your work will help you weather the change

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

When I changed careers at 30 to become a software engineer, I expected it to be hard. I expected to struggle to fit in, and I expected to bomb a lot of interviews (I did). What I didn’t expect was how few people would support me.

A career change is a risk, and the people who care about you tend to project their fears onto you. They don’t want to watch you struggle or fail, so they discourage you or just don’t offer much enthusiasm.

Right now is a strange time to be in engineering, or knowledge work in general. Plenty of us are excited about what AI means for our jobs. More of us are nervous, and I think that fear is justified. Employment for entry-level software developers has fallen nearly 20 percent since late 2022, according to Stanford’s 2026 AI Index, and it can feel like the knowledge we spent our careers building is being commoditized.

Lately I’ve seen a flood of social media content telling software developers to go into the trades. YouTubers are telling you to become a plumber or a goat herder.

But before you do that, I want to warn you, there is no EASY path. Even if you want to become a goat herder.

I’ve changed careers once so far, but my business has forced me through several pivots that felt a lot like career changes—new audiences, new skills, new identity. Here’s what I’d tell anyone considering a change, whether you’re moving into engineering, leaving it, or finding a new speciality.

This is exactly what I told my oldest son, who’s getting ready to enter the job market full-time. Outside of the primary social media feeds, the internet is full of free and paid communities on Facebook, LinkedIn, and other sites. Reddit works, too, if you can stomach the trolls, because there’s valuable information buried in there.

Many of these spaces are flooded with people trying to break in, so look for the ones full of people who already do the work and talk openly about what is and isn’t going well. Then find one or two people in your own circle who’ve done it and ask what the job takes.

You’ll often find the degree matters less than you assumed. Indeed Hiring Lab found the share of U.S. postings requiring a bachelor’s degree fell from 20.4 percent in 2019 to 17.8 percent in early 2024, and more than half listed no education requirement at all.

Yes, you’ll probably need to do some work for free, or at least far cheaper than you’re used to. I’ve had to do this in my business over and over. Nobody cares that I’ve been a software engineer for 12 years. They want to know whether I can do the thing they need.

When I started pitching businesses, I offered to build something for free as a case study, then used it to land clients who paid well. You can copy this in most fields. Say you want to get into marketing: Learn how Facebook ads work, find a friend or small business that needs help, and run the campaigns at a low price. Now you’ve picked up the jargon, and you have something concrete to show a hiring manager.

It may be corny, but change is the only constant. If you’re a software engineer, you could argue you’re in the middle of a career change already, whether you opted in or not. Programmers in the 1990s had the same experience when the web showed up and they had to quickly learn new tools just to stay relevant.

If you’re looking for stability, you’re in the wrong place, and I think it will get scarcer as AI and other forces reshape work. The best move is to build a strong foundation so you can adapt when the ground shifts. I wrote about the foundational skills to focus on if you’re interested.

Roboticist Barbara Mazzolai is a prime example of someone who advanced her career by switching fields—and now, she’s helping to create a new one. Learn how her background in biology led her to co-author a manifesto on “sustainability robotics.”

The transition from a technical role to a leadership position can be challenging. To help seasoned professionals navigate the shift, IEEE is hosting its first International Leadership Conference in Budapest.

Every year, IEEE recognizes engineers whose technical achievements and leadership have made a lasting impact with its Technical Field Awards. See who’s on the 2027 list of awardees, which was announced in late September.

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, an online education platform that helps people break into AI and modern software roles through project-based learning and one-on-one mentorship with senior developers. #316. This Apple Watch Series 10 Is $120 Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon has dropped the 46mm Apple Watch Series 10 (GPS + Cellular) to $679 from $799, taking $120 off this titanium model. Although it's no longer Apple's newest smartwatch, the Series 10 still has plenty going for it, with PCMag giving it an "outstanding" rating and an Editors' Choice award, along with naming it the best Apple smartwatch of 2024. Much of its appeal comes down to the design, which is thinner and more comfortable than the Series 9, with a larger always-on OLED display that gives you more room to read notifications and messages without making the watch feel particularly bulky. The titanium case also gives it a more polished appearance than most smartwatches, especially if you plan to wear it beyond workouts.

The cellular connectivity is particularly useful if you like leaving your iPhone behind occasionally, since an active carrier plan lets you make calls, reply to messages, stream music, and receive notifications directly on the watch, even when your phone isn't nearby—in practice, that means your phone can stay on the kitchen counter during a morning jog or a quick trip to the corner store, and you’ll still be able to pick up a call from work or reach someone if something goes wrong. It also supports Apple Music playback through its built-in speaker, though you'll probably want to connect wireless headphones for longer listening sessions.

The watch is just as capable as a health tracker, logging your heart rate and sleep, taking ECG and blood oxygen readings, and using its accelerometer to spot breathing disturbances overnight that could point to sleep apnea. Swimmers get a depth gauge and water temperature sensor as well, handy for seeing whether you’ve drifted a few feet below the surface while snorkeling or how chilly the lake is once you’re in. As for battery life, PCMag recorded around 36 hours in testing (though using LTE regularly can drain it faster), which is decent for an always-on smartwatch but still falls short of the Apple Watch Ultra 2. You’ll also need an iPhone to use it, since the Series 10 doesn’t work with Android devices.

#317. Tmux and Claude Code: Sessions, Send-Keys, and the Ceiling

A working tmux setup for running Claude Code and other AI agents: session-per-project naming, pane layouts, send-keys for scripting an agent, capture-pane for reading one back, and the status-line monitor. Plus the limits you hit at four agents.

tmux runs your AI coding agents in named, detachable sessions that survive a closed terminal or a dropped SSH connection. You get one window holding many agents, send-keys to type into any of them from a script, and capture-pane to read one back. That combination is why people use it.

Before you build any of it by hand, check the built-in path: recent versions of Claude Code can create the worktree and the tmux session for you with claude --worktree --tmux. This guide covers that first, then everything it doesn’t reach, then the point where tmux itself stops.

A coding agent is a long-running process that wants to keep talking to a terminal. Three properties of tmux match that shape:

It survives disconnection. The tmux server owns the pty, not your terminal window. Close the window, lose your SSH link, put the laptop to sleep: the agent keeps working and is still there when you reattach.

It holds many sessions in one window. Four agents become four named sessions you switch between with a keystroke, instead of four windows you hunt for in the app switcher.

It’s scriptable from outside. Any shell, anywhere, can type into a running agent or read its screen. No IPC to build, no API to wire up. This is the property people build on, and it’s why tmux keeps showing up in agent-orchestration scripts.

Claude Code ships with this wired up for the single-agent-on-a-branch case. Two flags, from claude --help on a recent version:

So the whole “isolate this task, give it its own session” move is one command:

Two details matter before you rely on it. --tmux errors without --worktree, so it’s a worktree feature that happens to make a session, not a general session flag. And on iTerm2 it uses native panes instead of tmux, which is nicer to look at and means the tmux commands in the rest of this page have nothing to attach to. Pass --tmux=classic when you want real tmux underneath, which you do if you plan to script against the session.

For a single agent on a single branch, that’s the answer. Use it and skip ahead.

What it doesn’t do: run several agents in one session, lay out panes so you can watch them, let you type into a running agent from a script, tell you which agent is waiting on you, or set any of this up on a remote box over SSH. Those are the rest of this guide, and each one is where people end up writing tmux by hand.

More on the worktree half of that flag in git worktrees for parallel development.

The organizing rule that keeps this usable: one tmux session per repo, named after the repo. Not per task, not per agent. Tasks come and go; the project is the stable thing.

-A is attach-or-create. It makes a single command safe to run repeatedly, which is what you want in a shell function:

Session names can’t contain . or : (tmux uses them as target separators), hence the tr.

Inside a session, give each agent its own window, named for the task:

Windows are better than panes for agents you’re not actively watching, because a window costs no screen space. Panes are for the two or three you want side by side right now:

#{pane_current_path} is easy to leave off. Without it a new pane opens in the directory the session started in, not the directory you’re actually in, and the agent you launch there is pointed at the wrong repo.

Two layouts by name: tiled for an even grid of agents, and main-vertical for one big pane (the agent you’re driving) with the rest stacked beside it.

Percentage values for main-pane-width need tmux 3.2 or newer. On older builds use an absolute column count (main-pane-width 120). Check with tmux -V.

These are the lines that matter for agent work specifically. They’re not a full config, they’re the delta from defaults that a fleet of agents makes you want.

Agent TUIs like to set the terminal title, so without allow-rename off your carefully named auth window becomes whatever the agent felt like calling itself.

escape-time 10 fixes the “my arrow keys are laggy inside the agent” complaint. The default delay exists to disambiguate a real Escape key from an escape sequence, and it makes interactive TUIs feel mushy.

send-keys types into a pane as if you were at the keyboard. This is how you script an agent from cron, from a git hook, or from another agent.

Three things go wrong here, in order of how often:

Bare arguments get interpreted as key names. Enter, C-c, Escape, and Space are keys, not text. If your prompt contains one of those words as a standalone argument it gets sent as a keypress. Use -l to send a literal string:

-l disables key-name lookup entirely, so the newline has to be a second call.

Semicolons end the tmux command. A trailing ; in your text is read as a command separator. Escape it as \;.

Agent TUIs need a beat between the text and the newline. Many agent input boxes debounce or re-render on paste, and an Enter arriving in the same frame as the text gets swallowed. The reliable pattern:

Interrupting a runaway agent is the same mechanism:

capture-pane dumps a pane’s contents to stdout. It’s the read half of the pair.

-J matters more than it looks. Without it, a line that wrapped at your terminal width comes back as two lines, and every grep you write against the output is wrong at the seams.

For a continuous log rather than a snapshot, pipe-pane streams everything a pane produces to a command:

-o toggles, so running it twice turns it off. The output is raw, escape sequences and all, so pipe it through something like sed -E 's/\x1b\[[0-9;]*[a-zA-Z]//g' if you want it readable later.

Every person who runs several agents in tmux eventually builds this: a status line that tells you which agents are working and which are waiting.

The mechanism is #() in the status line, which runs a shell command and interpolates its output, refreshed every status-interval seconds.

And the script, which capture-scrapes each pane for a sign of life:

It works, and it’s worth building. Be clear-eyed about what it’s doing: string matching against a TUI’s rendered frame, on a five-second poll, for every pane you have open. The match strings are whatever your agent version happens to print this week.

The lighter-weight version uses tmux’s own activity tracking instead of scraping. monitor-silence fires an alert when a pane produces no output for N seconds, which is the closest native signal to “this agent stopped”:

Silence is a proxy for done, not a report of it. An agent thinking hard about a large file is silent too.

The tmux server is just a process owned by your user. Nothing about tmux makes it survive a reboot, and a session’s scrollback is lost when the server stops. If the transcript matters, pipe-pane it to a file or use a tool that persists history on its own.

One detail people trip on: a detached session’s panes are sized to the last client that was attached, or to 80x24 if there never was one. An agent TUI rendering into an 80-column pane while you’re away will look wrong when you reattach at 200 columns, until it redraws. set-window-option -g aggressive-resize on helps when several clients are attached at different sizes.

This is where tmux is genuinely hard to replace. Running agents on a remote box, over a link you don’t trust:

Your connection drops mid-task, you run the same command again, and you’re back in the same session with the agent still going. Pair it with mosh if your link is bad enough that SSH itself keeps dying.

The nested-tmux problem: if you run tmux locally and also on the remote box, both grab the same prefix. The two fixes are a different prefix on the remote (set -g prefix C-a), or pressing the prefix twice, which bind C-b send-prefix gives you.

For running agents on a machine that isn’t the one in front of you, see remote development.

tmux is good software. It solves multiplexing and persistence about as well as those can be solved, and it has been doing it since 2007. What it doesn’t do is anything specific to agents, because agents didn’t exist when its model was designed.

No visibility into which agent is parked. An agent waiting on an approval prompt looks exactly like an agent thinking, which looks exactly like an agent that finished twenty minutes ago. All three are “a pane with some text in it”. The status-line hack above exists to paper over this, and it papers by scraping.

No notification when one finishes. monitor-silence is the nearest thing, and it fires on any quiet pane for any reason. There is no event for “the agent is done” because tmux has no idea what an agent is.

Screen scraping is brittle by construction. capture-pane gives you the rendered frame: spinners, box drawing, truncated columns, ANSI. Not what the agent said, not which tool it called, not whether that call succeeded. Every parser you write against it breaks when the agent ships a UI change.

No shared state across sessions. Two agents in two tmux sessions have no way to see each other. If you want one to read another’s transcript or hand off work, you build that yourself, out of files and locks and polling.

Scrollback for several streaming agents is expensive. history-limit 100000 across a dozen panes of agent output is real memory, held per pane for as long as the server lives, and gone the moment it does. See terminal emulators for AI agents for why the rendering side of this gets costly too.

Nothing survives a reboot. Every session, every transcript, gone.

None of these are flaws. They are the edge of a tool built to multiplex shells for one person at a keyboard.

crystl is a macOS terminal built for the workload tmux was not shaped for: many agents at once, most of them off-screen, each one occasionally needing you.

The differences map almost one-to-one onto the list above.

The recommendation: keep tmux. It’s still the right answer for remote boxes, for long-running processes on servers, and for anything where the SSH link is the fragile part. Use it for that. When the thing you’re managing is six agents that each need a decision from you at an unpredictable moment, the problem stopped being multiplexing.

More on the organizing side of this in managing multiple AI coding sessions, and on keeping agents working rather than idle in running AI coding agents for longer.
