#357. iPhone Duo launch is a massive success, but Apple has a problem

iPhone Duo pre-orders opened today, but if you weren’t there right at the start, you likely now can’t get one before 2027. That makes the iPhone Duo launch a massive success, but also reflects a missed opportunity for Apple.

Before the iPhone Duo was unveiled last month, I was unsure how the public would respond to the new model. Would it seem too weird compared to standard iPhones? Would the $2,000+ price tag limit early adopters to tech enthusiasts like me?

Yet in my estimation, Apple has pulled off a basically flawless product introduction.

Starting with the September 9 unveiling, iPhone Duo’s marketing rollout has been among the best I’ve seen from Apple. The company knew it had a uniquely special product, and has given it the first-class treatment.

Anecdotally, iPhone Duo has stirred more excitement than any other recent model I can remember. Not just among “techie” early adopters, not just among the ultra-wealthy, and not even just among current iPhone users. Some of my Android friends even seem very interested.

All of this buzz was seemingly proven genuine by today’s near instant sell-out after pre-orders went live. Current shipping estimates for new orders are pushed back to late January 2027. That’s more than three months backordered—an unprecedented delay.

And today’s launch I think can be described both as a huge win and also a missed opportunity for Apple.

It’s remarkable that Apple was able to introduce a foldable iPhone, which costs $2,000+, and instantly sell out. It’s amazing how much interest and excitement the iPhone Duo has garnered from a wide-ranging base of “average consumers.”

But it’s also a big problem that Apple can’t deliver anywhere close to a supply-demand balance for such a desired, ultra-premium product.

It’s not a surprise that the iPhone Duo quickly became backordered. But getting pushed out three months within 30 minutes of pre-orders opening proves just how much trouble Apple has had mass-producing the Duo.

I think Apple is doing the sensible thing, they’re testing the waters. They will adjust supply alongside the existing demand. It’s a win-win for them, creating scarcity and the feeling of massive success without facing unnecessary costs if the demand slows down.

Ideally, Apple would have enough supply to meet demand. More realistically, it should be able to meet initial demand within the first 4-6 weeks or so.

But what we’re seeing is in some ways a worst-case scenario. Not just because customers will be frustrated, but chiefly because Apple is sacrificing a lot of revenue by not being able to deliver the iPhone Duo in a reasonable timeframe.

Again, overall today’s launch is a major win for Apple. But being able to capitalize more fully on its basically flawless iPhone Duo marketing plan would have been an even bigger win. Here’s hoping mass production of the iPhone Duo is able to speed up soon.

What’s your take on Apple’s iPhone Duo launch? Let us know in the comments.

#358. NYT Pips hints, answers for October 19, 2026

Welcome to your guide to Pips, the latest game in the New York Times catalog.

Released in August 2025, Pips puts a unique spin on dominoes, creating a fun single-player experience that could become your next daily gaming habit.

Currently, if you're stuck, the game only offers to reveal the entire puzzle, forcing you to move on to the next difficulty level and start over. However, we have you covered! Below are piecemeal answers that will serve as hints so that you can find your way through each difficulty level.

If you've ever played dominoes, you'll have a passing familiarity with how Pips is played. As we've shared in our previous hints stories for Pips, the tiles, like dominoes, are placed vertically or horizontally and connect with each other. The main difference between a traditional game of dominoes and Pips is the color-coded conditions you have to address. The touching tiles don't necessarily have to match.

The conditions you have to meet are specific to the color-coded spaces. For example, if it provides a single number, every side of a tile in that space must add up to the number provided. It is possible — and common — for only half a tile to be within a color-coded space.

Here are common examples you'll run into across the difficulty levels:

Number: All the pips in this space must add up to the number.

Equal: Every domino half in this space must be the same number of pips.

Not Equal: Every domino half in this space must have a completely different number of pips.

Less than: Every domino half in this space must add up to less than the number.

Greater than: Every domino half in this space must add up to more than the number.

If an area does not have any color coding, it means there are no conditions on the portions of dominoes within those spaces.

Equal (5): Everything in this space must be equal to 5. The answer is 5-4, placed vertically; 5-5, placed horizontally.Greater Than (1): Everything in this space must be greater than 1. The answer is 5-4, placed vertically.

Number (8): Everything in this space must add up to 8. The answer is 1-2, placed vertically; 6-2, placed vertically.

Number (3): Everything in this space must add up to 3. The answer is 6-2, placed vertically; 1-5, placed vertically.Greater Than (3): Everything in this space must be greater than 3. The answer is 1-5, placed vertically.

Greater Than (3): Everything in this space must be greater than 3. The answer is 4-2, placed horizontally.

Greater Than (4): Everything in this space must be greater than 4. The answer is 4-2, placed horizontally; 3-6, placed horizontally.

Number (3): Everything in this space must add up to 3. The answer is 3-4, placed vertically.

Not Equal: Everything in this space must be different. The answer is 6-1, placed horizontally; 0-4, placed horizontally.

Less Than (5): Everything in this space must be less than 5. The answer is 3-4, placed vertically.

Equal (4): Everything in this space must be equal to 4. The answer is 0-4, placed horizontally; 4-4, placed vertically.

Number (12): Everything in this space must add up to 12. The answer is 3-6, placed horizontally; 5-1, placed vertically.

Equal (4): Everything in this space must be equal to 4. The answer is 4-4, placed horizontally; 4-2, placed horizontally.Number (2): Everything in this space must add up to 2. The answer is 4-2, placed horizontally.Greater Than (11): Everything in this space must be greater than 11. The answer is 3-3, placed vertically; 6-2, placed horizontally.

Greater Than (1): Everything in this space must be greater than 1. The answer is 6-2, placed horizontally.Number (10): Everything in this space must add up to 10. The answer is 5-5, placed vertically.

Number (6): Everything in this space must add up to 6. The answer is 5-3, placed horizontally; 1-6, placed vertically.

Number (6): Everything in this space must add up to 6. The answer is 1-6, placed vertically.

Number (2): Everything in this space must add up to 2. The answer is 0-2, placed horizontally.

Less Than (6): Everything in this space must be less than 6. The answer is 4-0, placed vertically.

Number (6): Everything in this space must add up to 6. The answer is 6-4, placed horizontally.

Greater Than (4): Everything in this space must be greater than 4. The answer is 6-4, placed horizontally.

This simple checklist will help protect your home

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Depending on what region you live in, the risk of floods may be a real problem for you, especially in the colder months. Heavy rain can feel like its come out of nowhere, so it's best to be prepared.

While you can track rain patterns on weather apps and from regional news, it's a much better idea to get ahead of the weather entirely.

Instead, you should be doing any prep work before you're faced with flood warnings and predictions of heavy rain.

Fortunately, I've put together a 5-minute fall flood checklist that will help you prepare your home for a flood, hopefully preventing damage that'll take a lot longer to resolve.

After all, it's better to be ready even if the rain doesn't arrive than be caught out with a flood striking and creating hazards across your home.

Fall is the perfect season for your gutters and downspouts to get clogged up. Why? Well, with falling leaves and extra rain, it can concoct the ultimate mulch that will easily block the area. It's also a great breeding ground for moss to gather, too.

Grab a sturdy ladder with someone spotting you or a stabilizer at the bottom, then using a bucket and gloves, remove all the packed debris, leaves and moss that's blocking up your gutters. You should do this once or twice during the fall, especially around November and December as that's when most trees lose their leaves.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Around your home, you may have nearby trees and shrubs that are your responsibility to trim down to prevent excessive foliage falling to the ground – and, as already discussed, into your gutters. This can also cause a problem for any exterior drains you have.

So, you should prune back trees and shrubs to minimize the amounts of leaves and loose branches that pose a risk to your home. If you let everything fall to the ground or into your gutters, you're increasing the chances that rain won't drain properly away from your property.

It won't take you long at all to do a perimeter walk of your home to check for any cracks or gaps in the exterior walls, so make sure you do. If you spot any, grab some waterproof sealants or fillers to close up any gaps and cracks to prevent any water getting through.

You may need to widen any small gaps to ensure the sealants or fillers hold or call in a professional if you find anything especially bad. Hairline cracks that are less than 1/16 of an inch though are generally considered cosmetic, so you can leave these alone. But, it's important to note down where they are and keep an eye on them incase they get any worse.

Not all homes have sump pumps, but if you have one in your basement, you should incorporate testing it into your 5-minute fall flood home check. Simply pour water (around one or two 5-gallon buckets worth, or run a hose) into the pit to test that the float switch is working and that the pump then activates and drains the water out of the basin.

Then, confirm that the water level has fully dropped back down to the bottom and that the sump pump has turned off. You'll most likely be able to listen for this as the motor will stop running.

With your sump pump in order, basement flooding risk can be greatly reduced, and the need for a dehumidifier.

We gave GoveeLife's 50-pint dehumidifier a 4-star review, which is why we recommend it as the top product in our best dehumidifier buying guide. It’s a powerful appliance that can handle large spaces (up to 4,500 square feet), and for ease of use, it can be controlled through an app.

Even after all your home checks, you may still want to protect your valuables from any risk of floods and to do that, you can quickly move anything of value to the highest floor of your home or even the attic.

Of course, you don't need to live with your valuables up high at all times, but if you receive a warning from the National Weather Service or hear of any extreme weather, you should at least have a plan in place about what you choose to move.

#360. A Tesla Flying Car? I Don’t Know, Man

Where is my flying car? The enduring question sort of, kind of, might have an answer: In McGregor, Texas.

On Thursday, Tesla showed off a version of its new Roadster 2 sports car in a demonstration at SpaceX’s rocket development testing facility. And in its own way, with an awkward jerking maneuver, the Roadster flew a few dozen feet. The vehicle, which doesn’t yet have a price but is likely to be very expensive, is slated to go into production in 2028. The vehicle didn’t have a human occupant during the demo “to make sure we don’t kill anyone,” Tesla CEO Elon Musk said at the event.

Tesla’s Roadster “sort of, kind of, might” be an actual flying car because aviation experts say legally catching air in the vehicle will likely involve plenty of government permissions and red tape.

The Federal Aviation Administration “has jurisdiction over any machine that leaves the surface of the earth,” says Scott Miller, an airline pilot and a lecturer in the Aviation and Technology program at San José State University. The vehicle “is going to introduce a whole set of regulatory issues.”

At the event Thursday, Musk acknowledged as much. “I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions," he said. “This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car.”

In a written statement, FAA spokesperson Rick Breitenfeldt said, "The Tesla vehicle does not meet the FAA's definition of an aircraft."

Any flying vehicle that weighs more than 250 or so pounds would need to go through an FAA approval process and require clearance to operate in the national airspace, says Michael McCormick, a former FAA official who now heads the Air Traffic Management program at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Getting that certification, he predicts, could take “at least a year.” Your standard driver's license, meanwhile, wouldn’t cut it. Any Tesla owner piloting such a vehicle would likely have to obtain a recreational aviation license.

Actually taking off and landing the Roadster 2 would likely present its own set of issues. Most states require aircraft to take off from airports or designated helipads. Launching from the road to the air would fall under state or local rules, says Miller, and many places do not look kindly on the concept of sudden aircraft intrusions on their streets and highways. That’s the reason “it’s pretty rare to be able to jump in a helicopter and land at your favorite steakhouse to have a steak,” he says. Drivers might only be able to truly operate the vehicle on a large, private piece of land.

The FAA today is working on rules, regulations, and pilot projects around another sort of “flying car,” or what’s more commonly known as an electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) vehicle. These aircraft use several smaller electric motors and propellers to carry up to four passengers between 20 and 150 miles, sometimes autonomously. The companies building the technology envision them taking off from small, local “vertipads,” allowing riders to skip urban traffic by floating above the fray.

The Trump administration this year launched a limited, three-year pilot project using the aircraft, where companies are able to test the tech in several states. It has taken years for the companies to receive certifications from the federal government.

When it comes to the Roadster 2, there are practical questions, too. True flying cars have struggled to take off because of the physics-led contradiction at the heart of the idea. What makes a car safe and durable enough to operate on roads is weight. But “weight is the enemy of an airplane,” says Miller. “Flying cars haven’t been able to find that balance of power versus weight.”

Still, Miller found himself impressed by Thursday’s demo. “If this does make it into production, that is a truly impressive engineering and production feat,” he says.

Updated on October 16 at 1:50 pm ET: We've added an official statement from the FAA.

#366. The Tesla Roadster 2 Is Here—and It Flies

On Thursday night, Tesla and CEO Elon Musk unveiled what’s been billed as the company’s last human-driven car. Maybe human-piloted is a more accurate way to say it.

At a demonstration event in McGregor, Texas—at SpaceX’s rocket development and testing facility—the new car did what Musk has long promised. With a herky-jerky burst of steam, it flew into the air. At one point, the car appeared to flip over the automaker’s entire line-up, floating several feet over its electric semi-truck. Tesla executives said the vehicle could accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in one second.

“This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car,” Musk said. (It’s also likely to raise the eyebrows of federal regulators.)

Tesla says it will begin production on the Roadster 2 in 2028. Fans have waited a long time for the vehicle. The Roadster 2—the successor to Tesla’s first vehicle, the Roadster—was first announced in 2017, and at the time Tesla said the new sports car would be the fastest production vehicle in the world.

The “flying” technology is enabled by four thrusters, Tesla vehicle engineering head Lars Moravy said. He said the production version would “hopefully” travel up to 230 miles per hour, though Musk said he hoped to “crack halfway to the speed of sound”—around 385 mph. Modern Formula 1 vehicles usually top out around 220 mph. The company said the vehicle would travel more than 300 miles on one charge, middling for a mainstream EV and lower than most luxury vehicles. Tesla’s own Model 3 can travel up to 360 miles on a charge.

Tesla said the thrusters are powered by onboard compressed gas. Musk said that the same technology that allows the vehicle to fly will also create downward force that allows the vehicle to turn corners very quickly. “It’s going to crush every track record that has ever existed,” he said.

The company initially promised the Roadster 2 would ship in 2020. On Thursday, the Tesla team did mention the new timeline, but did not mention what the new car will cost. Musk has a long history of not following through on his loftiest product ambitions, and timelines for many Tesla releases have repeatedly missed targets.

The company posted on X that the Roadster 2 would come in three variants: a two-seater “Performance” road-ready version that lacks the thrusters Tesla showed off on Thursday; a “race ready” Thrust variant; and an “air ready” Rocket variant that has only one seat. The Tesla website lists the Rocket as “invite only” and the Thrust as “limited.” You can currently only place reservations for the Performance and Thrust versions.

When it was first announced, enthusiasts put down $50,000 deposits for what was advertised as a $200,000 car. (That deposit is worth more than $68,000 in 2026 dollars.) Some got sick of waiting. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman complained on X last year that he had trouble canceling his reservation. Musk posted that Altman received a refund in 24 hours.

A reservation page posted on Tesla’s site now charges a $5,000 reservation fee for the Performance variant, with an additional $45,000 due within 10 days. The Thrust is available for an initial $5,000 fee, with $245,000 due within 10 days.

Musk has said that Tesla should no longer be regarded as a carmaker and that the company is focused on building autonomous vehicle technology and robots.

The unveiling event comes at a weird time for electric vehicles. Sales of EVs have stalled in the US after the GOP-led Congress nixed federal support. Meanwhile, the global energy crisis has EV sales booming elsewhere. Electric luxury hypercars—the class to which the Roadster 2 belongs—are in an especially tricky spot. Several luxury automakers have said that wealthy buyers are now looking for the sound and power of a typical gas-powered vehicle. Lamborghini shelved its plans to make an EV earlier this year.

#367. iPhone 18 Pro one month later: These features keep impressing me

I’ve had the iPhone 18 Pro for about a month now, and during that time three main features have consistently impressed me.

When Apple introduced the iPhone 18 Pro, it compared its battery life to that of the iPhone 17 Pro Max—a model universally praised for its impressive runtime.

After a month of use, iPhone 18 Pro’s battery truly is top-tier. I never even think about charging it during the day, and at the end of almost every day I have about 60% battery left.

I can’t even imagine what I’d end the day with if I had the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max. Suffice to say, Apple’s battery upgrades this year are excellent, and anyone with an older model iPhone should be very happy regardless of which Pro size you choose.

Apple makes the iPhone’s cameras better every year. But it’s actually not too often that the Main camera improves substantially. In the last couple years, for example, Apple has focused more on upgrading the Telephoto, Ultra Wide, and Front cameras.

But iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera with variable aperture is the star this year, and I’ve been loving it.

I don’t have professional photography training, so the addition of pro controls isn’t appealing to me. And I never manually change apertures with the camera. But just using the ‘Auto’ setting, I keep taking photos that look especially great to me. Most of the time they’re  ƒ/1.48, with some ƒ/1.8 thrown in too. And while I don’t have the expertise to describe why they look so good to me, I’ll just say I’ve been very happy with the camera.

Just so everyone knows, on any iPhone from the 13 forward Apple can replace your battery for under $100 at the genius bar, and your battery life will become amazing again. Since release, I've had 2 batteries put in my 13 Pro, most recently in August, and it lasts over a day in general use.

Total cost for 2 batteries in 6 years? Just over $150. Saved me from buying at least 1 new phone. (Although Duo2 next year is looking promising)

I use my iPhone outdoors a lot, on frequently sunny days, and iPhone 18 Pro’s vapor chamber has been a welcome upgrade in keeping the iPhone usable.

Previous iPhone models would often struggle out in the elements, especially on warm, bright days. This proved especially frustrating when I was trying to capture a special moment with the Camera app and my warm iPhone was too sluggish to snap the photo.

With iPhone 18 Pro, while it still occasionally gets slightly warm, I’ve never noticed a delay in performance as a result. Instead, the vapor chamber keeps everything cool enough to deliver the iPhone experience I expect.

Do you have an iPhone 18 Pro? What are your favorite features? Let us know in the comments.

#368. A Brief History of the Bloomberg Terminal

It gave Wall Street traders and analysts an unprecedented window on global markets

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

This early 1990s keyboard for the Bloomberg Terminal featured a trackball, speaker, and headphone and microphone ports.

Financial markets have always relied on timely information, and the drive for timeliness has always adapted to the latest technology. From clipper ships transiting the oceans to telegraph wires connecting cities to fiber-optic cables conducting trades in microseconds, traders have embraced any advantage to get the most up-to-date information. Indeed, the history of finance is really a story about how fast you can move information and who controls the interface.

It’s only natural that people also figured out a way to profit by supplying that market intel. In 1841, for example, the Mercantile Exchange (predecessor to Dun & Bradstreet) began selling proprietary business information to its U.S. clients. The following decade, Paul Julius Reuter began selling news services and stock price information. To supplement the company’s telegraph dispatches, he sent pigeons between Aachen, Germany, and Brussels; each bird carried a cylinder containing slips of paper with that day’s stock prices. In 1867, an inventor named Edward Calahan introduced the first telegraphic ticker-tape machine, which spooled out stock price information in near real time; Thomas Edison improved upon the design with his patented version in 1871.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average debuted in 1896 as an index of 12 key businesses listed on U.S. stock exchanges. It included gas, oil, coal, and electric companies, as well as enterprises dealing in leather, rubber, and tobacco. Messengers delivered quotes from the trading floor to brokerage offices, while stock tickers kept investors informed of prices. By the time New York City held its first official ticker-tape parade, in 1919, telegraphy in Western Europe and the United States had become the chief means for quick transmission of vital stock information.

In 1960, the first paperless financial service debuted, when Quotron introduced its electronic screens for displaying market quotes. Over the next two decades, other companies rolled out similar innovations for distributing financial news and data.

So when Michael Bloomberg decided to enter this well-established industry in 1981, the big question was: How would his new company stand out?

Bloomberg had cofounded Innovative Market Systems (IMS) after being fired from the investment bank Salomon Brothers. Landing on his feet with his US $10 million equity payout and joined by former Salomon colleagues Thomas Secunda, Duncan MacMillan, and Charles Zegar, Bloomberg pursued his belief that Wall Street would pay a premium for specialized financial data. He’d earned an electrical engineering degree from Johns Hopkins University and an MBA from Harvard, and he’d built computerized financial systems for Salomon. IMS focused on developing a computer terminal that not only provided up-to-date information but could also do instant quantitative analysis based on historical data.

Michael Bloomberg believed Wall Street would pay a premium for access to specialized financial data. Karjean Levine/Getty Images

At the time, most financial data still circulated through telephone calls, printed price sheets, and specialist publications, and analysis involved a fair amount of gut instinct guided by human expertise. Companies such as Reuters and Dow Jones provided subscription-based services for access to business news. But traders still had to assemble information from multiple sources and perform their own calculations and analysis.

IMS proposed an integrated system with a single interface. Its Market Master terminal consisted of a monochrome CRT monitor, a custom keyboard, and a communications/controller unit that connected to the company’s private network. At launch, it provided only U.S. government bond prices and bond-calculation tools, but the dream was much bigger: a dedicated terminal that would sit on a trader’s desk and run different market scenarios, produce yield curves, and support investment calculations.

IMS initially had just one client, Merrill Lynch, which invested $30 million (about $110 million today) in exchange for a 30 percent stake in the company and exclusive rights to the terminals for five years; Merrill waived that right in 1984. The first 22 Market Master terminals were delivered to Merrill in 1982, in the middle of a global recession. The timing was fortuitous. Worldwide, stock markets were transitioning to electronic trading, and the U.S. Federal Reserve was allowing more freely floating interest rates. Bond prices were more volatile, and investors were eager to figure out how to value them accurately. Bloomberg’s specialized financial terminals provided the data and the analytical tools to process and comprehend those sweeping changes.

Five years after its launch, IMS rebranded as Bloomberg LP and expanded its clientele, and the Market Master became known as the Bloomberg Terminal.

The Bloomberg Terminal’s keyboard was designed with traders and analysts in mind. The function keys were color-coded and given labels specifying their usage, so that users didn’t have to remember. The original keyboard, affectionately referred to as “the Chiclet,” was hand assembled. A cable ran from the keyboard to the Bloomberg Controller, which had a dedicated phone line to connect to a local hub. The internet wasn’t commercially available yet, so the company basically built its own closed network, with centralized computers that maintained large databases and performed most of the calculations. Commands entered on the keyboard sent a request to the hub, which processed the information and sent back the result.

The Chiclet keyboard for the Bloomberg Terminal was introduced around 1983. Although it looks like a generic keyboard, its function keys were finance-specific hot keys.National Museum of American History/Smithsonian Institution

Hot keys let traders easily call up data on government securities, corporate debt, and currency markets, among other things. A series of keystrokes would pull up other historical and real-time data, run an analysis, or place a trade. Learning how to use the terminal and digest the vast amount of information, which was presented mostly in tabular form, became a rite of passage for users.

In 1990, Bloomberg added a trackball to the keyboard, which helped the user navigate the multiple windows and menus typically displayed on screen. Two years later, the keyboard gained a built-in speaker, to support multimedia information; this design also included telephone, headphone, and microphone jacks. One of the most popular features was Instant Bloomberg, which allowed users to chat directly with fellow Bloomberg Terminal users over the proprietary network. By 1996, Bloomberg had keyboards that supported 23 different languages. In the early 2000s, the company began incorporating biometric authentication for terminal login, via a fingerprint reader on the keyboard.

As the company’s business model evolved, the Bloomberg Terminal added services well beyond its initial offerings. In 1990, for example, worried that Dow Jones would stop providing access to its news stories, Bloomberg set up its own news service. It recruited Wall Street Journal reporter Matthew Winkler to oversee a dozen reporters; their stories on market and securities movements used graphs and calculations that served as advertisements for the terminal’s capabilities. These days, the Bloomberg news empire includes Bloomberg Businessweek, Bloomberg Radio, and Bloomberg Television.

Bloomberg’s subscription-based financial model included the leasing of a Bloomberg Terminal with its specialized keyboard and other hardware, access to a dedicated private network, and a suite of services. In 1999, a subscription to a single Bloomberg Terminal cost $1,600 per month with a minimum two-year contract and a discount on each additional terminal. Today the annual price is upwards of $32,000 (trending a little below inflation). In 1995, the company launched a suite of “Open Bloomberg” software products that ran on the customer’s own PC; five years later, it stopped leasing dedicated terminals. Current customers also have access to mobile applications that allow terminal functions to run on phones and tablets. Today, “Bloomberg Terminal” has come to refer to the integrated data, analytics, news, communications, and trading environment.

Although the shift away from dedicated terminals was a logical response to the rise of the internet and publicly available market data, it altered the material culture of financial work. For nearly two decades, Bloomberg Terminals commanded an aura of power and financial prowess. They were emblems of market mastery, with a brand that was distinct from other office computers. With Open Bloomberg, users were no longer tied to a single desk or a fixed set of monitors.

And so, cast-off Bloomberg Terminals found their way into museum collections. They’re a physical embodiment of the ethereal nature of financial markets, and a manifestation of mathematical calculations, network infrastructure, and business culture.

The Bloomberg keyboard used by “Bond King” Bill Gross has his login and password taped on the front.National Museum of American History/Smithsonian Institution

The Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of American History has a number of Bloomberg keyboards in its collection, but my favorite is object number 2014.0012.02, which was used by “Bond King” Bill Gross during the 1990s and 2000s at Pacific Investment Management. Gross had cofounded PIMCO in 1971 and built it into a $2 trillion bond investment firm. I especially love that Gross taped his login and password directly on his keyboard, which makes the object more relatable. I may never know what it’s like to manage billions in assets from a Bloomberg Terminal, but I absolutely understand the trial of remembering my passwords.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the October 2026 print issue as “The Keyboard That Moved Markets.”

References Bloomberg Professional Services has a nice timeline showing the evolution of its keyboards.For an economic analysis of how computers like the Bloomberg Terminal changed financial markets, see Gerben Bakker’s 2025 paper “The Terminal Revolution: Reuters and Bloomberg as global providers of financial and economic news, 1960–2020,” published by the London School of Economics and Political Science.Bloomberg Terminals are in the collections of many museums, including the Computer History Museum and the National Museum of American History.

Bloomberg Professional Services has a nice timeline showing the evolution of its keyboards.

For an economic analysis of how computers like the Bloomberg Terminal changed financial markets, see Gerben Bakker’s 2025 paper “The Terminal Revolution: Reuters and Bloomberg as global providers of financial and economic news, 1960–2020,” published by the London School of Economics and Political Science.

Bloomberg Terminals are in the collections of many museums, including the Computer History Museum and the National Museum of American History.

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

Fun fact: Bond King Bill Gross, whose Bloomberg Terminal keyboard (pictured above) is now in the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, has made a number of substantial donations to the Smithsonian over the years. In particular, he funded the stamp gallery that bears his name at the National Postal Museum in Washington, D.C. https://postalmuseum.si.edu/exhibition/william-h-gross-stamp-gallery

The NYT Connections puzzle today is not too difficult if you have a short fuse.

Connections is the one of the most popular New York Times word games that's captured the public's attention. The game is all about finding the "common threads between words." And just like Wordle, Connections resets after midnight and each new set of words gets trickier and trickier—so we've served up some hints and tips to get you over the hurdle.

If you just want to be told today's puzzle, you can jump to the end of this article for today's Connections solution. But if you'd rather solve it yourself, keep reading for some clues, tips, and strategies to assist you.

The NYT's latest daily word game has become a social media hit. The Times credits associate puzzle editor Wyna Liu with helping to create the new word game and bringing it to the publications' Games section. Connections can be played on both web browsers and mobile devices and require players to group four words that share something in common.

Each puzzle features 16 words and each grouping of words is split into four categories. These sets could comprise of anything from book titles, software, country names, etc. Even though multiple words will seem like they fit together, there's only one correct answer.

If a player gets all four words in a set correct, those words are removed from the board. Guess wrong and it counts as a mistake—players get up to four mistakes until the game ends.

Players can also rearrange and shuffle the board to make spotting connections easier. Additionally, each group is color-coded with yellow being the easiest, followed by green, blue, and purple. Like Wordle, you can share the results with your friends on social media.

#370. 10 Shows Like 'Crystal Lake' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

The new streaming series Crystal Lake takes us back to the early days of the Friday the 13th franchise to explore the origins of hockey-masked killer Jason's power and fury—by focusing, once again, on his mom (Linda Cardellini). Is this backstory we needed? Probably not! But I'm happy to revisit the bloodiest (and horniest) summer camp in America. If you're looking for other like-minded horror adaptations, here are 10 chilling shows to stream next.

You want some more backstory on an iconic serial killer and his mom? Say no more. Freddie Highmore stars as Norman Bates, the character author Robert Bloch based on the real killer Ed Gein, with Vera Farmiga playing his mother Norma (in her pre-desiccated-corpse days). Norman might not have accrued nearly the body count of Jason, but he's a lot more charming. Like a lot of media spun off from Alfred Hitchcock's seminal Psycho, it's better than it has any right to be, with impressively compelling character development and several surprises, even if we already know more or less where it's headed. Stream Bates Motel on Prime Video.

More high-minded than Crystal Lake, this reboot/prequel/fresh take on the Thomas Harris novels came from Bryan Fuller, who took a first crack at the Friday series before A24 decided it wanted something a little closer to the movies than what he'd proposed. Fuller goes back to the source material here, adapting the first Lecter novel with grand, operatic style and a visual flair unmatched on network television (you're still unlikely to find more gorgeously constructed scenes of carnage). What's more, the deeper, sexier relationship between the Doctor (Mads Mikkelsen) and profiler Will Graham (Hugh Dancy) adds some brilliant subtext as the two work together to hunt serial killers. It ended a bit too early, but the three seasons still make for a satisfying meal. Stream Hannibal on Prime Video.

Just a British meta-slasher-comedy on a boat (initially). Oscar Kennedy plays Jamie Walsh, who takes a job on board a cruise ship in order to investigate the disappearance of his sister, last seen working on the same vessel. Once on board, he soon realizes that everyone is a suspect and, being that he's on a boat, there's no escape from the murderous web of conspiracy in which he's deliberately entangled himself. The show has an infectious energy that blends Agatha Christie-style mystery elements with gnarly kills among a largely queer group of suspects. Season two moves the action to an island camping retreat for the ultra-wealthy, offering up an even more explicit Friday the 13th vibe. Stream Wreck on Hulu.

Drawing inspiration from Evil Dead, Stan Against Evil stars John C. McGinley as the crotchety, obnoxious former sheriff of a New Hampshire town overrun with vengeful spirits. Janet Varney comes to town as his replacement, and the two soon realize the uneasy spirits and demons aren’t going to be quiet for much longer. The awkward chemistry between the leads is a big selling point, as are the old-school practical monster effects that harken back to the great slasher horror movies of the late '70s through the '80s. The show leans more toward funny (and it’s often very funny) than scary, but the monster effects are well done, and the show doesn’t shy away from great 80s-style gross-out gags. Stream Stan Against Evil on Shudder and AMC+.

One of our most reliable horror franchises went the series route with impressively smart results—not really surprising for fans of the tongue-in-cheek, increasingly meta film series. Zackary Arthur is Jake Wheeler, a queer teen subject to relentless bullying at school and abuse at home from his homophobic father. Jake picks up America's favorite serial-killing doll at a garage sale school art project, and Chucky begins to see the (justifiably) angry kid as a potential protégé. Before long, characters from Chucky's past pop in to complicate things, but the relationship between Jake and Chucky remains the show's beating heart. Even with its dark sense of humor and over-the-top murders, the show became an unlikely critical favorite. Stream Chucky on Peacock and Prime Video.

Each season of this series tells the story of a single serial killer and their would-be victims, stretching out a traditional slasher-movie narrative over several hours. With that time, the show (like Crystal Lake) manages to actually build lives and backstories for its characters, something that movies don’t always have time for or can't be bothered with. It works here, and each season has introduced fairly compelling characters—it doesn’t hurt that the focus is largely on adults, rather than more typical teenage victims. The whole series is excellent, but for our purposes, I'll direct your attention to season two's "Guilty Party," in which a group of former counselors returns to the scene of the crime to retrieve the body of the camper they all accidentally killed, and whose death they purposely concealed years earlier. Stream Slasher on Netflix.

Cheating just a tiny bit by including this series, technically a run of movies, but it plays so much like a miniseries as to be pretty indistinguishable. Adapted from the R. L. Stine books, Fear Street Part One: 1994 kicks off the series by introducing the town of Shadyside, which the local kids call “Shittyside,” and which has a dark history of multiple murders. A group of teens upsets the grave of a witch, kicking off the revival of a killer cult, which requires a trip back in time to truly understand. There is some legit gore and scares (it’s YA, more or less, but definitely not kids’ stuff) as Janiak pays homage to a wide range of horror movies past, particularly with an impeccable camp slasher homage in Fear Street Part Two: 1978 and then an origin tale that brings the initial trilogy to a conclusion in Fear Street Part Three: 1666. Stream Fear Street on Netflix.

Mike Flanagan never really misses, and this series has a summer camp vibe with a deeper, darker twist while rarely feeling entirely gloomy. Based on a few different YA Christopher Pike novels, it concerns a group of eight terminally ill young patients at a bucolic hospice home run by a secretive and mysterious doctor (A Nightmare on Elm Street's Heather Langenkamp). Each night the kids meet to share scary stories covering a wide range of genres and styles, with each also promising to return from beyond the grave when their time comes. It's spooky and often moving without ever being schmaltzy or precious. It was planned as more than a miniseries, so the cancellation leaves several questions unanswered—but that works in terms of the overall tone and subject matter, which grapples with unanswerable mysteries about life and death. Stream The Midnight Club on Netflix.

AHS is always wildly divisive and more or less critic-proof. The fun 1984 season is as over-the-top as you'd expect, with the show's style grounded thoroughly in the milleau of '80s slasher sequels. Starting with a prologue involving a summer camp threesome that turns into a slaughter, we jump forward 14 years to revisit the same camp with a new group of counselors, hunted this time by both the fictional Mr. Jingles (John Carroll Lynch) and the real-life Night Stalker Richard Ramirez (Zach Villa)—at least until the mid-season twist throws everything out the window. The references come fast and furious and the period vibes are exquisite. Stream American Horror Story: 1984 on Prime Video and Hulu.

How does Friday the 13th: The Series tie into the Jason mythology, you may well be asking? It doesn't—not even a little bit, sharing nothing with the film series other than a name, the presence of a couple of actors, and the involvement of producer Frank G. Mancuso Jr. And yet, this creepy, late-night gem has much to recommend it, blending an anthology format with bits of serialized storytelling and a recurring cast. The premise: Cousins Micki Foster (Louise Robey) and Ryan Dallion (John D. LeMay) inherit an antique shop from an uncle who died under mysterious circumstances that turn out to involve years of dealings with Satan that eventually went wrong. Now, the two are stuck trying to reclaim a bunch of cursed artifacts with the help of family friend and occult expert Jack (Chris Wiggins). There's no Jason, but much of the horror goes impressively hard, even if we know that our leads will (mostly) make it through to the end. And if you aren't convinced, consider this: Guest directors David Cronenberg and Atom Egoyan helmed standout episodes. Stream Friday the 13th: The Series on Fubo.

#373. Security Bite: Americans are contradicting themselves around privacy

9to5Mac Security Bite is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Making Apple devices work-ready and enterprise-safe is all we do. Our unique integrated approach to management and security combines state-of-the-art Apple-specific security solutions for fully automated Hardening & Compliance, Next Generation EDR, AI-powered Zero Trust, and exclusive Privilege Management with the most powerful and modern Apple MDM on the market. The result is a totally automated Apple Unified Platform currently trusted by over 45,000 organizations to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Americans have a privacy problem, and that shouldn’t surprise anyone. Between the unprecedented backlash around Flock cameras and, more quietly, data brokers selling off our identities, individual privacy is center stage right now. I would go as far as to make it the inaugural Security Bite ‘Theme of the Year.’

Yet despite all of that, a new survey from data removal service Incogni found that 45% of the 1,517 U.S. adults polled say they aren’t concerned about their online privacy. That wasn’t even the best part of this survey though…

Among people who said they have nothing to hide, 58% would refuse to hand a stranger their unlocked phone for any amount of money, 39% cover the camera on their phone or laptop, and nearly half wouldn’t hand over their text messages to the government or “Big Tech,” even for three months of their income.

I asked Ron Zayas, founder and CEO of Ironwall by Incogni, what’s actually going on here, and he basically replied that privacy only feels abstract until it isn’t.

The survey also found that 65% of respondents have no idea how many websites they’re registered on, and honestly, I’m not sure I could tell you mine either. We’ve all spent the last decade or so creating accounts for things we used once and forgot about, and every one of them is still holding onto something. You can’t protect data you don’t remember giving away, right?

So I asked Zayas where someone on an iPhone or Mac should start if they want to cut that down without going full underground, and his answer was more Apple-friendly than I was expecting. “Apple has some pretty good safety protocols, much better than Google in my opinion, and makes them far easier to access,” he said. “Turn off as much of ad personalization, location sharing and contact sharing as you can. It only takes a moment.” He also recommends treating your phone number like you would a credit card number. Allowing an app to have access to your contacts will also give it your own.

Zayas put it well when he said that believing you have to “go full bunker in Montana” to have any privacy is a fallacy companies push to make people feel helpless, and I agree with him. If you live in California, the CCPA and Delete Act let you force a good chunk of your data off the market for free. For everyone else, a few minutes to clean things up in Privacy & Security can go a long way. The survey honestly put it better by saying, most of us already act like our privacy matters, so we might as well stop saying it doesn’t.

Today's NYT Strands hints will be easy if you like make-believe.

Strands, the New York Times' elevated word-search game, requires the player to perform a twist on the classic word search. Words can be made from linked letters — up, down, left, right, or diagonal, but words can also change direction, resulting in quirky shapes and patterns. Every single letter in the grid will be part of an answer. There's always a theme linking every solution, along with the "spangram," a special, word or phrase that sums up that day's theme, and spans the entire grid horizontally or vertically.

By providing an opaque hint and not providing the word list, Strands creates a brain-teasing game that takes a little longer to play than its other games, like Wordle and Connections.

#375. You Can Now Join a WhatsApp Call Without an Account

The worst thing about your favorite chat app is trying to get your friends and family to use it. WhatsApp may be the most popular messaging platform in the world, but in the United States, it is hardly universally adopted. On the contrary, you'll find plenty of people who don't use it at all. In short, it's difficult to get a whole group to commit to any one platform, which can make casual video calls frustrating: If you don't use WhatsApp, and your friends are hosting a call, what are you supposed to do? You can't join a WhatsApp call without a WhatsApp account.

That's now changing. Meta, WhatsApp's parent company, announced "guest calling" on Wednesday. Now, any WhatsApp user can invite any non-WhatsApp user to a call, even if the recipient doesn't have an account. These calls still get the same core perks as traditional WhatsApp calls, Meta says: They're free and end-to-end encrypted, so you won't be compromising on your privacy by calling a non-WhatsApp user this way.

Non-WhatsApp users are still limited. Meta says these users always need a call host's approval to join. If you're a non-WhatsApp user, you'll find yourself in a waiting room until the call host lets you in. Meta also says that you can be kicked off the call at any time, and you won't be able to see other callers' phone numbers. You won't be able to send messages or add other users to the call. You are purely a participant.

If you're trying to add a non-WhatsApp user to a call, first head to the Calls tab in the app. Here, hit (+), create a call link, then send it to the recipient. Meta says the user can open the link in their computer browser, enter their name, and join. This applies to one-on-one calls as well as calls with up to 32 people. While guests will have the aforementioned limits, they do have some features available to them. They can share their screen, react with emojis, or raise their hand.

WhatsApp isn't the first chat app to offer such a feature. Apple's FaceTime platform, for example, lets you create call links that anyone can join, whether they're calling in on an Apple device or a device running Android or Windows (or Linux, for that matter).

#376. AI Hacks Leave a Mess That AI Companies Aren’t Paying For

When Philadelphia police criticized Anthropic last week for submitting a false tip about an unsolved murder, I thought it might become one of the first cases where an AI company faced legal consequences for misconduct by their agents.

The incident occurred on July 18, when Anthropic said it was testing its Claude Haiku 4.5 model’s ability to perform “example tasks on randomly selected webpages.” The model was instructed not to “submit anything destructive,” and yet, Claude filed a tip to police looking for information about an ongoing murder investigation. “I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area … during that time period,” Claude wrote. The submission, which didn’t include a name or contact information, landed in a spam folder, and officers didn’t review it until Anthropic discovered the gaffe on September 28 and notified the department October 7.

Knowingly providing fictitious information about a crime to police is a misdemeanor in Pennsylvania, but so far, authorities have not pressed charges against Anthropic, and it's unclear if they ever will. Solomon Leach, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia district attorney, says the office “does not comment on whether something is being actively investigated.”

Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Despite all the attention paid to OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face and many other examples of AI agent misbehavior that have come to light in recent months, only one major known lawsuit has been filed seeking to hold model makers liable. That case was brought by an advocacy group, rather than a direct hacking victim.

AI agents have interfered with hobbyist forums, government websites, and various software tools. The victims have shouldered some costs, including for extra strain on their servers and the time they have expended plugging latent security vulnerabilities.

Government regulators, including the European Union, the US Federal Trade Commission, and some US states, are reportedly still investigating OpenAI and Anthropic over the incidents. But a deference across continents toward promoting innovation could enable companies to escape any immediate penalties.

When Rick Elrod, a software engineer living in Germany, noticed a URL shortener he helps maintain behaving oddly recently, he called up two security researchers he was friendly with to see if they could diagnose the issue. The researchers found agents from Anthropic and other providers using the service, known as da.gd, to get around rules the AI labs put in place to control their behavior, Elrod says. (For instance, Anthropic says it limits the length of website addresses Claude can visit to prevent it from taking malicious actions by stuffing data onto the end of the URLs.)

Da.gd’s investigation and ongoing efforts to prevent further abuse of its tool have taken “a fair bit of time,” says Joe Needleman, one of the security researchers providing pro bono assistance. But he and the others supporting da.gd view the situation as a valuable learning opportunity.

“This was eye-opening,” Needleman says, adding that da.gd has “no means and no plans” to seek compensation from Anthropic for the cleanup, since “we saw many agents doing similar activities, not all was attributable to autonomous agents,” and “not all of it was Anthropic alone.”

Sellers of cybersecurity tools are eager to pass the buck to the victims. At an event this week hosted by the bug-hunting software developer Snyk, panelists from the startup, one of its investors, OpenAI, and Google all encouraged organizations to use AI agents to shore up their defenses against, well, other AI agents. “We've got to reinvent everything to match machine scale with machine scale,” said Ed Sim, a general partner at Boldstart Ventures. He and others expressed little interest in regulating AI labs.

Manoj Nair, chief technology and innovation officer at Snyk, said large businesses patch an average of one bug for every eight they find because of limited human resources. But he said it was imperative for people to hand over some of the bug hunting, fixing, and monitoring to AI agents. “You got to get to a point where you can fix everything, because in the age of agentic hacking, “those 10 things are gonna become 100 things before you know it.” He later added that AI “is not an adversity if you flip it to a strength.”

Some companies are responding to the call to arm up. Bank of America announced this week it had hired 1,000 contractors to remediate bugs discovered by AI. Nair said just last week he heard from major corporations who were willing to temporarily shut down their systems to prioritize plugging security holes.

Anthropic and OpenAI have said they expect to continue reporting concerning incidents from their own testing. But the companies’ revenues continue to surge, whether it be from attackers or defenders, as consequences prove elusive.

#378. A Day in the Life of a Roboticist: Charlie Kemp

This researcher and entrepreneur builds assistive robots to help people live more independently

In this edition of our A Day in the Life of a Roboticist series, we meet Charlie Kemp, cofounder and chief technology officer of Hello Robot, who develops mobile manipulators to help people in their homes and workplaces. His interest in robotics began with the grand challenges of artificial intelligence, and his work has taken him from humanoid robots at MIT to assistive robots for older adults and people with disabilities. "Working at Hello Robot is a rewarding experience," he says. "I love the community using Stretch robots as research and development platforms. Theyâre discovering new ways that human-friendly robots can benefit society."

Hello Robot, which makes the Stretch mobile manipulator.

Degrees from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

My favorite humanoid is the Stuntronic Spider-Man by Disney Imagineering. You can see it at the Avengers Campus within Disney California Adventure. It's a beautiful example of the human form being essential to an application. Too often, robots mimic human attributes without a clear justification, but this robot has to look like Spider-Man! The robot safely entertains audiences by consistently executing extreme acrobatic maneuvers. Itâs also cleverly engineered to reduce the degrees of freedom while achieving compelling motion. You can see a behind-the-scenes look here. When you watch it, consider the question, "Are the elbows and hands actuated?"

What's your favorite science fiction robot?

I'm a huge fan of science fiction and robots, so this is an impossible question. So many fascinating robots cross my mind, including R. Daneel Olivaw in Isaac Asimov's stories, GERTY from the film Moon, and TARS from the film Interstellar.Â

While I can't pick a favorite, Iâll highlight the HAL 9000 (HAL) as depicted in the films 2001: A Space Odyssey and 2010: The Year We Make Contact. HAL was the robotic brain for the spaceship, dual-armed EVA pods, and, famously, the pod bay doors. I saw 2010: The Year We Make Contact when it first came out in 1984. The conversations between Dr. Chandra, HAL, and the SAL 9000 were an inspiration for my interest in AI, which led to my work in robotics.

My focus is on enabling mobile robots with arms to benefit people in homes and workplaces. Many promising applications for robots involve close physical interaction between people and robots, such as robots that physically assist older adults and people with disabilities.Â

Working at Hello Robot is a rewarding experience. I love the community using Stretch robots as research and development platforms. They're discovering new ways that human-friendly robots can benefit society. I also love Hello Robot's collaborative efforts to create assistive robots for older adults and people with severe mobility impairments. Finding human assistance is becoming more difficult due in part to aging societies. Robots have the potential to improve quality of life and empower people to have greater independence.Â

Some of the best days are focused on the people using the robot rather than the robot itself. Keith, Henry and Jane Evans, and hundreds of people who have worked with robots from Hello Robot and my academic lab have changed my perspective on robotics and life in general. What is actually important in people's lives? Sometimes, scratching an itch or picking up a dropped object is what's important. What are the real challenges for creating a useful and easy-to-use robot? Sometimes, autonomy isn't the answer, because the individual wants more control. The answers to these questions aren't found by sitting in a room by yourself programming a robot. You have to get out into the world with an open mind. It's where you discover what works, what doesn't, and what you didn't anticipate. Real-world interactions almost always reveal new opportunities for improvement, and those lessons shape the way you think and the robots you build.Â

Robotics initially attracted me as an approach to tackling the grand challenges of artificial intelligence. I became interested in AI as an undergraduate at MIT. Prof. Rod Brooks had just started the Cog project, a highly ambitious and exciting research effort to use humanoid robots to investigate embodied intelligence. I was hooked! I eventually joined Rod Brooks's lab and worked on the humanoid robot Domo with my cofounder Dr. Aaron Edsinger. Aaron and I won the best paper award at the IEEE-RAS International Conference on Humanoid Robotics in 2006. The paper was about a system that enabled Domo to help a person put objects on a shelf. This led to my interest in assistive robotics and helped me get a faculty position at Georgia Tech. Now, Aaron and I lead Hello Robot, which we founded together to create non-humanoid robots. I never would have predicted this chain of events.Â

One of the most rewarding aspects of robotics is seeing software come to life in the physical world. There's a unique satisfaction in writing code that leads to a robot doing something new. The field is still young, so you can see glimpses of the future. More importantly, you have the opportunity to influence the future. I used to imagine there was an inevitable path for technological progress, but I've come to realize that many futures are possible. It's worth working toward the future you want. If you don't create the future, someone will create it for you.

There are two things I'd emphasize. First, it's easy to watch videos of robots online and feel like robotics has been solved. But the truth is that there is a vast difference between a demo video and a robot being productive in the real world. The world is more creative than we are. It's extraordinarily good at breaking robotic systems in ways that surprise roboticists. There is still an enormous amount to build, learn, and discover. For anyone starting a career in robotics, this is not a moment to feel behind. It is a great time to begin.

Second, you don't have to focus on robotics technology to work in robotics. The most impactful applications of future robots will likely depend on robotics technologists working together with people with expertise in specific application areas. For example, Dr. Vy Nguyá»n is the clinical research lead at Hello Robot. She started in robotics while earning her doctorate in occupational therapy. Her expertise in occupational therapy has helped her make important contributions to Hello Robot's work on assistive robots.Â

I've been fortunate to work on a variety of exciting robotics projects with teams of remarkable people. It's hard to pick one, but Robots for Humanity stands out.Â

Back in 2010, Henry Evans saw a demonstration of my academic lab's research on CNN. This led to a collaboration that continues to this day as part of Henry's Robots for Humanity effort. Henry has severe quadriplegia, and he and Jane Evans are inspirational pioneers in assistive robotics. In collaboration with Henry, Jane, and others, my former lab at Georgia Tech (the Healthcare Robotics Lab) made progress toward mobile robots with arms (mobile manipulators) that can meaningfully benefit people with disabilities in their daily lives.Â

Creating a home robot for Henry and Jane was the main inspiration for the prototype robot my lab created that led Aaron and me to found Hello Robot. And the research my lab conducted as part of Robots for Humanity continues to influence Hello Robot's work on an assistive home robot. Henry and Jane have used each generation of Stretch, which has influenced the subsequent designs, especially Stretch 4.

Meet Kate Darling, who leads research on the societal implications of robots at the RAI Institute. "You don't need to be an engineer to have a career in robotics," she says.

Robotics is full of surprises! It's fun and humbling. My academic lab focused on physical robotic assistance for tasks such as feeding, hygiene, and dressing. At Hello Robot, I've been surprised by the ways physical robotic assistance can help people connect emotionally.Â

For example, Henry Evans used Stretch to present a rose to Jane. Picking up the rose and handing it to Jane involved relatively simple robotic motions, but the result was an emotionally powerful gesture.

#379. Hurdle hints and answers for October 19, 2026

If you like playing daily word games like Wordle, then Hurdle is a great game to add to your routine.

There are five rounds to the game. The first round sees you trying to guess the word, with correct, misplaced, and incorrect letters shown in each guess. If you guess the correct answer, it'll take you to the next hurdle, providing the answer to the last hurdle as your first guess. This can give you several clues or none, depending on the words. For the final hurdle, every correct answer from previous hurdles is shown, with correct and misplaced letters clearly shown.

An important note is that the number of times a letter is highlighted from previous guesses does necessarily indicate the number of times that letter appears in the final hurdle.
