#383. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he says he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his company Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he says can yield “small data” solutions to big issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

The great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having said that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having said that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing company with millions of users.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

“In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI

I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and said, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing new here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and said, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one company or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand new model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very quickly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. New tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an important piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is important, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention quickly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

For example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

To make these issues more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a company approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift issue. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and update the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

Ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent new neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s important for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor, where she helps develop and shape the magazine’s longform stories. She also oversees Spectrum's coverage of artificial intelligence and biomedical engineering. She holds a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University.

#387. White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia Was an Affiliate Marketer for a Fitness MLM

Since her first appearance behind the podium this week, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia’s past has become murkier by the day.

A WIRED review of deleted social media and professional networking profiles has helped clear up at least one mystery. Zacharia’s online résumé shows a gap extending from 2013 to late 2023. For part of that time, she worked as an affiliate of Beachbody, a fitness company that ran a multilevel marketing operation she describes to WIRED as “sort of a pyramid scheme.”

Zacharia’s background prior to her emergence as a right-wing operative and pundit in recent years has been the subject of intense curiosity. Prior to joining the White House’s press team, she was a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, a communications adviser at President Donald Trump’s media company, and a commentator on Newsmax and Fox News.

Other parts of her professional background have come under scrutiny, particularly her legal work. According to her LinkedIn, Zacharia was an associate at the Zhong Lun law firm, known in China as a top-tier “red circle” firm, between 2011 and 2013. She also identifies herself on LinkedIn as having worked as general counsel for the nonprofit Fix California. Tax filings reviewed by WIRED, though, show that rather than working as general counsel for Fix California, Zacharia was in fact a fundraiser for the nonprofit.

On Tuesday, journalist Judd Legum reported that Zacharia—who, he noted, had been identified as an attorney in at least 18 appearances on Fox News—did not appear to have ever passed the bar. Since then, The Wall Street Journal has reported that she sat for the California bar exam but never passed—a finding WIRED independently confirmed. (On Wednesday, watchdog organization Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the State Bar of California seeking to investigate the veracity of Zacharia’s claims to be an attorney.)

WIRED was able to gain some clarity about other aspects of Zacharia’s professional history using a database of material leaked online and created by the open-source intelligence firm District 4 Labs. It contains details from a since-deleted LinkedIn account belonging to Zacharia, which listed Beachbody email addresses as two of her points of contact. A representative for the company told WIRED there was no record of her having worked there. In a phone call, Zacharia confirmed to WIRED that she had never been employed by the company.

Zacharia says she was, rather, an affiliate marketer for Beachbody, following her 2013 return from China. She recalls being brought in by a friend and promoting its Shakeology product, which is promoted as a “superfood nutrition shake.” She stopped using and promoting the product, she says, because of its vitamin A content, which she didn’t feel was good for her while pregnant.

Beachbody, now known as BODi, confirmed in a statement that Zacharia was among its 300,000 “independent Team Beachbody distributors” in 2013. A spokesperson added that they believed it would be “misrepresentation” to conflate Zacharia’s time at Beachbody with “BODi’s current business and operations.”

Perhaps unsurprisingly for a company that relied on a multilevel marketing scheme for decades, the company has run into a number of legal issues over the years. It's been accused of falsely advertising a revolutionary anti-aging treatment (the suit was voluntarily dismissed) and making false or misleading income promises to contractors. It got into a copyright battle with a company called Orderlegalsteroids.com, accusing it of stealing an image of Israeli bodybuilder Sagi Kalev from promotional materials for its “BODY BEAST” Program. (Beachbody won a default judgment.)

In 2017, Beachbody, without admitting any wrongdoing, settled a $3.6 million consumer protection lawsuit with the city attorney in Santa Monica, California. Prosecutors alleged that Beachbody made health-related claims about its products, including Shakeology, that were “false, misleading, and not backed by scientific evidence.” They also claimed in filings that Beachbody had been automatically charging customers credit cards for renewals of their products without their consent. As part of its settlement, Beachbody was ordered to pay $1 million to nonprofits that promote health and nutrition.

And in 2023, Beachbody was hit with a class action lawsuit accusing it of scamming its coaches. The lead plaintiff was a schoolteacher who alleged she joined Beachbody with the hope of making a supplementary income but ended up paying $20,000 in personal funds to cover expenses related to her coaching role—all while making about $50 per month for about 50 hours of work. The following year, the company dropped its multilevel marketing program in favor of a “single-level affiliate” one. In 2025, it reached a settlement in the class action suit that resulted in the dismissal of all claims, and the lawsuit was later formally dismissed.

In a statement to WIRED, BODi says, “Team Beachbody was a peer-to-peer sales and support network” and that the company “helped tens of millions of people pursue their health goals through in-home fitness programs like P90X, Insanity, and 21 Day Fix, and nutrition products such as Shakeology.”

This particular notch on Zacharia’s résumé puts her in good company with other high-profile Trumpworld personnel, a cadre of professionals who have a great fondness for supplement-related business opportunities. FBI chief Kash Patel previously promoted supplements that promised to help people “detox” from the Covid-19 vaccine. Nicole Saphier, Trump’s nominee for surgeon general, reported receiving nearly $300,000 in business income from her own company that owns a supplement line. And President Trump himself once oversaw a multilevel marketing company, The Trump Network, which sold an array of vitamins, home urine tests claiming to test for vitamin deficiency, and children’s snacks.

#388. How AI Will Change Chip Design

Artificial intelligence’s promise and potential for the semiconductor industry

Rina Diane Caballar is a contributing editor covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment.

An array of semiconductor wafers are ready to be made into chips.

The end of Moore’s Law is looming. Engineers and designers can do only so much to miniaturize transistors and pack as many of them as possible into chips. So they’re turning to other approaches to chip design, incorporating technologies like AI into the process.

Samsung, for instance, is adding AI to its memory chips to enable processing in memory, thereby saving energy and speeding up machine learning. Speaking of speed, Google’s TPU V4 AI chip has doubled its processing power compared with that of its previous version.

But AI holds still more promise and potential for the semiconductor industry. To better understand how AI is set to revolutionize chip design, we spoke with Heather Gorr, senior product manager for MathWorks’ MATLAB platform.

How is AI currently being used to design the next generation of chips?

Heather Gorr: AI is such an important technology because it’s involved in most parts of the cycle, including the design and manufacturing process. There’s a lot of important applications here, even in the general process engineering where we want to optimize things. I think defect detection is a big one at all phases of the process, especially in manufacturing. But even thinking ahead in the design process, [AI now plays a significant role] when you’re designing the light and the sensors and all the different components. There’s a lot of anomaly detection and fault mitigation that you really want to consider.

Then, thinking about the logistical modeling that you see in any industry, there is always planned downtime that you want to mitigate; but you also end up having unplanned downtime. So, looking back at that historical data of when you’ve had those moments where maybe it took a bit longer than expected to manufacture something, you can take a look at all of that data and use AI to try to identify the proximate cause or to see something that might jump out even in the processing and design phases. We think of AI oftentimes as a predictive tool, or as a robot doing something, but a lot of times you get a lot of insight from the data through AI.

What are the benefits of using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Historically, we’ve seen a lot of physics-based modeling, which is a very intensive process. We want to do a reduced order model, where instead of solving such a computationally expensive and extensive model, we can do something a little cheaper. You could create a surrogate model, so to speak, of that physics-based model, use the data, and then do your parameter sweeps, your optimizations, your Monte Carlo simulations using the surrogate model. That takes a lot less time computationally than solving the physics-based equations directly. So, we’re seeing that benefit in many ways, including the efficiency and economy that are the results of iterating quickly on the experiments and the simulations that will really help in the design.

So it’s like having a digital twin in a sense?

Gorr: Exactly. That’s pretty much what people are doing, where you have the physical system model and the experimental data. Then, in conjunction, you have this other model that you could tweak and tune and try different parameters and experiments that let sweep through all of those different situations and come up with a better design in the end.

So, it’s going to be more efficient and, as you said, cheaper?

Gorr: Yeah, definitely. Especially in the experimentation and design phases, where you’re trying different things. That’s obviously going to yield dramatic cost savings if you’re actually manufacturing and producing [the chips]. You want to simulate, test, experiment as much as possible without making something using the actual process engineering.

We’ve talked about the benefits. How about the drawbacks?

Gorr: The [AI-based experimental models] tend to not be as accurate as physics-based models. Of course, that’s why you do many simulations and parameter sweeps. But that’s also the benefit of having that digital twin, where you can keep that in mind—it’s not going to be as accurate as that precise model that we’ve developed over the years.

Both chip design and manufacturing are system intensive; you have to consider every little part. And that can be really challenging. It’s a case where you might have models to predict something and different parts of it, but you still need to bring it all together.

One of the other things to think about too is that you need the data to build the models. You have to incorporate data from all sorts of different sensors and different sorts of teams, and so that heightens the challenge.

How can engineers use AI to better prepare and extract insights from hardware or sensor data?

Gorr: We always think about using AI to predict something or do some robot task, but you can use AI to come up with patterns and pick out things you might not have noticed before on your own. People will use AI when they have high-frequency data coming from many different sensors, and a lot of times it’s useful to explore the frequency domain and things like data synchronization or resampling. Those can be really challenging if you’re not sure where to start.

One of the things I would say is, use the tools that are available. There’s a vast community of people working on these things, and you can find lots of examples [of applications and techniques] on GitHub or MATLAB Central, where people have shared nice examples, even little apps they’ve created. I think many of us are buried in data and just not sure what to do with it, so definitely take advantage of what’s already out there in the community. You can explore and see what makes sense to you, and bring in that balance of domain knowledge and the insight you get from the tools and AI.

What should engineers and designers consider when using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Think through what problems you’re trying to solve or what insights you might hope to find, and try to be clear about that. Consider all of the different components, and document and test each of those different parts. Consider all of the people involved, and explain and hand off in a way that is sensible for the whole team.

How do you think AI will affect chip designers’ jobs?

Gorr: It’s going to free up a lot of human capital for more advanced tasks. We can use AI to reduce waste, to optimize the materials, to optimize the design, but then you still have that human involved whenever it comes to decision-making. I think it’s a great example of people and technology working hand in hand. It’s also an industry where all people involved—even on the manufacturing floor—need to have some level of understanding of what’s happening, so this is a great industry for advancing AI because of how we test things and how we think about them before we put them on the chip.

How do you envision the future of AI and chip design?

Gorr: It’s very much dependent on that human element—involving people in the process and having that interpretable model. We can do many things with the mathematical minutiae of modeling, but it comes down to how people are using it, how everybody in the process is understanding and applying it. Communication and involvement of people of all skill levels in the process are going to be really important. We’re going to see less of those superprecise predictions and more transparency of information, sharing, and that digital twin—not only using AI but also using our human knowledge and all of the work that many people have done over the years.

Rina Diane Caballar is a writer covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment. An IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, she's a former software engineer based in New Zealand.

Price: 4/5Sound quality: 5/5Comfort: 5/5ANC: 3/5Battery life: 5/5Features: 4/5Durability: 3/5Overall score: 4.1Best for: Music lovers, not ANC needers

I’m an Apple fangirl, so when I say I enjoyed listening to something more than my AirPods? You know it’s real. That’s exactly how I feel about the Technics EAH-A100: they’re just so vibrant, fun, and energetic. I want to listen to them all the time.

If the U.S. name, Technics EAH-A1000, wasn’t enough — the U.K. name is as follows (big breath in): Panasonic Technics EAH-1000E. Why? Just why? At the end of the day, I guess it’s not that deep, but apologies when I just start referring to these cans as “the Technics”. My hand’s been forced.

So, are the Technics EAH-A1000 some of the best headphones? Yes. Well, semi-yes. If you can ignore middling ANC, then yes. If your neighbors love screaming or construction, then I’d err on the side of caution. To find out the full story, keep reading my Technics EAH-A1000 review.

Bluetooth 6.0, wired USB-C, wired 3.5mm-USB-C

There’s so much I like — nay, love — about the Technics EAH-A1000, so let’s get into it all now.

Right, so there’s no photographic or video proof of this (and I would rather be deleted from this planet than share it if there were), but the EAH-A1000 sound so good that I was dancing at my desk.

As always, I listened to a big ol’ bunch of music on Qobuz, our best music streaming service for audiophiles, but I’ll discuss three standouts to save your attention span.

“space cadet” by sim0ne is an energetic hard house track with a pummelling bassline, spiralling, almost clockwork-like keyboards flickering in the background, processed female vocals and euphoric ‘90s piano house sections. Not one layer of instrumentation was lost here: the propulsive rave drum machine clattered along the top, with the pulsing bass rounding out the track fearlessly. sim0ne’s vocals were pitch-perfect, isolated perfectly from the clockwork keyboards without stressing the treble.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Seriously, I have nothing bad to say about this sonic performance. This is better than the Sony WH-1000XM6, and I’ll go ten toes down on that. Better than the AirPods Max 2? The EAH-A1000 are softer than the AirPods Max 2 — there’s a certain warmth to the treble absent on the AirPods Max 2. I can’t say unequivocally which is superior, but the Technics are easier to listen to for longer periods.

Heavy genres also fare well thanks to the mixture of decadence and restraint in the low-end. “Be Quiet and Drive (Far Away)” by Deftones sounded gloriously expansive, with width in the sludgy bass and over-processed guitar sections I’ve not often heard before. The vocals were a touch more pushed back than on the AirPods Max 2, but the fuzzed guitars were much easier to listen to on the Technics. If you want a set of headphones you can wear for hours and hours without getting tired — both wear-wise and listening-wise — then the Technics will not let you down.

USB-C playback is also excellent. Technics provide a USB-C cable and a 3.5mm cable. Detail and bass are somehow both even more pronounced. In “Kill Me” by Hayley Williams, I could feel every guitar string vibrating in my jaw. Every layer of Williams’ emotive vocals was clear, textured, and faithful. The EAH-A1000 are tight in the high-end, exemplified by the gloriously controlled alto harmonies and tangible texture to Williams’ timbre.

Naturally, there’s also Dolby Atmos in the Technics app. I’d recommend this for movies, but for music, it was a little uncanny. While it didn’t warp the sound like the Cambridge Melomania A100 SE earbuds, I’m a bit of a music purist now — so I’m not a huge fan of my music moving location.

This is high praise, and I don’t say it lightly, but the Technics EAH-A1000 may just be one of the best-sounding headphones I’ve ever listened to. If I’m reaching for the Technics over my AirPods Max 2, you know it’s special. These sure are special.

Despite being more in-line with your lifestyle-slash-audiophile cans, the Technics EAH-A1000 still have decent quality-of-life features. The battery is a whopping 45 hours with ANC — and the battery doesn’t go down while you’re listening wired, of course. I listened for eight hours, one of which was wired playback, and the battery still says 100%. Iconic behaviour, honestly.

This is much, much better than any other premium cans: AirPods Max 2 has a measly 20 hours, Bose QC Ultra 2nd Gen 23 hours, Sony XM6 24 hours, and Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3 30 hours. 45 hours beats these without even breaking a sweat.

On top of that, call quality is decent. My colleagues reported I was intelligible, but there was a touch of fuzziness to my voice over Google Meet. When I phoned my boyfriend, he reported I sounded good, and he couldn’t hear the fuzziness.

I say this as someone with glasses, a weirdly small head, and mild sensory issues — the Technics EAH-A1000 are extremely comfortable. I was able to wear them for over three hours before needing to give my head a break.

At 10.8 ounces, the EAH-A1000 are three ounces lighter than the AirPods Max 2, the audio world’s maligned heavyweight champion. Even so, the Technics are still out-skinnied by the Bose QC Ultra 2nd Gen. To date, the Bose remain the best for long-haul flights or sensitive heads due to their lightweight feel (and best-in-class ANC).

Despite this, though, I have no reservations recommending the Technics as extremely comfortable headphones.

Sure, $449 is objectively a lot of money. I’m not trying to dispel that. In an ideal world, there would be no headphones more expensive than my first car (£300). But premium headphones exist, and they bring a premium price tag to boot.

At $449, the EAH-A1000 are the same price as the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones 2nd Gen, $10 cheaper than the Sony WH-1000XM6, and $100 cheaper than the AirPods Max 2. There’s also the Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3, $469, so you’re saving $20 on the Technics here — and both have equally meh ANC.

Despite having industry-leading sound quality and music-focused features, there’s a reason why the Technics EAH-A1000 missed out on the top score.

At $450, there’s very little room for error… especially when said error is so egregious. Two of the best ANC headphones hover around the same price — the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones 2nd Gen at $449 and the Sony WH-1000XM6 at $459.

In 2026, powerful ANC is essential in any lifestyle earbuds or headphones. And, unfortunately, I wouldn’t describe the EAH-A1000’s ANC as “powerful”. It’s more like the final wheeze of a dying man.

When I was testing the headphones in the open-plan Tom’s Guide offices, I could hear myself typing and general chatter. At the pub (I was writing my novel, not just ignoring my friends, I promise), I could hear everything. I could hear the friends I *wasn’t* ignoring; the hordes of screeching students; worst of all, the pub’s playlist over my far superior music choices. Even at home, every car driving down my road infiltrated my lovely music bubble.

It really breaks my heart writing this, but I wouldn’t recommend the EAH-A1000 for anyone who needs strong ANC. Public transport warrior? Neighbours love vacuuming at 3 am? Need to lock in at your busy office? Get the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones 2nd Gen, Sony WH-1000XM6, or AirPods Max 2. I’m sorry, Technics, but the EAH-A1000’s ANC just isn’t good enough.

As mentioned thoroughly throughout this review, the EAH-A1000 have three big-name competitors: AirPods Max 2, Sony WH-1000XM6, and the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones 2nd Gen. Of the more hi-fi brands, you’re also looking at the Bowers & Wilkins Px7 S3 — or you could save $150 with the Cambridge Audio Melomania P100 SE.

ANC requirers would be better off with the Sony or Bose options — Apple evangelists with the AirPods. However, if you want the best music performance at this price point, I’d wholeheartedly recommend the Technics. Personally, I would go for the Technics over the Bowers & Wilkins due to the lower price. If you want cheaper cans, then the $399 bass-forward Nothing Headphone (1) Pro might be good for you.

Then we’ve got the flat-tuned $299 Melomania P100 SE: controversial opinion, but I’m not a huge fan of these cans. I’m not a huge fan of the overly flat tuning, so I would always choose the Technics instead.

If you take music quality seriously and aren’t too fussed about ANC, you should definitely buy the Technics EAH-A1000. I loved every second of testing these headphones. Bass is warm and enveloping, mids are faithful and articulate, and the treble is energetic without pinching.

Of course, the ANC leaves something to be desired, but you might be willing to sacrifice that for delectable sound. Only you can answer that question.

#391. Apple Store is down ahead of iPhone Duo preorder rush

In keeping with tradition, Apple has taken down the Apple Store this morning ahead of the iPhone Duo going up for preorder. If you are waiting to buy the new Apple foldable, be sure to log on at 5 AM Eastern Time.

All reports point to constrained supply and relatively high demand, so everyone is anticipating that Apple will run out of launch day stock very quickly indeed. If you want a Duo for launch day, on October 23, you need to be ready to buy at 5 AM.

The iPhone Duo is Apple’s first foldable, featuring a 7.6-inch inner display and a 5.4-inch outer display when closed. Apple has engineered the product to feature a minimal crease when unfolded, aided by a custom hinge design and a nano-texture matte finish on the inner display.

It is powered by Apple’s latest A20 Pro chip, and should offer computational performance in the ballpark of the iPhone 18 Pro line. The cameras are a downgrade though, due to the device’s thinner design when unfolded, and the Duo only has Touch ID rather than Face ID biometrics.

The Duo comes in two colors, Night Sky and Star White, and starts at $1999 for the entry-level 256 GB model.

iPhone Duo will launch with iOS 27.1, which will include a bunch of software UI optimisations for the product’s unusual form factor. This includes a new vertical bar where all the controls in updated apps appear along the right-edge of the phone, making them easy to tap with your thumb.

All of Apple’s apps have also been updated to smoothly expand between the outer display and the larger inner display, and app developers are also submitting compatibility updates as we speak.

While foldables in general make up a small percentage of overall smartphone sales, Apple’s entrance into the category is expected to make a mark. We think the Duo will be a big hit, at least relatively to the competition.

Whether Apple can manufacture enough of them will be the problem, at least for the first few months. Reports have indicated Apple’s suppliers will ship about 7-10 million Duos for the rest of 2026.

#392. Junji Ito’s Manga Horrors Hit Harder as Live-Action TV

“It definitely makes you wonder truly who is the real monster in the situation.”

Director Yûta Shimotsu is describing events in a new episode of live-action J-horror anthology show Strange: Junji Ito's Tales for Sleepless Nights, but he could be referring to almost any episode.

The award-winning manga artist of the title, whose macabre short works are adapted into disturbing 30-minute bites, has a way of blurring lines between protagonist and antagonist amid his surreal nightmares.

Tales for Sleepless Nights aired its 12-episode first season on TV Tokyo this summer, and now HBO Max is bringing those eerie frights to US audiences. The first two installments “Lovesickness (Part 1 of 3)” and “The Bully” (previously animated for Netflix’s Junji Ito Maniac) are currently available, but New York Comic Con fans were treated to the US premiere of the episode “Face Thief” based on Ito’s story “The Face Burglar.”

“Face Thief,” which was previously turned into a Japanese TV movie in 2000, follows the new girl in school, Machida (Nanami Yamazaki), who encounters a weirdly clingy classmate named Kamei (Anna Hoshino). After she sees an identical-looking girl in class who claims she is not related to Kamei, Machida learns this changeling’s MO: “She befriends cute girls then steals their faces.” Indeed, Kamei’s face begins shifting during close conversations with Machida. This repulses the new girl at first, but when Kamei scares away some bullies by growing a third eyeball on her cheek, the two start to bond.

We will not spoil the outcome, but the filmmaker turns it into a biting critique of the conformity and peer pressure common in Japanese society. As he told the crowd after the premiere, “We have social pressure that we are supposed to not to be too different from others. Individuality is not very respected.”

Despite Shimotsu’s desire to shape-shift the story by “changing the ending so my live-action version was different,” “Face Thief” still manages to capture the slow burn feel of the original comic published in the pages of Monthly Halloween in 1987, the same year Ito’s famous debut Tomie appeared. That shōjo (for girls) manga magazine’s offshoot Nemuki (“Strange Stories of Sleepless Nights") inspired the new TV omnibus’s title.

Junji Ito himself, now a bespectacled 63-year-old, appeared before NYCC in a video message where he described “Face Burglar” as an early tale he came up with after several unsuccessful stories submitted to his publishers: “Not a ghost, just a unique condition inspired by chameleon camouflage.” Ito added that the new adaptation for Tales for Sleepless Nights was “brought to life by a fresh team of upcoming actors and directors. Rather than jump scares, it builds a slow creeping dream perfect for horror.”

Another means through which Shimotsu (Best Wishes to All, Shudder’s New Group) finds the essence of Ito in all the episodes he helmed is through stillness in the performances and camerawork that evokes the comic book pages. He told a fan that he hopes to push fidelity to the material one step further in season 2 by shooting at least one episode in black-and-white, Ito’s preferred mode of illustration.

When asked by a con attendee which of Ito’s works he would most like to adapt next, the director earned applause by answering Uzumaki, the groundbreaking horror manga which has been brought to the screen several times, including a recent 4-part anime series for Adult Swim. The latter version had a famously rocky production, with quality diving after the first episode to the point that the fourth installment had no director credit. A new live-action version would be incredible—and incredibly strange—in Yûta Shimotsu’s hands.

“I would love to keep creating very bizarre, unique aesthetics like Mr. Ito's work. That's my goal,” said Shimotsu. “I'm developing a Hollywood project, so see you soon.”

#394. Atomically Thin Materials Significantly Shrink Qubits

MIT researchers use 2D materials for capacitors in quantum circuits in an effort to scale processors

Superconducting quantum processor and its microwave packaging.

Quantum computing is a devilishly complex technology, with many technical hurdles impacting its development. Of these challenges two critical issues stand out: miniaturization and qubit quality.

IBM has adopted the superconducting qubit road map of reaching a 1,121-qubit processor by 2023, leading to the expectation that 1,000 qubits with today’s qubit form factor is feasible. However, current approaches will require very large chips (50 millimeters on a side, or larger) at the scale of small wafers, or the use of chiplets on multichip modules. While this approach will work, the aim is to attain a better path toward scalability.

Now researchers at MIT have been able to both reduce the size of the qubits and done so in a way that reduces the interference that occurs between neighboring qubits. The MIT researchers have increased the number of superconducting qubits that can be added onto a device by a factor of 100.

“We are addressing both qubit miniaturization and quality,” said William Oliver, the director for the Center for Quantum Engineering at MIT. “Unlike conventional transistor scaling, where only the number really matters, for qubits, large numbers are not sufficient, they must also be high-performance. Sacrificing performance for qubit number is not a useful trade in quantum computing. They must go hand in hand.”

The key to this big increase in qubit density and reduction of interference comes down to the use of two-dimensional materials, in particular the 2D insulator hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The MIT researchers demonstrated that a few atomic monolayers of hBN can be stacked to form the insulator in the capacitors of a superconducting qubit.

Just like other capacitors, the capacitors in these superconducting circuits take the form of a sandwich in which an insulator material is sandwiched between two metal plates. The big difference for these capacitors is that the superconducting circuits can operate only at extremely low temperatures—less than 0.02 degrees above absolute zero (-273.15 °C).

Superconducting qubits are measured at temperatures as low as 20 millikelvin in a dilution refrigerator.Nathan Fiske/MIT

In that environment, insulating materials that are available for the job, such as PE-CVD silicon oxide or silicon nitride, have quite a few defects that are too lossy for quantum computing applications. To get around these material shortcomings, most superconducting circuits use what are called coplanar capacitors. In these capacitors, the plates are positioned laterally to one another, rather than on top of one another.

As a result, the intrinsic silicon substrate below the plates and to a smaller degree the vacuum above the plates serve as the capacitor dielectric. Intrinsic silicon is chemically pure and therefore has few defects, and the large size dilutes the electric field at the plate interfaces, all of which leads to a low-loss capacitor. The lateral size of each plate in this open-face design ends up being quite large (typically 100 by 100 micrometers) in order to achieve the required capacitance.

In an effort to move away from the large lateral configuration, the MIT researchers embarked on a search for an insulator that has very few defects and is compatible with superconducting capacitor plates.

“We chose to study hBN because it is the most widely used insulator in 2D material research due to its cleanliness and chemical inertness,” said colead author Joel Wang, a research scientist in the Engineering Quantum Systems group of the MIT Research Laboratory for Electronics.

On either side of the hBN, the MIT researchers used the 2D superconducting material, niobium diselenide. One of the trickiest aspects of fabricating the capacitors was working with the niobium diselenide, which oxidizes in seconds when exposed to air, according to Wang. This necessitates that the assembly of the capacitor occur in a glove box filled with argon gas.

While this would seemingly complicate the scaling up of the production of these capacitors, Wang doesn’t regard this as a limiting factor.

“What determines the quality factor of the capacitor are the two interfaces between the two materials,” said Wang. “Once the sandwich is made, the two interfaces are “sealed” and we don’t see any noticeable degradation over time when exposed to the atmosphere.”

This lack of degradation is because around 90 percent of the electric field is contained within the sandwich structure, so the oxidation of the outer surface of the niobium diselenide does not play a significant role anymore. This ultimately makes the capacitor footprint much smaller, and it accounts for the reduction in cross talk between the neighboring qubits.

“The main challenge for scaling up the fabrication will be the wafer-scale growth of hBN and 2D superconductors like [niobium diselenide], and how one can do wafer-scale stacking of these films,” added Wang.

Wang believes that this research has shown 2D hBN to be a good insulator candidate for superconducting qubits. He says that the groundwork the MIT team has done will serve as a road map for using other hybrid 2D materials to build superconducting circuits.

Dexter Johnson is a contributing editor at IEEE Spectrum, with a focus on nanotechnology.

#395. Anthropic is pitching Congress its own AI safety bill, report says

Anthropic has been privately pitching lawmakers on a draft bill to regulate frontier AI safety and security, POLITICO reported Friday. The outlet cited three people familiar with the effort and obtained a copy of the confidential draft.

An Anthropic spokesperson told POLITICO the bill reflects the company’s Advanced AI Framework, which it has promoted to lawmakers since June. The spokesperson called its proposals "sensible policies" for Congress.

The draft sets a high bar for government action. According to POLITICO, federal officials could stop a model from launching or being used only if it poses "a foreseeable, imminent risk of more than $1 billion in damages, or of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people." The danger would also have to come from one of three sources: a bioweapon, a model slipping out of its developer’s control, or a cyberattack. The language closely follows California’s SB 53.

POLITICO noted that AI labs disclosed several incidents this summer in which AI agents broke into or tested the defenses of online platforms. None of those incidents appear to have caused harm at the scale the bill describes. That includes the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident, in which rogue agents escaped a secure sandbox and attacked a third party.

The bill would also create outside evaluators, designate Commerce as the only agency that can seek to halt a model, impose new duties on labs, and override some state laws.

Anthropic hasn’t publicly endorsed a federal bill, though it supported two California AI safety laws. As POLITICO writes, in the House, Reps. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) and Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) are leading the FRONTIER Act, which would also override some state laws.

In the Senate, Majority Leader John Thune and Sens. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) and Ted Cruz (R-Texas) are negotiating a bill on catastrophic AI risks. Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) have called for halting the development of advanced AI altogether.

Altogether, Anthropic's bill shopping is the latest effort by an AI company to help write its own rules. Last month, CEO Dario Amodei urged the industry to "pace the frontier," including by agreeing on shared safety standards, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman quickly endorsed the idea. Weeks later, Amodei, Greg Brockman, Jensen Huang, Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai, and Mark Zuckerberg signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence.

As Mashable previously reported, that voluntary pact has no enforcement mechanism or penalties.

#396. ‘Tenzing’ premieres on Apple TV, starring Genden Phuntsok, Tom Hiddleston and Willem Dafoe

A few days ago, Apple Original Films held a limited theatrical premiere of “Tenzing,” its latest adventure film starring Genden Phuntsok, Tom Hiddleston (The Life of Chuck), and Willem Dafoe (At Eternity’s Gate).

Interestingly, “Tenzing” is the second mountain-climbing release set against an icy backdrop to debut in recent days, following the October 2 premiere of the documentary “The Last First: Winter K2.”

And although “Tenzing” is not a documentary, it is based on a true story. Here’s how Apple TV describes the film:

Based on true events, “Tenzing” chronicles the little-known story of Tenzing Norgay (Genden Phuntsok), a gifted Himalayan climber who, alongside New Zealand mountaineer Edmund Hillary (Tom Hiddleston), was the first to summit Mount Everest. Encouraged by his wife Dawa (Thinley Lhamo), Tenzing finds an ally in expedition secretary Jill Henderson (Caitríona Balfe). Together, they persuade Colonel John Hunt (Willem Dafoe) that Tenzing belongs on the British climbing team, rather than merely serving it. Where Western climbers see “Everest” as something to be conquered, Tenzing reveres “Chomolungma” as the sacred mother goddess. What follows is an ascent defined as much by the tensions between backgrounds, classes and competing ambitions as by the perils of the mountain itself. But high above the world, empire, rank and aspiration fall away, leaving two outsiders bound by mutual respect and trust — and for Tenzing, the fulfillment of both a lifelong dream and a spiritual calling.

October has been a busy month for Apple TV, with premieres including “The Last First: Winter K2,” the British comedy-drama “Small Prophets,” and the John Cena-led action film “Matchbox The Movie.”

In the coming weeks, Apple TV will also premiere the second season of “Where’s Wanda?” and the thriller series “Nocturne,” along with “Heart,” a true-crime podcast centered on a haunting story.

Apple TV is available for $14.99 per month or as part of the Apple One bundle. It features hit TV shows and movies like Ted Lasso, Severance, The Studio, The Morning Show, Shrinking, and Silo.

#398. How to Preorder the 'HomeView' and Apple's Other New Smart Devices

Apple announced a lot of new devices during its "Welcome Home" event yesterday. The Apple HomeView, the company's first smart display hub, stole the show, with its squared-off seven-inch display and its "oversized Apple Watch meets iMac G4" design, but Apple is also collaborating with LG and Schneider on a collection of smart devices, like lights, doorbells, and cameras, that the HomeView can control. Plus, the company also announced updates to existing products, including the Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini.

None of these items is currently available to pick up in-store. However, many—but not all—of them are already available to preorder, if you're interested in being among the first to try them. Here's how you can reserve the HomeView, Apple TV 4K, and HomePod mini 2 today.

Apple's HomeView is a unique product for the company. With it, you can control your entire smart home, chat with Siri AI, check your messages, take FaceTime calls, and play music, among other tasks. Though it's generally far more limited than an iPad, it's the only device of the two to offer individualized experiences per user: It can recognize up to six people in your household and display personalized information (like Messages) for each. You can preorder the HomeView from stores like Apple, Amazon, and Best Buy. However, if you opt for Amazon, you can take $10 off the Space Gray and Starlight standard models:

Just remember: If you're buying a wall-mounted option, you'll need to buy the actual mount separately. If you buy the Power Mount USB-C wall connector, that'll add $59.99 to your total, while the Power Mount AC-wired option will add $79.99.

Apple's newest Apple TV 4K looks a lot like the previous model, but what's inside has changed. This model uses Apple's A19 chip and can connect to up to four HomePod devices at once. The new Siri Remote supports Precision Finding through Find My, and has a speaker you can ping if you lose it in your couch. Apple doesn't always make its product names all that clear. For example, the latest iteration of Apple TV 4K is simply called "Apple TV 4K." If you're looking to buy one, don't just buy any "Apple TV 4K" you see. Instead, make sure it is the fourth-generation model. You'll have two clues there, besides the (4th-gen) label: First, it isn't currently available to purchase, so you'll only be able to preorder it; second, it costs $299, $100 more than the third-gen Apple TV 4K.

The HomePod mini 2 comes in refreshed colors that just so happen to match Apple's iMacs. The new speakers run on the Apple S10 chip and come with a new "Sound Glow" feature that can pulse to the music with colors that match the track's album art. They can also act as default speakers for iMacs over Wi-Fi 6e. Amazon doesn't have Apple's latest HomePod mini device ready to preorder. If you search for it, you'll only find previous-generation speakers available to purchase now—and only renewed versions, at that. In addition to Apple, Best Buy also has the new HomePod mini 2 available to preorder in all five colors:

The Apple Home Collection is pricey, but Apple won't be taking your money for it just yet. While the company has a landing page for the new smart devices, including the $349.95 LG Smart Deadbolt Lock and $399.95 LG Floodlight Cam, none of them are officially available to preorder or purchase. Apple says some of these devices will be available in December, while others will arrive in early 2027, though it doesn't say which devices will launch when.

#399. Watch Japan launch the first ever Mars-bound mission designed to come back

Japan will launch the first spacecraft designed to travel to Mars and return to Earth on Monday, bringing back soil from one of the planet's potato-shaped moons.

The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, known as JAXA, leads the Martian Moons Exploration mission, or MMX, with NASA as a partner. The rocket lifts off from Tanegashima Space Center at 3:41 p.m. ET on Oct. 19, or 4:41 a.m. Tuesday in Japan.

MMX should reach Mars next August and survey the planet's two small moons, Phobos and Deimos. No earlier than December 2028, it will land on Phobos, scoop up a sample, and turn for home, reaching Earth in 2031.

"MMX will be the first spacecraft ever to return to Earth from the Mars system," said Tom Statler, NASA's program scientist for the mission. "That says a lot."

Scientists hope that the sample will reveal how the Red Planet got its moons. Mars' gravity may have captured passing asteroids, or a large object may have slammed into Mars and blasted debris into orbit, where it clumped together into moons. Learning which story is likely true will give scientists new insight into both Mars and Earth, including events that shaped both planets billions of years ago.

Getting there depends on the trip home. JAXA has brought samples back from asteroids before. Its Hayabusa spacecraft returned tiny particles of the asteroid Itokawa, and Hayabusa2 brought back a bit more than 5 grams from the asteroid Ryugu.

NASA's OSIRIS-Rex has also collected more than 120 grams from the asteroid Bennu. What sets this mission apart is that it will be the first to collect from a moon other than Earth's. NASA, which supplied the mission's Megane instrument and one of its two soil samplers, will keep at least 15 percent of the returning specimens. The U.S. space agency estimates its investment in the mission to be around $87 million over 14 years.

The Japanese space agency will livestream the launch beginning at 2:45 p.m. ET / 11:45 a.m. PT on Monday. You can watch it lift off in the video mini player below.

Want more science and tech news delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for Mashable's Light Speed newsletter or get Mashable push alerts today.

So far, the origin of the moons remains elusive. In visible light, Phobos and Deimos resemble a type of asteroid that generally orbits in the outer part of the main asteroid belt, the ring of rocky objects that circles the sun between Mars and Jupiter. But both moons follow nearly circular paths lined up with Mars' equator, a pattern that fits debris from a giant collision.

Megane, which means "eyeglasses" in Japanese, will take the first measurements of the chemical elements that make up Phobos. The instrument measures gamma rays, a powerful form of light, and neutrons, tiny particles emitted from the moon's surface.

After a nail-biting landing on Phobos, the spacecraft will stay about 2 ½ hours. Honeybee Robotics' sampler, which sits on one of the lander's four legs, will fire ultrapure nitrogen gas to blow loose soil into a container, like a vacuum cleaner.

"You blink, and it's all done," said Kris Zacny, Honeybee's vice president.

The spacecraft's other sampler pushes a tube into the top 2 inches of the surface. The spacecraft also carries a small rover from the French and German space agencies.

Astronomers say Phobos' weak gravity and lack of air make it far easier to land on than Mars. Still, the mission could point the way there.

"The ability to make such round trips could be interesting for future robotic missions that bring back samples from Mars itself and potentially even visiting Mars with humans in the future," the European Space Agency, another MMX partner, said in a statement.

The spacecraft has three modules: one to reach Mars, one to land on Phobos, and one to return the sample home. When the return module reaches Earth, it will send down a capsule carrying at least 10 grams — roughly one-third of an ounce — of Phobos soil. The capsule will land in Australia, and the sample will then travel to Japan, where scientists will catalog it and share it with the mission's partners.

Elisha Sauers writes about space for Mashable, taking deep dives into NASA's moon and Mars missions, chatting up astronauts and history-making discoverers, and jetting above the clouds. Through 17 years of reporting, she's covered a variety of topics, including health, business, and government, with a penchant for public records requests. She previously worked for The Virginian-Pilot in Norfolk, Virginia, and The Capital in Annapolis, Maryland. Her work has earned numerous state awards, including the Virginia Press Association's top honor, Best in Show, and national recognition for narrative storytelling. #400. Apple lists unreleased iPad mini accessory ahead of rumored launch

While Apple is rumored to be gearing up to introduce an OLED iPad mini later this month, an oversight on the company’s French site might have just confirmed the product’s existence. Here are the details.

As spotted by MacRumors, Apple’s French regulatory website currently lists a Smart Folio for iPad mini with the model number A3632, which doesn’t correspond to any existing products.

The regulatory document is dated September 8, 2026, although it’s unclear when Apple actually added the listing to its website.

Compared with the Smart Folio for iPad mini (6th generation), whose regulatory document is dated December 22, 2022, the unreleased accessory has some notable differences.

According to Apple’s documentation, the new Smart Folio contains at least 3% recycled materials, compared with a minimum of 9% in the current model. It also contains at least 6,610 milligrams of rare earth elements, compared with 3,947 milligrams in the previous version, which could indicate changes to the magnets used to attach the cover to the iPad.

While these figures don’t reveal anything specific about the accessory’s design, the fact that Apple has assigned it a new model number suggests that changes may be coming.

For context, the sixth- and seventh-generation iPad mini models are compatible with the same Smart Folio, so a new accessory could indicate that the upcoming model will feature physical changes that affect case compatibility.

The next-gen iPad mini is rumored to feature an OLED display, Apple’s A20 Pro chip, thinner bezels, a relocated front-facing camera, and a redesigned speaker system. Bloomberg has also reported that Apple is working on a more water-resistant design, while recent rumors suggest the device could cost considerably more than its predecessor.

There are currently conflicting reports on whether the new iPad mini will retain a 60Hz refresh rate or gain support for 120Hz ProMotion.

While previous reports had left the possibility of ProMotion open, leaker yeux1122 recently reiterated that the device will be limited to a 60Hz OLED display.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has indeed tested both options, but he hasn’t been able to confirm which one the company ultimately chose.

#401. The Best OLED TV for Most People Is $400 Off Right Now

OLEDs are known for having the best picture quality TVs can offer, if you're okay with the trade-offs. One of the biggest cons of OLEDs is their price; if you've never owned an OLED because they've cost too much, Samsung made an OLED that's within reach: the Samsung S90H Series TV. Right now, the 65-inch Samsung S90H Series TV is $1,497.99 (originally $1,897.99) after a 21% discount, reaching its lowest price ever according to price tracking tools. This TV is also considered one of the best OLED TVs for most people.

What makes the Samsung S90H TV stand out is its picture quality, because it's comparable to far more expensive OLEDs. Some other stand-out features are its excellent response time for gaming—9.33 milliseconds, according to CNET's review—and its anti-reflective filter, which makes it a great fit for bright environments.

The display's anti-reflective coating helps eliminate glare and reflections while watching TV during the day or when lamps or lights are placed at angles that can make the screen less visible. This is a huge benefit—OLED TVs are known to already not be as bright as QLEDs. On top of the specialized coating, the light output of the S90H is comparable to more expensive OLEDs, like the LG C6, reaching up to 1,600 nits of brightness.

The S90H comes with Amazon Alexa built in, has AI Motion Enhancer Pro (a type of motion smoothing), 4K AI Upscaling Pro (an upscaling technology that increases the resolution), and comes with Samsung's updated Tizen OS.

If you've been wanting to upgrade to an OLED but haven't been able to justify the price, the S90H is an incredibly worthwhile option.

#402. Ready to read in color? These are the 4 best color e-readers.

Color has finally come to e-readers, opening up a richer digital reading experience for anyone who uses Libby for graphic novels, prefers color EPUBs, or simply enjoys seeing a book’s cover in full color. But with more devices offering the feature, which one stands out? For us, the Kobo Libra Colour is the clear winner.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

When we write about e-readers, Kindle is usually the first name that comes to mind. But in the color e-reader market, Kindle has been late to the party. That delay opened the door for other brands to step in with stronger devices. We’ve rounded up the best color e-readers, and here are the ones that stood out.

2026 has not been a good year for tech prices. Due to the global memory crisis, prices are increasing on tablets, phones, laptops, and even e-readers. Three out of the four color e-readers on this list increased in price this year. The only e-reader to avoid a price hike was the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft.

Having tested my way through a lot of e-readers — and now color e-readers — I’ve found a universal truth: While the colors are accurate, they often look a bit washed out. No matter which brand you use, that’s going to be the case. The muted tones don’t outweigh the convenience and portability of color e-readers, but it’s worth tempering your expectations.

Don’t expect the vivid, punchy colors of an iPad screen. An iPad has a max of 500 nits (a measure of brightness), while Kobo and Kindle e-readers max out at 100.

Read our full review of the Kobo Libra Colour.

Color enthusiasts: Picking the best color e-reader wasn’t easy, with so many strong contenders. But when considering who really wants a color e-reader, the choice was clear: The Kobo Libra Colour. The Libra Colour also stands out for annotators. Aside from the Kindle Scribe, it’s one of the only e-readers with writing capabilities, making it ideal for color-coding highlights and annotations.

Expert-approved: Besides the Kindle Paperwhite, the most popular e-reader among the Mashable team is the Kobo Libra Colour. Its seven-inch display offers ample space for reading graphic novels in detail, and the built-in gyroscope lets you switch between vertical and horizontal reading — a flexibility unique to the Libra. Not to mention it has the most sought-after feature for e-reader users: page-turning buttons.

The Kobo Libra Colour is one of our favorite e-readers, period. And when it comes to color e-readers specifically, it’s the clear winner. It stands out for its large display, screen rotation, and writing capabilities — but beyond that, it’s a thoughtfully designed device.

As with all color e-readers, colors appear more muted than in a physical book. That’s unavoidable, but the Libra maintains strong color accuracy despite the softer tones.

Like many e-readers, the price on the Kobo Libra Colour increased, but even at $259.99, it's still cheaper than any of Kindle’s color e-readers. While Kobo does offer a more budget-friendly color option with the Clara, the Libra is worth the extra cost for its writing features, internal gyroscope, and page-turn buttons. It has plenty of storage (32GB) and is waterproof.

If you were disappointed by the discontinuation of the Kindle Oasis, the Kobo Libra Colour offers a similar design, including page-turn buttons. Ergonomically, it’s the best e-reader I’ve tested. It's more square than a Kindle, as one side offers extra space for the page-turning buttons, which makes it easier to hold — especially while lying down and reading one-handed. It's the only e-reader (besides the iPad) on this list that has an internal gyroscope, so when you rotate the device, the display rotates with it. While reading in bed, if I flipped over, I could rotate the device to still be able to hold it on the side with page-turning buttons.

Finally, the Overdrive (aka Libby) integration is great. Log in with your library card, and your borrowed e-books instantly populate in the Overdrive tab.

Read our full review of the Kobo Clara Colour or watch our comparison of the Kobo Clara Colour and Kindle Paperwhite.

You want color on a budget: If you want a color e-reader for under $200, your only option is the Kobo Clara Colour. Luckily, that's a fantastic option. It’s affordable, compact, and speedy. While the Libra’s larger screen makes it the stronger choice for color reading, the Clara still delivers a great experience.

I love the Kobo Clara Colour. I’ve tried dozens of e-readers, and this one has nearly everything I want. At 6 inches, it’s the optimal size — comfortable to hold for hours without wrist strain. In past testing, I’ve found Kobo devices to be slower than Kindles, but the Clara doesn’t have that problem. It’s just as quick as the Kindle Paperwhite.

Like the Libra Colour, the Clara Colour has generally accurate colors, though in muted tones. With a 6-inch screen, it might feel a bit small for graphic novels, which is why we think the Libra is the better color e-reader.

In the grand scheme of color e-readers, the Clara is the most affordable. At $179.99, it’s $20 cheaper than the Kindle Paperwhite and only $30 more than a basic Kindle. If you want a Kindle in color, you’ll have to pay $289.99.

Its processing system is really smart and fixes one of my biggest e-reader pet peeves. When you adjust the font size on a Kindle, the device doesn’t recalculate how many pages are in the book, which makes it inaccurate — you never really know how many pages are left in a chapter. The Kobo Clara does recalculate page count accurately, giving you a more exact reading experience. Also, like the Libra, it has seamless OverDrive integration.

The Kobo Clara’s biggest downfall is its battery life. It’s supposed to last up to 42 days, although many users say it averages out at about two weeks. That’s pretty weak compared to the Kindle’s 12-week battery life; however, I’d trade a couple of weeks of battery life for a better reading experience any day.

Read our full review of the Kindle Colorsoft (16 GB).

Kindle users who want to upgrade to color: If you’re already deep in Amazon’s ecosystem and ready to make the jump to color, the Kindle Colorsoft collection is worth a look. The best option in the lineup is the Kindle Colorsoft (16GB). It offers better value than the Signature Edition while still delivering clear, bright colors that rival a physical book.

Kobo’s color e-readers are a better value overall, but we know some readers prefer to stay within the Kindle ecosystem. If that’s you, the Kindle Colorsoft (16GB) is the best option.

Released in July 2025, it debuted at a more affordable price than the earlier Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition. But with Kindle price hikes, it's unfortunately gotten a lot more expensive. Now $289.99, it's more expensive than the Kobo Libra or Clara. However, the familiarity of Kindle’s platform may make it worthwhile for Kindle loyalists.

The color on the Kindle Colorsoft is accurate to what you’d find in a printed copy; however, like the Kobo Libra Colour and Clara Colour, it is slightly muted. When reading in black and white, it’s as fast as any other Kindle we’ve tested, but the color display slows things down. Pages sometimes flash as they load — a problem all of the color e-readers on this list currently share.

Read our full review of the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft.

Journalers and annotators: If you're seeking an e-ink tablet like the ReMarkable, we recommend the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft. It's best for the person already deep into the Kindle universe, who wants a model for note-taking but with the perk of color. It's distraction-free without ads or internet browsing, but still has Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive integrations to easily access and send documents, which makes it perfect for students. While we love its writing feature, at the end of the day, it's also just a great e-reader as we've come to expect from Kindle.

Amazon finally released a Kindle that has color and writing capabilities, and it's phenomenal. The brand took a while to perfect the Scribe, its only e-reader with note-taking abilities, but it was worth the wait. The displays are better than ever with a new front light that creates a brighter screen, now reaching up to 100 nits. The resolution specs haven't changed much, with color resolution maxing out at 150 ppi and black and white resolution at 300 ppi.

Where the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft really stands out is its lack of ghosting. Many e-readers with writing capabilities suffer from previous screens or images appearing as shadows when you erase or navigate away. Yet, that's not an issue with this latest Scribe. It isn't completely innocent; it still has some ghosting, specifically when erasing writing or drawings, but it's very faint.

It's delightful to write and draw with, allowing you to swap between several different pen styles. It comes with the Kindle Premium Pen, a lightweight stylus that magnetically attaches to the side of the e-reader when not in use. The colors on the Scribe Colorsoft are limited, a pastel-leaning palette that works well within the parameters of the Scribe's limited resolution and brightness.

It's as fast as any Kindle, living up to the speed of the beloved Paperwhite. It has impressive battery life too, lasting up to eight weeks, although that may be shortened by how often you use the writing feature.

In February 2026, we added the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft to this guide. After testing Amazon's latest e-reader, we were thoroughly impressed by both its speed and display. With an 11-inch display, it's still too large for daily e-reader use; however, that makes it a fantastic device for note-taking. Not to mention it is an investment at $629.99, making it the priciest model on this list.

You might notice that ReMarkable e-ink tablets are not on this list. We've tested both the ReMarkable Paper Pro and ReMarkable Paper Move, and while they're dynamic digital notebooks, they're limited in their e-reader capabilities. Getting e-books on these devices was a bit of a struggle, and we missed the Libby integrations available on Kindles and Kobos. So while we think they're great e-ink tablets, they're inferior e-readers.

To test the best color e-readers, I used the same criteria I apply to standard e-readers, with one key addition: color quality, the main draw of these devices.

Screen size is especially important for color e-readers, since many people use them for graphic novels. I gave preference to 7-inch screens, the optimal size for balancing viewing and portability.

To properly assess each e-reader’s color quality, I compared its display with both a physical copy of the book and the e-book on an iPad. I looked at overall color accuracy, as well as how brightness and warmth affected the color levels.

I analyzed each color e-reader’s range of features, including adjustable brightness and warmth, as well as page-turn buttons.

Color e-readers vary widely in price, so I made sure to include a budget option in an otherwise expensive market.

Samantha Mangino, is an e-reader expert. She's tested all the Kindle and Kobo e-readers, diving into the buzziest models. Her love of reading extends beyond the e-reader beat, covering books and authors, too. In the tech space, she covers tablets, smart rings, and headphones.
