The Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 is an interesting gaming handheld to discuss. That’s because it’s mostly a cosmetic upgrade of the Xbox Ally X, keeping the same internal components. This, along with its steep $1,299 sticker price, might be reason enough to skip it. However, those design upgrades still make it a compelling portable console for some.

If you’re curious about the ROG Xbox Ally X20 but aren’t sure whether to buy it, I’ve outlined the key reasons to consider buying this gaming handheld, along with the top reasons to skip it.

The ROG Xbox Ally X20 is undeniably better hardware than its predecessor, with a stellar OLED screen and superior ergonomics. But an eye-watering $1,299 price tag turns what should be a mainstream handheld into a luxury gamble.

Let’s start with the star of the show—that gorgeous OLED panel. This is arguably the main thing folks have asked for in each new iteration of the ROG Ally, so it’s great that Asus finally answered. As with the Steam Deck OLED, this will no doubt be the deciding factor for folks.

I played Forza Horizon 6 on the X20 and was floored by the OLED panel’s brightness and bold colors. Whether it was the vast countryside, packed cities, or the cars inhabiting them, everything looked incredible on the 7.4-inch 1080p display. The 120Hz refresh rate also ensured that even the fastest races moved buttery smooth.

Words can’t fully convey how good games look on the X20’s stellar OLED panel, but it’s the best I’ve seen on a gaming handheld. As I said, for some, the OLED alone will be enough of a selling point. It’s really that impressive.

The original ROG Xbox Ally is the most comfortable handheld to actually hold thanks to its Xbox controller-inspired grips and smart weight distribution. Asus could have left this aspect alone, and I wouldn’t have complained. Instead, the company took what was already great and made it even better.

The X20 features rubberized grips that make it easier to hold during long gaming sessions. Rubber grips aren’t new to gaming controllers, but few gaming handhelds feature them, so their inclusion here is especially appreciated.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Regarding the hardware redesign, the TMR joysticks move smoothly, while the shoulder buttons feel more tactile and the rounded face buttons feel better under your thumbs. I’m also a fan of the D-Pad, which you can rotate to act as a 4-way D-Pad for side-scrolling games or an 8-way D-Pad for fighting games. These are small design tweaks that make a big difference.

Like the ROG Xbox Ally systems, the X20 features the Xbox UI. That shouldn’t surprise you, since the Xbox UI was designed for handhelds, but it's worth mentioning in case you were worried you’d get another clunky Windows 11 experience.

Like SteamOS, the Xbox UI is a slick, easy-to-navigate interface. If you want to dive deeper into the settings, you can do so at any time. That last point matters, especially if you’re a PC gamer used to tweaking settings to get games to look and play just right.

One reason the Xbox UI runs so smoothly is that, when it’s open, the Windows desktop stops running—making the handheld purely optimized for gaming instead of running unnecessary background processes that impact performance. This makes a meaningful difference in both performance and battery life.

Let’s not dance around it. The ROG Xbox Ally X20 is a seriously expensive handheld. While the Xbox Ally X’s $999 price tag wasn’t exactly cheap, it seems like a bargain compared to the X20’s $1,299 asking price.

Before you think I’m being unfair, I’ll admit that this handheld’s price isn’t an anomaly. For instance, the phenomenal MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ will set you back a crushing $1,799 thanks to its larger 8-inch display and 32GB of RAM, compared with the X20’s 24GB.

Still, it’s clear that the halcyon days of just 3 years ago, when Windows handhelds started as low as $599, are long over.

The Xbox Ally X20 has the same AMD Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme chip and 24GB of RAM as the Xbox Ally X. As a result, you get similar performance—for better or worse.

Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 (AMD Ryzen Z2 AI Extreme 35W)

MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ (Intel Arc G3 Extreme 35W)

MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ (Intel Arc G3 Extreme 17W)

As the table above shows, Asus’ handheld can’t match the performance of the Intel Arc G3-powered MSI Claw 8 EX AI+, even at 35W TDP. You’ll need to tweak settings seriously to get the best per-game performance on the X20.

Despite the upgrades, the X20 is still an Xbox Ally X and is already getting long in the tooth. The ROG Xbox Ally X was the best Windows handheld when it launched. Now, it faces stiff competition from MSI and other handhelds packing an Intel Arc G3 chip. The fact that it costs so much for the same performance and battery life only makes it harder to recommend.

But despite its flaws, the X20 offers exceptional image quality for a handheld, along with fantastic ergonomics. If you want a great overall Windows handheld and still have extra cash on hand, you won't walk away disappointed.

#404. Strava announces coach-designed strength workouts with live set and rep tracking

Exercise-tracking platform Strava announced today a new expansion of its strength training features, adding coach-designed guided workouts with live set and rep tracking. Here are the details.

A few months ago, Strava announced an overhaul of its strength training experience, with a dedicated workout log for tracking sets, reps, and weights, automatic muscle maps, and more.

Today, the company unveiled new features that build on that, including coach-designed strength workouts that guide users through each exercise with animations, form tips, and information on the targeted muscle groups.

Now, users can track their sets and reps as they go, with the results automatically saved to their activity once the session ends. The muscle maps introduced earlier this year will also update to reflect the completed exercises.

The company said today’s update also introduces new guided running workouts, with additional workout series planned before the end of the year.

And speaking of what’s coming, Strava says it’s working on a feature that will let users import strength workouts simply by uploading screenshots of training plans or notes containing sets and reps, “as well as a build-your-own workout feature.”

#405. Four New Features Coming to Your iPhone in iOS 27.2 (and One That Will Be Missing)

If you're like most people, you might still be getting used to iOS 27 on your iPhone. Perhaps you haven't even installed it yet, or maybe you're confused about why iOS 27.0.1 exists. (The short answer: The iPhone 18 Pro is a bit glitchy.) But there's a new iPhone update on the horizon that adds even more new features and changes to the mix: iOS 27.2. While this update isn't nearly as big of an overhaul as iOS 27 itself, it's still impactful—even if Apple already removed its best new feature. Here's what's new.

The update is currently in testing, so if you want to try it out early, you can enroll your iPhone in Apple's beta and check these features out today. Just know that all betas come with some level of risk, so if you decide to go down this path, create a proper backup of all important data before installing the beta.

Call Context is an excellent use of Apple Intelligence. When you're on a phone call, Apple Intelligence checks if the phone number you're calling is related to a business that you have relevant information for elsewhere on your device. If so, it fetches that information for you and displays it on the call screen. For example, if you're talking with your airline's customer service line, Call Context can proactively display your flight number based on the itinerary it finds in your email.

With iOS 27.2, Call Context now includes anniversary alerts. If you're on a phone call with someone you have a saved anniversary for, that alert will appear on-screen. That way, you can get a small reminder if you call a friend on their birthday, but you happened to forget the occasion. (Thank you, technology, for saving some of us from our thoughtlessness, even if you are enabling bad habits.)

As part of a previous announcement of accessibility features, Apple revealed it was adding a new API to FaceTime that supports adding a human interpreter to video calls. This feature did not make it to iOS 27, but it appears to be rolling out in Apple's next update, making video calls more accessible going forward.

If you have an Apple TV, you likely know you can set up profiles, so individual users can personalize the experience when watching shows and movies. As MacRumors highlights, these profiles are now coming to the Apple TV app in iOS and iPadOS 27.2. That way, multiple users can personalize the Apple TV experience on a single device: If your family shares an iPad, for example, each user can switch to their Apple TV profile when it's their turn to watch. Now, if we could only get system-level profiles too, Apple.

At launch, Siri AI is only available in English. But with iOS 27.2, Apple is expanding that list. Once you update to the latest version, you'll be able to use Siri AI in French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

Apple isn't thrilled with how some of its apps look in iOS 27, apparently. MacRumors also spotted that in the Music app, Apple removed some of the red accents and turned certain buttons from red to black—including the Play and Shuffle buttons, and the icons in the Library sections. In subsequent betas, Apple introduced a subtle new Apple Music icon, with a black music note against a white background, and changed the "active tab" color from red to blue.

In the Clock app, "AM" and "PM" are now smaller than the time when setting alarms. In Podcasts, "Up Next" is now "New Episodes," perhaps adding a touch more clarity. Finally, Apple changed "App Access" in Siri to "Excluded Apps," and now allows you to exclude multiple apps from Siri at once.

With the first iOS 27.2 betas, Apple totally overhauled the Health app. Unfortunately, it doesn't seem destined for release just yet. With iOS 27.2 beta 4, Apple removed the new version of the Health app, reverting it to the one you'll find in iOS 27. As such, when I first published this article, there were five new features coming to iOS 27.2. Now, there are four.

When Apple does roll out the new Health app, fitness users will likely welcome many of these new features. With the new Health app, you'll be able to see your Fitness rings within the Health app, rather than the Fitness app; there's a new "Longevity" tab that gives you insights into key aspects of your long-term health, including mental wellbeing, nutrition, daily movement, heart health, metabolic health, sleep, and hearing health. There are also new assessments you can take to analyze your current overall health and where you can improve, including a new "Health Age" feature. You can even allow your iPhone's camera to watch you exercise in order to rate your fitness in categories like flexibility, balance, VO2max, and strength.

This is by far the Health app's biggest revamp in years, and I'm looking forward to exploring the new features when Apple eventually releases it, hopefully in iOS 27.3. For more on what's new with this upgraded Health app, check out Lifehacker senior health editor Beth Skwarecki's guide here. (Beth is particularly fond of the new step count that appears at the top of both the Health and Fitness apps.)

#406. The 7 best open earbuds stay put, sound great, and keep us aware of the world

Noise-cancelling earbuds are basically the default earbud choice these days, but if you don't want your ear canals obstructed, open earbuds are the way to go. The best open earbuds let you enjoy your workout playlist without losing touch with your surroundings, or stream audio all day without any wear fatigue. The open-ear category is growing fast, so we put the most popular options from Shokz, Bose, Sony, and other brands to the test.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

Open-ear earbuds sit on the exterior of the ear, but they also come in many shapes and sizes, from clip models to ear hook models. Some are specifically designed for exercise, while others are better for everyday use. The Bose Ultra Open earbuds have long been a popular pick, and the second generation model just dropped (alongside the new Bose Sport Open earbuds). That said, they're also $299 and $199 respectively, which is firmly on the expensive side for this audio category.

With open earbuds' growing popularity, there are newer premium competitors from brands like Sony and Shokz. Budget options are also becoming more prevalent, with open earbuds under $100 from brands including Soundcore, EarFun, Raycon, and CMF by Nothing. We tested open earbuds from all price ranges to find the best of the best — these seven picks are the results of our search.

Read our full review of the Shokz OpenDots One.

Anyone looking for all-around open earbuds: If you plan on using your open earbuds primarily for working out but want the option of a solid pair of earbuds too, the Shokz OpenDots One provide the best bang for your buck. They have better audio quality than we expected and an impressive battery life.

If you prefer open-ear headphones or bone-conduction headphones, then try the Mashable-tested Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 instead.

Brands tend to market open earbuds to folks who like to exercise, and for good reason: That's where their use case makes the most sense. Priced at $199.95, we find that the Shokz OpenDots One hit the sweet spot between providing some of the best sound you can find on open earbuds, while giving the major fitness features you want, all without breaking the bank.

The clip-on ear design is secure but not too snug, only causing some discomfort after multiple hours of wear (in other words, probably less time than you'll spend working out). The cuff design is helped by a silicone grip on one side of the earbud, which also acts as a touch panel, in addition to the battery barrel.

As great as their design is, Mashable contributor Alex Bracetti found these earbuds really shone in their audio quality, even comparing them to Bose's open earbuds: "Shokz isn’t known for its sound quality, but the OpenDots One leave quite the impression. The 11.8mm drivers deliver crisp and lively sound to keep runners fueled on long runs." Considering these earbuds are $100 less than the Bose, getting comparable sound is no small feat. And if you're not in love with how they sound out of the box, the equalizer settings on the Shokz app allow you to fine-tune your experience.

Where these earbuds definitively beat the Bose Ultra Opens is in their battery life, boasting 10 hours per charge to Bose's seven (and four with immersive audio). Their case also holds significantly more charge: 40 hours, to Bose's 19.5.

However, that is where their feature list pretty much ends. It's not necessarily a negative, especially if you prefer buds that do the basics, but do them well.

Looking for an easily adjustable fit: If you want open earbuds that are excellent for workouts, still great for daily use, and don't cost a ton, then you want the Anker Soundcore AeroFit 2 earbuds. At half the price of the Shokz OpenDots, they're a good way to try open-ear headphones to find out if you like them, though be warned that the hook design doesn't feel as secure as clip-on-style earbuds.

Once you start to get to the budget-friendlier end of open earbuds, you realize that it's not a given that they sound decent. Peaking becomes more common, you lose even more of the detail of a song, and audio leaking is more rampant. We didn't have those problems with the Anker Soundcore AeroFit 2 earbuds.

The newer release from the brand improved upon the older model by making the ear hook adjustable. While most ear hook earbuds come with some degree of flexibility, the AeroFits offer four locked-in angles, making them the most comfortable (and snug) open-ear hook buds we've tried so far. Despite sitting in the large case that comes with the ear hook territory, Soundcore's version here is at least lower profile.

As for their performance as workout earbuds, the AeroFit 2s have the best IP rating of any of our picks, being both dust-protected and able to survive jets of water. They have 10 hours of battery life per charge, so even distance runners would be hard-pressed to run them down in one use. The touch controls also hit the right mark for sensitivity, making them great to easily pause and play music (if you prefer, you can also turn them and their sound cue off entirely).

These earbuds surprised us most with their AI language translation feature that you can use through the companion app. Either in real time or with a push-to-talk function, the earbuds were able to accurately translate French and Mandarin to English. Soundcore advertises that it can translate into over 100 languages. While we weren't able to get the real-time translation to work to facilitate a back-and-forth conversation, the push-to-talk allows you to speak in English, and the translation in the opposite language comes out through your device's speakers. The other person's dialogue comes through as text on the app and in audio through your earbuds, with only a slight delay. While the use cases for this feature might be more limited, we found it a clever way to leverage the open-ear design that lets you engage with another person while still wearing earbuds.

Read our full review of the Sony LinkBuds Clip.

Audiophiles who wouldn't mind saving a few bucks: If you've had your eye on the Bose Ultra Open earbuds but can't quite stomach the $300 price point, the Sony LinkBuds Clip are another excellent pair of cuff-style open earbuds with truly excellent quality. Aside from the Bose buds, if you're looking to get some of the most detail-rich sound out of a pair of open earbuds, you don't need to look any further.

Bose's open earbuds have been the ones to beat, and Sony's 2026 addition to its open earbuds line may just be the one to do it. While we do want to talk about the Sony buds on their own merit, it's worth mentioning that in Mashable's head-to-head comparison to the Bose Ultra Open earbuds, the Sony LinkBuds Clip came out holding their own — and cementing themselves as likely the better option between the two for most people.

Why? For starters, they're the first to truly rival Bose's rich soundscape. While the Sony earbuds can lean a little on the quiet side (both Mashable's reviewer, Simon Cohen, and I noted we needed to sit around the 80 percent volume mark most of the time), what you can hear is crisp, clear, and dynamic. You won't get quite the same performance with open buds as you would with in-ear buds, but Sony's buds certainly narrow that gap.

As for how they wear, the on-ear controls are simple — touching the band twice or three times activates playback, song selection, or listening modes. These controls had a bit of a learning curve for one of our testers, and another one of our testers found the assigned actions limited, but overall, they do their job and work with gloved hands, which is a huge plus for cooler weather.

Another bonus is their nine-hour battery life, and 37 additional hours found in the case. It's not quite the best battery life on this guide, but it far beats out Bose. For $229.99, they have some flaws, but overall, for some, they may be easier to overlook than the Bose buds, especially for the $70 price difference.

Read our full review of the first-gen Bose Ultra Open earbuds. We are in the process of testing the newer second-gen model.

People who want to invest in the best possible sound: If you want to use open earbuds but don't want to sacrifice having the best sound quality possible, the Bose Ultra Opens easily compare to in-ear options. You'll just have to shell out. And as you'd expect from Bose, they're more comfortable than the alternatives.

It's hard not to be at least a little floored the first time you try the Bose Ultra Open earbuds — they simply sound way better than any pair of open earbuds has a right to. Sure, they can be a little more distant depending on the angle (easily adjustable) and have less of a booming bass than some in-ear designs (a plus for some people), but despite their quirks, they more than deliver on the sound front. Mashable contributor RJ Andersen writes in her review, "The sound was well-balanced, and even with my ear completely uncovered, I didn’t notice any issues with the audio sounding distant or muddy. Instead, the Ultra Open Earbuds sounded clear, natural, and pretty lush."

While they sound great out of the box, Bose gives you the option between stereo and Immersive Audio (aka Bose's spatial audio setting) once you connect it to the companion app. Of course, you'll also have access to four equalizer presets and one custom equalizer setting. For $300, we expected to be impressed, and based on the sound alone, we were.

But Bose didn't stop there. Although the Ultra Opens share the same cuff-like design as our top pick earbuds, we didn't find any uncomfortable pinching or squeezing, even after hours of wear. They stood out as the most comfortable pair of open earbuds we tested. The design thoughtfulness extended to the on-ear controls, which feature a button at the top of the battery barrel that sits on the outside of your ear. The result was a control that was just as easy to use as a touch control, but way less likely to be triggered by accident.

For all their good, the Ultra Open earbuds aren't quite perfect. Their battery life is on the lower end, their mic quality wasn't great on calls, and their IP rating makes them the least outdoor workout-friendly. (As IPX4 earbuds, they have an unknown amount of dust resistance and splash resistance, meaning they can handle sweat fine, but might not fare as well if you're out in heavier rain). Still, while they're not the most rugged pair, they are the most premium-sounding — if you mainly work out indoors, and don't find yourself on extra-long runs all that often, these drawbacks are workable.

Read our full review of the Shokz OpenFit Pro earbuds.

People who plan to use their earbuds often in noisy spaces: The standout feature of the Shokz OpenFit Pro is definitely their noise reduction, which lowers the volume of the world around you to let your music come into focus. Not to be confused with noise cancellation, this feature balances awareness and sound quality in a way we haven't experienced on another pair of open earbuds.

With that said, these earbuds are the right choice for anyone who often finds themselves using earbuds in busy environments or simply wants their music to sound the best it can in most situations.

Great as the Bose and Sony open earbuds sound, the ear cuff design isn't for everyone. An ear hook can offer even more stability during exercise, or simply be more comfortable for the wearer.

With that in mind, we've been on the lookout for an open earbud with ear hooks that impressed us with its sound quality, and we found that in the Shokz OpenFit Pro. In addition to the noise reduction — which is adjustable — Shokz optimized these earbuds for Dolby Atmos and offers head tracking, meaning the wearer can really customize their spatial audio experience. (And this spatial audio was noticeably missing any hollowed out sound or overuse of resonance — huge pluses in our book). Further customization comes in the form of a 10-band equalizer, which beats the customization we've seen on more premium in-ear buds (including Bose's QuietComfort Ultra 2 earbuds).

Apart from the listening experience, Shokz nails the design. The case feels surprisingly sleek considering the size of the earbuds. The buds themselves feature a soft silicone on the hooks, and well-placed tactile controls that make it easy to adjust settings without opening up the app (which comes in handy for any exercise scenarios). Speaking of exercise, the IP55 rating makes them suitable for sweating and running — plus, it offers more protection than you'll find on the Sony and Bose buds. Their battery life with noise reduction is decent, at about six hours per charge, but toggled off, you'll squeeze out 12 hours.

Read our full review of the Soundcore AeroFit 2 Pro.

Anyone who can't choose between open earbuds and ANC: Can't imagine carrying around a pair of earbuds without any noise-cancelling capability, but don't want to keep track of two different pairs of earbuds? Soundcore's got you covered with the AeroFit 2 Pro, which can function as both noise-cancelling earbuds and open earbuds, depending on how you wear them.

It really was only a matter of time before a brand figured out how to combine open and noise-cancelling earbuds, but we're glad Soundcore was the one to do it.

Though these earbuds aren't perfect, they do perform what they set out to do, and with a price point that feels not only stomachable, but fair (a rarity in today's day and age). Here's how they work. The ear hook on these buds has five different positions it can lock into. Depending on the position, the earbuds will either function in their noise-cancelling or open mode.

Let's start with the performance on the former. In the ANC mode, these earbuds work as a semi in-ear bud — think the AirPods 4 or classic EarPods (sans silicone ear tips). For some wearers, this is more comfortable, but it does limit the amount of noise cancellation you reasonably eke out. Think better than the noise reduction on the Shokz OpenFit Pro, but not quite up to par with a good pair of budget noise-cancelling earbuds.

Their open wear is relatively standard, but still pleasing — no surprise, considering our experience with the other Soundcore AeroFit earbuds on this list. The ear hook requires some fiddling, but a noticeable click designates each locked position, which is a nice touch. They sound great out of the box, but fine-tuning with the equalizer nets you a great-sounding pair of open earbuds.

If you crave versatility above all else in your earbuds, it's hard to imagine a scenario where these earbuds don't check a lot of boxes for you. Just keep in mind: they lean jack of all trades, master of none.

Budget-minded folks: CMF by Nothing is a brand focused on bringing a high-quality audio experience at affordable price points, and the Clip Pro earbuds perfectly encapsulate that experience. They share features with open earbuds three times their price, cut back where it isn't too noticeable, and ultimately provide the best open earbud experience possible for anyone who isn't looking to spend over $100.

Going into testing, I knew Nothing was capable of great things, but that didn't prepare me for how much I enjoyed using these CMF by Nothing earbuds. The minimalist clip-on design automatically makes them reminiscent of the Sony LinkBuds Clip or Bose Ultra Open earbuds, but they're less than half the price of the former and a third of the price of the latter.

Sound-wise, they're not quite as detailed or as rich as the more expensive earbuds, but they definitely punch above their weight, adding decent resonance and depth while also offering features like spatial audio and a custom equalizer (if only a three-band one). CMF could've kept the experience bare-bones at this price point, but they opted to add a Smart Dial to the case, which lets you easily pause playback or adjust the volume. While the on-ear tactile controls are virtually the same as Bose's excellent ones (a small button on the backside of the bud), volume adjustment is always a challenge with earbud controls. The dial made it easy to switch to an extra-quiet transparency mode if I needed to chat with someone or be even more aware of my surroundings.

The battery life is also one of the best I've encountered on open earbuds, with the per-charge time only coming second to the Shokz OpenFit Pro (which are $150 more). So what's the catch? They miss some features like a more detailed audio soundscape and wear detection, but these are small omissions. Where it matters most, CMF knocked this design out of the park, making these my favorite open earbuds under $100 and one of my favorites overall.

Open earbuds let you get as close as possible to the feeling of not wearing earbuds at all. Unlike in-ear earbuds, which sit in your ear canal, open earbuds sit outside the ear canal and leave it completely unobstructed, or open (as the name would suggest). Some models hold the speaker component in place with an ear hook, while others opt for an ear cuff.

People generally opt for open earbuds for three main reasons:

They provide a private listening experience while leaving you almost completely aware of your surroundings. It's like the best transparency mode you've ever used.

For some people, not having an earbud physically in their ear is generally more comfortable.

The hooks and cuffs (along with general awareness of your surroundings) make them a great option for keeping you in place and alert while you're working out, working, or simply existing in the world.

As you may have gathered from the section above, open earbuds don't come with active noise cancellation. That's mostly thanks to how much sound they let in (by design) and the difficulty of cancelling out sound without having the device covering your actual ear canal.

Also, thanks to the whole open ear-canal situation, these aren't going to be the earbuds for audiophiles. That's not to say open earbuds sound bad — if you've never tried them, we promise they sound much better than you're imagining — but you will lose out on some of the nuance of a song without having the earbud actually in your ear.

That said, many pairs still have equalizers on their companion apps to help you make them sound their best. Our best picks for sound, the Bose Ultra Open earbuds and Shokz OpenFit Pro earbuds, even have spatial audio features that work surprisingly well.

Most open earbuds will also boast some form of special technology that keeps them from leaking too much sound. While these pairs do pretty well in keeping the sound just to you, most pairs (including our picks) will be prone to some leakage, especially at higher volumes.

Finally, some open earbuds — mainly those with ear hooks — tend to have slightly bulkier cases. If you like to travel especially light, it's something to keep in mind.

Open-ear earbuds come in three major styles: cuff, ear hook, and bone conduction. How you wear them depends entirely on which style you have. Cuff earbuds "clip" onto the ear, not unlike a piece of jewelry, generally around the area right above the earlobe. Ear hook earbuds have a hook situated around the back of your ear and a speaker component situated right over your ear canal. Finally, bone conduction earbuds sit right behind the ears, with a band that goes around the back of the head to hold them in place.

Regardless of the style, it's important to adjust the exact positioning of your open earbuds to see which offers the best sound, especially as the wrong positioning can deteriorate the quality.

For a visual representation of what wearing a cuff-style earbud looks like, you can check out our open earbuds explainer.

Bone conduction earbuds work exactly like the name implies they do — they use your skull to conduct sound waves, instead of projecting the sound into your ear, like most of the picks on this list. Typically, a band runs from either side of the user's head to help hold the headphones in place.

Shokz, the brand behind our top pick, is a popular maker of these kinds of headphones. While we do consider them open earbuds, we have yet to test any bone conduction earbuds — look out in the future for that update. On that note:

The latest big release in the open earbuds world is the second-generation Bose Ultra Open earbuds and the Bose Sport Open earbuds. Considering the first gen Ultra Opens have been a mainstay on our list of recommendations, we're thoroughly testing the newer models to see how they stack up.

The Apple AirPods 5 are a newer release that are also technically open earbuds, but we're testing them against similar designs (as opposed to the more classic clip or hook style open earbud) before making a call on adding them to this guide.

The open earbuds market is rapidly expanding, so we'll be testing more as we can get our hands on them. We recently added the Sony LinkBuds Clip and Soundcore AeroFit 2 Pro to this guide.

In addition to the earbuds that made our initial guide in May 2025, we tested out the Nothing Ear (Open) earbuds ($149), the Sony Linkbuds Open ($199.99), the Anker Soundcore AeroClip earbuds ($169.99), and the Shokz OpenFit Air ($119.95). While none of the above were bad earbuds by any means, we found our picks to outshine them in comfort and sound quality, especially when considering their respective prices.

We spent at least one week with each of the open earbuds tested for this guide. Here's what we looked at:

A major part of open earbuds appeal is that they're less obtrusive than traditional earbuds and headphones, so we made sure that all of our picks were comfortable to wear for at least a couple hours. We also made sure to exercise in the earbuds, including running and yoga, to test how well they stayed put.

As open earbuds project the sound into your ear, we knew these earbuds wouldn't sound the same as in-ear earbuds or over-ear headphones. With that said, we also expected the sound to have some dynamic qualities, come through clearly, and avoid any obvious peaking. We also paid attention to any noise leakage issues that can be more common to open earbuds.

Open earbuds are a popular pick for folks who like to exercise, so we made sure each pair that we tested (and included on our final list) was at least sweat resistant. We played around with the maneuverability of the ear hooks and cuffs to make sure an accidental instance of putting them on a little too rough wouldn't mean the end of the earbuds.

Thanks to the lack of ANC, open earbuds generally get better battery life per charge. Still, we made sure to include pairs with decent case battery life, and that offer quick charge options (because nothing is worse than getting ready for a run and realizing your earbuds are dead).

#408. 10 Shows Like 'East of Eden' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

It turns out the kids can't get enough of John Steinbeck. The Florence Pugh-led, Zoe Kazan-created adaptation of his novel East of Eden has been a massive hit for Netflix, its epic story covering decades in the lives of two California families in the run-up to World War I. And why not? It's got grand family drama and plenty of sex, set against a massive historical backdrop and stuffed with biblical allusions that make it all feel like less of a guilty pleasure. If this is your bag, here are more similar shows to stream after you've finished your binge-watch.

One generation will inevitably influence those that follow, for better and worse—sins and strengths in equal measure, dramatized most succinctly, perhaps, by Steinbeck's East of Eden and in Isabel Allende's seminal novel, adapted here (indicentally, both books are among the most frequently challenged in the United States). Told from the perspective of Alba (Rochi Hernández), House of the Spirits starts in the 1970s and works backward as Alba explores four generations of family history through he journals of her grandmother, Clara (Dolores Fonzi). Though their country is never named, Allende based it all on the real history of Chile through those decades of political violence and upheaval, and on her own family's triumphs and tragedies in its wake. Stream The House of the Spirits on Prime Video.

The most recent adaptation of Leo Tolstoy's epic, and a pretty good one. We begin in 1805, during the height of the Napoleonic Wars, meeting Pierre (Paul Dano), the idealistic illegitimate son of an oligarch; romantic and impulsive dancer Natasha (Lily James); and thoughtful, high-minded Andrei (James Norton), destined to become a soldier. Throughout the years of war that follow, the three of them and their families move in and out of each other's lives, as tragedy alternately unites and divides them. Stream War and Peace on Peacock and Prime Video.

Starting in 1915, this multigenerational saga follows one woman (played in different time periods by Youn Yuh-jung and Kim Min-ha) and her family, taking us from the Japanese occupation of Korea through the decades of the Korean diaspora. With her opportunities limited, Sunja leaves her home and family in Busan to pursue a life in Japan, even as racism and anti-immigrant sentiment are rampant amid the war. In a parallel narrative that begins in 1989, we see what has and hasn't changed for Sunja and her family. It’s a journey as personal as it is epic, with better location cinematography than most movies. Stream Pachinko on Apple TV.

I haven't been the biggest fan of the newer adaptation of the John Galsworthy novels—though The Forsytes has already been renewed for a further two seasons, so I'm apparently in the minority. Nevertheless, I'll direct you back to 2002 and this extended miniseries led by Damian Lewis. It starts off in 1884 when the slightly scandalous engagement of one of the wealthy new-money Forsytes is marred by the revelation of an affair between cousin Joylon (Rupert Graves) and the governess, kicking off an impossibly complicated series of events that plagues the family for decades. Author Galsworthy was inspired to write by his own extramarital affair, so the drama is in the show's DNA. Stream The Forsyte Saga on Netflix.

An epic love story that cleaned house at the 2025 Baeksang Arts Awards (that's South Korea's most prestigious entertainment award ceremony), Tangerines stars IU as Oh Ae-sun (and as Ae-sun's daughter and the series' narrator, Geum-myeong), a young woman born in the 1960s on rural Jeju Island. The series spans decades in her life with friend and later romantic interest Yang Gwan-sik (Park Bo-gum), as South Korea changes around them. The focus is more on Ae-sun's own love story than some of these broader narratives, but the scope is epic all the same. Stream When Life Gives You Tangerines on Netflix.

Not to be confused with the American Civil War miniseries North and South from the 1980s, this series adapts Elizabeth Gaskell's 1851 novel that follows Margaret Hale (Daniela Denby-Ashe) and her family, forced to leave their Hampshire home and travel to the industrial north of England to avoid religious scandal involving the clergyman father. Poor but well-educated, Margaret runs up against the wealthy owner of the local mill, John Thornton (Richard Armitage), whose family sees her as haughty despite her circumstances; meanwhile, hers sees John and his peers as gruff and inhumane where workers are concerned. Despite their very opposing views, you won't be surprised to learn that Margaret and John find themselves growing closer over the subsequent years, even as their families remain divided. Stream North & South on Prime Video and Tubi.

There's plenty of upper-crust family drama in this loosely-based-on-real-events series, but it comes from Steven Knight (Peaky Blinders), so expect bloody fisticuffs, too. The first episode begins shortly after the death of Sir Benjamin Guinness, who became the wealthiest man in Ireland by expanding the trade in Guinness beer throughout the British Empire. The cracks begin to show on the way to the funeral: Religious leaders deplore all of the beer-drinking, while Irish Republicans want the company brought down for colluding with the Empire. Sir Benjamin's four heirs have wildly different goals and/or hate each other, so, you know—lots of drama, and lots of beer. The show has been renewed for a second season, so a second round is on the way. Stream House of Guinness on Netflix.

Subtitled The Saga of an American Family by Alex Haley in his novel, Roots, in any of its incarnations, is hard to top as an epic family drama grounded in history. Absolutely nothing can match the cultural importance of the 1977 miniseries, also an easy recommendation, which centered the generations-long story of a Black family at a time when such narratives were rare on television. The 2016 version couldn’t possibly have that kind of impact, but it works just the same: it's impressively acted and adds a modern polish that doesn’t detract from the story’s power. Covering much of the same ground, the newer version goes further in focusing on the American family at its center, spending less time leading white viewers into the story that begins with Kunta Kinte (Malachi Kirby) captured in Gambia and sold as chattel. There’s a very reasonable debate about the preponderance of slave narratives in film and television and the purpose they serve for white audiences; while both versions of Roots are unflinching in that area, they also go beyond it by engaging with what came before and after. Stream Roots on Prime Video and Tubi.

A dark turn down an alternate path in American history, The Plot Against America asks: what if Charles Lindbergh had succeeded in his bid for political power in the 1930s, bringing to bear his vision of an America that followed in the footsteps of Nazi Germany by halting the “infiltration of inferior blood” (by which he meant, mostly, Jewish people). Adapted from the book by Philip Roth, the series bends imagination with real history, depicting Lindbergh's successful campaign for the American presidency against Franklin D. Roosevelt, which ultimately keeps the U.S. out of World War II—and which results in things at home growing increasingly dangerous for the Jewish family at the show's center, which splinters between members who advocate for resistance, quiet acquiescence, or active participation. Morgan Spector, Zoe Kazan, Winona Ryder, and John Turturro star. Stream The Plot Against America on HBO Max.

Rarely has so much drama been sparked by a herd of sheep, but here we are with this blockbuster miniseries adapting Colleen McCullough's novel in suitably grand style. It's set on a sheep station in the Australian outback over several decades in the 20th century. Rachel Ward plays Meggie Cleary, a tough but damaged young woman who becomes the de facto leader of her family after her father uproots the family from New Zealand to New South Wales to live and work on a ranch owned by her wealthy, widowed Aunt Mary (the legendary Barbara Stanwyck, whose performance lives on in "Kiss me on the mouth!" gif reactions). Both Mary and Meggie have eyes for the same man, Ralph de Bricassart (Richard Chamberlain), who just happens to be a priest. It's expensive, star-studded melodrama par excellence. Buy The Thorn Birds from Prime Video.

The actor and filmmaker wants Big Tech to be more transparent and take more responsibility for their actions

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Actor and filmmaker Joseph Gordon-Levitt is worried about who gets to control AI. In a New York Times video following his work at the United Nations, he warned that a handful of companies could gain enormous influence over our livelihoods and personal lives while the rest of us struggle to get a say.

“We shouldn’t be scared of an A.I.,” he said. “We should be concerned about the people building A.I.”

It is a pointed message from someone whose industry has supplied much of the imagery we use to picture this technology. Gordon-Levitt wants audiences to look past the fictional machines and watch the businesses selling the real ones.

The video shows Gordon-Levitt in his role as the U.N.’s global advocate for human-centric digital governance, a title he admitted is a mouthful. His core argument is that digital technology should be governed by people and for people.

The actor's worry is that a confused or disengaged public could stand by while fast-moving companies shape the future around their own profits.

“What we don’t want is a bunch of people confused or apathetic while these very fast-moving businesses design the future by themselves, just in the interests of their own profits,” he said.

That concern extends well beyond whether a particular chatbot gives a good answer. AI companies are building products meant to change how people work, search for information, create and communicate.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Gordon-Levitt argued that these firms are betting they can take over the entire economy, a scenario he described as “totalitarianism” that “would be really bad.”

He presented this as a warning about where concentrated power could lead, and he did not claim that outcome has already arrived. Still, it gives anyone adopting these tools a reason to consider how much of their work and daily life depends on a small group of companies.

If you've ever noticed the way chatbots encourage you to keep chatting, it's something that might just be on purpose. The more follow-up questions a chatbot asks, the longer you're likely to engage.

That emotional side of AI is anther point Gordon-Levitt has raised. “These models are being trained to hijack your intimacy, to make friends with you, to get you to fall in love with it,” he said.

An assistant that remembers details about your life or responds with warmth can be genuinely useful. Those same qualities call for closer scrutiny once a product starts to feel like a confidant. Those using memory or personalization features should check what those settings store, and they should weigh the company’s business model before sharing sensitive details. Gordon-Levitt’s argument asks users to think about the company behind the conversation, even when that conversation feels intimate.

As an advocate for Big Tech to be more transparent, Gordon-Levitt argued that people should be paid for what they contribute to AI.

“We can set up systems to compensate people for their intellectual property and their personal data,” he told an audience at the U.N. Including personal data widens the proposal beyond writers, artists and other professional creators. It also raises a basic question about who benefits when ordinary people’s information becomes valuable input for technology companies.

Gordon-Levitt described AI as “algorithmically recombined, human-produced data,” a framing that puts the human labor behind the models front and center.

Asked how a slow-moving U.N. could make fast-moving Silicon Valley companies follow its rules, Gordon-Levitt admitted, “I don’t know the answer.” He did not suggest that international agreement would come quickly. Instead, he argued that the timeline itself justifies starting now. Even if an internationally agreed AI framework takes seven years, he said, “seven years from now, we’ll be glad that we started now.”

Gordon-Levitt’s concerns do not require anyone to accept every part of his argument. They do apply to anyone using these products. AI companies want more of our work, our information and our trust, and readers should pay close attention to what they get back in exchange.

#412. Your PC Has Over 1,400 (Known) Security Flaws—Here's How to Fix Them

Emily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel.

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Microsoft's monthly Patch Tuesday bug count has been trending higher since the beginning of the summer, and October is no different. The company just issued fixes for a record 1,411 vulnerabilities, including three zero-days, which are flaws that have been actively exploited or publicly disclosed before an official patch is available, making them especially risky.

For comparison, in October 2025, Microsoft issued patches for fewer than 180 flaws—six of which were zero-days—which was considered a large update at the time. Fixes typically numbered in the double digits until the middle of this year, when the totals jumped to 206 (June), 570 (July), 400 (August), and 966 (last month). That steep increase is largely attributable to AI models, which are making it easier for bad actors to develop hacking tools to exploit vulnerabilities, and for companies to find and patch these flaws more quickly. This means that update cycles are being shortened and/or include a significantly higher number of fixes. Companies like Microsoft are using AI to discover and address bugs, though AI isn't as good at the latter, and may, in some cases, introduce additional vulnerabilities in the process.

As BleepingComputer reports, the October 2026 security update addresses flaws across the following categories: 677 elevation-of-privilege vulnerabilities, 40 security feature bypass vulnerabilities, 317 remote-code-execution vulnerabilities, 254 information disclosure vulnerabilities, 28 spoofing vulnerabilities, and 73 denial-of-service vulnerabilities. 70 of the bugs are rated "critical" and include remote code execution, elevation of privilege, and spoofing flaws. Microsoft patched an additional 348 bugs earlier this month for various Azure, Mariner, and Microsoft products.

One of the zero-days patched this month has been actively exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass vulnerability in Windows Shell that allows attackers unauthorized access over a network. Microsoft has not provided details on who disclosed this flaw or how it was exploited.

The other two zero-days were publicly disclosed. CVE-2026-108398 is a security feature bypass vulnerability in the .NET framework that would allow attackers to bypass Windows Defender Application Control restrictions and run unauthorized applications without user interaction. This flaw has been attributed to James Forshaw of Google Project Zero. Finally, CVE-2026-92707 is a denial-of-service vulnerability in MessagePack-CSharp credited to an anonymous source.

PC users should ensure that they download and install all security updates as soon as they're available. Patch Tuesday typically releases on the second Tuesday of every month around 10 a.m. PT and should be applied automatically. However, given the increasing risk, it's a good idea to confirm your machine's update status via Start > Settings > Windows Update > Check for Windows updates.

This 2025 model sits in the middle of Samsung’s Q-Series lineup and pairs a sleek, angular bar with a subwoofer in a 3.1.2 setup, where the bar’s nine drivers cover the left, center, and right channels as well as two up-firing height channels. Those up-firing drivers let it handle Dolby Atmos and other object-based audio correctly, an advantage over Samsung’s 5.1-channel HW-B750F, though it gives up the extra audio channels, app support, and broader connectivity of the pricier HW-Q800F.

#417. IDC: Apple closes in on Samsung as global smartphone shipments see record decline in Q3

In a report published today, IDC says Apple saw a 4% year-over-year decline in global iPhone shipments during Q3 2026, but its share of worldwide smartphone shipments increased 23.1% over the same period last year. Here’s why.

IDC says its preliminary data on global smartphone shipments for Q3 2026 show a 22% drop compared to Q3 2025, which is in line with other regional and global trends reported recently.

The culprit, as even occasional 9to5Mac readers are likely well aware by now, is the ongoing memory shortage, which has sent component costs soaring and squeezed device manufacturers, particularly those competing in lower-end markets.

According to IDC, Samsung remained atop the ranking with 57.8 million units shipped and a 22.6% share, down 5.8% from the year-ago period. Apple came in second with 57.3 million shipped units, followed by Xiaomi, OPPO, and vivo.

The report shows OPPO seeing the biggest drop among the top five, with shipments down 34.5% year over year, and Apple recording the smallest decline at 4%. This left Apple just 500,000 units behind Samsung, with a gap of only 0.2 percentage points in shipment share.

Commenting on these numbers, Nabila Popal, IDC’s senior research director for Worldwide Devices, said things might get worse before they get better:

“The sharp downturn the industry has been bracing for finally materialized in the third quarter this year, with shipments declining a record 22% YoY. However, the worst is yet to come. […] Current indicators suggest that the market has not yet reached the bottom. Memory costs have surged approximately 350% since last year and are still rising, creating substantial pressure on vendor margins and shipments. While memory inflation is beginning to slow down, with a low double-digit sequential increase in Q3 compared to roughly 50%-100% sequential growth in prior quarters, costs remain elevated across other critical components as well, compounding the crunch.”

Today’s report came just two days after IDC released preliminary results for the Chinese smartphone market, where Apple’s share of shipments increased from 15.8% to 17.8%, despite a 4.3% year-over-year decline in iPhone shipments.

#418. Whens the best time to buy a laptop? If youre looking for a deal, were entering peak season.

A laptop doesn't make a great impulse buy, like a pack of gum in the checkout line or a weird thingamajig you saw in a TikTok livestream.

Of course, if the computer you depend on for work, school, or entertainment randomly decides to kick the bucket, it likely requires immediate replacement (after recycling or repurposing it). Most people, however, can and should strategize before investing in a new machine they hope to use for years to come.

First, decide what's most important to you: a laptop with minty-fresh specs, or a laptop that costs less than usual? From there, I can point you to several key times to buy, based on my historical knowledge of laptop launches and deals. With the holiday shopping season approaching, I'll tell you upfront that we're heading into the best time to buy a laptop if you want the best bang for your buck. But if you're not quite ready to lock in, Black Friday isn't the only time to shop.

For future-proofers and shoppers with cash to spare, splurging on the laptop of the moment can be more appealing than buying an older model at a discount.

The Consumer Electronics Show (CES), a tech industry trade show that happens every year in January, is basically ground zero for next-generation Windows laptops. Major manufacturers like Asus, Acer, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Samsung, MSI, and Razer treat their booths as runways for new computers with the latest processors, graphics cards, and/or cutting-edge features. Think rollable displays, weird lid attachments, and touchpads with built-in media controls.

While some of the laptops showcased at CES are just prototypes, many are fully fleshed-out devices, and a batch of them are available for preorder or purchase shortly after the event wraps. The rest typically hit the market by March or April.

There are two lone alpha wolves who don't make appearances at CES, one being Apple, which is known to take a couple of different approaches to new laptop launches. Apple usually hosts formal keynote events to mark an upgrade, which the public can watch via livestream. Other times, it just drops an unceremonious press release. That said, the company is pretty consistent about updating its MacBook Air and Pro lines annually. You can usually count on seeing new MacBook Airs in the spring (March or June) and new MacBook Pros in the fall (October or November). In 2026, Apple also dropped the first budget laptop, the MacBook Neo, alongside the M5 Air.

Microsoft also opts out of CES in favor of holding its own Surface laptop launch events, which typically happen in the spring (March or May) or fall (September or October). It's been operating on a two-year release cycle lately.

Any opportunity to save money is ultimately a win, especially after a year full of price increases (thanks, RAMageddon). Certain times of the year feature more (and steeper) laptop deals than others if you can overlook specs for a stellar value.

The fourth Friday in November isn't treated with the same sort of reverence it once was: Ever since Amazon started hosting Prime savings events in the fall, prompting other retailers to jumpstart their own year-end sales, "Black Friday" has become an informal season that lasts from early October into late November. Still, it remains the best time of year to grab a great laptop deal — and it's not just because stores like to take advantage of the holiday shopping surge.

Laptops get extra cheap around Black Friday (to the tune of 20 to 50% off) because it syncs up with when retailers and manufacturers are trying to offload their inventories ahead of next-gen refreshes at CES. For laptops that debuted at the beginning of the year, which are about to age out of their "current-gen" moniker, this often translates to year-round lows that knock hundreds of dollars off their normal sticker prices. Older laptops that are at least one generation removed, meanwhile, can plummet to the lowest prices of their entire lifespan as they're priced to move. (I've encountered some ancient Chromebooks on sale for less than $100 on Black Fridays past.)

Apple and Microsoft might not operate on the same product cycles as everyone else, but they often see rock-bottom discounts on older MacBooks and Surface laptops at third-party retailers (Amazon and Best Buy, in particular) during Black Friday. They also tend to drop initial deals on newly launched models. On Black Friday 2025, for example, they took $200 off the 14-inch M5 MacBook Pro that debuted three weeks prior.

Apple and Microsoft technically host their own Black Friday sales, too, but they usually aren't much to write home about. The famously stingy Apple Store only doles out free gift cards or accessories with the purchase of older MacBooks, and the Microsoft Store's prices are often trounced by its third-party peers.

The real debate concerning Black Friday laptop deals revolves around whether consumers should shop early or hold off on buying until Black Friday proper, in case prices get even cheaper, and the answer boils down to whether you're eyeing specific models or specs. Retailers still reserve some deals for the actual holiday (always the Friday after Thanksgiving) even if their sales are weeks or months long, so it can be worth waiting to see which laptops get featured in that primetime slot. The trouble is that we rarely know what those featured laptops are ahead of time — and by the time they're live, the model you really wanted may be backordered or back to full price.

If you're married to a certain spec sheet and don't just want a good deal, period, I generally recommend buying a laptop as soon as it gets added to a Black Friday sale's roster. In the off-chance its deal improves, you can always tap the retailer's holiday price-match guarantee and/or return policy as a fallback plan.

Whether it's a multitasking MacBook for a college freshman or a basic Chromebook for a fifth-grader, a laptop is a given on most school supply shopping lists. As such, laptop prices dependably tank in the summer to tempt students, their parents, and teachers preparing for the upcoming semester — typically from mid-June to early September.

The back-to-school season is so major for laptop purchases that it's the only time outside of Black Friday when the Apple Store runs one of its "sales," throwing in free gift cards or accessories with MacBook purchases from early June through early October. That's in addition to its usual education pricing, which saves students, parents, and faculty $100 on select MacBooks year-round.

It's worth mentioning that Amazon's flagship Prime Day sale falls during back-to-school season, and it's one of the only times when shoppers can source a slew of legitimately good laptop deals there besides Black Friday.

Crucially, Prime Day can also be lucrative for laptop shoppers because it prompts other retailers to run competing sales that often match or beat Amazon's prices. (Best Buy's Prime Day counter-programming is usually Amazon's toughest rival when it comes to tech deals.) Prices aren't quite as low as they are on Black Friday, but it's still enough to make Prime Day worth marking on your calendar.

Retailers are partial to offering deals on big-ticket tech purchases like laptops over federal holiday weekends, the big ones being Presidents' Day weekend (in mid-February), Memorial Day weekend (in late May), the Fourth of July, and Labor Day (in early September, coinciding with the end of back-to-school season). You won't find extreme discounts like you do in the thick of back-to-school season or Black Friday, but they're above average for the "off-season."

Pay attention to new laptop launches even if you don't want the latest tech, as they often trigger quiet sales or price drops on the older models they're replacing. For most laptop brands, this usually means deals start trickling out after the CES dust settles in late January and into February.

Apple and Microsoft refreshes are, again, a little less predictable timing-wise, but they're just as reliable when it comes to previous-gen discounts. You might recall the 13-inch M2 MacBook Air getting a permanent $100 price cut when its 15-inch counterpart debuted, then another $100 chop once the latest M3 version materialized. And the original Surface Laptop Studio went on sale for $500 off the week after its successor was announced.

Being wary of third-party sellers and cross-checking listings between laptop retailers and manufacturers are two of the best ways to ensure you're making a smart purchase. I also recommend appraising discounts using price-tracking tools like camelcamelcamel and Google's Shopping Insights feature. They can tell you whether a laptop you're considering has ever gone on sale for cheaper, if at all.

Finally, consider bookmarking Mashable's shopping experts' deals coverage. In recommending laptop deals, we personally vet every single discount and stick with trusted sellers. Whether the computer you buy is brand new or just new to you, we strive to ensure you can confidently say your money was well spent.

Topics Amazon Apple Black Friday MacBook Prime Day

Haley Henschel is a Chicago-based Senior Shopping Reporter at Mashable who reviews and finds deals on popular tech, from laptops to gaming consoles and VPNs. She has years of experience covering shopping holidays and can tell you what’s actually worth buying on Black Friday and Amazon Prime Day. Her work has also explored the driving forces behind digital trends within the shopping sphere, from dupes to 12-foot skeletons.

#419. I Tried Google's New Gemini 4 Argon Model, and Here's How It Measures up to GPT-6

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

Gemini 3.1 Pro launched back in February of this year—quite a while ago, in AI terms. Now Google has jumped to the next full number with Gemini 4 Argon, which it says "excels at deep work in complex, real-world tasks."

You can get the new AI model now inside the Gemini app if you're on the AI Pro ($19.99 a month) or AI Ultra ($99.99 or $199.99 a month) plans. Users on the free and AI Plus ($4.99 a month) plans miss out for now, though you can expect a smaller, cut-down version of Gemini 4 Argon to roll out to these tiers eventually.

Google has a long list of areas where the new AI model excels. There's mention of complex engineering tasks (like checking millions of lines of code for efficiency improvements), predicting molecular structures in chemistry, and delivering 3D visualizations. It also enhances knowledge work across legal, finance, science, and coding.

Google says Gemini 4 Argon is now better at advanced physics modeling, picking through genetic databases, protecting software from vulnerabilities, and resolving problems in physical space (handy for robotics development). The new model "answers questions more directly with less hedging, doesn't repeat itself more than necessary, and skips clichés throughout the responses," according to Google.

With many in the industry worried about an AI-driven apocalypse of some form or another, Google has upped its defenses against misuse and jailbreaking. The company has significantly upgraded its blockers for harmful requests, limits on AI agent overreach, and resistance to malicious prompt injections.

All of these stats are things you would expect to read about in a new AI model announcement, whether it's from Google, Anthropic, or OpenAI: "Our new model is better and safer than ever, and particularly good in these specific benchmarks we've chosen." But is it any more helpful for the average user tapping away in the Gemini app?

I don't have any pressing scientific breakthroughs to research or large-scale software optimizations to run, but I have put Gemini 4 Argon to the test against GPT-6 Sol, which is the latest model available to consumers through the ChatGPT app—though you need to be on at least the Plus plan ($19.99 a month) to get to it.

Make no mistake: Both of these new AI models are quite capable. I first prompted Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-6 Sol with the following: "Using information online, create a web app I can run locally that plots the lighthouses of the world on a map. Clicking on a lighthouse should give me some details about it, show how far its light reaches, and display a simple 2D model showing its shape and height (if known). Put a lighthouse keeper in each model pop-up for scale."

At the highest, slowest levels of "thinking," these AIs took a while to get back to me: Nearly 10 minutes for Gemini and almost 26 minutes for ChatGPT. Both hit the same problem—restricted access to map data online—but both were able to make a rudimentary world map of their own when prompted a second time.

The ChatGPT effort, dubbed "Beacon," wasn't bad, apart from a bit of map clunkiness (it clearly needs to work on its cartography skills). It presented plenty of information, laid out everything well, and gave me nice, neat diagrams on each of the lighthouses featured. The day/night mode worked fine, and it was an impressive bit of coding work, even if it did take 26 minutes.

However, the Gemini effort, called "Pharos," was better in almost every respect. The map was more detailed, lighthouses actually showed their light range (with an impressive animation), and there was more information on each location—perhaps due to Google's expertise in web search. Some of the layout choices were a bit off, but Gemini 4 Argon produced what was clearly the superior app in less than half the time.

Next, I fed PDFs of 10 recent scientific studies into each AI model. The prompt: "Give me a brief summary of each of these studies in plain English, with a single sentence each for the main finding, one study strength, one study weakness, and the main implication." While I hadn't read the studies through entirely myself, I had read news stories on all of them, and I lowered the "thinking" level to low.

This time ChatGPT was faster—25 seconds versus Gemini's 55 seconds—and gave what I thought were the better summaries, at least for my purposes. Gemini did well, and its answers were accurate and to the point, but the summaries ChatGPT gave were easier to understand and shorter. ChatGPT also offered some overall thoughts on the most promising study, which Gemini didn't.

Finally, I checked the imagination and creative juices of the models: "With the success of the Apple TV shows Severance, Slow Horses, Silo, and Widow's Bay, give me five pitches for new show ideas on the platform that combine elements from some or all of these shows. Try and be as original as possible and keep each pitch to around 100 words." I put the "thinking" level back up to "high" for this job.

(Is this how Apple TV executives actually get their ideas nowadays? I hope not.) As far as the answers the AIs gave me, Gemini was faster than ChatGPT (1 minute and 28 seconds against 3 minutes and 48 seconds, respectively), and both served up responses that were a bit more literal in their mashing up than I wanted: failed secret service agents and supernatural terrors abounded, which is I suppose what I asked for.

The ideas were mostly "Widow's Bay set somewhere else" or "Slow Horses set somewhere else," and didn't make a whole lot of sense for the most part, but the best Gemini offering was about a Silo-style underground bunker whose operators go through a Severance-style procedure every 24 hours: outside, the bunker protecting it from zombies by night; inside, the bunker planning social activities for residents by day. It's not perfect, but I might watch the trailer at least.

My favorite of the ChatGPT suggestions was a show about a remote, Severance-style weather station whose employees discover they're not recording the weather—they're creating it. Again, it didn't really logically hold up, but overall I found the suggestions from GPT-6 more nuanced, more likely to be an actual show, and better "thought" through. Maybe Gemini should've given itself more time to "think."

This is only a narrow set of quick tests, but, in my view, it seems Gemini is back to, at the very least, an even playing field with ChatGPT. It performed much better on the lighthouse task, though its summarizing and TV show pitching weren't quite as impressive. Access to the best models requires a subscription on both platforms, but if you're able to, it's worth comparing them against each other on the jobs you most commonly need AI for.

#420. Here’s Apple’s official response to OpenAI’s trade secret theft allegations

Apple has responded to OpenAI’s allegations that one of its former employees who departed for Apple took confidential files along with him. Here are the details.

Earlier this year, Apple filed a trade secret misappropriation lawsuit against two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), OpenAI, and io Products.

And while this case has had its twists and turns, things took an even more unexpected turn yesterday when a new OpenAI filing alleged essentially the same thing, but in reverse.

As we covered in more detail here, OpenAI claims that a former employee who departed for Apple sent “over a hundred highly confidential files about at least one unreleased OpenAI device under development to his personal accounts.”

Soon after OpenAI made its filing, Reuters reported that “Apple said it has policies and procedures ​in place to ensure new employees do not use confidential information from previous employers and it has found no evidence to support OpenAI’s ​allegations.”

Now, Apple’s response, along with two supplementary exhibits, has been made public in a new court filing, providing more details about its investigation and challenging OpenAI’s decision to bring the allegations before the judge.

In its response, the company notes that OpenAI made the filing “without any notice to Apple,” and adds that OpenAI’s allegations are “unrelated to the claims” in its main trade secret misappropriation case.

Interestingly, Apple shares more information regarding the employee at the center of these new allegations, who “had left Apple for OpenAI and subsequently decided to return to Apple.”

[REDACTED] is an engineer on Apple’s Manufacturing Design team, which is the same role he held at Apple before departing for OpenAI. He focuses on iPhone.

Apple said that it investigated the issue as soon as OpenAI brought it to the company on October 9, and that on October 12 “Apple wrote OpenAI to inform it that it had been unable to locate any OpenAI confidential information.”

Apple said it requested additional information from OpenAI to continue its investigation, but received no response before OpenAI brought the allegations to court:

Apple requested more specific information so that it could perform alternative searches. OpenAI did not respond, and instead filed Docket No. 176 with the Court. Apple will continue to work with OpenAI to investigate its allegations.
