#421. AdultFriendFinder vs. Grindr: Which is better for hooking up?

Unless you've been living under a rock, you probably already know that Grindr has opened up access to everyone, including women, trans, and non-binary people, which now means it can compete in the larger hookup category rather than the more specific gay hookup category when it comes to comparisons.

And that got us thinking: how does Grindr stack up against the web's oldest, raunchiest hookup site, AdultFriendFinder? Specifically, when it comes to hookups, is one service much better at finding you something fun, flirty, and short-term? What are each service's strengths and weaknesses?

We put these two hookup juggernauts to the test across four major categories to see which one will work best for you. The best hookup apps, reviewed by our experts AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections Tinder — top pick for fast hookups Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups Pure — best for anonymous hookups OkCupid — best app for inclusivity Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections

Tinder — top pick for fast hookups

Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups

Pure — best for anonymous hookups

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity

Let's start with Grindr. According to their Investor Relations report, Grindr boasts 15 million active monthly users, which really does make them, in their words, the "Global Gayborhood in Your Pocket."

AdultFriendFinder, on the other hand, boasts nearly 8 million active users (7,288,978, to be precise!), but in our experience on the site, many of them are bots.

Grindr, with nearly twice as many active users, is the clear winner, then, right? Not so fast! The answer depends on what you're looking for. While AdultFriendFinder definitely has a skewed gender ratio (65 percent men, 35 percent women, according to a recent DatingAdvice breakdown), Grindr still hasn't escaped its reputation as being an app exclusively for gay men, since, according to the latest DatingNews report, Grindr's members are a whopping 93 percent male.

In other words, if you're a gay man looking for a hookup, Grindr is the clear favorite, but if you're anyone else… AdultFriendFinder still retains the edge.

The big drawback of AdultFriendFinder is that the site was founded all the way back in 1996, and though it's undergone some updates through the years, it definitely looks its age. The aesthetics, navigation tools, and even the profile photo limitations don't reflect what modern technology is capable of, so you have to get comfortable with a dated interface. On the plus side, though, AFF has one of the most comprehensive offerings of any dating site, with blogs, discussion boards, live webcam feeds, and even user-generated sex tutorials you can peruse when you're tired of looking at profiles.

Grindr, being a mobile app, operates very differently and is powered by more impressive tech. The focus of Grindr is its location-based grid, which shows you the nearest Grindr users to within 100 meters, which is about as efficient as any hookup app can get.

Other features are also much better executed on Grindr. Profile photos are larger and crisper, messages are easier to read and allow for modern conveniences like location sharing and voice notes, and the navigation bar makes it easy to switch between the main grid, your profile, and your conversations in the blink of an eye. And best of all, for those of us who prefer a computer or tablet to a smartphone, Grindr even has a web app, Grindr Web, so you can enjoy all the above perks with a full-size keyboard to boot.

Another major difference between AFF and Grindr is where their users are located. Because Grindr operates on proximity, showing you the profiles of people closest to you first, it is most effective in large metropolitan areas where you're constantly surrounded by people. On the other hand, if you live in a small town or rural community, not only are you unlikely to have many fellow Grindr members nearby, but your profile is at an inherent disadvantage since you live farther away from the core Grindr userbase.

If, for example, you live 30 minutes outside of Manhattan, there's a good chance your profile won't appear to Manhattan Grindr users, unless they manage to swipe through the millions of Grindr profiles on the island.

Which, in turn, demonstrates the beauty of AdultFriendFinder: you can be from anywhere, including rural Alaska, and still let your freak flag fly prominently, without being penalized because you don't live near a large, active member community.

This one is a bit of a toss-up, since Grindr is arguably the most effective app for people living in cities, but, for the same reason, it's much less effective for everyone else.

If you narrowly define a hookup as something that exclusively happens in person, there's a clear winner in this category: Grindr. Its location-based matchmaking algorithm and culture of horny singles constantly on the lookout for novelty make hooking up nearly as fast and efficient as ordering food for delivery. Just look at any social media site, and you'll find hundreds, if not thousands, of people talking about using Grindr and meeting people from the app. AFF? Not so much.

On the other hand, if you expand the definition to include online hookups, whether that's sexting or sharing a live webcam interaction, AdultFriendFinder has a lot going for it, beginning with the fact that you aren't limited to the people in your immediate vicinity.

For in-person fun, though, Grindr takes the victory.

Does this ultimately mean that a heterosexual male will be better off creating a Grindr profile than an AdultFriendFinder one? No, of course not. If you're a man and not at least heteroflexible, Grindr will be an exercise in disappointment, and you're automatically better off on AdultFriendFinder. But if you're gay, lesbian, or bisexual, Grindr has the goods and is clearly the future of hookup apps.

Say hello to Logitech’s best gaming keyboard in years

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A few months ago, I got the chance to test the Logitech G512 X 75 TMR, a mechanical gaming keyboard that saw the company step outside its comfort zone in many ways. For starters, it's a hot-swappable design, allowing users to easily remove the stock switches and replace them with alternatives of their choosing. More impressively, it features 39 Dual Swap switch beds that support both Logitech's TMR analog switches and standard 3-pin or 5-pin mechanical switches, allowing users to mix and match switch types across the same board. That's something I haven't seen on any other keyboard I've tested, even if the implementation feels a little half-baked.

As much as I liked that keyboard, I was instantly more enamoured by Logitech’s new G Pro X2 Rapid, despite the fact that it doesn’t break anywhere near as much new ground. It’s not hot-swappable, it doesn’t use TMR switches, and its design is far less gamer-coded. However, over the past few weeks I’ve repeatedly found myself thinking this is probably the company's strongest gaming keyboard in years, largely because Logitech has focused on its strongest attribute — polish.

I've tested plenty of keyboards over the last year that take very different design approaches. The MelGeek Made68 Ultra V2 won me over with its slick styling and enthusiast-inspired aesthetic, while the anime-themed MelGeek Centauri60 proved that a keyboard can have plenty of personality without feeling childish. Then there's the GravaStar Mercury V60 Pro, which embraces an entirely different philosophy with its sci-fi-inspired exposed-frame design. I genuinely enjoy all three, but the Logitech G Pro X2 Rapid stands out because it doesn't try nearly as hard.

Rather than relying on bold colours, elaborate themes or attention-grabbing design flourishes, it leans into restraint. The white model I tested here is particularly stunning, pairing crisp doubleshot PBT keycaps with a clean, sharp aesthetic that's clearly designed to sit alongside Logitech's G Pro X2 Superstrike gaming mouse. In my opinion, it's one of the few gaming keyboards that looks just as appropriate in a professional workspace as it does in a dedicated gaming setup.

That's also why I think it has broader appeal than some of the more adventurous keyboards I've tested recently. The Made68 Ultra V2, Centauri60 and Mercury V60 Pro all have stronger visual identities, which will undoubtedly appeal more to users who fully embrace their gamer style. The G Pro X2 Rapid, however, feels more timeless. Its understated design lets the materials, finish and overall build quality do the talking.

And that build quality goes a long way towards reinforcing the premium feel. The moment I picked it up, the keyboard felt reassuringly solid, with a rigidity that's often missing from lighter gaming boards. Despite that sturdiness, it never feels unnecessarily heavy or cumbersome on the desk.

Logitech also includes a silicone wrist rest in the box. It's not especially soft compared to memory foam alternatives, and it doubles as a remarkably effective cat hair collector, but I found it comfortable during longer gaming and typing sessions. Combined with the keyboard's excellent fit and finish, it helps create a package that feels convincingly high-end from the moment it's unboxed.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Looks aside, the Pro X2 Rapid packs all the magnetic switch features I'd expect from a flagship gaming keyboard. The factory-lubed KS-20 POM switches allow actuation points to be adjusted in tiny 0.05mm increments from 0.1mm to 4mm, giving me plenty of flexibility to tailor the typing and gaming experience. Rapid Trigger is equally well implemented, helping movement inputs feel quicker and more immediate in competitive shooters like Call of Duty and CS:GO.

Add SOCD Key Priority options, polling rates of up to 8,000Hz and Logitech's extensive KeyControl suite, and there are few complaints to be made with the performance-focused features. You can even browse and apply presets used by professional players and the wider Logitech community.

But I'd argue those features aren't really what make this keyboard special. Rapid Trigger, adjustable actuation and advanced key-prioritisation options have become baseline expectations among high-end magnetic keyboards. What impressed me more was everything Logitech built around them.

While G Hub remains the main hub for customisation, handling everything from Lightsync RGB effects to custom key assignments, the small OLED display in the keyboard's top-right corner makes quick adjustments far easier. Being able to tweak actuation settings, Rapid Trigger and key priorities without tabbing out of a game is genuinely useful and helps the keyboard feel more thoughtfully designed.

Logitech has also put considerable effort into the G Pro X2 Rapid’s acoustics. A six-layer dampening system featuring PORON and IXPE foam helps reduce unwanted resonance and gives the keyboard a deeper, fuller sound profile than many previous Logitech boards. The custom screw-in stabilisers also do an excellent job minimising wobble in larger keys, helping the overall experience feel more premium than many gaming-focused alternatives.

That's not to say it's the best-sounding Hall-effect keyboard I've used. Several rivals I’ve tested still offer a creamier keypress and a slightly snappier rebound. Even with the improved dampening, some of the familiar plastic raspiness that's long been associated with Logitech's mechanical keyboards is still present.

Thankfully, it's nowhere near enough to spoil the experience. The switches remain smooth, keypresses feel consistent, and there's enough substance to each press to make both gaming and everyday typing genuinely enjoyable.

Normally, it would be easy for me to focus on the Pro X2 Rapid's Hall-effect credentials, and to Logitech's credit, they're implemented exceptionally well. However, the reality is that most premium magnetic keyboards now offer the same level of actuation and customisation, more or less. What sets the Pro X2 Rapid apart is the level of polish surrounding these features.

Its gorgeous finish, excellent build quality, thoughtful acoustic tuning and understated industrial design give the Logitech G Pro X2 Rapid a level of refinement that, in my humble opinion, many gaming-focused keyboards struggle to match. It may not offer the creamiest typing experience in its class, but few keyboards combine performance, build quality and visual appeal as successfully as this.

#424. 10 Hacks Every YouTube TV User Should Know

YouTube TV is one of several streaming services for live TV—and a particularly good pick for sports fans who want to be able to watch and record every matchup from their favorite leagues. If YouTube TV is your platform of choice, here are the tips and tricks to optimize your experience.

If you and members of your household have wildly different streaming tastes, you can create unique profiles for each person to prevent recommendations from one from influencing another and to separate DVR libraries. A single subscription can be shared with five additional family members, who technically must reside in the same household, and those who are outside of the home need to check in once every three months (more on that below) to maintain access. You're also limited to three active streams at a time, so six people can't be watching on six separate devices at once.

If you travel frequently or are part of family sharing based anywhere besides your home, make sure you launch YouTube TV whenever you are in the account's home area. YouTube TV requires all users to check in every 90 days to avoid losing access when away from your home area. (For baseball fans, MLB imposes viewing restrictions after just 30 days.) If you get in the habit of resetting your 90-day window, you're less likely to find yourself locked out when you're on the road.

YouTube TV has pre-built multiviews that show you three or four channels at once—these are often either several games across a single sport or a combination of sports channels. Earlier this year, the platform launched customizable multiview, which allows you to select up to four channels across content categories. This means you can choose the specific games you want or mix and match sports with news, TV shows, and movies so that everyone in your household can be entertained. From any livestream, press the down button and select Multiview > Your multiview to choose up to four channels.

YouTube TV is heavy on features benefiting sports fans. If you can't begin a broadcast when a game starts, the platform offers you several options when you launch the stream: Start from the beginning, join live, or catch up to live through key plays. The latter shows you only the highlights of the action then drops you into the live stream, so you don't miss anything important but don't have to watch or fast-forward through the entire game to see what's happening now. You can also find the key plays view via Scores & stats at the bottom of the screen. This feature is supported for events from the NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL, college football, and college basketball.

Another way to avoid spoilers for live sports is to hide scores, which prevents final scores or live previews from launching before you start watching. For NFL, NBA, and MLB games, you can hide scores on a team-by-team or league-wide basis. If a league doesn't have pages for individual teams, you can hide scores for the whole league. On the team or league page, go to More and turn on Hide all scores for this team/league.

If you aren't sure what you want to watch on YouTube TV and none of the recommendations do it for you, you can use the platform's Live Guide just like the channel guide from traditional cable. However, this version is customizable, so you don't have to scroll through dozens of channels you never watch to reach the ones you do. On the web browser or app, go to Settings > Live Guide to reorder, favorite, or hide channels from your list. This can't be done directly from a streaming box, but when you open the live guide on your TV, select the Custom filter view to see your updates.

Your watch history informs recommendations on YouTube and YouTube TV, which is useful for discovering new content but also means that your algorithm can be influenced by anything and everything you watch. If you don't want certain content affecting what you're served—let's say you're binge-watching a show you wouldn't normally or you have someone staying at your house and using your account—you can pause your watch history temporarily. Tap your profile photo, go to Settings > Privacy, and toggle on Pause watch history.

YouTube TV has unlimited DVR, but that doesn't mean you need to fill your storage with content you don't plan to watch. You can record everything from an entire sport or league, or you can select only the specific teams or franchises you care about. This depends on how you set up recording: You can search for the league and tap Add + or the "+" icon to get every game, or search for your favorite team or individual matchup. DVR playback has similar options to live events you start on delay, including resuming where you left off and watching key plays.

Some content you record from the live feed may also be available as video on demand (VOD). With the former, you can fast-forward through ads; with the latter, ads can't be skipped. However, you may be able to choose your version if you used DVR. Click down on the stream to see whether you're on VOD or DVR, then go back to the show page and select Choose a Version > DVR (if available).

If you have technical issues with YouTube TV, the built-in Stats for Nerds feature can help you diagnose the problem (and whether it's coming from your network or YouTube TV itself). For example, if your resolution drops significantly, connection speed, buffer health, and dropped frames can give you a clue as to whether your wifi is the culprit. Access Stats for Nerds on your TV via player controls > More > Bug icon. On your computer, right-click on the video player; on mobile, tap More > Stats from the video player.

#426. Apple Photos in iOS 27 upgrades one of my favorite features in a big way

Apple Photos is full of exciting updates in iOS 27, including for one of my favorite features in the app: iCloud Shared Albums.

Apple’s Photos app is one of my most-used apps, as I suspect it is for many iPhone users. It’s where all of the photos and videos I capture live, plus screenshots, pictures shared by friends, and more.

But did you know that the Photos app also has a social media-style feature?

I’m not big on social media, but I do enjoy having a private, social-lite way to share memories with loved ones. And iCloud Shared Albums offers exactly that.

With iCloud Shared Albums, you can create an album that’s shared with only the people you choose. Anyone invited can add their own photos and videos, and you’ll get notified when they do. You can also ‘like’ shared photos and comment on them—just like a proper social network.

I’ve used and enjoyed Shared Albums for a long time, but the feature has felt in need of some upgrades. Fortunately, iOS 27 provides them.

In iOS 27, Shared Albums now support full-resolution photos and videos. That’s a huge item checked off my wish list.

Additionally, iOS 27 expands how you can react to a photo or video. Now you can use any emoji of your choosing as a reaction—you’re not limited to just ‘likes.’

For the first time, Android and Windows users can contribute to the album via the web. Previously, they could only view content shared by Apple users.

Apple has also made it easier to save shared photos with a tap. And you can set new participant permissions and optionally have your album expire at a later date.

These upgrades address all of the complaints I’ve previously had about Shared Albums. Combined with the other improvements in iOS 27, it’s a big year for Apple Photos.

Apple’s latest flagship headphones, the AirPods Max 2, are currently $429 (down from $549.99) on Amazon—taking $120 off every available color and bringing them within $30 of their lowest price ever, according to price trackers. They’re still a considerable investment, but the AirPods Max 2 have plenty going for them, earning a spot on our shopping editor Daniel’s list of the best over-ear headphones of 2026. PCMag is similarly impressed, giving them an “outstanding” rating for their excellent sound quality, noise cancellation, and seamless integration with Apple devices.

Much of what makes the AirPods Max 2 an improvement over their predecessor comes down to two hardware changes: a new high-dynamic-range amplifier and Apple’s H2 chip, replacing the older H1. The amplifier delivers cleaner audio, fuller bass, and better instrument separation with minimal distortion, while spatial audio makes movies and compatible music feel more immersive. Meanwhile, the H2 chip improves active noise cancellation, Transparency mode, and Voice Isolation, which helps callers hear you more clearly when you're speaking from a crowded environment.

Also, noise cancellation is now adaptive, meaning it adjusts how much outside sound comes through as your surroundings change, saving you from constantly switching listening modes. You’ll also find some useful additions beyond audio performance, including Live Translation, which lets you hear supported foreign-language conversations translated through the headphones when paired with a compatible iPhone. The buttons on the headphones can also act as a remote shutter for your iPhone’s camera, which could come in handy for group photos or hands-free recording. All said, the AirPods Max 2 makes the most sense for someone already invested in Apple's ecosystem, since several of their more interesting features depend on compatible Apple devices and software.

You can’t just snap any ordinary MagSafe power bank onto the back of the iPhone Duo. #431. Four Ways the Fitbit Edge Is Better Than the Charge 6, and Two Ways It Isn’t

The Fitbit brand has long been defined by fitness trackers with tiny screens, yet it's been three years since it released a new one. Now that the Fitbit Edge has been announced (and pre-orders have opened), longtime Fitbit users are probably wondering how it compares to the last Fitbit release with a screen, the Charge 6.

The design is the first clear difference: The Edge fits in perfectly between the screenless Fitbit Air and the smooth, curved screen of the Pixel Watch. It runs on the same operating system as the Fitbit Air, which is slightly different from the OS that runs on Pixel watches. Like other Fitbits, the Edge pairs with both iPhones and Android devices. Now, let's look at what Google has added since the Charge 6—and what it took away.

I just unboxed the Fitbit Edge that Google sent me to review, and can confirm: There is a physical button on the right side of the casing. It makes an audible click when you press it in, even when the device is turned off. The Charge 6 has a "button" that is just a haptic nub—squeeze it, and if you're lucky it might recognize your touch and buzz in response. (Sadly, I found it often didn't work.)

The altimeter is a brand-new bit of hardware in the Fitbit Edge. You have to go back to the Charge 4 to find a Fitbit tracker with an altimeter. This is the sensor that tells you your altitude and enables a measurement of how many "floors" you have climbed throughout the day. It also allows for more accurate tracking of hills on your hikes and hilly runs.

The Charge 6 and the Edge both have GPS capabilities, allowing the device to know where you are in the world, even if you left your phone at home. (The Fitbit Air, by contrast. does not have its own GPS and has to pester your phone to find out where you are and how fast you're running.) The Charge 6's GPS has some serious flaws, the main one being that tightening the wristband too much could strain the GPS antenna, leading to comically distorted maps, as you can see from my testing. Google says the Fitbit Edge has better GPS hardware. I believe them, but mainly because it would be hard for it to be worse.

This is the biggest downgrade: With the Charge 6, you could set up Google Wallet and be able to tap your Fitbit to pay for things at stores. That's a convenient feature if you like to run or walk without your phone and still be able to buy a drink at a convenience store. But the Fitbit Edge dropped this capability, probably to make room for other internal components. If you loved Google Pay on your older Fitbit, you'll miss it if you upgrade to the Edge.

The Charge 6's music player is one of the most frustrating things about it. The music controls only work for Youtube Music. That's a premium service, meaning you need to pay a monthly subscription fee just to be able to control music playing on your phone, and it has to be a subscription to Youtube Music—Spotify or Apple Music users are out of luck.

Fortunately, that's been fixed in the Fitbit Edge. Google says it will be able to control whatever is playing on your phone (like pretty much every other watch in existence) rather than relying on a specific app.

At launch, the Fitbit Edge doesn't support Google Maps directions—but Google's spec sheets say it's "coming soon." To be fair, Google Maps directions were never particularly useful. They lived in their own little app, and only gave you turn-by-turn directions, not a map view showing where you are. In the long run, this isn't likely a difference that matters, since Google plans to bring this feature to the Edge. But if you enjoy it on your Charge 6, you should know it's not going to be available right away on the Fitbit Edge.

#433. Apple execs talk Samsung’s role in creating iPhone Duo display

Apple is widely reported to have Samsung as its key supplier in building the iPhone Duo’s folding display. As a result, some have claimed that Apple is just “using a Samsung display.” Here’s how Apple addressed that question in a new interview.

Last month, YouTuber MrMobile (Michael Fisher) had the chance to interview a trio of key Apple staff who were involved in iPhone Duo’s development.

The sit-down took place following the iPhone Duo introduction, but the interview just went live on YouTube yesterday.

It’s a great video that’s well worth watching if you’re interested in the iPhone Duo. But one noteworthy portion involves the question of Samsung’s involvement in building the Duo’s display.

Here’s what Rich Dinh (VP of Hardware Engineering) and JP Guillou (Senior Director of Display Technology for iPhone) had to say:

Michael Fisher: What on the iPhone do is like straight out of the Samsung factory and what is Apple designed?

Rich Dinh: Everything that we design internally comes from the place of servicing the experience at the end of the day. And so whether it’s the display, whether it’s the hinge, whether it’s the enclosure, the chip, there are manufacturers that we work with, a number of them, incredible manufacturers that we work with. But at the end of the day, we start with, “What are we trying to accomplish?” And we start internally with, “What are we trying to accomplish in the design? What are some of the challenges we’re trying to solve for?” And then we work with our manufacturers to help us develop those parts.

Fisher then presents a contrast between the display and hinge, He suggests that Apple gets shipped a pallet of “display things” from Samsung to make the iPhone Duo, then says, “That doesn’t include the hinge, right? The hinge is not in that thing. You guys whip that up yourselves.” Here’s how Apple responds:

JP Guillou: Maybe I can say: the display doesn’t exist at the vendor until we start working on it.

Fisher: They don’t start working on it until you make an order with your specifications.

Dinh: Yeah, there’s not a, unfortunately [laughter] there’s not a pre-cooked shelf of components that we can go to.

Guillou: And certainly not ones that would meet our demands, expectations, requirements, specifications.

Fisher: Everything is a custom order for you guys.

Dinh: We really did start from the ground up. Now, there’s partners that we work with out there that are incredible partners in helping us to manufacture these designs, but it always starts with, like, we customize down to the nanometer.

Other key topics addressed in the video include iPhone Duo’s durability, the choice to use an under-display camera on the folding screen, how Apple approaches product design, and more.

What are your takeaways from MrMobile’s interview? Let us know in the comments.

#436. Hurdle hints and answers for October 18, 2026

If you like playing daily word games like Wordle, then Hurdle is a great game to add to your routine.

There are five rounds to the game. The first round sees you trying to guess the word, with correct, misplaced, and incorrect letters shown in each guess. If you guess the correct answer, it'll take you to the next hurdle, providing the answer to the last hurdle as your first guess. This can give you several clues or none, depending on the words. For the final hurdle, every correct answer from previous hurdles is shown, with correct and misplaced letters clearly shown.

An important note is that the number of times a letter is highlighted from previous guesses does necessarily indicate the number of times that letter appears in the final hurdle.

#440. Meta launches new Muse Spark Open model, optimized to run on Mac Studio

Meta today unveiled Muse Spark Open, which it says is the “most capable US open-weight model to date.” For Apple users, Meta says Muse Spark Open is optimized to run on the Mac Studio powered by M5 Ultra.

In a blog post, Meta explains that Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and brings “leading agentic capabilities to your desktop for the first time.”

Today, we’re releasing the weights for Muse Spark Open, the most capable US open-weight model to date. Muse Spark Open is a natively multimodal model with 816B total parameters (42B active) and a 1M-token context window. Built for coding and agentic work, it excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning.

Meta’s blog post specifically touts that Muse Spark Open leverages Apple’s latest version of MLX. MLX is an open source array framework created by Apple and optimized for the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon.

Using the latest version of MLX, Meta says that Muse Spark Open was optimized for Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, and that “together they’re the best way to run a powerful model on your own desktop.”

Apple’s unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra’s integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip’s 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory.

We tested a range of agentic workflows running entirely on-device, using Muse Code powered by Muse Spark Open, including shipping real iOS changes to Ice Cubes (an open-source Mastodon client) — bug fixes, new features, full build — and driving DaVinci Resolve end to end, with the model reviewing footage frame by frame to find the strongest moments and crop them vertically.

Muse Spark Open is available now through Hugging Face. Apple has also published a new article on its Machine Learning Research website touting how MLX on Mac “lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private environment.”

Apple and Meta working together is a surprise given the icy history between the two companies. In an interview with Axios, Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said they are “excited for mommy and daddy to be playing nice again.” Wang explained that Apple and Meta have been working together for several months. Wang credits Daniel Gross, a former Apple executive, with playing a “really big role in kind of getting the two companies to work nicely together.”

#441. Should You Buy Apple's New HomeView, or Is an iPad Enough?

Apple's new HomeView smart hub is fun. It looks like a cross between an iMac G4 and an Apple Watch, especially if you opt for the one with the stand—which you should probably do, seeing as the wall-mounted option requires separate hardware purchases. If you have more than one Apple user in the house, it's certainly a tempting product. But as sleek as the HomeView looks, I can't help but wonder: Is this really a better decision than an iPad on a stand?

After all, you can already control smart devices from the Home app on your iPad, not to mention take FaceTime calls, play music, check the weather, etc. And, since it's an iPad, it's inherently more versatile than a device made as a smart hub. Would you be better off buying one of Apple's tablets with a stand, and calling a day? The short answer: maybe, but not necessarily. After thinking it through, it might not make sense for everyone to splurge on the iPad in this scenario.

Despite being a new product, there's a lot of crossover between the HomeView and your average iPad. They both support FaceTime, and both place the camera along the top bezel—at least, if you have one of Apple's modern iPads. (For years, the company put the camera along the short side of the iPad, which meant it was always off-center for landscape video calls.) They both run the Home app, which means both can control your compatible smart devices. You can access Apple Music on both devices, as well as the Messages app. To that point, they both run some of the same first and third-party apps, including Calendar, Weather, Podcasts, and Find My, but it's a bit too early to know the full list of compatible apps. That said, Apple told The Verge that any app that works with CarPlay and supports audio and video streaming will appear on your HomeView if you have it on your iPhone or iPad.

Both devices also come with Safari. That's obvious on the iPad, but it's a welcome addition on the HomeView. I'm not seeing much about how Safari works on HomeView, however, other than the fact you can tap "Start Cooking" on a recipe you find in the browser to see the steps in a "streamlined format." While you can do many things on HomeView with simple gestures and voice commands, Apple also includes an on-screen keyboard here, so the iPad isn't the only device of the pair you can type on. Depending on the iPad, HomeView might actually be on-par power-wise, as well: Apple outfitted this device with the A18 chip, one generation newer than the A17 Pro in the iPad mini, and two generations newer than the chip in the A16 iPad. That runs Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, a big selling point for Apple with this device. Like other smart displays, the company wants you to ask Siri AI complex questions and make requests across your apps. That's something you can do on certain iPads too, as long as they support Apple's AI suite.

It might sound like the HomeView and the iPad are surprisingly similar, but there's a wide array of features that are exclusive to Apple's dedicated tablet. Perhaps most importantly, you have a dedicated OS to work with on iPad. It might not be macOS, but you can run multiple apps side-by-side, including with desktop-like window management, if you'd like. Speaking of apps, you'll have many more options on iPad than on HomeView. It's great that there's third-party support on HomeView, but your iPad can also tap into the entire App Store; HomeView can't.

iPads have mouse and keybord support as well, in case you don't want to rely on gesture and touch controls for everything. There's also Apple Pencil support; optional, but useful. And while both devices have front-facing cameras, all iPads have rear cameras—some better than others, but they come in handy. If you're on a FaceTime call, you don't have to turn the entire device to show someone something in front of you. There's a host of other smaller features that may matter to some, but not all, like a USB-C port, or external drive support.

On the flip side, there are perks you get with a HomeView that you just don't get on an iPad. While you can place an iPad on a stand in your kitchen, you won't be able to take advantage of HomeView's dedicated "faces." That includes the Home face, which puts all your smart devices on-screen in tiles. If your home is relatively smart, this is useful (not to mention sleek), and is a bit more streamlined than moseying over to the Home app on your iPad. To that point, HomeView's other faces make it stand out in your room: You can use it as a dynamic clock or calendar, with fun designs and effects. Even the Weather app's face looks better on HomeView than the Weather app on iPad.

The HomeView really shines if you have multiple people in your house—at least, on paper. Apple says the device can recognize up to six different users, and personalize the experience to each. You can have a custom Home Screen layout, and only be able to access your own data (like Messages); then, when a different member of your household looks at HomeView, they can access their personal setup. This type of personalization is great, and is sorely missing from the iPad. Hopefully, Apple adds profiles to iPadOS at some point in the future, like it does on macOS. Until then, HomeView offers a much better experience for multiple users.

HomeView also has the advantage when it comes to speakers—particularly if you buy the model with the stand. Apple says the screen comes with two full-range drivers, while the base has a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators. If you opted for an iPad on a stand, you'd need some sort of external audio solution to match that, which would only increase your costs.

If you're torn on buying an iPad as a HomeView alternative, the cost might just be the decision maker here. Apple is pricing the HomeView on a stand at $299, which, to me, sounds a bit pricey at first. But you get a lot for that money, especially when you consider the other option: Apple's cheapest iPad is still quite expensive, retailing for $449. The iPad mini, which gives you a more comparable display size to the HomeView, is even more expensive. Your best bet would be to find a refurbished iPad, but even then, you're likely still spending more than the cost of the HomeView. That's before you factor in a stand, or even alternative audio solutions, like a Bluetooth speaker or HomePod mini.

If you plan to use your iPad as a dedicated tablet in addition to a smart home display, that additional cost might be worth it. After all, you can switch from taking FaceTime calls in the kitchen to sending emails, making music in GarageBand, or playing games like Minecraft and Stardew Valley. But if your main goal is finding a smart display that fits in well with your existing Apple ecosystem, the HomeView isn't a bad buy.

#443. NYT Pips hints, answers for October 18, 2026

Welcome to your guide to Pips, the latest game in the New York Times catalog.

Released in August 2025, Pips puts a unique spin on dominoes, creating a fun single-player experience that could become your next daily gaming habit.

Currently, if you're stuck, the game only offers to reveal the entire puzzle, forcing you to move on to the next difficulty level and start over. However, we have you covered! Below are piecemeal answers that will serve as hints so that you can find your way through each difficulty level.

If you've ever played dominoes, you'll have a passing familiarity with how Pips is played. As we've shared in our previous hints stories for Pips, the tiles, like dominoes, are placed vertically or horizontally and connect with each other. The main difference between a traditional game of dominoes and Pips is the color-coded conditions you have to address. The touching tiles don't necessarily have to match.

The conditions you have to meet are specific to the color-coded spaces. For example, if it provides a single number, every side of a tile in that space must add up to the number provided. It is possible — and common — for only half a tile to be within a color-coded space.

Here are common examples you'll run into across the difficulty levels:

Number: All the pips in this space must add up to the number.

Equal: Every domino half in this space must be the same number of pips.

Not Equal: Every domino half in this space must have a completely different number of pips.

Less than: Every domino half in this space must add up to less than the number.

Greater than: Every domino half in this space must add up to more than the number.

If an area does not have any color coding, it means there are no conditions on the portions of dominoes within those spaces.

Greater Than (3): Everything in this space must be greater than 3. The answer is 1-4, placed horizontally.

Number (5): Everything in this light blue space must add up to 5. The answer is 5-1, placed horizontally.

Number (5): Everything in this purple space must add up to 5. The answer is 1-4, placed horizontally; 5-1, placed horizontally; 1-6, placed vertically; 1-1, placed horizontally.

Number (9): Everything in this space must add up to 9. The answer is 1-6, placed vertically; 3-4, placed horizontally.

Greater Than (7): Everything in this space must be greater than 7. The answer is 5-3, placed vertically.

Number (4): Everything in this space must add up to 4. The answer is 4-4, placed vertically.

Not Equal: Everything in this space must be different. The answer is 4-4, placed vertically; 5-2, placed vertically; 3-6, placed vertically.

Equal (2): Everything in this space must be equal to 2. The answer is 2-1, placed horizontally; 5-2, placed vertically; 2-4, placed horizontally.

Less Than (2): Everything in this space must be less than 2. The answer is 2-1, placed horizontally

Less Than (5): Everything in this space must be less than 5. The answer is 2-4, placed horizontally.

Number (10): Everything in this space must add up to 10. The answer is 6-4, placed vertically.

Number (2): Everything in this space must add up to 2. The answer is 2-0, placed horizontally.

Less Than (2): Everything in this space must be less than 2. The answer is 1-4, placed vertically.

Less Than (9): Everything in this space must be less than 9. The answer is 2-3, placed horizontally; 3-5, placed vertically.

Number (5): Everything in this light blue space must add up to 5. The answer is 3-5, placed vertically.

Number (9): Everything in this space must add up to 9. The answer is 6-3, placed horizontally.

Less Than (5): Everything in this space must be less than 5. The answer is 1-3, placed vertically.

Equal (6): Everything in this space must be equal to 6. The answer is 6-6, placed vertically; 6-2, placed horizontally.

Number (12): Everything in this space must add up to 12. The answer is 4-6, placed vertically; 2-2, placed horizontally.

Equal (2): Everything in this space must be equal to 2. The answer is 6-2, placed horizontally; 2-2, placed horizontally; 2-1, placed vertically; 2-5, placed vertically; 2-1, placed vertically.

Less Than (2): Everything in this space must be less than 2. The answer is 2-1, placed vertically.

Greater Than (4): Everything in this space must be greater than 4. The answer is 2-5, placed vertically.Greater Than (7): Everything in this space must be greater than 7. The answer is 2-5, placed vertically.

Number (3): Everything in this space must add up to 3. The answer is 3-0, placed vertically.

'It Follows,' 'Smile,' and more nightmare fuel worthy of your weekend

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Anyone looking to embrace the Sunday scaries rather than chase them away with a feel-good comfort watch (hey, no judgement — time's are tough), Paramount+ just added over 20 new horror movies to kick off spooky season. I'm a huge horror movie fan, and of the batch, these are the top 3 that deserve a spot on your watchlist.

From the deeply unsettling "Smile" and the haunting found-footage of "Sinister" to the slow-burn dread of "It Follows," there's something for everybody on this list. I've ranked them by least to most scary, so if you're hemming and hawing about diving into the horror genre, no sweat. Start with "It Follows," see how that goes, and then let us know how it went in the comments — I'm interested to hear your thoughts!

Whether you’re a longtime horror fan or just looking for one last thrill before the work week starts, I'm rounding up some of the best scares currently streaming on Paramount+. So dim the lights, get comfy, and check out these horror movies worth adding to your watchlist this weekend.

I'll shout out "It Follows" every chance I get because it's a great movie to help non-horror fans dip their toes in to the genre. The ending feels a little corny, but I was on the edge of my seat up until that point, so it's easy enough to roll with the peak campy slasher vibes. Maika Monroe stars as Jay, a young woman who's stalked by a terrifying supernatural entity after hooking up with a guy. This thing will follow her to the end of the Earth, and it can look like anyone.

The only way to escape the curse along is to have sex with someone else to give whatever the hell it is a new target. As Jay and her friends scramble to find a way to break the curse without condemning someone else, paranoia gets its hooks in them. Its slow-burn tension and ever-present sense that anyone could be a threat make “It Follows” the kind of movie that’ll have you obsessively scanning the background and hiding behind your hands any time someone gets just a little too close.

Moving now to a horror movie for horror fans, "Smile" plays in the same sandbox of paranoia and mounting dread as "It Follows." The final monster reveal is...laughable (my friends and I cackled in theaters at it), but everything up until that point is a genuine treat, riffing on the audience's expectations and trope of the unreliable narrator to terrifying ends.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

"Smile" follows a therapist named Rose (Sosie Bacon) caught up in an unsettling supernatural curse after a new patient, Laura (Caitlin Stasey), kills herself under Rose's watch — smiling creepily the entire time. Things get weirder when Rose starts seeing things and acting out of character with no memory of doing so. Her friends and family write off her fears as signs of a mental breakdown, leaving her on her own to break the curse before she becomes its next victim. If you like this one, the surprisingly competent sequel, "Smile 2," is also on Paramount+.

A decade before he terrified us as the Grabber in the phenomenal "The Black Phone," Ethan Hawke had a real horror protagonist moment in the early 2010s between "The Purge" and "Sinister." I'll always have a soft spot in my heart for the latter, because it's managed to claw its way back into my nightmares over the years. "Sinister" is haunting in every sense of the word, and I say that as someone who watches a lot of horror movies.

Hawke's sympathetic as struggling true-crime writer Ellison, who's stuck in a rut of writer’s block after his family's big move. While settling in, he finds a box of old film reels hidden in the attic — strange home movies that he's horrified to realize are of a string of brutal murders that have gone unsolved for decades. Ellison becomes obsessed, convinced he just found the key to his next bestselling novel. But as he digs deeper, forces beyond his understanding twist his psyche, and even after the family flees their new home, he can't escape the nightmare he's unleashed.

#449. How to Preorder the New Fitbit Edge (and Why You Might Want To)

Google announced the Fitbit Edge earlier this week, making it the company's first Fitbit with a screen since the Charge 6 was released in 2023. Pre-orders are open now, and the devices are expected to start shipping on Oct. 27.

The Fitbit Edge ($179.99) has features and a price that are right in between the Fitbit Air, which has no screen and retails for $99.99, and the Pixel Watch 5, a full-featured smartwatch that starts at $399.99.

You can pre-order the Fitbit Edge here. It comes in black with a black band, silver with a "fog" (gray) band, "champagne gold" with a salmon-pink band, and a metallic color they're calling "satin pyrite" with an olive green band. There's also a Steph Curry edition for $219.99 in gray and orange. The standard packages come with two bands, a small/medium that fits wrists 130 to 170 millimeters around, and a medium/large for wrists 170 to 210 millimeters. There are a few other bands available for an extra fee: an "active sport" band with larger holes for ventilation ($39.99), a magnetic band ($49.99), and a band with metal links ($149.99).

Unlike the screenless Fitbit Air, the Fitbit Edge adds its own GPS chipset, so you can track distance without bringing your phone, and an altimeter to detect elevation changes like hills. The latter also enables a "floors climbed" metric each day. The Fitbit Edge also has an ECG app, a morning report, and can control music playing on your phone no matter what app is playing it.

If you're upgrading from a Fitbit Charge 6, the Edge adds an altimeter and a morning report, and you'll be glad to see the music controls work for any music app, not just Youtube Music. The Edge is missing some features, though: With no NFC, it can't do tap-to-pay with Google Wallet. The Edge also does not have Google Maps directions at launch, although Google says these are coming soon. The EDA scan and stress tracking are also gone. (Personally, I'm glad about that. Stress tracking isn't accurate enough to be useful.)

#450. Apple SVP Greg Joswiak: ‘We don’t feel threatened’ by OpenAI hardware plans

Today in a new story at TIME, the publication interviewed CEO John Ternus but also spoke to Greg “Joz” Joswiak, Apple’s SVP of Worldwide Marketing, who addressed the “lunatic fringe” of AI in Silicon Valley, hardware threats from OpenAI, and more.

TIME picked the iPhone Duo as one of 2026’s best inventions and interviewed CEO John Ternus plus a few other Apple execs for the story.

One of those other interviewees, SVP of Worldwide Marketing Greg Joswiak, addressed Apple’s AI strategy, OpenAI hardware efforts, and more.

When asked about the ChatGPT maker’s hardware plans, Joswiak said: “We don’t feel threatened. The fact that we can do the integration that we can means we can create just a better experience than anybody else.”

Apple’s integration of hardware, software, and services has long been central to the company’s product ethos. And it clearly believes those ecosystem strengths will be a strong defense against new competitors.

I think this is a great way of looking at it. Apple has always promoted Apple Intelligence as way to assist you in what you already do - not to completely take it over, and have you forget you ever did it.

AI is here, but for how long? With growing backlash, companies re-hiring employees once fired to be replaced by AI… backlash is growing.

AI was and IS being used a scapegoat by companies to lay off employees, and proclaim improvement of efficiency. While boosting stock prices temporarily.

These same companies should be taxed much higher than if they maintained employees. Having a human to authorize and final review proposes by AI should ALWAYS Be how it’s utilized.

If you lay everyone off, who’s going to have cash to buy your product?

We all learned during COVID, that the government is as slow as a snail when it comes to providing assistance in how much of us needed it.

We’re cutting SS, Medicare, and have been for decades. Where if AI were to layoff most people, how would Universal Basic Income work and be allotted for?

Joswiak also implies that perhaps OpenAI’s products won’t have as broad appeal as Apple devices do. From the story’s very next paragraph:

Joswiak adds that Apple isn’t making products for the die-hard AI believers chasing superintelligence. “We love them, and they can use it too, but that’s not our target,” he says. “It’s how to make it better for everyday people.”

This sort of split between the average person and the AI enthusiast is also highlighted by Joswiak elsewhere in the interview. Andrew Chow writes:

While Apple trains its own models, it is nowhere near the technology’s frontier, leaving the company vulnerable to being left behind if super-smart AI transforms industry and society in the coming years…But Ternus and other Apple executives say they aren’t concerned. In the midst of a populist AI backlash, they contend that they are building a modest but personalized and privacy-preserving form of AI that will actually help ordinary people as opposed to merely dazzling Silicon Valley’s “lunatic fringe,” as Greg Joswiak, senior vice president of worldwide marketing, puts it.

Joswiak doesn’t define this “lunatic fringe,” but by contrasting it with Apple’s own efforts to “help ordinary people,” he’s making a clear distinction.

What are your takeaways from Greg Joswiak’s remarks on AI? Let us know in the comments.

#451. NYT Connections hints today: Clues, answers for October 18, 2026

The NYT Connections puzzle today is not too difficult if you're a fashionista.

Connections is the one of the most popular New York Times word games that's captured the public's attention. The game is all about finding the "common threads between words." And just like Wordle, Connections resets after midnight and each new set of words gets trickier and trickier—so we've served up some hints and tips to get you over the hurdle.

If you just want to be told today's puzzle, you can jump to the end of this article for today's Connections solution. But if you'd rather solve it yourself, keep reading for some clues, tips, and strategies to assist you.

The NYT's latest daily word game has become a social media hit. The Times credits associate puzzle editor Wyna Liu with helping to create the new word game and bringing it to the publications' Games section. Connections can be played on both web browsers and mobile devices and require players to group four words that share something in common.

Each puzzle features 16 words and each grouping of words is split into four categories. These sets could comprise of anything from book titles, software, country names, etc. Even though multiple words will seem like they fit together, there's only one correct answer.

If a player gets all four words in a set correct, those words are removed from the board. Guess wrong and it counts as a mistake—players get up to four mistakes until the game ends.

Players can also rearrange and shuffle the board to make spotting connections easier. Additionally, each group is color-coded with yellow being the easiest, followed by green, blue, and purple. Like Wordle, you can share the results with your friends on social media.

#452. Garmin Just Launched a Luxury Smartwatch With a Price to Match

Yesterday the MARQ Gen 3 turned up on Garmin's support pages, and today, the company has made it official. Garmin launched its third-generation luxury smartwatch collection, a lineup of six models priced from $2,500 to $3,100. That sure is a lot of money for a watch. Let's take a look at what exactly you get with the new Garmin MARQ Gen 3.

The new collection consists of the MARQ Athlete, Adventurer, Aviator, Commander, Golfer and Diver. Across all six, Garmin has moved to larger AMOLED displays, added LTE and satellite connectivity, expanded its mapping, and brought in its latest health and fitness features that I detail in my review of Garmin's other recent release, the Fenix 9 Pro.

The hardware follows the luxury formula the MARQ line is known for. Each watch has a 47 mm Grade 5 titanium case, a sapphire crystal lens, and a ceramic bezel inlay. Each is 15 mm thick and carries a 1.4-inch AMOLED display, up from 1.2 inches on the previous generation.

At the bottom of the range, the MARQ Athlete is the entry point at $2,500. It comes on a silicone strap with VO2 max markings on the bezel, and includes Garmin's full collection of running and training features. The MARQ Adventurer costs $2,700 and pairs an Italian leather strap with a compass bezel. This one is aimed at hiking, navigation and climbing, and includes preloaded ClimbPro information.

And so on: The remaining four models are each built around a specific pursuit, as MARQ variants have been since the line debuted. The MARQ Aviator is the flight-focused model, the MARQ Commander is the tactical one, the MARQ Golfer is built for the course, and the MARQ Diver is the one for the water. Garmin's pricing and strap details for these four sit between the Athlete's $2,500 and the $3,100 top of the range.

In terms of software updates, the biggest addition is embedded inReach connectivity. All six watches support LTE calling, messaging and location sharing without a phone nearby, along with satellite messaging and emergency SOS through Garmin Response. Note: These services require a separate inReach subscription.

Garmin has also added a speaker, a microphone, and an LED flashlight. Other upgrades include the ECG app in supported regions, newer health and recovery metrics, and worldwide TopoActive maps with address search. Storage has jumped from 32GB to 128GB, and battery life reaches up to 18 days in smartwatch mode, or seven days with the always-on display enabled.

What's most exciting is how these changes bring the MARQ much closer to Garmin's latest high-end sports watches, as opposed to being more of an aesthetic purchase. Previously, MARQ buyers were paying a considerable premium for hardware that lacked some features already available elsewhere in the range. Honestly, the earlier MARQ was, in effect, a fancy-materials version of a watch you could get for less, with fewer capabilities.

Now, the MARQ Gen 3 is finally a watch that tops the Garmin lineup with all the features of a Fenix. And for the first time, the MARQ has pluses the Fenix doesn't, like increased storage and on-device mapping features. The question of whether such premium price Garmin has set is worth it? That's still up for debate.

Garmin says the collection is available now, with broader availability reportedly scheduled for Nov. 5. You can see the full lineup on Garmin's site here.

#454. Hands-on: Pokémon x Beats Pill is one of my favorite collabs yet [Video]

As someone who loves all things Apple and Pokémon, I never thought these worlds would collide, but here we are! Beats and the Pokémon Company have officially teamed up for a special edition Beats Pill, and man, did they nail this. This new collab features both Pikachu and Mimikyu, bringing a two-tone design, unique accessories, and some awesome attention to detail in a speaker that we know and love. I have been using mine for a few days and wanted to share my thoughts as a fan of both brands in this collaboration.

Be sure to check out our hands-on video to see what this new Beats Pill is really like!

With a collab and product like this, the design is the selling point. The first thing that stands out is the packaging. You get this awesome two-tone design that gives us Pikachu’s signature yellow color that pops, and on the other side, you get the more grayscale, monotone look associated with Mimikyu. They even have all the ears of each Pokémon pop up past the packaging, which is a fun touch. But the real magic is when you open this thing up.

Both Pokémon are featured directly on the speaker grill, giving the Pill a completely different personality from the standard versions. On the left, you see the grayscale Mimikyu, and on the right, you see the bright yellow and red-cheeked Pikachu. But they didn’t stop there. Around the Pikachu, there are protruding lightning bolts with chrome accents that literally pop off the speaker, giving it a nice look and texture. Then, my favorite part is that Beats is including a charm on the lanyard portion of the Beats Pill. The charm is a rubber, double-sided circle with one side showing the Beats logo and the other side showing a Poké Ball.

Between the unboxing experience and the product’s uniqueness, this feels more like a collectible than anything else. It just so happens to be a fantastic Bluetooth speaker as well, and I think that was the entire point.

As I mentioned, beneath all the Pokémon-themed goodness, this is the same Beats Pill we already know and that Apple has been selling for a bit. It comes with the same acoustic system, powerful bass in a portable design. You get:

Again, no major hardware differences compared to a Beats Pill. But the Pill already offers a great combination of sound, battery life, convenience, and portability. So this is just another one to add to the collection.

The Pokémon x Beats Pill is available starting today, October 15th at 11 AM EST. You can pick one up online or in-store at both Apple and Target for $149. For reference, a normal Beats Pill is the same $149 at Apple and $129 at Target and other retailers. Also, if you just want a Beats Pill and don’t care about the color, the Kim Kardashian version is on sale for $85 on Amazon.

Overall, I think Beats nailed this collab with the Pokémon Company. It’s fun and different, with fantastic attention to detail. If you are already a Pokémon fan and have been considering a portable speaker, then this seems like an obvious choice. I also think plenty of collectors will buy this and keep it sealed, so I assume it will sell out almost immediately. I do wish they made the pairing sound a Pikachu noise; that would have been the cherry on top! Maybe for the next one.

What do you think? Is this a collab you saw coming? Are you picking one up?

#456. Which Should You Believe After a Race, Your Official Distance or Your Watch?

You just finished running a race, but your watch disagrees with the official distance and timing. Which should you trust? While race organizers can screw up their distance or timing, they usually don't. Let's look at how races are measured and why they may disagree with your watch—which happens more often than you might realize.

Before we compare a watch time to an official race time, we need to know what kind of official race time we're looking at. There are two different numbers you might see from a race: gun time and chip time. They may differ from each other and from your watch. Here's where each comes from:

Chip time, also sometimes called net time, is the time from when you personally cross the start line until you personally cross the finish line. This is the time that matters for most of us.

Chips measure your personal start and finish because big races often have a crowd at the start line. If you’re running a big-city marathon, it could be 10 minutes or more of waiting and then slowly moseying forward with the crowd before you are able to cross the start line. In that case, your marathon could have a 4:40:00 gun time and a 4:30:00 chip time.

The “chip” in the name refers to a computer chip that is usually embedded in your racing bib (the numbers you pin to your shirt). The timing system registers a data point whenever you cross a timing mat on the ground. There is a timing mat at the start and another at the end of the race. (Longer races like marathons and half-marathons may also have timing mats at a few checkpoints along the way, such as the halfway point.)

Gun time is the time from when the race starts (often signaled by a starting pistol, hence “gun”) until you cross the finish line. This is also sometimes called clock time.

If you are trying to actually win the race, you may need to care about gun time. Sometimes the rules specify that the person who wins the race is the person who crosses the finish line first, regardless of when they crossed the start line. If you are an elite athlete who is in the running to win a big race, you’ll generally work out arrangements with the race organizer to be at the actual start line when the race starts, so that the gun time accurately reflects how long it took you to run the race.

But for the rest of us, gun time doesn’t matter at all. The exception is if you are in a very small local race that doesn’t use chip timing, or that only has one mat at the finish line (no mat at the start). In that case, only a gun time will be reported, and no chip time.

Watch time is the name I’m using here for the time you see on your wristwatch, or in your running app after the fact. If you start and end the timer exactly when you cross the start and finish lines, and never pause it in between, in theory, it should be the same as the chip time. All the major brands of running watches and smartwatches do an accurate-enough job in most situations. But you shouldn't trust it too much—let me explain why.

As I mentioned above, gun time only matters if there is no chip time, if you’re trying to win an award in a race that uses gun times for awards, or if you’re trying to qualify for the Olympics.

Use the chip time anytime you’re telling someone what you ran, or when you’re keeping track of your personal bests (PBs). (Only use a watch time if you ran a race with no chip time, and even then make sure to use your actual total time between the start and finish lines, no pausing. In that case, you're not trusting the watch over the chip time; you're just using it to estimate a missing chip time.)

Watch time should be the same as chip time if you started and stopped your watch at the start and finish lines. But it’s often not. Some of the reasons your watch time might be wrong:

Your watch auto-pauses. This is a convenient setting on training runs, if you often stop for a water break or to wait to cross a street. Your watch will pause your run when you stop, and resume recording when you move again. But during a race, stops aren’t free! If you stop to spend two minutes in a porta-potty, that’s still part of your race time.

Your app (such as Strava) might report a “moving” time. Same idea as above, but it happens even if your watch recorded the whole thing. For example, on one longish run I did, I remember stopping to tie my shoe. Strava shows this run as taking 1:17:02. But if I scroll down through the numbers it gives, I can also see an elapsed time of 1:17:28. I guess it took me 26 seconds to tie my shoe.

On Strava, you can make your elapsed time show up first by selecting Edit Activity and then changing Type of Run to Race. If I do that on my shoe-tying run, the elapsed time with the extra 26 seconds shows up on that Strava activity.

There is one other reason why your official race result might not make sense, even if it’s a chip time and it’s showing the same as your watch’s elapsed time: Every now and then, a race organizer fucks up.

One time, I was running a 2K race (1.2 miles) and was expecting a finish time somewhere between nine and 10 minutes. My watch registered a number in that range, but I knew it was probably off by a few seconds. When I checked the official results shortly after crossing the finish line, I had a time of 12:29, about three minutes longer than I was expecting! And in this case, I had started near the start line (it was a small, local race), so I couldn’t blame a gun/chip time difference. Turns out the timing service had accidentally added three minutes to everyone’s times. They noticed the error pretty quickly, though, and my official time was soon updated to 9:29. (I got an age group medal that day, and wrote my time on the back, which is why I remember it all these years later.)

So if your official race result is way off, consider speaking to the race organizer. There may have been an error that affects everybody, or they may only have a gun time and not a chip time.

There’s one other consideration here: not just the time on your watch, but the distance. You may find that your watch’s time was within a few seconds of your chip time, but the distance seems wrong—usually too long. Or if you upload your run to Strava, you may find that the notorious "Strava tax" has been applied, appearing to shave off a bit of distance. (My best 5K in the last few years was recorded on Strava as 4.99 kilometers and thus didn't update my 5K PR. Am I mad? OK, yes.)

The first thing to check is whether the race course was certified. (Most are.) The process of certifying a race course ensures that the course has been measured to be the correct distance. And that distance is nearly guaranteed to be shorter than most runners actually run. So, yes, you will probably run a smidge longer than 3.1 miles in a 5K (3.1 mile) race!

You can read the USATF course certification guidelines here. Of particular interest is this part: "A race course is defined by the shortest possible route that a runner could take and not be disqualified. A given runner might not follow the shortest possible route…[t]he actual path of any given runner is irrelevant. The shortest possible route is a reasonably well-defined and unambiguous route that ensures all runners will run at least the stated race distance." (Emphasis theirs.)

How does one find the shortest possible route? "You might envision the shortest possible route as a string, stretched tightly along the course so that it comes within 30 cm (one foot) of all corners, straight through S-turns, and diagonally between corners when crossing a street. You should measure the course following the same route as that hypothetical string." In addition, there is a 0.1% correction factor added to the measured distance, to ensure “that your course will not be short, even if you make small errors in following the shortest possible route.”

The only time your smartwatch’s distance should make you doubt the course measurement is if your watch thinks you covered a significantly shorter distance than the advertised length of the race. In that case, check your map to see if the GPS route looks like the route you actually ran. If you had poor GPS accuracy, your watch (or phone) might draw a line that cuts a corner that you did not actually cut.

If your map looks correct, but your distance is still short, it’s worth checking with other runners to see if they had a short distance as well. Mistakes in course measurement or signage are rare, but they happen! The San Francisco Marathon accidentally shaved half a mile off its half-marathon course once. If you think your race course was short, contact the race organizer.

Your PB, or personal best, can be whatever you want it to be in your heart. But if you want to brag about your times or compare them with other runners, you'll want to talk about chip time.

This is where the distance issue comes up. Maybe you finished your first 5K in 30:03 chip time, but your watch congratulated you on a 5K PR of 28:59. What gives? Check the distance, and you might see that your total race distance was 3.22 miles, with 28:59 being the time it took you to hit 3.1 (at which point the finish line was in sight, but you weren't actually done with the race). Sorry, but you didn't officially run a sub-30 5K.

This is why we distinguish race PBs from training PBs. The race course's timing is more accurate, and its certified distance is more accurate than your GPS even though the actual route that you personally run may be a bit longer than the certified distance. People tend to hit PBs at races because that's when you're the best prepared for a big effort and you have a crowd cheering you on. But the distance being potentially longer than advertised means that it is more of an accomplishment to run a "5K" race in a certain time than to run exactly five kilometers in that time.

So when another runner asks for your 5K time, they mean a race. You can proudly and accurately cite your chip time—in our example, 30:03. But you could also add: "My best training PB for that distance is 28:59, so I know I'm going to break 30 minutes officially soon." You will. I believe in you.

#457. John Ternus talks iPhone Duo, ‘cheap and crappy’ foldables in new interview

TIME has just published its list of the best inventions of 2026, and iPhone Duo made the list with John Ternus featured on the magazine cover. Here’s what Ternus said in his interview with TIME.

John Ternus sat down with TIME for a wide-ranging interview centered on iPhone Duo, but also covering a variety of other topics, including AI.

Regarding the iPhone Duo, which is hitting the market nearly a decade after other foldables, Ternus was involved in early foldable work at Apple all the way back in 2011.

In 2011, when many people still carried around flip phones, Ternus and five other engineers filed a patent application for foldable electronic devices, exploring what kind of batteries and circuit boards might be needed for such an idea. “It felt clear that we were going to eventually get to a place where OLED displays were going to be flexible,” Ternus says.

Ternus wasn’t a fan of early attempts at foldables from other companies in the 2010s. He says, “The other examples in the world felt kind of cheap and crappy.”

The drive to achieve a foldable unlike its competitors is evidenced by a story from Richard Dinh, Apple’s VP of Product Design.

Along the way, Ternus encouraged the team to invest more time and effort in the project, even as other foldables beat them to market. Dinh says that at one point, he asked Ternus whether his team should proceed with a top surface material similar to those of its competitors, which Dinh felt had flaws but was potentially good enough.

“And he was like, ‘Look, Rich, you’ll know when it’s the right thing.’ And that gave us the confidence to really push the boundaries on innovation and manufacturing, and fly worldwide to connect our suppliers together and come up with the nanotexture [a surface technology],” Dinh says. The result—a surface made from a custom polymer and built atop a hinge with more than 100 tiny interior precision components—has impressed its first users, who have said they can barely detect a crease at all.

We don't release products until they're ready. Also here's the new Siri AI that we had to use gemini for.

The story also mentions that Ternus “has devoted much of his early tenure as CEO to obsessing over design, spending multiple days a week in the studio with the industrial-design and human-interface teams.” This echoes previous Bloomberg reporting around Ternus’s early priorities.

#458. Wordle today: Answer, hints for October 18, 2026

Today's Wordle answer should be easy to solve if you like to get dolled up.

If you just want to be told today's word, you can jump to the bottom of this article for today's Wordle solution revealed. But if you'd rather solve it yourself, keep reading for some clues, tips, and strategies to assist you.

Originally created by engineer Josh Wardle as a gift for his partner, Wordle rapidly spread to become an international phenomenon, with thousands of people around the globe playing every day. Alternate Wordle versions created by fans also sprang up, including battle royale Squabble, music identification game Heardle, and variations like Dordle and Quordle that make you guess multiple words at once.

Wordle eventually became so popular that it was purchased by the New York Times, and TikTok creators even livestream themselves playing.

The best Wordle starting word is the one that speaks to you. But if you prefer to be strategic in your approach, we have a few ideas to help you pick a word that might help you find the solution faster. One tip is to select a word that includes at least two different vowels, plus some common consonants like S, T, R, or N.

It might feel like Wordle is getting harder, but it actually isn't any more difficult than when it first began. You can turn on Wordle's Hard Mode if you're after more of a challenge, though.

#461. Half of United flights have Starlink Wi-Fi – here’s how to check yours

United Airlines first introduced Starlink Wi-Fi on its flights starting early in 2025, the airline says nearly half of its flights currently offer the high-speed satellite internet service. It’s now introduced a new way to let you check whether your flight has the service …

The airline says that it intends to hit 100% Starlink coverage by the end of next year, while current installation rates depend on the fleet. For mainline aircraft flying long distance routes, the current figure is 37%, while United Express regional jets have significantly greater coverage at 68%.

United already has more Starlink-equipped planes than any other airline in the world and is installing it on about 20 aircraft per week with plans to complete installations by the end of 2027. More than 250,000 United customers on average fly on a Starlink-equipped plane every day onboard more than 2,500 flights – nearly half the airline’s daily departures.

Starlink is now active on more than 635 United mainline and United Express aircraft and the airline has already flown more than 37.7 million passengers on Starlink-powered aircraft across more than 538,000 flights, powering 14 million devices.

United already notifies you about the availability of Starlink Wi-Fi in preflight emails and texts, but it’s now introduced a tracker in case of any equipment changes on your route. Airlines do sometimes need to swap aircraft at relatively short notice to account for issues like technical faults and flight cancellations that leave planes incorrectly positioned for their next scheduled flight.

Simply go to this tracking link within two days of your departure, entering your flight number and departure date. If you check further ahead, the tracker will show you the percentage likelihood based on recent flights on the same route, but it’s only within 48 hours that you’ll get a generally reliable answer.
