#490. The 10 best cheap wireless earbuds, tested by audio experts

Contrary to what you might think, you don't need to break the bank to get a great pair of earbuds. We spend a lot of time fawning over the latest tech here at Mashable, but new tech is usually expensive tech, especially in 2026. And as much as we love nerding out over the newest Sony headphones drop, we know that not everyone wants to spend $450 on a pair of flagship noise-cancelling headphones. So, that's why we're here to talk about the best budget earbuds. All of the products in this guide have been rigorously tested by a member of the Mashable team, and we've included our favorite wireless earbuds from Beats, Nothing, Apple, and Bose.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

Let's be clear: Just because these earbuds are affordable, that doesn't mean they skimp on features.

Mashable audio experts have tested all of the most popular wireless headphones and earbuds (not to mention some wired options). And the very best noise-cancelling wireless earbuds typically cost $250 to $300 — the Apple AirPods Pro 3 retail for $249 (but often go on sale for $179), and Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (Gen 2) come in at $299.

Fortunately, you don't need to spend $300 to get a great pair of wireless earbuds; in fact, you don't even need to spend $100. The best cheap wireless earbuds under $100 include some great options from JBL, Nothing, Anker Soundcore, and Beats. And if you're willing to spend a little more, the newest Apple AirPods 5 sound great and include new AI features such as live translation.

When reviewing earbuds for this guide, we looked for features such as easy connectivity, rich and balanced sound, active noise cancellation, and a comfortable fit. And among all the earbuds we've tested, which is an extensive list, these are the best budget earbuds for 2026.

Those looking for the best all-around package for their dollar. Anker’s latest mid-range buds have the firepower and functionality of top-performing luxury buds. At $64.99, they’re the true embodiment of getting plenty of features without sacrificing affordability.

The P42i pack many of the same features as Anker’s premium models and performs nearly as well in audio, battery life, and noise cancellation — all at a third of the price. If you don't want to drop $150 on AirPods or Bose wireless earbuds, these are a great all-around pick under $100.

Anticipate crisp instrument separation, deep bass, and sharp vocals when plugging them into your ears. The Soundcore Signature preset is well-balanced, and there are additional presets and a customizable EQ to personalize the sound. Enabling the LDAC codec boosts fidelity to hear more detail and nuance when streaming music on Android devices. However, you’ll want to set up the HearID feature, as it intuitively creates a sound profile tailored to your hearing.

Noise cancellation is also pivotal to sound performance. It provides an uptick in bass that gives contemporary recordings more oomph. Multi-level ANC produces an extra layer of noise reduction to minimize unwanted noise. Standard mode silences low- and mid-frequency sounds with ease, especially when set to Ultra ANC. Adaptive mode scans the environment to achieve stronger noise neutralization. Wind Noise Reduction is great at reducing harsh wind effects. Transparency mode is equally excellent and has a HearGuard setting that protects your hearing by automatically adjusting the amount of loud noise entering the buds.

In addition to the aforementioned features, these buds come with a Fit Test, multi-device connectivity, wearing detection, and a Game Mode that reduces latency when gaming. There’s even AI integration (e.g., Live Translation, chatbot capabilities), which is much better than it was on past Anker releases.

Fast charging (10 mins=3.5 hours) is some of the best at this price point. A full charge provides up to 12 hours of listening time, depending on how you use the buds, and the wireless charging case provides up to 56 hours of listening time.

Flaws are very few. Spatial audio drastically hollows out the midrange, and the small-stem design with tiny capacitive sensors makes tap input difficult. Besides that, these are near-flawless buds at an unbeatable value.

Audio nerds on a budget who want extensive sound customization and hi-res streaming over Bluetooth. While they retail for $99.99, you can typically buy them on sale via Amazon for $79.99, making them a solid alternative to AirPods.

Our previous top pick for the best cheap earbuds under $100, the EarFun Air Pro 4, didn’t need a director’s cut. Nonetheless, we received one in the Air Pro 4 Plus.

EarFun’s new dual-driver acoustic system with balanced armature enhances bass response and treble for terrific low-mid presentation. Drums and synths sound pleasant and punchy. Mids and lows also receive proper attention. EarFun spared no expense, blessing the Plus version with top-tier Bluetooth audio codecs. AptX Adaptive/Lossless and LDAC provide dynamic scaling and higher streaming quality. Other wireless audio perks like Auracast and LE Audio are appreciated.

Battery life isn’t significantly higher; you’re only getting 1 hour more per charge and 2 hours more from the charging case. That works for us, as do other retained hallmarks, including a comfortable fit, instantaneous multi-device pairing, and serviceable EQ functions.

ANC performed well on the previous model. The same can’t be said here. While electronic humming and loud voices are silent, everything else is audible and disruptive. The multiple AI noise-cancelling modes do little to suppress external sounds. Even the two ambient listening modes perform unevenly. Default produces clear vocals, but it also makes environmental noises sound harsh. Natural softens ambient noise and drastically decreases vocal presence simultaneously.

It’s hard not to fault EarFun for mishandling noise cancellation on a next-gen release. At the same time, the company overdelivered on audio performance in ways we never expected.

Bargain-bin shoppers who prioritize substance over style; anyone looking for the best cheap earbuds under $50. Much of the FlyBuds C3’s charm is exhibited through wonderful sound performance that receives a nice boost from Tribit’s impressively engineered music presets.

Aesthetically, there’s nothing appealing about the FlyBuds C3. Their plain, long-stem design with a trite matte finish screams off-brand mediocrity. Yet what they lack in physical appeal, they vastly make up for in sound.

Are we talking Anker or JBL quality? No, but the buds still produce solid audio, and Tribit keeps the listening experience simple with user-friendly features in the mobile app to easily tweak performance on the fly.

Proprietary 10mm NdFeB drivers pump out satisfying frequencies. XBass technology sounds more balanced than ever on a Tribit product; the extra thump felt on bass-centric tracks is impactful and doesn’t bloat up the soundstage. It’s worth toying around with the EQ and presets for optimized sonic presentation with select music genres.

Niche features like antibacterial coating and Hearing Protection mode are overlooked. They help extend the buds’ lifespan and preserve your hearing, respectively. Multipoint technology also comes in clutch to seamlessly switch between two audio sources.

We'll be honest: ANC and spatial audio don’t contribute anything positive. Deluxe features like these aren’t necessary for $35. Great sound is, and the FlyBuds C3 guarantee it at a highly attainable MSRP.

Brand enthusiasts who want Sony audio quality and the best noise neutralization available for under $100. The fact that these buds come with nearly every Sony proprietary sound technology should make them cost double their sale price, which is consistently around $80. These were a popular pick in our guide to the best Sony headphones as well.

If the $328 Sony WF-1000xM6 are out of your financial reach, which is reasonable considering the current economy, then pick up the WF-C710N. They offer nearly everything their flagship counterpart does, from adjustable ANC to fidelity upscaling to multipoint technology.

You’re essentially getting a stripped-down version of the WF-1000xM5’s noise cancellation, which is still superior to most options in the budget and mid-range categories. It eliminates up to 85 percent of unwanted sounds. Most high-frequency noises are audible, but they end up sounding like background effects on most tracks. Then there’s the 20-level Ambient Sound mode that vastly increases awareness in all surroundings. The mics can pick up conversations from across the street and high-frequency noises from several blocks away.

Sony’s 5mm dynamic drivers dish out booming lows, expressive mids, and crisp highs, resulting in a well-balanced mix that complements most music genres and video content. Audiophiles have a plethora of sound features at their disposal, including a customizable multi-band EQ and various well-engineered presets. DSEE enhances the quality of compressed low-quality audio files to pull more detail from recordings. The WF-C710N also come with 360 Reality Audio, but the feature is underwhelming on these buds and limited to a handful of streaming services.

The long playtimes (up to 12 hours) allow for lengthy listening sessions, though your ears will need occasional breaks due to the buds’ uncomfortable oval design. Listeners with high pain thresholds shouldn’t experience any fatigue.

Fitness buffs in need of high-performance sports buds that sell for nearly a third of what Apple’s top models cost. They’re a much cheaper alternative to the AirPods Pro 3 and Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 and offer far more upside for the price.

It’s been several years since we’ve tested budget sports buds this great, but the Endurance Peak 4 blew us away on multiple levels.

JBL’s silicone hooks with memory wire are less stiff and more flexible than the Powerbeats Pro 2’s hooks. Even though the battery compartment is thick, it doesn’t weigh down your ears or cause wearer fatigue. Each set of tips forms a tight seal for passive noise isolation, though you can enable any of the three ANC modes — Noise Cancelling, Ambient Aware, and TalkThru – to effectively block out or let in ambient noise. Waterproof protection (IP68) comes as part of the package too.

There are several activity presets that JBL calls Sports Modes, which let you assign ANC and EQ presets to different profiles. Relax Mode plays peaceful ambient sounds to soothe the body for a set period.

Sports buds are nothing without energizing sound to push you through your workouts. The Endurance Peak 4 unleash bold bass response that pummels your eardrums. We recommend keeping the EQ off to get more mids and highs from your music. However, the best results come from the Personi-Fi feature, which optimizes sound to your hearing. It’s superb at balancing the low end with other frequencies.

The massive charging case is unflattering, while the unreliable touch controls can be frustrating to operate during breaks. But these shortcomings won’t get in the way of your workouts when you’re fully locked in.

Read our full review of the Apple AirPods 5.

Anyone who wants the Apple AirPods experience at a big discount. This fifth-gen model welcomes multiple upgrades and comes in at a lower price point than the AirPods 4.

Some of you may be willing to spend a few extra dollars for a little more performance, especially iPhone users. Those who can will want to look at the AirPods 5.

They come with new acoustic architecture and updated audio algorithms. The result is clearer and livelier sound. Bass has a nice kick to it and blends well with engrossing mids and airy highs. You’re not getting full, encompassing audio due to the open-ear design, but what projects from the drivers is compelling. Spatial Audio creates an immersive soundscape for Dolby Atmos content. The three-band EQ helps adjust sound to your liking. Adaptive Audio does an excellent job of blending ANC and Transparency modes, though you can use either mode independently to block out or let in ambient noise. Both work extremely well.

Now, if you’ve been an avid AirPods user, then you’re well accustomed to their flaws. Battery life remains poor at 4 to 5 hours with ANC on. That doesn’t factor in other features like Spatial Audio and Siri, which knock off another 1.5 hours. Android support is still lacking. Wireless charging also comes at a premium.

Regardless, you already know what you’re getting from a product five generations deep like the AirPods: exceptional overall quality.

If you're looking for the best Beats earbuds to buy on sale, then this is our top pick. Android and iOS users who want the closest thing to AirPods for as little as possible. These buds bridge the gap between the two mobile platforms, while combining midrange-heavy sound with strong noise cancellation to deliver a fantastic value.

Multiple price drops have now placed the Studio Buds Plus firmly in the budget category. That’s huge considering how much firepower they possess.

Beats’ fine-tuned drivers produce cleaner bass with “ultra-low distortion.” Mids and highs are given plenty of room to breathe on a wider soundstage. Spatial audio may not perform as well as it does on the AirPods or Beats’ upscaled entries (*cough* the Powerbeats Pro 2 cough), but it can make certain Dolby Atmos tracks feel more spacious.

Noise cancellation is superior to the AirPods 4 with ANC; Apple’s open design lets in more ambient noise. Low- and mid-frequency noises are handled surprisingly well. Transparency mode is equally effective at increasing situational awareness, and neither mode compromises sound quality.

Battery life has been increased to give listeners roughly two days of moderate use (3-4 hours daily) before recharging. The pebble-shaped charging case and cool colorways, including the translucent option, also give these buds a distinctive look.

The lack of head tracking and wireless charging may sway some users to spend more on the AirPods. Neither omission is a dealbreaker, especially when considering that the pros outweigh the cons by a 2-to-1 margin.

Business-class types who want prime call quality and productivity-focused features. Nothing’s powerful mic array doesn’t just demonstrate stellar vocal capture for phone calls and transcriptions. It also filters out a large amount of ambient noise for distraction-free listening and Zoom chats.

In an oversaturated category, the Nothing Ear (3A) offer more than enough performance to earn serious consideration.

Voice communication is their biggest selling point. You’re getting first-rate call quality that rivals many luxury competitors. Conversations are loud and clear on both ends, and Nothing’s noise-canceling technology puts a kibosh on most external sounds during voice and video calls. Niche AI features like Audio Snapshot and call recording further boost productivity by recording and transcribing chats up to 2 hours long.

The Nothing X app comes stocked with performance-enhancing upgrades, minus the presets and spatial audio, which are bloated-sounding misfires. Multi-level ANC grants full control of noise reduction, with the High setting eliminating close to 80 percent of unwanted noise. Adaptive mode works reasonably well in rowdy environments.

The buds sound great right out of the box. Bass performance is refined. Mids and highs won’t blow you away, but they have enough presence to balance the frequency range. What’s most intriguing is how consistent the sound remains with or without ANC enabled.

Read our full review of the Skullcandy EcoBuds.

If you're environmentally conscious, then buying tech is a constant dilemma. While the most sustainable tech will always be what you already have, if you've run your earbuds into the ground, turn to Skullcandy EcoBuds. The brand reduced its product's usual carbon footprint by 50 percent, using less plastic and metal. While this has scaled back on some features we like in wireless earbuds like ANC or a self-charging case, these buds still bring crisp audio for vibrant music listening.

The Skullcandy EcoBuds are an interesting competitor in the earbud market. The buds are made of 65 percent recycled plastic and contain fewer metals, so they lack some features. But if you don't need a lot of flair in a pair of earbuds, these ones are a steal.

All of the other earbuds on this list have charging cases that hold enough power to recharge the buds. However, there's no battery in this case. Instead, there's a built-in USB-C charger to plug into your computer, smartphone, or the wall. So, despite not being able to charge on its own, the built-in charger makes up for that. There's also no lid to the case, which means the buds tend to fall out easily — not great for the clumsy.

These earbuds have audio performance that shines. In our tests, we were impressed with how they picked up the beat of pop songs and the nuances of live performance recordings. However, they don't have ANC, so you'll have to crank up the volume to drown out the world.

All this to say, at $39.99, these Skullcandy Ecobuds are totally affordable, especially when they're on sale for even less.

If you really want to stay on a tight budget but don't want to sacrifice features, your best bet is the Anker Soundcore P30i earbuds. They're extremely affordable (they retail for $49.99 but are often on sale for $25 or less), but you still get the perk of active noise cancellation and powerful sound.

The Anker Soundcore P30i earbuds prove that you don't need to spend even $25 to get the perks of a more expensive pair of headphones. We didn't expect much from a pair of super cheap earbuds, but they proved to be a surprisingly solid pair, and with active noise cancellation, too.

The active noise cancellation on them is impressive for their price, able to block out the bustle of busy streets or the noisy gym. That being said, it isn't the best noise cancellation or sound we've ever experienced. A $50 pair of earbuds just can't compete with a $300 pair, so we weren't entirely surprised to find that the P30i earbuds occasionally had some buzzy ANC or tinny audio.

That being said, for everyday use, our reviewer found them to be a great pair of headphones for running errands. Advanced audiophiles on a budget will enjoy the addition of custom EQs and multi-point connection.

Our main word of caution is that we find these earbuds to be a bit slippery. If you're a sweater, these earbuds get slippery fast, so we don't recommend wearing them to work out.

Otherwise, they're a decent pair of headphones that you really can't beat for the price.

Budget is a relative term. We know the Apple AirPods 5 ($129 to $149) and Bose QuietComfort Earbuds ($149.99 on sale) aren't budget earbuds for everyone, but there are plenty of good options under the $100, $50, and even $25 mark.

Our top pick is the Anker Soundcore P42i, which have a list price of $64.99, and have the noise cancellation of a much more expensive pair of earbuds. Going the budget route might mean making compromises, but not sacrifices. For under $100, you can still get active noise cancellation and self-charging cases.

We do include a model closer to $200, which we get isn't exactly everyone's idea of budget-friendly. The Apple AirPods 5 with ANC is that model. Compared to premium options, the fifth-gen AirPods offer an awfully similar experience for significantly cheaper and allow folks who want to stay in the Apple ecosystem without having to jump to the Pros.

Three other pairs of earbuds that are currently in consideration for this list are the CMF Buds 2, JBL Vibe Beam 2, and Sony WF-C510. We're currently testing these earbuds and will update this guide once complete.

The models on this list are pulled from our extensive testing here at Mashable. One of our previous top picks on this list was the Apple AirPods 4; however, the AirPods 5 have replaced them, making them more expensive, and they also lack great Android compatibility.

Another pair we considered for this list were the Skullcandy Method 360 ANC earbuds with sound by Bose. We tested these buds, and while they're pretty good for $100, they have a bad case design and just aren't that comfortable compared to other models on this list — plus, the $100 introductory price went up to $129.99.

Mashable writers, editors, and contributors tested every product on this list — and a lot that didn't make the cut. We pulled from our extensive reviews and testing experience to find a selection of affordable wireless earbuds that strike the right balance of performance and price.

When testing earbuds, we consider criteria such as:

The selections on this lift were driven first by price, as we wanted the options here to be truly affordable. All of the products in this guide are under $150, with a focus on models that are mostly under $100.

We tested these earbuds with various songs, from live performances to bass-heavy electronic music, R&B, rock, and folksy guitar songs. We evaluated how they sounded out of the box, along with any EQ presets or custom controls.

Though this category can be subjective, we made sure each of our selections had at least several different ear tip sizes and was comfortable to wear for three hours or more.

Realistically, you'll make calls when using your earbuds, which is why we put each of these earbuds through a call test, making sure the person on the other end of the phone could hear us clearly and consistently.

#492. How to Try WhatsApp's New Scheduled Messages Feature Early

All messaging apps should let you schedule texts by default. Sometimes, you need to send a message to a friend or family member, but you don't want them to get it just yet. Maybe they're in a different time zone, and it's too early or late to politely text them; maybe they're in an important meeting, and you don't want their phone sounding or buzzing as a distraction. Either way, a scheduled message can save you: You won't forget to text them later, and they'll get the message whenever you think they should. Win-win.

Of course, this is not a standard feature in all apps yet. Some apps have it, like Telegram or iMessage, and it's a great addition when you need it. Others, like Messenger or WhatsApp, are sorely missing it. While Meta doesn't appear to have any plans to bring scheduled texts to Messenger, it does seem like WhatsApp users are getting the upgrade on the horizon. In fact, you might be able to try it out today.

As reported by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is currently testing a new feature for users to schedule texts, photos, and videos to send at a later time. At this time, the feature works even when you're offline, so your scheduled messages will still send even if you don't have a wifi or cellular connection. In addition, the feature is not limited to single chats, as so many new messaging features are. You can schedule texts in both one-on-one and group chats, and all scheduled messages are still end-to-end encrypted.

At this time, it looks like Meta is only testing scheduling messages on WhatsApp for Android. The bright side for iPhone users is that this test is quite limited: Only select users are getting the feature at this time—and, while it's no guarantee, you should enroll in the WhatsApp beta if you want a chance at trying it out early. To start, head to WhatsApp's official beta tester page on the Google Play Store. Here, make sure you're logged into your Google Account, then enroll in the beta. Head back to the official WhatsApp Play Store page, and you should have a new update. This is the beta.

Once you're on the WhatsApp beta, you can check if you have the feature like so: Craft a new message in any chat, then tap and hold on the send button. If you have it, WhatsApp will present a pop-up, letting you cycle through a date and time to schedule your message. (You can choose to send the message in as little as 10 minutes, or as long as two weeks.) When you're ready to schedule, you can tap the green schedule button at the bottom of the menu. You can then tap the contact or group name at the top of this window, then tap "Schedule messages" to manage all scheduled texts in that thread.

#495. Mars without its makeup can look a little blue. Heres why.

On a summer morning on Mars, NASA's Curiosity rover woke in its usual crater, opened its shutter, and snapped a sprawling view carpeted in blues and grays.

The panorama subverts the usual perception of the Red Planet, a reputation that dates to ancient civilizations. Romans called it Mars, the god of war, because its color reminded them of blood. Egyptians called it Her Desher — "the red one." Even people today associate Mars with rust: dry, desolate, and caked with iron minerals that oxidize red.

Curiosity captured this scene on Aug. 11, around 8:30 a.m. local time with its Mastcam instrument. A pale custard sky hangs above slate-colored terrain.

What makes the image strange is what the U.S. space agency didn't do. The team almost always adjusts the colors in Mars photos before releasing them. This time, it skipped that step and kept the dim morning light as the camera recorded it. In a news release, NASA called it "an artistic choice."

Which brings up a surprisingly complex question. No human has ever stood on Mars, so what would the planet actually look like to someone who did? The answer depends on several factors: the weaker sunlight to its farther distance, the dust suspended in the air, the minerals on the ground, the camera's sensor, the editing software, and, not to be underestimated, the eye of the beholder.

When mission teams tweak the photos, scientists say the goal is to make the rocks look as they would in sunlight on Earth. Martian dust tints everything the sun touches, so removing its influence shows the rocks' intrinsic colors.

In photography, that correction is called white balancing. The phone in your pocket already does it, shifting every picture so the scene looks lit by ordinary daylight.

"The surface of Mars is covered with pink-red dust that disguises the surface geology," Mike Malin, principal investigator for Curiosity's Mastcam instrument, told Mashable. "That dust is also suspended in the atmosphere, and sunlight passes through it to illuminate the surface. If you have ever been near a forest fire or something like that, the coloring of the sunlight is not unlike the coloring of the sky on Mars most of the time."

Correcting for that haze gives geologists a stable reference point, whether it's a dusty or clear day, said Mark Lemmon, a co-investigator on the Perseverance rover's Mastcam-Z, who wasn't involved in processing this particular image. It also lets scientists compare the terrain to Mars-like places on Earth where they have done much of their fieldwork. Without it, everything takes on the same dusty cast, and the color differences that reveal detail fade away. When a global dust storm engulfed the planet in 2018, the uncorrected view turned "virtually monochrome," he said.

So is the editing tricking us? In a sense, yes. But the unedited image can't claim to show the real Mars, either. True color, meaning what a person would actually see, is hard to pin down. The planet orbits about 1 1/2 times farther from the sun than Earth, so it gets less than half as much sunlight, Malin said. A visitor standing beside Curiosity that morning probably would peer into a murky landscape and see distant cliffs of light tan. The shadows would reveal little color or detail.

Want more science and tech news delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for Mashable's Light Speed newsletter or get Mashable push alerts today.

But the visitor's own eyes would complicate things further because they don't hold a fixed setting. Given time, a person's brain would start doing what software does.

"If you spend time in a very colored environment, the brain starts to white balance the scene," Lemmon told Mashable. "So there is also something human in the white balancing."

Is the camera tricking us, then? Mostly not. Lemmon traces the blue to the ground itself. Rocks scoured clean of dust and patches of wind-driven sand look gray to blue-gray, and against the surrounding reds, oranges, and yellows, they tend to look especially blue, he said.

But the camera can deepen the effect, Malin said. A quarter of the sensor's light-detecting elements are designed to catch blue light, yet Martian sunlight carries very little of it. When the team calibrates the camera to compensate for that weak signal, the boost can overshoot and give gray rocks and dark shadows an extra blue tint. Even a well-calibrated camera records Mars in its dust-tinted light. Images that stop at calibration come out looking orange, he said, as the Viking landers' did in the 1970s.

For research, both scientists say they prefer the corrected view. Neither could recall a case where the raw image actually revealed something the balanced one hid. But Malin cautioned that it's possible to go too far. Some people process images with harsh contrast that turns the colors "garish," and that can distract other scientists trying to interpret the rocks.

Inspecting rocks is what Curiosity has done since 2014, slowly climbing Mount Sharp, a three-mile-high mountain in Gale Crater stacked in layers, each one recording a different chapter of Martian history. Those layers tell of a world that once held lakes and streams, then dried out billions of years ago and left salty minerals behind. In August, the rover passed one kilometer — about 0.6 miles — of elevation gain, the highest any rover has climbed on Mars.

The cliffs on the panorama's horizon are Curiosity's next major target. Scientists call them yardangs — ridges the wind carves over long stretches of time that form in sedimentary rock of a specific grain size, Malin said. They stretch about 10 miles across the mountain's northwest flank, and they puzzle the mission team.

"The yardang layer looks out of place," said Ashwin Vasavada, Curiosity's project scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in a statement, adding that its color is distinct from its surroundings, and the layer almost looks plastered on. One possibility is that ancient volcanoes blanketed the area in ash, but there are other hypotheses.

Color processing does somewhat shape how scientists read a feature like this, Lemmon said, and mostly for the better. But the yardang layer's prominence doesn't depend on editing.

"The yardang unit stands out in images from orbit, too," he told Mashable.

Scientists hope Curiosity will reach the base of the yardangs sometime in 2027, and the rover's robotic arm can then gather close-up evidence of what they are.

In the meantime, the panorama gives the public rare insight into whether the Red Planet lives up to its name. People tend to picture Mars redder than it is, Lemmon said: "It is frequently much more butterscotch."

#496. I Tried 'PhotoCraft,' the AI Clone of Photoshop, and It's Almost Exactly Like the Real Thing

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

Love it or hate it, AI is changing tech at a rapid pace. Case in point: AI is now being used to reverse-engineer big-name software packages. Once complete, developers upload the cloned versions online as open-source tools that anyone can use for free. It seems no company is immune from these dupes, no matter how big it happens to be. That includes Adobe, and its legacy software like Photoshop, which now has a free-to-download AI clone called "PhotoCraft." I gave this clone a shot, and while it isn't perfect, it's remarkable how similar it is to the real deal.

One of the developers leading this particular charge is Brandon Thomas, a seasoned software engineer who has used Claude Opus 5.5 to build copies of Adobe Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, Lightroom, Acrobat Pro, After Effects, and InDesign in the Rust coding language. They all get new names—Photoshop is PhotoCraft, Premiere is FilmCraft—but they're very similar in terms of features and layout to what Adobe puts out and charges a monthly fee for. It's another seismic industry shift driven by AI, and Thomas is apparently building clones of Microsoft Office apps next.

According to the developer, Thomas "got bit by the dark pattern 'cancellation fee' one too many times," which prompted the start of the project. "AI lets us take back tech and set the clock back to the pre-shitty era," says Thomas. "But now you can just create 1:1 functional equivalents, clean room, that are highly performant and cross-platform. Nothing is stopping you." In another comment, he declares, "Software is over."

It's not clear exactly how Thomas completed this project, but he has used the term "vibe coding," so it sounds like some kind of AI-powered observe-and-copy is going on here, even with his programming experience. The developer has also suggested this is a more worthwhile endeavor than supporting open source apps such as LibreOffice and GIMP as, in his view, "There is no reason to save broken software."

As Ars Technica points out, reverse engineering is usually tolerated as long as no code is directly copied, but if the new suite of tools too closely matches the look and feel of the apps they're cloning, that could mean legal trouble. The truth is, no one's sure yet—and it brings up again the legality of the AI models themselves, which have been trained on vast amounts of human-made code to get to this level.

Adobe is no doubt taking a very close look at this, but while it's still available, I decided to give the software a try myself. You can download the apps from the ArtCraft website, though they're labeled as "early alpha" and "in development" for now. According to Thomas, 99% feature parity with the Adobe equivalents should be "measured in months and not years".

The ArtCraft web portal offers a launcher app through which you can manage the entire 'Craft' selection of tools, but I focused on PhotoCraft as Photoshop is the only Adobe program I really make much use of. My first impressions: It definitely looks like a Photoshop rip-off.

PhotoCraft has the same color scheme, the same layout of panels, and the same menus in the same order—with the exception of Plugins, which I suppose will take a while. The keyboard shortcuts are the same, as far as I could tell, and the various preferences screens are very similar too—both in terms of the options you have and how they're laid out.

Most of the Photoshop work I do involves cropping and combining images, tweaking their colors and balance, and getting them in fixed formats for articles. I was able to transform my workflow from the Adobe app pretty much wholesale: The same panels, the same dialogs, and the same tools (from the clone stamp to the magic wand).

Plenty of image editors ape Photoshop, of course, because it's the industry leader—Pixlr, anyone?—but this seems on another level entirely. PhotoCraft is also fast and slick, and as far as I could tell, free from bugs. The only bumps I came across were some clunky snapping and selecting operations, which could definitely be improved upon but didn't actually break anything.

I'm by no means a power user of Photoshop, and people with more experience than me have found plenty of issues under the hood. I suspect that when it comes to playing around with more advanced tools and layer functions, cracks might start to show in the way you would expect from AI code trying to copy what another program does. I'm not sure "watch this program and make something that behaves the same" is the best way forward for software development.

That said, for me, PhotoCraft did everything I needed it to in terms of image manipulations, adjustments, and layer control, and did it well. How the app carries on long-term remains to be seen, as AI-written bug fixes and feature upgrades will presumably be piled on top of existing AI-written code—and that's assuming Adobe doesn't get involved.

Personally, I'm not going to cancel my Photoshop subscription: I can afford it, I use it, and I'm not yet ready to trust my projects to something that's been coded by AI. But this is the era we're in now, where AI can look at something—a painting, a website, a movie, a sprawling Adobe software application—and give you a very convincing imitation in not much time at all.

#499. The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: Why Are Kids Throwing Fruit in Toilets?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's deep dive into young people culture answers questions you may not have thought to ask, like, "Why are young people throwing fruit in their toilets?" "What does it mean when someone tells me to 'visualize spinning apples'?" "What is glass skin?" and "How can Minecraft help you understand the age of the universe?"

This is a weird one, but young people are throwing fruit in the toilet in honor of the rapper Lucki. Backstory: The Atlanta rapper best known for his track "New Drank" was attending ComplexCon in Los Angeles on Oct. 3 when an entourage vs. entourage tussle with rapper Playboi Carti's crew broke out and Lucki was stabbed.

In response, the hashtag #throwfruitinthetoiletforlucki appeared on Instagram and TikTok, and kids started throwing fruit in the toilet and posting videos like this one:

So that's what's happening; why it's happening is a little harder to explain. People posted screenshots indicating the lyrics to Lucki's "Y Not" include the line "When I get stabbed at ComplexCon, throw fruits in the toilet"—but the song doesn't actually include those lyrics and it's hard to imagine many fans bought into it. Some suggested that the trend is a dig at Lucki's lifestyle and weight: a not-subtle suggestion he eat more fruit. Maybe, but I think it's a classic online non sequitur. I don't think anyone is legitimately trying to honor Lucki by posting these videos. It seems like jokers trying to get fans of the rapper to throw fruit in their toilets so they can say, "Look at those weirdos! We tricked 'em into throwing fruit in their toilets!" But it doesn't seem to be working. All the fruit-throwers I've seen seem like they're "in on the joke," which actually reverses the joke. Anyway, Lucki is doing well and expected to make a full recovery.

The second fruit-related meme trending this week is "imagine spinning apples," a way to insult pretentious dinks online. It's a journey to explain how it came to mean that, so here goes.

Aphantasia is the inability to visualize things. If you can't imagine apples, you may have aphantasia. The idea that some people can imagine apples and some can't is big on 4Chan, Reddit, and other online communities populated by young people who would like to claim superiority over others, but can't do it based on money, attractiveness, or any other traditional measure of preeminence. Despite the actual neuroscience showing a correlation between aphantasia and a slightly higher IQ, these online weirdos decided that having aphantasia means you are dumb, or lack an inner life. Some took it even further and suggested that intelligence can be measured by the number of apples one can visualize and whether you can visualize them spinning.

started showing up as a way of clowning on people who boast about how smart they are using a metric that actually makes them look dumber. It's like bragging about the results of an online IQ test or joining Mensa.

Glass skin is a beauty trend taking over TikTok. It's based on Korean skin care trends and refers to skin so smooth, luminous, and clear, it seems to shine. How one can achieve this look is debatable, but there is no shortage of videos giving instructions and hawking creams and tinctures that promise to make your skin shiny as glass. Like this one:

I'm in favor of people looking as greasy as they want, but viral "glass skin" videos are not giving good advice—a recent study found that almost 95% of viral Korean skincare and “glass skin” TikToks are misleading, and many can even be dangerous.

Reports about the new "door kick challenge" are coming from all corners of the nation, from Portland to Phoenix to West Virginia to California this week.

Here's how West Virginia's Taylor County Sheriff's Office Deputy Sheriff Chris MacQueen describes the door kick challenge: "There is a new trend out that’s either referred to the 'door kick challenge' or 'donkey kick challenge' and what that essentially is, is teenagers late at night are donkey kicking doors and then recording their reactions as they run off. This is absolutely not ding dong ditch."

There's so much wrong with this statement. First, the "door kick challenge" isn't new. Here's a report from 2021 about the supposed challenge. Hundreds, maybe thousands, of similar news stories have been published regularly since, all across the country, a steady drumbeat of warning about this dangerous trend. But it doesn't seem to be real.

I've looked through TikTok's doorkickchallenge hashtag and similar places on other video platforms, and I can't find any evidence of any young people "recording their reaction" to kicking a stranger's door or mentioning the challenge in a "you should try this too" kind of way. There are plenty of videos of people kicking doors, but they're all shot from doorbell or security cameras, presumably posted by homeowners, and we have no idea who is doing the kicking or why. They could be stalkers, robbers, or angry because they left their keys on the coffee table. So there is no discernible trend or challenge, beyond the trend of more people having doorbell cameras.

The cop's last point, that "this is not ding dong ditch," is debatable. Ding dong ditch dates back to the early 1800s, and I can't find any evidence that the game has changed since then, or that more kids are kicking doors instead of ringing doorbells. No one keeps stats on it, but it seems reasonable to assume that kids today do dumb things as often as you and your friends did dumb things. That's where the safe money always is.

If police departments want to warn the public about a truly deadly trend, they could look at the number of adults who shoot teenagers on their porches. Then they could hold a press conference warning about the "murdering children for ringing your doorbell" challenge.

Looking at the volume of AI-generated brainrot that floods video-sharing platforms makes it easy to conclude that young people are not able to visualize apples spinning. But the counter evidence is out there, too. Like this week's viral video: "Running Minecraft Until It Beats Itself." It's a video about a kids' video game, but on a deeper level it's a video about deep time, evolution, the second law of thermodynamics, and more.

This video runs a simulation of a Minecraft world to prove that if you have the right starting seed and leave Minecraft running long enough with no input, the winning condition (the dragon being slain) would happen even if there was no player, by chance. You'd have to run your PC for a billion years instead of playing Minecraft for 100 hours, but it would happen.

The idea that anything that could happen will happen if enough time passes isn't new, but it's hard to grasp the concept of time scales so vast. This video uses a relatively simple model (that viewers understand intimately) to make the billions of years imaginable.

I have no doubt that the seven million people who have viewed this video (and played Minecraft enough to understand the implications) grasp the concept of a billion years better than the people who haven't: A billion years is about how long it would take for an Enderman to randomly drop a carved pumpkin on two snow blocks and for the resulting snow golem to lead a creeper to blow up next to the walls around the end portal so Endermen could randomly carry enough blocks from the Overworld to The End to make piles high enough that randomly moving snow golems would throw enough snowballs to destroy all seven crystals that protect the Ender Dragon.

#500. Apple Intelligence reportedly coming to China in December, but without Siri AI

Bloomberg reports that Apple plans to finally launch Apple Intelligence in China in December, although some important features could still be missing. Here are the details.

Earlier today, a report from the South China Morning Post claimed that Chinese regulators had approved the use of Alibaba’s AI models to power Apple Intelligence, following preliminary approval for the platform’s rollout in July.

The report noted that the timing of the approval was particularly relevant, as the iPhone Duo is scheduled to launch in China next week.

Now, Bloomberg reports that Apple “is planning to launch Apple Intelligence in the region in December as part of an upcoming iOS 27.3 update,” although the launch “will exclude the new Siri AI assistant and other features announced this year,” according to the publication’s sources.

The move comes after a lengthy and complicated effort to bring Apple Intelligence to China, where local regulations governing AI-generated content, security assessments, and algorithm registration have forced Apple to take a different approach than in other markets.

In order to get Apple Intelligence approved, the company had to make some concessions. Unlike in other countries, the platform has guardrails developed with China’s Alibaba Group Holding Ltd., including a filter that allows the government to approve ongoing updates to the AI models. Apple is also working with Baidu Inc. on features related to search and Siri.

On Sept. 29, Apple received Chinese permits allowing recent iPhones to support the use of Apple Intelligence and Alibaba AI models, including Tongyi Wanxiang and Qwen.

The report notes that Apple Intelligence’s launch in China will not feature “the company’s in-house image-generation tools,” while certain “features for generating text will also be limited in some applications.”

According to Bloomberg, the initial rollout will include Genmoji for creating custom emoji, Apple’s AI-powered notification summaries, writing tools, and the Clean Up feature in Photos, which lets users remove unwanted objects from images.

The report notes that it is unclear whether these features will be enough to win over Chinese consumers, as local smartphone makers have already introduced their own AI capabilities:

With AI services proliferating on rival phones from Huawei Technologies Co., Xiaomi Corp., Oppo Guangdong Mobile Telecommunications Corp., Vivo Mobile Communication Co. and others in China, it’s unclear how much Apple will benefit from launching a two-year-old set of relatively basic AI features in the country.

Interestingly, today’s report came just one day after Apple said in the footnotes of its HomeView announcement that it is “working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward” to launch Siri AI in Europe, where the assistant also remains unavailable due to regulatory issues.

Google's new Fitbit Edge is sleek and powerful but it can't match the Air in one key area

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Type: SmartwatchBest for: Fitness trackingSubscription: $9.99/month (optional)Warranty: 1-yearPrice: From $179.99 at Google (pre-order)

Type: Screenless smart bandBest for: ComfortSubscription: $9.99/month (optional)Warranty: 1-yearPrice: From $99.99 at Google

The new Fitbit Edge is making a push to be the best sleep tracker of 2026. Available for pre-order from $179.99 at Google, the Edge is sleek, affordable and has high-powered sensors to track every wake up and sleep stage.

But I test sleep tech for a living and the Google Fitbit Edge has left me feeling underwhelmed. I've been testing the cheaper Fitbit Air, from $99.99 at Google, and I think it's the stronger pick when it comes to sleep tracking.

In the battle of Fitbit Edge versus Fitbit Air for sleep tracking, it's all about the comfort (and price, let's be honest). So before you hit pre-order on the FitbitEdge, here's what you need to know.

The Fitbit Edge is the latest Fitbit release and is currently available for pre-order from $179.99 at Google or Amazon. The Fitbit Air, released earlier this year, is available from $99.99 at Google or Amazon.

These are highly competitive prices for a sleep and wellness tracker — the Oura Ring will set you back $399.99, while the Garmin CIRQA Smart Band comes in at $199.99.

All Fitbits use the Google Health app to track and store your data. Basic tracking is available for free, with no subscription required. Or you can upgrade to Google Health Premium, which offers additional support and coaching from $9.99 per month.

The Fitbit Edge is a competitvely priced smartwatch with a starting price of $179.99. Pre-orders are currently available with devices set to start shipping on October 27th.

The Fitbit Air is one of Google's most affordable trackers, with a starting price of just $99.99. Different and additional straps are available to accessorize the Air to suit your needs, with the new mesh band an attractive choice for everyday wear.

For the past few weeks I've been testing the Fitbit Air and it's impressed me with its accurate sleep tracking and detailed reports.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Fitbit uses dedicated sensors to gather essential sleep health metrics, including temperature and HRV. These are then fed to a powerful algorithm which uses the data to draw a picture of your sleep.

As well as your daily sleep score and nightly sleep stages, Google Health lets you know how your sleep will impact your energy levels that day — this is a nice heads-up in the morning when I've forgotten to open the app.

My colleague Nicola Appleton saw the same performance when testing the Fitbit Inspire 3. And I expect to see the same again from the Fitbit Edge. If you do opt for this tracker, you should find (nearly) everything you need to know about your sleep in the Google Health app.

The Fitbit Edge is a sleek take on a smartwatch. The slim screen gives you access to your important stats on the go, without the bulk of a watch face.

But the Air ditches the screen altogether. Placing a small tracker on the inside of a lightweight band, the screenfree design is all about simplicity. It's comfortable, even when you're tossing and turning.

And that's much, much better for sleep, from my experience. Because when it comes to a good night's rest, you don't want anything encroaching on your comfort.

A screen does have its advantages (no looking at your phone in the morning to see your sleep score). But I'd take a quick glance at an app over waking up at 3 a.m. because I've rolled over and now my watch is pressing painfully into my wrist.

The Fitbit Edge is an exciting new release if you're focused on fitness tracking. But if you want to learn more about your sleep, save your money and stick with the Fitbit Air.

Both options come with powerful sleep tracking features. And both also offer detailed analysis and coaching, should you pay for a subscription.

But the Fitbit Air has the edge (pun intended) when it comes to comfort. Smaller, sleeker and without a screen to leave red welts on your wrist, it's one of the best sleep trackers released this year. I doubt Google will top it any time soon.

#502. 9 movies like Mean Girls, for when you want Burn Book-level thrills

Mean Girls was more than a teen movie. When it hit in 2004, it was a comedy that defined a generation.

Screenwriter/comedian Tina Fey found inspiration for the film in Rosalind Wiseman's Queen Bees and Wannabes, a self-help book that explored how female friendships among girls could turn toxic. So, Mean Girls became more than a hilarious movie with lines we can't stop quoting; it became a parable about how to be a better friend and build a healthier clique.

Want more film and TV news and reviews delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for Mashable’s Top Stories newsletter or get Mashable push alerts today.

Mean Girls starred '00s It Girl Lindsay Lohan as Cady Heron, a naive new girl from Africa who's bewildered by the etiquette of American high school. Lucky for her, she's swiftly welcomed into the popular girl clique known as the Plastics, where Regina George (Rachel McAdams) rules with an iron fist and French manicure. But Cady has a secret that she's keeping from Regina and her henchgirls, Gretchen Wieners (Lacey Chabert) and Karen Smith (Amanda Seyfried). Aligned with misfits Janice Ian (Lizzy Caplan) and Damian (Daniel Franzese), this new girl is looking to bring the queen bee down by acting as an inside man. That is, if she can resist the lure of being popular.

But if you've rewatched this movie so many times you can recite it from memory, you go, Glen Coco! I mean, then maybe it's time to try something new? Want a comedy about female friendships surviving hilarious highs and wild lows? Want a teen movie that hits no matter your age? Want a film that will give you new vocal stims? We've got you covered.

Before there were the Plastics, there were the Heathers. Set at Westerburg High School in Sherwood, Ohio, this 1989 dark comedy follows the unraveling of a clique of preppy, popular girls named Heather Chandler (Kim Walker), Heather Duke (Shannen Doherty), Heather McNamara (Lisanne Falk), and Veronica Sawyer (Winona Ryder).

But when Veronica hooks up with bad boy J.D. (Christian Slater), she not only becomes increasingly fed up with her shallow and cruel besties, but she also begins to plot how to get revenge. One murder leads to more, and before long, Veronica needs to take some serious self-evaluation before her hot-and-heavy romance with J.D. blows up in her face.

This one is definitely darker than Mean Girls, and it's rated R because of it. But it's definitely influential in terms of female-friendship comedies. Plus, it has an unexpected fraternal connection, as Heathers was written by Daniel Waters, and Mean Girls was directed by his brother Mark Waters.

Starring: Winona Ryder, Christian Slater, Shannen Doherty, Lisanne Falk, Kim Walker, and Penelope Milford

How to Watch: Heathers is now playing for free on Tubi.

Another thing that Mean Girls and Heathers have in common is that each was adapted into a stage musical. In 2024, Reneé Rapp, who briefly played the role of Regina George on Broadway, reprised the role in the movie adaptation of the musical.

Members of the original film's cast make appearances, including Tina Fey and Tim Meadows, in roles as high school educators. But critics (myself included) noted that this music-driven reboot dulled the original's wit. As I wrote in my review, "It seems this team was trying to wed Mean Girls with High School Musical, bleeding out the bits that might have been too jolting for parents so that kids could expand the demographic. It's a strange call since both movies are PG-13. But there's no denying this Mean Girls is playing it safe. And that's not fetch."

Starring: Angourie Rice, Reneé Rapp, Auliʻi Cravalho, Christopher Briney, Jaquel Spivey, Avantika Vandanapu, Jenna Fischer, Busy Philipps, Tina Fey, and Tim Meadows

How to watch: Mean Girls is now streaming on Pluto TV.

Not all popular girls are mean! In writer/director Amy Heckerling's hit comedy from 1995, a new girl in school is swept up into a world of house parties, designer fashion, and deeply clueless L.A. socialites. But as it's based on Jane Austen's Emma, Clueless offers a clique that really is trying to do their best by others.

Cher Horowitz (Alicia Silverstone) is a bright and eager student at her Beverly Hills high school. And with her no-nonsense bestie Dionne Davenport (Stacey Dash) by her side, Cher thinks she can tackle any challenge, from fending off her annoying ex-step brother Josh (Paul Rudd), playing matchmaker to improve her grades, or giving new girl Tai (Brittany Murphy) a makeover to turn her into a total Betty. And what does she get for all her efforts? An insult so scorching it still has us saying, "Way harsh, Tai."

A true landmark in female friendship comedies, Clueless is funny, vibrant, and cool.

Starring: Alicia Silverstone, Paul Rudd, Stacey Dash, Brittany Murphy, Dan Hedaya, Jeremy Sisto, Breckin Meyer, Twink Caplan, Donald Faison, Wallace Shawn, and Elisa Donovan

How to watch: Clueless is now streaming on Paramount+.

Named after the Stevie Nicks song, The Edge of Seventeen is a sidesplitting comedy about a 17-year-old girl having a comically rough time. Rocked by the death of her father four years before, Nadine Franklin (Hailee Steinfeld) is a socially awkward misfit who struggles to connect to her image-conscious mom (Kyra Sedgwick) and her popular brother, Darian (Blake Jenner). Plus, she's flailing at getting her crush to notice her. The one person she can depend on is her bestie Krista (Haley Lu Richardson) — that is, until she catches Krista in bed with Darian.

Feeling betrayed, Nadine has an unhinged (and very funny) crash out, which involves turning to her sardonic teacher (Woody Harrelson) for help. Written and directed by Kelly Fremon Craig, The Edge of Seventeen is a wonderful movie that masterfully captures the agony and outrageousness of being a teen girl who's trying to make sense of life, loss, and the real meaning of friendship.

Starring: Hailee Steinfeld, Woody Harrelson, Kyra Sedgwick, Blake Jenner, Woody Harrelson, and Haley Lu Richardson

How to watch: The Edge of Seventeen is now streaming on Prime Video.

Olivia Wilde made her directorial debut with this critically praised coming-of-age comedy about two try-hard high school seniors who are desperate to shake up their reputation before graduation. See, Molly (Beanie Feldstein) and Amy (Kaitlyn Dever) are besties, who love each other — and overachieving. But once they learn that their hard-partying classmates also got into great colleges, they fear they're underachievers on the social front. So, time to cram four years of sex, drugs, and shenanigans into one night.

Booksmart plays like Superbad for those of us who fear we relate to Liz Lemon too much. The screenplay from Emily Halpern, Sarah Haskins, Susanna Fogel, and Katie Silberman is chock-full of jokes that go from raunchy and witty to brilliantly stupid. And a cast overflowing with terrific comedic talent assures that there's never a dull moment. But some of the cringe comedy here may have you covering your eyes.

Starring: Kaitlyn Dever, Beanie Feldstein, Jessica Williams, Lisa Kudrow, Will Forte, Jason Sudeikis, Billie Lourd, Skyler Gisondo, and Molly Gordon

How to watch: Booksmart is now streaming on Lionsgate+.

Another clever book adaptation, Easy A is a modern re-imagining of Nathaniel Hawthorne's 1850 novel The Scarlet Letter. Emma Stone stars as Olive Penderghast, a whip-smart 17-year-old girl who becomes the subject of much slut shaming when a prudish classmate starts rumors about her sex life. Rather than denying the claims, Olive leans in, wearing bustiers to school with a red "A" plastered on them, and accepting gift cards in exchange for letting boys lie about hooking up with her.

Written by Bert V. Royal and directed by Will Gluck, Easy A harkens back to the teen sex comedies of the '80s with less problematic sexual politics. Stone is sensational in the lead role of a wise-cracking rebel. Penn Badgley pops up as a love interest in a woodchuck costume. And Patricia Clarkson and Stanley Tucci play parents who are beautiful, funny, and cool in a way that's almost infuriating, because we want to go to there! Hilarious and heartwarming, Easy A is a great choice for a cozy night in.

In 2007, this comedy from screenwriter Diablo Cody became a sensation for its unique vision of teen angst and teen pregnancy. Elliot Page stars as Juno MacGuff, a quirky teen girl whose life is thrown into spin she realizes she's carrying a baby after a hook-up with her crush, Paulie Bleeker (Michael Cera). Thanks to encouragement from her best friend, Leah (Olivia Thirlby), she cooks up a plan to find some good grown-ups to adopt the kid. But prospective parents Vanessa and Mark Loring (Jennifer Garner and Jason Bateman) aren't as picture-perfect as they seem.

Cody won the Best Original Screenplay Oscar for Juno, and it's easy to see why. Rather than trying to encapsulate how teenagers in the '00s were using slang, she made up her own, building a unique world that invited all weirdos in warmly. From there, a vibrant color scheme, a terrific soundtrack from Kimya Dawson, and a cast exploding with chaotic charisma makes Juno a movie that's timeless fun.

Starring: Elliot Page, Michael Cera, Jennifer Garner, Jason Bateman, Allison Janney, and J. K. Simmons

How to watch: Juno is available for rent or purchase on Prime Video.

Co-written and directed by Rachel Lee Goldenberg, this underseen buddy comedy offers a road trip like no other. Based on the novel of the same name by Ted Caplan and Jenni Hendriks, Unpregnant stars Haley Lu Richardson as Veronica Clarke, a 17-year-old who seems to have her future at an Ivy League university all lined up — until she finds herself staring down a positive pregnancy test in the girls' bathroom.

Determined to get an abortion without her parents knowing, Veronica needs to travel across state lines. But her boyfriend is not the person she trusts to get her there. Instead, she turns to her former bestie, Bailey Butler (Barbie Ferreira), who is her real ride-or-die. While that sounds like the plot of the 2020 drama Never Rarely Sometimes Always, this bold PG-13 movie is firmly a comedy, turning America's culture war on bodily autonomy of pregnant people into a truly wild ride that's wonderfully funny. And beyond that, Unpregnant is a touching film about learning what it means to be a true friend.

Starring: Haley Lu Richardson, Barbie Ferreira, Alex MacNicoll, Breckin Meyer, Giancarlo Esposito, Sugar Lyn Beard, and Betty Who

The JBL Go 5 is down to $39.95 from $54.95 on Amazon, and price trackers show that this is its lowest price so far. At roughly four inches wide and just over half a pound, it is small enough to toss into a backpack, clip onto a bag, or keep on your desk without taking up much room. Battery life gets a modest improvement too, with JBL rating the Go 5 for up to eight hours of playback, or around 10 hours with Playtime Boost turned on. Its front-facing driver also makes placement more important, since the sound is noticeably stronger when you are sitting in front of the speaker than off to either side.

The Go 5 does add a few conveniences that make it easier to live with—you can now play audio over USB-C, Bluetooth 6.0 brings LC3 codec support, and AirTouch lets you pair two Go 5 speakers for stereo simply by bringing them together. #504. ElevationLab pulls AirTag Silencer after backlash over stalking concerns

Following intense criticism over the obvious fact that its AirTag Silencer could facilitate stalking and other forms of misuse of Apple’s AirTag, ElevationLab has now pulled the accessory. Here are the details.

A couple of weeks ago, Glenn Fleishman wrote a lengthy post over at Six Colors criticizing ElevationLab’s AirTag Silencer, which does pretty much what it says on the label.

Equipped with a piercing mechanism intended to neutralize the AirTag’s speaker without damaging the rest of the hardware, the accessory was announced on September 30 for $9.99.

Yesterday, as Fleishman noted in a new post on Six Colors, ElevationLab announced its decision to remove the product from sale, in a brief note acknowledging the obvious opportunity for misuse the accessory afforded.

We launched an AirTag silencing tool recently. We have always made products we want for ourselves, and this was no different – we wanted it for AirTags on our bikes. (Some of us here have bikes more valuable than our cars.)

In retrospect though, this also has the side effect of aiding someone with bad intentions to track someone that wouldn’t get phone notifications.

We have removed the product and will use our patent on it to prevent anyone else from making one in the future.

The product is also no longer listed on Amazon, although it still appears as an autocomplete suggestion in search results.

It is worth noting that the now-pulled product information page for ElevationLab’s AirTag Silencer noted that it worked “on multiple AirTags.”

As a longtime AirTag accessory maker, ElevationLab was certainly aware that one of the changes Apple made with the second-generation AirTag was making its speaker harder to remove, a change that could help discourage tampering and unwanted tracking.

Be that as it may, the product is no longer for sale, and it would be great if ElevationLab kept the public informed about its efforts to prevent similar devices from being sold through the promised enforcement of its patent.

#506. Google Finally Made Another Fitbit With a Screen

The rumors are true: Google has announced a new device, the Fitbit Edge. It’s a band with a narrow screen, much like the old Charge 6, but updated to match the look and some of the functionality of the Fitbit Air.

Before the Fitbit Air, which came out earlier this year, Google hadn’t come out with any new Fitbits since the Charge 6 in 2023. In the meantime, the Pixel Watch has gotten up to its fifth generation, and the Fitbit app became the Google Health app. I was worried the idea of a small-screen fitness tracker might have been lost for good. Fortunately, I was wrong.

A physical button on the side, unlike the Charge 6’s haptic nub

Its own GPS chipset, instead of relying on your phone.

An altimeter, which the Fitbit Charge 6 did not have (but many fitness watches do)

A seven-day battery life, or about two days if you enable the always-on display

Music controls that work with anything your phone is playing

Pre-orders open today, and the Fitbit Edge is expected to start shipping on Oct. 27. The retail price is $179.99, making it $20 more than the Charge 6’s regular price. For comparison, the Fitbit Air is $99.99, and the Pixel Watch 5 starts at $349.99. The Fitbit Edge’s price, size, and functionality put it right in between those two devices, and honestly it’s a well-rounded lineup.

Google representatives said in a briefing that it will be possible to connect both a Fitbit Air and Fitbit Edge to your phone, so that you can switch between them at will. (Previously, you could pair a Fitbit and a Pixel Watch, but not two Fitbits.)

Compared to the Charge 6, the Fitbit Edge gains an altimeter and more useful music controls; the Charge 6 could only control music playing on Youtube Music, which required a subscription. However, the Fitbit Edge will not have a tap-to-pay option like the Charge 6 did; it does not have NFC capabilities. Google says GPS tracking is more accurate on the Edge than the Charge 6, which isn’t surprising since that was a major weak point of the Charge 6. I’m looking forward to testing out the Fitbit Edge and reporting back on how well it performs in real-life use.

#507. Influencers are shilling libido products. Which ones should you use?

In our "maxxing" culture of optimization, no aspect of life is safe from attempts to make it as enhanced as possible. This includes our sex lives: We have to want more sex, have more sex, and have better sex.

And there are always products to help you do just that. In 2026, there are a ton of libido products on the market, especially for women and people with vulvas. Mashable checked with experts which ones are actually worth trying, with the knowledge that there's no end-all, be-all solution.

"Libido" is difficult to define. In general, though, it's about desire, interest in intimacy and sex, and thoughts about it, OBGYN and co-director of the University of Chicago Medicine Center for Women's Integrated Health, Dr. Melinda Lukens, told Mashable.

AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections

Tinder — top pick for fast hookups

Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups

Pure — best for anonymous hookups

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity

Libido is also incredibly personal and changes throughout a woman's lifespan, Lukens said. This is due to relationship changes, outside stressors, trauma, pregnancy and postpartum, as well as perimenopause and menopause.

And there are different types of desire: spontaneous desire and responsive desire, sexpert for sex toy brand LELO, licensed psychologist, and certified sex therapist Dr. Laurie Mintz told Mashable. Spontaneous desire is a male model and youth-oriented model — and it's unfortunately the one we see in the movies when someone is overcome with passion and wants sex immediately. People experiencing spontaneous desire might also feel the beginning stages of arousal, like tingling in the genitals, warmth, and lubrication, Mintz noted.

Responsive desire is wanting sex without feeling those physical feelings, she explains. Sexual activity comes first, then desire comes. And people want to have sex for a variety of reasons. In a 2007 paper titled "Why humans have sex," participants identified 237 individual ones. The top wasn't being horny, but being attracted to the person they had sex with. Next on the list was wanting to experience physical pleasure, and because sex feels good. (Being horny was reason #7.)

Most women — as they get older and/or are in long-term relationships — lose spontaneous desire. Mintz tells those women to have sex to get horny rather than waiting to be horny to have sex.

Both Lukens and Mintz said that desire is multifaceted and that there's no one-size-fits-all solution. The best place to start is a doctor's office.

With patients who come in who want to increase their desire for sex, Lukens first asks a number of questions: What exactly is bothering them? How long has this been going on, and why do they want to fix this now?

Then, she asks about the patient's relationship with their partner and what conversations they're having. She also asks if the patient has been able to orgasm during sex. Lukens utilizes the Female Sexual Function Index, which asks questions about desire, arousal, and satisfaction. She wants a deep history of what's been going on, and that can illuminate which direction to take this.

She recommends Mintz's book, A Tired Woman's Guide to Passionate Sex, to patients. Sometimes, the process of getting desire back also involves a therapist, a sexual health professional, or another mental health professional.

If a patient tells her she has a safe relationship with her partner, and she's able to enjoy sex and intimacy but needs a little bit more oomph to get things started, Lukens will talk about medication therapy. Her current go-to is testosterone therapy. (More on that below.)

If someone lost their desire because they hate their husband, they probably shouldn't take medication to get it back, Mintz said. But if someone lost their desire because of normative age-related changes, the first course of action would be to teach about responsive desire, scheduling sex, and the like.

"But there are some women who learn about responsive desire, they use it effectively, but they grieve. They grieve the feeling of being horny, because it's a glorious feeling, right?" Mintz said. "And for those women, I think these medicines can be extremely useful." She used to be against desire meds, but she's since changed her tune.

So what products do the experts actually recommend?

"If I had a woman coming to me with desire issues, my first thing would be the psychological stuff," Mintz said, such as being mindful during sex.

"Mindfulness, responsive desire, all that," she said. "If she says, 'Yeah, yeah, yeah, but I really miss feeling horny,' I'd send her to a sexual medicine physician for something FDA-approved or testosterone, Addyi, Vyleesi, and I would also tell her about vibrators and marijuana because the evidence is strong there."

Testosterone isn't yet FDA-approved for women, but both Lukens and Mintz mentioned it as an option for post-menopausal women. Like any of these medications, it's not a cure-all. Lukens pointed out that 40 percent of women see improvement over placebo, but she said it's a nice option for someone who's already exhausted other avenues.

Vyleesi is the brand name for a medication called bremelanotide, an FDA-approved injection for premenopausal women. Patients inject Vyleesi around 45 minutes before sexual activity, and it can't be used more than once in a 24-hour period or 8 times in one month. There's no safety data for pregnant people using Vyleesi, so it's advised to use reliable contraception.

Lukens doesn't prescribe Vyleesi, but found that the treatment effect was modest in absolute terms. In one study, around 24 percent of bremelanotide patients achieved a more than 1.2-point increase in their desire score versus 18 percent with placebo, as measured by the Female Sexual Function Index. The change in the number of satisfying sexual events wasn't significantly different from placebo, though a post-study analysis showed a higher percentage of these events with the drug, Lukens said.

Patients with high blood pressure should avoid using Vyleesi. It's also advised to avoid if you're taking naltrexone (used to treat alcohol use disorder and opiate use disorder). Side effects include nausea, transient increase in blood pressure and decrease in heart rate, and hyperpigmentation (patients with darker skin have a higher risk of this).

But, positively, it doesn't interact with alcohol the way Addyi does.

Addyi (the drug flibanserin) is a daily oral pill that's also FDA-approved. Lukens said it also has a modest benefit to increase the number of satisfying sexual experiences by around 0.5 per month. Common side effects include dizziness and fatigue. This also has interactions with alcohol that cause low blood pressure, so you shouldn't drink while taking this.

Mintz pointed out that studies have shown a link between cannabis and higher sexual desire and performance, in small doses. In higher doses, though, it's associated with the opposite (which makes sense — you might fall asleep before anything sexy happens).

Vibrators aren't just linked to greater sexual satisfaction. Studies have shown that vibrators can also increase sexual desire. So if you've been wanting an excuse to buy a new sex toy, here it is — and Mashable has lots of suggestions on which vibrators to buy.

No need to shun your Heated Rivalry fan fiction habit. Erotic literature has also been shown to increase desire and satisfaction compared to a placebo.

There are many supplements and pills out there that claim to boost libido. Just one example is Lemme Play Gummies, from the Kourtney Kardashian-owned brand Lemme. On its website, it claims these gummies are for "daily intimacy." They have ingredients like ashwagandha, maca root, nitric oxide, and horny goat weed.

Only one of those ingredients, ashwagandha, has clinical trials, said Mintz, who recommends only FDA-approved drugs or products with clinical trials published in scientific journals. Maca root has suggested evidence, and nitric oxide has nothing to do with desire, just blood flow to tissues. Horny goat weed has nothing studied, she said.

"So what do I think of those products? Not much," she said. "They're taking things that have evidence or not, making them go together and saying this is a desire pill. And my thinking is, first of all, we have FDA-approved medicines, and if you want to take something with evidence, then take the one ingredient that has evidence, ashwagandha." But you need to talk to your doctor about whether to take certain ingredients. People with thyroid issues, for instance, shouldn't take ashwagandha.

Lukens said, "The truth is that so many of these supplements do not have actual evidence behind them. They really aren't held to the same premarket efficacy and safety standards as something that's FDA approved," but companies can market them however they'd like.

"Women deserve to know what evidence is really behind what they're putting in their bodies," she continued.

People might experience a change because they believe a product they're using works — that's the placebo effect. "Our mind and body — everyone says they're connected. They're not connected. They are one," Mintz said. "They're more than connected. They're the same thing."

But the problem with the placebo effect is the cost, Lukens said, monetary and potentially otherwise (such as taking an ingredient that has a negative impact on your body).

Lukens has noticed an increase in the last three to five years of women coming to her to talk about their libidos. Historically, she said, women were shamed for being sexual, but now it seems that we're swinging in the opposite direction and women can feel like they're supposed to want more sex.

"I'm glad we're talking more openly about women's sexual health, but I do worry that with…all this talk online, that we're starting to replace one kind of pressure with another," she said.

Research fellow at the Kinsey Institute, Dr. Jaclyn Siegel, told Mashable over email that she believes the push to sell women things to "fix" their "broken" sex drive instead of understanding the circumstances to affect their desire to have sex — such as working multiple jobs, childcare, uneven domestic labor, and pain during sex — is a money grab.

"Supplements also aren't regulated. I empathize with women who feel broken in some way, but this does not seem like the way," Siegel said.

Similarly, Lukens said, "Some of these companies online and these social media influencers are really pathologizing libido," she said. Despite what you see on Reels, you won't feel like your 20-year-old self again if you just take one supplement or medication.

But that doesn't mean there's nothing to be done. There are a host of ways, medicinal or not, to try to increase your desire. Taking the pressure off yourself might be the first step.

Anna Iovine is the associate editor of features at Mashable. Previously, as the sex and relationships reporter, she covered topics ranging from dating apps to pelvic pain. Before Mashable, Anna was a social editor at VICE and freelanced for publications such as Slate and the Columbia Journalism Review. Follow her on Instagram.
