#553. Apple wins early access to OpenAI documents and employee testimony in trade secrets lawsuit

Judge Edward Davila today granted some of Apple’s requests for expedited discovery in its trade secrets lawsuit against former employees, OpenAI, and io Products. Here are the details.

A few months ago, Apple filed a trade secrets misappropriation lawsuit against two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), OpenAI, and io Products.

In a nutshell, Apple says Liu and Tan improperly accessed or used confidential information about its products and technologies to help advance OpenAI’s consumer hardware development efforts. Apple also accuses the defendants of improperly obtaining information from other Apple employees during recruitment interviews.

You can read more about Apple’s original filing here.

As part of the lawsuit, Apple asked Judge Edward Davila to issue a preliminary injunction to prevent the defendants from further embedding the alleged trade secrets in their hardware development while the case plays out.

Apple also requested expedited discovery, seeking early access to internal documents, forensic evidence, and testimony from OpenAI employees to better understand the extent of the alleged misappropriation and support its injunction request.

OpenAI opposed the motion, arguing that Apple’s demands were overly broad and that expedited discovery was unnecessary given that the regular process was about to begin.

In a decision issued today, Judge Davila granted most of Apple’s requests, while rejecting others and postponing a decision on those he considered overly broad.

That includes ordering the defendants to turn over several categories of documents and evidence, including:

Additionally, Judge Davila authorized Apple to depose Liu, Tan, and Yu-Ting “Alyssa” Peng, as well as corporate representatives from OpenAI and io Products.

On the flip side, Judge Davila rejected Apple’s request for expedited access to OpenAI’s research and development documents regarding metal finishes, power management, and battery functionality for consumer hardware products. Instead, he decided that these will be addressed through the regular discovery process.

Finally, he postponed a series of decisions involving what Apple described as “Apple Originated Information,” finding Apple’s definition “amorphous as currently defined.” On that point, Apple has five days to consult with the defendants and submit a narrower definition to the court if it wishes to take another crack at those requests.

#561. AdultFriendFinder vs. Feeld: Which is better for couples?

When dating sites and apps first emerged on the scene, they were not only fairly straightforward in their design and matchmaking abilities, but they were also very much conservative in their outlook, designed for heterosexual singles to find a monogamous relationship. Fast forward to today, however, and mainstream online dating has loosened its restrictions considerably, with a wider embrace of human sexual orientations and a greater legitimacy given to connections of all shapes, sizes, and durations.

Couples dating, however, is still not as widely supported, with only a handful of apps and sites offering native support for non-monogamous lifestyles. Two of the standouts in that respect are AdultFriendFinder, one of the internet's oldest adult dating sites, and Feeld (originally 3nder), an app designed from the ground up for practitioners of polyamory, kink, and swinging to connect.

Whether you're new to couples dating or only recently expanding your search to the digital world, you're probably curious about where it's best to start your search. We put AdultFriendFinder and Feeld in a head-to-head contest to see which one offers couples the best chance of finding connection, whether they're looking for other couples or simply another single to add to their fun.  The best hookup apps, reviewed by our experts AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections Tinder — top pick for fast hookups Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups Pure — best for anonymous hookups OkCupid — best app for inclusivity

AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections

Tinder — top pick for fast hookups

Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups

Pure — best for anonymous hookups

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity

One immediate difference between the two services is that Feeld looks and feels modern, while AFF's interface has not meaningfully changed in decades, so if you're a digital native with an affinity for apps over web-based dating, you're going to gravitate to Feeld.

However, as dated as the AFF interface looks, it offers fantastic native support for couples dating and does a great job integrating couples' accounts into its search algorithms. In other words, though it still looks every bit the '90s-era website, its functionality for couples dating is basically unmatched against other web-based dating sites.

In feel and design, Feeld is AFF's opposite, eminently modern and aesthetically pleasing, but Feeld and AFF share a common support for non-monogamous dating. From the signup screen, you'll be asked about the "group dynamics" that you're interested in, as well as how open you are to exploring outside your comfort zone. And if you are already in an open relationship with another Feeld user or users, you have the option to add them to your "Constellation," a collection of partnered profiles that will be visible to everyone who comes across you on the app and with whom you share an automatic ability to group chat.

A lot of the decision here comes down to whether you're more comfortable using your phone or computer, but since both services offer extensive native support for couples looking to date, we're not going to give the edge to either.

Both AdultFriendFinder and Feeld have remained relatively tight-lipped about their user counts. AFF has more than its fair share of bots and spam accounts, while Feeld users aren't all active when you want them to be. Feeld claims it has more than 14 million registered users worldwide, with roughly 30 percent year-over-year growth since 2022, while AFF claims to have more than 50 million active users worldwide and more than 100 million registered accounts.

So, in absolute terms, AFF has almost five times as many active users as Feeld has total users, but the differences don't end there. According to Feeld's own statistics, the most active users are between 28 and 32, while the average AdultFriendFinder user is between 30 and 38. Unfortunately for Feeld, this discrepancy can't exclusively be attributed to preference; Feeld is much less popular among the over-40 crowd, which means anyone middle-aged and above will probably have better luck on AFF.

There's one final difference worth mentioning, though it's harder to quantify with statistics: Feeld users are much more concentrated in cities, especially big cities like Los Angeles and New York, whereas AdultFriendFinder users are much more spread out geographically. If you're already in LA or NYC, you can definitely have great luck on Feeld, but if you live somewhere more remote, you'll quickly realize there just aren't many Feeld users in your area.

By far the most important aspect when evaluating a dating service for couples is the site's culture, since some sites or apps aren't always welcoming to non-monogamous daters. Religious dating sites, for example, don't even offer the option to date as a couple, while even hookup-oriented services like Tinder don't offer native support for joint profiles, and only recently offered listings for polyamory and ethical non-monogamy in dating profiles.

Thankfully, this is one area where both AFF and Feeld are clear standouts. Both services have an open-minded user base that doesn't just tolerate but openly accepts non-traditional dating practices.

In other words, from a culture perspective, you can't go wrong with either Feeld or AFF.

For all their other similarities in values and features, one obvious standout between Feeld and AFF is their value proposition. To do almost anything on AdultFriendFinder, from viewing profiles to sending private messages to other singles or couples, you have to have a paid membership. Feeld, on the other hand, operates much like Tinder, allowing non-paying users a wide range of features: swiping through profiles, sending likes and dislikes, and even chatting with matches. You don't even need to be a paying member to use Feeld's Constellation feature.

The major downside of being a free user of Feeld is that you can only send a limited number of likes per day (much like Tinder!), and that's not much of a downside at all if you're willing to be patient.

In terms of a value proposition, then, the choice is obvious: Feeld offers much more for less.

#563. NYT Connections Sports Edition today: Hints and answers for October 17, 2026

Today's Connections: Sports Edition will be easier for people who like college football.

As we've shared in previous hints stories, this is a version of the popular New York Times word game that seeks to test the knowledge of sports fans.

Like the original Connections, the game is all about finding the "common threads between words." And just like Wordle, Connections resets after midnight, and each new set of words gets trickier and trickier — so we've served up some hints and tips to get you over the hurdle.

If you just want to be told today's puzzle, you can jump to the end of this article for the latest Connections solution. But if you'd rather solve it yourself, keep reading for some clues, tips, and strategies to assist you.

The NYT's latest daily word game has launched in association with The Athletic, the New York Times property that provides the publication's sports coverage. The sports Connections can be played on both web browsers and mobile devices and require players to group four words that share something in common.

Each puzzle features 16 words, and each grouping of words is split into four categories. These sets could comprise anything from book titles, software, country names, etc. Even though multiple words will seem like they fit together, there's only one correct answer.

If a player gets all four words in a set correct, those words are removed from the board. Guess wrong and it counts as a mistake — players get up to four mistakes before the game ends.

Players can also rearrange and shuffle the board to make spotting connections easier. Additionally, each group is color-coded with yellow being the easiest, followed by green, blue, and purple. Like Wordle, you can share the results with your friends on social media.

#564. We Now Know When Apple Will Host Its Next Big Tech Event

Last month's Apple event was a big one. The company announced (and subsequently released) the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, Apple Watch Series 12, and Apple Watch Ultra 4. It also announced the iPhone Duo, though the company's first foldable phone still isn't out yet. Despite all these new products, Apple apparently wasn't finished. Next week, the company will host another product announcement, titled "Welcome Home." Here's what we know.

Apple's product announcement hints are usually pretty subtle. This time, it isn't. "Welcome Home" is almost assuredly referencing Apple's long-rumored smart home devices. Sure, the company makes some smart devices, like the HomePod and HomePod mini, but leaks suggest the company has some big updates up its sleeve.

Perhaps no announcement will be bigger than its smart home hub. This device, according to the rumor mill, will be a mix between an iPad and a HomePod, competing with similar devices from companies like Amazon and Google. It may ship with a six-inch display (some reports suggest the screen is a square), but it won't be like an iPad on a stand. Instead, the experience seems more focused, letting you control smart home devices, make and receive FaceTime calls, watch videos, display the news and water data, and check your calendar. Of course, it will likely work with Siri AI, the company's new AI-powered assistant.

Apple may even expect users to buy more than one of these hubs. The idea could be to have multiple hubs throughout your house, which could let you use them like intercoms. (Apple currently offers a similar feature with its HomePods.) If the rumors are to be believed, the smart hub will understand the voice of whoever is talking to it, and tailor the experience to that user personally. If you have guests over, you could switch to a "visitor mode" to avoid revealing sensitive information.

While the smart home hub may steal the show, Apple is planning some updates to existing devices as well. The HomePod mini may come in new colors, and is expected to get both the N1 chip for improvements to wifi and Bluetooth, as well as an upgraded S-series chip for Siri AI. Apple may also update the Apple TV 4K with the A19 or A19 Pro chip, as well as that new N1 chip, and a new Siri remote. Apple may take this opportunity to reveal its new OLED iPad mini, but the company may keep the focus on smart home specifically.

According to Apple's announcement, "Welcome Home" kicks off on Tuesday, Oct. 13 at 9 a.m. ET (6 a.m. PT). That's an early start time, considering the company is based in California, though it seems Apple is hosting the event in New York City this time around. For context, Apple's events usually kick off at 1 p.m. ET (10 a.m. PT) when the company hosts them in Cupertino. It's not yet clear if there will be a livestream of the event, or if it will be exclusive for invited members of the media.

Echoes of Sekigahara is the missing puzzle piece

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Ghost of Yotei is one of my favorite games of recent years. Even though I've achieved the Platinum trophy in the base game, I keep coming back to it as Ezo's beauty is just too addictive. So, when the Echoes of Sekigahara story expansion was announced, I couldn't wait to get my hands on it. And now that I have finished it, I love the game even more — and it's the puzzle piece Ghost of Yotei was missing all along.

This isn't the first time we've heard of Sekigahara. Atsu, the katana-wielding protagonist, mentions it a few times in the base game. She fought in and earned her laurels at the Battle of Sekigahara, but that's all we're told.

The Echoes of Sekigahara DLC takes you to Ashoro Foothills, located in the eastern part of the fogged-out map, and introduces you to Nagato from Atsu's past. What unfolds is a touching (albeit short) tale that sheds light on Atsu's humanity and emotions, and left me wanting even more Yotei.

The Ghost of Yotei Complete Edition includes the base game, Echoes of Sekigahara story expansion, Most Wanted (a combat survival mode), and new in-game masks and outfits.

Echoes of Sekigahara starts in Ezo. You pick up a bounty from a bounty board on a man called Nagato the Handsome. Turns out, Atsu knows him from her time during the Battle of Sekigahara, so she travels to Ashoro Foothills in the east. This isn't a very big area, and you can explore every aspect and complete all side activities in under 10 hours.

Though Atsu is at first reluctant due to their past, she teams up with Nagato to cut off resources to Lord Saito's army. You take on a new kind of enemy faction: the Vipers, the Snakes' followers, now without a leader (Atsu kills the Snake in the base game's intro).

There's a lot of infighting as mini-bosses, known as Snake Contenders, are vying to replace their slain leader. You seek them out and, of course, vow to put an end to them. You can wield heavy weapons (which break after about four or five hits), and I'll leave it for you to explore just how fun that is.

There are plenty of side activities to partake in, too, such as finding fox dens and hot springs, as well as a lovely Mythic Tale starring your wolf companion. Ashoro Foothills is visually stunning, and what I love a lot is that you see it flourish as the expansion pans out. At first a deprived area having been plundered by the Vipers, you rebuild Ashoro Springs, the main town, by helping the locals secure food supplies.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The story expansion explores Atsu's more intimate side. The Atsu we know is fuelled by vengeance, and she has no space for personal relationships — that much is clear in the way she treats Jubei, her brother, still being alive and having a daughter.

Echoes of Sekigahara humanizes her as we explore her and Nagato's relationship through playable flashbacks. The story feels a little predictable, much like the base game, but it's told in a compelling manner, and it still hits you like a ton of bricks, thanks to the somber music and original Japanese lyrics soundtracking their encounters.

While the Echoes of Sekigahara story expansion mode is fantastic, it's the DLC's Most Wanted mode that had me hooked for a few days after I wrapped everything up. This is a new roguelike combat-survival mode where you play as one of four characters: Atsu, Oyuki, Nagato, and everyone's favorite samurai, Jin Sakai.

You then pick up bounties on the Yotei Six and fight your way through waves of enemies. Ever wanted to fight the Kitsune as Oyuki, the one who held the mantle previously? Now you can.

Each character has their own unique play style. For instance, Atsu starts each bounty hunt with dual katanas, while Oyuki wields her trusty kusarigama. As the hunt continues and you defeat waves of enemies, you unlock new passive or active perks that aid in combat by triggering certain effects, like lightning strikes after every successful parry counter.

Most Wanted is seriously addicting. You face off against different types of enemies and mini bosses — agile archers, heavy brutes, you name it — and do whatever you can to best them. Fighting the members of Yotei Six, especially as Jin Sakai, was incredibly fun. While I love Ghost of Tsushima's story, I much prefer Ghost of Yotei's fluid combat system, and Jin's stances fit right into Yotei's world and Most Wanted's combat gauntlets.

But Most Wanted isn't for the weak. Waves of enemies can quickly overwhelm you and you can't always brute-force your way out of it. Instead, I had to think tactically, and choose my perks wisely.

My favorite, which I mentioned earlier, was triggering lighting strikes, and having my weapon set on fire after, say, hitting an enemy four times with my yari. It's ridiculously fun, and even if I was beaten by a mini boss before getting to the main bounty, I was compelled to try again — and this is coming from someone who sucks at punishing Soulslike games!

Echoes of Sekigahara is the story expansion Ghost of Yotei desperately needed. I loved the base game, but I know it didn't tell the strongest story, and it couldn't scratch the itch like Ghost of Tsushima did. The DLC slots in like a puzzle's missing piece. It massively aids Atsu's character development, and I'd recommend playing it before you head into the final quests in Oshima Coast.

Personally, I wasn't expecting to like Nagato as much as I did. He's sly and you don't know if you can trust him, but after finishing Echoes of Sekigahara, I kept wishing he was in the base game and that we got to know him more.

Regardless, the story expansion as well as the oh-so-fun Most Wanted mode have reaffirmed one thing for me: Ghost of Yotei is one of the best games of this generation, and one that keeps you coming back for more.

#567. NYT Pips hints, answers for October 17, 2026

Welcome to your guide to Pips, the latest game in the New York Times catalog.

Released in August 2025, Pips puts a unique spin on dominoes, creating a fun single-player experience that could become your next daily gaming habit.

Currently, if you're stuck, the game only offers to reveal the entire puzzle, forcing you to move on to the next difficulty level and start over. However, we have you covered! Below are piecemeal answers that will serve as hints so that you can find your way through each difficulty level.

If you've ever played dominoes, you'll have a passing familiarity with how Pips is played. As we've shared in our previous hints stories for Pips, the tiles, like dominoes, are placed vertically or horizontally and connect with each other. The main difference between a traditional game of dominoes and Pips is the color-coded conditions you have to address. The touching tiles don't necessarily have to match.

The conditions you have to meet are specific to the color-coded spaces. For example, if it provides a single number, every side of a tile in that space must add up to the number provided. It is possible — and common — for only half a tile to be within a color-coded space.

Here are common examples you'll run into across the difficulty levels:

Number: All the pips in this space must add up to the number.

Equal: Every domino half in this space must be the same number of pips.

Not Equal: Every domino half in this space must have a completely different number of pips.

Less than: Every domino half in this space must add up to less than the number.

Greater than: Every domino half in this space must add up to more than the number.

If an area does not have any color coding, it means there are no conditions on the portions of dominoes within those spaces.

Equal (2): Everything in this space must be equal to 2. The answer is 2-2, placed horizontally.

Greater Than (5): Everything in this space must be greater than 5. The answer is 6-0, placed horizontally.

Equal (0): Everything in this space must be equal to 0. The answer is 1-0, placed vertically; 6-0, placed horizontally.

Less Than (1): Everything in this space must be less than 1. The answer is 0-0, placed horizontally; 5-0, placed horizontally.

Number (2): Everything in this space must add up to 2. The answer is 2-0, placed horizontally.

Less Than (5): Everything in this space must be less than 5. The answer is 2-0, placed horizontally; 4-6, placed horizontally.Greater Than (8): Everything in this space must be greater than 8. The answer is 4-6, placed horizontally; 3-3, placed vertically.

Equal (5): Everything in this space must be equal to 5. The answer is 0-5, placed vertically; 5-5, placed horizontally.

Number (8): Everything in this space must add up to 8. The answer is 5-5, placed horizontally; 3-3, placed vertically.

Less Than (4): Everything in this space must be less than 4. The answer is 3-6, placed horizontally.

Equal (6): Everything in this space must be equal to 6. The answer is 3-6, placed horizontally; 6-2, placed horizontally.

Number (2): Everything in this space must add up to 2. The answer is 6-2, placed horizontally.

Number (8): Everything in this space must add up to 8. The answer is 6-1, placed horizontally; 2-2, placed vertically.

Number (4): Everything in this space must add up to 4. The answer is 6-1, placed horizontally; 3-5, placed vertically.

Number (5): Everything in this space must add up to 5. The answer is 3-5, placed vertically.

Number (5): Everything in this space must add up to 5. The answer is 5-0, placed vertically.

Number (3): Everything in this space must add up to 3. The answer is 3-2, placed vertically.Greater Than (1): Everything in this space must be greater than 1. The answer is 3-2, placed vertically.

Number (0): Everything in this space must add up to 0. The answer is 5-0, placed vertically.

Number (5): Everything in this space must add up to 5. The answer is 6-5, placed horizontally.

Number (2): Everything in this space must add up to 2. The answer is 2-0, placed horizontally.

Not Equal: Everything in this space must be different. The answer is 6-2, placed vertically; 3-0, placed horizontally.

Number (0): Everything in this space must add up to 0. The answer is 3-0, placed horizontally.

Number (5): Everything in this space must add up to 5. The answer is 1-4, placed vertically.

Equal (6): Everything in this space must be equal to 6. The answer is 6-6, placed horizontally; 6-3, placed vertically.

Number (10): Everything in this space must add up to 10. The answer is 6-3, placed vertically; 4-3, placed horizontally.

Equal (0): Everything in this space must be equal to 0. The answer is 0-0, placed vertically.

#569. These Fitness Tracker Deals Are Still Live After October Prime Day

October Prime Day has officially ended, but some of the deals are still going. Most of the deals I covered yesterday are still live, including on one of the cheapest good smart rings you're likely to find, as well as several on Garmins, and even a Fitbit or two.

RingConn makes some of the better subscription-free smart rings out there. I tested the Gen 2 and Gen 3 rings and found them to be decently good at sleep and lifestyle tracking, although not always great at workout tracking. (Add my standard disclaimer that rings are never good workout trackers.) In any case, the Gen 2 Air is on sale right now. This is a pared-down version of the Gen 2 ring, but honestly, you don't lose much—just sleep apnea monitoring and a few days of battery life. That still leaves the Air with a 10-day battery life, so it's a tradeoff that's well worth it if you want an affordable smart ring.

If you mainly want a general fitness tracker during the day, but would appreciate a precise and full-featured watch for workouts, something on the lower end of the Forerunner line can do both at a good price. Right now, the Forerunner 165 is $199.99, down from $249.99. This is an entry-level Forerunner from the previous generation (they're up to the 170 now), but I wouldn't call it out of date. Garmins age well, and the 165 is a solid pick that will give you many years of use.

Polar makes a screen-free smart band called the Loop that normally retails for $199.99, but right now it's on sale for $169.99 (and some colors are $161.99). The Polar Loop looks like a slightly more stylish Whoop. In my testing, I enjoyed the physical design, but was underwhelmed by the app (it's pretty barebones). Still, it has no subscription, and may be just the minimalist tracker you're looking for.

Fitbit's Charge 6 normally retails for $159.99, but right now it's on sale for $133.49. Or somewhere around there—I've been seeing the price jump up and down a few dollars throughout the day. You can read my review of the Charge 6 here. I found it a solid tracker if you just want the basics, but didn't love that it limits music playback to YouTube Music and requires your phone to be on hand for payments and maps. Still, it's one of the best options out there for a band that has a screen but isn't shaped like a watch. And if you don't ned GPS, you can save a few bucks and go for the Inspire 3, which is on sale for $74 to $88 depending on color.

#570. These Heart Rate Monitors Are Still on Sale After Prime Day

The heart rate sensors on smartwatches are usually good enough for casual training (and some of them are really good), but to get the best possible accuracy, you want a separate heart rate monitor—ideally a chest strap. Fortunately, these wearables are still on sale even after the end of October Prime Day. Heart rate monitors from Polar, Coospo, and more were available at discounts, and two of my favorite models are still discounted.

All electrical chest straps are good, but the consensus in the fitness world is that if you want the best, you get the Polar H10. It’s the chest strap that Apple used in its own heart-rate accuracy testing; it’s also the one I recall being put on me when I did a VO2max test in a lab. It retails for $104.95 but goes on sale from time to time, and now is one of those times: You can pick up a Polar H10 for $84.74.

I love when a budget option works as well as the top-of-the-line model, and that’s why I swear by my Coospo heart rate monitor. Full disclosure, the H6 model I used for over four years finally gave up its ghost, so I’ve moved on to a newer model, the H808S. Both are on sale: the H6 for $23.99, down from $29.99, and the H808S is $26.26, down from $36.99.

Heart rate monitors connect to your watch or to gym equipment wirelessly, usually with Bluetooth and sometimes with an older protocol called ANT+. (Many heart rate monitors can do both.)

You’ll need to set up the heart rate monitor to either broadcast your heart rate or to pair to another device. (Usually you broadcast to gym equipment, but pair to a watch or phone.) The specifics vary by brand, but it’s usually pretty straightforward. If you have a fitness watch like a Garmin, an Apple Watch, or a Samsung Galaxy Watch, pairing a chest strap is a simple job. Pixel Watches, unfortunately, can’t pair a heart rate sensor.

But even without a watch, you can use a sensor with your phone. I like the Polar Beat app as a simple heart rate tracker, but there are plenty of other options. The Apple Fitness app can use third-party heart rate sensors, and so can Strava.

Removing the camera actually made Meta's AI glasses more useful

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I've spent a week wearing Meta's new Ray-Ban Audio glasses, and I have a confession. At first, I wasn't particularly impressed.

They're essentially sunglasses with speakers built into the frames. Meta's AI assistant is there when you need it, but nothing about the glasses immediately feels groundbreaking. I've already spent time with Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses, so going from a pair that can see what I see to one without a camera felt like a step backward.

Except, a week later, I find myself reaching for the Ray-Ban Meta Audio Burbank glasses whenever I leave the house.

I've worn them to my son's soccer game, brought them to the trampoline park with my three kids and used them while driving and running errands. Somewhere along the way, I realized I was checking my phone a lot less.

The Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses offer many of the features of Meta's camera-equipped smart glasses, minus the camera. You can listen to music and podcasts, take calls, send messages, hear navigation directions and ask Meta AI questions without reaching for your phone. They also support live translation and hands-free voice commands. The lightweight design, comfortable fit and optional Transitions lenses make them easy to wear throughout the day. You won't be taking photos, recording videos or asking AI to identify what you're looking at, but that's the point. These glasses deliver everyday convenience without making everyone around you wonder if they're being recorded.

The biggest surprise wasn't something Meta added. It was what the company took away. I've never been completely comfortable wearing a camera on my face. Even when I'm not recording, other people have no way of knowing that. At my son's soccer game, I don't want parents wondering whether I'm filming their children. At the trampoline park, I want to watch my kids without feeling like I'm carrying surveillance equipment.

Removing the camera takes that awkwardness out of the equation. The glasses still have microphones, so they aren't completely free of privacy considerations, but they feel far more natural to wear.

And after getting past my initial skepticism, I discovered five unexpected ways these audio-only glasses could fit into everyday life.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Traveling somewhere you don't speak the language usually means pulling out your phone, opening a translation app and hoping everyone is patient enough to wait while you figure out what the other person just said. Ray-Ban Meta Audio offers another option.

The glasses support live translation, allowing you to hear translated speech through the built-in speakers while keeping your phone in your pocket. The person you're speaking with can read or hear your translated responses through the companion app.

Imagine getting into a taxi in Lisbon or checking into a hotel in Tokyo. Instead of holding a phone between you and another person, you can maintain eye contact and carry on a conversation with translated audio coming through your glasses.

Out of everything these glasses can do, translation is one of the features I'm most interested in testing further. And unlike camera-based AI, it doesn't require actually facing the people you're talking to.

As a journalist, this might be one of my favorite possibilities. Think about the last time you were speaking to someone and suddenly couldn't remember a date, a name or a statistic. Normally, you'd either admit defeat or reach for your phone.

With the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses, I can ask Meta AI questions without opening an app. The answer comes directly through the speakers, and I don't have to look away from whatever I'm doing.

That makes me think about how useful these could be for teachers, presenters and tour guides.

A teacher could check a historical date during a lesson. A tour guide could look up a detail about a landmark. Someone preparing to give a presentation could quickly confirm a fact before stepping in front of an audience.

It reminds me of the earpiece a television presenter wears when a producer needs to feed them information. There are some obvious limitations. The assistant can get facts wrong, and speaking a command aloud isn't invisible to the people around you. It also isn't going to quietly interrupt your thoughts with the perfect answer.

Still, for quick questions, conversions and facts that don't warrant pulling out my phone, it's a feature I can see myself using regularly.

This is where the glasses genuinely impressed me. As a parent of three, driving anywhere can get noisy. Between conversations, questions and whatever disagreement is happening in the back seat, I've occasionally struggled to hear my phone telling me where to turn.

With the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses, navigation instructions come directly through the speakers built into the frames. I don't have to turn up the car audio or ask everyone to be quiet just so I can hear the next direction.

The open-ear design is particularly useful because the glasses don't seal off my ears the way traditional earbuds do. I can still hear my surroundings, including my kids and important sounds outside the car.

That doesn't eliminate the need to stay attentive, and drivers should follow local laws on audio devices. I also wouldn't recommend carrying on a distracting conversation with an AI assistant behind the wheel.

But the navigation experience has been one of my favorite parts of wearing these glasses. And there's another benefit I hadn't initially considered: walking around an unfamiliar city.

I love exploring new places, but I hate the feeling of staring at Google Maps while everything interesting happens around me. With spoken directions, I can keep my head up, look at the buildings and actually enjoy where I am.

Here's a use I hadn't expected to appreciate: being able to make a call or send a message without visibly reaching for my phone. The glasses support hands-free calls and messaging through compatible services. That means I can ask them to contact someone while my phone stays in my pocket or bag.

Of course, that's convenient when I'm carrying groceries or juggling three kids' belongings. But I started thinking about situations where having your hands free could be more important.

If you're uncomfortable during a rideshare, walking home at night or on a date that isn't going particularly well, being able to contact a trusted person without searching for your phone could be useful.

You still need to speak a command, and anyone nearby may hear you. The glasses aren't an emergency alert system, and I wouldn't rely on them as my only way to get help. They also depend on having a working connection through a compatible phone. But I appreciate having another way to reach someone quickly.

This is the one that convinced me I would keep wearing the glasses. When I'm around my family I don't want to spend time looking at my phone. I want to stay as present as possible.

At the same time, I don't want to miss an important call, a message from my husband or something related to everyone's schedules. It's a familiar problem for parents. You want to be present, but you also need to be reachable.

At my son's soccer game, I could leave my phone in my bag and still use voice commands or ask Meta AI a question. When I took my kids to the trampoline park, I didn't feel the same need to keep checking my screen.

The glasses can handle calls, supported messages, reminders, music and podcasts. I can use them to ask a quick question while I'm doing something else, rather than stop what I'm doing to find my phone.

I especially love that the Burbank frames look like regular Ray-Bans. They're lightweight, comfortable and available with Transitions lenses, which makes wearing them indoors and outdoors much more practical.

I've worn glasses since I was two years old, so having another pair on my face feels completely natural. And unlike earbuds, they don't occupy my ears or leave me feeling cut off from everything happening around me.

I went into this experiment assuming Meta had made a less capable version of its smart glasses. I came away thinking the company may have made something more practical for everyday use.

The Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses don't replace my smartphone. They can't identify objects, read unfamiliar signs or menus through a camera, or capture those moments when I wish I'd taken a picture. They're also not cheap. Starting at $349, they're a significant purchase when you consider that a good pair of sunglasses and wireless earbuds can handle many of the same basic tasks.

Meta rates the glasses for up to 12 hours of mixed use, but continuous audio playback is rated for up to six hours. That's worth remembering if you plan to spend your day listening to music or podcasts.

Still, the fact that I don't have to pull out my phone nearly as often has changed how I think about these glasses. I can listen, communicate, navigate and get answers from AI while wearing something that looks and feels like ordinary eyewear.

And without the camera, I feel a lot more comfortable doing it.

#578. Apple's Latest Mac Mini Is Still at Its Lowest Price Ever After October Prime Day

Apple's smallest Mac is a favorite amongst AI enthusiasts and value-seekers alike. Despite its size, this Mac is as powerful as any other, which makes it as great an option for running AI agents as it is for handling simple macOS tasks.

While the "mini" isn't as affordable as it used to be—the memory crisis has certainly taken its toll—it's now cheaper than ever, even after October Prime Day has ended. If you've been thinking about picking up a Mac mini, now's the time to buy.

Apple's latest Mac mini runs the company's newest M6 chip, with a 12-core CPU, 12-core GPU, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage. This processor is so new, in fact, that the company hasn't ported it over to its laptops yet. That means the M6 Mac mini will largely outperform Apple's M5 laptops, like the M5 MacBook Air and M5 MacBook Pro, at a much lower price. Why the discount? It's a great value if you already have those peripherals on hand, but your investment does increase if you need to buy one, two, or three of those items.

Most users will likely connect one or two displays to this Mac mini, but it actually supports up to three. While it doesn't have a webcam, it does come with a built-in speaker, as well as a 3.5mm headphone jack. For ports, you have three Thunderbolt 4, two USB-C, HDMI, and 2.5Gb Ethernet—though you can upgrade to a model with a 10Gb Ethernet port. All that typically costs you $899. But as we close out October Prime Day, you can spend just $779.99 on this machine, saving around $120. While it's still more expensive than Apple's former Mac mini MSRP, it's the best price yet for the M6, and a great value for what you get.

If you think you'll need something a bit more capable, the upgraded Mac mini models are also on sale right now. The M6 Mac mini with a 512GB SSD currently costs $949.99, down from $1,099 (a $150 savings), while the M6 Pro Mac mini costs $1,149.99, down from $1,299. #579. The Best Apple Watch for Most People Is Still on Sale After October Prime Day

Last month, Apple released two new smartwatches: the Apple Watch Series 12 and the Apple Watch Ultra 4. These wearables offer brand-new features like a heart rate monitor that takes your pulse every five seconds; "Audio Intelligence," which can display a transcript of the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation; and Apple's new S11 chip, its fastest wearable processor yet.

Despite all these perks, neither the Series 12 nor the Ultra 4 is the best Apple Watch for most people. That title goes to the Apple Watch SE 3, which is currently as cheap as $219, even after October Prime Day.

The Apple Watch SE 3 doesn't have Apple's latest and greatest features, nor does it have its biggest and best display. It doesn't have to: The SE 3 comes with all the features and options most people expect from an Apple Watch. It is available in two sizes, 44mm or 40mm, both with Always-On OLED displays and brightness up to 1,000 nits. The SE 3 has a heart rate monitor and can track both workouts and your sleep. It supports the Vitals app, which can report on heart rate, respiratory rate, wrist temperature, and sleep duration. It can track menstruation cycles and predict both period windows and ovulation estimates.

While it doesn't support Audio Intelligence, it does support Apple Intelligence—including the company's new Siri AI assistant. If the AI-powered Siri is important to you, you'll be able to use it with the SE 3 and your AI-capable iPhone. This watch also supports Emergency SOS, as well as fall and crash detection. That means your watch can call emergency services on your behalf if you become unresponsive after a fall or a collision. If you take the SE 3 swimming, you can dive as deep as 50m before you should worry about water resistance.

This watch doesn't have Apple's newest S11 chip, but it does come with last year's S10 chip, which should be plenty powerful for running watchOS for the foreseeable future. It gets up to 18 hours of screen-on time, and up to 32 hours when in Low Power Mode. You can fast charge the watch up to 80% in 45 minutes with the right charger, or get eight hours of use in as little as 15 minutes of charging.

Really, some of the bigger misses here won't matter to most people. The SE 3 doesn't have an ECG monitor, nor can it detect your blood oxygen levels or send you hypertension alerts. Its screen isn't as bright as the one on the Series 12 (2,000 nits) or Ultra 4 (3,000 nits), nor does it have Emergency SOS via satellite. It doesn't support Precision Finding for iPhone, nor does it have as long a battery life as Apple's other watches (24 hours on the Series 12, and 50 hours on the Ultra 4). But for everything save battery life, most users likely aren't going to be swayed, especially when you consider the price difference. Speaking of which, the SE 3 starts at $219 right now for the 40mm option—a bit higher than its October Prime Day low of $199. If you want the 44m option, you'll spend an extra $30, or $249.

#580. The AirPods Pro 3 Are Still $70 Off After October Prime Day

AirPods Pro are Apple's "premium" earbuds, but that definition isn't as clear-cut as it used to be. Active Noise Cancellation used to be a "Pro" feature, but now, Apple's standard AirPods come with it, too. So why spend $249 on the Pros when you can get AirPods with ANC for about half that? Tough question, but even though October Prime Day is done, Amazon is still making it a bit easier to answer, as right now, you can take $70 off the AirPods Pro 3, bringing the price down to $179. That's $10 more than the all-time low of $169 they hit back in June.

The new AirPods 5 may come with Active Noise Cancellation, but it's not quite as good as that on the AirPods Pro 3. According to Apple, the Pros can cancel sound up to three times more effectively than AirPods 5, which makes them the better choice for noisy environments like airplanes. Part of that may be due to the seal created by the Pros' silicone ear tips. While some prefer the one-size-fits-all approach of the AirPods 5, AirPods Pro 3 come with different-sized tips, so you can choose the size that fits your ears best.

Another "Pro" feature is the built-in heart rate sensor. If you don't have a fitness tracker, or just want to leave it at home, you can use your AirPods to keep tabs on your heart rate during workouts. While you shouldn't go swimming with them, the Pros are IP57 rated against dust and water, so working out in the rain shouldn't be a problem.

The Pros are also the only AirPods in Apple's lineup that are FDA-certified hearing aids. As part of that feature, you can take a hearing test with the AirPods Pro to learn more about your personal hearing health. In addition, the Pros come with hearing protection features, which can help block out loud sounds that might otherwise damage your hearing. AirPods Pro 3 also come with Adaptive Audio, which automatically blends Transparency and Active Noise Cancellation based on how loud or quiet your environment is. There's also Conversation Awareness, which automatically lowers the volume of your audio when you start speaking. A few seconds after you stop speaking, your AirPods will bring your audio back up again.

#581. Apple's AirPods Max 2 Are Still 22% Off After October Prime Day

I love my AirPods Max, but I have a hard time recommending them. They sound great, pair seamlessly with my other Apple devices, and offer excellent Active Noise Cancellation, so they're my go-to for long flights and travel days. And yet, I can't in good conscience advise most people to buy them, because of the price. $549 is way too much for any pair of headphones, even if they are my favorite pair I've ever used.

I have good news, however. Even though October Prime Day is over, Amazon is still discounting the latest model of the priciest AirPods. The AirPods Max 2 are now $429, down 22%, or $120, from the $549 list price. According to Keepa, that's the best price since August. While the headphones are still wildly expensive, it's much easier to recommend them at this price point than at their normal MSRP—at least while this deal is still live.

The AirPods Max 2 aren't expensive for nothing. They come jam-packed with features that make them Apple's best over-the-ear headphones yet. Apple says these AirPods support up to 1.5 times more Active Noise Cancellation than the original AirPods Max, though the benefits also extend to Transparency mode. These are Apple's first AirPods Max to come with Adaptive Audio, which automatically adjusts the loudness of sounds coming in through Transparency mode, as well as Conversation Awareness, which lowers audio when your AirPods detect that you're speaking. (The audio levels rise once the headphones note you've stopped speaking for a length of time.)

While these headphones sound great when used wirelessly, they're worth using with a USB-C cable, too. With it, you can listen to lossless music through a service like Apple Music, which offers more detail than lossy music over a Bluetooth. Apple says you can expect 20 hours of battery life on one charge when using Active Noise Cancellation, and although the company doesn't specify, you can presumably extend that usage with ANC or Transparency mode turned off. You can also get 90 minutes of playback on just five minutes of charging.

Like all AirPods, these headphones work best when you already have other Apple products. That's personally my favorite thing about AirPods in general: You can use your AirPods Max with your iPhone, then play a video on your Mac, and your AirPods will automatically switch to the new audio source. They're also easy to pair with an Apple TV, which makes for a great way to watch movies and shows without bothering others around you.

#583. You Can Get a MacBook Air for What It Cost Before the RAM Crisis

If you bought one of Apple's M5 MacBook Airs at launch, it would have cost you $1,099 for the base model. Then, the memory crisis took its toll, and all of a sudden, that same machine shot up in price by $200 without any new features or changes. The MacBook Air, which for years has started at $999 and jumped to $1,099 with the M5 (while also giving you more storage, at least), now starts at $1,299. If you want more storage, or to upgrade to the 15-inch model, it'll only cost you more.

These prices only push customers towards Apple's less expensive MacBook Neo. That's not necessarily a bad thing: the Neo comes with most of the features that people are looking for in an Apple laptop, at about half the cost of the MacBook Air. But these are not identical machines. Users choosing the Neo over the Air lose out on a bigger, higher-quality display; a processor made for macOS; a backlit keyboard; and MagSafe charging, just to name a few perks. These are all excellent features, but it's tough to justify the additional $600. But what if you could save $200? That makes those perks a bit more worth the upgrade.

Even though October Prime Day is over, Amazon has an excellent deal on the 13-inch M5 MacBook Air, taking $200 off Apple's new and beefier MSRP, bringing the cost down to...well, the M5's launch price. If you've been kicking yourself for not buying one of these machines between March and June, now's your chance to turn back the clock.

This MacBook Air comes with a 13.6-inch display (Apple calls it the "13-inch" for marketing purposes), with a resolution of 2560 by 1664 and a maximum brightness of 500 nits. You get the M5 chip, which, according to Geekbench, outperforms the MacBook Neo's A18 Pro by nearly 22% in single-core tasks and 134% in multi-core tasks. That extra $400 isn't just going towards an "Apple tax," as you'll notice real-world performance increases for your money. You'll also get a 12MP Center Stage camera for video conferencing and FaceTime calls, Touch ID built into the keyboard, and support for MagSafe charging—though you can also charge using either of the two USB 4 ports.

Importantly, this model comes with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage. That should be plenty for most users, but Amazon is also hosting discounts on both the 1TB model ($1,399 instead of $1,599), as well as the 1TB model with 24GB of RAM ($1,599 instead of $1,799). But again, most people will make do just fine with the base configuration. And for $1,099, it's a fantastic deal.

With this MacBook Air, you get a 15.3-inch display, Apple's M5 chip with a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU, 512GB of storage, 16GB of RAM, and up to 18 hours of battery life (according to Apple).

Apple's "Pro" MacBook Pro line used to start at $1,999. No longer: Apple's MSRP for the M5 Pro MacBook Pro is now $2,499. Expensive, but for many, worth it, since you get a powerful Mac chip with Apple's most feature-filled MacBook design. If you've been eyeing this model, good news: Amazon is currently taking $160 off. For $2,339, you can get a 14.2-inch MacBook Pro with a mini-LED display, the M5 Pro chip with 15-core CPU and 16-core GPU, 24GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD. If you're looking for even more power, Amazon has a number of M5 Pro configurations discounted, including the 18-core CPU/20-core GPU model with a 2TB SSD ($2,699, down from $3,199).

While the M5 chip in the MacBook Air is more than enough to handle most computing tasks, Apple's M5 Max is on a whole other level. For users who do intense graphics work or AI processing, there are few chips better than the one found in this 14-inch MacBook Pro. Of course, all that power comes at a cost: Apple's MSRP for this particular configuration is $4,099. But right now, Amazon has it discounted by $600. For $3,499, you get a 14.2-inch mini-LED display, the M5 Max chip with an 18-core CPU and 32-core GPU, 36GB of RAM, and a 2TB SSD.

Apple's Mac mini is a favorite among AI agent fans, as well as users who want the best possible value in a powerful Mac. You'll need to provide your own keyboard, mouse, and monitor, but Apple's latest Mac mini is currently 13% off during the last hours of Prime Day, $779.99 instead of $899. It comes with Apple's latest M6 chip, 16GB of RAM, and a 256GB SSD. You'll find a 14% discount if you upgrade to the 512GB SSD, and an 11% discount on the M6 Pro model with 24GB of RAM.

As much as I love my AirPods Max, I have a hard time recommending them because of the price—$549 is expensive for wireless headphones, and it's tough to ignore other excellent options that cost hundreds of dollars less than Apple's. However, they become easier to recommend when they're on sale. Right now, you can pick up Apple's AirPods Max 2 for $429—still expensive, but a bit more reasonable. These are Apple's latest AirPods Max, with "new" features like Live Translation and Adaptive Audio.

Apple's third-generation AirPods Pro are excellent, but they're also pricey. For $249, you get Apple's best earbuds, with Active Noise Cancellation, Adaptive Transparency, a built-in heart rate monitor, and interchangeable tips to fit the buds to your ears. While these earbuds are arguably worth their MSRP, they're especially worth it on sale: Right now, you can take $70 off the price of the AirPods Pro 3, as Amazon is currently selling them for $179. Apple also offers cheaper AirPods with similar features, so unless you need the Pros' exclusive perks, you can save even more with the new, full-featured AirPods 5 ($149 for the version with the wireless charging case).

If you're looking for a pair of AirPods at the lowest possible price, look at this deal from Best Buy. The retailer has the Apple AirPods 4 for just $79, down from their original list price of $129.99. These are one generation old at this point, and this model doesn't have Active Noise Cancellation, but for the price, this deal is an excellent way to get the AirPods experience.

Apple's basic iPad—sometimes called iPad (A16)—is the best iPad for most people. Most of us only need an 11-inch tablet with a chip capable of running iPadOS, with 12MP cameras on the front and back of the tablet. While there are iPads with bigger displays, including some with OLEDs, as well as more powerful chips and better cameras, this iPad will generally be more than enough. Right now, Amazon has the 128GB model discounted by 11%, bringing the price from $449 to $399. If you think you might need more storage, Amazon has smaller discounts on the 256GB and 512GB options, as well as on the 128GB and 256GB cellular models.

Apple's latest iPad mini doesn't have the 17% discount it did during October Prime Day, but you can still save 5% right now. This iPad mini comes with Apple's A17 Pro chip, an 8.3-inch display, 128GB of storage, and 12MP cameras on the front and back of the tablet. 128GB isn't much, though it can go a long way if you mostly keep your files in the cloud. If you think you need more storage, Amazon is taking 5% off the 256GB model.

Apple's 11-inch iPad Pro is powered by the same M5 chip as the MacBook Air—though it still runs iPadOS. Despite missing perks you get with a laptop, like a built-in keyboard, trackpad, and macOS support, this iPad Pro isn't too far off from the MacBook Air's price tag. Typically, this unit retails for $1,199, but Amazon has it listed at $100 off. Not the biggest discount, but you could apply those savings towards an Apple Pencil Pro—currently 23% off—or take a chunk off of Apple's Magic Keyboard. This model comes with an 11-inch OLED display, the M5 chip, and two 12MP cameras—one on the front and one on the back.

The Apple Watch SE 3 is the best Apple Watch for most people. Despite the existence of bigger and "better" Apple Watches, the SE 3 does everything most people want their Apple Watches to do. It tracks your workouts, lets you send and receive texts, keeps tabs on your sleep habits, and checks your heart rate. It may be missing perks like an ECG reader, the latest S11 chip, and Apple's new persistent heart rate monitor, but most of us don't need these extra features. What's more, the SE 3 is currently 20% off on Amazon. You can pick up a new SE 3 for as little as $219 for the 40mm model, or $249 for the 44mm option. You can also save on the 44mm cellular option, which is currently $299.

The new Series 12 already has a discount, but unfortunately not for the 42mm option. If you're eyeing the larger model, however, you can spend $399 for the 46mm instead of $449—though it does seem the sales are only for some colors. The Series 12 comes with Apple's latest S12 chip, as well as the new heart rate sensor that takes a reading once every five seconds, or 20 times a minute.

Apple's AirTags are excellent trackers for anyone in the Apple ecosystem. Once set up, you can place AirTags on or in any of your possessions (bags, bikes, keys, etc.) and track those items through Find My. While AirTags cannot connect to the internet themselves, they communicate with other Find My-enabled devices out and about. Those devices then securely and privately update your AirTags' locations. Right now, Amazon is taking $10 off a pack of four, or $5 off an individual AirTag.

People often make fun of Apple's Magic Mouse for its odd charging port location (since it's on the bottom, you can't use the mouse while it's charging) as well as its less-than-ergonomic design. But despite this, it's often the best mouse choice for Mac users, if for no other reason than its easy pairing and compatibility with macOS gestures. If you're looking for a new mouse for your Mac—or even your iPad—you can save 24% on the Magic Mouse at Amazon, bringing the price to $59.99 from $79.

Amazon's October Prime Day sale has wrapped up, but the Sonos Arc Ultra is still selling for $899, down from its usual $1,099. PCMag named it the best soundbar of 2024 and gave it an “outstanding” review. $899 is still a lot to spend on a single soundbar, and anyone shopping on a tighter budget will find more affordable picks in our Fire TV soundbar roundup.

For those who can make room in their budget, the next thing to plan around is space, since the Arc Ultra measures a little over 46 inches across and weighs about 13 pounds, making it a natural match for a larger TV. Despite all that width, it keeps a low profile at just under three inches tall, so it can sit beneath most screens without blocking the picture, or you can wall-mount it if you would rather keep your TV stand clear. All that size makes room for a 9.1.4-channel layout (a big step up from the original Arc) that gives Dolby Atmos effects more space to spread around and above you. Sonos also added a new Sound Motion driver that it says doubles the original Arc's bass, giving action scenes real weight without a separate subwoofer, though you can still add a Sub 4 later for more rumble.

At the other end of the sound spectrum, voices and dialogue come through clearly even at low volumes, and a Speech Enhancement mode lifts them further. Trueplay tuning then adjusts the sound to your room, with a quick version on Android and iOS and a more detailed one for iPhone owners. The biggest drawback is connectivity, since the Arc Ultra has a single HDMI eARC port with no passthrough, which can leave you short on inputs for a console or streaming box, and no optical port. It also lacks DTS:X support, a letdown for some Blu-ray collectors, and voice control is limited to Alexa or Sonos' own assistant, though Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and AirPlay 2 make streaming music from your phone easy.

Earlier this year, my colleague Jason England put the original Xreal One Pro AR glasses head-to-head against one of the best premium pairs of AR glasses, the Viture Beast.

This week, Xreal released an updated version of its flagship glasses dubbed the Xreal One Pro Plus, with an upgraded display and a more comfortable nose pad. We've already put the One Pro Plus to the test.

In the original battle, Viture's premium glasses just edged out the One Pro thanks to a lower price, slightly better specs, and a bit more versatility.

Does a refreshed Xreal take down Viture? It's a lot closer than you think.

The updated Xreal One Pro Plus packs a pair of gorgeous micro-OLED prism lenses with a 57-degree field of view. These are paired with a built-in X1 chip to handle 3DoF tracking entirely on the glasses. Plus, it features a redesigned nosepad to make the glasses more comfortable to wear.

The AR glasses cream of the crop — the Viture Beast pack amazing OLED display tech with a crispy 1200p resolution, camera-aided 3DoF tracking, and a massive 58-degree field of view.

3DoF (native) / 6DoF (with Spacewalker app)

Out of the box, the Plus glasses are basically the same as the original One Pro specs — which means all the advantages we highlighted before are still here.

Xreal upped the brightness from 700 nits to 1,200 (still 50 nits less than the Beast, but much closer), so the display is much better. They already featured flatter color science, making for more accurate video and photo editing. Plus, Xreal added three new modes: Reading, Standard, and Movie, which adjust the display depending on what kind of content you're viewing.

The new modes add more versatility and make reading websites or even an eBook a much better experience compared to the original glasses.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The built-in X1 chip gives you a lot of on-device ways to tweak the display. No, there isn't the ultra-wide display and screen-by-screen 3D like the Beast, but Viture's glasses do require the Spacewalker app for more versatility.

Xreal's glasses have real-time 2D-to-3D content transformation, which got a boost from 30FPS to 60FPS in the Plus version. It's a smoother upgrade.

Xreal gave the One Pros a permanent price cut to $599 earlier this year, and the new Plus version retains that price. However, to get the most out of the glasses you still need the $99 optional Eye Camera, which enables 6DoF anchoring compared to the native 3DoF.

Unfortunately, if you're traveling and lack the Eye camera, the Plus still gets, as Jason said, "bamboozled" when on a moving vehicle.

When the Viture Beast launched in January of this year, we didn't have much good to say. However, the company quickly added tweaks that make the glasses an actual animal.

Despite Xreal's updates, the Beast is still slightly better spec-wise. They feature a slightly wider 58-degree field of view, 50 nits higher brightness, better sharpness and color reproduction when it comes to gaming and streaming.

Display glasses are often marketed as an extension of your entertainment and the Viture Beast is a perfect example of that goal.

Compared to the Xreal glasses, productivity uses take a backseat. You can customize the color in the on-device menu, but the One Pro Plus, especially in reading mode, is better for work.

I don't notice the chromatic aberration as much on the edges. This is one of those cases where display preference is up to the individual.

The new modes do a lot to help Xreal catch up, but the Beast does feature an ultrawide monitor mode built into the glasses themselves, plus impressive 3Dof tracking. However, you do need the Spacewalker app for multi-screen support, 6DoF tracking and Immersive 3D for AI 3D content conversion.

In practice, that means that some phones might have compatibility issues. And some features are locked into the app's UI rather than featuring across different apps. For example, if you want to watch 3D movies on Netflix, you have to use the Viture browser rather than your Netflix app.

Still, in combination, the app and glasses do give you plenty of versatility in how you use the Beast for both work and play.

Before, we gave the edge to the Viture Beast thanks to the $50 savings, slightly wider FOV, and more versatility in tuning the glasses. All of those things remain true.

However, Xreal's refresh is much closer thanks to the updated display and new modes. At this point, I'd say that the Beast and One Pro Plus are on equal footing, and it all comes down to preference.

These are the cream of the crop when it comes to display glasses. Both have excellent electrochromic dimming on the lenses, pretty good audio, and are comfortable for long sessions; the Xreal even more so, thanks to the redesigned nosepad.

Here's the rub, though: when it comes to display glasses, most people don't need this much capability or to spend this much money.

You can get pretty good bang for your buck if you explore any of the budget-friendly models. Fortunately, both Xreal and Viture have excellent options in the $299 range that released this year.

The Xreal a01+ brings some flair to a pretty staid category of tech with glasses that actually look like sunglasses you'd wear out of the house. Viture dropped the updated Pro 2 AR glasses in August, prioritizing comfort and versatility over display upgrades, and it totally paid off.

If you'd like to know how they compare, I put the Viture Pro 2 and Xreal a01+ in their own head-to-head contest.

Otherwise, RayNeo is the king of budget display glasses, offering a lot in the $299 Air 4 Pro; you could also try out the new RayNeo GT.

Here's the one drawback to all of those budget options compared to the Beast and One Pro Plus: the FOV is much smaller. I won't get VR headset truther on you, but I promise a 57 or 58-degree field of view feels better and different than 50 or 46, like in the budget options.

My dream would be for Xreal and Viture to keep making excellent displays and bringing them down to the budget tier for the rest of us. Meanwhile, these are both excellent display glasses.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. Amazon’s October Prime Day event may be over, but the Bose SoundLink Max is still available for $279, down from its usual $399, keeping it at the lowest price we’ve seen so far, according to price trackers. Unlike many speakers in this price range, the SoundLink Max keeps things fairly simple, leaving out wifi, smart assistants, and speakerphone support. That lets Bose focus on what most people buy a portable Bluetooth speaker for in the first place: loud, well-balanced sound, long battery life, and a design that can handle being taken almost anywhere.

That practical approach carries over to the design—it has a steel frame that is wrapped in silicone for added durability (though the textured exterior tends to collect dust more easily than smoother finishes), and the woven carry handle makes it easy to grab before heading to the backyard, the beach, or a campsite. I also like that Bose uses physical buttons here instead of fussy touch controls. Inside, three front-facing drivers and dual passive radiators deliver a wide stereo sound with clear vocals and crisp instruments. According to this PCMag review, the mids and highs remain detailed even at higher volumes, though the deepest bass notes lose some impact when the speaker is pushed to its limits. Bose rates the battery life at up to 20 hours, and the IP67 rating means it can survive dust, rain, accidental splashes, and even a brief drop into water.

The companion Bose app adds a little extra flexibility without becoming a requirement. You can adjust bass, mids, and treble, switch between connected devices, and customize the shortcut button to launch Spotify or jump to the auxiliary input. Just don't expect dramatic changes from the equalizer; it is better suited for small tweaks than completely reshaping the speaker’s sound. Bose also does not include a shoulder strap in the box, which feels like an odd omission for a speaker this large. Even so, if you're looking for a rugged Bluetooth speaker that prioritizes sound quality over smart-home features, the SoundLink Max remains one of the stronger options in its class, especially at its current price.

#589. This Tiny E-Reader Has a Front Light and Touchscreen, and It's Even Cheaper After October Prime Day

I've read 25 books in the past year, all of them on an e-reader with a screen roughly the size of a credit card. If you think that sounds untenable, I say: Don't knock it 'til you've tried it. Once you're immersed in a book, you'll find it really doesn't matter, and the convenience of being able to slip it into any pocket and forget it's there means you need never be without it. If you're the kind of person who prefers a soothing e-ink screen to the harsh distractions of a smartphone, this is golden.

Right now, the best tiny e-reader I've tried so far, the Xteink X4 Pro, is on its best sale yet in the wake of October Prime Day (aka Prime Big Deal Days). This limited-time deal takes 15% off the usual $99 price, bringing it down to $84.15. This is the cheapest e-reader with a light and a touchscreen that you can buy right now, and it's well worth the money.

The X4 Pro is the newest and best e-reader from Xteink, the Chinese tech startup that turned the e-reading world upside down last year with the launch of the original X4 pocket e-reader. While the X4 Pro is the same size as the basic X4, it adds two big upgrades—a temperature-adjustable front light and a touchscreen—plus a faster processor and more memory. As a result, it costs a bit more, but you can pick one at a $15 discount right now. (Even at full retail, the X4 Pro is $50 cheaper than the entry-level Kindle after its recent price increase).

Now, as much as I love them, these minuscule e-readers aren't for everyone. Some may indeed find the screen too small (though if you've ever read a book on a phone, the experience is similar). Then there's the fact that they can't load your existing libraries of Kindle books; you'll need to source copies of e-books lacking Digital Rights Management (DRM) software. But if you can jump those hurdles, you might just discover it's the weirdest, most lovable piece of tech you've used in years.

As Amazon’s October Prime Day winds down, you can still find the Bose Lifestyle Ultra Soundbar on sale for $844.99 (originally $1,099), its lowest price yet, according to price trackers. It replaces the Smart Ultra Soundbar in Bose’s lineup and sits at the center of the company’s newer Lifestyle Ultra family, with matching speaker and a subwoofer available if you eventually want to build out a larger system. On its own, though, this is a substantial soundbar at 43.3 inches wide and 14.3 pounds, though its 2.6-inch height keeps the profile relatively low.

Inside are nine drivers arranged in a 5.0.2 configuration, including a center tweeter for dialogue and two upward-firing drivers for Dolby Atmos height effects, and the result is crisp, detailed audio with a convincing sense of space. It also skips DTS entirely and can't pair with Bose headphones for private listening. Anyone already invested in Bose speakers or planning to build out a full system around it will get the most from this discount, while those wanting deeper bass without buying a subwoofer may be better served by the Sonos Arc Ultra, which is also on sale for $899, though it comes with the same single-HDMI, no-DTS limitations.

People are often unprepared for the amount of work a house requires. It doesn’t matter if it’s a new build or a creaking classic; unless they’ve got the cash to just hire out for every little project, new homeowners are going to need tools. That makes a basic tool set the perfect housewarming gift, and this one from Black+Decker is my go-to when a friend buys their first home. It has everything a DIY newbie needs, and at this price you can buy a couple to have on hand for future gifting needs.

A basic tool kit like this is a great idea for folks who don’t have a lot of experience doing small repairs and DIY jobs around the house because it has all the basics (including a durable bag to carry it all around in):

A ratcheting screwdriver with a full set of bits

One Phillips and one flathead screwdriver

Those are the basic hand tools anyone looking to do small jobs around the house needs. They’re basic, but decent quality, so they’ll last a long time. They can also be upgraded one piece at a time as people gain knowledge and skills.

What really sets this kit apart from others is that it’s one of the only decent-quality beginner tool sets that includes a power drill (as well as a battery and charger). Sure, Black+Decker is happy to hook newbies into their battery ecosystem, but a power drill is a game-changer when it comes to DIY stuff around the house. The kit includes all the basic drilling, spade, and hole saw bits you might need for basic work (as well as the screwdriver bits listed above), and includes a magnetic bit holder to prevent bit loss.

If you or your gift recipient develop your DIY skills, you’ll definitely wind up replacing most of this kit with better, more capable tools. But for a complete newcomer who has just completed the stress and complexity of buying their first property, this kit gets them set up to tackle basic maintenance right off the bat—and at 20% off, it's a great value.

#592. These Are the Best Last-Minute Deals on Bluetooth Speakers Before October Prime Day Ends Tonight
